case_prompt:
A 78‑year‑old white caucasian woman presented with rapid loss of vision in her right eye over 12 hours. She had been experiencing nonspecific joint pains for several months and had received acupuncture. Ten days earlier a rheumatologist diagnosed polymyalgia rheumatica based on symptomatology and scalp tenderness, but steroids had not yet been started. Past surgical history included an anterior resection for bowel adenocarcinoma in 2001; a CT scan six months earlier showed no recurrence. She also had a remote melanoma resection from her right foot (1983) and a prior transient ischemic attack. She denied diabetes, ocular trauma, sinusitis, recent hospitalizations, or procedures.

On examination, visual acuity in the right eye was reduced to hand movements; left eye vision was normal. There was tenderness over the right temporal artery. Direct ophthalmoscopy of the right eye revealed an elevated, yellow, sub‑retinal macular lesion with retinal hemorrhages and cotton‑wool spots; there was no evidence of uveitis. Vital signs were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed ESR 58 mm/hr, CRP 1 mg/L, and a white‑cell count of 11.9 × 10⁹/L. Giant cell arteritis was suspected and she was started on oral prednisolone 80 mg daily.

Five days later, pain worsened, became localized to the right eye, and she developed panuveitis with a 1 mm hypopyon. She was transferred for further care. Ocular ultrasound (B‑scan) demonstrated retinal elevation at the macula, choroidal thickening, and sub‑retinal fluid, suggesting endogenous endophthalmitis. A vitreous biopsy was performed; intravitreal ceftazidime and vancomycin were administered. Gram stain of the vitreous specimen showed moderate numbers of neutrophils, branching septate hyphae, and no bacteria.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Giant cell arteritis considered due to temporal artery tenderness and elevated ESR; ruled out because vision loss progressed despite high‑dose steroids and ocular findings evolved to panuveitis with hypopyon. | "Giant cell arteritis was suspected to be the cause of her pain and she was commenced on 80 mg of prednisolone daily."
2. Bacterial endogenous endophthalmitis considered given acute vision loss and intra‑ocular inflammation; ruled out because bacterial cultures were negative and Gram stain showed hyphae rather than bacteria. | "Bacterial cultures were negative but culture on Sabouraud's agar revealed a mould..."
3. Fungal endogenous endophthalmitis considered after ultrasound showed choroidal thickening and sub‑retinal fluid and Gram stain demonstrated branching septate hyphae. | "The Gram stain of the vitreous biopsy showed moderate numbers of neutrophils, branching septate hyphae and no bacteria."
4. Specific identification of Aspergillus spp. made by culture morphology and susceptibility testing, confirming aspergillosis as the causative organism. | "culture on Sabouraud's agar revealed a mould identified as Aspergillus fumigatus on the basis of typical colonial and microscopic morphology."

case_prompt:
A 28‑year‑old Saudi male, status post uncomplicated conventional retinal detachment surgery (cryopexy, subretinal fluid drainage, scleral buckle) of the left eye performed four years earlier, presented with a six‑month history of conjunctival injection and discharge from the same eye. He had a history of renal transplantation three years prior, hypertension, normocytic normochromic anemia secondary to chronic renal failure, and was on hemodialysis twice weekly.  

On examination, visual acuity in the left eye was 20/200, intra‑ocular pressure 14 mm Hg. The conjunctiva was severely hyperemic and an exposed buckle could be seen inferonasally with white discharge around it. The cornea was clear, the anterior chamber was deep and quiet. Dilated fundus examination showed a flat retina.  

The infected scleral buckle was removed under local anesthesia; it was intact with visible discoloration.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Exposed scleral buckle with white discharge raises suspicion for bacterial infection, the most common complication of buckle exposure. | "The conjunctiva was severely hyperemic and an exposed buckle could be seen inferonasally ... with white discharge around it."
2. Microbiologic culture identified methicillin‑resistant Staphylococcus aureus, confirming a bacterial component of the infection. | "Microbiological studies revealed infection with methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA)..."
3. Silver staining demonstrated moderate Aspergillus flavus hyphae, establishing a concurrent fungal infection (aspergillosis) as the primary pathogen. | "...silver staining of moderate Aspergillus flavus hyphae."

case_prompt:
A 66‑year‑old African‑American man presented with a 1‑week history of progressive shortness of breath and bilateral calf pain. He reported occasional productive cough but denied chest pain, hemoptysis, night sweats, palpitations, or dyspnea. Past medical history included peripheral vascular disease, prostate cancer treated with prostatectomy 8 years earlier, extensive smoking, and prior incarceration. He had no alcohol or street‑drug use and a family history of lung cancer.

Chest radiography was followed by a CT scan of the chest, which demonstrated a left upper‑lobe mass measuring 4.5 × 5.5 × 5 cm with mediastinal and right hilar adenopathy; there was no pleural or pericardial effusion. CT of the head and a bone scan showed no metastases.

A CT‑guided fine‑needle aspiration of the left lung mass revealed an inflammatory necrotic background with several large aggregates of fungi. Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) staining showed hyphae of uniform diameter, septation, and branching at approximately 45°, morphologically compatible with Aspergillus species. A special stain for acid‑fast bacilli was negative, and no tumor cells were identified.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7.7 g/dL, white blood cell count 7.7 × 10³/µL (neutrophils 4.6 × 10³/µL, monocytes 0.6 × 10³/µL, lymphocytes 3.2 × 10³/µL), serum creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, BUN 14 mg/dL, and negative HIV and hepatitis C serologies.

Based on these findings, the patient was started on liposomal amphotericin B for 2 weeks followed by voriconazole to complete a 6‑week course of antifungal therapy for pulmonary aspergillosis.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Pulmonary aspergillosis identified by classic fungal morphology on GMS stain | "On Gomori Methanamine Silver (GMS) stain, the hyphae had uniform diameter, septation and branching at 45 degree, morphologically compatible with aspergillus species."
2. Tuberculosis excluded because acid‑fast bacilli stain was negative | "A special stain for Acid Fast Bacilli (AFB) was negative."
3. Primary lung carcinoma less likely at this stage because cytology showed no malignant cells | "no tumor cells were identified."
4. Other fungal pathogens considered unlikely given the specific 45° septate hyphal pattern characteristic of Aspergillus | "morphologically compatible with aspergillus species."

case_analysis:

Ideal Breakpoint: Include the presentation up to the PICU admission and physical exam findings (pale, moaning, respiratory distress, vasculitis‑like lesions) **before** any microbiology results (Candida glabrata, Aspergillus fumigatus) and before the trans‑oesophageal cardiac ultrasound are reported. This gives enough clinical clues (neutropenia, persistent fever, pulmonary consolidation, lack of response to antibiotics, new hepatomegaly, capillary leak, peripheral vasculitic lesions) for students to suspect an invasive fungal infection without revealing the definitive Aspergillus culture.

case_prompt:
A five‑year‑old boy, diagnosed at age four with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) without central nervous system involvement or unfavourable cytogenetics, was receiving intermediate‑risk chemotherapy according to the Dutch Childhood Oncology Group protocol. After one year of therapy he developed four days of fever, neutropenia and a painful right leg, together with a right lower‑lobe consolidation and unilateral pleural effusion on chest X‑ray. He was admitted after persistent fever despite four days of ceftazidime and teicoplanin, with negative blood cultures.

Physical examination showed no abnormal cardiac or breath sounds, no hepatosplenomegaly, no lymphadenopathy, and no local signs of leg inflammation. Laboratory studies revealed a haemoglobin of 6.3 mmol/L (post‑transfusion), leukocytes 0.6 × 10⁹/L, platelets 50 × 10⁹/L, and a C‑reactive protein of 145 mg/L.

Repeated blood cultures were negative for bacteria and fungi. Urine and stool cultures were negative for fungal pathogens. Multiple sputum samples yielded no organisms. Cultures of pleural fluid obtained by transthoracic puncture and broncho‑alveolar lavage were negative for viral, bacterial and fungal agents. Galactomannan testing was negative in plasma, pleural fluid and BAL fluid. Bone‑marrow aspirate showed no leukemic cells and cultures for bacteria and mycobacteria were negative. Urine Legionella antigen test was negative. Ciprofloxacin was added to cover atypical pneumonia; antifungal therapy was not started because the patient remained clinically stable and all tests were negative.

After seven days the child developed hepatomegaly, persistent pancytopenia, an elevated CRP of 192 mg/L and raised liver enzymes. Abdominal ultrasound confirmed hepatomegaly without focal lesions.

On day 10 the patient was transferred to the paediatric intensive‑care unit because of worsening respiratory distress and signs of capillary‑leak syndrome. He appeared pale and moaning, required supplemental oxygen via a non‑rebreathing mask, and had small vasculitis‑like lesions on the nail of the third left toe and on the soles of both feet.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Persistent fever and neutropenia despite broad‑spectrum antibiotics suggested a non‑bacterial source. | "Despite broad‑spectrum antibiotic treatment (ceftazidime, teicoplanin and addition of ciprofloxacin for two days), fever persisted although the clinical condition remained stable."
2. Extensive microbiologic work‑up failed to identify bacterial, viral or fungal pathogens initially. | "Blood cultures taken were repeatedly negative for bacteria and fungi... The multiple sputum cultures taken did not reveal any microorganisms... Cultures of both pleural fluid... and broncho‑alveolar lavage (BAL) were negative for viral, bacterial and fungal agents."
3. Negative galactomannan reduced the likelihood of invasive aspergillosis early on. | "Aspergillus‑antigen (galactomannan) was not detected in multiple plasma samples, pleural fluid and BAL fluid."
4. Bone‑marrow aspirate showed no leukemic relapse, ruling out disease progression as cause of fever. | "Bone marrow aspirate to rule out a relapse of his leukaemia showed no malignant cells..."
5. Lack of response to ciprofloxacin and negative Legionella antigen argued against atypical bacterial pneumonia. | "Ciprofloxacin was added to the antimicrobial therapy, to cover atypical causative agents of pneumonia... Urine tested negative for Legionella antigen."
6. Development of hepatomegaly and capillary‑leak syndrome raised suspicion for systemic infection, but abdominal ultrasound showed no focal lesions, making deep fungal lesions less evident. | "Ultrasound examination of the abdomen confirmed the hepatomegaly without any focal lesions which might have been suggestive for fungal infection."
7. Appearance of vasculitis‑like lesions on distal extremities suggested a disseminated infection with vascular involvement, compatible with invasive fungal disease. | "On the nail of digit III of the left foot and on the soles of both feet small vasculitis‑like lesions were noticed."
8. Subsequent positive cultures for Candida glabrata in urine/faeces and Aspergillus fumigatus in sputum provided direct microbiologic evidence of invasive fungal infection. | "the urine and faeces cultures became positive for Candida glabrata, while one out of many sputum samples grew Aspergillus fumigatus."
9. Transoesophageal echocardiography demonstrated a large intra‑atrial mass, consistent with a fungal vegetation or infected thrombus, supporting invasive aspergillosis with cardiac involvement. | "Transoesophageal ultrasound examination of the heart showed ... a round left intra‑atrial tumour mass, compromising almost the whole left atrium."
10. Based on the combination of neutropenia, refractory fever, pulmonary consolidation, negative bacterial work‑up, vasculitic skin lesions, positive Aspergillus sputum culture and cardiac mass, the authors concluded the diagnosis was invasive aspergillosis. | "Suspicion of a fungal mass or infected thrombus together with the recovery of fungal pathogens ... led to the initiation of antifungal therapy with liposomal amphotericin B."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: Identification: The patient’s ultimate diagnosis is active tuberculosis, which is included in the 21 SELECTED diseases list. Therefore the target diagnosis is “tuberculosis”.
2. Ideal Breakpoint: Stop the narrative just before the culture result is disclosed. Include chief complaint, HPI, past TB history, physical exam, imaging findings, negative sputum smear, bronchoscopy with negative BAL for TB/fungi/malignancy, and negative Aspergillus serology. Omit the sentence “Culturing was positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis…”.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished active TB from other causes of massive hemoptysis in silicosis by (a) demonstrating a cavitary lesion on HRCT, (b) performing bronchoscopy and BAL that were negative for TB smear but later yielded a positive culture, (c) ruling out chronic pulmonary aspergillosis with negative immunodiffusion, and (d) excluding malignancy via negative BAL cytology.
case_prompt:
A 55‑year‑old man, former smoker with a 14‑year history of occupational silica exposure leading to chronic silicosis, was admitted after expectorating >200 mL of blood. He had a one‑month history of productive cough with blood‑streaked sputum. His past medical history was notable for pulmonary tuberculosis treated two years earlier; he had been asymptomatic since that episode.

On examination the patient was emaciated and pale, blood pressure 100/70 mmHg, pulse 104/min, respiratory rate 20/min. Lung auscultation revealed rhonchi and wheezing bilaterally; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable. Laboratory screening was normal, HIV test negative, and Aspergillus immunodiffusion tests were negative.

Chest radiograph and high‑resolution CT of the thorax showed bilateral conglomerate masses, one with cavitation, multiple small nodules, calcified hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes, paracicatricial emphysema, architectural distortion, and enlarged central pulmonary arteries. No parenchymal findings were suggestive of active tuberculosis.

Sputum smear was negative for acid‑fast bacilli. Bronchoscopy demonstrated active bleeding; bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for tuberculosis, fungi, and malignancy on direct examination.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Reactivation pulmonary tuberculosis – culture later grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis, confirming active disease. | "Culturing was positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis..."
2. Chronic pulmonary aspergillosis – considered because cavitary lesions can harbor Aspergillus, but serology was negative and BAL did not reveal fungi. | "Immunodiffusion tests were negative for Aspergillus." … "Culturing was ... negative for fungi."
3. Primary lung malignancy – cavitary mass with hemoptysis raises concern for carcinoma, yet BAL cytology was negative for malignancy. | "Direct examination of the bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for ... malignancy."
4. Silicosis‑related bronchial artery hypertrophy causing hemorrhage – imaging showed hypervascular bronchial artery, which was embolized, but this is a mechanism rather than a primary disease; underlying infection needed to explain ongoing symptoms. | "Angiogram of the common bronchial trunk showed marked hypervascularity and enlargement of left bronchial artery..."
5. Non‑tuberculous mycobacterial infection – possible in silicosis, but culture specifically identified Mycobacterium tuberculosis, excluding other mycobacteria. | "Culturing was positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis..."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case culminates in invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (IPA) confirmed by histology and culture. Aspergillosis is on the 21 SELECTED diseases list, so the target diagnosis is aspergillosis.
2. Best Breakpoint: End the prompt after the repeat HRCT performed 4 weeks later that demonstrated new cavitary lesions, but before the thoracotomy, histology, and culture results that explicitly identified Aspergillus. This provides sufficient clinical, radiographic, and laboratory clues for learners to deduce invasive fungal infection without revealing the definitive diagnosis.
3. Author's Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished IPA from bacterial pneumonia, pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia, viral pneumonitis (RSV, influenza, CMV), and GVHD‑related pneumonitis by (a) negative bacterial/fungal cultures, (b) negative serum galactomannan early on, (c) lack of response to broad antimicrobial/antiviral therapy, (d) evolution from ground‑glass opacities to cavitary lesions, and (e) definitive histopathology and culture after surgical resection.
case_prompt:
A 40‑year‑old Chinese male underwent allogeneic peripheral blood hematopoietic stem‑cell transplantation (HSCT) for B‑cell prolymphocytic leukemia and subsequently developed steroid‑refractory grade III acute graft‑versus‑host disease of the liver, requiring prolonged immunosuppression with prednisolone, tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and sirolimus. He received dapsone and acyclovir prophylaxis but no antifungal prophylaxis.

In December 2007, nine months post‑transplant, he developed an acute dry cough and dyspnea after close contact with a person who had an upper respiratory tract infection. Initial chest radiograph was unremarkable. Over the next few days his respiratory status deteriorated, and one week after onset he required non‑invasive ventilation in the ICU for acute respiratory failure. He was afebrile; lung auscultation revealed bilateral rhonchi. Blood counts, renal and hepatic panels were normal. A chest X‑ray showed patchy bilateral lower‑zone and right upper‑zone air‑space opacities.

High‑resolution CT of the thorax demonstrated bilateral extensive, circumscribed ground‑glass opacities with a fine reticular pattern, interpreted as pneumonitis; no nodules or pleural‑based lesions suggestive of invasive fungal infection were seen. Empiric therapy with intravenous levofloxacin, trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole (for possible Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia), and oseltamivir (for possible influenza) was started.

Microbiologic work‑up showed negative aerobic bacterial, acid‑fast bacilli, and fungal cultures; nasopharyngeal PCR was positive for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) while viral culture was negative. Serial serum galactomannan and quantitative CMV PCR from blood were negative. Bronchoalveolar lavage was not performed because of concern for worsening hypoxemia.

The patient improved over a week, with decreasing oxygen requirements. A repeat HRCT performed four weeks later revealed new cavitary lesions in both lungs.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Community‑acquired bacterial pneumonia was considered because of acute cough and dyspnea, but cultures of respiratory samples were negative and the patient did not improve with levofloxacin alone. | "All microscopy and cultures of clinical samples were negative for aerobic bacteria..."
2. Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia was entertained, prompting TMP/SMX, yet lack of characteristic radiographic findings (no diffuse ground‑glass without nodules) and negative response made it unlikely. | "Empirical antimicrobial therapy with intravenous levofloxacin and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole was prescribed for community‑acquired bacterial pneumonia and possible pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonitis."
3. Influenza‑associated pneumonia was a possibility, leading to oseltamivir administration, but PCR for RSV was positive, influenza testing was not reported, and the clinical course did not align with typical influenza. | "Oseltamivir (Tamiflu) was added as the possibility of influenza‑associated pneumonia was entertained."
4. RSV infection was identified by PCR, providing a viral etiology for the initial symptoms; however, RSV typically does not produce cavitary lesions, and the patient’s radiographic pattern progressed despite supportive care. | "Reverse‑transcriptase polymerase chain reactions (PCR) performed on nasopharyngeal specimens were positive for RSV..."
5. Cytomegalovirus pneumonia was considered; serial serum CMV PCR remained negative, reducing its likelihood. | "Serial ... quantitative real‑time PCR for cytomegalovirus DNA from peripheral blood were all negative."
6. Acute GVHD‑related pneumonitis was plausible given recent severe GVHD and immunosuppression, but HRCT showed ground‑glass opacities without the typical interstitial pattern, and later development of cavitary lesions is atypical for GVHD alone. | "HRCT ... showed bilateral extensive, circumscribed areas of ground‑glass opacification ... in keeping with pneumonitis."
7. Invasive fungal infection (aspergillosis) became more likely after new cavitary lesions appeared on repeat HRCT, a classic evolution from early pneumonitis to necrotizing lesions in immunocompromised hosts, despite earlier negative serum galactomannan. | "A repeat HRCT thorax (Figure 3) 4 weeks later showed new cavitary lesions."
8. Other invasive fungal pathogens were less favored because initial imaging lacked nodules or halo signs, and the patient had no antifungal prophylaxis; the eventual histology and culture later confirmed Aspergillus fumigatus. | "The histology was consistent with IPA, while lung tissue cultures grew Aspergillus fumigatus."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case’s definitive diagnosis is infection with *Aspergillus fumigatus*, which maps to “aspergillosis” on the 21 SELECTED diseases list.  
2. Best breakpoint: End the prompt after the decision to obtain CT‑guided lung biopsy and stereotactic brain biopsy, but before any pathology or culture results are reported. This includes the patient’s acute respiratory and neurologic presentation, imaging findings, initial laboratory work‑up, and the differential considerations that led to biopsy, without revealing the fungal identification.  
3. Author’s analytic distinctions: The authors excluded metastatic/recurrent carcinoma and post‑transplant lymphoproliferative disease by obtaining tissue; they excluded other opportunistic infections with negative serologies/antigen tests; definitive diagnosis was made when histopathology demonstrated septated, branching hyphae and cultures grew *Aspergillus fumigatus*, which also correlated with clinical improvement on antifungal therapy.
case_prompt:
A 71‑year‑old woman with adult‑onset diabetes, hypertension, a history of rectal cancer, and end‑stage renal disease status post deceased‑donor kidney transplant 18 months earlier (immunosuppressed with belatacept as part of a study) presented acutely with dyspnea and substernal chest pain that had become constant. Seven days prior she had developed new word‑finding difficulty with inappropriate word substitution. She denied fever, chills, weight loss, or other constitutional symptoms.

On exam she was aphasic and had a firm, tender substernal mass; no other focal neurologic or physical findings were noted. Chest radiograph showed a mediastinal mass with a left lower‑lobe process; CT confirmed a mediastinal mass adherent to the pericardium and extending anteriorly.

During admission she developed right retro‑orbital pain with decreased vision. Neurologic re‑examination revealed a predominantly expressive aphasia, mild right pronator drift, and slight right nasolabial flattening. Ophthalmology identified a corneal erosion treated with topical polymyxin B. Head CT and MRI demonstrated a deep‑seated left frontal lesion, heterogeneously enhancing with gadolinium, measuring 25 × 18 × 10 mm, surrounded by perifocal edema and a mild midline shift. She was started on dexamethasone and levetiracetam.

Routine blood work (CBC, electrolytes, chemistries) was normal; baseline creatinine 0.8 mg/dL. Infectious work‑up included blood cultures (no growth), serum toxoplasma IgG/IgM, cryptococcal antigen, galactomannan, β‑D‑glucan, and urinary histoplasma antigen (all negative). CSF was not sampled due to concern for increased intracranial pressure.

Given her remote squamous cell carcinoma of the anus, the erosive mediastinal mass, and recent solid‑organ transplant, metastatic or recurrent malignancy and post‑transplant lymphoproliferative disease were considered. Accordingly, a CT‑guided transthoracic lung biopsy and, two days later, a stereotactic brain biopsy were planned.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Metastatic or recurrent malignancy was a primary consideration because of the patient’s prior squamous cell carcinoma and new mediastinal mass, but tissue diagnosis was required to exclude it. | "Given her history of a distant squamous cell carcinoma of the anus, the presence of an erosive mediastinal mass ... metastatic or recurrent malignancy ... were of concern."
2. Post‑transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD) was also in the differential due to immunosuppression, yet needed histologic confirmation. | "metastatic or recurrent malignancy as well as post‑transplant lymphoproliferative disease were of concern and it was felt that a biopsy was needed of both foci."
3. Other opportunistic fungal infections (cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis) were evaluated with antigen testing that returned negative. | "cryptococcal antigen, galactomannan and beta‑d‑glucan antigen tests were negative; urinary histoplasma antigen was also negative."
4. Toxoplasma infection was considered but serologies were negative. | "serum toxoplasma IgG and IgM ... were negative."
5. Bacterial infection was investigated through blood cultures, which showed no growth. | "Blood cultures for bacteria and fungus were obtained (but showed no growth)."
6. Aspergillosis was ultimately diagnosed when biopsy specimens revealed septated, branching hyphae and cultures grew *Aspergillus fumigatus*. | "Both yielded specimen demonstrating septated, branching hyphae with culture data that confirmed Aspergillus fumigatus."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient ultimately was diagnosed with invasive aspergillosis, which is on the 21 SELECTED diseases list. Therefore the target diagnosis is **aspergillosis**.
2. Ideal Breakpoint: End the presented case just before the laboratory confirmation of aspergillus antigenemia. Include the initial presentation, neurologic decline, imaging suggesting multifocal cerebral abscesses, and empiric antibacterial/antiviral therapy, but stop prior to the statement “During the infectious investigation, an aspergillar antigenaemia returned positive…”.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors differentiated invasive aspergillosis from bacterial septic emboli, viral encephalitis, and other opportunistic CNS infections by (a) negative bacterial cultures from CSF and blood, (b) negative cryptococcal and toxoplasma tests, (c) lack of pleocytosis in CSF, (d) positive galactomannan (aspergillus antigen) on multiple samples, and (e) histopathology showing Grocott‑positive, septate, branching hyphae consistent with Aspergillus fumigatus.
case_prompt:
A 66‑year‑old male smoker with diffuse atheromatosis presented with gradually worsening intracranial hypertension. Biopsy of a left occipital lesion revealed a WHO grade III–IV glioma located near the left ventricular atrium, deemed inoperable. He received 60 Gy radiotherapy with corticosteroids, which were well tolerated, and temozolomide chemotherapy was planned.

Several weeks later he developed left hip and sacral pain. MRI suggested aseptic osteonecrosis of the left femoral head secondary to corticosteroids. The pain intensified with swelling of the left lower limb; ultrasound showed an intra‑articular effusion but no venous thrombosis. A febrile syndrome ensued, but all bacteriological samples remained negative. Neurologically he became apathetic, drowsy, and exhibited memory disturbances, attributed to radiotherapy and opioid analgesics. He was transferred to the infectious disease unit where left hemiparesis was noted. Brain CT demonstrated multifocal hypodensities compatible with cerebral abscesses. Lumbar puncture revealed no pleocytosis and negative bacterial cultures. Empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics and intravenous anti‑herpetic therapy were initiated. His level of consciousness rapidly deteriorated, prompting cerebral MRI, which confirmed images suggestive of multifocal abscesses.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial brain abscesses were considered given the CT findings, but CSF cultures were negative and no elevated cell count was present, reducing bacterial likelihood. | "The lumbar puncture did not show elevated cell count; the bacteriological examination was negative."
2. Septic emboli from pulmonary sources were contemplated, yet thoracic CT showed only lesions later proved to be fungal on autopsy, and blood cultures remained sterile. | "Multiple lung lesions suggestive of septic emboli were noticed on the thoracic CT scan."
3. Viral encephalitis (e.g., HSV) was entertained, leading to the addition of anti‑herpetic therapy, but lack of CSF pleocytosis and negative viral studies made this less likely. | "A probabilistic biantibiotic therapy was established, in association with an intravenous antiherpetic treatment."
4. Toxoplasmosis was a differential, especially in immunosuppressed patients, but CSF PCR and staining were negative. | "Mycological and parasitological examinations were negative for cryptococcosis and toxoplasmosis."
5. Cryptococcosis was evaluated given the immunosuppressed state, yet CSF antigen testing and cultures were negative. | "Mycological and parasitological examinations were negative for cryptococcosis..."
6. Metastatic tumor progression or radiation necrosis could mimic abscesses, but the acute febrile syndrome, rapid neurologic decline, and systemic septic picture favored infection. | "A neurological syndrome ... likely secondary to the cerebral radiotherapy and morphinic painkillers" (initial hypothesis) versus later infectious findings.
7. Necrotizing fasciitis of the left lower limb provided a portal of entry for polymicrobial infection, but cultures grew only intestinal flora, not Aspergillus, indicating a separate invasive fungal process. | "The sample of necrotizing fasciitis was positive for polybacterial intestinal flora, compatible with anoperineal portal of entry."
8. Invasive aspergillosis was ultimately supported by repeatedly positive aspergillus antigenemia, histopathology showing Grocott‑positive, septate, branching hyphae, and multiple pulmonary and cerebral lesions consistent with fungal abscesses. | "During the infectious investigation, an aspergillar antigenaemia returned positive, confirmed on two other samples, suggestive of invasive aspergillosis."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The definitive diagnosis is infective endocarditis caused by Legionella longbeachae, which is not among the 21 SELECTED diseases. Therefore the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.  
2. Breakpoint: Present the case up to the initiation of empiric vancomycin + gentamicin for blood‑culture‑negative endocarditis (July 2008 admission), before valve‑tissue molecular testing and identification of L. longbeachae. This includes clinical presentation, imaging, laboratory data, and negative serologies, but excludes the surgical pathology and PCR results that reveal the organism.  
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors ruled out common causes of culture‑negative endocarditis (Coxiella, Bartonella, Brucella, Chlamydia, Mycoplasma, Legionella pneumophila, Aspergillus) via a comprehensive serologic panel; they used imaging (TEE) to demonstrate vegetation; they applied Durack and Richet scores to gauge likelihood of endocarditis; finally, they identified L. longbeachae by 16S rDNA sequencing, culture on buffered charcoal yeast extract, immunohistochemistry, and serologic confirmation.
case_prompt: In July 2008, a 73‑year‑old man was admitted to La Timone Hospital because of heart failure. He had received an aortic bioprosthetic valve replacement in January 2008 and, after returning home in March, performed gardening with potting mixes. On admission, transesophageal echocardiography showed displacement of the prosthetic valve with a false aneurysm and a 9 mm vegetation. Laboratory studies revealed a leukocyte count of 9.4 × 10⁹ cells/L, hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 53 mm, and C‑reactive protein 126 mg/L. Three blood cultures remained sterile. Serologic testing for Legionella pneumophila and urinary antigen testing for Legionella spp. were negative; only the serologic test for *Legionella* anisa was positive (titer 256). A diagnosis of blood‑culture‑negative endocarditis was made, and intravenous vancomycin (30 mg/kg/d) plus gentamicin (3 mg/kg/d) was started.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Culture‑negative endocarditis due to Coxiella burnetii considered but excluded by negative serologic test. | "Results of all tests (including transesophageal echocardiograph) were negative."
2. Bartonella spp. considered; serology negative, thus excluded. | "Results of all tests (including transesophageal echocardiograph) were negative."
3. Brucella spp. considered; serology negative, thus excluded. | "Results of all tests (including transesophageal echocardiograph) were negative."
4. Chlamydia spp. considered; serology negative, thus excluded. | "Results of all tests (including transesophageal echocardiograph) were negative."
5. Mycoplasma pneumoniae considered; serology negative, thus excluded. | "Results of all tests (including transesophageal echocardiograph) were negative."
6. Legionella pneumophila considered; urinary antigen test and serology negative, thus excluded. | "Results of serologic tests for L. pneumophila and the urinary antigen test for Legionella spp. were negative."
7. Aspergillus spp. considered; serology negative, thus excluded. | "Results of all tests (including transesophageal echocardiograph) were negative."
8. *Legionella* anisa seropositivity noted but deemed unlikely as the cause of endocarditis because only low‑titer positivity without supporting culture. | "Only the serologic test for L. anisa was positive (titer 256)."
9. Non‑infectious prosthetic valve dysfunction/failure considered; however, presence of vegetation on TEE and marked inflammatory markers supported an infectious etiology. | "Transesophageal echocardiograph showed... a 9 mm vegetation."
10. Endocarditis due to *Legionella longbeachae* confirmed by valve‑tissue 16S rDNA sequencing, culture on buffered charcoal yeast extract, immunohistochemistry, and serologic assays. | "We conducted bacterial 16S rDNA amplification and sequencing on the valvular tissue... found a sequence 100% similar to that of L. longbeachae... The valvular culture grew... identified as L. longbeachae... immunohistochemical analysis ... were positive for L. longbeachae."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case culminates in a diagnosis of hepatic aspergilloma, a manifestation of aspergillosis, which is included in the 21 SELECTED diseases list. Therefore, the target diagnosis is aspergillosis.
2. Best breakpoint: Include all clinical data up to the histopathologic observation of abundant fungal hyphae in the liver biopsy, but stop before the statement that A. fumigatus was isolated and before the authors explicitly concluded “liver aspergilloma.” This provides sufficient information (hepatic nodules, normal tumor markers, negative bacterial/viral studies, imaging, and fungal hyphae) for students to generate the differential and arrive at the diagnosis without the spoiler.
3. Author’s analytic distinctions: The authors first considered malignancy, bacterial/acid‑fast infection, viral hepatitis, CMV/EBV, and other liver metabolic disorders, ruling each out with specific tumor markers, cultures, serologies, and metabolic tests. Imaging excluded pulmonary or sinus aspergillosis, and a negative galactomannan test argued against systemic aspergillosis. Definitive proof came from histopathology showing fungal hyphae and culture growth of A. fumigatus, leading to the final diagnosis of liver aspergilloma.
case_prompt: A 55‑year‑old woman was referred for progressive discomfort in the hepatic region. She had a past history of chronic aplastic anemia treated with stanozolol and intermittent gamma‑globulin infusions, with documented remission on serial bone‑marrow examinations. On admission her vitals were: temperature 36.5 °C, pulse 75/min, blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO₂ 98% on room air. Physical examination revealed a softly palpated abdomen. Laboratory studies showed leukocytes 3.0 × 10⁹/L, hemoglobin 110 g/L, platelets 23 × 10⁹/L; AST 80 U/L and ALT 65 U/L. Immunologic work‑up (quantitative immunoglobulins, CD4/CD8 ratio, delayed hypersensitivity skin tests) was normal; HIV test was negative. Serum tumor markers (CEA, CA‑125, CA‑199, PSA, AFP, etc.) were within normal limits. Abdominal ultrasonography and MRI demonstrated multiple heterogeneous solid nodules in the right hepatic lobe; no abdominal lymphadenopathy or effusions were seen. Additional investigations—including ESR, CRP, galactomannan antigenemia, hepatitis viral serology, cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus serology, urinary copper, and serum ceruloplasmin—were unrevealing. Bacterial and acid‑fast smears and cultures from blood and the liver lesion were negative. An ultrasound‑guided fine‑needle aspiration of a liver nodule was performed. Histopathological examination revealed abundant fungal hyphae amidst necrosis and chronic inflammation.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Malignancy or metastatic disease was considered because of multiple hepatic nodules, but normal serum tumor markers (CEA, CA‑125, CA‑199, PSA, AFP) made this unlikely. | “Malignant ailments and metastatic diseases were initially suspected, but serum tumor marker screening … was within normal limits.”
2. Bacterial and mycobacterial infection were contemplated; repeated bacterial and acid‑fast smears and cultures were negative, excluding these etiologies. | “Bacterial and acid‑fast smears and cultures were negative.”
3. Viral hepatitis, cytomegalovirus, and Epstein–Barr virus infections were evaluated; serologic testing was negative, ruling them out. | “Complete liver disease studies, including hepatitis virology, cytomegalovirus, Epstein‑Barr virus serology … failed to lead a significant result.”
4. Metabolic liver disorders such as Wilson disease were excluded by normal urinary copper and serum ceruloplasmin levels. | “Urinary copper, serum ceruloplasmine failed to lead a significant result.”
5. Systemic or pulmonary aspergillosis was considered; however, chest and paranasal sinus CT showed no lesions and serial galactomannan antigenemia tests remained negative, making pulmonary involvement unlikely. | “A comprehensive whole body evaluation, including chest and paranasal sinus computed tomography (CT), did not indicated aspergillosis lesions. Regular GM tests continued to be negative.”
6. Other invasive fungal infections (e.g., mucormycosis) were less likely because the histopathology demonstrated septate hyaline hyphae typical of Aspergillus rather than the broad ribbon‑like, pauciseptate hyphae of Mucorales. (Implied from description of “abundant fungal hyphae” consistent with Aspergillus morphology.) | “Abundant fungal hyphae were observed in the background of necrosis and chronic inflammation.”
7. Definitive diagnosis of hepatic aspergilloma was established by culture growth of A. fumigatus from the biopsy specimen, confirming Aspergillus infection of the liver. | “A. fumigatus was subsequently isolated and cultured from the biopsy aspirate… On the basis of these findings, we concluded the diagnosis of liver aspergilloma.”

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case’s definitive diagnosis is invasive Aspergillus fumigatus infection of the central nervous system (aspergillosis), which is included in the 21 SELECTED diseases list.  
2. Best breakpoint: End the presented case just before the histopathology and culture results that explicitly identify Aspergillus. Include chief complaint, imaging progression, surgical intervention, postoperative sudden headache, CT showing subarachnoid hemorrhage, and CTA revealing multiple bleb‑like aneurysms. This provides sufficient clinical and radiologic clues (immunosuppressed host, orbital apex lesion, rapid progression, multiple intracranial aneurysms) to allow the learner to infer a fungal etiology without revealing the final microbiologic confirmation.  
3. Author’s analytic distinctions: The authors distinguished a fungal etiology from other possibilities (e.g., inflammatory pseudotumor, neoplasm, bacterial infection) by noting steroid unresponsiveness, radiologic progression, intra‑operative findings, and finally definitive histology (septate hyphae) and culture growth of Aspergillus fumigatus, which also explained the atypical “fungal aneurysms.”
case_prompt:
A 73‑year‑old woman with hypertension and rheumatoid arthritis (stage 4) on long‑term corticosteroids presented in August 2010 with a 2‑month history of progressive visual loss in the right eye and right periorbital pain. Earlier, in June 2010, brain CT and orbit MRI revealed a small enhancing lesion (≈1.2 × 1.1 × 1 cm) at the right orbital apex and superior orbital fissure with mild optic nerve encasement and extension into the right posterior ethmoid sinus. Pulse steroid therapy in the ophthalmology service was ineffective.  

On admission she had right‑eye blindness, right ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, and tingling in the ophthalmic branch of the right trigeminal nerve. Repeat MRI in August showed enlargement of the lesion to 1.5 × 1.3 × 1.2 cm. She underwent endoscopic endonasal trans‑ethmoid resection of the lesion on 19 August 2010. Post‑operatively she initially improved, but five days later she developed a severe headache followed by loss of consciousness. Emergent brain CT demonstrated diffuse high‑density acute subarachnoid hemorrhage in the basal cisterns, pre‑pontine cistern, ambient cistern, quadrigeminal cistern, cerebellomedullary cistern, and right sylvian fissure, with acute hydrocephalus. External ventricular drainage was performed, and CT angiography showed multiple bleb‑like wide‑base aneurysms over the right supraclinoid internal carotid artery; one 4‑mm aneurysm on the medial side of the right supraclinoid ICA demonstrated contrast extravasation, indicating rupture.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Steroid‑refractory orbital apex lesion suggested a process other than inflammatory pseudotumor | "She had pulse steroid therapy in ophthalmology service, but it was ineffective."
2. Progressive enlargement of the enhancing lesion on serial MRI indicated an aggressive pathology, raising concern for neoplasm or infection | "Repeated MRI of orbit after admission in August 2010 showed the progression of the lesion which enlarged up to 1.5 cm × 1.3 cm × 1.2 cm."
3. Immunosuppressed state (long‑term corticosteroids) predisposes to opportunistic fungal infection, especially Aspergillus | "past medical history of ... rheumatoid arthritis stage 4 under long‑term corticosteroid therapy."
4. Development of multiple wide‑base aneurysms with rupture in a patient with a CNS lesion is compatible with fungal (mycotic) aneurysms, which are most commonly caused by Aspergillus spp. | "Her intracranial aneurysms were probably fungal aneurysms, which are one of the sequels of central nervous system (CNS) fungal infection."
5. Definitive histopathology showed septate hyphae on H&E and PAS stains, confirming invasive fungal infection | "the histology examination reported that the lesion was composed of many fungal septate hyphae demonstrated on both HE stain and periodic acid‑Schiff (PAS) stain."
6. Culture grew Aspergillus fumigatus, establishing the specific pathogen | "The culture turned out to be Aspergillus fumigatus."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient’s definitive diagnosis is invasive pulmonary aspergillosis, which is on the SELECTED diseases list (aspergillosis).  
2. Breakpoint: End the presented information just before the CT‑guided pulmonary biopsy and culture results are disclosed. Include chief complaint, HPI, vitals, physical exam, initial laboratory data, imaging findings (pulmonary embolism and cavitary nodules with halo sign), and the positive serum galactomannan; exclude the biopsy histology and culture that directly confirm Aspergillus.  
3. Analytic Distinctions: The authors highlighted (a) the presence of a halo sign and cavitary nodules on chest CT suggestive of angioinvasive fungal infection, (b) a markedly elevated serum galactomannan supporting Aspergillus, (c) negative Cryptococcus and Histoplasma antigen assays to rule out those fungi, and (d) definitive demonstration of septate, acute‑angle‑branching hyphae on Gomori‑silver stain plus growth of Aspergillus fumigatus in culture, which cemented the diagnosis and excluded other possibilities.
case_prompt:
A 78‑year‑old woman with a right frontal glioblastoma treated with craniotomy, hypofractionated radiation, and temozolomide presented two days after completing chemoradiation with dyspnea and asymmetrical lower‑extremity edema. She denied cough, sputum, hemoptysis, chest pain, fever, chills, sweats, or weight loss. Past medical history included hypertension, well‑controlled type 2 diabetes, and a tapering dose of dexamethasone 4 mg/day. Medications: omeprazole, amlodipine, metformin, gliclazide, sitagliptin, and prophylactic sulfamethoxazole‑trimethoprim.

On examination, vital signs were normal; respiratory rate 18/min, oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Lower‑extremity exam showed asymmetric edema; lung auscultation revealed fine bilateral crackles. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL, platelets 67,000/mm³, leukocytes 7,030/mm³ with absolute lymphocytes 800/mm³; electrolytes, liver enzymes, and renal function were within normal limits.

A venous duplex scan demonstrated extensive deep‑vein thrombosis of the left common femoral vein. Thoracic CT angiography confirmed an acute pulmonary embolism and identified scattered lobulated nodules up to 2.7 cm, predominantly in the upper lobes, many with cavitation and a surrounding ground‑glass halo. No pleural effusion was seen. Additional findings included peribronchial infiltrates and centrilobular nodules. Serum galactomannan by ELISA was markedly elevated (optical density index = 6.7; ≥0.5 considered positive). Blood cultures and serum antigen assays for Cryptococcus neoformans and Histoplasma were negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Pulmonary embolism as cause of dyspnea was initially considered but did not explain the cavitary nodules and halo sign seen on CT. | "An angiotomography of the thorax diagnosed an acute pulmonary embolism and also revealed scattered lobulated nodules with areas of cavitation..."
2. Cryptococcosis and histoplasmosis were evaluated because they can produce pulmonary nodules; both were excluded by negative antigen assays. | "Blood samples obtained for culture and Cryptococcus neoformans and Histoplasma antigen assays were negative."
3. Invasive aspergillosis was favored due to the halo sign, cavitary lesions, and a highly positive serum galactomannan, which is characteristic for Aspergillus infection. | "Serum galactomannan levels... were elevated (optical density index = 6.7, optical density index >=0.5 is considered a positive result)."
4. Definitive confirmation came from histopathology showing septate, acute‑angle branching hyphae and culture growing Aspergillus fumigatus, which ruled out other fungal pathogens. | "Histochemical analysis (Gomori's silver stain) showed septate hyphal elements with acute-angle branching... culture of the pulmonary tissue was positive for Aspergillus fumigatus."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case centers on hemolytic anemia secondary to Clostridium ramosum septicemia, which is not among the 21 SELECTED diseases. Therefore, the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.
2. Best breakpoint: Include presentation, laboratory data, imaging results, and blood‑culture findings up to the point where C. ramosum is identified and the patient’s antimicrobial regimen is changed, but stop before the authors explicitly state that the hemolysis was caused by the C. ramosum infection. This provides enough information for learners to generate the diagnosis without revealing it.
3. Author's Analytic Distinctions: The authors used negative viral antigenemia (aspergillus, CMV), a negative Coombs test, a negative DIC panel, and the isolation of C. ramosum from blood cultures to argue for an infectious etiology. They correlated clinical improvement and decreasing LDH after targeted antibiotics to support C. ramosum‑induced hemolysis, while excluding other infectious and non‑infectious causes.

case_prompt:
A 48‑year‑old African‑American man presented with progressive generalized weakness three months after receiving a living unrelated kidney transplant for end‑stage renal disease of unclear etiology. He had been on hemodialysis for four years prior to transplant and received induction immunosuppression with antithymocyte globulin and methylprednisolone. Post‑operative course was complicated by delayed graft function requiring dialysis, ureteral obstruction treated with revision of the ureterocystostomy and placement of a double‑J ureteral stent on postoperative day 7, and a kidney biopsy showing no acute rejection. The stent was removed after 20 days. At discharge the serum creatinine nadired at 159 µmol/L; iron studies showed a ferritin of 1815 ng/mL with an iron saturation of 63 %. New‑onset diabetes mellitus developed during follow‑up, and serum bicarbonate remained normal.

On current admission the patient had acute kidney injury (serum creatinine 406 µmol/L) without volume depletion or tacrolimus toxicity. Blood glucose was 24.3 mmol/L, requiring three days for control. Renal ultrasound demonstrated an enlarged transplanted kidney. A chest CT revealed bilateral ground‑glass infiltrates, multiple nodular opacities, and a 3.1 × 3 cm cystic mass in the left lower lobe. Head CT showed no sino‑orbital or cerebral involvement. The patient’s prophylactic agents were held because of persistent neutropenia, and filgrastim was started. A nephrostomy tube was placed for ongoing hydronephrosis. Urine cultures from the nephrostomy and catheter grew no organisms. Bronchoalveolar lavage cultures were negative, and serum and BAL Aspergillus galactomannan assays were negative. Serum PCR for cytomegalovirus DNA was also negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:

2. Aspergillosis considered due to pulmonary lesions; excluded by negative fungal antigen testing: “Serum and BAL Aspergillus galactomannan antigen assays were negative.”  
3. Cytomegalovirus infection evaluated given immunosuppression; excluded by molecular testing: “Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay of the serum was negative for cytomegalovirus DNA.”  
4. Rejection was deemed unlikely early on because prior biopsy “showed no evidence of acute rejection,” and current presentation lacked classic rejection findings.  
5. Environmental mold exposure was noted (wife cleaned house windows of molds) but did not directly explain the invasive disease; the definitive tissue diagnosis later demonstrated non‑septate hyphae consistent with Mucorales, confirming mucormycosis as the cause.

case_prompt:
A 38‑year‑old man presented with two days of giddiness and uneasiness. He denied dyspnea or palpitations and had no prior comorbidities. Examination revealed bitemporal hemianopia. Laboratory evaluation showed hyponatremia, hypocortisolism, hypothyroidism, and elevated gonadotropins. MRI of the brain demonstrated a sellar‑supra‑sellar mass. After hormone replacement and electrolyte correction, he underwent gross‑total trans‑sphenoidal resection of the tumor. Post‑operatively he received hydrocortisone infusion (4 mg/h) and later 50 mg IV every 8 h, was discharged on oral hydrocortisone and thyroxine, and histopathology confirmed a gonadotropin‑secreting pituitary adenoma with clear dura, bone and sphenoid sinus mucosa.

Three weeks later he returned with intermittent fever and a five‑day history of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) rhinorrhea. He exhibited terminal neck rigidity. CSF analysis was consistent with pyogenic meningitis; culture grew Enterobacter species, prompting appropriate antibiotics. A CT scan showed pneumocephalus. Endoscopic repair of the skull‑base defect was performed after apparent control of infection, and CSF diversion was instituted via an external lumbar drain.

Despite repair, CSF rhinorrhea persisted and repeat CT demonstrated progression of pneumocephalus. A repeat CSF culture after one week grew Staphylococcus, and he was started on intravenous vancomycin and meropenin together with intrathecal vancomycin. His leukocyte count rose from 8,700 mm³ (71 % neutrophils) pre‑operatively to 15,800 mm³ (82 % neutrophils) on this admission; serum albumin was 4.5 g/dL and globulin 3.5 g/dL. HIV serology was negative. Throughout this period he remained on injectable hydrocortisone, oral thyroxine, and intermittent desmopressin for diabetes insipidus.

After three weeks of hospitalization he abruptly became unresponsive. Emergent CT revealed a subarachnoid hemorrhage with intraventricular extension. The cause of death was speculated to be due to rupture of an intracranial aneurysm. This may have been an association with the pituitary macroadenoma, weakening of the vessel wall from inflammatory exudates, or an inadvertent intra‑operative injury such as snapping of a distal perforator resulting in pseudoaneurysm formation.

1. Pituitary macroadenoma causing mass effect – considered because the initial MRI showed a sellar‑supra‑sellar mass and bitemporal hemianopia; excluded as the ultimate cause of death because the tumor was gross‑totally resected with clear margins. | "Histopathology and immunohistochemistry showed a gonadotropin secreting pituitary adenoma. The dura and bone was free of tumor..."
2. Post‑operative pyogenic meningitis due to Enterobacter – considered given CSF culture positive for Enterobacter and neck rigidity; excluded as the fatal event because the meningitis was treated, cultures later cleared, and the patient subsequently died from hemorrhage. | "CSF studies were suggestive of pyogenic meningitis, CSF culture showed Enterobacter species, and he was started on appropriate antibiotics."

Secondary bacterial meningitis with Staphylococcus – considered after repeat CSF grew Staphylococcus and prompted escalation of antibiotics; ruled out as primary lethal pathology because hemorrhagic catastrophe occurred despite antimicrobial therapy. | "Repeat CSF culture after a week grew Staphylococcus and he was started on intravenous Vancomycin and Meropenem..."

Pneumocephalus due to skull‑base repair failure – considered because CT demonstrated pneumocephalus and CSF rhinorrhea persisted; not the cause of death as imaging later showed subarachnoid hemorrhage rather than expanding air collection. | "CT scan showed pneumocephalus... Despite the repair, CSF rhinorrhea persisted, and CT scan showed the progression of pneumocephalus."

case_prompt:
A 61‑year‑old woman, never smoker, was referred for a 5‑year history of productive cough, dyspnea, and wheezing. She had peripheral eosinophilia (6–20 %) and recurrent transient infiltrates on serial chest radiographs. A prior diagnosis of eosinophilic pneumonia with bronchial asthma had been made, and oral prednisolone produced symptom remission lasting 2–3 weeks at a time.

She reported sputum production of up to 10 mL per day, purulent, malodorous, sometimes forming mucoid plugs. Current therapy included inhaled corticosteroids and long‑acting β‑agonists. Pulmonary examination revealed bilateral coarse crepitations with biphasic polyphonic rhonchi. Laboratory studies showed a total leukocyte count of 7 240 cells/µL with 11.9 % eosinophils (absolute eosinophil count 861/µL). Serum biochemistry was unremarkable. Aspergillus spp. IgG antibody was negative, total IgE was normal (70.36 IU/mL), but specific IgE for Aspergillus spp. was positive.

Chest X‑ray demonstrated infiltrates in the right lower lung. Computed tomography showed bilateral dilation of the central bronchi in the right upper lobe with hyperattenuating mucus, consistent with central bronchiectasis. Sputum microscopy identified Charcot‑Leyden crystals and septate, branching hyphae on KOH wet mounts of three consecutive specimens and of expectorated mucoid plugs. Culturing of homogenized sputum and mucoid plugs on Sabouraud’s glucose agar yielded green and white, wooly colonies after 4 days at 25 °C. One isolate was morphologically identified as Aspergillus fumigatus; the other produced similar colonies but could not be identified by morphology alone.

1. Eosinophilic pneumonia considered due to chronic eosinophilia and infiltrates, but the presence of central bronchiectasis and positive Aspergillus‑specific IgE argued against a purely eosinophilic process. | "She had a high eosinophil range of 6‑20% ... and transient recurrent infiltrates on serial chest X‑rays."
2. Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) entertained because of asthma, eosinophilia, central bronchiectasis, and positive Aspergillus‑specific IgE, yet Aspergillus IgG was negative and cultures grew an additional unidentified fungus, prompting broader mycotic investigation. | "Specific IgE for Aspergillus spp. was found to be positive." and "The patient was further investigated because saccular bronchiectasis is a feature of allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA)."
3. Mycobacterial infection ruled out: sputum smears negative for acid‑fast bacilli and no clinical evidence of tuberculosis. | "Microscopic assessment of sputum was negative for acid‑fast bacilli (AFB) and other bacteria."
4. Non‑fungal bacterial infection excluded by lack of pathogenic bacteria on culture and by the predominance of fungal hyphae on microscopy. | "Direct microscopy of KOH wet mounts ... revealed two types of septate and branching hyphae."
5. Co‑infection with a non‑Aspergillus fungus (Schizophyllum commune) considered after culture yielded an obscure colony and DNA sequencing identified its ITS/D1‑D2 regions as 100 % similar to S. commune; this explained the atypical presentation and confirmed allergic bronchopulmonary mycosis. | "The other (Fig 2B and D) remained obscure. case_prompt:
A 17‑year‑old Caucasian girl with common variable immunodeficiency presented with a 6‑day history of a non‑pruritic, photo‑distributed rash on her face, arms, and legs associated with swelling of the arms. The rash began after she spent a few hours playing on a sunny farm. She denied fever. She reported a burning sensation in her eyes for a few hours prior to admission, without drainage or blurred vision, and dryness with redness and early blistering of the lips. She had no recent sick contacts.

She was diagnosed with common variable immunodeficiency at age 3 after recurrent ear infections and bacterial pneumonia and receives monthly intravenous immunoglobulin. In the past 5 months she had recurrent cough and hemoptysis; chest CT showed a tree‑in‑bud pattern and bronchoalveolar lavage grew *Aspergillus fumigatus*. She was started on oral voriconazole 200 mg twice daily for 4 weeks, increased to 300 mg twice daily 10 days before presentation because of a sub‑therapeutic serum level. Other medications included Vynase (lesdexamphetamine) 50 mg daily; quetiapine had been stopped 10 days earlier due to potential QT prolongation with voriconazole.

On exam the teenager appeared well‑built and well‑nourished, alert but in moderate distress from burning of the arms and face. Vital signs: temperature 36.7 °C, heart rate 65/min, respiratory rate 14/min, blood pressure 117/69 mm Hg. There was an erythematous, shiny, tender rash on the face and both arms up to mid‑arm, extending to the neck and lower extremities, sparing the trunk, buttocks, and genital area. Lips were cracked with mild bleeding but no swelling or oral ulcers. The remainder of the examination was normal.

Laboratory studies: WBC 3,900/mm³ (neutrophils 74 %, lymphocytes 16 %, monocytes 8 %, eosinophils 2 %); hemoglobin 13.9 g/dL; platelets 196 × 10³/mm³; electrolytes normal; BUN 15 mg/dL, creatinine 0.7 mg/dL; liver enzymes normal. Blood cultures were negative. Voriconazole level was 2.5 µg/mL (therapeutic 2–6 µg/mL). Serum IgM for parvovirus B19, Mycoplasma, and HSV were negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Temporal relationship between recent voriconazole dose increase and rash onset suggests drug‑induced photosensitivity | "She was given oral voriconazole… increased to 300 mg twice daily, 10 days prior to presentation… The rash started after she was playing in the farm on a sunny day."
2. Photodistributed pattern sparing non‑exposed areas is characteristic of photosensitivity reactions | "The rash was photo‑distributed … sparing the truncal area, buttocks, and the genital area."
3. Absence of systemic symptoms and negative viral serologies argue against infectious exanthem | "Serum parvovirus B‑19, Mycoplasma, and herpes simplex IgM levels were all negative."
4. Histopathology consistent with photosensitivity supports the diagnosis (though not revealed in the prompt) | "Skin biopsy showed mild vacuolar interface dermatitis with necrotic keratinocytes and superficial vessel involvement consistent with photosensitivity reactions."
5. Rapid clinical improvement after discontinuation of voriconazole confirms drug causality | "Voriconazole was discontinued at the time of presentation… The rash gradually improved."

case_prompt:
A 29‑year‑old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus diagnosed three months earlier and end‑stage renal disease presented with melena. On examination she had anemia, temperature 38.4 °C, blood pressure 130/90 mmHg, pulse 90 bpm. Laboratory studies showed severe anemia (Hb 5.8 g/dL), thrombocytopenia (platelets 79 ×10³/mm³), and leukopenia (WBC 1.05 ×10³/mm³). Chest X‑ray was normal and the infection focus could not be identified. Emergency gastroduodenoscopy revealed several ulcers with hematoma in the stomach and duodenum; endoscopic hemostasis with hemoclips was successful and she received blood transfusions.

Four days later she complained of a right neck mass and palpitations. High‑frequency thyroid sonography showed diffuse enlargement of the right lobe (AP 2.1 cm) with an ill‑defined hypoechoic lesion, sonographic tenderness, and poor vascularity on color Doppler; the left lobe was normal and no cervical lymphadenopathy was seen. Thyroid function tests indicated thyrotoxicosis (TSH < 0.02 µIU/mL, FT4 4.05 ng/dL). Subacute thyroiditis with hyperthyroidism was considered, and she was started on a beta‑blocker and steroids.

Despite therapy she continued to have palpitations and the neck mass enlarged. Repeat thyroid function showed further rise in FT4 (7.83 ng/dL) with persistently suppressed TSH (0.02 µIU/mL). Propylthiouracil was added without significant effect, and the neck swelling progressed. Two weeks after the initial sonography, repeat imaging demonstrated a marked increase in thyroid size (AP 4 cm) with lobulated contours, irregular hypoechogenicity subcapsularly and isoechogenic central portions, suggesting progression of thyroiditis. Thyroid scintigraphy showed large photon defects in both glands. The team suspected other diseases such as fungal or suppurative thyroiditis rather than subacute thyroiditis. Chest CT showed no pulmonary fungal lesions, and sinus radiographs were normal. The next day the patient developed severe dyspnea and hypoxemia, requiring endotracheal intubation and stabilization of thyroid hormone levels before emergent total thyroidectomy.

1. Subacute thyroiditis was initially entertained because of painful thyroid enlargement, low vascularity on Doppler, and thyrotoxic labs; however, lack of clinical improvement with steroids and rapid gland enlargement argued against it. | "We considered subacute thyroiditis with hyperthyroidism. She was empirically treated with beta blocker and steroid for subacute thyroiditis... the patient continued to complain of palpitation with a growing neck mass."
2. Suppurative (bacterial) thyroiditis was considered given the inflammatory picture, but absence of fever spikes, negative sinus and lung imaging, and no purulent discharge made bacterial infection unlikely. | "We suspected other diseases such as fungal or suppurative thyroiditis rather than subacute thyroiditis. There was no evidence of fungal infection involving the lung in chest computerized tomography (CT). She had no symptoms of sinusitis."
3. Fungal thyroiditis became the leading hypothesis because of the patient’s profound immunosuppression (SLE, leukopenia), refractory hyperthyroidism despite steroids and PTU, rapid progressive enlargement, poor vascularity, and lack of alternative infectious sources. | "We suspected other diseases such as fungal or suppurative thyroiditis rather than subacute thyroiditis."
4. Definitive diagnosis of Aspergillus infection was established by histopathology of the thyroidectomy specimen, revealing necrotic tissue with fungal yeasts and hyphae characteristic of Aspergillus species. | "Histopathological examination and staining... revealed extensive necrotic tissue with many fungal yeast and hyphae characteristic of Aspergillus species."

case_prompt:
A 64‑year‑old male farmer presented to the oral medicine outpatient department with a 4‑month history of pain and pus discharge from the left upper back tooth region. The pain was slow‑onset, localized, dull, intermittent, and not modified by any factors. He also reported numbness of the left facial side for the past 2 months. Past medical history was notable for hypertension (5 years) and diabetes mellitus (4 years) on treatment.

Four years earlier he had been diagnosed by an ENT physician with nasal myiasis, for which surgical debridement and maggot removal were performed. More recently, plain and contrast computed tomography of the brain revealed a sharply defined, mildly hyperdense 24 × 19 mm lesion in the left temporal region with mild enhancement, hyperostosis and widening of the diploic spaces of the greater wing of the sphenoid, suggestive of a meningioma. He was admitted to a private dental hospital, consented, and underwent left‑side maxillectomy under general anesthesia. Two months of regular debridements and sterile wound cultures later, an acrylic palatal obturator was fabricated.

Extra‑oral examination showed marked facial asymmetry with a sunken left side and loss of the nasolabial fold. TMJ and neck nodes were unremarkable. Intra‑oral examination revealed a well‑defined surgical defect in the left maxillary quadrant; the base displayed a gray‑black necrotic pseudo‑membranous slough with interspersed yellowish areas. Multiple missing teeth were noted in both maxillae and periodontally compromised mandibular teeth.

Provisional diagnosis of osteomyelitis of the surgical defect was made. Differential considerations listed by the authors included tuberculosis, squamous cell carcinoma, tertiary syphilis, and fungal infections such as aspergillosis and mucormycosis.

Panoramic radiograph demonstrated extensive maxillary loss consistent with the left maxillectomy. Paranasal sinus view showed diffuse radiolucency with irregular borders involving the left maxillary antrum and deviated nasal spine. Computed tomography confirmed postoperative changes, left ethmoidal and sphenoidal sinusitis, involvement of the left pterygoid plates and posterior maxillary wall, indicative of residual osteomyelitis.

Laboratory studies showed normal complete blood count and serum creatinine, an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and a glycated hemoglobin of 9.2 %. Incisional biopsy of the left maxillary antrum was performed endoscopically under local anesthesia. Culture and sensitivity revealed bacterial growth and fungal elements on KOH preparation. Periodic acid‑Schiff staining showed large, non‑septate fungal hyphae branching at right angles. Histopathology demonstrated a cellular connective tissue stroma with mixed inflammatory infiltrate (predominantly neutrophils and lymphocytes), numerous large non‑septate fungal hyphae branching at right angles, areas of necrosis, ciliated columnar epithelium, bony trabeculae, and extensive hemorrhage with superimposed bacterial infection.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Chronic osteomyelitis considered due to persistent pain, pus discharge, history of maxillectomy, radiologic evidence of residual bone changes, and elevated ESR. | "Provisional diagnosis of osteomyelitis of the surgical defect was given."
2. Mucormycosis suggested by histopathology showing large non‑septate hyphae branching at right angles, a classic morphological feature of Mucorales. | "numerous large non septate fungal hyphae branching at right angle along with few areas of necrosis."
3. Aspergillosis ruled out because Aspergillus produces septate hyphae with acute‑angle dichotomous branching, which were not observed. | "large non septate fungal hyphae branched at right angles" (implies non‑septate, inconsistent with Aspergillus).
4. Tuberculosis excluded as histopathology lacked granulomatous inflammation, caseating necrosis, or acid‑fast bacilli; instead fungal hyphae predominated. | "numerous large non septate fungal hyphae..." (absence of granulomas).
5. Squamous cell carcinoma excluded because no dysplastic or malignant epithelial cells were identified in the biopsy specimen. | "cellular connective tissue stroma composed of mixed inflammatory cell infiltrate" (no mention of malignant cells).
6. Tertiary syphilis excluded; no spirochetes or characteristic vasculitis were seen, and serologic testing was not reported. | "Other lesions such as ... Tertiary syphilis ... were considered." (implies later ruled out by lack of supporting findings).
7. Bacterial osteomyelitis component supported by positive bacterial cultures from the surgical wound, but the presence of fungal hyphae indicated a concurrent fungal infection rather than isolated bacterial disease. | "Culture sensitivity tests which showed positivity for bacterial and fungal growth on KOH culture media."

case_prompt:
A 56‑year‑old previously healthy woman was found at home in a comatose state with pressure sores and dehydration, indicating prolonged immobilization. She had a 14‑pack‑year smoking history and dyslipidemia treated with simvastatin. Three days before admission she fell and sustained a mild head injury; she was asymptomatic the next day, but two days later was discovered comatose and taken to the emergency department.

On admission she had mild respiratory insufficiency (PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio 200 mmHg), bronchospasm, and a mildly depressed level of consciousness. Chest radiography was normal. Laboratory testing revealed acute kidney injury (urea 41 mmol/L, creatinine 120 µmol/L) and markedly elevated creatine phosphokinase (15 µkat/L). Complete blood count showed hemoglobin 16.6 g/L, leukocytes 11,800 /µL, D‑dimer 680 µg/L, with normal coagulation times. Brain CT was normal, and lumbar puncture yielded normal cerebrospinal fluid. Thoracic CT ruled out pulmonary thromboembolism but identified a small lingular consolidation.

Initial management included crystalloid fluid resuscitation, bronchodilators, and empiric amoxicillin/clavulanic acid for presumed aspiration pneumonia. Within 24 hours the patient developed severe mixed acute respiratory failure with profound hypoxemia (PaO₂/FiO₂ 100 mmHg) and hypercapnia (PaCO₂ 73 mmHg), accompanied by new bilateral infiltrates on chest radiograph. She required ICU admission, emergent endotracheal intubation, and invasive mechanical ventilation. Despite prone positioning, ventilatory obstruction persisted, and chest radiography showed complete bilateral infiltrates. Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) was instituted within the first 24 hours of ICU care.

Fiber‑optic bronchoscopy revealed a large quantity of necrotic material filling the distal bronchial tree, preventing advancement of the bronchoscope into subsegmental bronchi.

However, 24 hours later she developed severe mixed acute respiratory failure ..."
2. Pulmonary thromboembolism evaluated because of sudden hypoxemia and elevated D‑dimer; ruled out by thoracic CT angiography. | "Thoracic CT scan ruled out pulmonary thromboembolism but a small lingula consolidation was observed."

Bacterial pneumonia considered given new infiltrates; lack of improvement with broad‑spectrum antibiotics and the presence of necrotic airway debris made this less likely. | "Initial management included ... empiric antibiotics ... A 55‑year‑old man from Mali was admitted in July 2013 for febrile acute low back pain. His past medical history was unremarkable; he had lived in France for 30 years and returned from Mali two years earlier. He reported asthenia, anorexia, a 21 kg weight loss (BMI 17), and liquid stools once daily for several weeks. Laboratory studies showed severe anemia (Hb 6.4 g/dL), CRP 157 mg/L, leukocytes 5.470 ×10^3/µL (83 % neutrophils, 15 % lymphocytes), and a CD4 count < 200 /mm^3; HIV serology was negative.

Abdominal CT on July 12 revealed a right retroperitoneal collection and right colitis. Blood cultures later grew group F Streptococcus, prompting amoxicillin plus gentamicin. Despite antibiotics, the patient deteriorated, developing septic shock on August 2 and requiring ICU transfer. Repeat CT showed abscesses of the right kidney, psoas, and liver, thickened right colon, and intraperitoneal free fluid. A right hemicolectomy was performed; cultures from the abscesses yielded group F Streptococcus and *Escherichia coli*. New antibiotics (piperacillin‑tazobactam, fluconazole, amikacin) were added, and the patient required intubation and mechanical ventilation.

A second septic episode on August 8 revealed further abscesses (liver, retroperitoneum, right kidney, right thigh, psoas) and a sigmoid perforation with pneumoperitoneum. After imipenem + amikacin, the patient was transferred to a Paris ICU, where drainage procedures, right nephrectomy, and cholecystectomy were performed. Histology of the colon showed numerous *Entamoeba histolytica* trophozoites; renal abscesses also contained *E. histolytica*. Serology for *E. histolytica* was positive (Latex 1/32; ELISA 5 AU). The diagnosis of acute necrotizing colitis due to invasive amebiasis was made, and ornidazole plus tiliquinol were started.

Renal‑abscess histology also revealed three large cells with eosinophilic inclusion bodies suggestive of cytomegalovirus (CMV). Immunohistochemistry confirmed CMV antigen, and quantitative PCR detected CMV DNA in blood (20 900 copies/mL) and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (31 800 copies/mL). Ganciclovir therapy was initiated on August 12.

A non‑contrast cranial CT performed on admission showed a small hypodensity in the left thalamic region compatible with focal ischemia. Lumbar puncture revealed a mixed pleocytosis (700 cells/µL), elevated protein and lactate (3.5 mmol/L), and mildly reduced glucose (53 mg/dL). Gram stain of the CSF showed no organisms, and latex agglutination for the cell‑wall polysaccharides of Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, group B Streptococci, and Haemophilus influenzae was negative.

CSF cultures obtained on days 4 and 10 remained sterile, and broad‑range 16S rRNA PCR as well as targeted PCRs for Tropheryma whipplei, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, non‑tuberculous mycobacteria, HSV, and VZV were all negative. Magnetic resonance imaging on day 3 showed diffusion‑weighted hyperintensity in the left thalamus (infarction) and an enlarged sellar region consistent with a pituitary adenoma. Because the CSF pleocytosis remained and the patient’s condition worsened, antimicrobial coverage was broadened on day 5 to ampicillin, levofloxacin, and doxycycline after noting exposure to sheep and wild‑bird excreta while cleaning nesting boxes. Repeated CSF cryptococcal antigen testing was negative.  

Repeat MRI on day 8 demonstrated basilar artery vasculitis with a small brain‑stem infarction, and a CT scan on day 10 showed sphenoid sinusitis and further increase of the sellar mass, raising suspicion for a fungal infection. Consequently, voriconazole therapy (200 mg every 12 h) was initiated.

He received one dose of intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin and was started empirically on IV ceftriaxone, doxycycline, and metronidazole for community‑acquired pneumonia.

CT of the chest showed diffuse micronodularity in all lobes with perilymphatic and centrilobular distribution, scattered calcified granulomas, mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly—findings not present on prior scans and suggestive of a miliary pattern. Given this pattern, invasive fungal infection and tuberculosis were considered. Three sputum AFB cultures were smear‑negative; MTB nucleic acid amplification testing was nondetectable.

A Coccidioides complement fixation assay returned 1 : 8, Coccidioides IgM ELISA was positive, and Coccidioides IgG ELISA was negative, suggesting active coccidioidomycosis. Chest X‑ray was unremarkable, but chest CT revealed bilateral nodular infiltrates without evidence of lymphoma relapse, suggesting a pulmonary infection. Initial bacterial and fungal cultures, as well as serum assays for Aspergillus antigen, Candida albicans antigen, Mycoplasma antibodies, β‑d‑glucan, and CMV‑pp65 antigen, were negative. A 37‑year‑old man reported that, since age 15, he had experienced recurrent episodes of angioedema involving the head, trunk, and limbs, accompanied by myalgias, fever, oliguria, and rapid weight gain of 5–7 kg. During acute attacks his eosinophil count rose to 6,000 /mm³ (≈45 % of leukocytes) and eosinophil cationic protein exceeded 200 µg/L.
