case_prompt:
A 65‑year‑old woman, never‑smoker, was referred in January 2014 for a second opinion after an abnormal chest CT showed a mass in the right lower lobe. Her past history included a right‑sided mastectomy for breast cancer in 2006, with no adjuvant therapy. At that time, a 30‑mm lobulated, FDG‑negative solitary lung mass was incidentally noted and followed for five years without change.

In August 2013 she presented with a three‑month history of productive cough, dyspnea on exertion, fatigue, and weight loss. Fever and night sweats were absent. A PET‑CT demonstrated an intensely FDG‑avid right lower‑lobe mass adjacent to the old lesion, with intense hilar lymphadenopathy. Bronchoscopy, CT‑guided biopsy, and EBUS‑TBNA yielded no malignant cells and cultures were negative. Transthoracic biopsy showed fibrosis with chronic histiocytic inflammation. Video‑assisted thoracoscopic wedge resection revealed fibrosis, bronchiectasis, focal inflammation, and bronchiolisation but no malignancy or organisms. A presumptive diagnosis of cryptogenic organizing pneumonia was made, and prednisone 0.5 mg/kg/day was started for two months, with limited clinical benefit.

By January 2014 the lesion had progressed on PET‑CT, invading mediastinum, a mediastinal node (station 4R), the right pulmonary artery, and the left superior pulmonary vein. Repeat bronchoscopy and mediastinoscopy again showed no malignancy or infection; occasional hyphae suggestive of Aspergillus were seen in bronchial aspirate cytology but cultures were negative, and were considered contamination. Prednisone was escalated to 1 mg/kg/day with a macrolide for three months under suspicion of organizing pneumonia, yet the lesion continued to enlarge. A CT‑guided biopsy and further surgical sampling were deemed unsafe because of bleeding risk.

In March 2014 the patient developed progressive right‑upper‑arm weakness and sensory loss, leading to hospitalization. Brain MRI demonstrated multiple lesions in the cortex, watershed regions, left corpus callosum, left thalamus, and right semi‑oval center, initially interpreted as metastases. A neuro‑radiologist reviewed the scans and suggested ischemia versus metastasis. The lesions were not biopsied due to size and location.

In May 2014 a follow‑up brain MRI showed two lesions markedly enlarged with perilesional edema, while other lesions shrank. The diffusion‑weighted imaging showed restricted diffusion, favoring atypical cerebral abscesses over metastases. The chest PET‑CT showed further growth of the right lower‑lobe mass without distant disease. Concurrently, multiple ill‑defined skin lesions appeared on the patient’s torso and extremities.

1. Malignancy (metastatic breast cancer or primary lung cancer) was initially favored because of an FDG‑avid pulmonary mass with mediastinal invasion and new brain lesions; however, repeated bronchoscopic, CT‑guided, EBUS‑TBNA, and surgical biopsies consistently failed to demonstrate malignant cells. | "Bronchoscopic sampling... showed neither proof of malignancy nor infection... Transthoracic biopsy of the mass showed fibrosis and a chronic inflammation... Pathologic analysis... showed fibrosis... but no malignancy"  
2. Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (COP) was considered due to histologic findings of fibrosis with bronchiolisation and initial response to low‑dose steroids; the diagnosis was questioned because high‑dose steroids and macrolide therapy did not halt disease progression. | "With a diagnosis suggestive of cryptogenic organizing pneumonia, prednisone 0.5 mg/kg/day was initiated... 3. Non‑Aspergillus opportunistic infection (e.g., bacterial, other fungi) remained a possibility; however, cultures from multiple bronchoscopic and biopsy specimens were repeatedly negative, and no organisms were identified on histology until later. | "Cultures were negative (Table 1)... Cytology of the bronchial aspirate showed sporadic hyphae (most probable Aspergillus), but without growth on culture and these were considered contamination or colonization."  
4. Cerebral metastases versus ischemia versus abscess: Brain MRI initially read as metastases, later re‑interpreted as possible ischemia; the later MRI showed restricted diffusion and perilesional edema, favoring atypical cerebral abscesses, which kept infection on the differential. | "The radiologic appearance with restrictive diffusion of these lesions ... was suggestive for (atypical) cerebral abscesses rather than metastases."

A 55‑year‑old woman presented to the emergency department with severe lower flank pain radiating to the lower abdomen and chest. She also reported cough, night sweats, chills, and a 31‑lb (14 kg) unintentional weight loss over three months. Physical examination revealed bilateral axillary lymphadenopathy. Positron‑emission tomography (PET)‑CT demonstrated highly metabolically active lymphadenopathy in the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis but minimal to no PET avidity within the RUL cavitary lesion. She had a 30‑pack‑year smoking history, chronic bronchitis, sinusitis, and occasional scant hemoptysis. Serum TB‑Quantiferon was negative. Chest CT confirmed severe emphysema, multiple indeterminate pulmonary nodules, and a 1.7 × 1.1 cm subpleural thin‑walled cavitary lesion with spiculated margins in the RUL. The initial differential diagnosis included primary or metastatic carcinoma, less likely lymphoma, subacute or chronic infections (e.g., tuberculosis, fungal infection), and vasculitis. Bronchoscopy was unremarkable; bronchoalveolar lavage contained 87% macrophages, 10% neutrophils, and 2% lymphocytes, with no malignant cells. Respiratory cultures grew 1+ Aspergillus flavus. Serum antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies and rheumatoid factor were negative. A short‑interval (2‑month) follow‑up CT showed stable pulmonary nodules but persistence of the RUL cavitary lesion. case_prompt:
A 62‑year‑old woman was admitted in April 2016 with severe, persistent, deep‑throbbing headache localized to the right retro‑orbital region, unresponsive to common non‑steroidal anti‑inflammatory drugs. Neurological examination showed no focal deficits; ophthalmic fundus examination was normal with normal intra‑ocular pressure. A brain CT performed at that time revealed no parenchymal abnormalities but demonstrated obliteration of the right sphenoidal sinus, interpreted as sinusitis. After a month of oral antibiotics and corticosteroids, the headache partially improved, leaving a latent headache. In March 2017 she returned with recrudescent throbbing headache and posterior nasal drip.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and sinuses was obtained using a 1.5 T Siemens MAGNETOM Aera scanner with standard T1, T2, T2‑FLAIR, T2* GRE, diffusion‑weighted, and post‑contrast T1‑MPRAGE sequences. Brain parenchyma showed only incidental chronic hypoxic lesions. The right sphenoid sinus displayed irregular, hypertrophic mucosa with prolonged T2 hyperintensity and a central area of hypointensity, which appeared as low signal on T2* GRE images and hyperintense on T1‑weighted images. After gadolinium administration, the mucosa enhanced, while the sinus contents did not. The left sphenoid sinus showed only minimal T2‑hyperintense mucosal thickening without other abnormalities.

A repeat CT scan of the paranasal sinuses demonstrated total obliteration of the right sphenoid sinus with streak‑like calcifications (corresponding to the T2* blooming artefacts) and a sclerotic bony wall without cortical breach. The remaining sinuses had minimal mucosal thickening and tiny calcifications but no bony changes. Laboratory studies revealed no significant immune abnormalities.

Based on these radiological findings, the authors hypothesized a chronic non‑invasive fungal infection (fungal ball) of the right sphenoid sinus. The differential diagnosis considered included mucocele, inverted papilloma, sinonasal mucosal melanoma, and mature nasal osteoma.

case_prompt:
A 76‑year‑old woman presented to the department of oral pathology and microbiology with a one‑week history of difficulty eating. She reported having had pain in the upper right posterior tooth region for eight months, which led to extraction of teeth #16 and #17 because of periodontal compromise; the pain temporarily subsided after the extractions. 

Intra‑oral examination revealed a well‑defined, 2.5 cm × 1.5 cm lesion with everted, slightly indurated margins on the edentulous alveolar ridge at the sites of the missing teeth, extending into the vestibule. The patient denied nasal regurgitation but noted a nasal twang to her voice. She has a history of diabetes mellitus, treated for the past eight months. Bilateral submandibular lymph nodes were mildly enlarged and mobile. 

Radiographs showed irregular alveolar bone loss on the orthopantomogram and slight haziness of the right maxillary sinus with adjacent bone loss on the Water’s view. The patient reported renewed discomfort in the same area for seven days and supplied a fragment of tissue that had detached while eating. The specimen was decalcified, processed, and examined histopathologically. The decalcified sections demonstrated abundant bony trabeculae with empty osteocytic lacunae, loss of osteoblastic rimming, and prominent resting and reversal lines. Numerous fungal hyphae and spores of varying morphology were seen in the marrow spaces.

1. Chronic bacterial osteomyelitis considered because of longstanding tooth loss, bone loss on imaging, and necrotic bone; however, “numerous fungal hyphae and spores of varying morphology were seen in the marrow spaces,” indicating a fungal component rather than a purely bacterial process. |
2. Actinomycosis considered due to presence of “numerous actinomycotic colonies… in close association with peripheral bony trabeculae,” but the coexistence of abundant fungal elements suggests an additional infection beyond actinomycosis alone. |
3. Mucormycosis considered given the patient’s diabetes and sinus haziness; the authors later distinguished this organism by “broad, aseptate and ribbon‑shaped hyphae… representing Mucorales species,” separating it from the septate hyphae. |
4. Aspergillosis considered because septate, acute‑angle‑branching hyphae are characteristic; the authors identified this component by describing “thin and septate… branching at acute angles representing Aspergillus species” and confirmed species as Aspergillus niger and Aspergillus flavus. |
5. Neoplastic processes (e.g., maxillary carcinoma) were less likely; the lesion was primarily ulcerative with fungal infiltration and lacked atypical epithelial cells or invasive carcinoma features on histology. |
6. The combination of chronic osteomyelitis with mixed fungal infection best fits the authors’ final synthesis: “chronic osteomyelitis associated with a combination of mucormycosis, aspergillosis and actinomycosis.”

Computed tomography demonstrated diffuse osteolytic changes of the femoral necks and thoracic vertebrae.

A lymphogram failed to localize the leakage site. Sirolimus was started at 0.88 mg/m²/day; after one month the dose was increased to 1.3 mg/m²/day. Sirolimus trough levels ranged from 3.4 to 8.9 ng/mL, which is not considered elevated. After a further pause of sirolimus, pleural fluid volume remained unchanged, yet no additional DIC episodes occurred. Initiation of the herbal formula Eppikajyutsuto (0.2 g/kg/day) led to a marked reduction in pleural fluid, allowing removal of the thoracostomy tube 40 days after oral therapy began. No re‑accumulation of fluid was observed over the subsequent 18 months.

A 46‑year‑old woman with a history of tobacco dependence presented to the emergency department with low‑grade fever and sudden, severe right upper‑quadrant abdominal pain accompanied by nausea and vomiting. Emergent computed tomography of the chest and abdomen revealed an intraluminal polypoid filling defect arising from the isthmus of the aorta that projected into the proximal descending aorta, as well as infarctions of the spleen and right kidney. Because of the fever, broad‑spectrum antibiotics were initiated. Heparin was started but later discontinued to avoid hemorrhagic transformation of the infarcts. 

A transthoracic echocardiogram showed no valvular or cardiac source of embolus, and an agitated saline bubble study demonstrated no intracardiac shunting. Transesophageal echocardiography identified a large echogenic mobile mass attached to the wall of the descending thoracic aorta. Bilateral lower‑extremity arterial Doppler studies demonstrated severe popliteal‑tibial arterial disease in the left leg. 

Extensive infectious testing—including bacterial cultures, fungal studies, HIV, Bartonella henselae, Coxiella burnetii, Leptospira, syphilis, Aspergillus galactomannan, and Histoplasma antigen—were all negative. Hypercoagulability screening (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibodies, homocysteine, paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, protein C and S activity, antithrombin, factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene) was unrevealing. Autoimmune serologies (ANA, ANCA, dsDNA, RF, CCP, Sjögren antibodies, MPO, PR3, complement levels, Smith, RNP) were also negative. 

Given the absence of an acute limb‑threatening ischemia, the largely negative work‑up, and the lack of a straightforward method for removing the aortic lesion, the team opted for medical management. The patient was transitioned from inpatient heparin to oral apixaban 5 mg twice daily and aspirin 81 mg daily, with plans for close outpatient follow‑up.

Infectious etiology (septic emboli, mycotic aneurysm) considered due to fever, yet “infectious work‑up was negative and included testing for bacterial infection, fungal infection, HIV, Bartonella henselae antibody, Coxiella burnetii antibodies, Leptospira antibodies, syphilis, aspergillus galactomannan antigen, and histoplasma antigen.”

case_prompt:
A 93‑year‑old Caucasian woman was referred for cervical adenopathies of 3‑month duration. Four years earlier she had been treated surgically for cutaneous sarcomatoid carcinoma of the face. She denied fever, asthenia, weight loss, night sweats, respiratory symptoms, prior tuberculosis, and recent animal contact. Physical examination revealed an enlarged, mobile, painful right cervical lymph node; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable.

Cervico‑thoraco‑abdominal‑pelvic computed tomography demonstrated a right cervical mass with multiple adenopathies and fibrotic lesions in the upper right lobe; no other adenopathies or neoplastic disease were identified. Fine‑needle aspiration of the cervical node yielded a noncaseous granulomatous process; there were no Reed‑Sternberg or neoplastic cells, Ziehl‑Neelsen staining was negative, and PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis was negative. The patient was placed under close surveillance. An IgG lambda monoclonal gammopathy was identified; renal function, calcium metabolism, anemia, urinary free light chains, and β2‑microglobulin were normal. Peripheral‑blood immunophenotyping showed a polyclonal B‑cell population. Serologies for syphilis, HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C were negative, while QuantiFERON testing was positive.

Two months later the adenopathies enlarged and a cutaneous fistula with suppurative lymphadenitis developed. Swab culture grew Staphylococcus aureus; treatment with cefuroxime produced only slight improvement. Excisional biopsy revealed granulomas with caseous necrosis and suppuration. PCR assessment of the samples was negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Nocardia, Mycobacterium avium complex, Toxoplasma gondii, Aspergillus fumigatus, Bartonella spp., Treponema pallidum and Leishmania infantum.

1. Granulomatous lymphadenitis progressing to caseous necrosis strongly suggests tuberculosis | “Excisional biopsy … revealed granulomas with caseous necrosis and suppuration.”  
2. Positive interferon‑γ release assay (QuantiFERON) indicates latent or active Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection | “QuantiFERON testing was positive.”  
3. Broad PCR panel excluded other bacterial, mycobacterial, fungal, protozoal, and parasitic pathogens | “PCR assessment of the samples was negative for MT, Nocardia, Mycobacterium avium complex, Toxoplasma gondii, Aspergillus fumigatus, Bartonella spp., Treponema pallidum and Leishmania infantum.”  
4. Lack of neoplastic cells on cytology and absence of additional adenopathies on imaging argue against malignancy or lymphoma | “There was no evidence of Reed‑Sternberg cells or neoplastic cells; … no other adenopathies nor evidence of neoplastic disease.”  
5. Staphylococcus aureus infection alone is insufficient, as antibiotic therapy yielded only minimal improvement | “Microbiologic examination … positive for Staphylococcus aureus … displaying only slight improvement.”  
6. Serologic testing ruled out syphilis, HIV, and viral hepatitis as causes of granulomatous disease | “Serology tests for syphilis, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), hepatitis B virus and hepatitis C virus were negative.”  
7. Negative Ziehl‑Neelsen stain and initial PCR for MTB do not exclude TB, given known limited sensitivity of these tests in paucibacillary lymphadenitis | “Ziehl‑Neelsen staining was negative, as well as polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assessment for Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MT) and culture.”

Positive QuantiFERON together with caseous granulomas and exclusion of other etiologies consolidates the tuberculous diagnosis despite initial negative PCR. | “Considering the presence of persistent cervical lymphadenopathy with caseous granulomas, a positive QuantiFERON test, and the exclusion of other potential causes, the hypothesis of cervical tuberculous lymphadenitis was strongly suspected.”

case_prompt:
A 75‑year‑old Japanese man with hypertension and a prior ischemic stroke presented after accidentally falling into a creek, his face submerged in water. At the outside hospital he was hypothermic (33.4 °C) with a Glasgow Coma Scale of E3V3M6, bilateral coarse crackles, and required non‑invasive ventilation that progressed to intubation for worsening oxygenation (saturation 80 % on 100 % FiO₂). He was transferred to our tertiary center the same day.

On arrival he was sedated, temperature 36.4 °C, heart rate 104 bpm, blood pressure 123/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 /min, and oxygen saturation 91 % on 10 L/min supplemental oxygen. Physical exam was notable only for diminished breath sounds bilaterally. Arterial blood gas on 100 % oxygen showed pH 7.34, PaCO₂ 42 mmHg, PaO₂ 199 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 21.9 mmol/L.

Laboratory studies on day 1 revealed leukopenia (WBC 2,980/µL) with neutrophil predominance, hemoglobin 15.3 g/dL, platelets 159 × 10³/µL, CRP 0.6 mg/dL, and markedly elevated procalcitonin (59.37 ng/mL). Chest radiography and computed tomography demonstrated diffuse bilateral infiltrates without pleural effusion.

He was diagnosed with acute respiratory distress syndrome secondary to aspiration pneumonitis from drowning and septic shock, and treated with isotonic crystalloids, meropenem, vasopressors, and lung‑protective ventilation. Methylprednisolone 80 mg daily was started on day 3. On day 4 a β‑D‑glucan assay was elevated at 37.6 pg/mL (normal < 11.0 pg/mL). Vasopressors were weaned off by day 5, but hypoxia persisted. On day 6 tracheal aspirate culture grew *Aeromonas hydrophila*; blood cultures remained negative, and antibiotics were switched to piperacillin/tazobactam based on susceptibility. Despite these measures, his oxygenation worsened and he died on day 7.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Aspiration pneumonitis causing ARDS was initially assumed because the patient drowned and had diffuse infiltrates; the authors state, “The diagnosis was acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) caused by aspiration pneumonitis as a result of non‑fatal drowning and septic shock.”  
2. Bacterial pneumonia due to *Aeromonas hydrophila* was considered after the tracheal aspirate grew this organism; “On day 6, the tracheal aspirate culture was found positive for *Aeromonas hydrophila*… the patient was switched to piperacillin/tazobactam.”  
3. Septic shock was diagnosed based on hypotension requiring vasopressors and a highly elevated procalcitonin (59.37 ng/mL); “He was treated with… vasopressors…” indicating septic physiology.  
4. Pulmonary embolism was entertained after autopsy imaging, but not before death; the report later notes, “An embolus was detected in the right pulmonary artery,” suggesting a possible contributing factor, yet no clinical imaging had identified embolism prior to autopsy.  
5. Invasive fungal infection (aspergillosis) was ultimately identified by histopathology; the authors report, “Microscopic analysis with Grocott staining revealed diffuse filamentous fungi… the fungi were identified as *Aspergillus fumigatus*,” confirming invasive aspergillosis as the underlying cause of persistent hypoxia.

case_prompt:
In 2019 an 88‑year‑old autonomous woman with a past medical history of hyperparathyroidism, dyslipidemia, and non‑relevant cardiopathy presented to the emergency department after a day of vomiting and diarrhea following fish consumption. She reported months of diffuse abdominal pain for which she had self‑medicated with paracetamol and metamizole. 

On initial examination she was in good general condition but had an erythematous, painful left arm. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (7.3 G/L) with left shift and a C‑reactive protein (CRP) of 175 mg/L. Intravenous ceftriaxone was started and she was followed as an outpatient.

At the second consultation she demonstrated a deteriorated general state with disorientation, slowing, and a tendency toward hypotension. The left arm had worsened with swelling and livid skin discoloration, compatible with erysipelas. Her abdomen was distended, painful, and hypo‑peristaltic. Repeat labs revealed acute renal failure (creatinine 279 µmol/L), a CRP of 436.4 mg/L, rhabdomyolysis (CK 12 982 U/L) and metabolic acidosis (pH 7.26, HCO₃⁻ 12.3 mmol/L, lactate 2.8 mmol/L). An urgent CT scan showed nonspecific diffuse intestinal dilatation without perforation or free fluid; the lungs displayed only dorsal right dystelectasis and no infiltrates. 

Because of rapid clinical decline, blood cultures were drawn, broad‑spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin‑tazobactam, clindamycin) were initiated, and the patient was transferred to the intensive‑care unit with a diagnosis of sepsis secondary to erysipelas of the left arm, suspected fasciitis. In the ICU she became increasingly agitated, requiring dexmedetomidine, fluid resuscitation, noradrenaline, and supplemental oxygen (3 L/min via nasal cannula). Progressive abdominal distension and an unclear infectious focus prompted an exploratory laparotomy, during which multiple adhesions with low‑vascular‑perfusion signs were noted, but no perforation. An accidental colonic injury led to a split colostomy.

Post‑operatively the patient remained mechanically ventilated with hemodynamic instability. Over the next days lactate and inflammatory markers improved. One week after surgery the stoma was covered with a large amount of filamentous material described as compatible with fungal colonization; surface cultures were obtained and a local amphotericin B treatment was started. The following day the patient’s condition rapidly worsened with rising inflammatory parameters and renewed renal dysfunction, necessitating increased vasoactive support. Given an advance directive limiting aggressive measures, a joint decision with the family was made to initiate comfort‑focused therapy. The patient died a few hours later after a week in the ICU.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Erysipelas of the left arm with possible necrotizing fasciitis was considered the primary source of sepsis because of the erythematous, painful, swollen arm with livid discoloration and high inflammatory markers. | "sepsis due to erysipelas of the left arm with suspected fasciitis."
2. Intra‑abdominal bacterial sepsis or ischemia was entertained after the patient developed abdominal distension, renal failure, and CT showed diffuse intestinal dilatation. | "CT showed unspecific diffuse intestinal dilatation without signs of perforation or free fluid."
3. General septic shock of unknown focus remained a working diagnosis when the patient’s condition deteriorated despite broad‑spectrum antibiotics and negative blood cultures. | "rapid clinical deterioration, no clear focus of infection."
4. Fungal infection was suspected only after filamentous structures were observed on the colostomy stoma, prompting local antifungal therapy. | "stoma was covered with a large quantity of filamentous structures compatible with fungal colonization."
5. Bacterial causes were ultimately excluded by repeatedly negative cultures from blood, arm tissue, and intra‑operative samples, as well as by the absence of pulmonary infiltrates that would suggest typical bacterial pneumonia. | "blood cultures, ... negative results in the cultures the following days."
6. The definitive diagnosis of invasive aspergillosis was confirmed by histopathology and molecular testing demonstrating Aspergillus fumigatus in gastric, intestinal, and pulmonary tissues, distinguishing it from colonization or other fungal pathogens. | "presence of Aspergillus fumigatus was confirmed" (post‑mortem).

case_prompt:
A 45‑year‑old male farmer presented with blurred vision in his left eye that began 2 months earlier after mud was flung onto the eye during farming. He washed the eye with tap water and continued working. Two weeks later he developed redness, blurred vision, mild pain and a small white opacity. A private physician diagnosed an eye infection and prescribed topical terramycin ointment, but redness and the opacity persisted. A second physician prescribed tobramycin‑dexamethasone drops, again without improvement. Over time he lost useful vision in the left eye and sought further evaluation.

On examination, left‑eye visual acuity was hand movement with poor light projection; color perception was intact and a relative afferent pupillary defect was absent. Slit‑lamp examination revealed a very thick yellow plaque forming a rounded mass covering the entire corneal surface, measuring approximately 9 × 9.5 mm with a maximal depth of 2 mm centrally. No prolapse of intra‑ocular contents was seen, but associated scleritis was present. Ocular ultrasound showed only a few vitreous cellularities. The right eye was normal with 20/20 vision.

The plaque did not stain with fluorescein, lissamine green, or rose bengal dyes. Careful scraping yielded a semi‑solid, friable material without bleeding. Giemsa stain of the corneal scraping showed numerous hyphal elements.

1. Bacterial keratitis considered because of initial red eye and opacity; excluded due to lack of clinical improvement despite two courses of topical antibiotics (terramycin, then tobramycin‑dexamethasone) | "He was started on topical terramycin ointment... no improvement" and "prescribed him a regimen consisting of tobramycin-dexamethasone drops, again with no improvement".  
2. Non‑infectious inflammatory corneal disease considered given the large plaque and scleritis; excluded because the plaque failed to stain with epithelial dyes and microscopic examination demonstrated fungal elements | "The plaque did not stain with fluorescein, lissamine green, and rose bengal dyes" and "Giemsa stain of the corneal scraping showed numerous hyphal elements".  
3. Other filamentous fungi (e.g., Fusarium) were possible etiologies of fungal keratitis; narrowed to Aspergillus after culture grew Aspergillus sp., but the presence of septate hyphae on Giemsa already favored Aspergillus as a common cause in traumatic agricultural inoculation | "Culture of the plaque later revealed to be positive for Aspergillus sp." (used later to confirm).  
4. Viral keratitis (e.g., HSV) considered less likely because viral ulcers typically stain with fluorescein and lack hyphal elements; the negative dye staining and presence of hyphae argued against it | "The plaque did not stain with fluorescein..." combined with "numerous hyphal elements".

case_prompt:
A 55‑year‑old Chinese man presented in 2016 with a 2‑month history of cough and expectoration, increasing shortness of breath, headache and hoarseness for 1 week. He was a farmer from Zhejiang province and had previously worked in Guangzhou. Two months before admission he took unknown medications for his headache and noted a forehead scalp mass one month before admission. He denied high‑risk sexual behavior and blood transfusions and had no other past medical history.

Physical examination revealed a 3‑cm ill‑defined tough mass in the right forehead and he was febrile at 38.5 °C. Lung examination showed decreased breath sounds in the lower left lung; the rest of the exam was unremarkable. Oxygen saturation was 97 % on room air.

Laboratory studies: hemoglobin 122 g/dL, leukocyte count 27,900/mm³ with 87.3 % neutrophils and 6.7 % lymphocytes, platelet count 243,000/mm³, ESR 78 mm/h, CRP 184.9 mg/L, albumin 28 g/L, procalcitonin 0.611 ng/mL. HIV antibody, hepatitis B and syphilis serologies were negative. NK cells 63.1 % (11,800/mm³), CD4⁺ 23.6 % (2,785/mm³), CD8⁺ 35 % (4,130/mm³), CD4⁺/CD8⁺ ratio 0.67. Aspergillus serology (including galactomannan and 1‑3‑β‑D‑glucan) was negative. Acid‑fast bacillus smear of sputum and purified protein derivative test were negative.

Chest contrast‑enhanced CT showed a high‑density lesion in the left lower lobe with marked enhancement and necrotic mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Cranial CT and MRI demonstrated osteolytic destruction of the right frontal bone with adjacent soft‑tissue infiltrate. No vertebral lesions were seen.

Endobronchial ultrasound‑guided transbronchial needle aspiration and CT‑guided percutaneous needle aspiration of lung and lymph node yielded only acute and chronic inflammation; no tumor cells were identified. Cultures of blood, sputum, mediastinal lymph node aspirate, and lung tissue were all negative for pathogenic bacteria.

He was started on meropenem, but persisted with fevers up to 40 °C, rising leukocyte count and CRP, and decreasing hemoglobin and albumin. New subcutaneous masses appeared in the right neck and left chest wall. On hospital day 16, pus was aspirated from the fluctuating frontal mass; gram smear, fungal stain, and acid‑fast stain were all negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial infection initially suspected due to fever, neutrophilia, and pulmonary infiltrate, but repeated cultures from blood, sputum, mediastinal lymph node, and lung tissue were all negative. | "the culture of blood, sputum, mediastinal lymph node puncture and lung puncture were all free of pathogenic bacteria."
2. Tuberculosis considered because of necrotic mediastinal nodes and lung lesion; excluded by negative acid‑fast bacillus smear and negative PPD test. | "Acid-fast bacillus test of sputum smear was negative. Purified protein derivative (PPD) test was negative."
3. Invasive aspergillosis entertained given the immunocompromised appearance; ruled out by negative aspergillus serology, galactomannan and 1‑3‑β‑D‑glucan assays. | "Pastorex aspergillus testing with patient's serum, including galactomannan testing and fungi 1-3-beta-D glucan testing, was negative."
4. Malignancy (primary lung cancer or metastatic disease) considered because of mass lesions and lymphadenopathy; needle biopsies showed only inflammation and no tumor cells. | "the endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration and the CT-guided percutaneous needle aspiration all showed acute and chronic inflammation pathological change, but no tumor cell was found."
5. Other deep fungal infections (e.g., cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis) were in the differential but lacked supporting laboratory evidence; fungal antigen testing was negative. | "Pastorex aspergillus testing ... and fungi 1-3-beta-D glucan testing, was negative."
6. The definitive diagnosis was established when T. marneffei grew from pus, bone‑marrow, blood, and sputum cultures after several days of incubation. | "T. marneffei was isolated from pus after 4 days of pus culture. On the same day, T. marneffei was isolated from bone marrow culture, blood culture and sputum culture."

case_prompt:
A 53‑year‑old man with no significant past medical history presented with intermittent fevers up to 40 °C, weight loss, and right inguinal lymphadenopathy that began in December 2017. In February 2018, CT scanning revealed multiple subphrenic lymphadenopathies. Blood cultures grew methicillin‑resistant Staphylococcus aureus, and gastrointestinal endoscopy showed widespread esophageal candidiasis. In March, he developed a herpes zoster infection. An excisional biopsy of the right inguinal node was performed.

On admission, laboratory studies were notable for: WBC 14,400/µL (bands 3 %, segs 81 %, monocytes 8.5 %, lymphocytes 7.5 %), hemoglobin 9.0 g/dL, platelets 1.83 × 10⁵/µL, CD4⁺ T‑cell count 678 cells/µL (50.3 % of T cells), AST 16 U/L, ALT 15 U/L, BUN 5.3 mg/dL, creatinine 0.60 mg/dL, CRP 26.52 mg/dL, IgG 1764 mg/dL, soluble IL‑2R 16,523 U/mL. HIV, HTLV‑1, MAC antibody, candida antigen, aspergillus antigen, and interferon‑γ release assay were negative. PCR for T‑cell receptor clonality in peripheral blood was negative, and the lymphocyte blastoid transformation test by PHA was 29,300 cpm (normal 20,500–56,800), indicating no apparent T‑cell dysfunction.

PET‑CT demonstrated multiple enlarged subphrenic lymph nodes and a right inguinal node with SUVmax 11.1. Histopathologic examination of the inguinal node showed destruction of normal architecture with a mixture of abnormal large lymphoma cells and epithelioid cell granulomas. Hodgkin cells, Reed‑Stenberg cells, and Lacunar cells were identified. Immunohistochemistry revealed the malignant cells to be CD30‑positive and PD‑L1‑positive, partially CD15‑positive, and negative for CD3, CD4, CD8, and CD20. In situ hybridization for EBV‑encoded RNA (EBER‑ISH) was positive, and LMP‑1 and EBNA‑2 were partially positive, indicating EBV infection with latency type III. Ziehl‑Neelsen staining of the biopsy specimen demonstrated acid‑fast bacilli within granulomas. PCR tests for Mycobacterium tuberculosis and MAC on the node tissue were negative, as were bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial cultures.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Classic Hodgkin lymphoma was considered because Reed‑Sternberg and Lacunar cells were present, but the EBV latency pattern (type III) and CD20 negativity were atypical for EBV‑associated HL, which usually shows latency type II. | "EBV‑associated HL typically shows EBV infection with latency type II."
2. Other EBV‑driven lymphoproliferative disorders (e.g., EBV‑positive diffuse large B‑cell lymphoma) were evaluated; however, the lack of CD20 expression and the presence of Hodgkin‑like morphology favored an EBV‑positive LPD with Hodgkin‑like features. | "These malignant cells were ... negative for CD20 in immunohistochemistry."
3. Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection was a differential for granulomatous lymphadenitis, but PCR for M. tuberculosis and MAC were negative, and cultures failed to grow organisms. | "PCR tests of the right inguinal lymph node were negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis and MAC, and culture tests of bacteria, fungi, and mycobacterium species were also negative."
4. Non‑tuberculous mycobacterial infection remained possible because Ziehl‑Neelsen staining showed acid‑fast bacilli within granulomas, indicating mycobacterial presence despite negative cultures. | "Ziehl‑Neelsen staining of the biopsy specimen showed acid‑fast bacilli in granulomas."
5. HIV‑associated lymphadenopathy and opportunistic infections were ruled out by negative HIV serology and a normal CD4⁺ count. | "HIV antibody ... were negative. CD4‑positive T cell count of 678 µL."
6. HTLV‑1 infection and other opportunistic pathogens (MAC, Candida, Aspergillus) were excluded by negative serologies and antigen tests. | "HTLV‑1 antibody, mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) antibody, candida antigen, aspergillus antigen ... were negative."
7. T‑cell lymphoma was considered but dismissed due to absent T‑cell receptor clonality on PCR and a normal PHA lymphocyte transformation test, indicating no T‑cell dysfunction. | "PCR assays for the detection of clonally rearranged T cell receptors in the peripheral blood showed no clonality... lymphocyte blastoid transformation test ... suggested no apparent T cell dysfunction."
final_diagnosis: EBV-positive LPD with Hodgkin lymphoma-like features -> OUT_OF_SCOPE

case_prompt:
A 41‑year‑old morbidly obese woman with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (B‑cell type, Rai stage 0, 13q deletion, IGHV‑mutated) on active surveillance presented to urgent care after four days of nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and a low‑grade fever of 100.8 °F (38.2 °C). She received intravenous fluids and anti‑emetics and was discharged with a presumptive diagnosis of acute gastroenteritis. Over the next week her gastrointestinal symptoms improved but did not fully resolve.

Ten days after symptom onset she returned to the emergency department with two days of dry cough, dyspnea, myalgias, and persistent fevers of 102 °F (38.9 °C). In the ED she was hypoxic (SpO₂ 85% on 6 L/min nasal cannula) and was placed on a non‑rebreather mask, then electively intubated and started on lung‑protective mechanical ventilation. Empiric antimicrobial therapy with cefepime, linezolid, and doxycycline was initiated. A posteroanterior chest radiograph showed bilateral diffuse lung opacities.

Laboratory studies revealed a white blood cell count of 11,700/µL with 61 % neutrophils and 35 % lymphocytes (relative lymphocytopenia in the setting of CLL), troponin <6 ng/L, and total IgG 839 mg/dL. A nasopharyngeal swab was negative for common respiratory viruses and for SARS‑CoV‑2 by rRT‑PCR. A chest CT on hospital day 2 demonstrated bilobar, multi‑segmental ground‑glass opacities distributed centrally and peripherally. A second nasopharyngeal SARS‑CoV‑2 PCR obtained later was also negative. Blood cultures, serum Aspergillus antigen, β‑(1,3)‑D‑glucan, and urine Legionella antigen were all negative.

1. Bacterial pneumonia considered because of acute hypoxemic respiratory failure and bilateral infiltrates; excluded by negative blood cultures and lack of clinical improvement despite broad‑spectrum antibiotics. | "Blood cultures, serum Aspergillus antigen, β‑(1,3)‑D‑glucan, and urine legionella antigen were all negative."
2. Atypical pneumonia (Legionella) considered; excluded by negative urine Legionella antigen. | "urine legionella antigen were all negative."
3. Other viral respiratory infections (influenza, RSV, etc.) considered; excluded by negative nasopharyngeal panel for common respiratory viruses. | "A nasopharyngeal (NP) swab specimen was negative for common respiratory viruses."
4. SARS‑CoV‑2 infection initially considered despite negative NP swabs because of typical imaging and epidemiology; finally confirmed by BAL PCR. | "Despite negative testing, COVID‑19 pneumonia was highly suspected... The BAL rRT‑PCR for SARS‑CoV‑2 was positive on HD 4."
5. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) considered given immunocompromised state; excluded by negative BAL PCR for pneumocystis. | "The BAL specimen was negative for … pneumocystis jirovecii PCR."
6. Invasive aspergillosis considered; excluded by negative serum Aspergillus antigen and negative BAL Aspergillus antigen. | "The BAL specimen was negative for aspergillus antigen... Blood cultures, serum Aspergillus antigen… were all negative."
7. Cytomegalovirus pneumonia considered; excluded by negative BAL CMV PCR. | "The BAL specimen was negative for … cytomegalovirus PCR."
8. COVID‑19 remained the most plausible diagnosis because of bilateral ground‑glass opacities, hypoxemia, and eventual positive BAL SARS‑CoV‑2 PCR despite prior negative NP tests. | "A second NP swab specimen for SARS‑CoV‑2 was performed and reported negative... The BAL rRT‑PCR for SARS‑CoV‑2 was positive on HD 4."

case_prompt: A 45‑year‑old Chinese woman presented in May 2019 with a 2‑week history of cough and sputum production. Physical examination was unremarkable. Initial laboratory studies—including complete blood count, serum biochemistry, and tumor markers—were within normal limits. Bacterial pneumonia was considered initially because of cough and sputum, prompting moxifloxacin therapy; however, the lesion showed only minimal improvement on repeat CT, suggesting an atypical or non‑bacterial process. | "The enhanced CT was performed after 2 weeks' treatment with oral moxifloxacin on June 7, which revealed a little progress of the lesion."

case_prompt:
A 79‑year‑old man with hypertension and chronic lymphocytic leukemia presented with dysphasia after his first cycle of chlorambucil and obinutuzumab. He had been diagnosed with CLL a year earlier and started therapy for fatigue and progressive anemia (hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL). Baseline counts were: ANC 2.7 × 10⁹/L, ALC 16.3 × 10⁹/L, AMC 0.3 × 10⁹/L; IgG 805 mg/dL. He had no prior infections, corticosteroid use, or other immunosuppressants. He previously worked in construction and was active in gardening.

On exam, only a slurred speech was noted; the remainder was unremarkable. Brain MRI demonstrated three distinct left temporal and parietal lobe abscesses with significant edema. He was started on high‑dose dexamethasone 4 mg four times daily. Chest CT showed a pulmonary nodule.

Initial laboratory studies were negative: blood cultures, serum cryptococcal antigen, Aspergillus antigen (galactomannan, Platelia assay), and β‑D‑glucan. Stereotactic brain biopsy of an abscess was nondiagnostic because the necrotic core was not sampled. Plasma cell‑free DNA next‑generation sequencing revealed a strong signal for Nocardia abscessus. He was discharged on dexamethasone 4 mg twice daily, ceftriaxone, minocycline, and linezolid (later stopped due to thrombocytopenia).
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Nocardiosis identified by molecular testing; the cfDNA NGS result provided definitive evidence of Nocardia infection. | "Plasma cell‑free DNA next‑generation sequencing (cfDNA NGS) showed a strong signal for Nocardia abscessus."
2. Common bacterial pathogens were deemed unlikely because peripheral blood cultures were sterile. | "Blood cultures ... were negative."
3. Fungal etiologies such as Aspergillus and Cryptococcus were considered but largely ruled out by negative serum biomarkers. | "Serum cryptococcal Ag, Aspergillus Ag (galactomannan, using the Platelia Aspergillus enzyme immunoassay (EIA)), and beta‑D‑glucan (betaDg) were negative."
4. The stereotactic brain biopsy failed to provide a diagnostic tissue sample, limiting histopathologic confirmation of any organism. | "Stereotactic brain biopsy of one of the abscesses failed to include its necrotic core and was nondiagnostic."
5. The pulmonary nodule raised the possibility of a metastatic or infectious lesion, but lack of microbiologic data kept it from being the primary diagnosis at this stage. | "Chest CT revealed a pulmonary nodule."

case_prompt:
A 60‑year‑old woman from Moradabad, India, presented to the otorhinolaryngology department with a 7‑day history of insidious swelling that had gradually progressed, causing nasal blockage. She also reported loss of vision in the left eye for the past 7–10 days. There was no purulent nasal discharge, epistaxis, prior photophobia, diplopia, squint, facial weakness, or facial expression changes. Past medical history was notable for diabetes mellitus (5 years) and hypertension (10 years), with intermittent treatment.

The patient was admitted to the intensive care unit for septic shock. Antimicrobial therapy was changed to cefepime and azithromycin, and therapeutic anticoagulation was initiated. On hospital day 2 the left antecubital fossa became erythematous and painful with purulent fluid expression; preliminary cultures grew gram‑positive organisms, prompting addition of nafcillin and continuation of vancomycin.

Vascular ultrasound (September 1) demonstrated right‑lower‑limb intermuscular venous thrombosis, enlarged inguinal lymph nodes and subcutaneous edema. case_prompt:
An 86‑year‑old woman with well‑controlled type 2 diabetes and glaucoma presented with a 2‑week history of right ear pain, right frontal headache, and right facial pain lateral to the nose. She reported painful right extraocular movements, decreased vision, and thick purulent nasal discharge. Vital signs were normal (BP 132/70, HR 78, RR 14, SpO₂ 97 % on room air, T 36.7 °C). Examination showed hand‑motion vision in the right eye, severely restricted right eye movements, ptosis, and excyclotorsion. 

CT of the head and orbits demonstrated soft‑tissue thickening and loss of fat planes around the right optic canal and orbital apex, with extension of paranasal inflammatory disease into a bone defect of the right lateral sphenoid sinus wall, right anterior ethmoidal mucosal disease, and complete opacification of the right maxillary antrum. MRI of the brain (with and without IV contrast) revealed right‑sided paranasal sinus infection extending transsphenoidally into the right orbital apex and cavernous sinus, consistent with orbital apex syndrome. 

ENT performed a right nasal endoscopy, finding purulent material obstructing the right middle meatus and the sphenoid ostium. Nasal swab was sent for bacterial culture. Infectious disease initiated IV vancomycin, cefepime, metronidazole, and dexamethasone. 

On hospital day 3 the patient underwent extensive endoscopic sinus debridement, including total right ethmoidectomy, frontal sinusotomy, sphenoidotomy, tissue biopsy, and orbital apex washout. Cultures from the right naris and right ethmoid sinus grew methicillin‑susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA). Frozen‑section pathology showed mixed acute and chronic inflammation at all sites. Antibiotics were narrowed to IV cefazolin on hospital day 5.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial sinusitis/ orbital cellulitis due to MSSA was considered because nasal cultures grew methicillin‑susceptible Staphylococcus aureus. | "Tissue from the right naris and right ethmoid sinus grew methicillin‑susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA)."
2. Invasive fungal infection (Aspergillus) was ultimately identified when a fungal culture from orbital apex tissue yielded Aspergillus fumigatus and pathology showed tissue‑invasive hyphae, confirming the diagnosis. | "On hospital day 6, one colony of Aspergillus fumigatus grew from a culture of the right orbital apex tissue. The pathology revealed fungal hyphae consistent with Aspergillus spp. and related molds, with tissue invasion in the orbital apex."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case identifies Aspergillus niger cultured from ear pus, which falls under the SELECTED disease “aspergillosis”. No other SELECTED disease is present.
2. Best Breakpoint: End the prompt after the plan for a 6‑week ciprofloxacin ear‑drop course and the scheduled 6‑week follow‑up, but before any mention of the culture result, the resolved discharge, or the later grommet insertion. This supplies the chronic refractory otitis externa picture, the lack of response to antibiotics, and the swab being sent, allowing deduction of a fungal etiology without revealing the organism.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors demonstrate that conventional bacterial cultures were performed, yet only when a fungus was suspected were specific media (Sabouraud Dextrose with amikacin) used; the growth of a characteristic black‑spored fungus on these media confirmed Aspergillus infection, thereby ruling out bacterial causes and supporting a diagnosis of otomycosis (aspergillosis).
case_prompt: A 5‑year‑old girl was referred to the ENT clinic at a tertiary hospital with a 5‑month history of right‑ear otalgia and foul‑smelling otorrhea. The symptoms had not resolved despite two courses of oral co‑amoxiclav prescribed by a private general practitioner and a local clinic, as well as a 6‑week course of ciprofloxacin ear drops (three drops every 8 hours). The child was otherwise healthy; HIV screening was negative. On examination she was afebrile and systemically well. Nasal passages were clear. Otoscopy showed blood and pus in the right external auditory canal; a pus swab was taken in the outpatient department. The child did not tolerate aural toilet in clinic and was booked for examination under anaesthesia. In theatre an intact tympanic membrane was seen on the right, with prominent pus, debris, and a cotton‑wool‑like foreign body in the external auditory canal. The left ear displayed only wax. Both ears were cleaned, but no specimens were sent from theatre. The patient was discharged on ciprofloxacin ear drops for an additional 2 weeks (total of 8 weeks of fluoroquinolone therapy) and a follow‑up appointment was scheduled in 6 weeks.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial otitis externa considered because of otalgia, foul discharge, and initial empiric use of co‑amoxiclav and ciprofloxacin ear drops; ruled out by persistent symptoms despite appropriate antibacterial therapy. | "Symptoms had not resolved, despite two courses of oral co‑amoxiclav ... and a 6‑week course of ciprofloxacin ear drops."
2. Chronic suppurative otitis media considered given the chronic discharge, but excluded by intact tympanic membrane on examination under anaesthesia. | "Findings in theatre included an intact tympanic membrane on the right ..."
3. Mycotic otitis externa (otomycosis) considered due to refractory course, cotton‑wool‑like material in the canal, and lack of bacterial response; confirmed when culture on Sabouraud Dextrose media grew a characteristic black‑spored fungus identified as Aspergillus niger. | "In this case Aspergillus niger was grown at 25 °C and 35 °C on SabDex media with amikacin... The reverse of the fungus on the culture media plate had a cream colour."
4. Other systemic fungal infections (e.g., histoplasmosis, cryptococcosis) not supported by the localized ear findings and lack of systemic signs; therefore excluded. | "The patient was apyrexial and systemically well."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: Identification: The case centers on organizing pneumonia (OP), which is not in the 21 SELECTED diseases list. Although the patient had a prior episode of pneumocystis pneumonia (pneumocystis, which is on the list), the current diagnostic challenge is OP. Therefore, the target diagnosis is an OUT_OF_SCOPE disease.
2. Ideal Breakpoint: Include presentation, vital signs, physical examination, initial laboratory and imaging findings, negative infectious workup, lack of response to broad‑spectrum antibiotics, and the rapid clinical improvement after initiating high‑dose intravenous methylprednisolone. Stop before the description of the later CT‑guided biopsy results and the subsequent macrocytosis/MDS work‑up, to avoid revealing the definitive OP diagnosis.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors ruled out bacterial, viral, fungal, mycobacterial, and pneumocystis infections through cultures, serologies, and PCR; excluded eosinophilic lung disease by the absence of eosinophilia; and highlighted the dramatic steroid response as the key clue supporting organizing pneumonia, later confirmed by biopsy.
case_prompt:
A 72‑year‑old woman with chronic atrial fibrillation and heart failure presented to the emergency department in June 2019 with fever and productive cough. Chest X‑ray showed a new infiltrate. Arterial blood gases on room air revealed PO₂ 53 mmHg, PCO₂ 33 mmHg, pH 7.50, HCO₃⁻ 25 mmol/L. She had previously received a 30‑day taper of oral methylprednisolone (April–May 2019) for a small right‑lower‑lobe consolidation and, in early May, had been hospitalized for pneumocystis pneumonia treated with trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole and prednisolone.

On admission she was alert (GCS 15), temperature 35.8 °C, pulse 94 bpm, blood pressure 142/81 mmHg. Cardiac and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. Lung auscultation revealed rales over the mid and lower right lung fields; lung ultrasound showed consolidation in the same areas without pleural effusion.

Laboratory studies: WBC 6,800/µL, hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL, lymphocytes 600/µL, eosinophils 200/µL, platelets 350,000/µL, ESR 120 mm/h, CRP 23.94 mg/dL, INR 1.3; electrolytes, creatinine, liver function tests, and urinalysis were normal.

Microbiologic work‑up: blood and sputum cultures negative; serologies for Cryptococcus and Aspergillus negative; sputum negative for pneumocystis and acid‑fast bacilli; viral panel (including cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, HIV) negative; autoimmune panel (immunoglobulins, complement, ANCA, rheumatoid factor) unremarkable. No eosinophilia in blood or sputum.

She received oxygen therapy and broad‑spectrum antibiotics (initially piperacillin‑tazobactam, ciprofloxacin, linezolid, later switched to colistin and fluconazole) while continuing prophylactic trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, without clinical improvement. Because bronchoscopy could not be performed and CT‑guided biopsy was delayed, intravenous methylprednisolone 40 mg was started, after which the patient rapidly improved.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial pneumonia considered but antibiotics failed to produce improvement and cultures were negative. | "broad‑spectrum antibiotics... without improvement."
2. Viral etiologies (CMV, EBV, HIV) considered; viral testing was negative. | "negative viral testing (including cytomegalovirus, Epstein‑Barr virus, human immunodeficiency virus, etc.)."
3. Fungal infections (Cryptococcus, Aspergillus) considered; serologic tests were negative. | "negative serological test for Cryptococcus and Aspergillus."
4. Tuberculosis considered; sputum was negative for acid‑fast bacilli and cultures remained sterile. | "negative sputum for acid‑fast bacilli."
5. Pneumocystis pneumonia considered given prior episode; current sputum was negative for PCP. | "negative sputum for PCP."
6. Eosinophilic pneumonia considered; no eosinophilia in blood or sputum. | "She had no elevated eosinophils, either in blood or in the sputum."
7. Organizing pneumonia diagnosis supported by dramatic clinical improvement after high‑dose steroids, consistent with typical steroid‑responsive pattern. | "steroids were initiated with 40 mg intravenous methylprednisolone, and the patient rapidly improved."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: Identification: The case ultimately identified Aspergillus niger infection of the lung (invasive pulmonary aspergillosis). “aspergillosis” is on the 21 SELECTED diseases list, so the target diagnosis is aspergillosis.  
2. Ideal Breakpoint: Include all data up to the initiation of corticosteroid therapy on day + 7 (history, physical, eosinophilia, CT findings, bronchoscopy/BAL results, wedge‑resection pathology, negative microbiology and serologies, PET‑CT, and start of steroids). Omit the later microbiology culture that grew black colonies and the PCR result that confirmed Aspergillus, because these reveal the target diagnosis.  
3. Author's Analytic Distinctions: The authors ruled out mycobacterial infection (negative culture, Ziehl‑Neelsen, PCR, IGRA), autoimmune vasculitis (negative ANCA, ANA, complements), allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (negative IgE/galactomannan, no hyphae on pathology), and neoplastic processes (pathology showed organizing pneumonitis, no malignancy). Persistence of eosinophilia and the black indurated mass prompted repeat fungal culture, which finally established Aspergillus infection.
case_prompt:
A 27‑year‑old man presented to the emergency department with a several‑week history of cough, recurrent hemoptysis, weight loss and nocturnal sweating. He had no past medical problems, recent corticosteroid use, or substance abuse. He had lived in Belgium for six months and previously resided in Spain and Morocco.

On arrival, physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a markedly elevated eosinophil count (1.46 × 10³ /mm³) with normal C‑reactive protein, total white‑cell count and D‑dimer levels.

Chest CT demonstrated bilateral apical ground‑glass opacities together with an atypical consolidation in the apical segment of the left upper lobe. The patient was admitted and underwent bronchoalveolar lavage on day + 1; cultures, Ziehl‑Neelsen staining for mycobacteria, and PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis were negative.

Because hemoptysis persisted and worsened, a thoracoscopic wedge resection of the left upper lobe lesion was performed on day + 3. Intra‑operatively a blackish indurated mass was observed and resected. Histopathology revealed foci of pneumonia with numerous eosinophilic polymorphonuclear cells and features consistent with bronchiolitis obliterans organizing pneumonitis; no branching hyphae were seen.

During the subsequent days the patient’s symptoms resolved without specific therapy. On day + 5 an extensive etiologic work‑up was performed, including ANA, ANCA, complement levels (C3, C4, CH50), protein electrophoresis, HIV serology, CD4/CD8 counts, immunoglobulin levels, IGRA, sputum smear, and serum galactomannan; all were normal, although hypereosinophilia persisted.

A PET‑CT performed on day + 8 showed moderate hypermetabolism at the left lung apex (the resection site) with no other active lesions. On day + 7, before any microbiologic identification, the patient was started on methylprednisolone 64 mg daily.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Tuberculosis considered because of hemoptysis and weight loss, but mycobacterial cultures, Ziehl‑Neelsen staining, PCR for M. tuberculosis, and IGRA were all negative. | "Cultures, Ziehl‑Neelsen staining for mycobacteria and PCR Mycobacterium tuberculosis were negative... Interferon‑gamma release assays (IGRA) ... were negative."
2. ANCA‑associated vasculitis (e.g., GPA) considered given pulmonary infiltrates and hemoptysis; excluded by normal ANCA and other auto‑immune panels. | "auto‑immune tests (anti‑nuclear antibodies and anti‑neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies) ... No abnormalities were found."
3. Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis considered because of eosinophilia and pulmonary lesions; excluded by negative serum galactomannan, lack of IgE data, and absence of fungal hyphae on pathology. | "Serum galactomannan optical density index was also negative. No branching hyphae were observed."
4. Primary eosinophilic lung disease (e.g., chronic eosinophilic pneumonia) considered due to marked eosinophilia and organizing pneumonia pattern; less likely because symptoms resolved rapidly without targeted therapy and a distinct black indurated mass was present. | "Pathologic examination revealed the presence of foci of pneumonia with numerous eosinophilic polynuclear cells... marked hypereosinophilia."
5. Malignancy (primary lung cancer) considered given a black indurated mass; excluded by histopathology showing organizing pneumonitis without neoplastic cells. | "Anatomopathological examination showed features consistent with a bronchiolitis obliterans organizing pneumonitis and marked hypereosinophilia. No branching hyphae were observed."
6. Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis ultimately diagnosed when culture of the lung specimen grew black colonies resembling Aspergillus niger and PCR for Aspergillus was positive with a low cycle threshold (17 cycles). | "Microbiology culture of the lung sample revealed black colonies ... reminiscent of Aspergillus niger... PCR Aspergillus on the lung sample was positive with a low cycle threshold (17 cycles)."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case’s definitive diagnosis is infection with *Histoplasma capsulatum* (histoplasmosis), which is included in the 21 SELECTED diseases list. Therefore, the target diagnosis is histoplasmosis.
2. Best Breakpoint: Include all clinical presentation, physical exam, initial laboratory data, imaging findings, surgical intervention, and initial pathology/stain results, but stop **before** reporting the fungal culture growth, Histoplasma serology, and urine antigen results that confirm the diagnosis. This provides sufficient clues (immunosuppression, endemic exposure, tenosynovitis without bacterial growth) for students to work toward histoplasmosis without spoilers.
3. Key Analytic Distinctions: 
   - Authors ruled out bacterial infection by noting sterile cultures and negative Gram stains. 
   - Mycobacterial TB was considered but excluded through negative acid‑fast stains and an indeterminate QuantiFERON‑TB. 
   - Other endemic fungi were excluded by negative serologies for Blastomyces, Aspergillus, and Sporothrix. 
   - Imaging demonstrated tenosynovitis without septic arthritis, supporting an infectious but non‑septic process. 
   - Persistent inflammation despite steroids raised the possibility of IRIS, but the eventual identification of Histoplasma in cultures and tissue confirmed the fungal etiology.
case_prompt:
A 46‑year‑old woman with dermatomyositis diagnosed 5 months earlier presented with a 1‑month history of pain, warmth, redness and swelling of the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) and proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints of the left hand, accompanied by limited finger and wrist movement. She reported intermittent low‑grade fever, occasional night sweats, a dry cough, and loose stools for the past week. Her immunosuppressive regimen included prednisone 60 mg daily and mycophenolate mofetil 1500 mg twice daily for 4 months; hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily had been added 2 weeks prior, and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole thrice weekly was used for Pneumocystis prophylaxis.

She was born and raised in the upper Midwest, had a history of camping and freshwater lake swimming one year prior, occasional gardening, and extensive travel throughout the United States.

Physical examination showed a well‑appearing woman, blood pressure 134/80 mm Hg, heart rate 77 bpm, respiratory rate 18/min, temperature 36.9 °C. The left dorsal hand was swollen over the ulnar aspect with pain on gentle range of motion of the left wrist and fourth/fifth MCP joints; other joints were non‑painful. No active synovitis elsewhere. A dermatomyositis rash was present on the chest, shoulders, forearms and dorsal hands over the MCP joints. No open wounds.

Laboratory studies: white blood cell count within normal limits, platelet count normal, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 32 mm/h (↑), C‑reactive protein 52 mg/L (↑), ALT 77 U/L (↑), AST 28 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 51 U/L. QuantiFERON‑TB Gold Plus was indeterminate; HIV screen negative. Chest X‑ray was clear.

Imaging: Ultrasound of the left hand showed tenosynovitis of the fourth dorsal compartment with subcutaneous edema. Post‑contrast T1‑weighted fat‑suppressed MRI demonstrated peripherally enhancing tenosynovitis of the extensor compartment without evidence of septic arthritis or osteomyelitis.

Orthopedic hand surgery performed tenosynovectomy and irrigation/debridement of the extensor tendons. Intra‑operatively, the fourth extensor compartment displayed edema and fluid but no frank pus. Specimens were sent for bacterial, fungal and mycobacterial cultures, and for Gram, fungal and acid‑fast stains.

Pathology of the tenosynovium revealed fibrinous exudate and severe chronic inflammation. Gram, fungal and mycobacterial stains on fresh tissue were negative. No growth was reported on bacterial cultures at this point.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial septic tenosynovitis considered but deemed unlikely because cultures showed no growth and stains were negative. | "There was no growth on bacterial cultures." and "Gram, fungal and mycobacterial stains on fresh tissue were negative."
2. Mycobacterial infection (e.g., tuberculosis) entertained given immunosuppression; excluded by negative acid‑fast stains and indeterminate interferon‑γ release assay. | "QuantiFERON‑TB Gold Plus was indeterminate" and "Gram, fungal and mycobacterial stains on fresh tissue were negative."
3. Other endemic fungal infections (Blastomyces, Aspergillus, Sporothrix) were investigated but serologies were negative, making them less probable. | "Serology for Blastomyces, Aspergillus and Sporothrix were negative; Histoplasma serology and urine antigen were positive." (serology negativity part used to rule out these fungi)
4. Inflammatory tenosynovitis secondary to dermatomyositis was a consideration, yet imaging showed peripheral enhancement suggestive of infectious tenosynovitis and the lack of bacterial isolates directed the work‑up toward a fungal cause. | "MRI ... peripherally enhancing tenosynovitis ... no evidence of underlying septic arthritis or osteomyelitis."
5. Opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis jirovecii were on the differential due to high‑dose steroids, but prophylaxis with TMP/SMX and lack of respiratory findings made this unlikely. | "trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole ... for Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis."
6. Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) was later contemplated after initial antifungal therapy, but at this stage the persistent tenosynovitis prompted further microbiologic investigation. | "There was a concern that the fistulizing tracks with tenosynovitis could represent immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS)."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient’s ultimate diagnosis was hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, which is not on the 21‑disease SELECTED list; therefore the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.  
2. Best breakpoint: Stop the narrative just before the serologic result confirming hantavirus (i.e., after reporting that TB, leptospirosis, and Q‑fever tests were negative). This provides the full clinical picture, exposures, and extensive infectious work‑up without revealing the final diagnosis.  
3. Author’s analytic distinctions: The authors systematically ruled out common bacterial, viral, fungal, and atypical organisms (e.g., Legionella, MRSA, SARS‑CoV‑2, TB, CMV, Nocardia) through cultures, antigen tests, serologies, and bronchoalveolar lavage; they also considered non‑infectious etiologies such as pulmonary edema from alcoholic hepatitis and DAH. After exclusion, targeted hantavirus serology was ordered, leading to the final diagnosis.
case_prompt:
A 33‑year‑old Native American man, a welder, with past medical history of alcohol use, hypertension, and asthma presented with a 4‑day history of cough that began dry and progressed to productive with occasional hemoptysis, dyspnea, orthopnea, new lower‑extremity edema, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. He denied abdominal pain, melena, or hematemesis. He quit smoking six years ago.

On examination he was restless; temperature 98.5 °F, blood pressure 158/91 mm Hg, respiratory rate 30/min, pulse 116 bpm, oxygen saturation 96 % on 2 L nasal cannula, BMI 39.3. Laboratory studies showed WBC 16.3 K/µL, hemoglobin 8.6 g/dL, platelets 124 K/µL, Na⁺ 125 mmol/L, K⁺ 3.0 mmol/L, Mg²⁺ 1.6 mg/dL, folate 5.7 ng/mL, CK 455 U/L, LDH 310 U/L, albumin 2.9 g/dL, CRP 16.9 mg/L, lactate 3.1 mmol/L, procalcitonin 0.14 ng/mL, D‑dimer 10.56 µg/mL FEU, ethanol 96.7 mg/dL, AST 132 U/L, ALT 33 U/L, ALP 219 U/L. SARS‑CoV‑2, HIV, influenza, and MRSA nasal screens were negative.

CT pulmonary angiogram showed bilateral infiltrates (more extensive on the left) and excluded pulmonary embolism. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated hepatomegaly. Echocardiogram revealed an EF 65‑70 % with moderate LV hypertrophy, left atrial enlargement, and right atrial dilation.

He was started on ceftriaxone and doxycycline for suspected bacterial pneumonia and received thiamine, folic acid, and CIWA protocol for possible alcoholic hepatitis. By hospital day 2 his hemoptysis and respiratory status worsened, WBC rose to 18.1 K/µL, and supplemental oxygen requirements increased. Chest X‑ray showed worsening left infiltrates. Antibiotics were broadened to cefepime and vancomycin. Urine Legionella antigen, Streptococcus pneumoniae antigen, and serologies for Aspergillus, Blastomyces, Coccidioides, and Histoplasma were negative; repeat SARS‑CoV‑2 test was negative. Blood and sputum cultures showed no growth.

Bronchoscopy revealed diffuse alveolar hemorrhage thought secondary to pulmonary edema; intravenous steroids were initiated. Bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for acid‑fast bacilli, Nocardia, and CMV DNA. The patient required intubation, aggressive diuresis, and later was extubated after a week with resolution of hemoptysis. He completed a 10‑day course of antibiotics and was switched to oral prednisolone 40 mg daily.

Further history uncovered exposure to sick kittens and mice a few days before admission. Testing for hantavirus, Q‑fever, leptospirosis, and toxoplasmosis was ordered, and doxycycline was continued for three weeks. TB testing (QuantiFERON, sputum AFB smear, and PPD) and antibodies for leptospirosis and Q‑fever were all negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial pneumonia was initially suspected and treated empirically with ceftriaxone and doxycycline. | "He was started on empiric treatment with ceftriaxone ... and doxycycline ... for suspected bacterial pneumonia."
2. Legionella infection was considered but urine antigen testing was negative. | "Urine Legionella antigen ... were all negative."
3. Streptococcus pneumoniae infection was evaluated with a direct antigen test that returned negative. | "Streptococcus pneumoniae direct antigen ... were all negative."
4. MRSA colonization was screened and found negative; vancomycin was added empirically but later deemed unnecessary. | "Testing for ... MRSA nasal screen was negative."
5. SARS‑CoV‑2 and other viral pneumonias (influenza, HIV) were excluded by negative testing. | "Testing for SARS‑CoV‑2, Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV), influenza ... were negative."
6. Pulmonary embolism was ruled out by CT angiography. | "CT pulmonary angiogram ... excluded pulmonary embolism."
7. Pulmonary edema secondary to alcoholic hepatitis was considered given volume overload and hepatomegaly; bronchoscopy suggested DAH due to edema. | "Bronchoscopy was performed revealing DAH thought secondary to pulmonary edema."
8. Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage was identified on bronchoscopy as a possible cause of hemoptysis. | "Bronchoscopy revealed DAH thought secondary to pulmonary edema."
9. Fungal infections (Aspergillus, Blastomyces, Coccidioides, Histoplasma) were evaluated and serologies were negative. | "Aspergillus, Blastomyces, Coccidiodes, histoplasma antibodies ... were all negative."
10. Tuberculosis was investigated with QuantiFERON, sputum AFB smear, and PPD, all negative. | "TB testing (QuantiFERON, sputum acid‑fast bacilli, and PPD) ... were all negative."
11. Cytomegalovirus infection was excluded by negative BAL CMV DNA. | "Bronchoalveolar lavage sampling was negative for ... CMV DNA."
12. Nocardia infection was ruled out by negative BAL cultures. | "Bronchoalveolar lavage sampling was negative for ... Nocardia cultures."
13. Q‑fever was considered given rodent exposure but serology was negative. | "Antibodies for ... Q fever were all negative."
14. Leptospirosis was evaluated because of exposure to rodents and was seronegative. | "Antibodies for ... leptospirosis ... were all negative."
15. Toxoplasmosis was tested given animal exposure; empirical doxycycline covered it while awaiting results. | "He was tested for Hantavirus, Q fever, leptospirosis, and toxoplasmosis, and empiric treatment with doxycycline ... was initiated."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: Identification: The case centers on chronic eosinophilic pneumonia (CEP), which is not among the 21 SELECTED diseases; therefore the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE. No SELECTED disease is present.
2. Ideal Breakpoint: Present the case up to, but not including, the sentence “He was diagnosed as CEP in a similar fashion as the first case…”. This provides the chief complaint, vital signs, physical exam, laboratory data, imaging findings, and initial work‑up without revealing the ultimate diagnosis.
3. Author's Analytic Distinctions: The authors differentiate CEP from asthma exacerbation, bacterial pneumonia, EGPA, and ABPA by (a) marked peripheral eosinophilia (42%), (b) CT pattern of multifocal micronodular and acino‑alveolar opacities, (c) negative Aspergillus‑specific IgE, (d) negative ANAs/ANCA, and (e) lack of systemic vasculitic features, leading to the CEP diagnosis.
case_prompt:
A 48‑year‑old Saudi man with a history of bronchial asthma, allergic rhinitis, and type II diabetes mellitus presented in February 2018 with a 5‑day history of dry cough and progressive dyspnea that soon occurred at rest. He also reported nasal congestion and otalgia but denied fever, chest pain, hemoptysis, skin rash, joint pain, or swelling. He was a non‑smoker and had prior bilateral tympanectomy for partial deafness and a history of eosinophilic colitis diagnosed by colonoscopy in 2017.

On examination he was obese, blood pressure 140/70 mm Hg, pulse 120 beats/min, respiratory rate 32 breaths/min, temperature 36.9 °C, and SpO₂ 89 % on room air (improved to 95 % with 2 L nasal cannula). Cardiac exam showed normal, accentuated heart sounds without murmurs; neck veins were not distended. Lung auscultation revealed bilateral equal air entry with vesicular breath sounds and bibasilar early fine inspiratory rales. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 16.8 g/dL, white blood cell count 15.6 × 10⁹/L with eosinophils 42 % (6 552 cells/µL), C‑reactive protein 80 mg/L, arterial blood gas PaO₂ 58 mm Hg and oxygen saturation 87 % on room air, serum creatinine 150 µmol/L, total IgE 260 IU/mL, and negative Aspergillus fumigatus‑specific IgE. Liver function tests and urinalysis were normal.

Chest radiograph was normal. Chest CT demonstrated multifocal micronodular and acino‑alveolar opacities suggestive of an infectious process possibly spread by bronchogenic and hematogenous routes. Abdominal CT revealed mesenteric panniculitis with lymphadenopathy and right‑colon pneumatosis coli with small pockets of pneumoretroperitoneum.

He was admitted with a provisional diagnosis of asthma exacerbation with possible community‑acquired pneumonia and started on empirical antibiotics, oxygen, intravenous corticosteroids, nebulized bronchodilators, and fluids. Additional work‑up showed negative antinuclear and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies and normal nerve conduction studies.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Asthma exacerbation considered because of known asthma and acute dyspnea | "He was admitted as a case of asthma exacerbation with possible community‑acquired pneumonia."
2. Community‑acquired bacterial pneumonia considered due to acute respiratory symptoms and CT findings suggestive of infection | "CT chest showed multifocal, micronodular, and acino‑alveolar opacities primarily raising the possibility of an infectious process likely spread by bronchogenic and hematogenous routes."
3. Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) considered given asthma and marked eosinophilia, but excluded by negative ANCA and absence of systemic vasculitic signs | "Subsequent investigations were negative for ANAs and ANCA."
4. Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) considered because of asthma and elevated total IgE, but excluded by negative Aspergillus‑specific IgE | "Aspergillus fumigatus Immunoglobulin E (IgE) was negative."
5. Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia ultimately favored due to high peripheral eosinophilia, characteristic CT pattern, lack of infection markers, and exclusion of other eosinophilic lung disorders | (implicit synthesis of the above findings).

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient was ultimately diagnosed with Aspergillus flavus infection of the aortic valve. Aspergillosis is included in the 21 SELECTED diseases list; therefore the target diagnosis is **aspergillosis**.
2. Best Breakpoint: End the presentation after the statement that the fungal stain from the aortic valve tissue was positive and amphotericin B was added (“the fungal stain was positive from the tissue culture of the aortic valve; hence, amphotericin B was added”). This provides all clinical, imaging, and laboratory data needed for learners to suspect a fungal (Aspergillus) etiology, but before the definitive culture result (A. flavus) is disclosed.
3. Author's Analytic Distinctions: The authors highlighted (a) negative blood cultures despite persistent fever, (b) lack of response to broad‑spectrum antibacterial therapy, (c) embolic complications (splenic infarct, cerebral lesions, aortic thrombus, gangrenous bowel), and (d) intra‑operative findings of aortic valve abscess with a vegetative mass, all supporting an infectious endocarditis of fungal origin and ruling out purely bacterial or non‑infectious thromboembolic causes.
case_prompt:
A 49‑year‑old man with diabetes mellitus and coronary artery disease presented to the emergency department with one week of intermittent fever and left upper‑quadrant abdominal pain. He had undergone mitral valve fibroelastoma resection and coronary artery bypass grafting one year earlier. He denied smoking, alcohol, or substance use. On arrival he was afebrile; vital signs were otherwise normal. Abdominal examination revealed left upper‑quadrant tenderness without guarding. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL) and an elevated C‑reactive protein level (147.5 mg/L); renal and hepatic panels were within normal limits. Contrast‑enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated a wedge‑shaped hypodense lesion in the spleen consistent with splenic infarction. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed moderate aortic regurgitation and a new rounded 1.5 × 1 cm mass attached to the left coronary cusp of the aortic valve, not seen on the prior study a year earlier.

Empiric antimicrobial therapy was started, and because the patient remained febrile and blood cultures remained negative, antibiotics were escalated to cefepime and vancomycin. Chest radiography showed extensive bilateral infiltrates, predominantly in the medial right upper lobe and mid‑lower bilateral lungs, and he was diagnosed with community‑acquired pneumonia, discharged with continuation of home azithromycin and a 5‑day course of cefpodoxime. He returned the next day with persistent, worsening symptoms and was transferred to our institution.  

In the emergency department he was afebrile but hypoxic (SpO₂ 82 % on room air). Physical examination revealed bibasilar crackles and wheezes.
