case_prompt:
A 49‑year‑old man with a history of mantle cell lymphoma treated with autologous stem cell transplant in 2017 and maintenance rituximab until July 2020 was hospitalized in November 2020 for COVID‑19 pneumonia. From November 2020 to March 2021 he required four additional hospitalizations for shortness of breath and fever; each admission was labeled “recurrent pneumonia” based on clinical symptoms and pulmonary infiltrates on chest imaging. An extensive infectious work‑up during these episodes was repeatedly negative, including repeat COVID‑19 testing. He reported daily fevers, chills, night sweats, reduced appetite, and a 35‑lb weight loss over the preceding four months.

He presented again in March 2021 with shortness of breath and a temperature of 102 °F. Chest radiograph showed multifocal pulmonary opacities thought to represent cryptogenic organizing pneumonia or interstitial pneumonia. CT angiography demonstrated patchy bilateral lung infiltrates and interstitial thickening suggestive of pneumonia with pulmonary edema. Comprehensive infectious studies—including gram stain, respiratory cultures, fungal cultures, AFB smear and culture, testing for blastomycosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis, legionella, and aspergillus—were all negative. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and trans‑bronchial lung biopsy revealed chronic inflammation but no organisms on cultures and no evidence of malignancy. Laboratory testing demonstrated severe hypogammaglobulinemia (IgG 260 mg/dL, IgA 19 mg/dL, IgM 7 mg/dL). His risk factors for hypogammaglobulinemia included prior hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, recent rituximab therapy, and multiple short courses of glucocorticoids.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Recurrent bacterial pneumonia – considered because of fever, cough, infiltrates; excluded by serial negative bacterial cultures and lack of sustained response to antibiotics alone. | "Infectious disease workup was negative, including gram stain, respiratory culture…"
2. COVID‑19 reinfection – considered given prior COVID‑19 pneumonia; excluded by repeated negative SARS‑CoV‑2 testing. | "Infectious disease workup … was negative, including … recurrent COVID‑19 infection."
3. Fungal infections (aspergillosis, histoplasmosis, blastomycosis) – considered due to immunosuppression and pulmonary infiltrates; excluded by negative fungal cultures and specific antigen testing. | "Infectious disease workup … was negative, including … blastomycosis, histoplasmosis, … aspergillus."
4. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia – considered because of rituximab‑induced B‑cell depletion; excluded by negative pneumocystis testing on BAL. | "Infectious disease workup … was negative, including … pneumocystis."
5. Legionella infection – considered in the setting of fever and pneumonia; excluded by negative legionella testing. | "Infectious disease workup … was negative, including … legionella."
6. Mycobacterial infection (TB, atypical mycobacteria) – considered due to chronic pulmonary symptoms; excluded by negative AFB smear and culture. | "Infectious disease workup … was negative, including … AFB smear and culture."
7. Relapsed mantle cell lymphoma involving the lung – considered given prior hematologic malignancy; excluded by lung biopsy showing no malignancy. | "Lung biopsy … was negative for … malignancy."
8. Drug‑induced lung injury / steroid‑withdrawal effect – considered because of recent steroid courses; deemed less likely as imaging favored organizing pneumonia and there was chronic inflammation without eosinophilia. | "CT … showed patchy bilateral lung infiltrates and interstitial thickening concerning for pneumonia with pulmonary edema."
9. Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia / interstitial pneumonia – favored diagnosis because imaging pattern of multifocal opacities, negative infectious work‑up, and biopsy showing chronic inflammation are characteristic of organizing pneumonia. | "Chest x‑ray revealed multifocal pulmonary opacities concerning for cryptogenic organizing pneumonia or interstitial pneumonia… Lung biopsy … showed chronic inflammation."
10. Hypogammaglobulinemia‑associated immune deficiency – identified as a predisposing factor that explains recurrent infections and may contribute to non‑infectious inflammatory lung disease. | "Laboratories were significant for hypogammaglobulinemia… The patient had several risk factors for hypogammaglobulinemia."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient ultimately developed invasive pulmonary aspergillosis, which is included in the 21 SELECTED diseases list. Therefore, the target diagnosis is **aspergillosis**.
2. Best Breakpoint: Present the case up to the point where the sputum cultures first returned positive for Aspergillus (three separate occasions). This includes the progressive cavitary lung lesions, immunosuppressive therapy, negative bacterial cultures, and imaging findings, but stops before the detailed antifungal treatment course and later bronchoalveolar lavage results, so the diagnosis remains unsolved for the learner.
3. Key Analytic Distinctions: The authors evaluated and excluded tuberculosis, bacterial infection, sarcoidosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and neoplastic processes through smear/PCR, histopathology, serology (ANCA, RF), imaging, and clinical criteria, ultimately attributing the progressive cavitary disease to an invasive fungal infection (Aspergillus) based on repeated positive sputum cultures and radiologic progression despite antibiotics.
case_prompt:
A 28‑year‑old Saudi man, previously healthy, presented with a 40‑day history of dry cough, fever, fatigue, red eyes, and abnormal chest radiographs dating back to January 2020. He smoked 10 pack‑years and had undergone lumbar laminectomy in August 2019. Prior to admission he complained of dry cough, bilateral red eyes, blurred vision, arthralgia of both knees, and low back pain. Chest X‑ray showed an isolated right upper‑lobe pulmonary nodule, prompting referral to a pulmonary clinic.

Because pulmonary tuberculosis is common locally, outpatient sputum acid‑fast smear and PCR were performed and were negative. A repeat chest X‑ray two weeks later demonstrated bilateral pulmonary nodules, the largest in the right upper lobe. He was hospitalized elsewhere, where flexible bronchoscopy with trans‑bronchial biopsy of the right upper lobe showed no endoluminal lesion.

On examination he was afebrile (37.0 °C), BP 130/80 mm Hg, pulse 110 beats/min, SpO₂ 95 % on room air, BMI 30.5 kg/m². Eyes were bilaterally red without discharge; an ophthalmologist diagnosed bilateral episcleritis. No nasal polyps, rash, arthritis, lymphadenopathy, or organomegaly were noted. Chest auscultation was normal.

Subsequent chest radiographs revealed enlargement of the right upper‑lobe nodule with cavitation and growth of a left lower‑lobe nodule. A February 10, 2020 imaging study showed multiple bilateral nodules, an enlarged right upper‑lobe mass, and mediastinal lymphadenopathy.

Laboratory studies disclosed microscopic hematuria, proteinuria, and mild eosinophilia. Immunologic testing was positive for c‑ANCA and rheumatoid factor, negative for p‑ANCA, ANA, and anti‑CCP. A CT‑guided lung biopsy of the cavitary right upper‑lobe lesion showed necrotizing vasculitis with granulomatous inflammation and multinucleated giant Langerhans cells, suggesting an overlap of granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA); EGPA was excluded based on lack of asthma, atopy, and significant eosinophilia.

He was started on high‑dose intravenous methylprednisolone followed by oral prednisolone 50 mg daily and methotrexate. After three months of therapy there was no clinical or radiologic improvement, and rituximab was added; the fourth dose caused a severe allergic reaction.

On 17 September 2020 he developed fever, worsening cough with yellowish, sometimes bloody sputum, fatigue, dyspnea, recurrent red eyes, and arthralgia. Vitals: temperature 39 °C, pulse 140 beats/min, respiratory rate 28 breaths/min. Examination revealed dullness over both lung bases, distant breath sounds, and no lower‑limb edema, rash, or murmur. Repeat chest X‑ray showed enlarging cavitary lesions with air‑fluid levels. Blood and sputum bacterial cultures were negative, but sputum cultures grew **Aspergillus** on three separate occasions. Serum galactomannan tests were repeatedly negative, and COVID‑19 PCR remained negative. The patient’s inflammatory markers were elevated, and he had recently been diagnosed with type‑2 diabetes, for which he was on insulin.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Tuberculosis considered due to endemicity and cavitary lesions; excluded by negative sputum AFB smear and PCR. | "Since pulmonary tuberculosis is common in our area, we performed outpatient tuberculosis screening by sputum analysis for acid fast bacteria by smear and PCR. The result of the test was negative."
2. Bacterial pneumonia considered because of fever, productive cough, and infiltrates; excluded by repeated negative blood and sputum bacterial cultures. | "Blood and sputum cultures were negative for bacteria."
3. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) considered based on c‑ANCA positivity, granulomatous lung biopsy, and cavitary lesions; supported but not definitive, leading to immunosuppressive therapy. | "His immunological profile showed positive results for antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) C... Histopathology... suggested an overlap syndrome between GPA and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis."
4. Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) considered; excluded due to absence of asthma, atopy, and significant peripheral eosinophilia. | "Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis was ruled out in this case based on the clinical history (no asthma, no atopy, and no significant peripheral eosinophilia)."
5. Sarcoidosis considered as a granulomatous disease; excluded because biopsy showed necrotizing vasculitis with fibrinoid necrosis rather than non‑caseating granulomas typical of sarcoidosis. | "Sarcoidosis and granulomatosis with polyangiitis are other differential diagnoses."
6. Neoplastic process (lung cancer) considered given mass and mediastinal nodes; excluded by lack of malignant cells on bronchoscopy and biopsy. | "The possibility of a neoplastic process also cannot be ruled out."
7. Mycotic infection (fungal) considered early; ultimately supported by repeated positive sputum cultures for Aspergillus and progressive cavitary lesions despite antibiotics. | "Sputum cultures were positive for Aspergillus on 3 occasions."
8. COVID‑19 considered during the pandemic; excluded by repeatedly negative PCR tests. | "COVID‑19 was repeatedly negative."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case ultimately identifies a localized Aspergillus infection of the ascending aorta. Aspergillosis is on the 21 SELECTED diseases list, so it is the primary target diagnosis.
2. Best breakpoint: End the prompt after the statement that a tissue biopsy was obtained and sent for microbiological and histobiological analysis, but before any description of the microscopic findings that name Aspergillus. This provides all clinical, laboratory, and imaging data needed for learners to consider infectious, autoimmune, traumatic, or neoplastic causes of a pseudoaneurysm without revealing the definitive fungal identification.
3. Author's Analytic Distinctions: The authors systematically excluded pulmonary embolism (repeat CTA negative), bacterial/fungal cultures (negative), autoimmune vasculitis (negative serologies), and non‑infectious causes (no trauma, surgery, or connective‑tissue disease). Definitive diagnosis was made by histopathology showing characteristic hyphae, establishing Aspergillus as the etiologic agent.
case_prompt:
A 45‑year‑old white male presented for follow‑up of a pulmonary embolism diagnosed one year earlier. A repeat pulmonary computed tomography (CT) angiogram showed no evidence of embolism but incidentally revealed a new ascending aortic pseudoaneurysm with surrounding hematoma. Review of prior imaging suggested the original diagnosis of pulmonary embolism had been erroneous, and the patient had been on oral anticoagulation since.

His past infection history was notable only for an uncomplicated community‑acquired Klebsiella pneumonia three years prior, fully resolved after a 5‑day hospitalization. He denied diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, joint pain, skin rash, weakness, neurological or constitutional symptoms, trauma, surgeries, recent travel, or high‑risk sexual activity. He reported no exposure to humidity, moisture, or dust at home or work (employed at a water desalination plant). Family history was non‑contributory. He is a former smoker with a 14‑pack‑year history.

Physical examination showed poor oral hygiene and dental caries. Body mass index was 24.2 kg/m². Blood pressure differed between arms (120/83 mm Hg left, 107/46 mm Hg right) with weaker radial and femoral pulses on the right, raising concern for a structural vascular lesion. Laboratory studies revealed C‑reactive protein 13 mg/L, procalcitonin 0.1 ng/mL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 10 mm/h; complete blood count, cardiac enzymes, BNP, renal, hepatic panels, and coagulation profile were normal. Electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm. Autoimmune work‑up (ANA, ANCA, anti‑dsDNA, C3, C4) and infectious screening (HIV, syphilis, blood and urine bacterial and mycological cultures) were all negative.

Chest X‑ray demonstrated an increased transverse cardiac diameter, obliterated right cardiophrenic angle suggesting mild right pleural effusion, and clear left cardiophrenic angle; lungs were clear without nodules or consolidation. Transthoracic and trans‑esophageal echocardiograms showed normal left ventricular systolic function (EF 55 %), moderate tricuspid regurgitation, and no valvular vegetations. Brain CT angiography was negative for aneurysms or vascular malformations. Chest CT angiography identified a focal pseudoaneurysm (2.4 × 1.5 cm) on the right anterior wall of the ascending thoracic aorta, 2.5 cm above the aortic valve, with a 1.1 cm neck, accompanied by a large anterior mediastinal and intrapericardial hematoma, pericardial thickening, and a mild hemorrhagic pericardial effusion.

The patient was admitted for further evaluation and underwent surgical ascending aortic repair with pericardial debridement. Intraoperatively, a thick, adherent pericardium without a clear tissue plane was encountered, with contained cheesy material and hematoma over the right ventricle and ascending aorta. The pseudoaneurysm defect was patched with bovine pericardial material. A tissue biopsy was taken and sent for microbiological and histobiological analysis.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Misdiagnosed pulmonary embolism excluded – repeat CT angiogram demonstrated “no evidence of pulmonary embolism” while revealing the pseudoaneurysm. 
2. Bacterial and non‑aspergillus fungal infection ruled out – “precipitating infections (human immunodeficiency virus, syphilis testing, blood and urine bacterial and mycological cultures) were all negative.” 
3. Autoimmune vasculitis considered but excluded – “autoimmune profile (antinuclear antibodies, anti‑neutrophilic cytoplasmic antibody, anti‑double stranded DNA antibodies, Complement 3, Complement 4) … were all negative.” 
4. Traumatic or iatrogenic cause unlikely – the patient “has never had … trauma, nor any past surgeries,” and denied environmental exposures that might predispose to infection. 
5. Definitive fungal etiology identified by tissue pathology – “Hematoxylin and Eosin stain and methenamine silver stain revealed fungal organisms with thin separate hyphae and regular branching, morphologically consistent with Aspergillus species.” 
6. No evidence of disseminated disease – “As revealed in the previous labs and imaging results, the patient had no evidence of disseminated Aspergillosis.”

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case ultimately identified an invasive Trichosporon asahii infection, which is not among the 21 SELECTED diseases; therefore the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.  
2. Best breakpoint: End the prompt after describing the patient’s clinical deterioration, re‑intubation, death, and the fact that repeated cultures remained negative. Do not include the PCR array results that identified Trichosporon DNA, so the mystery diagnosis remains undisclosed.  
3. Analytic distinctions: The authors highlighted (a) the failure of conventional blood and respiratory cultures to isolate a pathogen, (b) the use of a broad‑range fungal PCR array covering common molds and yeasts, (c) detection of Trichosporon DNA (reaction F) whereas other branch‑specific reactions were only cross‑positive, and (d) species confirmation by sequencing, which together established Trichosporon asahii as the causative organism and excluded other molds or yeasts.
case_prompt: The patient was receiving antifungal therapy with voriconazole 400 mg twice daily after susceptibility testing. Clinical condition improved and extubation was possible on the fourth day of treatment, with chest CT showing reduction of pulmonary lesions. Eight days later, septic symptoms recurred, acute respiratory failure developed, and massive fluid accumulation occurred in the lungs, necessitating re‑intubation. Despite four pairs of blood cultures and twice‑daily respiratory specimens, no pathogen was detected in this final episode. The patient subsequently died from multi‑organ failure.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Persistent septic picture despite negative cultures suggested an unidentified pathogen | "Despite four pairs of blood cultures and twice daily respiratory specimens being used for culture, no pathogen could be detected in the patient's final episode of illness."
2. Broad fungal PCR array was employed to detect common moulds and yeasts, covering Aspergillus, Penicillium, Rhizopus, Mucor, Fusarium, Cryptococcus, Candida, etc. | "The array consists of… A set of two pan‑fungal reactions… Seven branch‑specific reactions (A‑G) for the detection of common moulds… and yeasts…"
3. Trichosporon DNA was uniquely identified by reaction F in all subcultures and in the patient’s EDTA blood, pointing to Trichosporon as the culprit | "With reaction F (Fig. 2), Trichosporon spp. DNA was detected in subcultures from all blood culture bottles and, importantly, also in the patient's EDTA blood sample from the first day of voriconazole treatment."
4. Other branch‑specific reactions (B and C) showed cross‑positivity but did not yield definitive identification, reducing the likelihood of those molds (e.g., Rhizopus, Mucor, Absidia) | "Two further branch‑specific reactions (B and C, Fig. 2) showed cross‑positivity."
5. Sequencing confirmed the organism as T. asahii, establishing the final diagnosis and ruling out other fungal species | "Sequencing of the PCR product… allowed species identification of T. asahii in all samples."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case centers on invasive aspergillosis (selected disease). Cytomegalovirus infection is also present but serves as a co‑infection; the primary mystery to be solved before autopsy is the invasive fungal disease, which is on the SELECTED list.
2. Best Breakpoint: End the presentation after the patient’s transfer to the pediatric ICU on day 83, noting persistent positivity for Aspergillus and pan‑fungal antigens and ongoing CMV‑DNA detection. Omit the sudden massive oral bleeding, resuscitation attempts, death, and all autopsy findings.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: Diagnosis of invasive aspergillosis was supported by documented galactomannan and β‑D‑glucan positivity, negative bacterial/fungal cultures, and histopathologic demonstration of hyphae; CMV infection was identified by PCR/DNA but was distinguished from the primary cause of airway ulceration by tissue findings.
case_prompt: A child younger than 6 years was diagnosed with pre‑B acute lymphoblastic leukemia with TEL/AML1 rearrangement and started on the AIEOP2017 chemotherapy protocol. On day 52 of treatment the patient developed fever (38.6 °C) and a 20‑day catarrhal cough and was treated with piperacillin‑tazobactam; respiratory secretions were positive only for rhinovirus. The child was discharged on day 63 in good general condition but returned to the emergency department on day 66 with recurrent fever. Laboratory evaluation revealed profound bone‑marrow aplasia with leukopenia (0.3 × 10³/µL), thrombocytopenia (7 × 10³/µL) and anemia (Hb 7.0 g/dL, requiring hospitalization). Serum testing was positive for Aspergillus antigen and pan‑fungal markers (galactomannan and β‑D‑glucan) while mycete cultures from nasopharyngeal aspirate and peripheral blood were negative. Cytomegalovirus DNA was also detected. Chest computed tomography showed a worsening interstitial pneumonia. Treatment was instituted with piperacillin‑tazobactam, oral foscarnet and amphotericin B (initially 3 mg/kg/day, later increased to 5 mg/kg/day). On day 83 the patient was transferred to the pediatric intensive care unit; positivity for Aspergillus and pan‑fungal antigens persisted together with detectable CMV DNA.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Invasive aspergillosis is likely because of documented positivity for Aspergillus antigen and pan‑fungal markers (galactomannan and β‑D‑glucan) in serum. | "Positivity for Aspergillus and pan‑fungal antigens (i.e., galatomannan and beta-D-glucan, respectively) was detected."
2. The presence of hyphae on tissue staining confirms invasive fungal infection. | "the presence of hyphae was detected by Grocott‑Gomori's methenamine silver (GMS) staining."
3. Bacterial bacterial pneumonia was considered (initial empiric piperacillin‑tazobactam) but was less likely due to negative cultures. | "mycete culture in nasopharyngeal aspirate and peripheral blood were negative."
4. Rhinovirus infection explained the initial catarrhal cough but did not account for the persistent febrile neutropenia and imaging findings. | "Positivity only for Rhinovirus in the superficial respiratory secretions."
5. Cytomegalovirus reactivation was identified (CMV DNA present) and could contribute to interstitial pneumonia, yet the tissue demonstrated both CMV‑related changes and fungal hyphae, indicating a dual infection with aspergillosis being the invasive component. | "Cytomegalovirus (CMV) presence was also shown." and "interstitial pneumonia evidence, consistent with CMV etiopathogenesis."
6. The persistent interstitial pneumonia on CT supported an infectious etiology, but the combination of antigenemia and histologic hyphae favored invasive aspergillosis over isolated viral pneumonitis. | "a computed tomography (CT) scan showed the presence of a worsening interstitial pneumonia."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case resolves around chronic pulmonary aspergillosis (CPA). Aspergillosis is included in the 21 SELECTED diseases list → target diagnosis = aspergillosis.  
2. Breakpoint: End the presentation just before the authors state “The patient met diagnostic criteria for CPA …” and before antifungal therapy is initiated. This includes history, imaging of a cavitary lesion, bronchoscopy findings, elevated CRP, positive Aspergillus precipitins, and negative bacterial/Mycobacterial work‑up, giving sufficient data for a learner to deduce CPA without revealing the definitive label.  
3. Analytic Distinctions (from authors): – Exclusion of active tuberculosis by negative Ziehl‑Neelsen stain, CB‑NAAT and cultures. – Exclusion of bacterial infection by repeated negative sputum and bronchial wash cultures despite empirical antibiotics. – Exclusion of lung‑cancer recurrence by CT‑guided fine‑needle aspiration and bronchial biopsies showing no neoplastic cells. – Support for CPA by the presence of a thick‑walled cavitary lesion in a post‑TB/ post‑radiotherapy lung, positive Aspergillus fumigatus precipitins, and later culture positivity.
case_prompt:
A 54‑year‑old female smoker (35 pack‑years) with a remote history of pulmonary tuberculosis in adolescence presented to the Department of Lung Diseases and Tuberculosis with a 6‑month history of productive cough, weakness, low exercise tolerance, and a 7‑kg weight loss. Prior to this admission she had undergone radiochemotherapy for locally advanced non‑small‑cell lung cancer of the right upper lobe three and a half years earlier; treatment consisted of three cycles of platinum‑based chemotherapy with etoposide and radical radiotherapy (66 Gy). Follow‑up CT scans performed every 6 months had revealed a cavitary lesion developing at the site of the original tumor two years after completion of cancer therapy.

Current chest CT showed an irregular cavity in the upper right lung with thick walls, a posterior‑wall mass, surrounding solid consolidation, a dilated adjacent bronchus, and emphysema. PET‑CT demonstrated hypermetabolic right‑lung masses deemed more likely inflammatory than malignant. Physical examination revealed wheezes and rales. Bronchoscopy confirmed purulent bronchitis. Laboratory testing showed a markedly elevated C‑reactive protein (90 mg/dL, normal < 5 mg/dL). Pulmonary function testing demonstrated a moderate reduction in TLCO (41 % predicted) without obstruction or restriction.

Microbiological studies of sputum and bronchial wash were negative for bacteria and fungi on smear and aerobic/anaerobic cultures. Ziehl‑Neelsen staining, cartridge‑based nucleic acid amplification testing (CBNAAT), and cultures for mycobacteria were also negative. Serum Aspergillus fumigatus precipitins were positive by Ouchterlony double immunodiffusion. Empiric intravenous ceftriaxone and levofloxacin were administered with only moderate clinical effect; repeat bronchoscopy showed partial reduction of purulent mucus. Fine‑needle aspiration of the cavity margin yielded only macrophages and inflammatory cells; bronchial forceps biopsy was negative for neoplastic cells. No additional clinical or radiographic signs of malignancy were identified.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Chronic pulmonary aspergillosis (aspergillosis) is supported by a thick‑walled cavitary lesion in a previously diseased lung, positive Aspergillus fumigatus precipitins, and later culture positivity, fulfilling CPA criteria. | "The patient met diagnostic criteria for CPA and antifungal treatment with itraconazole was initiated..."
2. Active tuberculosis was considered because of prior TB and cavitary disease, but excluded by negative Ziehl‑Neelsen staining, CBNAAT, and cultures. | "Ziehl‑Neelsen staining, cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification test (CBNAAT), and culture of sputum and bronchial wash did not show evidence of Mycobacterial infection."
3. Bacterial infection was a differential due to purulent bronchitis and elevated CRP; however, repeated sputum and bronchial wash cultures (aerobic and anaerobic) were negative, and empirical antibiotics yielded only modest improvement. | "Microbiological tests (smears, aerobic and anaerobic cultures) of the sputum and bronchial wash were negative for bacteria and fungi."
4. Recurrence of lung cancer was entertained given the prior malignancy and hypermetabolic PET‑CT lesions, but excluded by CT‑guided fine‑needle aspiration showing only inflammatory cells and bronchial biopsy lacking neoplastic cells. | "forceps biopsy of bronchial tissue ... was negative for neoplastic cells."
5. Other fungal pathogens were less likely; initial fungal cultures were negative, and specific identification of Aspergillus fumigatus precipitin antibodies pointed toward Aspergillus species. | "Aspergillus fumigatus precipitins were positive in serum."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case ultimately establishes a diagnosis of extracavitary primary effusion lymphoma (PEL), which is not among the 21 SELECTED diseases. HIV/AIDS is a SELECTED disease but is only mentioned as past medical history without a diagnostic work‑up in this report. Therefore, the target diagnosis is an OUT_OF_SCOPE condition.
2. Best Breakpoint: Include all presenting symptoms, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial laboratory/imaging results up to the CT neck description that reveals a heterogeneous right sternocleidomastoid/jugulodigastric mass. Exclude any histopathologic, immunophenotypic, or genetic data that leads to the definitive lymphoma diagnosis, as well as the PET‑scan follow‑up.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors systematically excluded common opportunistic infections (PJP, TB, fungal, viral) via DFA, sputum AFB staining, urine antigen testing, and CSF studies; they highlighted nonspecific imaging that raised concern for a lymphoproliferative disorder, prompting biopsy that confirmed extracavitary PEL.
case_prompt:
A 31‑year‑old man presented in November 2019 with three days of worsening dyspnea, excruciating throbbing headache, photophobia, and visual spotting. He reported insidious symptom onset beginning in July 2019, with progressive dyspnea, non‑productive cough, recurrent fevers and chills, leading to hospitalization in October for empiric treatment of pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia (PJP). He was discharged on HAART and Bactrim, but adherence was poor. Three weeks later he was re‑hospitalized for worsening dyspnea, headache, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and a syncopal episode; he required supplemental oxygen but not intubation. After a brief discharge while off HAART, he returned within three weeks with rapid worsening of the same symptoms.

Past medical history included HIV/AIDS for 10 years (poor HAART adherence after the first three years), neurosyphilis, and hypertension.

On exam he was tachypneic, mildly hypoxic, tachycardic, and hypotensive; neck was supple without cervical lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed elevated lactate, normal LDH, CD4 count 267 cells/µL, HIV RNA viral load 5.27 log. Direct fluorescent antibody testing of bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for Pneumocystis jirovecii, influenza A/B, parainfluenza 1‑3, adenovirus, and RSV. Sputum AFB stain and culture were negative; QuantiFERON‑Gold was not performed. EBV serology was not obtained due to sample lipemia. Buffy‑coat smear and urine Histoplasma antigen were negative; aerobic and anaerobic blood cultures were sterile. Chest radiograph demonstrated retrocardiac atelectasis without overt pneumonia or edema. CT pulmonary‑embolism protocol showed no embolus or right‑heart strain, but noted increased soft‑tissue density in the right lower neck, described as nonspecific and possibly representing contusion, neoplasm, or a lymphoproliferative disorder/HIV‑related process. Nuclear‑medicine ventilation‑perfusion imaging indicated low probability of PE.

Given the headache and photophobia, emergent head CT and MRI were unrevealing. Lumbar puncture yielded clear CSF with normal protein and no pleocytosis; CSF studies were negative for cryptococcal antigen, VDRL, treponemal antigen, fungal antibodies (aspergillus, blastomyces, histoplasma), and HSV/VZV PCR.

Due to progressive symptoms and right‑neck edema, a dedicated neck CT performed four days later showed an enlarged, heterogeneous right sternocleidomastoid muscle and a confluent right jugulodigastric mass measuring ~7.4 cm craniocaudally, with compression of the right internal jugular vein and proximal occlusion. Abdominal ultrasound was unremarkable except for mild hepatosplenomegaly.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Consideration of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) – empiric treatment was initiated because of HIV status and prior hospitalization, but DFA of bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for Pneumocystis jirovecii. | "DFA studies on a bronchial alveolar lavage sample revealed neither Pneumocystis jirovecii organisms..."
2. Tuberculosis – evaluated due to cough and fever; sputum AFB stain and culture were negative and QuantiFERON‑Gold could not be performed. | "Workup on sputum samples detected no acid‑fast bacilli... A QuantiFERON Gold test was ordered but was not performed..."
3. Fungal infections (cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis) – CSF cryptococcal antigen and urine Histoplasma antigen were negative; serum antibodies to Aspergillus, Blastomyces, Histoplasma also negative. | "CSF... negative for cryptococcal antigen... urine histoplasma antigen were negative."
4. Viral opportunistic infections (CMV, EBV, HSV, VZV) – DFA panel excluded influenza and RSV; EBV serology not obtained; CSF PCR for HSV/VZV negative. | "DFA studies... revealed neither ... influenza A and B, parainfluenza 1, 2, and 3, adenovirus, nor respiratory syncytial viruses." and "CSF... negative for herpes simplex virus and varicella zoster virus DNA by polymerase chain reaction."
5. Bacterial sepsis – multiple aerobic and anaerobic blood cultures were sterile. | "Anerobic and aerobic blood cultures were negative."
6. Non‑infectious pulmonary causes (pulmonary embolism, edema) – CT PE protocol and ventilation‑perfusion scan showed no embolus or right‑heart strain; chest X‑ray lacked edema. | "CT for the pulmonary embolism protocol ... showed neither evidence of pulmonary embolism nor right heart strain." and "Nuclear medicine imaging also showed low probability of pulmonary embolism."
7. Lymphoproliferative or neoplastic process – neck CT revealed a large heterogeneous mass with jugular vein occlusion, described as possibly neoplasm or HIV‑related lymphoproliferative disorder, prompting tissue diagnosis. | "CT of the neck soft tissue ... revealed an enlarged and heterogenous right sternocleidomastoid muscle and a heterogenous right jugulodigastric confluent mass ... may represent contusion, represent neoplasm, or be related to a lymphoproliferative disorder or HIV."
8. Primary CNS infection (meningitis, encephalitis) – CSF normal cell count, protein, and negative for cryptococcal antigen, VDRL, fungal and viral PCRs, making meningitis unlikely. | "CSF analysis revealed a clear sample with a normal protein level and no pleocytosis... CSF studies were negative for cryptococcal antigen, VDRL and treponemal antigen..."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: Identification: The patient was ultimately found to have a brain infection caused by Nocardia thailandica, which falls under “nocardiosis,” one of the 21 SELECTED diseases. Although the autopsy later revealed aspergillosis and disseminated candidiasis (OUT_OF_SCOPE), the instructional focus is on diagnosing the Nocardia brain abscess before those results are disclosed.  
2. Ideal Breakpoint: End the case presentation at the point when intra‑operative puncture fluid showed Gram‑positive bacilli positive on Kinyoun stain and the Nocardia genus was suggested, but before the species‑level identification (N. thailandica) and before any mention of the eventual fungal autopsy findings. This provides sufficient clinical, imaging, and microbiologic data for students to infer a Nocardia brain abscess without revealing the final diagnosis.  
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished Nocardia infection from other causes of cerebral abscess by (a) imaging characteristics of a multilocular ring‑enhancing lesion, (b) intra‑operative Gram‑positive bacilli on Kinyoun stain suggestive of filamentous organisms, (c) subsequent molecular identification (16S rRNA sequencing, MALDI‑TOF) confirming Nocardia, and (d) exclusion of common bacterial pathogens (negative cultures for typical cocci) and later exclusion of fungal etiology (autopsy findings).

case_prompt:
A 50‑year‑old woman presented with nausea and vomiting. She had a 30‑year history of ulcerative colitis treated with steroids and had undergone aortic root surgery with mechanical valve placement at age 48, for which she was on a vitamin K antagonist. On examination she was obtunded (Glasgow Coma Scale 3‑4‑6) and her systolic blood pressure exceeded 200 mm Hg; temperature was normal.

Laboratory studies showed a white‑blood‑cell count of 11 300 /µL, hemoglobin 11.1 g/dL, C‑reactive protein 0.17 mg/dL, INR 2.47, and D‑dimer 5.7 µg/mL. Two sets of blood cultures and a urine culture were negative.

Brain CT demonstrated a left occipital subcortical hemorrhage with intraventricular extension and acute hydrocephalus. No sinus fluid or bone destruction was seen. 3‑D CT angiography identified a distal left posterior cerebral artery aneurysm. The patient became comatose, prompting emergent intubation and bilateral external ventricular drainage.

On postoperative day 2 her consciousness improved (GCS 1‑t‑4) and digital subtraction angiography showed a wide‑necked aneurysm of the left parieto‑occipital artery, 5.6 mm in diameter. Direct surgery was undertaken the same day. In the prone position, a left occipital craniotomy was performed; intra‑operative ultrasonography confirmed the hematoma location. After corticotomy of the superior occipital gyrus the hematoma was evacuated, revealing the aneurysm adherent to the parent artery with intra‑aneurysmal thrombosis. Because the aneurysm neck was fragile, the aneurysm was removed and an end‑to‑end anastomosis of the proximal and distal portions of the artery was performed.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial infectious aneurysm considered due to intracerebral hemorrhage and immunosuppression, but ruled out because “Two sets of blood cultures and a urinary culture were negative.”  
2. Aspergillus‑related mycotic aneurysm considered given the immunocompromised state, yet excluded by negative serology: “Tests for serum beta‑D‑glucan and Aspergillus antigen were negative on POD 9.”  
3. Non‑infectious causes (e.g., hypertensive or atherosclerotic aneurysm) were entertained because of the patient’s severe hypertension, but the intra‑operative finding of a fragile, thrombosed aneurysm wall with surrounding necrosis suggested an infectious etiology.  
4. Mucormycosis ultimately identified by histopathology showing characteristic right‑angled branching hyphae, confirming a fungal mycotic aneurysm: “Immunohistochemical analysis performed with Grocott’s stain revealed that the coenocytic hyphae varied in width and exhibited right‑angled branching, which are characteristics of zygomycetes…These findings were consistent with Mucormycosis.”

case_prompt:
A 3‑year‑old girl (weight 16 kg) presented with a week‑long history of vomiting, weakness, and right‑angle mouth tremor. She was hospitalized, discharged, and a week later developed right‑sided head tilt while speaking and reduced activity, prompting readmission for brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and brain tissue biopsy.

Initial work‑up: first brain MRI showed a large (≈7.8 × 8.1 × 7.9 cm) lesion involving the corpus callosum and bilateral frontal lobes with perifocal edema, additional smaller lesion in the left parietal lobe, and multiple contrast‑enhancing nodules in the left frontal, bilateral parietal, and left temporal lobes. The radiologic impression suggested glioblastoma with a differential of necrotizing toxoplasma encephalitis.

Brain tissue biopsy revealed necrotic tissue with caseous necrosis, lymphocytes, macrophages, and epithelioid‑like cells. The initial pathology concluded chronic inflammation consistent with brain tuberculosis, and anti‑tuberculosis therapy was started.

One week after anti‑tuberculosis treatment the patient worsened: fever 39 °C, Glasgow Coma Scale 7 (E2V2M3), asymmetric sluggish pupils, tetraparesis (strength 1/5), hyperreflexia, positive Babinski, spasticity, and hand tremor. Laboratory studies showed markedly elevated transaminases; serologies for CMV, HSV‑1, HSV‑2, syphilis, and tuberculosis were negative.

A second brain MRI performed three days after admission demonstrated lesions in the subcortical and juxtacortical regions of bilateral fronto‑temporo‑parietal lobes, right occipital lobe, bilateral parieto‑occipital lobes, bilateral caudate heads, putamen, and globus pallidus without mass effect. These lesions contained early sub‑acute hemorrhage and cortical laminar necrosis in the frontal and bilateral parietal lobes. Spinal MRI was normal.

Comprehensive respiratory viral panel (adenovirus, several coronaviruses, SARS‑CoV‑2, metapneumovirus, rhinovirus/enterovirus, influenza A/B, parainfluenza 1‑4, RSV) and bacterial PCR (Bordetella pertussis/parapertussis, Chlamydia pneumoniae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae) were all negative. Cerebrospinal fluid was clear, with 100 % mononuclear cells, leukocyte count 2 cells/mm³, protein 3 mg/dL, glucose 59 mg/dL, negative Non‑ne test, positive Pandy test, negative tuberculosis Gene Xpert and acid‑fast bacilli, and sterile bacterial cultures.  

The second MRI showed hemorrhage and necrosis that were inconsistent with expected resolution of a tuberculoma.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Tuberculoma initially favored by imaging and biopsy but later deemed unlikely because CSF Gene Xpert and acid‑fast stains were negative and the second MRI revealed new hemorrhage and necrosis inconsistent with lesion resolution. | "negative of tuberculosis (Gene Xpert and fast acid bacilli examination)" and "The second MRI showed hemorrhage and necrosis, which were inappropriate with the resolution of tuberculoma."
2. Glioblastoma considered due to large heterogeneous lesion with contrast‑enhancing nodules, yet excluded by biopsy showing necrotic inflammatory tissue without malignant cells and by lack of progressive mass effect on follow‑up imaging. | "This condition suggests glioblastoma with a differential diagnosis of necrotizing toxoplasma encephalitis." and "The result showed a necrotic mass and inflammatory cells, suggesting an inflammatory process without malignancy or tuberculosis."
3. Necrotizing toxoplasma encephalitis entertained because of multiple enhancing nodules, but excluded by negative toxoplasma serology and the absence of typical ring‑enhancing lesions on MRI. | "with a differential diagnosis of necrotizing toxoplasma encephalitis."
4. Herpes simplex virus encephalitis entertained (prompted initiation of acyclovir) but not supported by negative HSV‑1/2 serology, negative CSF PCR panel, and the pattern of bilateral deep gray‑matter involvement rather than classic temporal lobe predominance. | "IV acyclovir was started with consideration of HSV infection as an etiology of ANEC."
5. Broad viral and atypical bacterial infections were systematically ruled out by a negative respiratory viral RT‑PCR panel and negative bacterial PCR, making an infectious etiology other than ANEC unlikely. | "Several viral ... and bacterial infection ... were excluded by real time‑polymerase chain reaction (RT‑PCR) examination."
6. Autoimmune encephalitis considered; serum autoimmune panel for encephalitis and MOG antibodies were negative, lowering its likelihood. | "Examination of serum showed the negativity of ... autoimmune panel for encephalitis, and Ab MOG."
7. The constellation of rapid clinical deterioration, fever, elevated transaminases, bilateral deep gray‑matter lesions with hemorrhage, and cortical laminar necrosis aligns with acute necrotizing encephalopathy of childhood (ANEC), a diagnosis made after other possibilities were excluded. | "The second MRI showed hemorrhage and necrosis, which were inappropriate with the resolution of tuberculoma; then, the diagnosis ANEC was considered."

case_prompt:
A 28‑year‑old woman was admitted because of recurrent cough for 6 years and wheezing for 7 months, worsening over the preceding half month. She had a history of cough with sputum since September 2014; tuberculosis was initially suspected and anti‑tuberculosis therapy was given, with symptom improvement. In 2015 she developed cough with fever during anti‑tuberculosis treatment and was evaluated at our hospital. Laboratory tests then showed leukocytosis, elevated ESR, CRP, and a serum total IgE of 2 500 IU/mL (normal < 130). Chest CT demonstrated multiple cavitary lesions in both upper lungs and the dorsal segment of the left lower lung, together with bilateral bronchiectasis. Sputum and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid cultures grew Aspergillus spp. and Staphylococcus aureus; she received teicoplanin and itraconazole with symptomatic relief.

She remained stable until 2019, when intermittent cough recurred and progressed to dyspnea and wheezing. At her second admission in December 2020, blood work revealed eosinophilia (0.97 × 10⁹/L) and again markedly elevated IgE (>2 500 IU/mL). Aspergillus‑specific IgE, IgM, and IgG were all elevated. Pulmonary function testing showed a moderate obstructive pattern with a positive bronchodilator response. Chest CT now showed bilateral multiple bronchiectases, pulmonary bullae, and atelectasis of the right middle lobe. A diagnosis of allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis was made; she was treated with voriconazole, methylprednisolone and inhalers, without sufficient improvement. Omalizumab was started in February 2021, but cough and wheezing worsened, prompting readmission.

On physical examination she weighed 58 kg, had facial flushing, a full “moon” face, buffalo‑back, and scaly scalp lesions. Moist rales were audible bilaterally. Laboratory studies on admission showed a CRP of 33.6 mg/L (reference 0–6), normal leukocyte count and ESR, and a serum IgE of 770 IU/mL. Serum β‑D‑glucan, galactomannan, ANA, ANCA, vasculitis antibodies, antiphospholipid antibodies, ENA panel, and rheumatoid factor were all negative. Pulmonary CT revealed diffuse multiple ground‑glass shadows, scattered striae, and numerous cystic lesions, more extensive than prior scans. Bronchoscopy demonstrated viscous jelly‑like secretions filling the tracheal lumen. The next‑generation sequencing (NGS) of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid was performed.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Opportunistic infection with Pneumocystis jirovecii considered because of diffuse ground‑glass opacities in an immunocompromised host and high‑read NGS detection. | "The next‑generation sequence (NGS) of BALF indicated Pneumocystis jirovecii (sequence reads 34909)… With classic diffuse ground‑glass lesions… we identified that the patient had … P. jirovecii coinfection."
2. Cytomegalovirus infection considered given elevated NGS reads and compatible imaging, and treated accordingly. | "The next‑generation sequence (NGS) of BALF indicated … Human Herpes Virus Type 5 (also named CMV, sequence reads 1843)… SMZ‑TMP and ganciclovir were given and symptoms were gradually relieved."
3. EBV infection excluded as pathogenic because read count was negligible. | "The sequence reads of EBV, which is ubiquitous in most of the population, were too few to be identified as pathogenic."
4. Active tuberculosis ruled out by lack of microbiologic evidence and negative recent cultures, despite remote history. | "A combined infection of aspergillosis and Staphylococcus aureus was confirmed… Anti‑infection… was prescribed, and her symptoms were relieved on therapy." (absence of TB organisms on later cultures)
5. Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis excluded as the current pulmonary infiltrates were not typical of ABPA (negative galactomannan, absence of new eosinophilic exacerbation). | "Serum -beta‑D‑glucan test, galactomannan test… were negative."
6. Bacterial pneumonia excluded due to negative sputum/BALF cultures at the time of presentation. | "A combined infection of aspergillosis and Staphylococcus aureus was confirmed… she remained stable until 2019…" (no bacterial growth now)
7. Autoimmune/vasculitic lung disease excluded by comprehensive negative autoantibody panel. | "Anti‑nuclear antibody, anti‑neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, vasculitis antibodies… were negative."
8. Non‑infectious drug‑induced lung injury excluded (no recent offending drug exposure reported). | "The patient denied any history of food or drug allergies."

case_prompt:
A 47‑year‑old man with a 30‑pack‑year smoking history was diagnosed with ankylosing spondylitis (AS) HLA‑B27 positive at age 30. Over several years he experienced cervical morning stiffness, axial inflammatory pain, bilateral sacroiliitis grade IV, lumbar spine ankylosis, syndesmophytes, and a restrictive ventilatory pattern. He received infliximab for almost 2 years after a negative latent TB screen performed 4.5 years prior, discontinued biologic therapy, and stopped rheumatology follow‑up 3 years ago.

He presented to the pulmonary department with a 3‑month history of worsening dyspnea, productive cough with mucopurulent sputum, evening sweats, fever, anorexia, and unquantified weight loss. Physical exam showed BMI < 18.5 kg/m², muscle wasting, pronounced thoracic kyphosis, reduced chest expansion, and crepitant rales over the upper thirds of both lungs. Laboratory studies revealed ESR 120 mm/h, CRP 23 mg/dL, Hb 10.3 g/dL, and albumin 3.1 g/dL. Chest X‑ray demonstrated hypotransparency of the upper lung zones with volume loss and a right upper‑lobe cavity. CT confirmed right upper‑lobe consolidation with cavitation, left upper‑lobe peripheral consolidation with air bronchogram, marked upper‑lobe volume loss, and multiple cylindrical bronchiectases.

Sputum molecular testing identified Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, and standard anti‑TB therapy was started. Persistent fever and cough led to flexible bronchoscopy, which isolated methicillin‑resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) on bronchial biopsies; appropriate antibiotics produced improvement. After seven months of anti‑TB treatment he developed a dry cough; repeat CT showed retractile fibrobullous disease (AFBD) with extensive volume loss, bronchiectasis, and a bulky right upper‑lobe cavitated lesion abutting the mediastinum. A second bronchoscopy with washings and biopsies yielded no microbiologic growth or characteristic histopathology, and the working diagnosis was progressive AFBD secondary to AS aggravated by TB sequelae. He was referred for rehabilitation, rheumatology reassessment, and thoracic surgery evaluation.

Nine months later (16 months after the initial admission) he returned with a 1‑month history of worsening productive cough, increased purulent sputum, hemoptysis, and further weight loss. Examination revealed pronounced muscle wasting, low oxygen saturation, and bilateral crepitant rales. Labs showed microcytic hypochromic anemia (Hb 9.2 g/dL), leukocytosis 18,100 µL with 93 % neutrophils, and CRP 18.7 mg/dL. Chest X‑ray displayed a markedly enlarged right upper‑lobe cavity and bilateral reticular infiltrates. Empiric antibiotics were initiated. CT demonstrated enlargement of the right upper‑lobe cavity, consolidation with air bronchograms in the upper lobes, a mass‑like lesion within the left upper‑lobe cavity, diffuse multifocal ground‑glass opacities, sub‑pleural micronodules, and tree‑in‑bud pattern. Sputum microbiology was inconclusive.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Active pulmonary tuberculosis was initially suspected due to cough, fever, weight loss, and cavitary lesions; confirmed by sputum molecular detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, prompting anti‑TB therapy. | "Sputum molecular tests detected Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTC) and first‑line anti‑bacillary therapy was initiated."
2. Superimposed bacterial infection with MRSA was considered after persistent fever and cough despite anti‑TB treatment; bronchoscopy isolated MRSA, leading to targeted antibiotics and clinical improvement. | "a methicillin‑resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) was isolated on bronchial biopsies."
3. Progressive ankylosing spondylitis‑associated fibrobullous disease (AFBD) aggravated by prior TB was proposed to explain ongoing cavitation, bronchiectasis, and volume loss when repeat bronchoscopy yielded no organisms or characteristic pathology. | "The diagnoses of progressive AFBD secondary to AS aggravated by TB sequelae were assumed."
4. Reactivation or persistence of tuberculosis was re‑evaluated after clinical worsening; repeat bronchoscopy and biopsies failed to isolate MTC or show typical histopathology, making active TB unlikely. | "Flexible bronchoscopy with bronchial wash and biopsies was repeated, with no microbiological isolation or characteristic histopathological findings."
5. Chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis became the leading diagnosis after a third bronchoscopy isolated Aspergillus fumigatus, showed elevated bronchial wash galactomannan, and increased serum Aspergillus IgG, confirming fungal colonization of the cavity. | "A new flexible bronchoscopy was performed and Aspergillus fumigatus (AF) was isolated in the bronchial wash with an elevated bronchial wash Galactomannan antigen test and elevated serum AF IgG levels."

case_prompt:
A 53‑year‑old lifelong nonsmoker woman presented to the emergency department with acute‑onset pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath that began a few hours earlier. She denied cough, sputum production, hemoptysis, fever, weight loss, anorexia, or night sweats. No family history of asthma, malignancy, or venous thrombosis was reported, and she does not keep pets.

On examination, vital signs were within normal limits except for a respiratory rate of 20 breaths per minute. Chest examination revealed reduced expansion and diminished breath sounds. Other system examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed peripheral eosinophilia with an absolute count of 1.0 K/µL (16% of leukocytes), an elevated C‑reactive protein of 13 mg/dL, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 60 mm/hr. D‑dimer was elevated at 0.72 µg/mL FEU. Chest radiography demonstrated bilateral opacities in the right middle and left lower zones. A computed tomography pulmonary angiogram was performed because of the pleuritic pain and raised D‑dimer; it was negative for pulmonary embolism but revealed soft‑tissue density masses in both lungs.

The patient was initially treated with intravenous levofloxacin, bronchodilator therapy, analgesia, and prophylactic anticoagulation, and was referred to the respiratory service for possible lung mass evaluation.

Further history uncovered intermittent shortness of breath with wheezing triggered by dust and smoke, with previous improvement after nebulized bronchodilators, though she had never been prescribed long‑term inhalers.

Flexible bronchoscopy showed a whitish, cheesy, very viscous mucus plug that was difficult to suction. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) revealed 9% eosinophils and 68% segmented neutrophils. BAL cultures grew *Streptococcus pneumoniae* and an unspecified *Aspergillus* species. Cytology and acid‑fast bacilli stains and cultures were negative.

Given the asthma‑like symptoms, peripheral eosinophilia, radiographic abnormalities, and the mucus plug, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis was suspected, and total IgE and Aspergillus‑specific IgE testing were ordered.

Primary asthma considered because of wheeze triggered by dust/smoke, yet the presence of peripheral eosinophilia, bilateral opacities, and an Aspergillus‑laden mucus plug indicated a hypersensitivity component rather than isolated asthma. | "In view of asthma‑like symptoms, peripheral eosinophilia, radiological changes, and mucous plug, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis was suspected."

case_prompt:
A 62‑year‑old man with known systemic AL amyloidosis was admitted because of fever. One year earlier he had developed bilateral leg edema and proteinuria; a renal biopsy had confirmed AL amyloidosis involving the heart, intestines and tongue. He had undergone autologous peripheral blood stem cell transplantation followed by six courses of melphalan and dexamethasone. On admission his C‑reactive protein was 5.29 mg/dL, complete blood count was normal, serum creatinine 1.08 mg/dL, and IgG 753 mg/dL. Tests for β‑D‑glucan, Aspergillus galactomannan, cytomegalovirus antigen, anti‑glycopeptidolipid‑core IgA for Mycobacterium avium, and interferon‑γ release assay were all negative.

Chest radiograph showed right pleural effusion and bilateral ground‑glass opacity. CT of the chest demonstrated right pleural effusion and multiple randomly distributed micronodules throughout both lung fields. Echocardiography revealed low ejection fraction with moderate left ventricular hypertrophy and a granular myocardial appearance.

Miliary tuberculosis was suspected, and sputum, urine and blood smears were examined; Ziehl‑Neelsen staining showed no acid‑fast bacilli. Thoracentesis yielded an exudate, but cultures of the pleural fluid did not grow common bacteria or acid‑fast organisms.

Because the risk of malignancy was deemed higher than that of transbronchial lung cryobiopsy (TBLC) in this patient with lung volume loss and reduced ejection fraction, he underwent flexible bronchoscopy. The bronchial mucosa appeared normal. Specimens were obtained from the right B2b, B3a and B4a using both forceps biopsy and TBLC under radiographic guidance.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Miliary tuberculosis considered due to micronodular pattern and pleural effusion | "Hence, miliary tuberculosis was suspected."

A 30‑year‑old individual with a Phe508del/Y1092X genotype, diffuse bronchiectasis colonised by *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* and exocrine pancreatic insufficiency experienced an infectious exacerbation in 2017 that precipitated a sharp decline in pulmonary function (nadir FEV₁ 0.63 L, 23 % predicted) and severe malnutrition (BMI 16 kg/m²). Transthoracic echocardiogram at that time showed a dilated right ventricle, an estimated systolic pulmonary artery pressure of 50 mmHg, and a patent foramen ovale, prompting discussion of lung transplantation, which the patient declined. Over the subsequent years FEV₁ stabilised around 0.8 L (30 % predicted) but remained precarious during exacerbations. In February 2019, prior to antibiotic treatment for another exacerbation, FEV₁ fell to 0.57 L (21 % predicted).  

In August 2020, a triple combination therapy (elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor) was initiated via compassionate access. One month later FEV₁ rose to 1.09 L (40 % predicted), BMI improved to 18.2 kg/m², and no further exacerbations requiring systemic antibiotics occurred.  

An unplanned pregnancy began in December 2021, four months after therapy start. Obstetric monitoring confirmed normal fetal anatomy, growth and development. Up to the 31st gestational week maternal pFEV₁ remained between 35 % and 40 % of predicted, similar to pre‑pregnancy values. Resting and nocturnal oxygen saturations were maintained, although the 6‑minute walk test showed exertional desaturation. Repeat echocardiograms at 13 weeks and 31 weeks no longer showed a patent foramen ovale or pulmonary hypertension. There was no evidence for allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis at any time point; gestational diabetes did not develop, and iron‑deficiency anaemia was corrected intravenously at weeks 31 and 32.  

At 31 weeks the patient presented with threatened preterm labour and was hospitalised; tocolysis with atosiban and nifedipine was administered, and betamethasone was given for fetal lung maturation. Concurrently she contracted a rhinovirus infection causing productive cough and bronchial congestion, and nocturnal desaturation required supplemental oxygen. Respiratory physiotherapy frequency was increased and inhaled formoterol/budesonide was started. She declined antibiotics and discharged after one week.  

At 33 weeks she developed symptomatic polyhydramnios, which was managed by amniocentesis and drainage of 2700 mL of fluid. After 12 hours of observation she returned home. At 36 weeks spontaneous rupture of membranes occurred, and she delivered a healthy 2.7 kg infant vaginally. Post‑partum, nocturnal hypoxemia resolved rapidly, oxygen therapy was stopped, and at four months postpartum FEV₁ was 1.07 L (40 % predicted), comparable to pre‑pregnancy levels. The infant’s growth and development remain normal at 12 months.

A 51‑year‑old woman with hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and a history of dysfunctional uterine bleeding presented with three weeks of progressive lower‑extremity swelling, pain, and tenderness without warmth or erythema. She noted heavy menses for five years that ceased after menopause two years earlier. She denied chest pain, dyspnea, orthopnea, cough, fever, weight loss, or dysuria and had no history of intravenous drug use.  

On examination she was afebrile, with jugular venous distention and +3 bilateral pedal edema. Cardiac auscultation revealed a grade III/VI holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border; lungs were clear. Abdomen was soft, mildly tender suprapubically, with active bowel sounds; no skin lesions or stigmata of chronic liver disease were noted.  

Laboratory studies showed mild thrombocytopenia with normal ESR and CRP. ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm and incomplete right bundle‑branch block. Transthoracic echocardiography identified severe tricuspid regurgitation and a tricuspid valve vegetation with preserved left‑ventricular ejection fraction. CT pulmonary angiography revealed a filling defect in the left lower pulmonary artery suggestive of a calcified embolus and multiple bilateral sub‑centimeter pulmonary nodules appearing contiguous with the vasculature.  

Transesophageal echocardiography confirmed a large vegetation oscillating between the right ventricle and right atrium on the posterior and septal leaflets of the tricuspid valve, with additional small vegetations on the anterior leaflet.  

Extensive infectious work‑up—including multiple blood cultures and serologies for *Chlamydophila pneumoniae*, *C. psittaci*, *Brucella*, *Bartonella*, *Coxiella burnetii*, and *Legionella*—was negative, as was a full autoimmune panel.  

Given the absence of an infectious or autoimmune source, metastatic disease was considered. Abdominal CT and MRI demonstrated a large fundal uterine fibroid with cystic degeneration and an exophytic fibroid extending toward the left adnexa. Endometrial biopsy showed endometrial and endocervical tissue with tubal metaplasia without atypia or malignancy.  

Because of severe symptomatic tricuspid regurgitation from the aseptic vegetation, the patient underwent cardiothoracic surgery. Intraoperatively a discrete 2.37 × 1.15 cm mass attached to tricuspid valve tissue was excised; severe degeneration and destruction of all valve leaflets were noted, a sub‑valvular abscess was debrided, and the valve was replaced with a #31 Epic St Jude tissue valve. The postoperative course was uneventful, and follow‑up showed marked improvement in dyspnea and edema.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Infectious tricuspid endocarditis considered but deemed unlikely because “Infectious workup, including multiple blood cultures… were all negative.”  
2. Autoimmune aseptic vegetations entertained yet excluded as “All autoimmune workup was negative.”  
3. Metastatic malignancy raised as a possible etiology after infectious and autoimmune causes were ruled out: “Computed tomography pulmonary angiogram appeared to be consistent with septic emboli; however, given the lack of infectious and autoimmune source, metastasis was suspected.”  
4. Benign metastasizing leiomyoma ultimately identified by histology showing a smooth‑muscle neoplasm with strong desmin, smooth‑muscle, estrogen, progesterone, and WT‑1 positivity, supporting a uterine origin: “Microscopically… it was smooth muscle neoplasm… Diffuse and strong positivity for desmin… and Wilms tumor gene 1, suggesting likely uterine origin, and represented BML.”

case_prompt:
In July 2008, a 73‑year‑old man was admitted to La Timone Hospital, Marseille, because of suspected displacement of an aortic bioprosthetic valve that had been implanted in January 2008 for aortic insufficiency. After returning home in March, he performed gardening activities and used potting mixes to plant flowers.

In April, he presented to a general‑hospital emergency department with fever (38.9 °C). Leukocyte count was 12 × 10⁹ cells/L. He received amoxicillin/clavulanic acid plus ciprofloxacin empirically. Chest radiograph, transesophageal echocardiography, three blood cultures, urine analysis, and Legionella urinary antigen test failed to identify an infectious agent, and antibiotics were stopped after 24 h.

In May, he had a second fever episode (39 °C) with a 20‑kg weight loss over three months and was admitted to the cardiology department. An endocarditis diagnostic kit was performed, including serologies for Coxiella burnetii, Bartonella spp., Brucella spp., Chlamydia spp., Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Legionella pneumophila, L. anisa, and Aspergillus spp.; all were negative. The modified Durack score yielded only two minor criteria and the Richet score was 3 (fever, male sex, previous valvular pathology). He was discharged without antimicrobial therapy.

In July, he was readmitted for heart failure. Transesophageal echocardiography showed displacement of the aortic bioprosthesis with a false aneurysm and a 9 mm vegetation. Laboratory studies revealed leukocytes 9.4 × 10⁹ cells/L, hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, ESR 53 mm, and CRP 126 mg/L. Repeat endocarditis serologies remained negative except for a positive L. anisa titer of 256. Blood cultures were sterile. Blood‑culture‑negative endocarditis was diagnosed, and intravenous vancomycin (30 mg/kg/d) plus gentamicin (3 mg/kg/d) was started.

After 30 days, because of persistent heart failure, cardiac surgery was performed; the aortic bioprosthesis was replaced.
diagnostic_reasoning:

The radiology report concluded a “likely abscessual lesion.” The authors considered this inconsistent with the normal white‑cell count and atypical for hepatocellular carcinoma, which usually appears hypodense on CT.

He denied exposure to contaminated water or travel to epidemic areas. His mother had pulmonary tuberculosis 10 years earlier. Spectral Doppler showed markedly increased peak systolic velocities in the origins of the superior mesenteric artery (643 cm/s) and celiac artery, suggesting significant stenosis.

No pathogenic microorganisms were identified in biopsy tissue. Cytomegalovirus DNA and IgM were repeatedly negative, and cytomegalic inclusion bodies were absent.

Given the exposure history and regional epidemiology, serologic testing for Brucella was performed. Two months later he returned with intermittent headache, fever, unsteady gait, and vomiting. Lumbar puncture showed elevated protein, neutrophilic pleocytosis, and normal glucose; empiric antibiotics for meningitis were started. Repeated lumbar punctures continued to show substantial pleocytosis and elevated protein. Additional evaluations—including head‑and‑neck vascular imaging, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, temporal artery biopsy, brain biopsy, and ophthalmologic exam—were nondiagnostic. Broad‑spectrum antibiotics failed to improve his condition, and his functional status steadily declined. On a subsequent admission he was found in generalized non‑convulsive status epilepticus; steroids and antiepileptic drugs were initiated, leading to near‑immediate improvement in mental status. Despite this, periodic fevers and rash recurred roughly every two weeks. Over the next several months intravenous immunoglobulin and mycophenolate were trialed; however, the patient continued to be readmitted on a monthly basis.

A 70‑year‑old Kuwaiti man with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, atrial fibrillation, and a pacemaker placed a year earlier presented after a mechanical fall. He reported dizziness, urinary incontinence, intermittent subjective fever, nausea, and a brief episode of non‑bilious, non‑bloody vomiting. He had recently traveled to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and drank unpasteurized camel milk.

On admission he was febrile (38.9 °C); hemodynamics and respiratory status were stable. Physical examination noted a new pansystolic murmur; there were no classic stigmata of infective endocarditis, joint pain, or musculoskeletal findings. Laboratory studies showed a normal white‑blood‑cell count and differential, mild hyponatremia, and hypoglycemia. Acute abdominal series and head CT were unrevealing. Because of the discordance with the pacemaker leads, a transesophageal echocardiogram was performed at a specialized center. Seven days prior to admission she had sought medical help for the same pain, which was deemed musculoskeletal and she was prescribed diclofenac 50 mg PO twice daily; the drug was stopped on admission. Blood biochemistry at that initial visit was normal. After three days of diclofenac she developed nausea, vomiting, and jaundice but continued the medication. Past medical history included primary myelofibrosis diagnosed two years earlier, arterial hypertension treated with quinapril for 15 years, and heterozygosity for beta‑thalassemia trait. She denied use of herbal agents, dietary supplements, illicit drugs, or alcohol, and had no prior liver disease. Physical examination showed hepatosplenomegaly and deep jaundice without signs of hepatic encephalopathy.

Laboratory abnormalities were: hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL, platelets 73 × 10³/µL, INR 2.32, albumin 3.3 g/dL, total bilirubin 21.6 mg/dL (direct 15.4 mg/dL), AST 717 IU/L, ALT 679 IU/L, γ‑GT 56 IU/L, IgG 1760 mg/dL (ULN = 1500). Chest X‑ray demonstrated a left pleural effusion; ECG showed a right bundle‑branch block. Arterial blood gas analysis revealed respiratory alkalosis (pH 7.52, pO₂ 68 mmHg, pCO₂ 28 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 22.9 mEq/L).

Because of the pleural effusion, right‑bundle‑branch block, and respiratory alkalosis in a pro‑coagulant patient, CT pulmonary angiography was performed and excluded pulmonary embolism or thrombosis. Liver biopsy was not undertaken at this stage due to absolute contraindications.

The differential diagnosis considered all potential causes of acute severe hepatitis. Acute viral hepatitis was excluded by negative serologies. Budd‑Chiari syndrome and ischemic hepatitis secondary to massive pulmonary embolism or thrombosis were considered but ruled out by imaging. Alcoholic hepatitis was excluded based on the patient’s denial of alcohol use. An idiosyncratic drug‑induced liver injury (DILI) from recent diclofenac use was also seriously considered.

Ischemic hepatitis from massive pulmonary embolism/thrombosis considered given respiratory alkalosis and pleural effusion, but CT pulmonary angiography ruled out embolism. | "ischemic hepatitis as a consequence of massive pulmonary embolism or thrombosis were also considered. Further evaluation was performed because of persistently elevated ESR and aortic regurgitation of unclear etiology. Physical exam showed decreased deep‑tendon reflexes. Initial labs: WBC 3,650/mm³ (44% neutrophils, 56% lymphocytes), hemoglobin 13 g/dL, platelets 259,000/mm³, ESR 29 mm/hr, CRP negative. ANA was 1:2,560 and anti‑dsDNA was positive. Cerebellar testing revealed abnormal finger‑to‑nose and tandem gait. Cerebrospinal fluid, brain MRI, chest X‑ray, and abdominal‑pelvic ultrasound were normal. EMG and nerve conduction studies showed absent compound sensory nerve action potentials. He was diagnosed with Guillain‑Barre syndrome (GBS) per Asbury criteria and received intravenous immunoglobulin, without improvement; he developed severe headaches and disrupted sleep. Bone‑marrow aspiration was normal. Cardiology evaluation found mild mitral and tricuspid regurgitation. Additional labs (CK, LDH, thyroid panel, immunoglobulins, anticardiolipin, anti‑Smith, β2‑glycoprotein, lupus anticoagulant) were negative or normal. Serologies for brucellosis, mononucleosis, tuberculosis, bacterial and fungal infections, and throat culture were negative. Urinalysis was normal. His condition improved, gait disorder lessened, and he was discharged.

Two weeks later he was readmitted with leg pain, loss of balance, walking instability, lower‑extremity weakness, and anorexia. Cerebellar testing and DTRs remained abnormal; distal strength in upper and lower limbs was reduced. Vitamin B12 and E levels were normal. Total spinal MRI was normal. EMG/NCV again demonstrated chronic mild sensory‑motor demyelination. He was treated with a 5‑day pulse of methylprednisolone followed by oral prednisolone for 3 months, then tapered. One month after stopping prednisone, he developed severe weakness of all limbs, walking instability, and gait disorder, with persistent decreased lower‑extremity DTRs and cerebellar testing abnormalities. Laboratory tests were ordered again due to the possibility of lupus.

An 80‑year‑old man with arterial hypertension and advanced clear‑cell renal carcinoma (diagnosed 2015) had been treated sequentially with sunitinib (first line), axitinib (second line) and, after progression, nivolumab as third‑line therapy. After four cycles of nivolumab he was admitted for severe asthenia and uncontrolled pain from subcutaneous tumor infiltration. He denied chest pain.  

Vital signs on admission were notable for atrial fibrillation and a left bundle‑branch block on electrocardiogram. Laboratory studies showed markedly elevated cardiac enzymes: creatine kinase 1,853 U/L (normal 38‑174), troponin I 19.4 ng/mL (normal < 0.1), and brain natriuretic peptide 1,413 pg/mL (normal < 100). Inflammatory markers were high (C‑reactive protein 151.8 mg/L, normal < 5) with lymphopenia (670/µL, normal > 1,000).  

A transthoracic echocardiogram performed at admission revealed preserved left‑ventricular systolic function with mild concentric hypertrophy and dyssynchrony, unchanged from an examination 4 months earlier. High‑dose intravenous methylprednisolone (2 mg/kg/day) was started. Subsequent labs showed decreasing CK (1,275 U/L), troponin I (14 ng/mL) and CRP (108.3 mg/L).  

Comprehensive infectious work‑up was negative: serologies for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV, varicella‑zoster, Epstein‑Barr, cytomegalovirus, parvovirus, and bacterial agents associated with myocarditis (Brucella, Treponema pallidum, Leptospira, Borrelia, Rickettsia) were all non‑reactive. Cardiologists judged the presentation non‑ischemic. Repeat echocardiography 4 days later showed a slight reduction in left‑ventricular ejection fraction to 50 %.  

Autoimmune evaluation identified elevated anti‑acetylcholine‑receptor antibodies (2.06 nmol/mL, normal < 0.45) and positive anti‑striated‑muscle antibodies; antinuclear and anti‑smooth‑muscle antibodies were negative.

2. Ischemic myocardial injury deemed unlikely: “cardiological evaluation… reported that the clinical presentation was not suggestive of ischemia” and the patient had no anginal symptoms.  
3. Bacterial infection as cause of myocarditis ruled out: “serologies of bacteria that could potentially cause myocarditis… (brucella, treponema pallidum, leptospira, borrelia, rickettsia) were negative.”  
4. Autoimmune myasthenia gravis identified, suggesting an immune‑mediated process: “elevation of antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor… compatible with immunological diagnosis of myasthenia gravis” and “antibodies against striated muscle were also positive.”  
5. Immune checkpoint inhibitor–related myocarditis favored due to temporal relationship with nivolumab therapy, lack of infectious/ischemic explanations, and immunologic findings: “He had no history of autoimmune disorders before nivolumab treatment… the ratio of CD8/CD4 cells was 80%/20%, and 40% of all lymphocytes were PD‑1 positive,” supporting a drug‑induced T‑cell–mediated myocardial inflammation.

She reported longstanding dystrophic nails of the hands and feet, previously labeled onychomycosis for at least five years with multiple antifungal courses that yielded no clinical improvement and no fungal growth on culture. Her sister had juvenile idiopathic arthritis and died of chronic renal failure at age 13.

On first examination she weighed 24 kg (<3 percentile) and measured 132 cm in height (<3 percentile), demonstrating failure to thrive. Musculoskeletal examination revealed limited left elbow dorsiflexion, restricted hip abduction, swelling of both knees, and Achilles‑tendon tenderness. Dermatologic assessment identified nail psoriasis with onycholysis, leukonychia, and nail‑plate crumbling (Figure 1). Laboratory studies showed: WBC 7,960/mm³ (56 % neutrophils, 44 % lymphocytes), hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL, hematocrit 32.8 %, platelets 392,000/mm³, CRP 5 mg/dL (norm < 0.5), ESR 105 mm/hr (norm < 15), IgG 2,230 mg/dL, IgM 242 mg/dL, IgA 201 mg/dL (hypergammaglobulinemia). Total IgE, eosinophil count, lymphocyte subsets, and granulocyte oxidative burst were within normal limits. Tuberculosis evaluation revealed two BCG scars, a negative tuberculin skin test, and a negative QuantiFERON‑TB Gold assay. Abdominal and renal ultrasonography were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies demonstrated leukocytosis (12.4 × 10⁹ cells/L), mild anemia (hemoglobin 130 g/L), and an elevated C‑reactive protein (87.3 mg/L). Five sets of blood cultures obtained before antibiotics remained negative after 7 days, and cultures of the excised valve and vegetation on standard enriched media were also negative. Indirect detection assays were performed and were negative, including specific PCRs on oropharyngeal samples and valve tissue for Chlamydophila pneumoniae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Bordetella spp., Treponema pallidum, Tropheryma whipplei, Brucella spp., Bartonella henselae, and Bordetella quintana; a Legionella pneumophila urinary antigen test; and serologies for Coxiella burnetii, Bartonella henselae, and Brucella spp. Broad‑range 16S rDNA PCR on a valve fragment was likewise negative. A 75‑year‑old cattle farmer underwent an uneventful left‑sided cemented total hip replacement for degenerative disease. Six months later his cattle herd was slaughtered after detection of brucellosis, and one month thereafter he was admitted for fever and generalized fatigue. Six months after completing therapy he noted occasional left hip pain; examination revealed tenderness over the greater trochanter. An x‑ray showed the prosthesis in satisfactory position but mild loosening of the acetabular component. C‑reactive protein was 3 mg/L and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 18 mm/h. Intra‑operative samples grew Staphylococcus epidermidis, and he was treated with two weeks of intravenous flucloxacillin followed by suppressive oral flucloxacillin and fusidic acid. He declined a two‑stage revision and was followed annually with stable clinical status and normal inflammatory markers while on oral flucloxacillin.

Thirteen years later he again reported left‑sided hip pain. Radiographs demonstrated loosening and a cavitary defect of the acetabular component of the cemented hip replacement. He consented to a two‑stage reconstructive surgery. During the first stage, three of six tissue specimens cultured on enrichment medium grew a Gram‑negative coccobacillus.
