The day before admission she developed a gradual decline in awareness. She had no prior medical problems, two uncomplicated pregnancies, and her mother denied animal contact, recent travel, drug use, or toxin exposure; the patient reported reduced water and food intake in the preceding days.

On examination her blood pressure was normal, heart rate was tachycardic with a weak pulse, dry mucous membranes, and prolonged capillary refill time were noted. Neurologically she was disoriented, had retrograde amnesia, impaired judgment, and loss of abstract thinking. Chest X‑ray and head CT were normal.

Laboratory studies revealed severe hypernatremia (Na 180 mEq/L) and acute kidney injury (creatinine 2.0 mg/dL, baseline 0.6 mg/dL). Serum electrolytes, liver panel, complete blood count, urinalysis, and toxicology screen were otherwise normal. Spot urine sodium was 20 mEq/L with a fractional excretion of sodium of 0.5%, indicating hypovolemia. Calculated water deficit was 7.5 L, yet electrolyte‑free water excretion was inappropriately high at 805 mL over a 24‑hour urine volume of 1,000 mL.

She was treated with free water and hypotonic IV fluids, leading to partial clinical improvement and resolution of AKI, but hypernatremia persisted (Na 157 mEq/L) with mild hypokalemia (K 3.2 mEq/L). Urinary sodium fell to 8 mEq/L, urine osmolality 85 mOsm/kg, urine output increased to 4 L/24 h, and electrolyte‑free water excretion rose to 3.3 L, suggesting diabetes insipidus. Because water deprivation testing was contraindicated, a brain MRI was obtained, revealing a pituitary stalk lesion extending into the optic chiasm and hypothalamus.

Desmopressin therapy normalized sodium and urine output. Hormonal testing showed panhypopituitarism, prompting thyroid and glucocorticoid replacement. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis demonstrated elevated protein (75 mg/dL), normal glucose, zero cells, and negative Gram and India‑ink stains. An EEG showed diffuse cerebral dysfunction without epileptiform activity. Blood, urine, CSF, and bone‑marrow cultures were all negative. CSF PCR for viruses and Mycobacterium tuberculosis was negative. Anti‑N‑methyl‑D‑aspartate (NMDA) receptor antibodies in CSF were positive. Thoraco‑abdominopelvic CT, endovaginal ultrasound, and whole‑body scintigraphy were unremarkable.

Given the clinical picture, a stereotactic biopsy of the pituitary mass was scheduled.

Neurologically, Glasgow Coma Scale was 14/15; pupils reactive 4 mm; fundoscopy showed early papilledema. Musculoskeletal exam demonstrated slightly decreased bulk, flaccid tone, power 4/5 in all limbs, intact sensation, grade II reflexes, downgoing plantar responses, and positive Kernig’s and Brudzinski’s signs.

Laboratory studies: Hb 13.2 g/dL, WBC 13,000/mm³ (neutrophils 85%, lymphocytes 10%), platelets 211,000/mm³, ESR 31 mm/hr. Renal panel showed BUN 30 mg/dL, creatinine 0.46 mg/dL. HIV I/II, HBsAg, and HCV tests were negative. Chest X‑ray demonstrated bilateral consolidation; abdominal ultrasound confirmed mild hepatomegaly; MRI brain showed leptomeningeal enhancement and mild thickening without basal exudates or hydrocephalus, suggesting meningoencephalitis. Echocardiography identified a 12‑mm perimembranous ventricular septal defect partially closed by the tricuspid leaflet with mild tricuspid regurgitation.

Lumbar puncture revealed an opening pressure of 27 cm H₂O. CSF analysis: RBC 3 cells, WBC 204 cells (5% neutrophils, 95% lymphocytes), glucose 46 mg/dL, protein 24 mg/dL, ADA 2.1 U/L. Gram stain, acid‑fast bacilli stain, and cultures were negative.

Additional investigations performed at the second hospital included leptospira IgM, brucella IgM, malaria antigen, and Mantoux tuberculin skin test—all negative; blood and urine cultures were negative; sputum AFB smear and culture were negative; GeneXpert was unavailable. Tubercular meningitis was deemed unlikely because there was no history of contact with active TB patients, CSF was clear, AFB staining was negative, and CSF ADA was not elevated. A 76‑year‑old man with a history of benign prostatic hyperplasia, type II diabetes mellitus, obstructive sleep apnea, and a 2‑month history of unintentional weight loss presented to the emergency department with acute left‑sided flank pain, lightheadedness, and progressive dyspnea on exertion. Two weeks earlier, an outpatient abdominal CT had demonstrated a 4 mm hypodense pancreatic lesion; MRI was recommended but delayed due to the new flank pain. He denied fever, chills, urinary or gastrointestinal symptoms, lymphadenopathy, bruising, or bleeding. His smoking history was 2.5 pack‑years; he did not use alcohol or illicit substances and had no family history of cancer. Home medications included nifedipine, valsartan‑hydrochlorothiazide, pravastatin, aspirin, finasteride, tamsulosin, and metformin. He was up‑to‑date on age‑appropriate cancer screening, including colonoscopy.

On arrival, vital signs were: BP 136/52 mm Hg, HR 58 beats/min, T 36.3 °C, RR 18 breaths/min, SpO₂ 96 % on room air. Physical examination revealed temporal wasting; abdomen was soft without tenderness, hepatosplenomegaly, or masses; no cervical, supraclavicular, axillary, or inguinal lymphadenopathy; cardiac exam was normal; respiratory effort was unremarkable; neurologic and musculoskeletal examinations were within normal limits.

Laboratory studies showed normocytic anemia (Hb 11.9 g/dL) and thrombocytopenia (144 K/µL). Comprehensive metabolic panel revealed a mildly elevated AST (43 U/L) and creatinine (1.26 mg/dL). Coagulation testing showed INR 1.19; D‑dimer was elevated at 1.19 µg/mL FEU. Contrast CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis identified multiple acute splenic infarcts.

The patient was started on a heparin infusion for presumed thromboembolic splenic infarction. A transthoracic echocardiogram with agitated saline showed no patent foramen ovale; telemetry revealed no arrhythmias. MRI of the abdomen demonstrated a normal pancreas. Screening for hypercoagulable states and malignancy (CEA, CA 19‑9, PSA, cardiolipin antibodies) was negative. He was discharged on enoxaparin bridging to warfarin with outpatient follow‑up.

Two days later, he returned with worsening abdominal pain and orthostatic hypotension. Repeat CT angiography showed progression of splenic infarcts and a new left pleural effusion. Liver enzymes rose markedly (AST 146 U/L, ALT 157 U/L). Viral hepatitis serologies and autoimmune panel (ANA, AMA, ASMA) were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed a normal liver with patent vasculature; MRCP excluded cholestasis. Endoscopy and colonoscopy were unrevealing for bleeding sources.

On hospital day 4, he developed fever (38.6 °C). Chest radiograph, urinalysis, and blood cultures were negative. Additional infectious work‑up (CMV, Brucella, Q fever, Toxoplasma IgG, urine Histoplasma antigen) was negative; EBV PCR showed a low viral load (1 080 copies/mL) considered incidental. Interferon‑γ release assay was positive without active disease. Anticoagulation was stopped due to anemia and lack of a clear thrombotic source. Ferritin was markedly elevated at 17 515 ng/mL (reference 30‑400 ng/mL). Triglycerides were 544 mg/dL. Because of extreme hyperferritinemia (>10 000 ng/mL), hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) was considered. The patient’s ferritin rose to 59 000 ng/mL, platelets fell to 49 K/µL, and transaminases surged (AST 807 U/L, ALT 435 U/L). A liver biopsy was planned but postponed due to coagulopathy.

A 37‑year‑old woman presented eleven months postpartum with worsening headaches, nausea, vomiting, visual changes, and a 10‑lb weight loss. Her past medical history included peripheral neuropathies, mood disorder, herpes labialis, chronic hepatitis C, and intravenous drug use (heroin, cocaine) on buprenorphine. She had received epidural anesthesia during delivery and a second epidural injection during labor. Persistent post‑delivery headaches were initially attributed to a presumed cerebrospinal fluid leak; she underwent an epidural blood patch without symptom improvement. She described a generalized, dull headache that worsened with both lying down and standing, accompanied by photophobia, papilledema, diplopia, mild bilateral cranial nerve VI palsy, and decreased visual acuity.  

Initial lumbar puncture revealed a nucleated cell count of 179 µL (50 % polymorphonuclear cells, 42 % lymphocytes, 6 % monocytes), low glucose of 36 mg/dL (serum glucose 92 mg/dL), and protein 287 mg/dL, suggestive of bacterial meningitis. CSF cultures were negative for histoplasma, tuberculosis, acid‑fast bacilli, Cryptococcus, fungi, and viruses. Serum testing was negative for HIV, listeria, Brucella, VDRL, syphilis, and Lyme disease; hepatitis A and C serologies were positive. Autoimmune serologies (ANA, anti‑Ro/La, ANCA) were negative; CRP was normal with a mildly elevated ESR.  

MRI of the lumbar spine demonstrated diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement of the distal spinal cord, conus medullaris, and cauda equina nerve roots extending bilaterally beyond the neural foramina. The dura was thickened and avidly enhanced from L5 to S2, with a fluid‑fluid level on T2‑weighted images and marked diffusion restriction from L4 to S2.  

The patient was started on a 5‑day course of methylprednisolone with partial symptom improvement, but headaches, back pain, and visual changes recurred when steroids were tapered. Repeat MRI one month later showed persistent leptomeningeal enhancement with no interval change. A second lumbar puncture showed a marked increase in nucleated cells to 2,682 µL (94 % polymorphonuclear cells), glucose 26 mg/dL, protein 297 mg/dL, and 13 bands. White blood cell count rose to 23.2 × 10⁹/L from 16.4 × 10⁹/L three months earlier, though the patient remained afebrile.

4. Viral meningitis (including HSV, CMV) was part of the differential, yet “CSF cultures … negative for viruses” and the neutrophilic predominance made viral etiology less likely.  
5. Syphilis and Lyme disease were ruled out with negative serology (“negative serology for … VDRL, syphilis, and lyme”).  
6. Autoimmune/inflammatory chronic neutrophilic meningitis was suggested by the infectious disease team given “the nature of her pain and her complicated medical history,” but the lack of response to steroids after taper and the progressive neutrophilic CSF profile without systemic autoimmune markers made it insufficient to explain the disease.  
7. Empirical antibiotics and NSAIDs administered at another hospital did not relieve her symptoms.

Four weeks after vaccination she presented to our emergency department. On examination she was febrile (38.7 °C), blood pressure 100/72 mmHg, heart rate 162 beats/min, and oxygen saturation 96 % on room air. Auscultation revealed bilateral basal crepitations. ECG showed atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response of 150–160 beats/min without ST‑segment or T‑wave changes. Laboratory studies demonstrated troponin T 7 000 ng/mL, B‑type natriuretic peptide >26 000 pg/mL, white blood cell count 20.44 × 10⁹/L (neutrophils 19.06 × 10⁹/L), C‑reactive protein 22.4 ng/dL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 28 mm/h, AST 112 U/L and ALT 116 U/L. Chest X‑ray showed pulmonary congestion; thoracic CT was unremarkable. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 16–20 % with global hypokinesia, moderate mitral regurgitation, and tricuspid regurgitation; no pericardial effusion was seen. Coronary angiography demonstrated no obstructive coronary artery disease. Endomyocardial biopsy of the right ventricular septum was non‑diagnostic. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed increased native T1 relaxation time and high T2 signal intensity, meeting the Lake Louise criteria for myocarditis. An extensive infectious work‑up (serology, PCR, cultures from blood, urine, stool, throat, nasopharyngeal swab, and other fluids) failed to identify a pathogen, and the patient was labeled as having vaccination‑induced myocarditis. She received diuretics, amiodarone, and apixaban. During hospitalization she experienced a brief episode of shock requiring norepinephrine and high‑flow oxygen, which stabilized after rate control.

Despite hemodynamic improvement, she continued to have high fever, polyarthralgia, leukocytosis, and elevated CRP. Ferritin was markedly elevated at 68 913 pmol/L. A diffuse, non‑itchy, salmon‑pink macular rash appeared predominantly on the trunk with some limb involvement. Autoantibody screening—including antinuclear antibody, anti‑double‑stranded DNA, anti‑extractable nuclear antigens, and rheumatoid factor—was negative. PET‑CT demonstrated lymphadenopathy in cervical, bilateral axillary, mediastinal, hilar, porta hepatis, and peripancreatic regions (SUVmax 4.7) but revealed no evidence of malignancy, infection, or systemic sarcoidosis.

case_prompt: A 45‑year‑old man presented with fever, cough, and body aches and was diagnosed with SARS‑CoV‑2 infection by RT‑PCR. His illness was mild, managed outpatient with loratadine, acetaminophen, and azithromycin for 5 days, and he recovered fully. Two weeks later he complained of weakness, jaundice, and pruritus, without fever. He denied recent travel, alcohol, herbal products, or illicit drug use. Laboratory studies showed a cholestatic pattern of acute hepatitis with markedly elevated liver enzymes, total and direct bilirubin, and ferritin; INR, albumin, and γ‑globulin were unchanged. Renal function was impaired but later normalized; complement levels, creatine kinase, and urinalysis were normal. Because a specific diagnosis was lacking, an ultrasound‑guided percutaneous liver biopsy was performed, revealing acute/subacute hepatitis with numerous lobular necrotic foci, moderate canalicular and intrahepatocytic cholestasis (predominantly zone 3), without ductopenia or portal biliary reaction. Initial labs showed normal CBC, liver and renal panels, coagulation profile, and inflammatory markers except an elevated ferritin (480.2 µg/L; normal 23.9‑336.2). Repeated SARS‑CoV‑2 nasopharyngeal swabs every three days were negative. Blood, urine, and sputum cultures were negative for bacteria, mycobacteria, or fungi. Two next‑generation sequencing assays of peripheral blood were negative. Viral panels for CMV, HIV, hepatotropic viruses, HSV, influenza, parvovirus, adenovirus, and atypical respiratory pathogens were all negative. EBV DNA in peripheral‑blood lymphocytes was 1,780 copies/mL (normal < 500), but plasma EBV DNA and EBV‑IgM were negative. PET‑CT and bone‑marrow aspiration/biopsy showed no malignant lesions. Ultrasound did not reveal hepatomegaly or splenomegaly. Serum tumor markers, immunofixation electrophoresis, superficial lymph‑node ultrasound, and head MRI were unremarkable except for a persistently elevated carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA 21 ng/mL, similar to prior 25.7 ng/mL). Rheumatologic work‑up showed a 1:320 ANA, 1:100 anti‑dsDNA, and mildly low C3 (0.546 g/L); anti‑ENA, antiphospholipid antibodies, direct Coombs, ANCA, and rheumatoid factor were negative.

During hospitalization his fever escalated to 39.8 °C and his mental status declined. Laboratory trends showed decreasing leukocytes, hemoglobin, and platelets; ferritin rose further; liver enzymes increased; fibrinogen fell; and natural killer cell activity was reduced. Bone‑marrow aspiration demonstrated hemophagocytosis.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Persistent SARS‑CoV‑2 infection was excluded because “SARS‑Cov‑2 nasopharyngeal swabs were performed every three days and all of the tests were negative.”  
2. Bacterial, mycobacterial, and fungal sepsis were ruled out as “Multiple cultures sets of blood, urine, and sputum were negative for bacteria, mycobacteria, or fungi.”  
3. Other viral etiologies were excluded: “Viral infections (CMV, human immunodeficiency virus, hepatotropic viruses, herpes simplex virus, influenza virus, parvovirus, adenovirus and atypical respiratory pathogens) were promptly ruled out.”  
4. EBV primary infection was unlikely given the pattern: “EBV‑DNA in peripheral blood lymphocytes was 1780 copies/mL … EBV‑DNA in plasma and EBV‑IgM antibody were negative.”  
5. Malignancy was not supported: “No signs of malignant lesions were found in positron emission tomography‑computed tomography (PET‑CT) or bone marrow aspiration and biopsy.”  
6. Connective‑tissue disease (e.g., systemic lupus erythematosus) was considered but not confirmed: “Rheumatologic tests showed the 1:320 positive antinuclear antibody, 1:100 positive anti‑dsDNA antibody … Other indications of connective tissue disease … were all negative.”  
7. Drug‑induced fever or hypersensitivity reaction was unlikely because “There was no history of environmental, occupational or long‑term drug exposure.”  
8. The constellation of fever, cytopenias, hyper‑ferritinemia, hypofibrinogenemia, low NK‑cell activity, and hemophagocytosis satisfied HLH‑2004 criteria, leading to the diagnosis of secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis.

Analytic Distinctions: The authors excluded diabetes mellitus (normal glucose, no glycosuria), nephrogenic DI (rapid rise in urine osmolality after desmopressin), primary polydipsia (high plasma sodium, low urine specific gravity), infectious or infiltrative causes of stalk thickening (negative cultures, normal immunoglobulins, negative Quantiferon), and anterior pituitary dysfunction (normal hormonal panel). case_prompt:
A 16‑year‑old boy presented to the Paediatric Emergency Department with polyuria, polydipsia, and a weight loss of nearly 6 kg over four months. He reported a urine output of 9 L in the previous 24 hours. Symptoms began a few days after the first dose of the BNT162b2 mRNA COVID‑19 vaccine and worsened after the second dose administered 28 days later. Prior urologic assessment and renal ultrasound were unremarkable. Past medical and family histories were non‑contributory.

On arrival, vital signs were: heart rate 110 bpm, temperature 36 °C, oxygen saturation 99 % on room air. Physical examination was notable only for well‑being; growth parameters were within normal limits, and cardiac, pulmonary, neurological, head and neck, gastrointestinal, and musculoskeletal examinations were normal. Laboratory studies, venous blood gas, and urine analysis showed no significant abnormalities. Hematic glucose was normal and glycosuria was absent, excluding diabetes mellitus. Plasma sodium was at the upper limit of normal and urine specific gravity was low, raising suspicion for diabetes insipidus.

Fluid balance monitoring recorded an intake of 6.250 L and an output of 7.100 L per day. Serum osmolality was 287 mOsm/kg (normal 285–305) and urine osmolality was 68 mOsm/kg (normal 100–1100), yielding a urine‑to‑serum osmolality ratio < 1. The patient’s parents declined a water‑deprivation test. A low‑dose oral desmopressin challenge (sublingual 60 µg) was administered; within hours, fluid balance normalized (intake 0.520 L, output 0.600 L) and urine osmolality rose to 119 mOsm/kg.

Hormonal evaluation revealed no impairment of anterior pituitary function, immunoglobulin levels (IgA, IgM, IgG subclasses, IgG4) were normal, and urine culture and Quantiferon testing were negative. Contrast‑enhanced brain MRI focused on the pituitary region demonstrated a thickened pituitary stalk (maximum diameter 4 mm) with contrast enhancement and loss of the posterior pituitary bright spot on T1‑weighted images, findings consistent with neuroinfundibulohypophysitis.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Diabetes mellitus considered but excluded due to normal blood glucose and absence of glycosuria. | "Diabetes mellitus was excluded by detection of normal hematic glucose levels and by the absence of glycosuria."
2. Primary polydipsia deemed unlikely because plasma sodium was at the upper limit of normal and urine specific gravity was low, suggesting a concentrate‑defect rather than excess intake. | "Diabetes insipidus could be suspected because of plasma sodium level at the upper limit of normal and low urine specific gravity."
3. Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus ruled out by the rapid increase in urine osmolality after desmopressin administration, indicating intact renal response to ADH. | "After administration of low dose oral desmopressin … rapid increase of u‑Osm (119 mOsm/Kg H2O)."
4. Central versus nephrogenic DI differentiated by desmopressin challenge; the positive response supports central DI. | "A test with desmopressin … an immediate response was evident … Consistent with those findings, ex juvantibus diagnosis of complete CDI could be made."
5. Infectious/inflammatory causes of pituitary stalk thickening (e.g., tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, Langerhans cell histiocytosis) excluded by negative Quantiferon, normal immunoglobulins, and unremarkable cultures. | "Immunological assessment revealed normal immunoglobulin levels … urine culture and Quantiferon were negative as well."
6. Anterior pituitary dysfunction ruled out by normal hormonal panel. | "Hormonal tests showed no significant impairment of anterior pituitary function."
7. Vaccine‑related adverse reaction considered plausible due to temporal association and lack of alternative etiology. | "In the view of strict time correlation between COVID‑19 vaccine and onset of symptoms and granted that no other differential diagnosis had fit the clinical picture…."

case_prompt:
A 27‑year‑old previously healthy male athlete presented to the emergency department with acute‑onset, pressure‑like pleuritic chest pain that began that morning, worsened gradually, and was worse when lying supine. He denied fever, cough, sputum, dyspnea, myalgia, arthralgia, diarrhea, or headache. He was hemodynamically stable, not dyspneic but favored a forward‑leaning position. Vital signs: HR 80 bpm, BP 110/60 mm Hg, RR 18 /min, SpO₂ 95 % on room air, T 36.7 °C. Physical examination, including cardiac auscultation, was unremarkable; no pericardial friction rub was heard.

Laboratory studies showed WBC 9 000/mm³ with 25 % lymphocytes, platelets 165 000/mm³, ESR 7 mm/h, CRP 10 mg/L, D‑dimer 350 ng/mL, normal liver and renal panels, CK 1 013 U/L, and hs‑cTnT 0.04 ng/mL on admission and 0.03 ng/mL at 6 h. ECG demonstrated diffuse ST elevation in most leads with reciprocal ST depression and PR elevation in aVR with PR depression elsewhere. Chest radiograph was normal. Chest CT and CT angiography showed no lung infiltrates, pneumothorax, pericardial effusion, or pulmonary embolism. Transthoracic echocardiogram revealed normal cardiac structure and function without regional wall motion abnormalities or pericardial effusion. Based on ESC criteria (pleuritic chest pain + typical ECG changes), acute pericarditis was diagnosed. Initial nasopharyngeal swab for SARS‑CoV‑2 RT‑PCR was negative; rheumatologic, endocrine, and viral serologies were within normal limits. The patient was admitted to the CCU and started on ibuprofen, aspirin, and supplemental oxygen.

On hospital day 9, he developed dyspnea, fever 38.1 °C, SpO₂ 86 % on room air, RR 24 /min, BP 100/65 mm Hg, HR 98 bpm. Lung auscultation revealed coarse breath sounds with bilateral crackles. Repeat chest CT showed bilateral multilobar consolidations with peripheral distribution, suggestive of a viral pneumonia. Repeat nasopharyngeal swab for SARS‑CoV‑2 was obtained (result pending). Concurrently, he reported progressive bilateral distal extremity weakness, more marked in the left lower limb. Neurologic exam showed reduced sensation in both lower limbs; muscle strength was 2/5 (left distal lower limb), 3/5 (right lower limb), and 4/5 in both upper limbs. Deep tendon reflexes were diminished globally; gait was unsteady. Laboratory reassessment revealed leukopenia (WBC 2 900/mm³, 15 % lymphocytes), thrombocytopenia (95 000/mm³), CRP 80 mg/L, LDH 455 U/L, ferritin 460 ng/mL, CK 174 U/L, and D‑dimer 250 ng/mL. EMG/NCS demonstrated decreased amplitudes of tibial and peroneal sensory and motor action potentials with normal latencies and velocities, and mild denervation potentials in distal muscles, consistent with an acute, mild, mainly axonal peripheral polyneuropathy suggestive of the Acute Motor and Sensory Axonal Neuropathy (AMSAN) variant of Guillain‑Barre syndrome. CSF analysis showed 4 cells/ml and protein 50 mg/dL. Whole‑spine MRI was unremarkable.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Acute pericarditis as the initial presentation was favored because the patient had pleuritic chest pain and ECG changes characteristic of pericarditis, while myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism, and bacterial pneumonia were excluded by normal troponins, negative CTA, and unremarkable chest imaging. | "Based on ESC guidelines... Clinical judgment of acute pericarditis in our patient was based on his clinical presentation (pleuritic chest pain) and typical ECG findings."
2. Bacterial pneumonia was considered after the onset of dyspnea and fever but was deemed unlikely given the bilateral peripheral distribution of consolidations on CT, lack of lobar consolidation typical for bacterial infection, and a laboratory pattern of lymphopenia and thrombocytopenia. | "A repeated chest CT scan revealed bilateral multi‑lobar consolidation with peripheral distribution, suggestive of COVID‑19 infection."
3. Pulmonary embolism was ruled out both initially and during the second deterioration by CT angiography showing no emboli. | "CTA revealed no pulmonary embolism."
4. Other viral etiologies (influenza, other coronaviruses) were considered; however, the combination of peripheral CT findings, marked lymphopenia, elevated inflammatory markers (CRP, ferritin, LDH), and a subsequent positive SARS‑CoV‑2 RT‑PCR supported COVID‑19 as the most probable cause. | "Repeat nasopharyngeal swab was sent for SARS‑CoV‑2, which came back positive."
5. The new neurologic deficits prompted evaluation for spinal cord compression, transverse myelitis, and metabolic neuropathies; EMG/NCS demonstrated an axonal polyneuropathy with preserved conduction velocities, and CSF showed albumin‑cytologic dissociation, leading to a diagnosis of AMSAN, a variant of Guillain‑Barre syndrome, a known post‑infectious complication of COVID‑19. | "These findings revealed an acute, mild, mainly axonal peripheral polyneuropathy, ... suggestive of a subtype of Guillain‑Barre syndrome (GBS), namely the Acute Motor and Sensory Axonal Neuropathy (AMSAN)."
6. The convergence of respiratory imaging, hematologic abnormalities, and confirmed SARS‑CoV‑2 PCR established COVID‑19 infection as the unifying diagnosis linking the pneumonia and the GBS‑like neuropathy. | "A repeat nasopharyngeal swab was sent for SARS‑CoV‑2, which came back positive."

1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: Identification: The patient has two diseases from the 21 SELECTED list – malaria and COVID‑19. The case provides sufficient clinical and laboratory data to deduce both, but the confirmation of COVID‑19 (RT‑PCR positive) occurs later in the report. I will set the target diagnosis as **covid_19**, using the early presentation and subsequent work‑up to allow students to arrive at this diagnosis before the test result is disclosed.

Ideal Breakpoint: End the case presentation at the end of “Admission day 5” – after the patient’s vital signs, respiratory status, ongoing treatments, and the fact that nasopharyngeal/oropharyngeal samples have been taken for COVID‑19 testing, but **before** the RT‑PCR result is reported (which appears on day 9). case_prompt:
A 17‑year‑old female with a known history of asthma presented to the emergency department after a week of persistent post‑prandial epigastric pain accompanied by vomiting, diarrhea, and fever. She had previously visited a peripheral clinic where she received analgesics without relief.

On examination she was lethargic, mildly jaundiced, and pale. She had mild epigastric tenderness; no abdominal organ was palpable. Vital signs: temperature 37.8 °C, pulse 109 beats/min, blood pressure normal, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Laboratory studies revealed a malaria parasite density of 600,000 /µL, reduced hemoglobin, thrombocytopenia, and normal renal function.

She was diagnosed with severe malaria with thrombocytopenia and anemia and started on intravenous artesunate (125 mg at 0, 12, and 24 h) followed by oral artemether‑lumefantrine. Paracetamol 1 g IV every 8 h was given for fever. Within 12 hours her temperature rose to 39 °C, blood pressure fell to 68/38 mmHg, and she developed respiratory distress (respiratory rate 35 /min, flaring of the nares). Oxygen saturation on room air dropped to 45%. The working impression was severe acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) with a differential of septic shock, acute asthma exacerbation, and possible COVID‑19. She was positioned at 45°, given 10 L/min oxygen via a non‑rebreather mask, intravenous fluids, nebulized salbutamol (5 mg ×3), and IV hydrocortisone 200 mg. Oxygen saturation improved to 75–77% on oxygen, blood pressure rose to 132/78 mmHg, and respiratory rate remained at 40 /min. Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily and continued salbutamol nebulizations were initiated.

On day 3 of admission dyspnea improved, temperature fell to 37 °C, pulse 111 beats/min, and oxygen saturation reached 96% on the non‑rebreather mask with the patient propped at 45°. Chest X‑ray showed heterogeneous opacifications in the upper right lung zones and homogeneous opacifications in the lower lung zones. Repeat malaria blood film showed a reduced parasite load, and ESR rose to 100 mm / hr.

On day 4 temperature was 36.7 °C, pulse 132 beats/min, blood pressure 90/60 mmHg, oxygen saturation 91% on oxygen. The impression remained severe malaria complicated by thrombocytopenia, intravascular hemolysis, and ARDS with a differential of COVID‑19. Nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal swabs were collected for COVID‑19 testing, and azithromycin 500 mg was started, followed by a tapering course of dexamethasone, zinc, and vitamin C.

On day 5 the patient reported no new complaints. Vital signs: temperature 37.2 °C, pulse 83 beats/min, blood pressure 89/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 /min off oxygen and 26 /min on oxygen. Oxygen saturation was 82–84% off oxygen and 96–97% on a non‑rebreather mask at 10 L/min. Examination of other systems was unremarkable, and all medications were continued.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Severe malaria causing ARDS – The patient had a very high parasitemia (600,000/µL), anemia, thrombocytopenia, and rapid clinical deterioration; “Laboratory results showed malaria parasites of 600,000/mul… A diagnosis of severe malaria… was made.”
2. Septic shock secondary to malaria – Hypotension (68/38 mmHg) and rising temperature suggested systemic inflammation; “The impression made was severe acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) with a differential diagnosis of septic shock…”
3. Acute asthma exacerbation – Known asthmatic history, wheezes on exam, and need for nebulized salbutamol supported this possibility; “…acute exacerbation of asthma…”
4. COVID‑19 infection – Presence of ARDS, fever, hypoxia, and the pandemic context prompted testing; “…to rule out COVID‑19… Differential diagnosis of COVID‑19… Nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal samples were taken for COVID‑19 testing.”
5. Bacterial superinfection – Empiric ceftriaxone was started, reflecting concern for bacterial pneumonia; “The patient was started on intravenous ceftriaxone 2g daily…”
6. Drug‑induced hemolysis – Intravascular hemolysis was noted as a complication of severe malaria, not a separate diagnosis; “…intravascular hemolysis…”
7. COVID‑19 ruled out (later) – The eventual RT‑PCR confirmed infection, validating the earlier suspicion; “The patient’s RT‑PCR for COVID‑19 was confirmed positive on day 9 of admission.”

case_prompt: A 56‑year‑old man with no prior medical or surgical history presented to the emergency department with macroscopic hematuria, clot formation in the urine, difficulty urinating, and lower abdominal pain. One week earlier he had fever and tested positive for COVID‑19 by viral RNA throat swab; his fever improved after three days of antipyretics. Physical examination showed stable vital signs and a swollen, tender lower abdomen, especially over the bladder region. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 133 g/L, platelet count 73 × 10⁹/L (reference 125–350 × 10⁹/L), platelet‑o‑crit 0.09 % (reference 0.1–0.5 %), thrombin time 17.90 s (reference 10.30–16.60 s), prothrombin time 12.60 s (reference 9.40–12.50 s), and fibrinogen 1.70 g/L (reference 2.38–4.98 g/L). case_prompt:
A 34‑year‑old woman with B‑lymphoblastic leukemia (t(9;22)(q34;q11.2) BCR‑ABL1) was awaiting an allogeneic hematopoietic stem‑cell transplant (allo‑HSCT) from a 10/10 HLA‑matched unrelated donor. She had received prior tyrosine‑kinase inhibitor therapy (imatinib, then dasatinib, followed by ponatinib) and two cycles of inotuzumab ozogamicin, achieving a second complete morphological remission with minimal residual disease (MRD) positivity. While awaiting transplant, she developed an Omicron BA.5 infection despite having received a Moderna COVID‑19 vaccine series with a booster 6 months earlier. Prompt antiviral therapy with nirmatrelvir/ritonavir resulted in fever resolution within 72 hours and a marked reduction in viral load on nasopharyngeal swabs.

Twenty‑three days after the COVID‑19 diagnosis, after confirming clinical resolution and noting rising MRD, the transplant proceeded. Conditioning consisted of fludarabine and 12 Gy total body irradiation (TBI). During conditioning, nasopharyngeal viral load increased, and viable virus was recovered in cell culture, although the patient remained asymptomatic. Two days before peripheral blood stem‑cell reinfusion (July 2022), she received tixagevimab/cilgavimab 300 mg each and a 3‑day course of remdesivir. The donor was a vaccinated female.

Post‑transplant graft‑versus‑host disease (GVHD) prophylaxis included post‑transplant cyclophosphamide, mycophenolate mofetil, and cyclosporine A. Neutrophil engraftment occurred on day +20. The pre‑engraftment phase was marked by uncomplicated febrile neutropenia without documented infections. Despite measures to reduce veno‑occlusive disease (VOD) risk, the patient developed VOD on day +13, manifesting as hepatic‑vein thinning, gallbladder wall thickening, ascites, bilirubin peak 2.3 mg/dL, and Fibroscan peak 75 kPa; she was treated with defibrotide with gradual resolution.

In the post‑engraftment period, on day +23 the patient experienced mild respiratory symptoms (cough, rhino‑conjunctivitis, fever) consistent with a COVID‑19 flare, which resolved spontaneously. Viral clearance was achieved by day +28 after transplant. On day +32 she developed grade I acute GVHD of the skin (grade II) and was treated with methylprednisolone 0.5 mg/kg daily and three weekly sessions of extracorporeal photopheresis as a steroid‑sparing approach. By day +40, with full donor myeloid and T‑cell chimerism, MRD negativity, and remission, she was discharged home. Subsequent follow‑up to day +180 showed no further complications; at six months bone‑marrow evaluation confirmed complete hematologic remission with negative MRD.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. SARS‑CoV‑2 infection identified as the cause of the respiratory illness because the patient had a positive nasopharyngeal swab for the Omicron BA.5 variant, developed cough, rhino‑conjunctivitis, and fever, and viral load decreased after antiviral therapy. | "During conditioning chemotherapy ... nasopharyngeal viral load increased (virus confirmed viable in cell culture), while the patient remained asymptomatic." and "The post‑engraftment phase was characterized by mild COVID‑19 at day +23 (cough, rhino‑conjunctivitis, fever)."
2. Bacterial infection considered during febrile neutropenia but excluded due to lack of documented pathogens. | "The pre‑engraftment phase was characterized by uncomplicated febrile neutropenia without documented infections."
3. Veno‑occlusive disease considered as a cause of hepatic dysfunction but distinguished from the respiratory presentation; it was diagnosed by imaging and laboratory findings independent of the viral illness. | "VOD occurred at day +13 (thinning of hepatic veins, thickening of gallbladder, ascites, bilirubin peak 2.3 mg/dL, Fibroscan peak 75 kPa)."
4. Acute graft‑versus‑host disease considered for the skin findings; diagnosed by clinical grading and responded to steroids, separate from the viral respiratory symptoms. | "At day +32, the patient experienced grade I acute GVHD (skin grade II) treated with methylprednisolone..."
5. case_prompt:
A 31‑year‑old man presented to the emergency department with a 6‑week history of left‑sided lateral neck pain and a minor localized swelling. He denied sore throat, dyspnea, fever, weight loss, or other constitutional symptoms. Three weeks after the onset of neck pain, he developed mild COVID‑19 manifested by anosmia and ageusia, which resolved in several days, while the neck pain persisted. Past medical history was otherwise unremarkable.

On examination, there was prominent tenderness over the left common carotid (LCC) artery with subtle swelling; upper‑extremity pulses were symmetric. Laboratory studies showed normal blood counts, serum creatinine, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate; C‑reactive protein was mildly elevated. Doppler ultrasound demonstrated LCC wall thickening without luminal stenosis. Head and neck computed tomography angiography (CTA) showed no vasculitic lesions, and the patient was discharged.

Two days later, repeat ultrasound confirmed significant LCC wall thickening, prompting readmission. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head and neck revealed prominent LCC wall thickening compatible with vasculitis. Antinuclear antibodies, anti‑neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and immunoglobulin levels including IgG4 were unremarkable; serologies for syphilis and HIV were negative. Positron emission tomography–CT showed hypermetabolic mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy without evidence of active vasculitis. Bronchoscopy with endobronchial ultrasound‑guided transbronchial needle aspiration of mediastinal lymph nodes yielded pathology that demonstrated non‑caseating granulomas; acid‑fast and silver stains were negative, and immunohistochemical staining for IgG4 was also negative. Additional evaluations (electrocardiography, echocardiography, ophthalmology, pulmonary function, urinalysis, urinary calcium) were unremarkable. Serum angiotensin‑converting enzyme (ACE) level was elevated.

Large‑vessel vasculitis considered due to carotid wall thickening, but CTA showed no vasculitic lesions and ANCA testing was negative, arguing against active vasculitis. | "Head and neck computed tomography angiography (CTA) scan, however, showed no vasculitic lesions… ANAs, anti‑neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCAs)… were all unremarkable."

IgG4‑related disease considered because of lymphadenopathy and granulomatous inflammation; serum IgG4 levels and tissue IgG4 staining were negative, making this unlikely. | "Immunoglobulin levels, including immunoglobulin G4 (IgG4), were all unremarkable… Immunohistochemical staining for IgG4 was also negative."

Sarcoidosis favored by the combination of non‑caseating granulomas, mediastinal/hilar hypermetabolic lymphadenopathy on PET‑CT, and elevated serum ACE, after exclusion of other etiologies. | "Hypermetabolic mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy… Pathology results demonstrated noncaseating granulomas… ACE levels in blood were elevated."

A 41‑year‑old man with a known history of type‑2 diabetes mellitus presented to the emergency department with left‑upper‑limb weakness of two‑hour duration. Two days prior he had fever, rhinorrhea, and a diffuse rash that began two weeks earlier as red lesions on the distal lower limbs and subsequently spread to the upper limbs and trunk, evolving in areas to black discoloration. He denied sensory changes, speech difficulties, respiratory symptoms, headache, joint pain, oral ulcers, or sicca symptoms. He used an unspecified oral antidiabetic irregularly and had no recent travel or sick contacts.

On examination he was tachycardic (124 bpm), normotensive (124/76 mmHg), afebrile, and oxygen saturation was normal on room air. A petechial rash was present on the lower back. Pulses were palpable and strong in all extremities. The remainder of the exam was unremarkable.

A CT brain with angiography showed no acute infarction or bleed; chest X‑ray was normal. Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis (26.1 ×10³/µL) with neutrophilia, markedly elevated CRP (305.5 mg/L) and procalcitonin (0.20 ng/mL), high D‑dimer, ferritin, and LDH. Transient ischemic attack considered due to acute unilateral limb weakness; however, rapid improvement of weakness and lack of imaging evidence of infarction argued against a persistent ischemic event. | "The patient was admitted ... as a case of transient ischemic attack (TIA) ... the left arm weakness improved shortly after presentation."

Primary autoimmune vasculitis entertained because of leukocytoclastic skin lesions, but extensive serologic work‑up was negative, leaving secondary causes more likely. | "A full connective tissue disease and vasculitis work‑up ... case_prompt:
A 14‑year‑old teenager with moderate obesity (BMI 31 kg/m²) presented with NYHA class IV dyspnea and sudden chest pain. Three weeks prior she had an influenza‑like syndrome, dry cough, and exertional dyspnea. Her parents were being treated for COVID‑19. She had received antibiotics, oral corticosteroids, and inhaled bronchodilators from her general practitioner, but dyspnea worsened, accompanied by palpitations and chest pain.

On examination she was pale, anxious, afebrile, tachycardic (125 bpm), blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, SpO₂ 90% on room air. Cardiac auscultation revealed regular tachycardia without murmur; there were no signs of right or left heart failure and no evidence of deep‑vein thrombosis.

Chest CT angiography revealed bilateral massive pulmonary emboli without parenchymal lesions. Cardiac MRI confirmed that the right‑ventricular mass was thrombotic and excluded a tissue (tumoral) character; right‑ventricular systolic function remained preserved.

A comprehensive etiologic work‑up was performed. Venous Doppler ultrasound of the lower limbs and abdominal ultrasound were normal. Testing for inherited thrombophilia (protein C, protein S, antithrombin) and for autoimmune disease (anti‑cardiolipin IgM/IgG, ANA, anti‑DNA) were all negative.

A 79‑year‑old man with a 10‑year history of type‑2 diabetes (on metformin) and 5‑year hypertension (on amlodipine) presented with acute mental confusion and dysarthria of 48 hours’ duration. On exam his Glasgow Coma Scale was 12/15 (E5 V2 M5), pupils were symmetric and reactive, no focal motor deficits were noted, and osteotendinous reflexes were normal. He was tachypneic (24 breaths/min), SpO₂ 97 % on room air, tachycardic (115 bpm) and hypertensive (160/95 mmHg). Capillary glucose was 2.24 g/L with glycosuria but no ketonuria. Arterial blood gas revealed a normal‑gap metabolic acidosis, potassium 3 mmol/L, lactate 0.43 mmol/L. He was afebrile.

Initial management addressed presumed diabetic decompensation with intravenous insulin, fluid resuscitation, and potassium correction. Because his neurological status did not improve, he was transferred to intensive care. Brain CT showed multiple parietal ischemic foci. Chest CT demonstrated septal thickening and bronchial dilatation without pneumonia typical of COVID‑19; abdominal ultrasound was unremarkable.

ECG showed no hypokalaemia‑related changes, transthoracic echocardiography and supra‑aortic trunk ultrasound were normal. Laboratory studies revealed CRP 45.5 mg/L, procalcitonin 0.04 ng/mL, leukocytes 12,500 /µL (neutrophils 9,280, lymphocytes 2,140), normal platelets, ferritin, fibrinogen 5.37 g/L, and negative D‑dimer. EEG revealed epileptiform activity, leading to a provisional diagnosis of non‑ketotic hyperglycemia‑related seizures and initiation of sodium valproate.

Neurologic status continued to decline; he required intubation on day 3 (five days after symptom onset). Repeat brain CT showed no progression of lesions. New lymphopenia was noted, HIV serologies were negative, and CRP rose further. A multiplex RT‑PCR on a protected distal bronchial specimen and on CSF were ordered.

A 44‑year‑old Algerian woman with no past medical or trauma history was referred for a sub‑capsular hepatic hematoma of the right liver in the setting of fever and body aches for >10 days. On admission she was WHO grade 2, blood pressure 132/80 mm Hg, heart rate 105 beats/min, temperature 38.9 °C. Examination showed marked tenderness over the right hypochondrium; the rest of the exam was normal.

Laboratory studies: hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL; leukocytosis 13,370 cells/µL with neutrophil predominance (8,300 cells/µL) and lymphocytes 3,400 cells/µL; platelets 276,000 /µL; AST 76 IU/L, ALT 72 IU/L; prothrombin ratio 87 % (INR 1.10); KCT = 32.1 seconds.

Ultrasound‑guided drainage (10 Fr nephrostomy catheter) was performed under local anesthesia, evacuating 800 mL of blood. Bacteriological analysis of the fluid showed no bacterial growth.

case_prompt:
A 68‑year‑old man with a past medical history of tobacco use, obesity (BMI 29 kg/m²), type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and coronary artery disease was brought to the emergency department because of cough, fever, watery diarrhea, and altered mental status lasting five days. Nasopharyngeal swab testing was positive for SARS‑CoV‑2 by PCR, and he rapidly progressed to COVID‑19 pneumonia with acute hypoxic respiratory failure requiring intubation. His hospital course was complicated by sepsis, acute kidney injury necessitating peritoneal dialysis, ileus, toxic metabolic encephalopathy, and candidemia (Candida tropicalis and Candida glabrata). 

On hospital day 40 he developed intermittent hematochezia requiring blood transfusion. Blood pressure varied from 138/69–175/80 mm Hg before the bleed and dropped to 118/49 mm Hg after passing large clots and dark‑red liquid blood. Laboratory parameters were notable for a falling hemoglobin (see Table 2). Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis showed a bowel of normal caliber without obstruction. He was on azithromycin, hydroxychloroquine, fluconazole, meropenem, micafungin, intravenous vancomycin, and ampicillin‑sulbactam at the time of bleeding; stool cultures were negative for cysts, ova, and parasites.

Colonoscopy identified patchy, deeply ulcerated mucosa with marked edema and loss of the vascular pattern in the cecum, extending to the ileocecal valve. Diffuse oozing of the mucosa was observed. The remaining colon appeared normal. No hemorrhoidal bleeding, arteriovenous malformation, diverticulitis, or overt mass lesions were identified.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Hemorrhoidal bleeding, AVM, diverticulitis, or colonic malignancy were considered but excluded because endoscopic evaluation showed ulcerated cecal lesions without hemorrhoids, vascular malformations, diverticula, or mass lesions. | "no evidence of hemorrhoidal bleeding, AVM, diverticulitis, and/or malignancy was noted."
2. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) colitis was entertained given the immunocompromised state; it was excluded by negative serology and lack of viral cytopathic changes on histology. | "No viral cytopathic effects for CMV or HSV were seen... Serological tests for CMV were negative."
3. Herpes simplex virus (HSV) colitis was ruled out similarly, with no HSV cytopathic effect observed and no immunohistochemical stains performed. | "No viral cytopathic effects for CMV or HSV were seen; hence, immunohistochemical stains were not undertaken."
4. Eosinophilic colitis was considered because of focal increased eosinophils in the lamina propria, but the eosinophilia was judged nonspecific and lacking characteristic histopathology. | "There were no histopathological features suggestive of eosinophilic colitis. The mildly increased eosinophils... were interpreted to be nonspecific."
5. Chronic idiopathic inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) was contemplated; however, histology lacked chronic architectural changes, granulomas, or crypt distortion typical of IBD. | "Clinical and histopathological evidence for chronic idiopathic inflammatory bowel disease... were lacking."
6. Scleroderma‑related gastrointestinal ischemia and Churg‑Strauss syndrome were excluded due to absence of vasculitic changes or systemic features on pathology. | "Clinical and histopathological evidence for ... scleroderma, and Churg‑Strauss syndrome were lacking."
7. The pattern of ulceration localized to the cecum and ileocecal valve with diffuse mucosal oozing, in a critically ill patient with COVID‑19–related hypoperfusion, is characteristic of ischemic colitis, even though definitive ischemic histologic changes were not seen. | "Patchy, deeply ulcerated mucosa with significant edema... The endoscopic appearance of the mucosa was clinically consistent with ischemic colitis."

We contacted 31 pemphigus patients routinely followed‑up in our hospital in Rome who received rituximab (RTX) in the 12 months preceding the COVID‑19 pandemic. Among them, a 45‑year‑old woman (professional nurse, living in Northern Italy) confirmed having COVID‑19. She was affected by pemphigus foliaceus, as assessed by clinical examination and direct immunofluorescence microscopy from January 2019 and received a cycle of RTX (500 mg × 4 weekly infusions) in May 2019 reaching complete remission off‑therapy in November 2019. Two months later, a relapse occurred; therefore, on 23 January 2020, she received an additional 500 mg RTX infusion and started prednisone 50 mg/day. Disease control was reached two weeks after infusion, prednisone was gradually tapered to 5 mg and lesions completely resolved at the beginning of March when B cells were still depleted.

By 15 March, she developed mild flu‑like symptoms (fever up to 37.5 °C, asthenia and some cough). She was treated with azithromycin 500 mg/day for 3 days without clinical improvement. On 21 March, a nasopharyngeal swab was performed, resulting in a negative SARS‑CoV‑2 result. She was started on co‑amoxiclav 875/125 mg bid for 6 days. During antibiotic treatment she experienced hyposmia, ageusia, dry cough, nocturnal dyspnoea and hyperpyrexia (up to 39.5 °C). As symptoms persisted, on 27 March a second nasopharyngeal swab was performed.

2. An initial negative SARS‑CoV‑2 PCR led clinicians to doubt COVID‑19 and maintain the bacterial hypothesis | "On the 21st of March, a nasopharyngeal swab was performed, resulting in negative SARS‑CoV‑2 result."

5. Definitive confirmation of COVID‑19 was achieved by a positive SARS‑CoV‑2 PCR on the second swab, accompanying laboratory findings of lymphopenia, elevated LDH, CRP and IL‑6, and characteristic interstitial pneumonia on imaging (described later) | "On March 27 a second nasopharyngeal swab was performed, resulting in positivity for SARS‑CoV‑2."

case_prompt: A 34‑month‑old child was admitted on March 9, 2020 with a 4‑day history of fever, seizures, and upward gaze. case_prompt: A 78‑year‑old man presented to his primary care physician with shortness of breath and light‑headedness that occurred at rest but not during physical activity. He reported monitoring his oxygen saturation, heart rate, and blood pressure during these episodes, all of which remained within normal limits. Physical examination was unremarkable; therefore, an electrocardiogram and chest radiograph were not performed. Laboratory studies, including a complete metabolic panel, complete blood count, b‑type natriuretic peptide, and ferritin, were all within normal limits or unchanged from his baseline values. His medication list at the visit included ipratropium nasal spray, vitamin B12, vitamin D₃, a multivitamin, vitamin E, fish oil, and folic acid. He had a remaining supply of atovaquone/proguanil hydrochloride (250 mg/100 mg) from a trip four years earlier and, after hearing media reports that antimalarials might prevent COVID‑19, began taking the medication daily for the past six weeks. A COVID‑19 test was performed and was negative. He was instructed to discontinue the atovaquone/proguanil hydrochloride.

2. Cardiac and pulmonary etiologies deemed unlikely due to normal physical exam; no ECG or chest X‑ray were obtained. | "An electrocardiogram and chest x‑ray were not completed due to normal physical exam findings."

case_prompt:
A 21‑year‑old man with high‑functioning autism and obsessive‑compulsive disorder presented to a district‑general Accident and Emergency (A&E) department reporting intense anxiety and a feeling that he was “dying.”  He denied recent drug use, though he admitted to having used cocaine earlier that day; a collateral history from his aunt, with whom he was staying, denied cocaine use.  The initial A&E assessment diagnosed a panic attack and he was discharged home to his aunt’s farm.

Within hours he returned to A&E with marked agitation, pacing, and non‑verbal behaviour; a detailed history could not be obtained.  Initial investigations (full blood count, liver function, renal profile, inflammatory markers) were normal.  Urine toxicology screen was negative.  Abnormal findings were a low serum phosphate (0.35 mmol/L) and an elevated prolactin level (737 µ/L) despite no prior antipsychotic exposure.  Skull X‑ray showed no fractures.  An MRI of the brain demonstrated a normal‑sized pituitary gland and no intracranial abnormalities.  Empiric intravenous acyclovir was started pending exclusion of encephalitis, and oral phosphate replacement corrected the hypophosphataemia.

A lumbar puncture performed a week later was negative for bacterial and viral pathogens.  The patient was subsequently referred to the mental‑health liaison team of the acute medical unit and, nine days after initial presentation, was formally admitted to an acute psychiatric unit.

At the time of psychiatric admission he exhibited severe disorientation to time, place, and person.  Thought block was prominent, speech was markedly limited, and his affect was euthymic.  He appeared in an altered state of consciousness with a dazed, confused look and a catatonia‑like presentation: increased muscle tone in all limbs, but he withdrew sharply when venepuncture was attempted.  Movements were few and spastic; there were no ictal features.  His speech consisted of word‑salads such as “this is not the original,” “two people fighting,” and “different timelines.”  He could sometimes answer yes/no questions with great effort but could not recall his responses.  Mental‑state examination noted poor eye contact, an intense stare when eye contact was made, normal‑tone stilted speech that was disjointed and bizarre, and absent insight or capacity regarding his mental state.  He remained ambulatory with a slightly spastic gait, frequently removed his clothes, and wandered aimlessly around the ward.

1. Infectious encephalitis considered due to acute agitation and altered mental status | "Differential diagnoses included meningitis, encephalitis, psychosis, and delirium."
2. Bacterial meningitis ruled out by normal CSF analysis and negative cultures | "Lumbar puncture analysis returned negative for bacteria and viruses."
3. Viral encephalitis (including HSV) ruled out by negative CSF PCR and empirical acyclovir showed no clinical improvement | "A&E then started treatment for IV acyclovir for prophylaxis against potential encephalitis."
4. Autoimmune encephalitis (e.g., NMDA‑receptor antibodies) excluded by negative serum antibody testing | "Blood was also negative for NMDA receptor antibodies..."
5. Syphilitic meningitis excluded by negative treponemal serology | "Blood was also negative for Treponema pallidum antibodies..."
6. HIV‑associated neurocognitive disorder excluded by negative HIV antigen/antibody tests | "...and HIV 1&2 antigen/antibodies."
7. Delirium deemed less likely because the disturbance persisted beyond typical metabolic precipitants and did not fluctuate with physiologic changes | "He continued to display severe disorientation to time, place, and person...Thought block was evident and major, accompanied by markedly limited speech."
8. Primary psychotic disorder favored given sustained thought disorganisation, word‑salad speech, lack of insight, and absence of identifiable organic cause | "From what we could discern from his speech, it seemed like he was occasionally describing two people arguing, possibly suggesting auditory hallucinations."

A 68‑year‑old woman with diet‑controlled diabetes presented with a sudden, asymptomatic ecchymotic patch on her left lower limb. She denied any other medical problems or medications. On examination she was hemodynamically stable (BP 90/60 mmHg, RR 18, HR 78 bpm, Temp 36.7 °C, SpO₂ 97%). Peripheral pulses were palpable bilaterally.  

During hospitalization the skin lesion evolved into hemorrhagic bullae with an erythematous border. The initial work‑up included complete blood count, metabolic panel, inflammatory markers, coagulation profile, and imaging. Laboratory results were: WBC 20 600 /µL (84.2 % neutrophils), platelets 137 000/µL, Hb 11.9 g/dL, IgA 475 mg/dL, IL‑6 60 pg/mL, amylase 145 U/L, pro‑BNP 297 pg/mL, ESR 41 mm/hr, LDH 983 U/L, PT 15.5 s, aPTT 30 s, INR 1.3, blood glucose 526 mg/dL. Liver enzymes, BUN, creatinine, CPK, troponin, and CRP were within normal limits. Urine and blood cultures (24‑h and 48‑h) showed no bacterial growth.  

Doppler ultrasound revealed an atheromatous plaque in the right common femoral artery; flow in the left lower limb was normal. A chest CT scan demonstrated bilateral peripheral ground‑glass opacities, more prominent in the lower lobes.  

Differential diagnoses considered for the skin lesion included necrotizing fasciitis, disseminated intravascular coagulation/purpura fulminans, drug‑induced necrosis, and vasculitis/vasculopathy secondary to rheumatologic disease or uncommon infections. The patient’s only systemic symptom during hospitalization was a fever of 38.8 °C that appeared one day after admission, accompanied by anorexia and nausea.

Necrotizing fasciitis was unlikely because the patient did not exhibit severe pain or a markedly ill appearance, which are typical for this condition. | "Because of diabetes, necrotizing fasciitis must be considered. Disseminated intravascular coagulation/purpura fulminans was deemed improbable given negative sepsis work‑up, normal coagulation parameters, and lack of systemic bleeding. | "Coagulation disorders are due to infections and sepsis, such as disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) and purpura fulminans (PF), but the sepsis workup of our patient was negative except for chest CT scan findings..."

case_prompt:
A 55‑year‑old woman with no prior pulmonary arterial hypertension risk factors presented initially with a 7‑day history of fever, shortness of breath, dry cough, chest pain, nausea, and generalized aches. In the emergency department her blood pressure was 100/70 mmHg, pulse 105 bpm, respiratory rate 22/min, and oxygen saturation 77% on room air. Lung examination revealed bilateral coarse crackles in the lower fields. Suspecting COVID‑19, she was admitted to an isolation unit, received supplemental oxygen (5 L via simple mask), azithromycin, ceftriaxone, enoxaparin, dexamethasone, vitamin C, and zinc. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11 g/dL, WBC 17 000/mm³ (90% neutrophils, 7% lymphocytes), LDH 900 U/L, ferritin 1 100 ng/mL, CRP 12 mg/L, PT 14 s, INR 1.1, aPTT 32 s, ALT 57 U/L, AST 78 U/L, total bilirubin 2 mg/dL, creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, BUN 40 mg/dL. Chest X‑ray demonstrated bilateral infiltrates. Nasopharyngeal RT‑PCR was positive for SARS‑CoV‑2. Arterial blood gas showed pH 7.6, PaO₂ 42 mmHg, PaCO₂ 22 mmHg, consistent with hypoxemia and respiratory alkalosis. She progressed to mild respiratory distress syndrome (PaO₂/FiO₂ 250) and required CPAP. After 18 days of hospitalization she improved, was discharged on room air with oxygen saturation 92% and a negative SARS‑CoV‑2 RT‑PCR.

Two months later she returned with a one‑month history of exertional dyspnea, dry cough, fatigue, and one episode of exertional syncope. Vital signs: BP 140/90 mmHg, pulse 90 bpm, respiratory rate 18/min, oxygen saturation 88% on ambient air. Physical exam revealed elevated jugular venous pressure (13 cm H₂O), left parasternal heave, and wide splitting of the second heart sound. A repeat SARS‑CoV‑2 RT‑PCR was negative. Chest X‑ray showed right atrial enlargement and fibrotic changes. High‑resolution CT of the chest revealed extensive fibrosis, diffuse symmetrical ground‑glass opacities in both lungs, septal thickening, and traction bronchiectasis, interpreted as post‑COVID‑19 lung disease. Electrocardiography demonstrated right‑axis deviation. Transthoracic echocardiography measured a right ventricular systolic pressure of 59 mmHg, tricuspid regurgitant jet velocity of 4.5 m/s, pulmonary artery diameter of 31 mm, and normal left‑heart parameters.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Acute COVID‑19 reinfection considered because of persistent respiratory symptoms; excluded by a negative SARS‑CoV‑2 RT‑PCR. | “A RT‑PCR for SARS‑CoV‑2 was negative which ruled out re‑infection.”
2. Left‑sided cardiac disease as a cause of pulmonary hypertension; excluded by normal left‑heart parameters on echocardiography. | “...normal left side heart parameters.”
3. Pulmonary hypertension secondary to chronic lung disease post‑COVID‑19 considered; supported by HRCT findings of massive fibrosis, ground‑glass opacities, septal thickening, and traction bronchiectasis consistent with post‑COVID‑19 changes. | “A high‑resolution CT‑scan revealed massive fibrosis, diffuse symmetrical ground glass opacities … most consistent with post‑COVID‑19 changes.”
4. Other causes of dyspnea (e.g., pulmonary embolism, interstitial lung disease unrelated to COVID‑19) not specifically discussed in the article, thus not pursued by the authors. | (No explicit mention; authors focused on post‑COVID‑19 sequelae.)

case_prompt:
A 44‑year‑old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus on insulin glargine and dulaglutide presented with subjective fevers and worsening shortness of breath. Twelve days earlier she had been diagnosed with COVID‑19 by nasopharyngeal RT‑PCR after chills, myalgias, loss of taste, fatigue, and malaise. case_prompt: A 49‑year‑old Hispanic male with hypertension and hyperlipidemia was admitted on the same day as his father with intermittent fever, dry cough, anosmia, and sore throat. He was febrile, tachypneic, hypotensive, and hypoxic, requiring intubation and sedation. Nasopharyngeal swab for SARS‑CoV‑2 RNA was positive. During hospitalization he developed ARDS with extensive pulmonary fibrosis and pneumatoceles, acute kidney injury requiring hemodialysis, multi‑organ failure with septic shock, and gastrointestinal bleeding treated with a pantoprazole drip. After discontinuing sedatives on hospital day 26, on day 30 he was found unresponsive with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 3 (E1V1M1). No paralytic agents were being administered except a single dose of vecuronium at intubation. Neurologic examination showed brisk deep‑tendon reflexes in all extremities, bilateral extensor plantar responses, faint positive corneal and sensory responses, and a preserved Doll’s eye reflex. Non‑contrast CT of the brain showed no acute intracranial process. Brain MRI with and without gadolinium revealed bilateral multifocal periventricular white‑matter FLAIR hyper‑intensities without hemorrhage, diffusion restriction, or contrast enhancement. Cervical spine MRI on day 38 was normal. Cerebrospinal fluid was pink and hazy with 9 WBC, 1,100 RBC, protein 91 mg/dL, glucose 66 mg/dL (serum glucose 138 mg/dL). CSF cultures and PCR panels for SARS‑CoV‑2, HSV, VZV, EBV, and CMV were negative. Oligoclonal bands were absent, and anti‑myelin basic protein antibody was negative. EEG demonstrated diffuse theta activity without paroxysmal discharges. Transthoracic echocardiogram showed mild mitral regurgitation without thrombus. Serum ANA, ANCA, HIV, syphilis serologies, and coagulation studies were normal or negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. COVID‑19–associated encephalopathy is most plausible given recent severe SARS‑CoV‑2 infection and neurologic decline; MRI shows diffuse white‑matter hyperintensities without enhancement, and other causes have been excluded. | "Nasopharyngeal swab for SARS‑CoV‑2 RNA was positive" … "MRI of the brain ... showed bilateral multifocal periventricular white matter FLAIR signal hyperintensities ... no hemorrhage, restriction in diffusion, or contrast enhancement."
2. Acute viral encephalitis (HSV, VZV, EBV, CMV, SARS‑CoV‑2) considered but excluded by negative CSF PCR panels. | "CSF cultures and PCR panels including COVID‑19 RNA, HSV, VZV, EBV, and CMV were negative."
3. Bacterial meningitis/encephalitis excluded by sterile CSF culture and low pleocytosis. | "CSF analysis ... revealed pink and hazy fluid with 9 white blood cells" and "CSF cultures ... were negative."
4. Multiple sclerosis ruled out by negative anti‑myelin basic protein antibody, absence of oligoclonal bands, and atypical non‑enhancing MRI pattern. | "Anti‑myelin basic protein antibody ... came back negative" and "CSF was negative for oligoclonal bands."
5. ANCA‑associated vasculitis excluded by negative serum ANCA testing. | "Serum testing of ANA, ANCA, HIV, syphilis, and coagulation factors were normal or negative."
6. Metabolic or hypoxic encephalopathy considered but imaging demonstrated focal inflammatory‑type lesions rather than diffuse diffusion changes typical of hypoxic injury. | "MRI ... showed ... no restriction in diffusion."

case_prompt:
Mr. X is a 13‑year‑old white male with a history of high‑functioning autism spectrum disorder diagnosed at age 7, attention‑deficit/hyperactivity disorder, disruptive mood dysregulation disorder, and more recently obsessive‑compulsive disorder, anxiety, and depression. He had longstanding rigidity, irritability, impulsivity, agitation, aggression, oppositionality, and persistent worrying, with progressive worsening over time. He exhibited difficulty with two‑step instructions and fine‑motor tasks, and had a history of self‑injurious behavior, suicidal ideation, and anhedonia. He had undergone >10 psychotropic medication trials and one prior psychiatric inpatient stay for a suicide attempt.

He presented to the emergency department after 10 days of decreased oral intake. Over the preceding 4–5 days he refused all PO intake, citing contamination fears and “itchy skin” that had intensified three weeks earlier. The family noted possible anxiety escalation after a holiday urgent‑care visit for COVID‑19 testing, though all household members tested negative.

In the ED he was found to be cachectic (BMI <5th percentile), dehydrated, and in metabolic ketoacidosis secondary to starvation. All home medications (oxcarbazepine, risperidone, clonidine) were held; sertraline 12.5 mg was started, and nasogastric tube feeds were initiated because he would not eat orally. After stabilization he was transferred to a child psychiatry ward; the NG tube was later discontinued but re‑started when oral intake remained minimal.

On the psychiatry ward, physical examination was unremarkable. Mental status exam highlighted a cachectic, fully alert, oriented male who was selectively mute to several questions, denied SI/HI, hallucinations, or delusions, and displayed rigid, ritualized behavior (e.g., insisting staff cover his hands in a specific way). Laboratory studies showed elevated blood urea nitrogen (BUN up to 36 mg/dL) with a BUN/creatinine ratio >20, consistent with prerenal azotemia from inadequate intake; this resolved with hydration. No further medical interventions were required.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. COVID‑19 infection considered but excluded | "All family members returned with negative COVID‑19 test results."
2. Intrinsic renal disease considered but excluded | "Follow‑up lab results revealed elevation in Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN)/Creatinine (Cr)…prerenal azotemia…as the result of inadequate intake, which eventually resolved following adequate hydration."
3. Diabetic ketoacidosis considered but excluded; starvation ketoacidosis identified | "He was found to have ... metabolic ketoacidosis secondary to starvation."
4. Primary psychiatric eating disorder (anorexia nervosa) identified as the underlying cause of refusal to eat | "He refused all PO intake for 4‑5 days...his condition was so dire that he required several days of stabilization…He was cachectic…BMI <5th percentile."
5. Obsessive‑compulsive contamination fears contributing to food refusal | "He refused all PO intake…exhibiting OCD symptoms of fear of touching objects…contamination fears."

case_prompt: A 55‑year‑old man with known HIV infection on antiretroviral therapy presented to the emergency department on May 26, 2021 with five days of sudden‑onset shortness of breath that had become progressively worse. He reported a productive cough, high‑grade fever, malaise, severe headache, loss of appetite, weight loss, chest pain, night sweats, and fatigue. One month earlier he had experienced bloody sputum. He admitted poor adherence to his ART and intermittent missed doses of cotrimoxazole prophylaxis. On examination he appeared acutely ill; blood pressure was 110/60 mm Hg, temperature 39.3 °C, pulse 112 beats/min, respiratory rate 38/min, and oxygen saturation 87 % on room air. He was tachypneic with shallow breathing, using accessory muscles. Lung examination revealed dullness over the left lower lobe, markedly reduced breath sounds at the left base, and coarse crepitations over the left upper and lower zones; the right lung was vesicular. He was alert and oriented. Laboratory studies showed random glucose 110 mg/dL, leukocytosis 15.2 × 10³/µL with lymphocytic predominance, ESR 86 mm/h, normal blood film, serum creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, and unremarkable liver function tests. Chest X‑ray demonstrated perihilar patchy opacities. The patient was placed on nasal oxygen and admitted as a medical emergency.
diagnostic_reasoning:

2. COVID‑19 considered given acute fever, severe dyspnea, hypoxia, and elevated respiratory rate; later confirmed by nasopharyngeal PCR positivity. | "nasopharyngeal sample for SARS CoV‑2 PCR was positive"

case_prompt: In November 2020, a 57‑year‑old woman with no prior medical problems presented to the emergency department with cough and dyspnea. A nasopharyngeal swab was obtained for SARS‑CoV‑2 testing. Chest computed tomography showed bilateral patchy ground‑glass opacities. Initial laboratory studies revealed severe neutropenia (neutrophils 0.55 × 10⁹/L), mild thrombocytopenia (platelets 115 × 10⁹/L), and marked anemia (hemoglobin 50 g/L). She was admitted to the intensive‑care unit, started on piperacillin/tazobactam, posaconazole, dexamethasone per institutional COVID‑19 protocol, and received CPAP with pronation. Because of a sharply rising D‑dimer on hospital day 2, a contrast chest CT was performed, which confirmed the ground‑glass opacities and demonstrated bilateral pulmonary emboli; low‑molecular‑weight heparin was added. Given the unexplained severe cytopenias, a bone‑marrow aspirate was performed to investigate the abnormal blood counts.

case_prompt:
A 34‑year‑old Caucasian man with a history of borderline hypertension, hypothyroidism and transient arthralgia two years earlier was admitted in November 2020 to a pulmonology ward for fever (up to 38.5 °C), dyspnoea, haemoptysis and bilateral pneumonia. He tested positive for SARS‑CoV‑2. During hospitalization he developed alveolar haemorrhage and acute kidney injury, prompting transfer to a nephrology clinic on 21 November 2020.

On admission to nephrology he was afebrile, had mild haemoptysis, conjunctivitis, oxygen saturation 86‑94 % on 10‑15 L /min oxygen, blood pressure 120/70 mmHg, and urinary analysis showed numerous erythrocytes and proteinuria 0.47 g/L. Laboratory tests showed anaemia, leukocytosis, hypoproteinaemia, dysproteinaemia, markedly elevated D‑dimer (2 378 µg/L, later 4 053 µg/L), increased C‑reactive protein, interleukin‑6, creatinine and urea; coagulation parameters were normal. Chest CT demonstrated findings consistent with both viral pneumonia and alveolar haemorrhage.

Serologic work‑up revealed negative anti‑glomerular basement membrane antibodies, negative antinuclear antibodies, negative cytoplasmic ANCA (c‑ANCA) and a high‑titer perinuclear ANCA (p‑ANCA > 200; normal < 1:20), suggesting p‑ANCA vasculitis complicating COVID‑19.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Pulmonary‑renal syndrome in a COVID‑19 patient raised concern for anti‑GBM disease, but anti‑GBM antibodies were negative, making anti‑GBM vasculitis unlikely. | "anti‑glomerular basement membrane antibodies (anti‑GBM) ... were negative"
2. Systemic lupus erythematosus was considered given renal involvement, yet antinuclear antibodies were negative, excluding lupus nephritis. | "antineuclear antibodies (ANA) ... were negative"
3. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (c‑ANCA vasculitis) could explain pulmonary haemorrhage, but c‑ANCA was negative, reducing this possibility. | "cytoplasmic anti‑neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (c‑ANCA) were negative"
4. Pure COVID‑19‑related lung injury was plausible because of viral pneumonia on CT, but the presence of high‑titer p‑ANCA and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis pointed toward an ANCA‑associated vasculitis rather than isolated viral damage. | "p‑ANCA were found with a high titer (>200; N: <1:20), suggesting p‑ANCA vasculitis complicating COVID‑19"
5. Bacterial superinfection was considered given haemoptysis and leukocytosis, but cultures were not highlighted and the dominant clinical picture was vasculitic rather than infectious. | "owing to the alveolar haemorrhage and probable bacterial superinfection, clarithromycin and piperacillin with tazobactam were ordered"
6. The combination of alveolar haemorrhage, pauci‑immune renal pathology (crescents with no immune deposits) and p‑ANCA positivity confirmed the diagnosis of p‑ANCA‑associated rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. | "Immunofluorescence did not reveal any deposits of immunoglobulins nor complement components"

case_prompt: A 17‑year‑old adolescent with no significant past medical history presented to the emergency department after 5 days of headache, diarrhea, fever, abdominal pain, and musculoskeletal pain. Inflammatory biomarkers were markedly elevated, including C‑reactive protein, procalcitonin, ferritin, and syndecan‑1; sublingual video microscopy showed altered microvascular parameters. case_prompt:
A 30‑year‑old man with end‑stage renal disease underwent a living donor kidney transplant in March 2013. Post‑transplant he was maintained on tacrolimus (trough 5 µg/L), mycophenolic acid 1 g/day, and prednisone 2.5 mg/day, with stable renal function (serum creatinine ≈138 µmol/L) as of early January 2020. 

On 31 January 2020 (day 0) he developed a fever of 39 °C, myalgia, anorexia, and a heart rate of 120 bpm. A nasopharyngeal swab was obtained. A computed‑tomography scan of the thorax showed extensive ground‑glass opacity involving the left lung field. Routine blood work demonstrated lymphocytopenia. He subsequently required supplemental oxygen via a non‑rebreather mask, and his immunosuppressive regimen was modified (prednisone dose increased, mycophenolic acid withdrawn, later tacrolimus held). Intravenous immunoglobulin was administered from days 7 to 9. By day 26 his symptoms had resolved, the chest CT improved, and repeat nasopharyngeal testing was negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:

2. Influenza – considered because oseltamivir was administered as part of empiric therapy. | "He clinically deteriorated and received supportive therapy with oseltamivir, antibiotics, and supplementary oxygen..."
3. Bacterial pneumonia – considered and empirically treated with antibiotics, but the lack of a focal consolidative pattern on CT and the rapid progression suggested a viral etiology. | "He clinically deteriorated and received supportive therapy with oseltamivir, antibiotics, and supplementary oxygen..."
4. Non‑infectious pulmonary edema – contemplated given the CT findings and hypoxia, but the presence of ground‑glass opacities bilaterally and lymphocytopenia favored an infectious process. | "CT which demonstrated pulmonary oedema consistent with severe COVID‑19."

case_prompt: A 62‑year‑old man presented to the emergency department with recurrent fainting episodes, asthenia, and a dry cough that began one week earlier. His past medical history was notable only for hypertension treated with four antihypertensive agents (losartan, hydrochlorothiazide, amlodipine, and furosemide). On arrival his blood pressure was 97/52 mmHg and heart rate 100 bpm. Chest X‑ray showed converging diffuse condensations in both pulmonary fields, predominantly central, suggestive of an evolving SARS‑CoV‑2 infection. Arterial blood gas revealed hypoxemia and hypocapnia; laboratory studies demonstrated leukocytosis with neutrophilia and an elevated D‑dimer. Because of hypotension, global respiratory insufficiency, and high suspicion for SARS‑CoV‑2 infection, a CT pulmonary angiogram was obtained to exclude pulmonary embolism. The scan demonstrated bilateral patched consolidations with open bronchi and ground‑glass opacities, and no filling defects were seen in the pulmonary arteries. Incidentally, the lower images revealed a left adrenal mass measuring 8 × 7.4 cm with a cystic component and a large calcification, interpreted as possibly a hematoma or pseudocyst.

2. Pulmonary embolism ruled out because CT pulmonary angiogram showed no arterial filling defects. | "no filling defects were observed in the pulmonary arteries"  
3. Adrenal hemorrhage or pseudocyst considered for the left adrenal mass because of its size, cystic component, and calcification on imaging. | "suggestive of a hematoma or pseudocyst"  
4. Pheochromocytoma later favored after biochemical evidence of markedly elevated plasma and 24‑h urinary metanephrine/normetanephrine levels, despite initial imaging uncertainty. | "Elevated plasma and 24‑h urinary metanephrine and normetanephrine were detected"  
5. Bacterial pneumonia less likely given the lack of focal lobar infiltrates, absence of sputum production, and the presence of typical viral imaging patterns. | (implicit from imaging description and clinical context)  
6. Sepsis secondary to adrenal hemorrhage considered but excluded after hemodynamic instability improved with supportive care and the underlying tumor was identified. | (implicit from clinical course)
