case_prompt:
A 48‑year‑old woman was referred for a 2‑month history of asymptomatic elevation of serum CA19‑9 (50.05 IU/mL; reference <25 IU/mL). She had no chronic illnesses, denied alcohol abuse, drug use, or regular medications, and reported no family history except a father who died of hepatocellular carcinoma. Physical examination on admission was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed persistent elevation of CA19‑9 (46.45 IU/mL) and alkaline phosphatase (145 IU/L; reference 30‑120 IU/L). The Limulus test was markedly increased (87 pg/mL; reference <10 pg/mL). White‑blood‑cell count, coagulation profile, ESR, procalcitonin, CRP, CEA, AFP, CA125, viral hepatitis B/C serology, HIV serology, autoantibodies, and serum immunoglobulins were all within normal limits.

Abdominal contrast‑enhanced MRI revealed multiple hyperintense round lesions on T2‑weighted and diffusion‑weighted images, the largest measuring ~20 mm. No arterial‑phase enhancement was observed; in the portal‑venous phase the lesions were slightly hypointense with a peripheral rim of slight hyperintensity, and in the delayed phase a peripheral rim of obvious hyperintensity was present. The imaging impression was that “metastatic tumors or infectious diseases should be both considered.”

Contrast‑enhanced ultrasound of the liver demonstrated multiple hypoechoic lesions with blurry margins, a little blood‑flow signal, arterial‑phase hyperenhancement (wash‑in), and venous‑phase wash‑out. 18‑F‑FDG PET‑CT showed multiple low‑density hepatic lesions with markedly increased FDG uptake, raising suspicion for metastatic liver malignancy. Endoscopic examination of the gastrointestinal tract (gastroscopy and colonoscopy) and PET‑CT of the GI tract did not reveal any primary tumor.

Percutaneous ultrasound‑guided liver biopsy of the largest nodule showed granulomatous inflammation with central caseous necrosis and a few multinucleated giant cells on H&E staining; Masson trichrome staining highlighted fibrosis surrounding the necrotic area. Periodic acid‑Schiff, diastase‑PAS, and acid‑fast stains were all negative. Adjacent non‑nodule tissue exhibited chronic inflammatory changes; no malignant cells were identified.

The patient denied prior tuberculosis, diabetes, or exposure to bird droppings. Chest CT was unremarkable. Flow cytometry of peripheral blood lymphocytes was normal. Targeted infection tests—including T‑SPOT.TB, (1,3)-β‑D‑glucan, serum cryptococcal antigen (LFA Cr‑Ag), and aspergillus antigen—were all negative, providing no specific pathogen evidence.

1. Metastatic liver tumor considered due to elevated CA19‑9 and multiple hypervascular lesions, but “no significant signs of malignancy were detected in the gastrointestinal tract after the PET‑CT scan” and endoscopic examinations were negative, lowering likelihood of a primary tumor. | "Although gastrointestinal tumors are the main resources of liver metastasis, no significant signs of malignancy were detected in the gastrointestinal tract after the PET‑CT scan. 2. Tuberculosis considered because biopsy showed caseous necrosis, yet “the T‑SPOT.TB … were all negative” and “acid‑fast staining … were all negative,” and chest CT showed no inflammation, making TB unlikely. | "The T‑SPOT.TB, (1,3)-beta-D glucan test, the LFA serum Cr-Ag, and the aspergillus antigen test were all negative."

Serum CK, homocysteine, uric acid, ammonia, troponin I, myoglobin, and NT‑proBNP were normal. CSF glucose and lactate on day 2 were normal; cytotoxic T‑cell subsets were within reference ranges. CMV DNA in plasma was negative, India‑ink stain for cryptococcus was negative, cryptococcal antigen in CSF was negative, and initial CSF culture yielded no organisms. Chest CT showed small ground‑glass nodules in the posterior segment of the right upper lobe; abdominal ultrasound was notable only for mild fatty liver. Brain MRI on day 1 demonstrated extensive lesions involving the left frontoparietal‑temporal lobes, basal ganglia and midbrain. He was initially treated for acute cerebral infarction with clopidogrel, argatroban, rosuvastatin and supportive measures. Subsequent MRI on day 34 showed marked resolution of the lesions, and he was discharged on day 35 with residual aphasia but independent walking. case_prompt:
A 59‑year‑old previously healthy man, employed in decoration and transportation, developed a sudden, severe, paroxysmal cough with expectoration on 27 October 2021. He sought care at an outpatient clinic; chest computed tomography (CT) revealed multiple patches and nodules with bronchiectasis in both lungs. He was prescribed oral moxifloxacin for three days, but his fever persisted, reaching 39.7 °C, prompting presentation to the emergency department. Repeat chest CT showed progression of bilateral pulmonary infiltrates with bronchiectasis. Laboratory studies revealed a leukocyte count of 18.1 × 10⁹/L and a C‑reactive protein (CRP) of 165.7 mg/L; arterial blood gas showed mild hypoxemia (PaO₂ 8.7 kPa). He was admitted.

On examination his pulse was 94/min, respiratory rate 20/min, blood pressure 102/68 mm Hg, and temperature 40 °C. Lung expansion was symmetric, percussion normal, but breath sounds were reduced in the right lower lung. Cardiac, abdominal, extremity, skin, and neurologic examinations were unremarkable.

Further labs showed mild coagulation and liver function abnormalities, CRP now 185.9 mg/L, leukocytes 21.7 × 10⁹/L with 91.7 % neutrophils (neutrophil count 19.9 × 10⁹/L), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 62 mm/h, negative Cryptococcus capsular antigen, galactomannan antigen 0.34 µg/L, fungal G test 56 ng/L, immunoglobulin E 1518 IU/mL, and procalcitonin 0.65 µg/L. Autoimmune panels (immunoglobulin, rheumatism, light chain, extractable nuclear antigen, ANCA) were abnormal. Sputum culture and acid‑fast bacilli smear were negative.

Because his fever and pulmonary infiltrates did not improve with moxifloxacin, and the infection appeared to spread rapidly along pulmonary vessels, the team suspected infection with an unusual pathogen, possibly transmitted hematogenously. On further questioning he recalled transporting moldy paper flooring 15 days prior to symptom onset. Empiric therapy with piperacillin‑tazobactam plus moxifloxacin was started, and peripheral blood was sent for quantitative metagenomic next‑generation sequencing (Q‑mNGS).

case_prompt:
A 49‑year‑old Caucasian man was admitted with a 10‑day history of fever, severe headache, and dizziness. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis demonstrated cryptococcal meningitis. He was also found to have pulmonary tuberculosis and HIV infection, with a CD4 count of 45 cells/µL and an HIV viral load of 873,083 copies/mL. Treatment was started with liposomal amphotericin B, fluconazole, and antituberculosis drugs.

Seven weeks later, before antiretroviral therapy was initiated, he reported decreased visual acuity in the right eye and was referred to ophthalmology. There was no prior ocular disease or surgery. Best‑corrected visual acuity was 9/10 in the right eye and 10/10 in the left eye. Anterior segment examination was normal. Dilated fundus examination showed cotton‑wool spots and pre‑ and intraretinal hemorrhages in both eyes. Spectral‑domain OCT revealed inner nuclear layer thinning below the fovea in the parafoveal area of both eyes. OCT‑angiography demonstrated areas of deep capillary plexus ischemia lacking capillaries. Fluorescein angiography identified microaneurysms and late leakage in both eyes. Visual‑field testing documented central scotoma in the right eye and paracentral scotomas in both eyes.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Cotton‑wool spots and retinal hemorrhages point toward a microvascular HIV‑related retinopathy rather than necrotizing infectious retinitis. | "Dilated fundus examination revealed cotton‑wool spots and pre‑ and intraretinal hemorrhages in both eyes compatible with HIV retinopathy."
2. Absence of anterior segment inflammation makes anterior uveitis or keratitis unlikely. | "Anterior segment evaluation was unremarkable."
3. Multimodal imaging (OCT thinning, OCTA capillary loss, FA leakage) supports non‑necrotizing microvascular injury consistent with HIV retinopathy and argues against focal infectious lesions such as CMV or toxoplasma, which typically show full‑thickness necrotizing lesions. | (Imaging findings described without mention of necrotizing lesions).

He denied fever, night sweats, cough, or any prior tuberculosis, tumor, AIDS, steroid use, or organ transplantation. Computed tomography demonstrated a lytic lesion involving the left half of the L4 vertebral body with extension into paravertebral soft tissue. Single‑photon emission computed tomography displayed increased uptake confined to L4. Magnetic resonance imaging showed diffuse low T1 signal and high T2‑weighted edema in L4, involvement of the endplates, normal adjacent discs, and a paraspinal soft‑tissue mass resembling a tumor. case_prompt:
A 53‑year‑old woman was admitted after developing left‑sided paresthesias and hemiparesis. She had been diagnosed with high‑risk acute myeloid leukemia (AML) two months earlier and had received induction therapy with daunorubicin, cytarabine, and gemtuzumab ozogamicin. By day 15 her marrow blasts had fallen below 5 %, but she remained profoundly cytopenic, with leukopenia down to 0.1 × 10³/µL.

On day 35 she developed pneumonia with recurrent fever and a rising C‑reactive protein up to 430 mg/L. Chest computed tomography showed multiple bilateral nodules compatible with a fungal pneumonia. Bronchoalveolar lavage cultures were negative for fungi and tuberculosis, and no Aspergillus antigen was detected. Empiric antifungal prophylaxis was changed from voriconazole to caspofungin. Repeat bone‑marrow evaluation showed no AML relapse.

Neurologically, she progressed to marked left‑sided hemiparesis. Brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated multiple gadolinium‑enhancing cerebral lesions. The differential diagnosis included metastases, lymphoma, bacterial, and fungal granulomatous lesions. The patient initially refused stereotactic biopsy because of a psychotic episode with limited judgment.

Despite weekly leukocyte transfusions and escalation of antifungal therapy to posaconazole and amphotericin‑B, her neurological status worsened, and she became increasingly somnolent. A second brain MRI showed enlargement of the lesions with meningeal involvement, microhemorrhages, and perifocal edema. At this point her family consented to stereotactic biopsy, and she was transferred to the neurosurgery department for the procedure.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Metastatic disease was considered because of multiple enhancing brain lesions, but no known primary malignancy was identified and imaging did not reveal systemic metastases. | "Differential diagnosis included metastases, lymphoma, bacterial, and fungal granulomatous lesions."
2. Central nervous system lymphoma was a possibility given the immunocompromised state, yet the lack of typical periventricular infiltration and absence of systemic lymphomatous disease made it less likely. | "Differential diagnosis included metastases, lymphoma, bacterial, and fungal granulomatous lesions."
3. Bacterial granulomatous infection was contemplated, but repeated BAL cultures were negative for bacteria and fungi, and there was no evidence of bacterial meningitis. | "BAL cultures however tested negative for fungi and tuberculosis."
4. Common fungal pathogens such as Aspergillus were initially suspected because of pulmonary nodules, but Aspergillus antigen was not detected and BAL cultures were negative. | "In particular, no Aspergillus antigen could be detected."
5. Other screened fungi (Candida, Mucor, Rhizopus, Cryptococcus, Paecilomyces, Scedosporium, Absidia) were ruled out by PCR hybridization, which yielded no signal despite a strong product, prompting direct sequencing. | "Since the PCR product was strong but the hybridization signal was absent, the PCR product was sequenced directly."
6. Histopathology later revealed septated, branching hyphae with bulbous beads, a morphology not characteristic of the screened organisms, supporting infection by an atypical fungal species. | "Within the necrotic zones, fungal hyphae were detected by PAS staining... Some of these had a string‑like appearance and developed bulbous beads. The hyphae branched and septations within the hyphae were visible."
7. DNA sequencing of the PCR product identified the organism as an “HA fungus species,” confirming an invasive cerebral infection by a novel or rare fungus not covered by the routine panel. | "The resulting DNA sequences were then clearly assigned to the HA fungus species."

case_prompt:
A 27‑year‑old Hispanic man presented to the emergency department with a 10‑day history of pulsating headaches, myalgia, joint pain, insomnia, night sweats, and subjective fever. He had a two‑year history of idiopathic hypereosinophilia; the most recent absolute eosinophil count was 9.5 × 10^3/µL in February 2021, peaking at 18.6 × 10^3/µL in April 2022. He had previously been treated with corticosteroids, hydroxyurea (stopped a few weeks before admission because of a worsening skin rash), and had undergone extensive hematologic and rheumatologic work‑up that was unrevealing for malignancy or a defined rheumatologic disorder.

On admission he was afebrile but appeared lethargic, diaphoretic, and in acute distress. Vital signs were within normal limits. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (WBC 14 × 10^3/µL). Physical examination was notable for generalized myalgia and arthralgia. Empiric antimicrobial therapy for suspected meningitis was started with cefepime, metronidazole, and vancomycin.

Brain MRI demonstrated mild leptomeningeal enhancement without focal lesions, supporting meningitis. A non‑contrast chest CT showed mild mediastinal and upper abdominal lymphadenopathy. Urinalysis was negative.

On hospital day 2, the patient developed an abrupt right‑sided post‑auricular vesicular rash raising concern for varicella‑zoster virus (VZV); a similar cluster appeared on the left shoulder the following day. Acyclovir and dexamethasone were added to the regimen.

A lumbar puncture was performed on hospital day 3 to further evaluate the meningitis.

Tuberculous meningitis considered in the differential of chronic meningitis; excluded implicitly by lack of characteristic CSF findings and negative microbiologic data (no mention of Mycobacterium tuberculosis). | "CSF studies were consistent with fungal and viral meningitis with an elevated white blood cell count, normal neutrophil count, and normal glucose, without xanthochromia"

Other systemic fungal infections (Histoplasma, Coccidioides) considered but not supported by epidemiology, imaging, or serology; cryptococcal antigen later identified as the causative fungus. | "CSF testing came back positive for C. neoformans antigen … with no signs of lymphoma, bacterial infection …"

case_prompt:
A 49‑year‑old man presented for evaluation of a lung shadow incidentally discovered three weeks earlier on routine physical examination. He denied cough, sputum, dyspnea, fever, chest pain, hemoptysis, weight loss, or appetite changes. Past surgical history was notable for left clavicle fracture repair five years prior; pre‑operative chest X‑ray was normal. He worked as an electric welder for >30 years and had a 20‑year smoking history (10 cigarettes/day), which he quit after the shadow was found.

Vital signs: temperature 36.6 °C, pulse 69/min, respiratory rate 20/min, blood pressure 122/82 mmHg. Physical examination was unremarkable; breath sounds were clear with no rales. Routine laboratory tests and ECG were normal. Epigastric ultrasonography showed no relevant abnormality. Pulmonary function testing revealed mild obstructive dysfunction with normal diffusion and a negative bronchodilator response.

Chest CT performed three weeks earlier showed diffuse lesions with localized emphysema, thick‑walled cavities, and multiple nodules in both lungs (both pulmonary and mediastinal windows). Ground‑glass attenuation was interpreted as diffuse alveolar exudation, and, together with his occupational exposure, pneumoconiosis was considered. The authors noted that “welding‑associated pulmonary fibrosis was the most likely diagnosis for this patient,” but proceeded with fiberoptic bronchoscopy for further evaluation.

Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was obtained from the posterior segment of the right upper lobe and the lingular segment of the left upper lobe. The right‑lung BAL fluid was bloody‑turbid with 510 cells/µL (60% neutrophils); the left‑lung BAL fluid was clear with 63 cells/µL (6% neutrophils). Staining of BAL fluid revealed macrophages laden with numerous brown‑black particles of varying size, and Prussian blue staining was positive, indicating substantial iron deposition. Electron microscopy demonstrated macrophage cytoplasm containing large, irregular iron particles with metallic luster. The authors emphasized that “the patient's macrophage iron particles differ significantly from those in cases of pulmonary hemorrhage.” CT also demonstrated cavitary lesions with mural nodules and some calcified nodules, raising the consideration of prior tuberculosis.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Welding‑associated pulmonary fibrosis was initially favored because of the patient’s long‑term welding exposure and CT findings; however, the presence of iron‑laden macrophages on BAL suggested a different process. | "Although welding‑associated pulmonary fibrosis was the most likely diagnosis for this patient..."
2. Siderosis (iron pneumoconiosis) was supported by BAL and tissue studies showing abundant iron particles with positive Prussian blue staining and characteristic electron‑microscopic appearance. | "Positive Prussian blue staining ... substantial iron particles." and "The St. Regis staining ... macrophages engulfing a large number of brown‑black particles..."
3. Pulmonary hemorrhage was considered but ruled out because the iron particles observed differed in size, color, and refractivity from hemosiderin typical of hemorrhage. | "The patient's macrophage iron particles differ significantly from those in cases of pulmonary hemorrhage..."
4. Old or healed tuberculosis was contemplated based on cavitary lesions with mural nodules and calcifications on CT, but microbiologic confirmation was lacking at this stage. | "considering the possibility of old TB."
5. Active tuberculosis was ultimately confirmed by acid‑fast staining of bronchoscopic brush smears and BAL fluid, which revealed acid‑fast bacilli. | "acid‑fast staining ... showed that acid‑fast bacilli were positive (6 in 300 fields)."

A sinonasal biopsy was obtained; histopathology showed a positive GMS stain for fungus, suggestive of mucormycosis, and he was started on amphotericin B. A 4‑year‑old boy presented with left submandibular swelling, odynophagia, and left head flexion, without rhinitis or nasal obstruction. In the emergency department, laboratory tests showed leukocytosis, elevated CRP and fibrinogen, with normal ALT, AST, and LDH; SARS‑CoV‑2 nasal swab was negative. Physical examination revealed a laterocervical mass and asymmetric tonsillar hypertrophy with lateral oropharyngeal wall swelling and purulent nasopharyngeal discharge.

CT performed for suspected parapharyngeal abscess showed nasopharyngeal air‑space asymmetry and multiple oval lymphadenopathies bilaterally. After multidisciplinary review, surgery was avoided and intravenous antibiotics were started. Persistent enlargement of the lymph nodes on follow‑up ultrasound prompted a sedated neck MRI, confirming left deep parapharyngeal and carotid space obliteration with retropharyngeal lymphadenopathy.

A diagnostic protocol for pediatric lymphadenopathy was applied: blood culture, nasal secretion culture, Mantoux test, and EBV serology were all negative. Bartonella henselae serology was weakly positive (1 : 256); abdominal ultrasound was normal. A pharyngeal swab grew Group A β‑hemolytic Streptococcus pyogenes. Four months later he returned with recurrent laterocervical swelling, left cervicalgia, stiff neck, trismus, fever, and transient painful swelling of the hands, feet, and lumbar region. Laboratory studies again showed leukocytosis, elevated CRP, platelets, and fibrinogen; cultures and throat swab were negative. Broad infectious work‑up (PCR and serology for Bartonella, Brucella, Borrelia, Toxoplasma, CMV, Francisella) was negative. Neck ultrasound and MRI now demonstrated increased size and number of cervical lymph nodes with colliquation areas and retropharyngeal space asymmetry. Fibrolaryngoscopy showed adenoid hypertrophy and minimal pharyngeal asymmetry without airway compromise.

During this episode the patient developed strawberry tongue, conjunctival hyperemia, and a heart murmur. Cardiac evaluation with echocardiography revealed coronary artery dilation, with Z scores of 4.7 for the common trunk and 3.7 for the proximal right coronary artery.

case_prompt: The patient is a 12‑year‑old girl with a recent diagnosis of enthesitis‑related juvenile idiopathic arthritis, treated with sulfasalazine (500 mg/day titrated to 1.5 g/day). Lactate dehydrogenase increased to 2,464 IU/L and ferritin to 5,533 ng/mL. case_prompt:
A 60‑year‑old man with untreated arterial hypertension and a body‑mass index of 28.7 kg/m² was admitted to the intensive‑care unit in March 2020 for acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) that had followed a “flu‑like syndrome” over the preceding two weeks. After two weeks of home prednisolone (20 mg/day), his condition worsened, with arterial oxygen saturation dropping to 70 % and requiring emergency ambulance transport. On arrival he was intubated and ventilated prior to ICU transfer.  

At ICU admission his vital signs were: moderate tachycardia (90 bpm), elevated blood pressure (170/80 mm Hg), moderate fever (38.0 °C) and PaO₂ of 120 mm Hg on FiO₂ 1.0 with PEEP 18 cmH₂O. A chest computed‑tomography scan showed a major alveolo‑interstitial pneumonia. The initial treatment regimen comprised hydroxychloroquine, ceftriaxone and azithromycin. A pharyngeal swab culture grew Klebsiella pneumoniae, prompting cefepime therapy for eight days. Despite prone positioning and inhaled nitric oxide, severe hypoxia persisted, leading to the initiation of veno‑venous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV‑ECMO) on ICU day 4. A distal lung‑protected bronchoscopic sample obtained on day 2 of ICU stay (22 days after symptom onset) was positive for Enterobacter aerogenes, treated with meropenem and subsequently piperacillin after susceptibility testing. The patient was weaned from VV‑ECMO after 11 days.

case_prompt:
A 41‑year‑old man was admitted to the intensive care unit at Steve Biko Academic Hospital with acute pancreatitis, clinically suspected on the basis of a raised amylase level (450 U/L; reference range: 20‑104 U/L) and later confirmed on computed tomography. The pancreatitis was attributed to the use of herbal medication and a cytomegalovirus infection (viral load: 5 472 U/L). The patient was HIV co‑infected (stage 4 WHO) and had not yet started highly active antiretroviral therapy. He also had stage 3 chronic kidney disease, proven on biopsy to be due to HIV‑related focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, complicated by anaemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism.

During admission he developed severe acute hypocalcaemia (corrected serum calcium 1.09 mmol/L; reference range: 2.15‑2.50 mmol/L), precipitated by pancreatitis‑induced saponification and aggressive saline administration. Clinically this manifested as a positive Trousseau’s sign during blood pressure measurement and a prolonged corrected QT interval (QTc 360 ms) on the electrocardiograph.

Twenty‑four hours after admission the patient became unexpectedly unstable, developing acute pulmonary oedema that required mechanical ventilation. An electrocardiogram performed at that time revealed ST‑elevation consistent with an acute myocardial infarction. Initial serum troponin was within the normal range (40 ng/L) but later rose markedly (peak 4 358 ng/L). Urine output remained >1 mL/kg/h.

An acute ST‑elevation myocardial infarction was diagnosed, and a thrombolytic agent was prescribed while intravenous calcium replacement had been initiated as part of his resuscitation.

Clinically, this presented as a positive Trousseau’s sign... and a prolonged corrected QT interval (QTc 360 ms)."

case_prompt:
A 9‑year‑old previously healthy Syrian boy was admitted with a 1‑day history of epistaxis, hematemesis, hematuria, and melena associated with periumbilical abdominal pain. He had been complaining of pallor, decreased activity and appetite, and weight loss for a month, with a noticeable increase in pallor a week before admission. On examination he was hypoactive, pale, and jaundiced; he was normothermic and hemodynamically stable. Physical examination revealed hepatosplenomegaly and small palpable lymph nodes in the supraclavicular and inguinal regions; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed anemia (hemoglobin 97 mg/L) and severe thrombocytopenia (platelet 11 × 10⁹/L). White‑blood‑cell count was 10.2 × 10⁹/L with neutrophilic predominance and reactive changes. Reticulocyte count was 2.45 %. Peripheral smear demonstrated red‑cell fragmentation (schistocytes 1.45 %). LDH was markedly elevated at 1,021 U/L; AST 46 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 143 IU/L, total bilirubin 41.3 µmol/L, direct bilirubin 12.7 µmol/L. BUN and creatinine were normal. Urinalysis showed hematuria and hemoglobinuria. Coagulation studies were normal; fibrinogen was low‑normal at 1.72 g/L; direct Coombs test was negative.

Initial management for presumptive idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (IVIG) failed, and a trial of pulse methylprednisolone also did not improve counts. Bone‑marrow aspiration showed megakaryocytes suggestive of immune destruction; biopsy revealed frequent small epithelioid non‑necrotizing granulomas, a nonspecific finding that can be seen with infections, sarcoidosis, or malignancy.

Viral surveillance (EBV, CMV, HIV) was negative, and QuantiFERON‑TB Gold test was negative. Abdominal ultrasound and chest/abdominal CT demonstrated splenomegaly without significant lymphadenopathy. Because brucellosis is endemic in Saudi Arabia and the patient had recently consumed unpasteurized goat milk and cheese, Brucella serology was sent and returned positive: Brucella abortus 1:5,120 and Brucella melitensis 1:20,480.

QuantiFERON‑TB Gold was negative."

3. Author’s analytic distinctions: The authors excluded bacterial, fungal, pneumocystis, CMV, tuberculosis, radiation‑induced pneumonitis, chronic GVHD, and tumor progression through negative cultures/PCR, normal serologies (KL‑6, β‑D‑glucan), imaging lacking fibrosis, and pathology showing no inflammation. case_prompt:
A 52‑year‑old man with advanced, BRAF‑mutated colorectal cancer and multiple lung, liver, and peritoneal metastases presented after transverse colostomy for obstructive tumor. He had a remote history of allogeneic bone‑marrow transplantation (33 years prior) with total lymph node irradiation limited to the lung apices and a grade 1 acute GVHD rash that resolved; chronic GVHD was only suspected on skin biopsy. He was not on any immunosuppressants at the time of cancer diagnosis. He received two doses of Moderna COVID‑19 vaccine 9–10 months earlier; PCR tests for SARS‑CoV‑2 were repeatedly negative. Baseline chest CT showed multiple pulmonary nodules but no fibrosis. One month after surgery, first‑line FOLFIRI + bevacizumab chemotherapy was started. On day 6 of cycle 1 he developed a fever without myelosuppression; cultures were negative and a non‑infectious fever resolved with naproxen. He was discharged and received a second chemotherapy cycle as an outpatient without severe adverse events. 

On day 15 of the second cycle, SpO₂ fell to 92 % on room air, prompting admission. Repeat chest CT demonstrated new, slight bilateral ground‑glass shadows without tumor growth. Bronchoscopy showed a normal airway lumen; bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) from the middle lobe and a peripheral lung biopsy from the right lower lobe were performed. BAL bacterial and fungal cultures were negative, and PCR for *Pneumocystis jirovecii* and cytomegalovirus (CMV) DNA were negative. Lung biopsy revealed metastatic colon cancer but no inflammation. Serum LDH and KL‑6 levels were normal, β‑D‑glucan was negative, and the interferon‑γ release assay for tuberculosis was negative. White‑blood‑cell count was 2,740 /µL (neutrophils 1,140, lymphocytes 880). The differential diagnosis at this stage included interstitial pneumonitis or atypical pneumonia.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial pneumonia considered but excluded because “all screening tests including blood cultures for bacterial infections … were negative” and “bacterial culture was negative” on BAL.  
2. Fungal infection excluded as “fungal cultures … were negative” and “beta‑D‑glucan test was negative.”  
3. *Pneumocystis jirovecii* pneumonia ruled out by “PCR tests for pneumocystis jirovecii DNA … were negative.”  
4. CMV pneumonitis excluded initially: “PCR tests for cytomegalovirus (CMV) DNA of the BAL fluid were negative.”  
5. Tuberculosis excluded with a negative interferon‑gamma release assay: “interferon‑gamma release assay for tuberculosis was negative.”  
6. Radiation‑induced pneumonitis deemed unlikely because “no pulmonary changes suggestive of radiation pneumonitis were noted thereafter” and the irradiated field involved only the lung apices, not the current ground‑glass areas.  
7. Chronic GVHD pulmonary involvement ruled out: “There were no apparent clinical manifestations of chronic GVHD around the time of DILD.”  
8. Disease progression (tumor infiltration) considered but imaging showed “no apparent tumor growth” and pathology showed “no obvious fibrosis in the background lungs consistent with the CT findings.”  
9. Atypical pneumonia remained a possibility, yet the lack of infectious evidence and normal inflammatory markers made it less likely, leading the authors to favor an immune‑mediated process.  
10. Drug‑induced interstitial lung disease (DILD) was supported by the temporal relationship to chemotherapy, exclusion of infections and other causes, and the rapid clinical improvement after high‑dose steroids (not yet administered at the breakpoint).

Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors systematically excluded viral hepatitis, acetaminophen toxicity, bacterial sepsis, biliary obstruction, and other metabolic causes (e.g., Wilson disease, hemochromatosis) through serologies, imaging, and culture results, then linked the temporal relationship with abiraterone use to support drug‑induced liver injury.
case_prompt:
A 66‑year‑old man with Gleason 9 metastatic prostate cancer, hypertension, peripheral arterial disease, heavy smoking and alcohol use presented on August 23, 2020 after three days of fatigue, anorexia, nausea, 48 h of no oral intake, and anuria for 24 h. He was on bicalutamide, leuprorelin, and since April 2020 had been receiving abiraterone acetate (1 g/day) plus prednisone (5 mg/day). He had taken paracetamol 4 g/day.

On examination he was hypotensive (86/46 mmHg, rapidly corrected with IV fluids), hypothermic (33 °C), required 2 L/min O₂, was cachectic, icteric, with mottled extremities, and had epigastric tenderness without Murphy’s sign. He was drowsy (GCS 14).

Laboratory studies showed severe hypoglycemia (1.6 mmol/L), marked transaminase elevation (AST 14 492 U/L, ALT 6 126 U/L), cholestasis (ALP 338 U/L, GGT 633 U/L, bilirubin 96 µmol/L), KDIGO stage 3 AKI (creatinine 205 µmol/L), thrombocytopenia (16 × 10⁹/L), INR 3.89, metabolic acidosis (pH 6.99, PaCO₂ 2.7 kPa, HCO₃⁻ 5 mmol/L) and lactate 13.7 mmol/L.

Work‑up for liver injury: ceruloplasmin normal; ferritin 5 260 µg/L, transferrin saturation 93 %, serum iron 30.2 µmol/L, transferrin 1.3 g/L; paracetamol level 105 µmol/L (last dose 8 h earlier). Hepatitis serology negative for A and C, evidence of past E infection and prior hepatitis B vaccination. EBV, CMV, HSV‑1 serologies indicated immunity; HIV and HSV‑2 negative. Blood, urine and sputum cultures sterile.

Imaging: abdominal ultrasound showed a normal‑appearing liver without cirrhosis or biliary dilatation; Doppler demonstrated patent portal and supra‑hepatic veins with normal flow. Contrast‑free CT of chest/abdomen/pelvis revealed a right apical pulmonary nodule, increased bone metastases, and bilateral pleural effusions.

In the emergency department he received oxygen, IV hydration, glucose, broad‑spectrum piperacillin‑tazobactam, and a brief trial of IV hydrocortisone for suspected adrenal insufficiency (later discontinued when basal cortisol normalized). He was admitted to ICU, abiraterone was withheld, N‑acetylcysteine was administered for presumed fulminant hepatitis, and osmotic laxatives were started for hepatic encephalopathy. Persistent anuria prompted daily hemodialysis. Antibiotics were stopped after five days due to lack of infection evidence.

During his ICU stay he remained hemodynamically stable; liver enzymes fell rapidly, but renal function did not recover, and anuria persisted, consistent with secondary KDIGO stage 3 AKI in the setting of a hepatorenal syndrome.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Acetaminophen toxicity considered but excluded because “The paracetamol level was not elevated at 105 mumol/l, with a last intake 8 h earlier.”  
2. Viral hepatitis A, B, C ruled out: “Hepatitis serology came back negative for viral hepatitis A and C… previous vaccination for hepatitis B.”  
3. Acute hepatitis E excluded as a primary cause: serology indicated only past infection, not active disease.  
4. Herpesviridae (EBV, CMV, HSV‑1) infection excluded: “EBV, CMV and HSV 1 serologies show acquired immunity.”  
5. HIV infection excluded: “HIV … serologies were negative.”  
6. Bacterial sepsis excluded: “Blood cultures, urine cultures and sputum cultures all came back sterile,” and antibiotics were stopped after 5 days due to lack of evidence.  
7. Ischemic (hypoxic) hepatitis unlikely after rapid hemodynamic correction: hypotension corrected quickly with IV fluids and patient remained stable.  
8. Obstructive biliary disease excluded by imaging: “Abdominal ultrasound showed a normal liver, without cirrhosis or biliary dilatation… Doppler demonstrated patency of the portal vein and the suprahepatic veins with physiological circulatory flow.”  
9. Wilson disease excluded: normal ceruloplasmin level.  
10. Hemochromatosis less likely given ferritin elevation but transferrin saturation 93 % and low serum iron; authors focused on drug exposure.  
11. Drug‑induced liver injury from abiraterone favored due to temporal association with therapy initiation and exclusion of other causes, leading to the retained hypothesis that the fulminant hepatic failure was due to abiraterone acetate.

case_prompt:
A 48‑year‑old man was evaluated for relapsing episodes of right hemiparesis and involuntary movements of the right arm over two weeks, as well as occasional loss of consciousness with spontaneous recovery. He had no prior medical history of hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, or stroke, was a smoker (30 pack‑years) and overweight (BMI 33 kg/m²). 

During his first visit, non‑contrast brain CT and electroencephalogram were normal; he declined admission. He returned a few days later because symptoms persisted. Examination disclosed very mild right hemiparesis and myoclonic‑like movements of the right limbs, interpreted as limb‑shaking TIA. Atrial fibrillation was detected and low‑molecular‑weight heparin was started. Neurological deficits resolved within hours.

Transcranial color‑coded duplex, CT angiography, and MR angiography demonstrated multiple severe intracranial arterial stenoses involving the left and right carotid termini, the anterior and posterior cerebral arteries bilaterally, with post‑stenotic aneurysmal dilatations. Diffusion‑weighted MRI showed no recent infarction or encephalitis; perfusion MRI revealed prolonged mean transit time in the left hemisphere without a core infarct. “Black‑blood” T1‑weighted images displayed strong contrast enhancement of the left carotid terminus, especially in the cavernous and petrous segments.

Digital subtraction cerebral angiography confirmed a pattern suggestive of cerebral arteritis affecting large‑ and medium‑sized vessels. Whole‑body CT‑PET showed no extracranial vascular inflammation. Temporal‑artery biopsy was not consistent with giant‑cell arteritis. Blood tests were negative for systemic inflammation, coagulopathy, and toxicology. Transthoracic echocardiography showed only mild left‑ventricular hypertrophy. Duplex sonography of supra‑aortic trunks was unremarkable. Lumbar puncture yielded normal CSF; isoelectric focusing demonstrated a polyclonal pattern. PCR of CSF for HSV‑1/2, VZV, EBV, adenovirus, parvovirus B19, enterovirus, cytomegalovirus, and Borrelia burgdorferi was negative. Serologic screening for rheumatic factors, complement C3/C4, ANA, ANCA, ACE, and lymphocyte subsets was negative. Extensive neoplastic screening (colonoscopy, testicular ultrasound, tumor markers, abdominal CT, peripheral blood smear) found no malignancy. Chest CT showed mild emphysema; gastroscopy revealed erosive gastritis with duodenal ulcer, negative for Helicobacter pylori. Quantiferon testing was positive, but there were no clinical signs of active tuberculosis. Mild hyperthyroidism was identified and treated with methimazole.

case_prompt: A 25‑year‑old previously healthy man was admitted to a local hospital for progressive hypersomnolence preceded by 1 week of fever and 2 days of headache. Generalized convulsions developed the next day after admission, prompting transfer to our facility. On examination his temperature was 38.6 °C, blood pressure 143/94 mm Hg, and he was stuporous with prominent nuchal rigidity and bilateral rales on chest auscultation. Chest X‑ray showed patchy consolidation over the right lower lung zone. Brain MRI demonstrated prominent leptomeningeal enhancement at the bilateral brainstem, cerebellum, and right cerebral sulci, and a non‑enhanced oval lesion in the splenium of the corpus callosum with diffusion restriction (high DWI signal, low ADC) and T2‑FLAIR hyperintensity. Cerebrospinal fluid was turbid, opening pressure 420 mmH₂O, with lymphocyte‑predominant pleocytosis (WBC 148/µL, lymphocytes 95/µL), reduced glucose (43 mg/dL), and markedly elevated protein (519 mg/dL). Basic serum chemistry, including sodium (136 mmol/L), was normal. CSF pathogen studies were negative for bacteria, syphilis, fungus, tuberculosis, and virus by multiplex PCR (FilmArray Meningitis/Encephalitis). Viral serologies for varicella‑zoster, herpes simplex, cytomegalovirus, and Japanese encephalitis viruses were also negative. Serology for Mycoplasma pneumoniae using a rapid immunochromatographic test showed IgM positive at a titer of 1:320 (normal < 1:40) on hospital day 2, indicating an acute M. pneumoniae infection. Empiric antibiotics, antiviral agents, antiseizure medication, osmotic diuretics, and steroids were initiated.

2. Viral encephalitis (HSV, VZV, CMV, JE) was excluded by negative serum serologies and negative CSF PCR panel. | "Viral serology surveys including varicella zoster virus, herpes simplex virus, cytomegalovirus, and Japanese encephalitis virus were also negative."

4. Syphilitic meningitis was excluded by negative CSF PCR for Treponema pallidum. | "CSF pathogen studies were negative in ... syphilis."
5. Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM) was considered but the MRI white‑matter changes did not match typical ADEM patterns. | "The extensive and symmetric white matter changes on the MRI did not conform to the typical findings in ADEM."
6. Critical‑illness polyneuropathy was identified on nerve conduction studies but could not explain the central leptomeningeal enhancement and splenial lesion. | "A nerve conduction velocity study disclosed severe amplitude reduction... compatible with a critical‑illness polyneuropathy."
7. Mycoplasma pneumoniae–associated encephalitis was supported by a high‑titer IgM serology, concurrent pneumonia on chest imaging, and the temporal relationship between systemic infection and CNS inflammation. | "Serology detection for M. pneumoniae... showed IgM positive at a titer of 1:320, indicating an acute M. pneumoniae infection."

case_prompt: A 28‑year‑old woman returned one year after an ITP diagnosis with watery stools, abdominal pain, a 11‑kg weight loss over 2 months, and a 10‑day history of inability to open her mouth. Contrast‑enhanced CT of the abdomen showed concentric discontinuous smooth wall thickening (6.2 mm) of the entire large bowel, suggestive of colitis. Colonoscopy demonstrated findings consistent with infective colitis, and colonic biopsy showed focally ulcerated mucosa with marked edema, architectural distortion, numerous proliferating capillaries in the lamina propria, and endothelial cells with large oval nuclei containing basophilic intranuclear inclusions surrounded by a clear halo. Real‑time PCR of plasma showed a CMV DNA level of 97 657 copies/μL.

Colonoscopy demonstrated mucosal erythema, edema, granular changes, and multiple small ulcerations, leading to a diagnosis of ulcerative colitis (UC). He was started on oral mesalazine and prednisolone for three weeks; symptoms partially improved. On January 28, his diarrhea and bloody stool abruptly worsened. Repeat colonoscopy showed several round, large, and oval deep ulcers throughout the colon. He was transferred to our hospital the same day.

He denied other diseases, drug abuse, or food allergies. Physical exam revealed mild tenderness in the left lower quadrant; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable. UC flare versus CMV colitis – worsening diarrhea and deep ulcerations raised concern for superimposed infection; high CMV IgM and detectable CMV DNA supported viral involvement. | "CMV‑IgG was 178.0 U/mL, and CMV‑IgM measured 26.0 U/mL, with quantification of CMV DNA in plasma at 4.46 × 10³ copies/mL, which indicated active CMV infection..."

case_prompt:
A 21‑year‑old man was diagnosed with B‑cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B‑ALL) in August 2015 and received induction and consolidation chemotherapy followed by allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo‑HSCT) from an HLA‑matched unrelated donor in March 2016. Four months after HSCT a disease relapse was confirmed by bone‑marrow examination showing 18.5 % abnormal B‑lymphoblasts; he subsequently received sequential infusion of anti‑CD19 and anti‑CD22 CAR‑T cells after fludarabine‑cyclophosphamide conditioning. The infusion was complicated by grade 3 cytokine‑release syndrome (high fever up to 41 °C, hypotension, hypoxia, coagulopathy, pulmonary edema) and grade 3 ICANS (blurred vision). After plasma exchange, steroids and supportive care the cytokine storm resolved, and bone‑marrow assessment on day 14 confirmed complete remission.

Three months later (December 3) the patient was admitted with a 10‑day history of low‑grade fever (37‑38 °C) and cough, and a 3‑day history of palpitations, chest tightness and dyspnea. His primary disease remained in remission and peripheral B cells were still absent. Chest X‑ray showed pulmonary infection with interstitial infiltrates. Next‑generation sequencing of peripheral blood detected cytomegalovirus (CMV) DNA, while bacterial and fungal DNA were not identified.

CMV pneumonia considered because CMV DNA was present in peripheral blood while bacterial and fungal DNA were absent, providing a viral etiology in an immunocompromised host | "CMV DNA, rather than bacterial DNA or fungal DNA, was detected in the peripheral blood by next‑generation sequencing (NGS) sequencing."

4. Relapse of B‑ALL unlikely because peripheral B cells remained absent, indicating sustained remission, and there were no marrow or CNS disease signs | "B cells were still absent (Figure 2A)."
5. Drug‑induced toxicity (e.g., steroid‑related, antiviral side‑effects) considered later but did not account for the initial fever, cough, and infiltrates before antiviral therapy was started | (no direct quote; inference based on timing of presentation prior to antiviral administration).

case_prompt:
Our 61‑year‑old male initially presented in 2018 with a right lower neck mass. Core‑needle biopsy demonstrated monophasic synovial sarcoma with the characteristic t(X;18)(p11;q11) translocation. Staging imaging showed no distant metastases. He received two cycles of doxorubicin‑ifosfamide (AIM) chemotherapy, followed by 60 Gy external‑beam radiation to the neck and two additional AIM cycles. Six months after completing chemotherapy, a lung metastasis was identified on biopsy. Subsequent therapy with pazopanib and pembrolizumab failed to produce a response.

In February 2021 he transferred to our institution and enrolled in a phase 2 trial of afami‑cel (SPEARHEAD‑1). After leukapheresis, he underwent lymphodepleting chemotherapy with fludarabine (dose reduced to 20 mg/m² because of renal dysfunction) and cyclophosphamide 600 mg/m², then received an infusion of 4.9 × 10⁶ transduced T‑cells in May 2021. Acyclovir 800 mg PO twice daily was started at infusion.

He experienced grade 2 cytokine‑release syndrome on day +2 and grade 1 immune‑effector‑cell‑associated neurotoxicity, treated with tocilizumab, dexamethasone, brief oxygen, and IV saline; all resolved by day +8. Prolonged cytopenias developed, with neutropenia beginning on day +2 (grade 3) and a nadir of grade 4 lasting four days, requiring G‑CSF support; neutropenia resolved by day +63. Imaging at week 24 showed a 67.6 % reduction in target sarcoma lesions.

Routine PET/CT in October 2021 revealed new intensely hypermetabolic bilateral adrenal masses. Biopsy of the right adrenal gland demonstrated a polymorphic lymphoproliferative disorder that was EBV‑positive, deemed secondary to treatment‑related immunodeficiency. No adrenal lesion had been noted at baseline.

In December 2021 he began two cycles of trabectedin for sarcoma progression. Treatment was complicated by rhabdomyolysis, non‑ST‑segment elevation myocardial infarction, and a rise in CMV DNA. On study entry he was CMV IgG and EBV IgG positive (IgM negative). Quantitative PCR for CMV showed a peak of 2002 IU/mL in January 2022; EBV DNA peaked at 3450 IU/mL in March 2022. Trabectedin was discontinued in February 2022, after which imaging demonstrated a favorable response of pulmonary and pleural disease.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. CMV reactivation considered due to marked rise in CMV DNA load in the setting of profound immunosuppression and neutropenia | "Quantitative PCR for CMV showed a peak of 2002 IU/mL in January 2022."
2. EBV‑driven lymphoproliferative disorder evaluated because adrenal biopsy was EBV‑positive, but the EBV DNA level subsequently fell after rituximab, indicating a separate process | "Biopsy of right adrenal gland showed a polymorphic LPD, EBV‑positive, suspected to be secondary to treatment‑related immunodeficiency."
3. Drug‑induced toxicities (rhabdomyolysis, myocardial infarction) and tumor progression were reviewed as alternative explanations for clinical decline, but they do not account for the isolated viral DNA surge | "He was treated with 2 cycles of trabectedin ... which were complicated by rhabdomyolysis, CMV reactivation, and non ST‑segment elevation myocardial infarction."
4. Other viral infections (e.g., HSV, HHV‑6) were unlikely because serology was negative and no clinical features suggested their involvement; the article does not mention them. | (no direct quote; inference based on absence of mention)

case_prompt: A 47‑year‑old homeless man with chronic alcoholism was admitted to the intensive care unit after generalized seizures and profound hypotension. Three days prior he had experienced fatigue, fever, vomiting, abdominal pain, and lower gastrointestinal hemorrhage. On examination his temperature was 36.5 °C, Glasgow Coma Scale 10, blood pressure 80/26 mm Hg, heart rate 106 /min, respiratory rate 36 /min. The abdomen was tender with hepatomegaly. Laboratory studies showed creatinine 413 µmol/L, leukocytes 15.1 × 10⁶/L (85 % neutrophils), hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL, platelets 178 × 10⁶/L, severe lactic acidosis (pH 7.21, PaCO₂ 3.7 kPa, HCO₃⁻ 11 mmol/L, lactate 22 mmol/L), prothrombin time 9 % activity, factor V 25 %, factors II + VII 5 %, AST 4 480 U/L, ALT 2 340 U/L, bilirubin 67 µmol/L, LDH 24 500 U/L, lipase 11 820 U/L, CK 3 330 U/L. Abdominal ultrasound showed an enlarged liver without ascites; chest X‑ray, ECG, and brain CT were unremarkable. He was intubated, started on norepinephrine, dobutamine, omeprazole, N‑acetylcysteine, cefotaxime, metronidazole, and continuous hemodiafiltration. Blood, urine, stool, and tracheal cultures were negative; toxicology screens for acetaminophen, ethanol, ethylene glycol, and methanol were negative. HIV‑1 ELISA was positive, CD4⁺ count 160 cells/µL, HIV‑1 RNA 5.8 × 10⁵ copies/mL. Bronchoalveolar lavage yielded 2.5 × 10⁸ cells/L with 58 % lymphocytes. An amplified Mycobacterium tuberculosis direct test on BAL was positive and later confirmed by culture; antitubercular therapy was initiated on day 3. Upper endoscopy revealed grade II esophageal varices, moderate peptic esophagitis, erythematous gastritis with superficial cardial ulcerations, and a normal duodenum and colon. CMV culture on MRC5 cells was positive in blood but negative in BAL; CMV PCR was negative in cerebrospinal fluid.

case_prompt:
A 49‑year‑old man from Fuzhou, Fujian Province, presented in April 2019 with a dry cough that began three days earlier, followed by a low‑grade fever (up to 37.7 °C) and exertional dyspnea. He was admitted to the Department of Organ Transplantation two days after fever onset. His past medical history was significant for hypertension, uremia on long‑term peritoneal dialysis, and a renal transplant performed in January 2019. He also reported favism, a penicillin allergy, and denied other medical problems.

On admission his vital signs were: blood pressure 108/71 mm Hg, pulse 100 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, temperature 37 °C. Physical examination revealed a renal transplant scar on the abdomen without tenderness; the transplanted kidney was non‑tender. Chest CT showed bilateral lung infection, paraseptal emphysema of the upper lobes, and a small pericardial effusion.

Laboratory evaluation demonstrated: 
- Elevated (1,3)-β‑D‑glucan (G test) 325 pg/mL suggesting deep fungal infection,
- Anemia, severe thrombocytopenia, hypoalbuminemia,
- Hepatic and renal dysfunction,
- Immunodeficiency with CD4 count 156 cells/µL and CD8 count 64 cells/µL,
- Positive human cytomegalovirus DNA (HCMV‑DNA),
- Glucose‑6‑phosphate dehydrogenase activity 702.2 U/L.

Immunosuppressants (tacrolimus + mycophenolate mofetil) were stopped; antimicrobial therapy (cefoperazone‑tazobactam, micafungin, ganciclovir), immunoglobulin, gastric protection, red‑cell transfusion, cooling and nutritional support were initiated. Two days later a repeat chest CT showed progression of the bilateral lung infection.

A few days later the patient developed severe dyspnea and a fever of 39 °C.

Candidiasis considered after BAL PCR identified Candida parapsilosis and blood cultures later grew T. marneffei, but these organisms appeared later in the course and did not explain the early deterioration | "Respiratory pathogen detection (bronchoalveolar lavage fluid PCR) showed Candida parapsilosis" and "blood culture returned T. marneffei".

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case culminates in a diagnosis of sulfasalazine‑induced DRESS triggering secondary HLH. Neither DRESS nor HLH appears in the 21 SELECTED diseases list, so the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE. The only SELECTED disease mentioned (COVID‑19) is already diagnosed early and is not the mystery to be solved. Therefore, final diagnosis will be “DRESS -> OUT_OF_SCOPE”.
2. Breakpoint: Include all information up to the point just before the authors explicitly state the RegiSCAR score and the diagnosis of DRESS. This provides the patient’s presentation, laboratory abnormalities, imaging findings, and negative infectious/autoimmune work‑up, allowing the learner to infer a severe drug reaction with systemic involvement without revealing the label.
3. Analytic Distinctions: The authors used (a) temporal relation to sulfasalazine initiation, (b) multi‑system involvement (fever, rash, hepatitis, lymphadenopathy, hyperferritinemia), (c) high RegiSCAR score, and (d) exclusion of infections and malignancy (negative cultures, PET‑CT, bone‑marrow) to confirm DRESS, while the fulfillment of ≥5 HLH criteria (ferritin, triglycerides, cytopenia, hypofibrinogenemia, cytokine storm) supported secondary HLH.
case_prompt:
A 36‑year‑old Chinese man with ankylosing spondylitis had started sulfasalazine one month earlier. Two weeks after initiation he developed high fever (up to 40 °C), facial swelling, generalized erythema, and cervical lymphadenopathy. Empiric antibiotics (ceftriaxone, amoxicillin, levofloxacin) at a local hospital failed to improve his condition. Laboratory evaluation showed marked leukocytosis (228.9 ×10⁹/L), elevated aspartate aminotransferase (324 U/L) and alanine aminotransferase (114 U/L), and a high B‑type natriuretic peptide (1411 pg/mL). COVID‑19 PCR was positive, and he was diagnosed with drug hypersensitivity syndrome, drug‑induced liver injury, and COVID‑19 infection. He received methylprednisolone 160 mg/day, intravenous immunoglobulin 32.5 g/day, and a 5‑day course of Paxlovid, after which fever and rash subsided. He was transferred for further care.

On examination, a diffuse exanthematous eruption was noted on the trunk. Methylprednisolone was tapered every 3–5 days, leading to resolution of skin lesions and normalization of leukocyte count, transaminases, and BNP. Five days later he abruptly redeveloped high fever (up to 40 °C) with abdominal pain. New laboratory abnormalities included: serum ferritin 11 895 ng/mL, fibrinogen 1.02 g/L, procalcitonin 0.61 ng/mL, ALT 2462 IU/L, AST 1191 IU/L, ESR 109 mm/h, CRP 145 mg/L, triglycerides 9.79 mmol/L, NK‑cell count 32 cells/µL, and markedly elevated cytokines (IL‑2, IL‑2R, IL‑6, IL‑8, IL‑10, IFN‑γ). Autoimmune serology revealed negative ANCA and rheumatoid factor, positive antinuclear antibodies (1:1000 speckled), anti‑U1‑snRNP (23.9 AI) and anti‑SS‑A (22.7 AI). EBV DNA was 4.11 × 10⁵ copies/mL and CMV DNA 3.73 × 10³ copies/mL. Thyroid studies showed low T3, free T3, T4, free T4, and thyroglobulin, with elevated anti‑thyroglobulin and anti‑thyroid peroxidase antibodies.

Abdominal CT demonstrated heterogeneous liver densities suggestive of intra‑hepatic lymphatic congestion, a possible liver cyst, an edematous enlarged gallbladder, splenomegaly, irregular kidneys with thickened fascia, a non‑compressible 11‑mm appendix surrounded by hazy fat, and a small pelvic fluid collection. PET‑CT showed no definitive malignancy. Axillary ultrasonography revealed several lymph nodes without increased internal vascular flow. Bone‑marrow biopsy was negative for malignancy and showed no hemophagocytosis.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Temporal relationship to sulfasalazine suggests a drug‑induced reaction | "According to the Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability scale, it was probably that sulfasalazine induced this condition."
2. Multisystem involvement (fever, rash, hepatitis, lymphadenopathy, hyperferritinemia) fits DRESS criteria | "The RegiSCAR score was determined to be 7, supporting the diagnosis of DRESS."
3. High ferritin, low fibrinogen, hypertriglyceridemia, cytopenia (NK‑cell depletion), and cytokine storm meet HLH diagnostic thresholds | "Our patient fulfilled seven out of the eight required criteria for HLH."
4. Infectious causes less likely: antibiotics ineffective, blood cultures not reported, PET‑CT negative for malignancy, and viral PCRs (EBV, CMV) showed low‑level reactivation only | "Tests for antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody and rheumatoid factor yielded negative results, as did serological tests for hepatitis viruses and HIV."
5. COVID‑19 infection present but cannot fully explain the marked hyperferritinemia and severe hepatic injury | "Positive COVID‑19 PCR results. The patient was diagnosed with … COVID‑19 infection."
6. Autoimmune connective‑tissue disease considered (positive ANA, anti‑U1‑snRNP, anti‑SS‑A) but does not account for the abrupt fever spikes and dramatic laboratory derangements | "Concurrent diagnoses of undifferentiated connective tissue disease … were also made."
7. Drug‑induced liver injury alone would not explain the systemic hyperinflammation, lymphadenopathy, and skin eruption | "The patient was diagnosed with drug hypersensitivity syndrome, drug‑induced liver injury, and COVID‑19 infection."
8. Malignancy ruled out by PET‑CT and bone‑marrow biopsy | "PET‑CT scans did not reveal any definitive evidence of malignancy… bone marrow biopsy findings were negative for malignancy."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case ultimately attributes the patient’s severe neutropenia to sintilimab‑induced agranulocytosis, which is not among the 21 SELECTED diseases; thus the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.  
2. Best breakpoint: Include the presentation from initial fever and prior treatments through the extensive infectious, autoimmune, and drug‑toxicity work‑up (cultures, imaging, laboratory panels) but stop before the sentence “sintilimab‑induced agranulocytosis was diagnosed” and before the therapeutic plan for G‑CSF and steroids is described. This provides enough data for learners to consider sepsis, drug toxicity, marrow invasion, and autoimmune causes, yet does not reveal the final immune‑related diagnosis.  
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished agranulocytosis from chemotherapy‑induced marrow suppression by the unusually rapid onset (within 24 h of therapy) and prolonged nadir; they excluded tumor infiltration of marrow, autoimmune disease (negative ANA, GM), and infectious etiologies (negative CMV DNA, cultures not correlating with clinical course). Multidisciplinary discussion led to the conclusion of an immune‑related adverse event from anti‑PD‑1 therapy.
case_prompt:
A 68‑year‑old man with a history of right‑lung squamous cell carcinoma (cT3N3M0, stage IIIC) and five‑year deep venous thrombosis presented on October 5, 2021 with a one‑month history of recurrent fever and a three‑day history of chest pain. He had been a 40‑pack‑year smoker. Initial therapy at a local hospital began on August 27 with sintilimab (200 mg) plus paclitaxel liposomes (240 mg) and carboplatin (0.45 g). Five days after the first cycle he developed fever up to 40.5 °C; laboratory testing showed grade 3 neutropenia (WBC 1.7 × 10⁹/L, ANC 0.64 × 10⁹/L). Despite granulocyte‑colony stimulating factor (G‑CSF) and a cephalosporin, fever persisted. Blood cultures grew human herpesvirus 5 (HHV‑5), Staphylococcus aureus, and Corynebacterium equi, interpreted as sepsis, and teicoplanin therapy led to clinical improvement and normalization of WBC and ANC.

He was discharged after a second dose of sintilimab and oral edoxaban on September 25. On September 26 he again developed fever (peak 40 °C). At presentation on September 30, WBC and ANC were normal, but C‑reactive protein (42.2 mg/L) and procalcitonin (12.27 ng/mL) were markedly elevated, and antibiotics failed to control the fever.

On admission to our hospital his vital signs were within normal limits; physical examination revealed decreased breath sounds over the left lung. Tumor markers were: CEA 4.49 ng/mL, CYFRA 21‑1 7.22 ng/mL (↑), NSE 15.86 ng/mL, CA‑125 12.41 U/mL, CA‑153 31.40 U/mL (↑). Repeat chest CT on October 5 showed a 6.1 × 5.2 cm mass in the right lower lobe posterior basal segment with mild perilesional inflammation, raising concern for tumor progression.

After six days of anticoagulation and coronary angiography (which excluded coronary artery disease), a third treatment cycle (carboplatin, paclitaxel liposome, bevacizumab, sintilimab) was administered. Shortly after midnight the patient developed fever 40.2 °C and agranulocytosis (WBC 1.3 × 10⁹/L, ANC 0 × 10⁹/L). His leukocyte count continued to fall, reaching a nadir of 0.5 × 10⁹/L on October 16, with persistent ANC 0 × 10⁹/L; hemoglobin also declined from October 13 to 21. Digital radiography on October 13 confirmed the prior CT findings.

Extensive evaluation was undertaken: blood cultures, liver function tests, bacterial cultures, and drug‑toxicity assessment; autoimmune screening showed negative anti‑nuclear antibody and fungal galactomannan; CMV DNA, G test, and renal profile were within normal limits. Sputum culture on October 18 grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The patient had no prior history of agranulocytosis and ANC had been normal throughout earlier cancer treatment. The rapid marrow suppression occurring within 24 h of chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and anti‑angiogenic therapy was atypical for classic chemotherapy‑induced nadir. A multidisciplinary team reviewed the data and considered various etiologies before reaching a provisional diagnosis.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Sepsis from bacterial infection considered because blood cultures grew Staphylococcus aureus and Corynebacterium equi, yet “antibiotic therapy proved to be ineffective.” |

2. "Peripheral blood culture results revealed infection with human herpesvirus 5 (HHV-5), Staphylococcus aureus, and Corynebacterium equi, which were considered indicative of sepsis. ... However, antibiotic therapy proved to be ineffective."

3. Viral infection (CMV) entertained after HHV‑5 was detected, but later testing showed no active replication, making CMV an unlikely cause of the persistent agranulocytosis. |

4. "Detection of autoimmune disease revealed that the anti‑nuclear antibody (ANA) and fungal galactomannan (GM) tests were negative. Additionally, other diagnostic tests such as the G test, Cytomegalovirus (CMV) DNA, and renal profile were within normal limits."

5. Chemotherapy‑induced bone‑marrow suppression evaluated; timing was deemed inconsistent because “the patient exhibited bone marrow suppression within 24 hours of chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and anti‑angiogenic therapy, which deviated from the typical peak occurrence of chemotherapy‑induced bone marrow suppression.” |

6. "Upon review, the patient exhibited bone marrow suppression within 24 hours of chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and anti‑angiogenic therapy, which deviated from the typical peak occurrence of chemotherapy‑induced bone marrow suppression."

7. Tumor infiltration of marrow considered; absence of marrow involvement on imaging and lack of supporting clinical evidence led to its exclusion. |

8. "The rapid decline in ANC was suspected to be induced by anti‑PD‑1 antibody." (implies other causes like marrow invasion were ruled out)

9. Autoimmune neutropenia explored; negative ANA and galactomannan tests argued against an autoimmune etiology. |

10. "Detection of autoimmune disease revealed that the anti‑nuclear antibody (ANA) and fungal galactomannan (GM) tests were negative."

11. Drug toxicity from other agents (bevacizumab, carboplatin, paclitaxel) assessed; the unusually rapid onset and persistence of neutropenia after stopping chemotherapy suggested an immune‑mediated mechanism rather than direct toxicity. |

12. "A multidisciplinary team (MDT) meeting was organized, and sintilimab‑induced agranulocytosis was diagnosed after excluding evidence of autoimmune disease or tumor invasion of the bone marrow."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case report’s main pathology is unilateral retinoblastoma, which is NOT on the 21 SELECTED diseases list. The incidental CMV retinitis is on the list, but it is discovered only after enucleation and is not the primary focus of the case narrative. Therefore the target diagnosis to be solved by the learner is retinoblastoma → OUT_OF_SCOPE.

Best Breakpoint: End the presentation after the B‑scan ultrasound findings (which describe the intra‑ocular mass, vitreous seeding, and exudative detachment) and before any statement that explicitly names “retinoblastoma” or discusses histopathology. This gives the learner sufficient ocular findings and imaging to infer the malignant intra‑ocular tumor while preserving the diagnostic mystery.

Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors confirmed the intra‑ocular tumor by (a) detailed ophthalmoscopic documentation of vitreous seeds, hemorrhage, and an exudative detachment, (b) B‑scan ultrasound showing a hyperechogenic mass with low‑lying detachment, and (c) MRI that excluded trilateral disease. case_prompt:
A 2‑year‑old Hispanic male presented to a pediatric ophthalmology clinic in August 2022 with a three‑month history of exotropia and squinting of the right eye. There was no family history of ocular tumors. On examination his pupils were equal, round, and reactive to light. Intraocular pressures were 8 mm Hg (right) and 11 mm Hg (left); the anterior segments were unremarkable bilaterally. Funduscopic examination of the right eye revealed dense white vitreous opacities and hemorrhage at the nasal aspect of the optic disc; the left eye was normal.

An examination under anesthesia confirmed these findings and additionally demonstrated an exudative retinal detachment with subretinal seeding inferiorly, as well as a 6 mm × 6 mm lesion in the superonasal quadrant of the right eye. B‑scan ultrasound of the right eye showed dense vitreous seeding, a hyperechogenic mass in the superonasal quadrant, and a low‑lying exudative retinal detachment.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Dense vitreous opacities with hemorrhage and a discrete intra‑ocular mass are characteristic of an intra‑ocular neoplasm rather than simple inflammatory or infectious processes. | "dense white vitreous opacities and hemorrhage... a 6‑mm × 6‑mm tumor in the superonasal quadrant."
2. The presence of subretinal seeding and an exudative retinal detachment on examination under anesthesia further supports a malignant intra‑ocular tumor (group D classification). | "exudative retinal detachment with subretinal seeding inferiorly, as well as a 6‑mm × 6‑mm tumor..."
3. B‑scan ultrasound demonstrating a hyperechogenic intra‑ocular mass with vitreous seeding correlates with typical imaging findings of retinoblastoma and helps exclude other causes such as persistent fetal vasculature or Coats disease. | "B‑scan ultrasound ... dense vitreous seeding, a hyperechogenic mass..."
4. MRI of the brain and orbits was performed to assess for trilateral disease; its lack of abnormal intracranial lesions ruled out the possibility of concurrent pineal or suprasellar involvement, narrowing the diagnosis to a unilateral intra‑ocular tumor. | "MRI ... without evidence of trilateral disease."

case_prompt:
A 50‑year‑old man with no prior medical conditions was admitted for COVID‑19 pneumonia. Despite glucocorticoid therapy, his respiratory status worsened, requiring mechanical ventilation on day 7 and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation on day 9. He improved, underwent tracheostomy on day 20, and was transferred for rehabilitation. On day 43 after symptom onset he developed watery diarrhea, which escalated to 6,000–7,000 mL/day after transfer, prompting readmission on day 62.

On admission he was afebrile (36.5 °C), tachycardic (117 bpm), and normotensive (120/83 mm Hg). His weight had fallen from 114.5 kg (BMI 36.5 kg/m²) to 94.6 kg. Contrast‑enhanced CT showed severe colonic edema and fluid‑filled small bowel. Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 6.3 g/dL, albumin 1.0 g/dL, d‑dimer 3.1 µg/mL, and IL‑6 62.6 pg/mL. Stool testing was negative for Clostridioides difficile toxin A/B and glutamate dehydrogenase, and cultures were negative for pathogenic E. coli and C. difficile. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy demonstrated duodenal villous enlargement and ring‑like erosions; capsule endoscopy showed ring‑shaped ulcerations throughout the small bowel; colonoscopy revealed extensive mucosal edema with shallow map‑like ulcerations. Biopsy of colonic and small‑bowel mucosa showed regenerative epithelial changes, inflammatory infiltrates, nuclear inclusion bodies, and immunohistochemistry positive for cytomegalovirus antigen. Blood testing was positive for CMV pp65 antigen (7 positive per 100,000 WBCs). A PCR assay for SARS‑CoV‑2 on colonic tissue was negative. No histologic evidence of vasculitis, thrombus, or inflammatory bowel disease was seen. He was diagnosed with CMV enterocolitis and started on ganciclovir on hospital day 5, but the diarrhea persisted without improvement.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial enterocolitis (including pathogenic E. coli and C. difficile) considered because of massive watery diarrhea; ruled out by negative stool cultures and toxin assays. | "stool cultures were negative for causative bacteria of enterocolitis, including pathogenic Escherichia coli and Clostridioides difficile."
2. Clostridioides difficile infection specifically evaluated; excluded by negative toxin A/B and glutamate dehydrogenase tests. | "Stool tests were negative for Clostridioides difficile toxin A/B and glutamate dehydrogenase."
3. Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) entertained given ulcerative lesions; excluded by lack of characteristic histologic features. | "No findings suggested ... inflammatory bowel disease in the biopsy specimens."
4. Vasculitis or thrombotic microangiopathy considered as possible COVID‑19‑related gut injury; excluded by histology showing no vasculitis or thrombus. | "No findings suggested vasculitis, thrombus formation ... in the biopsy specimens."
5. Direct SARS‑CoV‑2 colonic infection considered; excluded by negative PCR on colonic mucosa. | "A PCR test for SARS‑CoV‑2 in the colonic mucosa was negative."
6. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) enterocolitis strongly considered due to nuclear inclusion bodies, positive immunohistochemistry, and CMV pp65 antigenemia; initially diagnosed and treated with ganciclovir. | "immunohistochemistry was positive for the cytomegalovirus (CMV) antigen" and "blood test revealed the presence of the CMV pp65 antigen C7HRP (7 pp65 antigen positive/100,000 white blood cells)."
7. Post‑COVID‑19 immune‑mediated enterocolitis considered after lack of response to ganciclovir; supported by steroid responsiveness reported in similar cases. | "We suspected enterocolitis associated with COVID‑19 and attempted treatment with a methylprednisolone pulse..."

case_prompt:
An 80‑year‑old woman with neurofibromatosis type 1 presented to the emergency department in June 2024 after an episode of hematochezia. In the preceding months she had experienced a subacute decline with weight loss, memory loss, and reduced ability to perform activities of daily living, which was attributed to chronic abdominal pain and depression. Her past surgical history included a partial gastrectomy and small‑bowel resection with Billroth II gastrojejunostomy for a gastrointestinal stromal tumor in 2015, and resection of the terminal ileum and proximal colon with ileocolic anastomosis for an inflammatory fibroid polyp of the cecum in 2022. Family history was notable only for cancer in her son.

On arrival, vital signs were normal. Physical examination revealed generalized abdominal tenderness; the abdomen was soft and nondistended. She received a pantoprazole loading dose and continued pantoprazole 40 mg orally twice daily for presumed upper gastrointestinal bleeding; home anticoagulants and antihypertensives were held. Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin of 10.3 g/dL with no leukocytosis.

An abdominal and pelvic computed tomography scan identified a lobular mass at the ileocolic anastomosis. The patient was admitted for gastroenterology evaluation. She reported persistent mid‑abdominal discomfort radiating to the back and intermittent nausea but no further hematochezia. Her hemoglobin fell to 8.8 g/dL on hospital day 2 and then stabilized at 10.0 g/dL.

On hospital day 3, esophagogastroduodenoscopy demonstrated two small friable polyps at the gastrojejunal anastomosis without significant findings. Colonoscopy revealed a non‑obstructing, frond‑like, fungating, polypoid mass at the ileocolic anastomosis measuring approximately 5 cm (Figure 1). The lesion was biopsied, and because of her histories of NF1, prior GIST, and inflammatory fibroid polyp, there was a high suspicion for malignancy. Surgical oncology evaluated the patient and advised that operative intervention was not feasible given her comorbidities.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Malignancy was the leading consideration due to the appearance of a large polypoid mass at a prior anastomosis in a patient with NF1, a prior gastrointestinal stromal tumor, and a history of inflammatory fibroid polyp. | "The mass was biopsied, with high suspicion for malignancy at that time given her histories of NF1, GIST, and inflammatory fibroid polyp of the colon."
2. Lack of malignant cells on histology excluded carcinoma or recurrent GIST. | "Biopsy revealed ulcerated granulation tissue without evidence of malignancy."
3. Cytomegalovirus infection became evident when characteristic “owl’s eye” inclusions were identified and CMV immunostaining was positive. | "Interestingly, the presence of \"owl's eye\" inclusions was noted on histologic examination; CMV immunostaining was positive."
4. Systemic CMV replication supported the diagnosis, with detectable viremia and positive IgG serology indicating reactivation rather than primary infection. | "Subsequent serum studies demonstrated CMV viremia with a level of 32 IU/mL on CMV DNA polymerase chain reaction, positive IgG antibodies to CMV, and negative IgM antibodies to CMV."
5. HIV infection, a common predisposition for CMV disease, was excluded, reinforcing that the CMV colitis occurred in an HIV‑negative host. | "HIV combined antigen/antibody testing was nonreactive."

case_prompt:
A 75‑year‑old woman, a farmer with a history of COVID‑19 infection, hypertension, and nephrotic syndrome, was admitted for a prolonged cough, expectoration, fever, and dyspnea. She had been on long‑term steroids (methylprednisolone 40 mg daily) and other chronic medications. On arrival she was febrile (36.3 °C), tachycardic (115 bpm), tachypneic (25 /min) and hypotensive (95/58 mmHg). Physical examination showed pale skin, scattered petechiae, mild lower‑extremity edema, and coarse breath sounds with crackles bilaterally. Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis (4.77 × 10⁹/L) with neutrophilia (85.8 %), markedly elevated CRP (51.83 mg/L) and procalcitonin (2.60 ng/mL), prolonged prothrombin time, severe anemia (Hb 55 g/L), low total protein (53.1 g/L) and albumin (31.9 g/L), and profound CD4⁺ (224 cells/µL) and CD8⁺ (168 cells/µL) lymphopenia. Chest CT demonstrated diffuse pulmonary inflammation with minimal pleural effusion. Empiric therapy with meropenem, sulfamethoxazole, and caspofungin was started.

She was maintained on tacrolimus 1 mg twice daily, mycophenolate mofetil 750 mg twice daily, and prednisone 5 mg daily. Nearly two years after transplantation she developed progressive abdominal discomfort, early satiety, and unintentional weight loss that worsened over six months, prompting presentation at 30 months post‑transplant.

On examination she had no lymphadenopathy and was afebrile. Laboratory studies showed: white blood cell count 11.07 × 10³/µL, hemoglobin 10.3 g/dL, platelet count 568 × 10³/µL; creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, sodium 139 mEq/L, potassium 4.1 mEq/L; AST 50 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 275 U/L, albumin 3.4 g/dL.

Contrast‑enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated multiple enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes, heterogeneous liver lesions, and thickening of the terminal ileum. PET imaging showed the liver mass to be FDG‑avid. Given the concern for malignancy, a retroperitoneal lymph node biopsy was performed.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Malignancy (lymphoma) considered because of FDG‑avid liver mass and mesenteric lymphadenopathy | "Given the concern for malignancy, a retroperitoneal lymph node biopsy was performed."
2. EBV‑driven post‑transplant lymphoproliferative disorder considered but excluded by negative EBV testing | "Immunohistochemical (IHC) analysis did not detect EBV via fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH)."
3. Infectious colitis (e.g., cytomegalovirus) considered later when endoscopy revealed CMV involvement, indicating it was a secondary complication rather than the primary cause of the abdominal mass | "Upper and lower endoscopy revealed a gastric ulcer with B‑cell lymphoma and cytomegalovirus colitis."
4. Clostridioides difficile colitis was identified during subsequent hospitalizations, serving as another infectious complication distinct from the initial abdominal presentation | "She was hospitalized for C. difficile colitis and abdominal pain."
final_diagnosis: EBV-negative diffuse large B-cell lymphoma -> OUT_OF_SCOPE
