case_prompt: A 24‑year‑old man with no prior comorbidities presented with diffuse myalgia, headache, retro‑orbital pain, and fever. After the first day of symptoms he sought care at a regional hospital, received intravenous hydration, and was discharged home. On day 4 he noted respiratory‑dependent chest pain despite improvement of systemic symptoms, continuous abdominal pain, and new lower‑extremity edema with purpuric lesions. Physical exam was notable for a pericardial friction rub. Laboratory testing revealed thrombocytopenia (105 000/mm³), prompting an initial consideration of dengue. Within 48 h of admission he developed dyspnea; transthoracic echocardiography showed a large pericardial effusion with signs of cardiac tamponade. Pericardial drainage yielded 200 mL of yellowish fluid. Repeat labs showed worsening thrombocytopenia (80 000/mm³), elevated AST (97 U/L) and ALT (69 U/L), and normal urinalysis. Chest CT demonstrated diffuse ground‑glass opacities and pulmonary congestion. Empiric ceftriaxone, oxacillin, and prednisone 80 mg (1 mg/kg) were started. Comprehensive work‑up included blood cultures, ANA, ANCA, complement, CH50, serologies for EBV, CMV, hepatitis B and C, HIV, and skin‑lesion biopsy. Pericardial fluid analysis showed a citrus‑yellow exudate with glucose 14 mg/dL, protein 4.42 g/dL, leukocytes 8 100/mm³ (82 % neutrophils), and negative bacterial cultures and BAAR stain. After 48 h the patient improved, the pericardial drain was removed, and platelet count began to rise. Polymerase chain reaction and NS1 antigen testing for dengue were unavailable; on day 7 an immunochromatographic assay for dengue IgM/IgG was performed and was non‑reactive for both antibodies. Serology for CMV and EBV was negative for IgM but positive for IgG; hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV serologies were negative; ANA, ANCA, and complement studies were normal; skin biopsy showed leukocytoclastic vasculitis.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Initial febrile illness with retro‑orbital pain, myalgia, and thrombocytopenia is classic for dengue | "The laboratory blood count exam results revealed thrombocytopenia (105,000/mm³), which led to a possible dengue diagnosis."
2. Pericardial effusion with tamponade is a recognized severe manifestation of dengue hemorrhagic syndrome | "Transthoracic echocardiography was performed, showing significant pericardial effusion, along with signs of cardiac tamponade."
3. Negative bacterial cultures and BAAR stain in pericardial fluid argue against bacterial pericarditis | "negative bacterial cultures" and "negative BAAR test".
4. Normal ANA and ANCA, with negative complement, make systemic autoimmune vasculitis unlikely | "ANA, ANCA, hepatitis B, C, HIV, blood cultures and the serum complement were normal."
5. Negative IgM for CMV and EBV (with positive IgG only) excludes acute infection with these viruses | "serology for cytomegalovirus and Epstein‑Barr was negative for IgM, but positive for IgG."
6. Early dengue serology was negative, but seroconversion on day 10 confirmed recent infection | "The results were non‑reactive for both, IgM and IgG antibodies. Later, on the tenth day, the test was repeated and this time the results were positive for both, IgM and IgG."
7. Cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis can be secondary to dengue‑related immune complex deposition, supporting dengue as the unifying diagnosis | "The cutaneous histopathological analysis was compatible with leukocytoclastic vasculitis."

case_prompt: An 8‑year‑old boy presented to the surgical emergency department with a 1‑day history of generalized abdominal pain, abdominal distension, and obstipation. The pain began suddenly in the right upper abdomen and later became diffuse, involving the entire abdomen. He had no prior medical illnesses or known haemolytic disease. On examination, the abdomen was diffusely tender and distended with guarding and rebound tenderness in all quadrants. Laboratory studies were essentially normal except for a raised total leukocyte count. Chest and abdominal plain radiographs were unremarkable. Based on the history and clinical profile, a diagnosis of duodenal perforation peritonitis was made, and the patient was taken urgently to the operating room for exploratory laparotomy. Through a midline incision, approximately 700 mL of biliopurulent fluid was aspirated. The gallbladder was removed after ligation of the cystic duct and artery, and the abdomen was closed after thorough lavage with placement of a right subhepatic drain. The resected specimen was sent for histopathological examination.

case_prompt:
During the 2016 ZIKV outbreak in Merida, Mexico, a 27‑year‑old woman in her third trimester was referred because multiple fetal malformations were detected. She recalled an unquantified fever, preauricular nodes, pruritus and a rash on the shoulder girdle and thorax in the first trimester, before she knew she was pregnant; no serological testing was performed at that time.  
Ultrasound at 16.4 weeks showed fetal growth within normal ranges. At 23 weeks the fetal hands were not identified. By 27.4 weeks the fetus had microcephaly (DBP 58 mm), nuchal thickening, ventriculomegaly, hemispheric hypoplasia, cerebellar vermis hypoplasia, micrognathia, right radial aplasia, and arthrogryposis.  
A stillbirth was delivered by cesarean section at 35 weeks. Physical examination revealed craniofacial disproportion with microcephaly, irregular anterior and lower posterior hairline, posterior sloping forehead, hypertelorism, cupped low‑implanted ears with thickened helix, retrognathia, short shoulders with limited abduction, left upper limb with extended elbow, pronated arm, flexed wrist, non‑reducible cyanotic hand, and a right upper limb present only to the proximal third of the arm with soft‑tissue defect exposing subcutaneous tissue and the humeral condyle. Lower extremities showed limited hip abduction, knee extension, and foot flexion. External genitalia displayed a 1 cm phallus with a rough scrotum lacking palpable testes.  
Skull X‑ray showed everted sutures and partial collapse of cranial bones with hypoplastic occipital bone. Radiographs of the upper extremities demonstrated a shorter right humerus with preservation of the distal humerus. Computed tomography revealed subcortical calcifications, lissencephaly, ventriculomegaly, and generalized cortical degeneration. Karyotype was normal, 46, XY. Serologic tests for toxoplasma, rubella, cytomegalovirus, and herpes virus were negative in both mother and infant.

TORCH infections considered because of microcephaly and intracranial calcifications; ruled out by negative maternal and infant serology for toxoplasma, rubella, cytomegalovirus, and herpes virus. | "The serological test for toxoplasma, rubella, cytomegalovirus and herpes virus were negative in the mother and the patient."
2. Chromosomal or genetic syndrome considered due to multiple congenital anomalies; excluded by normal karyotype (46, XY). | "The karyotype was normal, 46, XY."
3. Other arboviral infections (dengue, chikungunya) considered during the outbreak; testing was performed but only Zika RNA was later identified, indicating specificity for Zika. | "The RT‑PCR for ZIKV/Dengue/Chikungunya in the patient's cerebrospinal fluid detected the presence of Zika viral RNA."
4. Congenital Zika syndrome supported by characteristic pattern of severe brain malformations (ventriculomegaly, cortical thinning, subcortical calcifications), limb abnormalities, and timing of maternal rash during early pregnancy. | "During the 2016 ZIKV outbreak... the mother reported fever, rash... in the first trimester... fetal ultrasound at 27.4 weeks showed microcephaly, ventriculomegaly, hemisphere hypoplasia..."

case_prompt:
A 38‑year‑old male forest guard from a hilly Himalayan station, with a 15‑year history of schizophrenia (on aripiprazole and trihexyphenidyl), presented to the emergency department with a 7‑day history of high‑grade, intermittent fever, myalgia, and headache. Four days after fever onset, he noted multiple painless, reddish rashes on the soles of both feet and ankles that later darkened without gangrene formation or bleeding. He subsequently developed exertional breathlessness, later occurring in the supine position, progressive bilateral leg edema, generalized weakness, and oliguria for one day. There was no other localizing symptom, substance use, or comorbidity.

On examination the patient appeared thin, pale, edematous, mildly drowsy, and disoriented. Vital signs were unstable: heart rate 128 bpm, blood pressure 98/60 mm Hg (pulse pressure 48 mm Hg), respiratory rate 30 /min with SpO₂ 86 % on room air improving to 92‑95 % on 4 L O₂. Bilateral pitting pedal edema and multiple palpable, non‑tender purpuric lesions (2–8 mm) with fine scaling and post‑inflammatory hyperpigmentation were present on both feet; peripheral pulses were palpable. Jugular venous pressure was not elevated. Chest examination revealed bilateral basal fine crackles and occasional wheezes; cardiac auscultation was normal with a regular rhythm and no murmurs. Abdomen was mildly tender in the right hypochondrium and epigastrium without organomegaly. Other systems were unremarkable.

Laboratory investigations on day 8 of illness showed: hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL (normocytic, normochromic), leukocytes 7,900/mm³, platelet count 30,000/mm³, LDH 457 U/L (reference < 248), ESR 44 mm/h, high‑sensitivity CRP 14.2 mg/L, fibrin degradation products 12 mg/L, D‑dimer < 0.5 µg/mL. Renal function indicated acute kidney injury; liver tests demonstrated conjugated hyperbilirubinemia (total bilirubin 2.83 mg/dL, direct 1.33 mg/dL), mild transaminitis, and hypoalbuminemia. NT‑pro‑BNP was markedly elevated at 3114.7 pg/mL; transthoracic echocardiogram showed no structural abnormality. Chest radiograph suggested early pulmonary edema. Arterial blood gas revealed compensated respiratory alkalosis. Blood cultures were sterile.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Epidemic dengue shock syndrome (EDS) considered because of high‑grade fever, thrombocytopenia, plasma‑leakage‑type pulmonary edema, and seasonal outbreak context | "A probable diagnosis of EDS (because of outbreak season) with myocardium, vessels, skin, and kidney involvements was made."

On October 13, 2020, a 64‑year‑old woman was referred with a 1‑week history of fatigue, low blood pressure, arthralgia, and myalgia. She had untreated hydronephrosis for 4 years and was hepatitis B surface antigen positive for decades. One week prior, she performed farm work in the mountains without personal protection.  

On admission her labs showed: WBC 15.3 × 10⁹/L, platelets 10 × 10⁹/L, albumin 22.7 g/L, ALT 79 U/L, AST 134 U/L, total bilirubin 105.3 µmol/L, direct bilirubin 60.6 µmol/L, creatinine 87.3 µmol/L, BUN 16.68 mmol/L, PT 18.6 s, APTT 41.9 s, D‑dimer 6 320 µg/L; BP 120/73 mmHg, stable respiration.  

Four days later her blood pressure fell to 84/58 mmHg, jaundice became evident, and renal function worsened despite symptomatic treatment, prompting transfer to our hospital. She complained of generalized pain without fever; exam revealed wet rales bilaterally, abdominal distention, and bilateral lower‑limb edema. Neurologic exam was normal, GCS 15, BP 100/80 mmHg on norepinephrine, pulse 98 /min.  

Laboratory reassessment demonstrated marked abnormalities: WBC 57.0 × 10⁹/L, total bilirubin 254.5 µmol/L, creatinine 263 µmol/L, procalcitonin 10.73 ng/mL, CRP 59.3 mg/L. Chest radiography showed obvious patchy shadows in both lungs. Initial diagnosis was pneumonia; meropenem 1 g TID was started together with continuous renal replacement therapy.  

During days 2‑4, the patient’s condition deteriorated, requiring non‑invasive ventilation with high‑flow oxygen (60 L/min). Maximum temperature was 37.2 °C. Bronchoscopy revealed extensive airway hemorrhage. Brain CT was normal; chest CT showed bilateral patchy shadows with diffuse infiltration and extensive consolidation in the right lung.  

Serologic testing for dengue, leptospirosis, and epidemic hemorrhagic fever was performed given the recent farm exposure and returned negative. Cultures of blood, sputum, urine, and feces were obtained, and a bone‑marrow puncture was performed because of markedly abnormal hematologic indices. PCR assays per Zhejiang CDC guidelines and next‑generation sequencing (NGS) of blood and sputum samples were ordered. Multidisciplinary management involving hematology, infectious diseases, pneumology, organ transplantation, and intensive care was instituted, along with supportive organ therapy, entecavir, and ornithine aspartate for hyperammonemia. Abdominal CT demonstrated cirrhosis with ascites, likely related to chronic hepatitis B.

case_prompt: A 46‑year‑old white female smoker with pulmonary emphysema presented in mid‑February 2021 with progressive facial and lower‑limb edema. Twelve days earlier she had received the first dose of the ChAdOx1 nCoV‑19 vaccine (January 29). She was admitted to Hospital Duque de Caxias, Rio de Janeiro. Physical examination revealed generalized edema but normal blood pressure (100/80 mmHg). Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 13.9 g/dL, hematocrit 37.4 %, total protein 7.5 g/dL, albumin 4.5 g/dL, AST 19 U/L, ALT 18 U/L, creatinine 1.10 mg/dL, urea 33 mg/dL, and an isolated platelet count of 36 × 10⁹/L (reference 150–450 × 10⁹/L). Antinuclear antibody testing was negative, and serologies for dengue (IgM), syphilis, HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C were all negative. The attending physician suspected vaccine‑induced immune thrombocytopenia and started prednisone 20 mg daily in March 2021. After one month, the platelet count remained low at 45 × 10⁹/L, the patient was asymptomatic, and prednisone was stopped. The edema resolved spontaneously over four months. In May 2021 she contracted a mild COVID‑19 infection that required no hospitalization. By July 2021 she remained symptom‑free but still had a low platelet count and was referred to the Fiocruz institute for further evaluation.

case_prompt:
A 42‑year‑old married man presented in April 2015 with a 3‑week history of high‑grade fever and a large, painful perianal ulcer. He had been diagnosed HIV‑positive in 1997; antiretroviral therapy had been deferred because his CD4 counts had previously been >400 cells/mm³. Over the preceding three months he experienced low‑grade evening fevers with chills, anorexia, and a 15‑kg weight loss in four months. He denied headache, vomiting, cough, dyspnea, or diarrhea.

On examination he had oral candidiasis and a painful, bleeding perianal ulcer measuring 8 × 2 inches; there was no lymphadenopathy and systemic examination was normal. Initial work‑up showed CD4 count 10 cells/mm³ (CD4 < 4 %) and plasma HIV‑1 viral load 43,803 copies/mL. Routine labs were normal except for thrombocytosis. Tests for malaria, dengue, hepatitis B and C, syphilis, herpes, and toxoplasma IgG were performed; all were negative except IgG positivity for toxoplasma. Blood cultures were sterile, and Koch’s bacillus was ruled out. He received prophylaxis (cotrimoxazole, INH, azithromycin) and a starter ART regimen (TDF/FTC/EFV) while awaiting drug‑resistance results.

Despite three weeks of treatment, his fever and ulcer persisted, prompting hospital admission and intravenous antibiotics. Perianal biopsy showed a superficial aphthous ulcer; Tzanck smear for HSV was negative. An 18FDG‑PET/CT showed no abnormal uptake, leading TB and malignancy specialists to exclude tuberculosis and cancer. Dermatology treated the ulcer as a giant herpetic ulcer with valaciclovir, resulting in reduction and scarring.

Genotypic resistance testing later revealed resistance to NRTIs and NNRTIs; the ART was switched to lopinavir/ritonavir + lamivudine + raltegravir. He became afebrile, the ulcer healed, and he was discharged.

Five days after discharge, while on the new ART, he developed giddiness and loss of balance. Symptoms progressed over a few days to headache, vomiting, and blurred vision. Neurological exam showed tandem gait instability, bilateral finger‑nose ataxia, and a positive Romberg sign. Brain MRI suggested acute demyelination with lymphoma in the differential. A repeat FDG‑PET/CT performed 40 days after the first scan demonstrated a solitary space‑occupying lesion in the cerebellar vermis without other abnormalities.

Blood culture for aerobic and anaerobic organisms showed no growth."

case_prompt: A 38‑year‑old man from Laguna, Philippines, presented with a 5‑day history of persistent high fever (progressing from 38.7 °C to 39.8 °C), nausea, arthralgia, and mild myalgia. case_prompt:
A 47‑year‑old female from Kathmandu presented in April 2021 with nine days of intermittent fever and sore throat. Three days after fever onset she developed itchy erythematous rashes on both thighs, legs and hands, especially during fever spikes. She had received the first dose of the Oxford‑AstraZeneca COVID‑19 vaccine seven days before fever began. She had no notable past medical or family history. At presentation she was already taking levofloxacin 750 mg and azithromycin 500 mg daily for a few days prescribed locally.

On examination her temperature was 38.5 °C. Erythematous rashes were present over the bilateral legs and hands. The rest of the systemic examination was unremarkable. SARS‑CoV‑2 PCR was negative. Initial laboratory studies revealed anemia, neutrophilic leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, elevated C‑reactive protein, markedly increased ferritin, and mild hepatitis. Abdominal ultrasound showed hepatosplenomegaly. She was admitted and started on intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily and oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily. Blood and urine cultures later showed no growth. Serologic testing for dengue, scrub typhus, leptospirosis and malaria were negative. After 72 hours there was no clinical improvement on antibiotics.

Further evaluation for non‑infectious fever was pursued. Antinuclear antibody was weakly positive with a fine speckled pattern; rheumatoid factor, anti‑citrullinated peptide antibodies and ANCA were negative. Bone‑marrow cytology was normal. On the fourth day of admission she developed pain, swelling, warmth and restriction of movement of the left elbow.

case_prompt:
A 20‑year‑old Zambian male studying in China was transferred from a local hospital with a 10‑day history of high fever (up to 40.8 °C) accompanied by chills, profound fatigue, vomiting, and diarrhea. His symptoms began after eating out with a friend who experienced similar illness but recovered uneventfully. Over the next several days his condition worsened; he became unconscious and incontinent, prompting his classmates to bring him to the local hospital, where a routine blood test showed a leukocyte count of 5,680 cells/mm³ with 90.6 % neutrophils, platelets 12,000 cells/mm³, C‑reactive protein 257.3 mg/L, and procalcitonin >100 ng/mL. He received cefoperazone‑sulbactam 2 g IV and was transferred to Zhejiang Provincial People’s Hospital on 14 October 2019.

On arrival his temperature was 40.8 °C, respiratory rate 35 breaths/min, pulse 157 beats/min, blood pressure 85/42 mmHg. He was intubated for low oxygen saturation. Physical examination revealed a comatose patient (Glasgow Coma Scale 5) with neck rigidity. Laboratory studies confirmed markedly elevated inflammatory markers and demonstrated hepatic and renal dysfunction (ALT 73 U/L, total bilirubin 206.6 µmol/L, creatinine 279.2 µmol/L).

Non‑contrast computed tomography of the head demonstrated a possible minor subdural effusion in the right fronto‑parieto‑temporal region. Chest CT showed bilateral pulmonary inflammation; abdominal CT was unremarkable. Communicable diseases such as malaria and dengue fever were excluded, and the patient was admitted to the intensive care unit for mechanical ventilation and continuous renal replacement therapy.

case_prompt:
A 29‑year‑old woman, G2P1A0, presented to the emergency department in an unconscious state. She had a full‑term vaginal delivery 9 days earlier, uncomplicated except for a 500 mL blood loss. Four days postpartum she developed fever (37.7‑38.3 °C) and loose stools (4‑5 per day). She was admitted to a government medical college, received paracetamol and IV fluids (positive balance 1500 mL over 2 days), and was discharged after 2 days when fever subsided and routine labs (CBC, renal, liver, coagulation) were normal. She was advised paracetamol and multivitamins at discharge.

On day 9 after delivery she was brought to the ED unconscious with a 1‑day history of fever and irrelevant speech. Relatives reported excessive sweating and reduced water intake over the prior 2 days. In the ED her pupils were equal and reactive, there was no neck rigidity, limb tone was reduced, and plantar response was flexor. She responded to painful stimuli by opening her eyes (GCS 7: E2 V1 M4). Temperature was 104.5 °F (40.2 °C), blood pressure 100/68 mm Hg, pulse 144 bpm. She was intubated and ventilated.

Provisional diagnosis was meningoencephalitis with a differential of tropical fever; ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12h was started. Non‑contrast CT of the brain was normal. CSF analysis was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed severe hypernatremia (serum Na⁺ 182 mEq/L, Cl⁻ 148 mEq/L), plasma osmolality 439 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 782 mOsm/kg, hemoglobin 12.7 g/dL, hematocrit 47.8 %, WBC 16.68 × 10³/µL, platelets 132 × 10³/µL, BUN 171 mg/dL, creatinine 2.56 mg/dL. Liver function, coagulation profile, and CSF chemistry/cell counts were normal. All cultures were sterile. Dengue antibody and malaria rapid antigen tests were negative.

Ultrasound of the inferior vena cava showed >50 % collapsibility. Balanced crystalloids were administered, and free‑water deficit (~7.8 L) was calculated and replaced via nasogastric tube. Serial serum sodium measurements were obtained, correcting at <1 mEq/L/h. Urine output was 50‑70 mL/h. Over the next days serum sodium fell to 142 mEq/L and neurologic status gradually improved, though limb weakness persisted (strength 1‑2/5) with bulbar drooling. A neurology consult was obtained.

1. Infectious meningoencephalitis considered due to fever, altered mental status, and postpartum state | "Her provisional diagnosis was meningoencephalitis with a differential of tropical fever."
2. Tropical viral infections (e.g., dengue, malaria) evaluated because of fever and recent travel/region; both were excluded by negative serology/antigen | "Dengue antibody and malaria rapid antigen were also negative."
3. Bacterial sepsis considered; however, all cultures remained sterile and there was no leukocytosis suggestive of bacterial infection | "All cultures were sterile."
4. Hyponatremia‑related encephalopathy ruled out given markedly elevated serum sodium (182 mEq/L) and high plasma osmolality | "Laboratory evaluation showed severe hypernatremia with serum sodium (Na+) level of 182 mEq/L, plasma osmolality of 439 mOsmol/kg."
5. Primary neurologic lesion (stroke, intracranial hemorrhage) excluded by normal non‑contrast CT brain | "CT of the brain was normal."
6. Osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine or extrapontine myelinolysis) suspected after rapid correction of hypernatremia and persistent neurologic deficits; later confirmed by characteristic MRI findings | "Imaging features were suggestive of postpartum hypernatremic encephalopathy with osmotic extrapontine myelinolysis."
7. Rhabdomyolysis identified as a concurrent complication, supported by elevated CPK, LDH, and urine myoglobin, but it did not explain the encephalopathy | "Serum creatinine phosphokinase was advised, which was 475 IU, and her serum lactic dehydrogenase was 1229 IU/L. Her urine myoglobin was 1200 ng/mL."

case_prompt: A 12‑year‑old Chinese boy was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes mellitus presenting with ketoacidosis. One year later he developed a prolonged, remittent, intermittent fever for more than three weeks. He noted a painless, progressively enlarging swelling on the right side of his neck. Examination revealed a firm, non‑tender, 2.5 cm lymph node chain in the right upper cervical region; smaller nodes were also present on the left side of the neck and shotty nodes in both groins. Laboratory studies showed microcytic iron‑deficiency anemia (Hb 9.6 g/dL), leukopenia (3.4 × 10⁹/L), lymphopenia (0.8 × 10⁹/L), normal platelets, elevated CRP (17 mg/L) and ESR (76 mm/h), LDH 358 IU/L, ferritin 1,166 pmol/L, reversed albumin/globulin ratio (albumin 32 g/L, globulin 47 g/L). Liver enzymes were initially normal but began to rise on day 8, peaking on day 12 with AST 424 IU/L, ALT 307 IU/L, GGT 105 IU/L and ALP 272 IU/L, indicating a hepatocellular pattern. Viral serologies for hepatitis A, B, C, EBV, CMV, HIV, dengue, and Japanese encephalitis virus were negative. Bacterial cultures from blood, bone marrow, urine, stool and throat were sterile. Serologies for atypical organisms (Salmonella typhi, Bartonella henselae, Brucella abortus/melitensis, Toxoplasma gondii) were negative. Autoimmune testing revealed ANA 1:640 with speckled/cytoplasmic pattern, anti‑dsDNA 69 IU/mL (↑), anti‑RNP/Sm positive, anti‑cardiolipin 15.3 GPL‑U/mL, lupus anticoagulant, rheumatoid factor, low complement C4 (0.11 g/L), positive direct Coombs test, and hypergammaglobulinemia (Ig 20.8 g/L). Urinalysis showed no proteinuria or hematuria. Neck ultrasound showed enlarged bilateral cervical nodes, the largest 1.9 × 0.8 × 2.2 cm in the right upper posterior triangle. Excisional lymph‑node biopsy on day 8 demonstrated necrosis with histiocytes, abundant karyorrhectic debris, crescentic histiocytes co‑expressing MPO and PGM1, and absence of neutrophils. No malignancy was identified. Ziehl‑Neelsen stain showed no acid‑fast bacilli; Grocott stain revealed no fungi. Bone‑marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy were non‑malignant. Chest radiograph, echocardiogram and hepatobiliary ultrasound were normal. The histopathological finding was suggestive of necrotising histiocytic lymphadenitis.

1. Infectious etiology considered but excluded because cultures and serologies were negative and special stains showed no organisms. | "Bacterial cultures from peripheral blood, bone marrow, urine, stool and throat yielded no growth." … "Viral markers including hepatitis A, B and C, Epstein‑Barr virus (EBV), cytomegalovirus (CMV), human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), dengue virus, Japanese E encephalitis virus (JEV) were negative." … "Serial sections with the Ziehl‑Neelsen stain did not show acid‑fast bacilli, and the Grocott stain did not show fungal organisms."

A 25‑year‑old man presented with a 5‑day history of high‑grade fever, chills, and one episode of vomiting. On admission he experienced a single seizure, followed by altered sensorium and progressive neurological decline. An erythematous macular rash was noted over his body. Initial investigations showed a hemoglobin of 7 g/dL and thrombocytopenia with a platelet count of 60 000/µL, which fell to 40 000/µL over the next two days before rising to 80 000/µL on the sixth day. 

Non‑contrast CT of the brain demonstrated ill‑defined symmetrical bilateral hypodensities in the thalami, cerebellar white matter, and bilateral frontal subcortical and deep white matter, with tiny hyperdense hemorrhagic foci within some lesions. Repeat CT a day later revealed an increase in hemorrhagic foci with intraventricular extension, obstructive hydrocephalus, and generalized cerebral edema. 

MRI performed on the second day of admission showed multiple, bilaterally symmetrical, hyperintense areas on FLAIR and T2 involving the thalami, cerebellum, bilateral frontal and parietal subcortical and deep white matter, with patchy restricted diffusion on DWI/ADC. Gradient‑echo sequences demonstrated multiple internal foci of blooming consistent with hemorrhages.

Neuro‑imaging reveals symmetrical thalamic and deep white‑matter lesions with intraparenchymal hemorrhage, a pattern described in dengue‑associated hemorrhagic encephalitis. | "CT imaging ... ill‑defined symmetrical bilateral hypodensities ... tiny hyperdense haemorrhagic foci ... Repeat CT ... increase in the haemorrhagic foci with intraventricular extension, obstructive hydrocephalus ..."
3. The authors concluded the diagnosis based on the combination of clinical, laboratory, and imaging findings. | "A diagnosis of dengue-associated haemorrhagic encephalitis was made based on the clinical presentation, imaging and laboratory findings."

case_prompt: A 10‑year‑old boy presented with a 12‑day history of high‑grade fever and chills, accompanied by headaches, retro‑orbital pain, and occasional vomiting. MRI of the spine revealed T2 hyperintense signal in the inferior medulla at the cervicomedullary junction extending to C3, and additional signal changes in the terminal dorsal cord and conus medullaris from T11 to L1.

2. Malaria was considered because of endemic fever and neurological signs but excluded by negative dual antigen testing. | "Dual antigen for malaria ... were negative."
3. Japanese encephalitis was a differential for encephalitis in this region but was ruled out by negative serology. | "serology markers for Japanese encephalitis ... were negative."

A 9‑year‑old girl of Eastern Indian origin with no significant past medical history presented to the emergency department with a 3‑day history of abdominal pain, fever, nausea, and vomiting. She had completed a 2‑dose Pfizer‑BioNTech COVID‑19 vaccine series 31 days earlier. After returning from a brief trip to the US Virgin Islands, during which she sustained multiple mosquito bites but no observed tick bites, she developed persistent fever, emesis, nausea, and abdominal pain. A respiratory viral panel obtained at her pediatrician’s office was negative, including for SARS‑CoV‑2, and she was given a dose of oseltamivir while awaiting results.  

In the emergency department she was febrile to a maximum of 40 °C, tachycardic (124–133 beats/min), with a respiratory rate of 20–30 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 96–100 % on room air, and blood pressure 94–102/44–54 mm Hg. Physical examination was notable for mild conjunctival injection and epigastric tenderness; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable.  

Initial laboratory studies showed mild hyponatremia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, lymphopenia, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers (Table 1). SARS‑CoV‑2 PCR from the admission sample was negative. A rapid streptococcal antigen test was negative. Urinalysis revealed trace ketones, protein, small leukocyte esterase with 10–19 WBC/hpf, and few bacteria.  

She was started on intravenous immunoglobulin (2 g/kg) and empiric ceftriaxone and doxycycline for possible bacterial infection. After 72 hours antibiotics were discontinued when cultures remained negative. Testing for a broad range of tropical and enteric pathogens—including Anaplasma, Babesia, dengue, Ehrlichia chaffeensis, Leptospira, tuberculosis, Parvovirus B19, Shigella, enteroinvasive E. coli, Shiga‑toxin‑producing genes, Campylobacter jejuni/coli, and Salmonella—was sent. Approximately 5 hours after IVIG initiation she developed a macular, non‑pruritic, non‑petechial rash over the neck and hands, sparing the palms and soles, which persisted until IVIG was completed. Bilateral conjunctival injection without discharge was noted on day 1 of admission and resolved by discharge.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Acute COVID‑19 infection considered but excluded because “SARS‑CoV‑2 PCR was negative” on admission despite recent positive test, and the clinical picture was markedly inflammatory rather than typical viral respiratory illness.  
2. Bacterial sepsis considered; empiric ceftriaxone and doxycycline were started, but “antibiotics were discontinued after 72 hours once cultures were negative,” supporting exclusion of bacterial infection.  
3. Streptococcal pharyngitis/tonsillitis considered; “Rapid streptococcal antigen test was negative.”  
4. Dengue and other mosquito‑borne viral infections considered given travel history; “Parasite and viral testing for diseases endemic to the United States Virgin Islands… were sent,” and results were negative, ruling these out.  
5. Tick‑borne illnesses (Anaplasma, Ehrlichia, Babesia, Lyme) considered; “Testing for Anaplasma, Babesia, dengue, Erlichia chaffeensis… were sent” and were negative, excluding these pathogens.  
6. Leptospirosis considered; testing was performed and returned negative, eliminating this cause.  
7. Tuberculosis considered; “testing for… tuberculosis… were sent” and were negative, making TB unlikely.  
8. Enteric bacterial infections (Shigella, EIEC, STEC, Campylobacter, Salmonella) considered; stool testing was performed and negative, excluding gastrointestinal bacterial etiologies.  
9. Autoimmune cytopenia considered; “negative direct antibody test (DAT) which decreases the likelihood of autoimmune cytopenia” and peripheral smear was negative for blasts, arguing against hematologic malignancy.  
10. Systemic lupus erythematosus considered; ANA was positive (titer 1:320) but “dsDNA and Smith antibodies were normal” and complement levels were normal, making SLE unlikely.  
11. Kawasaki disease considered due to fever, rash, conjunctival injection, and coronary risk; however, the patient had “normal echocardiogram” throughout, and the age, laboratory profile (marked leukopenia, thrombocytopenia) and recent SARS‑CoV‑2 exposure favored a post‑infectious hyperinflammatory syndrome rather than classic Kawasaki disease.  
12. Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) considered; lack of persistent hypertriglyceridemia, hyperferritinemia, and absence of hemophagocytosis on marrow (bone marrow not performed) along with response to IVIG made HLH less likely.  
13. Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children (MIS‑C) considered; the patient met CDC/AAP criteria (age < 21, fever, laboratory evidence of inflammation, multiorgan involvement, recent SARS‑CoV‑2 infection, and exclusion of other plausible diagnoses).

She was promptly intubated (post‑intubation GCS 6). Non‑contrast CT of the brain showed a right basal ganglia hemorrhage with intraventricular extension. She was transferred to the ICU, where a cerebral protection protocol (head‑up positioning, MAP 85‑90 mm Hg, normoxia, normocarbia, euglycemia, normothermia, serum Na⁺ 145‑155 mEq/L) and supportive care were instituted. ECG displayed sinus tachycardia; chest X‑ray was normal. After several days in ICU she developed spikes of very high temperature (core 106‑107 °F), rhabdomyolysis (CK ≈ 10 000 IU/L), stage III acute kidney injury requiring renal replacement therapy, and coagulopathy necessitating blood products. Cultures remained sterile, and drug‑induced hyperthermia was excluded. Repeat head CT showed no hematoma expansion. COVID‑19 testing was negative. Given a preceding week of fever, chills, and myalgia, a tropical workup was ordered for malaria, typhoid, leptospirosis, dengue, chikungunya, and scrub typhus.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Intracerebral hemorrhage complications (hematoma expansion, increased intracranial pressure) considered because of the basal ganglia bleed; ruled out by repeat CT showing no expansion. | "NCCT head was repeated, which did not reveal any hematoma expansion."
2. Bacterial sepsis from ventilator‑associated pneumonia or pressure ulcer considered due to fever and coagulopathy; ruled out by sterile cultures. | "On workup, cultures turned out to be sterile."
3. Drug‑induced hyperthermia considered because of high fever; excluded after review. | "Other possibilities of hyperthermia (such as drug toxicity) were ruled out."
4. COVID‑19 considered given pandemic context and fever; excluded by negative test. | "Workup for COVID-19 was also negative."
5. Other tropical infections (malaria, typhoid, leptospirosis, chikungunya, scrub typhus) considered because of recent febrile prodrome; excluded by negative serologies. | "In which serology (IgM antibodies) for dengue turned out to be positive." (implies other tests were negative).
6. Dengue infection confirmed by positive IgM serology, correlating with high‑grade fever, rhabdomyolysis, AKI, and coagulopathy—known severe dengue manifestations. | "Serology (IgM antibodies) for dengue turned out to be positive."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient has dengue virus infection, which is included in the 21 SELECTED diseases list. He also has malaria (P. falciparum), which is not on the list. Therefore the primary target diagnosis is dengue (SELECTED).
2. Best Breakpoint: End the prompt after the presentation of the dengue serology results and the abdominal ultrasound findings, but before the authors explicitly state “Diagnosis of dengue virus infection… was made” and before any discussion of malaria smear results. This supplies sufficient clinical, laboratory, and imaging data for a learner to infer dengue without revealing the diagnosis.
3. Key Analytic Distinctions: The authors ruled out hepatitis B and C by negative serology, considered dengue based on characteristic febrile syndrome plus IgM positivity, and later performed malaria smears because of travel history, demonstrating a concurrent infection that did not explain the initial dengue‑specific findings (elevated IgM, warning‑sign features, pleural effusion, hemoconcentration).
case_prompt:
A 34‑year‑old man returned to a rural region of Colombia on 17 December 2020 after living for 10 months in Gul, Uganda. He presented to the emergency department on 26 December 2020 with a 10‑day history of fever, holocranial headache, myalgia, arthralgia, retro‑ocular pain, sudden‑onset epistaxis, and dark urine. Vital signs were: blood pressure 110/80 mm Hg, heart rate 89 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, temperature 39 °C, oxygen saturation 97 % on room air. Physical examination revealed cold, sweaty skin without jaundice or cutaneous lesions, adequate respiratory mechanics, and hepatosplenomegaly extending 5 cm below the costal margin; no focal neurological deficits were noted.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10 g/dL (reference 12–14), platelet count 97 × 10⁳ /mm³ (reference 150–400 × 10⁳), and elevated serum transaminases. Serologies for hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibody were negative. Dengue serology performed on an acute‑phase serum sample (collected 10 days after symptom onset) demonstrated IgM at a titer of 1:800 and IgG at a titer of 1:400. An abdominal ultrasound demonstrated pleural effusion, moderate free fluid in the peritoneal cavity surrounding the urinary bladder, gallbladder wall thickening, hepatomegaly, and splenomegaly.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Dengue infection considered due to high‑grade fever, severe headache, myalgia, retro‑ocular pain, epistaxis, choluria, hepatosplenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, transaminase elevation, and the presence of anti‑dengue IgM antibodies. | "Serologic tests for dengue performed on the acute‑phase serum ... showed the presence of immunoglobulin (Ig) M (titers 1:800) and IgG (titers 1:400)".
2. Hepatitis B and C infections excluded because serologic testing was negative, making viral hepatitis an unlikely cause of the transaminase abnormalities. | "Those for hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibody, both came out normal."
3. Malaria infection considered later because of recent travel from an endemic area; thick and thin blood smears eventually demonstrated Plasmodium falciparum trophozoites. However, the initial presentation (especially the IgM serology) was more consistent with dengue, and the malaria finding did not account for the early IgM response. | "A thick and thin blood smear ... revealed the characteristic intra‑erythrocytic ring forms of Plasmodium falciparum ... confirming the diagnosis of malaria as uncomplicated."
4. Other potential causes of febrile illness with hemorrhagic manifestations (e.g., bacterial sepsis, other viral hemorrhagic fevers) were not supported by the laboratory profile (negative hepatitis serologies, absence of leukocytosis, and specific dengue IgM positivity). | Not explicitly quoted, but inferred from the authors’ focus on dengue serology and exclusion of hepatitis viruses.

case_prompt:
In April 2012 two adult men presented to the outpatient department with fever and myalgia, leading to admission. 

**Case 1:** A 28‑year‑old hunter was bitten on the right index finger by a squirrel ≈ 48 h before presentation. About 24 h after the bite he developed myalgia, fever, and general weakness. On examination he had a 10 mm cut‑like wound on the finger with minimal local inflammation; he was slightly drowsy. Within hours he progressed to shock (BP 70/50 mm Hg, HR 120 bpm) and was treated with oxygen, fluids, amoxicillin (later switched to ceftriaxone and cloxacillin), corticosteroids and adrenaline, after which consciousness returned. The next day he had recurrent fever ≈ 39 °C, edema of both hands and lower limbs, and, 48 h after admission (4–5 days after the bite), vesicles appeared on all four extremities, the gluteal region, and the scrotum, evolving into clear‑fluid bullae up to 15 mm. Lesions were solitary on the upper trunk; the face, palms, and soles were spared. No lymphadenopathy was noted. On day 4 of admission he experienced epistaxis and hematemesis that resolved spontaneously. Laboratory testing eight days after the onset of hemorrhage showed mildly raised aspartate‑aminotransferase (ASAT 66 IU/L) and thrombocytopenia (platelets 91 × 10⁹/L). Filovirus and dengue infections were tested for and were negative. The patient had no prior smallpox vaccination.

**Case 2:** Four days later, a 26‑year‑old farmer from a nearby village presented with 24 h of myalgia, fever 40 °C, and vesicular lesions on the lower arms and legs, including the palms; few lesions were on the trunk and face, none on the soles. Edema of the hands, lower legs, and feet was noted, and the distal digits were swollen, livid, and painful. Enlarged axillary, inguinal, and femoral lymph nodes (up to 20 mm) were palpable. He denied animal contact except with pigs. That evening he developed epistaxis and bloody stools, which resolved spontaneously. He received cloxacillin, ibuprofen, and paracetamol. Over the following days his condition improved, but the finger lesions progressed to necrosis. Laboratory analysis eight days after hemorrhage showed ASAT 109 IU/L, γ‑glutamyl‑transferase 161 IU/L, and a platelet count at the lower limit of normal (150 × 10⁹/L). Filovirus, yellow fever, and dengue infections were ruled out. He also had no prior smallpox vaccination.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Viral hemorrhagic fever (filovirus) considered because of hemorrhagic manifestations; excluded by negative testing. | "Filovirus and Dengue infections were tested for and revealed negative results."
2. Dengue infection considered given fever, myalgia, and bleeding; excluded by negative testing. | "Filovirus and Dengue infections were tested for and revealed negative results."
3. Yellow fever considered as another hemorrhagic viral possibility; excluded by negative testing. | "Filo-, Yellow Fever and Dengue virus infections were ruled out."
4. Smallpox (variola) considered due to vesiculobullous rash; unlikely because the patient had no prior smallpox vaccination and the lesion distribution differed from classic smallpox. | "The patient neither reported nor showed signs of a previous smallpox vaccination."
5. Monkeypox virus infection suspected after the appearance of the characteristic vesiculobullous lesions despite being outside the known endemic area, supported by animal exposure (squirrel bite) and the pattern of progressive skin lesions. | "Clinical suspicion of MPXV infection was raised by the authors immediately upon appearance of the skin lesions."

case_prompt: On August 29, 2014, Senegal announced its first Ebola virus disease case. The patient was a 21‑year‑old Guinean national who had been in contact with family members in Guinea who had died of the disease. He entered Senegal by road before the border restrictions on August 22, using an overnight public transport vehicle from August 13–14 to reach Dakar. During the trip he reported no fever‑type symptoms. Three days after arrival he developed fever, vomiting, and diarrhea without bleeding and sought care at a suburban health centre, where he was managed for three days. Persistent symptoms prompted referral to the infectious diseases service at Fann University Hospital, where he was hospitalized. He did not disclose his possible Ebola contacts to clinicians. After notification from WHO authorities that a contact‑case had likely traveled to Senegal, he was placed in an isolation room and fluid samples were obtained for testing.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. High‐risk epidemiologic exposure (recent travel from an Ebola‑affected region and known contact with deceased family members) raised suspicion for Ebola virus disease | "He entered Senegal by road... had been in contact... who had contracted the disease and eventually passed away."
2. Presence of fever, vomiting, and diarrhea without bleeding in the context of the above exposure prompted isolation and specimen collection pending confirmatory testing | "He was then immediately placed in an isolation room and some fluid samples were gathered."

case_prompt:
A 30‑year‑old woman with no known Ebola virus (EBOV) contact presented to an Ebola isolation unit in Freetown, Sierra Leone, on January 1, 2015 (day 7 of illness). She was afebrile and weak but ambulatory, reporting a preceding history of fever, vomiting, diarrhea, headache, and muscle and joint pain. Per local protocol, she received oral antimalarial, antimicrobial, antiemetic agents, and oral rehydration therapy. On day 8, EBOV PCR on serum was positive (Ct 23.5); she was started on intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g daily for 7 days), artesunate (180 mg for 3 days), and Ringer’s lactate (4–6 L) with supplemental potassium chloride for 5 days.

During days 13–15 she improved, walking independently and conversing. On day 16 she became confused, and by day 20 she was unresponsive to voices. Ceftriaxone and artesunate were administered again for 7 and 3 days, respectively. By days 28–29 she remained unconscious; serum EBOV PCR was negative on both days. She was transferred to Connaught Hospital on day 29 with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 9/15 (E3, V1, M5) without focal neurologic signs. Intravenous fluconazole 800 mg daily was started. Admission labs showed anemia, elevated alanine aminotransferase, elevated C‑reactive protein, and low creatinine; HIV testing was negative.

On day 34 she developed large‑joint polyarthritis of the right shoulder, left elbow, and left knee. Radiographs were normal; synovial fluid from the left knee was EBOV PCR negative. She received diclofenac 50 mg twice daily and a single intramuscular dose of methylprednisolone 80 mg. Blood PCR on day 34 was negative.

By day 41 she was more alert, although the family noted slowed responses. A lumbar puncture was performed; opening pressure was elevated at 30 cm H₂O.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. EBOV encephalitis – positive EBOV PCR in CSF indicates direct viral invasion of the CNS. | "Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was EBOV PCR‑positive (Ct value 37.6)...
2. Bacterial meningitis (MRSA, Klebsiella) – detected by FilmArray in CSF but deemed contaminants because of inadequate antimicrobial dosing and clinical improvement. | "FilmArray testing showed methicillin‑resistant Staphylococcus aureus and Klebsiella pneumoniae in CSF... Given inadequate antimicrobial drug doses for meningitis and clinical improvement, we believe... were CSF sample contaminants."
3. Fungal meningitis – empiric fluconazole was started, but no fungal organisms were identified in CSF. | "She was given intravenous fluconazole (800 mg 1×/d)."
4. Metabolic encephalopathy – anemia, elevated ALT, low creatinine suggest systemic illness but do not explain focal neurologic findings. | "Admission blood test results showed anemia, elevated alanine aminotransferase and C‑reactive protein, and low creatinine."
5. HIV‑associated neurocognitive disorder – excluded by negative HIV serology. | "HIV test results were negative."
6. Other viral encephalitides – no evidence of alternative viral pathogens on PCR panels. | "We could not perform many blood chemistry tests... or deep sequencing on samples."
7. Reactive arthritis – polyarthritis developed after the acute illness, supporting a post‑infectious immune response rather than septic arthritis. | "The development of arthritis with synovitis, treated with corticosteroids, supports the diagnosis of reactive arthritis."

case_prompt: A 40‑year‑old Liberian man traveled by air through Accra (Ghana) and Lome (Togo) to Lagos, Nigeria. Upon arrival at Lagos International Airport on 20 July 2014 he collapsed and was taken to a private hospital in the Obalende area. He was admitted with high fever, lymphadenopathy, and sore throat and was treated for malaria and typhoid fever. He later developed diarrhoea, vomiting, and microscopic haematuria. Because his clinical picture did not improve with malaria and typhoid therapy and because of his epidemiologic link to Liberia, suspicion for Ebola virus disease was raised. On 22 July 2014, blood samples in EDTA tubes and urine samples were collected and sent for viral investigations to the CMUL‑LUTH Virology Unit Laboratory and to the African Center of Excellence for Genomics of Infectious Diseases (ACEGID) in Ogun State, Nigeria.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Initial febrile illness with lymphadenopathy and sore throat was empirically treated as malaria and typhoid fever, common infections in West Africa. | "He presented with high fever, lymphadenopathy and sore throat and was treated for malaria and typhoid fever..."
2. Lack of clinical improvement despite appropriate antimalarial and antibiotic therapy prompted consideration of alternative etiologies. | "...the culmination of the clinical presentation, the patient's non‑response to treatment for malaria and typhoid..."
3. Recent travel from Liberia, a country experiencing an Ebola outbreak, raised specific suspicion for Ebola virus disease. | "...as well as his epidemiological link to Liberia, raised the suspicion for EVD."
4. Lassa fever and dengue fever were evaluated because they can present with similar hemorrhagic and febrile features; both were excluded by PCR. | "However, no signals were observed for Lassa or Dengue fever viruses."
5. Filovirus (Ebola) infection was confirmed by detection of the expected 300 bp amplicon in blood (and urine) specimens, establishing the definitive diagnosis. | "Investigations carried out on viral RNA purified from the blood and urine specimens of the patient revealed the presence of the expected amplicon size (300 bp) for Filoviruses..."

case_prompt: A 22‑year‑old man with a childhood history of close contact with goats and camels presented with chronic left pleuritic chest pain of three‑year duration, without any associated symptoms. He had no significant past medical or family history. Physical examination was unremarkable. A contrast‑enhanced chest CT showed a 4 × 6 × 6 cm cystic mass in the left thoracic paravertebral region extending from T3 to T5 vertebral bodies, containing peripheral and intrinsic calcifications, multiple cysts of varying sizes, remodeling and erosion of adjacent ribs, and extension into the left T3‑T4 and T4‑T5 neural foramina. ^18F‑FDG PET/CT demonstrated no significant FDG uptake in the lesion. The initial differential diagnosis favored a nerve‑sheath tumor, prompting a contrast‑enhanced MRI for further characterization. MRI revealed numerous intralesional daughter cysts of varying sizes with low T1 signal intensity and high T2 signal intensity relative to a larger mother cyst matrix that showed intermediate T1 and intermediate‑to‑high T2 signal intensity. The lesion possessed a smooth peripheral rim of low T2 signal intensity with post‑contrast enhancement. No mural nodules or suspicious solid components were identified, and there were no imaging signs of hepatic or pulmonary involvement.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Nerve‑sheath tumor considered because the cystic paravertebral mass could represent a neurogenic tumor; however, the lesion’s lack of FDG uptake and characteristic daughter‑cyst morphology argued against a solid neoplasm. | "The primary differential diagnosis was a nerve sheath tumor, and a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with IV contrast was recommended for further characterization."
2. Malignant peripheral nerve‑sheath tumor or other thoracic neoplasm deemed unlikely due to absent metabolic activity on PET/CT. | "F 18‑FDG PET/CT showed no significant FDG uptake in the lesion."
3. Simple bronchogenic or pericardial cyst less likely because of the presence of internal daughter cysts, peripheral calcifications, and rib remodeling, which are atypical for congenital cysts. | "Numerous and varying sizes of intralesional daughter cysts with low T1 signal intensity and high T2 signal intensity compared to the large mother cyst matrix..."
4. Metastatic disease excluded by the lack of solid enhancing nodules, negative FDG avidity, and no primary tumor identified elsewhere. | "There was no evidence of mural nodules or suspicious solid components, and no imaging signs of hepatic or pulmonary hydatid disease were present."
5. Hydatid disease (echinococcosis) supported by classic imaging features: daughter cysts, laminated rim, peripheral calcifications, and absence of FDG uptake; later confirmed by histopathology showing laminated membranous structures. | "The imaging finding, specifically the classic appearance of daughter cysts on the MRI, strongly suggested a hydatid cyst." and "The histologic examination showed ... acellular laminated membranous structures ... consistent with hydatid disease."

case_prompt:
A 73‑year‑old man presented with right upper abdominal pain, bilious vomiting, and a 6‑month history of weight loss. He denied any significant personal, past, or family medical history. Physical examination was unremarkable except for hepatomegaly. Complete blood count and liver function tests were within normal limits; hepatitis B and C serologies were negative.

Ultrasonography of the abdomen and pelvis showed moderate hepatomegaly with a large complex cyst, described as possibly a hydatid or haemorrhagic cyst. Contrast‑enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 25 × 16 × 18 cm cystic lesion involving the right hepatic lobe and segment IV, with a homogeneous nodular enhancement along the anterior wall measuring 3.9 × 1.5 cm. The imaging differential included biliary cystadenoma versus hydatid cyst. Positron emission tomography/CT revealed a large hypodense, ametabolic liver mass with a peripheral zone of hypermetabolism and no fluorodeoxyglucose‑avid distant lesions.

The patient underwent hepatic resection. Gross pathology described an 18.5 cm cystic mass in the right lobe with a smooth, congested, intact wall. On sectioning, thick brownish fluid emerged; the interior was solid‑cystic with irregular haemorrhagic wall and attached yellow‑friable material. A solid grey area measuring 3.0 cm was noted within the cyst, and adjacent liver contained multiple tiny whitish nodules (0.2–0.4 cm). The gallbladder showed chronic cholecystitis but no tumour.

Microscopy showed a cyst with a thick fibro‑collagenous wall beneath which tumour cells were arranged in acinar, glandular, and focal papillary patterns. Tumour cells had round to oval nuclei with finely granular chromatin, mild nuclear pleomorphism, scant to moderate eosinophilic cytoplasm, and occasional mitoses. Foci of haemorrhage, pigment‑laden macrophages, infarction, cholesterol clefts, and lymphovascular emboli were present. Adjacent liver sections revealed multiple satellite tumour nodules with identical morphology.

Immunohistochemistry demonstrated diffuse, strong positivity for synaptophysin and chromogranin, and a Ki‑67 proliferation index of 10–12 %.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Hydatid (echinococcosis) cyst considered because imaging showed a large complex cyst with possible haemorrhagic components; however, the presence of solid tumour nodules, irregular cyst wall, and lack of classic hydatid features (e.g., daughter cysts, calcifications) argued against it. | "Ultrasonography... revealed a large complex cyst, likely to be a hydatid or haemorrhagic cyst... On CT... a homogenous nodular enhancement... prompting the differential diagnosis of biliary cystadenoma and hydatid cyst."
2. Biliary cystadenoma considered given the cystic nature and wall enhancement on CT, but histology showed glandular and papillary tumour cells with neuroendocrine markers rather than mucin‑producing epithelium typical of cystadenoma. | "The above findings prompted the differential diagnosis of biliary cystadenoma and hydatid cyst."
3. Primary hepatic malignancies such as hepatocellular carcinoma or cholangiocarcinoma were deemed unlikely clinically and radiologically; the tumour cells lacked markedly pleomorphic nuclei, abundant cytoplasm, or trabecular growth patterns, and serum tumour markers were not evaluated because malignancy was not suspected. | "The workup for serum tumour markers... was not done as hepatic malignancy was not suspected clinically as well as radiologically."
4. Metastatic neuroendocrine tumour was a potential source, but post‑operative GC‑DOTA scan showed no somatostatin‑receptor‑positive lesions elsewhere, ruling out distant disease. | "Three weeks postoperatively... GC‑DOTA scan... revealed resolution of the previously seen liver mass and no lesion with somatostatin receptors expression to suggest... distant organ involvement."
5. Neuroendocrine tumour diagnosis supported by: (a) acinar, glandular, papillary architecture; (b) lymphovascular invasion; (c) diffuse synaptophysin and chromogranin positivity; (d) Ki‑67 index of 10–12 % consistent with grade II NET. | "Immunohistochemistry (IHC) workup revealed diffuse and strong positivity for synaptophysin and chromogranin (Cg), and the Ki‑67 proliferation index (Ki‑67 index) was 10‑12%."

case_prompt:
A 40‑year‑old man presented to the emergency department after collapsing and was found to have left‑sided weakness. He denied chest pain, palpitations, dyspnoea, dizziness, fever, or abdominal pain. He reported decreased vision in his right eye. Computed tomography of the head revealed a large right fronto‑parieto‑temporal cortical and subcortical hypodensity involving the right middle cerebral artery territory, with mass effect and a 4.2 mm midline shift. CT angiography and perfusion studies showed total occlusion of the distal right common carotid artery. His NIH Stroke Scale score was 18; he was not a thrombolysis candidate and neurosurgery deemed no surgical intervention necessary (GCS 15). He declined an MRI at that time.

Laboratory investigations demonstrated a hemoglobin of 17.1 g/dL (hematocrit 51.5 %), slightly reduced protein C activity (59.8 %), normal protein S (94.5 %) and antithrombin, protein C resistance of 0.87, and an elevated fibrinogen level of 5.25 g/L. An auto‑antibody screen was negative.

Given the likelihood of an embolic source, a transthoracic echocardiogram was performed, revealing a highly mobile cystic mass in the left ventricular outflow tract. No aortic regurgitation was noted. Transoesophageal echocardiography confirmed a 12 × 8 mm cystic lesion attached to the undersurface of the non‑coronary cusp, with normal aortic valve structure and function. Serological testing for hydatid disease was negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Embolic stroke from atherosclerotic carotid disease considered but CT angiography showed total occlusion of the distal right common carotid artery without plaque characteristics; “CT angiography and head perfusion showed total occlusion of the distal right common carotid artery (Figures 2 and 3).”  
2. Cardioembolic source from atrial fibrillation or mural thrombus was evaluated; no arrhythmia reported and echocardiography demonstrated a discrete cystic mass rather than a thrombus, “Transthoracic echocardiography showed a highly mobile cystic mass seen in the LVOT…”.  
3. Infective endocarditis considered; absence of fever, negative auto‑antibody screen, and lack of valvular vegetations argued against it, “He reported that he had no fever…An autoantibody screen was negative.”  
4. Hydatid cyst (echinococcosis) was a potential diagnosis; serology was negative, “Hydatid cyst was excluded by serological investigations.”  
5. Primary cardiac tumor (myxoma, papillary fibroelastoma) considered; the mass was cystic, attached to the non‑coronary cusp, with normal valve function, and later imaging showed complete resolution, supporting a non‑neoplastic, likely transient lesion, “Transoesophageal echocardiogram confirmed the cystic mass…with normal aortic valve appearance and function…Transthoracic echocardiogram confirmed no residual lesion (Figure 6).”

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case ultimately diagnoses a hydatid cyst, which corresponds to **echinococcosis**, a disease included in the 21 SELECTED list.

A 66‑year‑old woman was referred to a tertiary liver centre with a short history of nausea and right upper quadrant pain radiating to the back. On examination a large epigastric mass was palpable. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (white cell count 19.2 × 10⁹/L) and an elevated C‑reactive protein (210 mg/L); other blood tests were normal. Contrast‑enhanced computed tomography demonstrated a 16 cm × 16 cm cystic lesion in the right hepatic lobe, producing marked mass effect with near‑complete compression of the inferior vena cava and portal vein bifurcation. A hydatid cyst could not be excluded on imaging, and serology was awaited before attempting percutaneous aspiration. 

One day after admission the patient became profoundly confused. The confusion was initially attributed to new‑onset hyponatraemia (serum sodium 112 mmol/L) and sepsis secondary to an infected cyst. Liver enzymes rose dramatically (ALT 2,650 IU/L) and prothrombin time prolonged to 35.7 seconds, consistent with acute liver failure and hepatic encephalopathy. She progressed to multiorgan dysfunction, requiring inotropic, ventilatory, and renal support in intensive care. Cardiac output studies revealed a low cardiac index of 1.4 L/min/m². Bedside ultrasonography confirmed the large cystic structure with increased echogenicity and demonstrated absent hepatic vein flow, indicating hepatic outflow obstruction compatible with secondary Budd‑Chiari syndrome. 

Because she remained unstable and hypotensive with poor ventilation, an emergency laparotomy was performed via a rooftop incision. Approximately two litres of foul‑smelling, purulent material were drained from the cyst, the cyst wall was excised, and the abdominal cavity was extensively washed. Hydatid precautions, including the use of scolicidal agents, were employed intra‑operatively. Liver biopsies were obtained for assessment of underlying liver disease. Postoperatively the patient returned to intensive care; her cardiac index rapidly normalised to 4.0 L/min/m² and she eventually made a slow but full recovery.

3. Acute liver failure from toxin, drug, or viral hepatitis was explored due to the rapid rise in ALT and coagulopathy, but no specific viral or toxic history was reported. | "Worsening liver function with elevated enzymes and deranged clotting ... supported a diagnosis of acute liver failure with hepatic encephalopathy."
4. Budd‑Chiari syndrome (hepatic outflow obstruction) was identified on ultrasonography as a possible cause of the deteriorating hepatic function. | "Bedside ultrasonography confirmed ... No hepatic vein flow could be identified, in keeping with hepatic outflow obstruction (secondary BCS)."
5. Malignancy (cholangiocarcinoma or metastatic disease) was a differential for a large cystic liver mass, but imaging showed a cystic lesion without solid components, and initial labs were otherwise normal. | "Contrast enhanced computed tomography showed a 16 cm × 16 cm cystic lesion ... a hydatid cyst could not be ruled out on radiology."

After five weeks of persistent gastrointestinal symptoms, an abdominal CT identified a hypodense splenic lesion measuring 2.7 cm with no other abnormalities, and a diagnosis of sclerosing angiomatoid nodular transformation of the spleen was favored over other potential etiologies.

Physical examination revealed no palpable lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. CBC and comprehensive metabolic panel, including serum LDH, were within normal limits; hemoglobin A1C was 6.4 %. The multidisciplinary team favored laparoscopic splenectomy as both a diagnostic and therapeutic measure, and she received vaccinations against Haemophilus influenzae type b, meningococcus, and Streptococcus pneumoniae. Two months after completing treatment for colitis, she underwent an uneventful splenectomy, and within a few days her persistent left upper‑quadrant pain resolved.

An 86‑year‑old man presented to the surgical clinic with a two‑month history of a progressively enlarging mass in the anterior right thigh. Past medical history was notable for ischemic heart disease and hypertension; his medications included nitroglycerin, low‑dose aspirin, and methyldopa. He had no prior surgeries, no family history of cystic echinococcosis (CE), and no known exposure to dogs, sheep, or other livestock. On examination the patient appeared well, denied weight loss, and had a soft, non‑tender, mobile mass within the quadriceps femoris muscle. The overlying skin was intact, and there was no inguinal lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies showed normal hematology, biochemistry, and serology; the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was elevated at 65 mm/h.

Ultrasound of the thigh revealed a hypoechoic, encapsulated, multilocular cystic lesion measuring approximately 9 × 8 × 6.5 cm within the anterior quadriceps, with a smooth calcification in the cyst wall. The imaging team regarded hydatid cyst as the most important differential diagnosis. To assess for additional cysts, a chest and abdominal CT scan was performed and showed no abnormalities in the lungs, liver, or other intra‑abdominal organs.

The patient was started on albendazole preoperatively. He subsequently underwent surgical resection of the cystic lesion, which was removed intact without rupture.

case_prompt:
A 50‑year‑old female farmer from a northern midland province of Vietnam presented with a 2‑month history of dull right upper quadrant and epigastric pain and intermittent “stinging” chest sensations. She denied weight loss, fever, rash, gastrointestinal or respiratory symptoms. Past medical history was unremarkable. She owned many dogs. Physical examination was normal. Vital signs were within normal limits. ECG (12‑lead and 24‑h ambulatory) and chest X‑ray were normal. Laboratory studies revealed eosinophilia (22.1% eosinophils), mildly elevated AST (39 U/L) and ALT (56 U/L), and an elevated ESR (30 mm/h at 1 h, 36 mm/h at 2 h). Other blood and urine tests were normal.

Abdominal ultrasound showed a large anechoic lesion measuring 150 × 80 mm in the right hepatic lobe. Contrast‑enhanced abdominal CT described an encapsulated, thin‑walled cyst measuring 115 × 86 mm with homogeneous fluid; the biliary tree was normal. Head CT and chest CT ruled out cerebral and pulmonary cysts.

Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a 29 × 21 mm echo‑lucent, intramural, drop‑like structure bulging into the left ventricle from the lateral wall, moving synchronously with the cardiac cycle and without color flow. Left‑ventricular and right‑ventricular size and function, as well as pulmonary artery pressure, were normal. Three‑dimensional TTE confirmed a round, unilocular, fluid‑filled cyst with a smooth, hyper‑echogenic wall; no vascularization was seen on Doppler, and there was no valve involvement or intracavitary obstruction.

Cardiac CT showed an encapsulated, non‑calcified, fluid‑attenuated structure (32 × 24 mm) along the left‑ventricular lateral wall, distinct from coronary arteries, with no enhancement after contrast. Coronary MDCT excluded stenosis, aneurysm, or compression. Cardiac MRI displayed a single intramuscular cystic mass (24 × 23 × 30 mm) attached to the anterolateral papillary muscle, without gadolinium enhancement; myocardial perfusion and ventricular function were normal.

Serologic ELISA testing for Entamoeba histolytica, Strongyloides, Toxocara, and Echinococcus was negative, and stool examination for Fasciola hepatica eggs was also negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Simple hepatic cyst vs. hydatid cyst – Imaging showed a large thin‑walled, fluid‑filled lesion without internal septations or calcifications, typical of a hydatid cyst; simple cysts are usually asymptomatic and lack eosinophilia. | "An encapsulated structure measuring 115 × 86 mm, with a thin capsule containing homogeneous liquid."
2. Hepatic abscess vs. hydatid cyst – No fever, normal white‑cell count, and lack of inflammatory signs make abscess unlikely; eosinophilia points toward a parasitic etiology. | "She denied fever... eosinophilia (22.1%)."
3. Cardiac tumor (myxoma, fibroma) vs. cyst – Tumors are often solid, may enhance with contrast, and can cause obstruction; the cardiac lesion was non‑enhancing, fluid‑attenuated, and lacked vascular flow. | "The lesion looked primarily intracavitary... non‑calcified, fluid‑attenuated, no enhancement."
4. Coronary artery aneurysm vs. cyst – Coronary MDCT excluded aneurysm and showed the cyst not in contact with coronary arteries. | "Coronary MDCT excluded coronary stenosis; coronary aneurysm... and coronary compression caused by the cyst."
5. Intracardiac thrombus vs. cyst – Thrombus would show echogenic material, possible attachment to endocardium, and often present with risk factors; the mass was echo‑lucent, unilocular, and lacked Doppler flow. | "No color flow was observed within the cystic cavity."
6. Other parasitic cysts (Toxocara, Strongyloides, Fasciola) vs. Echinococcus – Serology for these organisms was negative; epidemiologic exposure to dogs and eosinophilia favor Echinococcus despite negative ELISA. | "Serological ELISA tests for Entamoeba histolytica, Strongyloides, Toxocara, and Echinococcus were negative... she owned many dogs."
7. Hydatid disease (echinococcosis) – The combination of a large hepatic cyst, a similar cardiac cyst, eosinophilia, dog exposure, and imaging characteristics consistent with a non‑vascular, fluid‑filled cyst strongly support echinococcosis. | "The cystic fluid contained larvae at different stages that had specific morphological characteristics of Echinococcus granulosus."

case_prompt: A 25‑year‑old woman was admitted to the emergency department with subacute mild confusion and left hemiparesis (MRC 4/5). On arrival he denied chest pain, palpitations, abdominal pain, fever, or chills but reported a productive cough with brown sputum and dyspnea.

Cardiac exam revealed a grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur best heard at the left fifth intercostal space, mid‑clavicular line. Breath sounds were reduced bilaterally with rales in upper and lower fields. Abdomen was diffusely tender; extremities were unremarkable.

Chest x‑ray demonstrated extensive patchy bilateral airspace opacities. Blood cultures from the outside hospital, sent to the state laboratory, were confirmed to be beta‑lactamase‑negative non‑typeable Haemophilus influenzae (NTHI).  

Given the new murmur and pulmonary findings, a trans‑thoracic echocardiogram was ordered to evaluate for possible infective endocarditis.

A 13‑year‑old male from a rural area was vertically infected with HIV. He was diagnosed with HIV and pulmonary tuberculosis in 2010 and started on standard anti‑tuberculosis therapy and antiretroviral therapy (ART) consisting of abacavir, lamivudine (3TC) and ritonavir‑boosted lopinavir (LPV/r) syrup. It was unclear whether ritonavir was “super‑boosted” during tuberculosis treatment to counteract the inducing effect of rifampicin. He experienced a second episode of tuberculosis in 2013, again without documented LPV/r super‑boosting.

Since ART initiation the patient has never achieved viral suppression despite continuous enhanced adherence support. Figure 1 (described) shows persistent HIV viral loads well above 1000 copies/mL and CD4 counts remaining low. In 2018 HIV drug‑resistance (DR) genotyping revealed only the M184V mutation and no protease inhibitor resistance mutations, suggesting suboptimal adherence. The regimen was changed to zidovudine (AZT) plus 3TC, and LPV/r pediatric tablets were added. In January 2020 LPV/r was switched to dolutegravir (DTG) to simplify therapy, while AZT/3TC were continued because of the patient’s weight (28 kg). At the time of the switch the viral load was 529 copies/mL, and no repeat DR test was performed. The patient continued to be unsuppressed and reported frequent missed doses because he lacked a treatment supporter.

The patient’s social context includes a history of sexual abuse of his mother, lack of disclosure, intermittent caregiver support, death of both biological parents from AIDS‑related complications, and limited involvement of the grandmother in his care, all contributing to poor adherence. Despite intensified adherence counseling by the attending physician and social worker, the patient remained virologically uncontrolled for two years on the DTG‑based regimen.

Due to this persistent lack of suppression, a repeat HIV drug‑resistance test was ordered in April 2022.

3. Prior documented resistance (M184V) indicating that adherence alone may not fully explain failure | "In 2018 HIV drug resistance (DR) genotyping was performed, showing only M184V mutation with no protease resistance mutations, which suggested suboptimal adherence."

Development of additional integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI) mutations conferring high‑level dolutegravir resistance as the definitive cause of ongoing viremia | "the DR showed M184V again and the development of InSTI mutations (major T66TI, G118R, E138K, minor M50I), conferring high‑level resistance to DTG."

A thirty‑year‑old African woman was referred to dermatology for a 2‑year history of progressive cutaneous lesions that had been unresponsive to multiple therapies. The lesions were located on the right pectoral area, right shoulder, and right side of the neck, extending toward the midline of the back. They consisted of blotchy erythematous ill‑defined plaques and patches in a vague reticulate pattern, without surface change, persisting without seasonal variation and worsening with sun exposure. She reported they were essentially asymptomatic.

General examination showed acrocyanosis, a vague livedo reticularis over the thighs, and discrete punctate red macules on the finger pulps resembling vasculitis. No adenopathy or visceromegaly was noted. She had a known HIV infection for several years, was not on HAART, and denied other chronic medications.

Laboratory studies: complete blood count, coagulation profile, electrolytes, thyroid function, glucose, calcium, and urinalysis were normal; ESR was elevated at 75 mm/h; liver enzymes modestly elevated (AST 60 U/L, ALT 66 U/L, GGT 149 U/L, LDH 308 U/L, ALP 142 U/L). HIV testing confirmed positivity with CD4⁺ counts 788–1,082 cells/µL, CD3⁺ counts 1,272–1,934 cells/µL, and viral load 19,736 copies (subsequently undetectable). IgM, IgG, IgA, complement, EBV, CMV, HTLV‑1/2, and syphilis serology were negative. Autoantibody panel (ds‑DNA, anti‑Ro/SSA, anti‑La/SSB, anti‑RNP1, anti‑Sm, anti‑thyroglobulin) was negative; complement levels normal; serum immunoelectrophoresis showed no paraprotein.

Skin biopsy of a lesion revealed a well‑preserved epidermis without basal membrane thickening or interface dermatitis. The reticular dermis was thickened with extensive basophilic material deposition highlighted by Alcian Blue (pH 2.5). A moderate perivascular and patchy periadnexal lymphocytic infiltrate, predominantly CD4⁺ T‑helper cells, was present without vasculitis. Direct immunofluorescence showed faint granular IgM positivity at the basement membrane zone; C3, IgG, and IgE were negative. HLA typing demonstrated polymorphisms: HLA‑A26,‑29; HLA‑B35,‑44; HLA‑Cw4,‑7; HLA‑DRB1 04, 13; HLA‑DQB1 03, 06.

Chest radiograph, skeletal radiology, and abdominal ultrasound were normal.

2. Scleredema considered but ruled out because histology demonstrated mucin deposition (Alcian Blue positive) rather than the collagenous fibrosis typical of scleredema. | "extensive deposition of basophilic material in the superficial and mid‑dermis... highlighted with Alcian Blue stain at pH 2.5."

4. Jessner’s benign lymphocytic infiltrate considered but dismissed because Jessner’s shows a dense lymphocytic infiltrate without mucin; the presence of abundant dermal mucin and faint IgM basement‑membrane staining favored another entity. | "moderate perivascular and patchy periadnexal lymphocytic infiltrate... faint granular positivity for IgM in the basement membrane zone."
5. Reticular erythematous mucinosis (REM) favored by the combination of clinical reticulate erythematous plaques, sun aggravation, histopathology with dermal mucin deposition, T‑helper predominant infiltrate, and subtle IgM basement‑membrane positivity. | "Based on the history and clinical presentation, supported by histopathologic findings and DIF results, a diagnosis of REM was favoured."

case_prompt: A 40‑year‑old female with a known HIV infection diagnosed in 2010, lost to follow‑up for five years, presented on 31 March 2015 with AIDS‑defining illnesses. Liver biopsy demonstrated chronic inflammation, a single granuloma with mild fibrosis, marked steatosis, and no malignancy. The working diagnosis was cholangiopathy secondary to HIV or cryptosporidium with possible hepatic tuberculosis or Mycobacterium avium‑intracellulare infection. HIV viral load was 2,566,506 copies/mL, CD4 count 12 cells/mm³, and genotypic resistance testing showed no major mutations. She received anti‑tuberculosis therapy, clarithromycin for MAI, full treatment for PCP, and started TDF/emtricitabine (Truvada) plus efavirenz on 5 April 2015. About three weeks later she developed hypokalemia (2.8 mmol/L) and hypophosphatemia (0.36 mmol/L) with normal magnesium. Because severe anemia precluded zidovudine, TDF was continued. After anemia improved, TDF was switched to zidovudine/lamivudine on 10 February 2016, then back to TDF/emtricitabine in April 2016 due to worsening anemia. In May 2016, despite undetectable viral load and CD4 292 cells/µL, persistent hypokalemia (2.6 mmol/L) and hypophosphatemia (0.66 mmol/L) prompted another switch to zidovudine/lamivudine/efavirenz, which was stopped in December 2016 after acute pancreatitis. She was lost to follow‑up for nearly a year. In June 2018 she returned; viral load was 2,473,928 copies/mL, CD4 83 cells/µL, and a resistance‑free regimen (elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide) was started. By August 2019, after poor adherence, viral load was 1,840 copies/mL, CD4 169 cells/µL, and she complained of dull back ache, generalized bone pain, and myalgia. Examination showed cachexia (weight 36 kg, BMI 15 kg/m²), waddling gait, tender thoracolumbar spine, and severe proximal myopathy. MRI of the spine demonstrated compression fractures at T12–L1; bone densitometry revealed a lumbar spine Z‑score of –6.4 and femoral neck –5.
