case_prompt:
A 44‑year‑old homeless man with a history of intravenous cocaine and heroin use presented to the emergency department with a 24‑hour history of pain and swelling of the right hand following an unsuccessful injection into a hand vein. He was emaciated, febrile, and had extensive erythema and edema over the dorsum of the right hand and distal forearm. Blood pressure was 112/68 mmHg. Laboratory studies showed microcytic, hypochromic anemia (Hb 10.3 g/dL), neutrophilic leukocytosis (25 220/µL), and a markedly elevated C‑reactive protein (306 mg/L). HIV serology was positive (CD4⁺ count 898/µL, viral load 3 680 copies/mL) and HCV serology was also positive. One set of blood cultures was drawn before empiric therapy with piperacillin‑tazobactam, vancomycin, and intravenous fluids was initiated. No purulent discharge was present, so the skin lesion was not sampled.

Within the next 24 hours the local inflammatory signs progressed, with extensive bullae forming on the epidermis. A computed‑tomography scan demonstrated extensive soft‑tissue edema and extensor tendonitis but no myositis; wrist ultrasound excluded radiocarpal arthritis. After 41.7 hours of incubation, one bottle of the initial blood‑culture set flagged positive; Gram stain of the smear revealed large, “box‑car”‑shaped Gram‑positive rods with squared‑off ends and parallel sides. The result was initially interpreted as probable contamination, prompting collection of a second set of blood cultures. After 89.9 hours, one bottle of the second set also flagged positive, and Gram staining showed an identical morphology.

case_prompt:
A 51‑year‑old man presented to an infectious disease clinic in the northeastern United States with continuous fever for 2 weeks and watery diarrhea for 1 week. His past medical history included asthma, a right rotator cuff repair 3 months earlier, and HIV infection diagnosed 10 years ago, currently on emtricitabine/tenofovir and dolutegravir with an undetectable viral load. Two weeks before presentation he received the mpox vaccine (JYNNEOS); 2 h later he developed fever with rigors, and two days later severe watery diarrhea and mild dysuria. He denied nausea, vomiting, rash, recent travel, or sick contacts.

On exam he was febrile (100.9 °F) and tachycardic (110–120 bpm); respiratory rate and oxygen saturation were normal. Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable except for slight tenderness over the right shoulder surgical site.

Laboratory studies showed no leukocytosis, elevated C‑reactive protein (67.82 mg/L) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (38 mm/h). HIV viral load was undetectable; CD4 count was 673 cells/µL. Blood, urine, and stool cultures were negative; CMV PCR, respiratory viral panel, and STI testing (including chlamydia/gonorrhea NAAT) were negative. Chest radiograph was normal. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia; echocardiogram showed normal left‑ventricular function without vegetations; troponin was negative. A 7‑day cardiac monitor recorded sinus rhythm.

One week later he developed progressive pain, redness, swelling, and warmth of the left knee with pitting edema extending from the foot to the knee. Duplex ultrasound ruled out deep‑vein thrombosis. MRI of the left knee revealed a grade 2 tear of the medial collateral ligament, medial femoral condyle edema, and a joint effusion. Aspiration yielded 50 cc of clear fluid with a modestly elevated white‑cell count and protein level suggestive of inflammatory arthritis. Antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and HLA‑B27 were negative; synovial fluid crystals, bacterial cultures, and Lyme PCR were all negative.

Over the next days he developed further migratory arthritis involving the left elbow, right knee, and bilateral temporomandibular joints, as well as left‑eye redness, floaters, and decreased vision. Ophthalmologic examination showed circum‑corneal congestion, keratin precipitates, an irregular pupil, and anterior chamber cells consistent with anterior uveitis.

3. Lyme disease considered due to possible tick exposure; excluded by negative Lyme PCR on joint fluid. | "Joint fluid crystals, cultures, and Lyme PCR testing were negative."
4. Systemic autoimmune arthritis (rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus) considered; serologies (ANA, rheumatoid factor) were negative. | "Antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factors, and HLAB27 were negative."
5. Spondyloarthropathy (including reactive arthritis associated with HLA‑B27) evaluated; HLA‑B27 was negative, making an HLA‑B27‑positive spondyloarthropathy unlikely. | "Antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factors, and HLAB27 were negative."
6. Viral etiologies (e.g., cytomegalovirus) considered given immunocompromise; CMV PCR was negative. | "Cytomegalovirus PCR ... were negative."
7. General vaccine adverse reaction considered; however the pattern of preceding gastrointestinal infection, asymmetric migratory arthritis, dysuria, and anterior uveitis fits the classic triad of reactive arthritis. | "The patient's diarrhea, asymmetric arthritis, dysuria, and uveitis were believed to be due to reactive arthritis."

case_prompt:
A 52‑year‑old woman was admitted to the emergency room after experiencing seven self‑limited focal seizures affecting the right upper limb and ipsilateral face over the preceding 12 hours. Her past medical history included advanced HIV infection (currently on tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, lamivudine, dolutegravir) and a treated episode of cerebral toxoplasmosis 11 years earlier that had resulted in right hemiparesis. Following that episode she had achieved immune reconstitution with an undetectable viral load. In the intervening years she had two additional neurological events: six years ago she was hospitalized for focal seizures and received carbamazepine; one year ago she presented with self‑limited headaches. Serial MRIs during those episodes showed calcified lesions with surrounding edema that later resolved.

At the current visit she experienced two more focal seizures of the right upper limb. Neurological exam revealed mild distal weakness (4+/5) of the right upper limb, unchanged from her prior toxoplasmosis sequelae. Current medications also included lamotrigine 50 mg twice daily. Laboratory studies showed a CD4⁺ count of 2,269 cells/µL (30 %) and an HIV‑1 viral load < 40 copies/mL. Non‑contrast brain CT demonstrated two calcified foci, one with a mild perilesional edema. Corresponding MRI confirmed the calcifications; the lesion with edema showed increased gadolinium enhancement compared with prior studies. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was unremarkable. Serologic testing was positive for Toxoplasma gondii IgG and negative for cysticercosis antibodies. An electroencephalogram performed three days after the last seizure was normal.

4. Neoplastic processes (e.g., low‑grade glioma) considered less probable given the long‑standing calcified focus, prior documented resolution of edema after treatment, and the acute inflammatory change rather than progressive growth. | "MRI showed these calcifications and the lesion with perilesional edema was increasing after gadolinium administration."

case_prompt:
A 48‑year‑old man, originally from Jiayu County, Hubei Province, and residing in Guangzhou Province, developed a fever up to 39.5 °C in April 2019. Initial anti‑infective therapy at a local hospital was ineffective, and the fever recurred despite intermittent antimicrobial courses over the next two months. At the end of May 2019 he experienced melena after taking Chinese herbal medicine, accompanied by epigastric pain, anorexia, acid regurgitation, eructation, retching, and weakness, prompting admission to the gastroenterology department.

Past medical history included herpes zoster infection, chronic bronchitis, penicillin allergy, a 20‑year history of smoking and alcohol use, and he denied other illnesses. On admission his blood pressure was 100/69 mmHg, temperature 36.4 °C, pulse 124 beats/min, and respiratory rate 17/min. case_prompt: A 40‑50‑year‑old patient with chronic alcoholism was referred to the stroke unit for severe aphasia. Orthostatic headache and walking disturbance had been present for four months. On examination the patient was delirious, aphasic and had spastic hypertonia of all four limbs. Pulse oximetry and blood glucose were normal. Brain MRI showed bilateral thalamic diffusion and FLAIR hyper‑signals with apparent diffusion coefficient hyp‑signals, as well as a thin chronic right‑convexity subdural hematoma. Arterial 3‑D time‑of‑flight sequences revealed no arterial occlusions, and there was no evidence of cerebral venous sinus thrombosis. Laboratory work‑up demonstrated HIV infection with lymphopenia; SARS‑CoV‑2 PCR was negative. Four days after admission the patient became comatose (Glasgow coma score 6). Emergent brain CT demonstrated an acute bleed within the chronic right‑convexity subdural hematoma (13 mm thickness) producing a subfalcine herniation. The patient was intubated and underwent surgical evacuation of the hematoma; intraoperatively the brain did not re‑expand and venous bleeding from bridging veins was noted. An intracranial pressure (ICP) sensor was placed. Postoperatively, sedation was stopped on day 1 and the patient was extubated on day 5, yet he remained unresponsive (Glasgow coma score 10) with fluctuating eye opening and severe spastic tetraparesis. Repeat MRI and ICP measurements were pending. Electroencephalography showed no epileptic activity or toxic/metabolic encephalopathy. Extensive biological investigations ruled out viral and bacterial meningo‑encephalitis, autoimmune encephalitis, hyperammonemia, toxic encephalitis, and vitamin B1 deficiency. case_prompt:
A 63‑year‑old female farmer was admitted with fever, skin ulcers, subcutaneous nodules, and food regurgitation from the nose while eating. She had been diagnosed with AIDS two years earlier but had discontinued antiretroviral therapy for several months. Four months before admission she noted oral pain and a purulent nodule on the upper palate; one month later the nodule ruptured, forming a sinus that communicated with the nasal cavity, resulting in nasal food regurgitation. She also experienced intermittent fever and multiple subcutaneous nodules on the trunk and limbs that grew, ruptured, and became non‑healing ulcers. She denied cough, headache, abdominal pain, diarrhea, visual loss, visual field defects, or limb weakness.

On examination the largest ulcer measured about 5 × 4 cm, covered with necrotic tissue and purulent drainage. Subcutaneous nodules were mildly tender and poorly demarcated. The oral cavity showed leukoplakia and a 1‑cm sinus tract in the upper palate communicating with the nasal cavity, with a small adjacent unruptured purulent nodule. Neck was soft, vision normal, and no superficial lymphadenopathy.

Laboratory studies showed WBC 2.3 × 10⁹/L, hemoglobin 74 g/L, albumin 28.7 g/L, CRP 21.7 mg/L, ESR 27 mm/h, CD4⁺ count 4 cells/µL, HIV‑RNA 94,000 copies/mL. Serum β‑D‑glucan, galactomannan, and IGRA were negative; serology for syphilis, cytomegalovirus, and Epstein‑Barr virus was negative. Maxillofacial CT demonstrated sinus mucosal thickening, enhancement, and partial defects of the hard palate and nasal septum. Chest CT showed a mild left‑lung infection. Doppler ultrasound of a right‑leg nodule revealed a subcutaneous hypoechoic inflammatory mass.

Empiric therapy with fluconazole, cefotaxime/sulbactam, and trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole was started, but fever persisted and lesions did not improve. On day 3 a biopsy of the right hip subcutaneous mass was performed; specimens were sent for histopathology, metagenomic next‑generation sequencing (mNGS), and special stains. Peripheral blood was simultaneously collected for mNGS, and cytologic examinations of ulcer and sinus secretions were obtained.

1. Bacterial infection considered due to fever and skin lesions; empiric cefotaxime/sulbactam started – “blood cultures were reported as negative” and lesions did not improve, arguing against bacterial etiology.  
2. Common fungal infection considered; fluconazole administered – “Serological studies for (1, 3) beta‑D‑glucan, galactomannan (GM)… were negative” and special stains were negative, making fungal infection unlikely.  
3. Tuberculosis evaluated because of subcutaneous nodules – “interferon‑gamma release assay (IGRA) were negative” and acid‑fast staining showed no organisms, reducing the likelihood of TB.  
4. Cryptococcosis screened due to immunosuppression – “Cryptococcus neoformans capsule antigen, India ink stain… were all negative in the CSF,” excluding cryptococcal disease.  
5. Cytomegalovirus and Epstein‑Barr virus infection assessed – “Blood screening for… cytomegalovirus, and Epstein‑Barr virus was also negative” and CSF PCR for CMV and EBV were negative, arguing against these viral infections.  
6. Syphilis tested because of ulcerative lesions – “Blood screening for… syphilis… was also negative,” making syphilis improbable.  
7. Nocardiosis considered as an opportunistic bacterial infection – “Tissue periodic acid‑Schiff staining, Gram staining, silver staining, and acid‑fast staining were all negative,” and lack of response to antibiotics lessened its probability.  
8. Pneumocystis pneumonia considered given HIV status – patient received TMP/SMZ empirically, but chest CT showed only mild infection and no respiratory symptoms, suggesting PCP unlikely.  
9. Other viral pathogens (HSV) evaluated – “PCR for herpes simplex virus… were all negative in the CSF,” ruling out HSV involvement.  
10. Disseminated Acanthamoeba infection confirmed by positive mNGS and trophozoites – “mNGS results… revealed Acanthamoeba castellanii infection” and “Trophozoite‑like structures were observed… indicative of an amoebic infection.”

case_prompt:
A previously healthy 55‑year‑old woman presented in August 2021 with persistent low‑grade fever, peripheral edema, and night sweats. Routine blood tests were normal except for elevated immunoglobulin levels. Chest radiography revealed diffuse bilateral lung micronodules, prompting referral to pulmonology in December 2021. Computed tomography confirmed a bilateral diffuse micronodular interstitial pattern, predominating in the lower lobes, with small subpleural nodules, ground‑glass opacities, and mediastinal lymph nodes up to 2 cm. Spirometry showed a restrictive pattern with reduced diffusing capacity; echocardiography was unremarkable. Fiberoptic bronchoscopy was normal. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) for microbiology, including tuberculosis, was negative; cytology showed no malignant cells. BAL cellularity was 72 % alveolar macrophages, 18 % neutrophils, 10 % lymphocytes with immunophenotyping: B cells 9 % (112/mm³), CD4⁺ T cells 4 % (45/mm³), CD8⁺ T cells 88 % (1113/mm³), CD3⁺ T cells 91 % (1143/mm³), NK cells 0.4 % (5/mm³), CD4/CD8 ratio 0.04, total lymphocytes 1261/mm³. Transbronchial biopsy showed nonspecific B‑cell aggregates with isolated CD30⁺ cells and EBV‑encoded small RNAs (EBER) positivity; Ziehl‑Neelsen stain was negative.

A follow‑up CT in February 2022 demonstrated persistent pulmonary findings and new supraclavicular, mediastinal, inguinal, and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy (max 27 × 13 mm). Inguinal node biopsy revealed reactive follicular hyperplasia with CD20⁺/CD10⁺/BCL6⁺/BCL2‑ B cells. A repeat transbronchial biopsy showed septal infiltrates of CD20⁺ B cells, CD3⁺ T cells, and plasma cells, lacking CD30⁺ or IgG4⁺ elements; PAS, Grocott, and Ziehl‑Neelsen stains were negative.

Because dyspnea worsened in October 2022, a surgical lung biopsy was performed. Histology demonstrated perivascular lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates with focal angioinvasion, occasional follicular structures containing CD23⁺ dendritic cells, CD10⁺/BCL2‑ germinal centers, and Cyclin D1‑ mantle zones. The interstitium was rich in CD3⁺ T cells; scattered CD79a⁺ plasma cells were HHV8‑negative and showed no light‑chain restriction. A few atypical large lymphoid cells (4–5 per high‑power field) were CD20⁺, CD30⁺, PAX5⁺, ALK‑, and EBER⁺, consistent with an EBV‑related B‑cell lymphoproliferative disease (low‑grade lymphomatoid granulomatosis). In November 2022, the patient was referred to the hematology unit for further management.

1. Tuberculosis considered due to pulmonary micronodules and lymphadenopathy; ruled out because “Bronchoalveolar lavage for microbiological investigations (including research for tuberculosis) turned up negative” and “Ziehl‑Neelsen stain was negative.”

3. Primary pulmonary lymphoma entertained because of atypical CD20⁺ CD30⁺ cells; dismissed since “no evidence of immunoglobulin light chain restriction” and the infiltrate was polyclonal.

case_prompt: In March 2023, a 43‑year‑old Chinese man presented to a fever clinic with a one‑week history of fever (peak 39.8 °C) and right upper‑quadrant abdominal pain. Aerobic and anaerobic cultures of the drainage fluid, as well as pre‑antibiotic blood cultures (four bottles), grew Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serotype Typhi. Susceptibility testing showed the isolate was sensitive to ceftriaxone, and treatment with ceftriaxone 2000 mg daily was started. case_prompt:
A 35‑year‑old Caucasian woman was diagnosed with HIV‑1 infection in 1989 after heterosexual exposure. She began zidovudine intermittently in 1995; by 1997 her CD4 count was <100 cells/µL with a high viral load (>500 000 copies/mL). At that time indinavir was replaced by ritonavir/saquinavir 400/400 mg bid because of renal stones. A 32‑year‑old man with adjustment and developmental disorders presented with rapidly progressive neurological symptoms and altered consciousness over 10 days, prompting transfer from a preceding hospital. He had no prior opportunistic infections. Systemic evaluation suggested meningitis and led to a diagnosis of pneumonia; empirical antibacterial therapy with ceftriaxone and azithromycin was started. Laboratory studies showed WBC 9 600/µL, severe lymphopenia (lymphocyte 0.8 % = 77 cells/µL), and a CD4⁺ count of 5.5 %, indicating advanced HIV/AIDS. Chest CT revealed diffuse bilateral ground‑glass opacities, suspicious for pneumocystis pneumonia. case_prompt:
A 35‑year‑old man with known HIV infection and hepatitis C virus coinfection presented with an atypical pharyngeal lesion. His HIV history included intravenous drug use, cigarette smoking, a nadir CD4+ count <100 cells/µL after self‑cessation of antiretroviral therapy (ART), and re‑initiation of ART three months prior to lesion onset (emtricitabine, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, ritonavir‑boosted darunavir).  

Initially a small plaque‑like lesion near the right lower wisdom tooth was noted and treated empirically as oral hairy leukoplakia with valaciclovir and aciclovir, but it relapsed and remitted. Four months later, after CD4+ count rose to 340 cells/µL and HIV replication was suppressed, the lesion enlarged into a thick, white, well‑circumscribed, exophytic plaque covering the left tonsil, accompanied by uvular enlargement, voice change, dry cough, and bilateral otalgia. No cervical lymphadenopathy or systemic symptoms were present.  

Laboratory studies showed mild eosinophilia (0.46 × 10⁹/L) with otherwise normal leukocyte counts; syphilis serology was negative. A CT scan demonstrated a lesion extending from the nasopharynx to the oropharynx. Empiric oral amoxicillin/clavulanic acid produced no change, and a left tonsillar biopsy was performed, complicated by postoperative hemorrhage.  

Microscopic examination of the tonsil revealed a dense inflammatory infiltrate composed largely of plasmacytoid lymphocytes, plasma cells, and eosinophils. Eosinophils exocytosed into the overlying squamous mucosa, and there was lobular vascular proliferation of numerous thin‑walled capillary‑sized vessels. Areas of necrosis were present, some centered on blood vessels, without evidence of vasculitis. Immunohistochemistry showed a benign mixed B‑ and T‑cell pattern, excluding a lymphoproliferative process. Special stains were negative for fungi (methenamine silver, PAS), spirochetes (Warthin‑Starry), acid‑fast bacilli, and immunoperoxidase stains for cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, and EBV LMP1.

case_prompt: A 34‑year‑old man with no family history of autoimmune disease or thrombotic events and no known chronic illnesses awoke on 9 June 2025 at 8:30 a.m. with sudden‑onset paresthesia of the left side of his body lasting about two hours. Laboratory studies were unremarkable: triglycerides 158 mg/dL, LDL 52 mg/dL, HDL 15 mg/dL; PT 12 s, aPTT 28 s. 1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case’s definitive diagnosis is HHV‑8‑positive multicentric Castleman disease, which is not in the 21 SELECTED diseases list; the patient also has latent syphilis (a SELECTED disease). Breakpoint: Present the case up to the point when the patient is admitted to the tertiary hospital, including physical findings, laboratory results, and imaging (PET‑CT, chest and abdominal CT), but stop before the excisional lymph‑node biopsy histology and immunohistochemistry that confirmed Castleman disease. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished Castleman disease from lymphoma by noting diffuse symmetric FDG uptake without focal destructive lesions on PET‑CT, repeatedly non‑malignant needle biopsies, and finally the presence of HHV‑8‑positive “onion‑skin” mantle‑zone expansion on excisional biopsy. case_prompt:
A 65‑year‑old married male office worker with a known history of HIV infection diagnosed in 2011 (baseline CD4⁺ count 84 cells/µL; currently on bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide) presented with painless, progressive lymphadenopathy. He first noted cervical, axillary, and inguinal nodes in March 2022; the largest node was chestnut‑sized, firm, smooth, and mobile. He delayed seeking care.

In June 2022 he presented to Tianjin Second People’s Hospital. Physical exam showed mildly enlarged cervical nodes. A cervical‑node biopsy suggested reactive hyperplasia. PET‑CT on June 29 demonstrated widespread, symmetric lymphadenopathy with markedly increased FDG uptake (bilateral cervical SUVmax 11.03, axillary SUVmax 10.03, thoracic, abdominal, and inguinal nodes) and no focal destructive lesions, raising concern for lymphoma versus inflammatory process. He received glucocorticoids and was discharged.

On July 4 he returned with new fever (up to 39.5 °C), fatigue, anorexia, chest tightness, dyspnea, and further node enlargement. A repeat lymph‑node fine‑needle aspiration again showed reactive proliferation. Bone‑marrow biopsy and flow cytometry revealed no lymphoma infiltration. Metagenomic next‑generation sequencing of node tissue detected HHV‑8 and EBV. His symptoms improved with anti‑infective and glucocorticoid therapy and he was discharged after node regression.

He was readmitted on August 27 with recurrent high fever and worsening lymphadenopathy. Examination revealed firm, non‑tender, mobile cervical, axillary, and inguinal nodes, the largest being egg‑sized, without erythema or ulceration. Vital signs were stable. Laboratory studies showed CD4⁺ count 435 cells/µL, CD4/CD8 ratio 0.44, undetectable HIV viral load, thrombocytopenia (85 × 10⁹/L), mild anemia (Hb 118 g/L), ESR 69 mm/h, CRP 68.33 mg/L, IL‑6 21.86 pg/mL. Syphilis serology was positive (TPPA⁺, RPR 1:2). EBV IgG was positive, EBV DNA negative. Chest CT suggested possible lymph‑node space‑occupying lesions. Abdominal CT showed splenomegaly, retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy, and a cystic lesion in the right inguinal region.

1. Lymphoma considered due to generalized high‑FDG uptake on PET‑CT but excluded by multiple needle biopsies and bone‑marrow studies showing no malignant cells | "Although lymphoma was suspected, inflammatory changes were considered more likely. ... Bone marrow biopsy ... showed no lymphoma infiltration."
2. Reactive hyperplasia suggested by initial cervical‑node biopsy and repeat fine‑needle aspirates showing proliferative but non‑malignant tissue | "A biopsy on June 22 suggested reactive hyperplasia." / "Repeat lymph node puncture again indicated reactive proliferation."

case_prompt:
A 48‑year‑old black female presented to the Medunsa Oral Health Center with a large swelling of the left side of her face and proptosis of the left eye. The facial mass was firm, immobile, obliterated the nasolabial furrow, displaced the nose to the right, and was fungating from the left nostril. Intraorally a large soft‑tissue mass arose from the maxilla, crossing the midline, with extensive necrosis. She reported that the facial swelling had rapidly enlarged over the previous month and that she had recently lost vision in the left eye. Language and cultural barriers prevented clarification of prior medical care.

Microscopic examination of an intra‑oral biopsy showed a neoplastic plasma‑cell tumour composed of densely packed plasmablasts with prominent nucleoli. Aspiration of bone marrow from the femur revealed plasmacytosis (9 % of the myelogram) without an increase in blasts; plasma cells were mainly mature with occasional binucleated forms. A trephine biopsy was not performed, so clonality could not be assessed. Erythropoiesis was reduced.

Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation demonstrated an IgG‑kappa monoclonal protein. Serum IgG was 35.89 g/L (reference 7.00‑16.00) and kappa light chain 8.4 g/L (reference 0.6‑1.3). The patient was HIV‑seropositive with a CD4+ count of 41 × 10⁶/L (9.06 % of lymphocytes). Laboratory studies showed normocytic normochromic anemia, lymphopenia, and thrombocytosis; serum calcium and creatinine were normal. A skeletal survey (excluding the head) showed no abnormalities. Ophthalmologic examination confirmed blindness of the left eye.

Computed tomography revealed a 12 cm × 12 cm heterogeneous soft‑tissue mass destroying the left maxillary, ethmoid, and sphenoid sinuses and extending into the anterior cranial fossa. The intra‑orbital component caused severe proptosis. The tumour involved the left nasopharynx, parotid and masseteric spaces, buccal tissues, left submandibular space, and floor of mouth. The mandible was displaced but showed no lytic or sclerotic lesions. Bilateral enlarged cervical lymph nodes were noted.

1. The biopsy showed plasma‑cell morphology, directing the diagnosis toward a plasma‑cell neoplasm rather than other head‑and‑neck tumors. | "Microscopic examination of a biopsy specimen from the intraoral mass showed a neoplastic plasma cell tumour. The densely packed tumour cells were mainly plasmablasts with prominent nucleoli."
2. Serum protein studies demonstrated a monoclonal IgG‑kappa spike, supporting a clonal plasma‑cell disorder and excluding polyclonal inflammatory processes. | "Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation showed IgG kappa monoclonal protein."
3. Bone‑marrow aspiration revealed plasmacytosis (9 %) without blasts, indicating systemic plasma‑cell involvement rather than an isolated extramedullary plasmacytoma. | "Aspiration of bone marrow from the femur demonstrated plasmacytosis (9% of the myelogram) without an increased number of blasts."
4. Extensive bony destruction on CT with soft‑tissue mass and lack of other primary tumors argued against sarcoma or lymphoma and favored a malignant plasma‑cell process. | "CT revealed a large soft tissue mass... that had caused destruction of the left maxillary ethmoid sinus, the sphenoid sinuses and the left nasal cavity, and extended intra‑cranially..."

General examination was within normal limits; no cutaneous lesions, oral thrush, hepatosplenomegaly, or lymphadenopathy were noted. Pulmonary tuberculosis was not evident clinically or radiologically.

case_prompt:
An eight‑year‑old girl presented with painful blisters on the skin of 40 days duration. She also had fever with chills, cough, dyspnoea, and severe headache for the past one month. She had suffered from chickenpox four months back, which resolved uneventfully. She was anemic and had stunted growth. Chest examination revealed bilateral crepitations. She also had neck stiffness.

Multiple painful and tender vesicles and bullae of varying size were seen all over the body, predominantly over the acral areas. Few bullae were hemorrhagic. Warty excrescences were seen overlying some blisters. Oral erosions were noted. The skin lesions started as tiny vesicles, which evolved into larger bullae, some hemorrhagic, then progressed to form warty excrescences, and finally resolved with varioliform scars. New lesions continued to appear as older ones healed. There was no dermatomal grouping of the lesions.

Tzanck smear from the blisters showed multinucleated giant cells. Histopathology of the early vesicle revealed typical features of varicella blister, and that of late warty lesions showed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and papillomatosis without the classical features of viral blister.

Chest x‑ray showed pneumonitis. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed lymphocytosis. Complete hemogram was normal except for dimorphic anemia. Blood VDRL was nonreactive. Serum IgG and IgM for HSV‑1 and HSV‑2 were negative. Serum IgM for VZV was negative, but IgG for VZV was positive in very high titre.

2. HSV infection excluded by serology. | "Serum IgG and IgM for HSV‑1 and HSV‑2 were negative."
3. Primary VZV infection excluded; high IgG with negative IgM indicated past infection/reactivation. | "Serum IgM for VZV was negative, but IgG for VZV was positive in very high titre."
4. Multinucleated giant cells on Tzanck smear supported a herpes‑virus etiology rather than bacterial infection. | "Tzanck smear from the blisters showed multinucleated giant cells."
5. Systemic involvement (pneumonitis, meningitis) suggested disseminated viral infection in an immunocompromised host. | "Chest x‑ray showed pneumonitis, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed lymphocytosis."
6. HIV infection confirmed serologically. | "ELISA for HIV was done, which turned out to be positive. Western blot for HIV was also positive."

case_analysis:

Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished Penicillium marneffei infection from bacterial sepsis, mycobacterial disease, cryptococcosis, and other fungal pathogens by (a) lack of response to antibiotics, (b) negative bacterial and mycobacterial cultures, (c) negative serum cryptococcal antigen, and (d) characteristic yeast morphology (thin‑walled, central septation) on PAS/GMS stains of skin biopsy.
case_prompt:
A 14‑year‑old Thai girl presented to a provincial hospital with a 4‑week history of fever, oral ulcers, disseminated papular skin lesions, and polyarticular pain. Twelve weeks earlier she had been diagnosed with perinatal HIV infection after presenting with disseminated herpes zoster infection and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia; her CD4+ count at that time was 7.2% (39 cells/mm³). She was started on fixed‑dose combination antiretroviral therapy (stavudine, lamivudine, nevirapine) twice daily and on trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis. Eight weeks after ART initiation she developed the current symptoms, which did not improve with multiple oral antibiotics, prompting referral to Chiang Mai University Hospital.

On admission she was febrile (high‑grade temperature). Examination revealed painful ulcerated lesions on the lips and oral mucosa, and generalized non‑pruritic erythematous papules and nodules with central umbilication over the face, trunk, and extremities. Multiple joints (right shoulder, wrist, metacarpophalangeal joints, knees, ankles) were swollen, warm, and tender. No lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly was noted. Laboratory testing showed CD4+ count of 11% (51 cells/mm³) and plasma HIV‑RNA < 50 copies/mL. Chest radiograph was normal; wrist and ankle radiographs demonstrated multiple round radiolucent bone defects. Skin biopsy revealed necrotizing histiocytic granulomas with neutrophilic infiltration; PAS and Grocott methenamine silver stains demonstrated numerous intracellular and extracellular thin‑walled yeast cells with central septation. Bone marrow aspirate showed no organisms. Hemoculture, bone‑marrow culture, and skin culture did not isolate P. marneffei or any other fungus. Blood cultures for mycobacteria were negative, and serum cryptococcal antigen was negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial infection considered but deemed unlikely because the fever, skin lesions, and joint pain persisted despite multiple oral antibiotics. | "The symptoms did not respond to many kinds of oral antibiotics."
2. Mycobacterial infection entertained; however, blood mycobacterial cultures were negative, arguing against disseminated tuberculosis or atypical mycobacteria. | "Blood was also sent for mycobacterial culture with negative results."
3. Cryptococcosis evaluated; serum cryptococcal antigen testing was negative, making cryptococcal disease unlikely. | "Serum cryptococcal antigen was negative."
4. Other opportunistic fungal infections considered; however, hemoculture, bone‑marrow culture, and skin culture did not grow any fungus, decreasing the probability of other systemic mycoses. | "The hemoculture, bone marrow culture, and skin culture revealed no evidence of P. marneffei or other fungus."
5. The presence of characteristic intracellular and extracellular thin‑walled yeast cells with central septation on PAS/GMS staining of skin tissue strongly supports Penicillium marneffei infection. | "tissue sections ... revealed numerous intracellular and extracellular, round to oval, elongated, thin‑walled yeast cells with central septation."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case resolves to immune reconstitution disease (IRD), which is not on the 21 SELECTED diseases list. HIV/AIDS is present as a known past diagnosis, but the mystery to be solved is IRD → OUT_OF_SCOPE.
2. Breakpoint: Include all information up to the mycobacterial culture result that identifies Mycobacterium avium complex, and the therapeutic response (prednisone, aspiration), but stop before the authors explicitly state “the diagnosis was IRD.” This provides sufficient clinical, laboratory, and radiologic data for learners to infer IRD without revealing it.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors contrasted three possibilities (drug‑resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis, infection with MOTT/MAC, and IRD) and used culture results, drug‑sensitivity, CD4 trend, and response to steroids to favor IRD over a simple MAC infection or resistant TB.
case_prompt:
A 35‑year‑old man presented with a 5‑6‑day history of acute increase in bilateral neck swelling, neck pain, fever, and weight loss. He first noticed multiple small neck swellings two months earlier and had not sought treatment. He was subsequently hospitalized for altered sensorium; HIV serology was positive and fine‑needle aspiration cytology of a neck node suggested tuberculosis. CD4 count was 48 cells/mm³. Brain MRI was normal. He was started on Category 1 antitubercular therapy (2 HREZ + 4 HR) under the RNTCP, antiretroviral therapy (3TC + d4T + EFV), and prophylaxis with trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole and fluconazole for Pneumocystis and fungal infections. He reported symptomatic improvement, although the size and number of neck swellings did not appreciably change.

Two months later he experienced an acute aggravation of symptoms with a one‑week history of further increase in swelling size. Examination revealed multiple discrete, firm, mobile, tender, non‑warm, non‑reducible, non‑pulsatile lymph nodes on both sides of the neck, involving all cervical groups, ranging from 2 to 12 cm. No other peripheral lymphadenopathy was noted. Neck ultrasonography showed multiple bilateral enlarged conglomerated nodes in levels 2‑5. Chest radiograph was normal and sputum smears for acid‑fast bacilli were negative. CD4 count had risen to 100 cells/mm³.

Given the lack of response to antitubercular therapy and ART, the differential considered included infection with drug‑resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis, infection by nontuberculous mycobacteria (MOTT), and immune reconstitution disease (IRD). Prednisolone 25 mg daily was added and tapered over three weeks, after which the swellings softened, the overlying skin became tense and red, and approximately 100 cc of pus was aspirated and sent for mycobacterial culture and sensitivity. Culture (BACTEC/L‑J) suggested Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) based on NAP reaction and morphology, and sensitivity testing showed susceptibility to all first‑line drugs.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Drug‑resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis considered because the patient was on standard ATT yet lymphadenitis progressed. | "considering the fact that in spite of treatment with ATT+ART, the patient had presented with increase in size of neck swelling, we were considering a differential diagnosis of infection with drug‑resistant bacilli..."
2. Infection with nontuberculous mycobacteria (MOTT/MAC) considered due to persistent lymphadenitis despite ATT and the emergence of pus. | "we were considering a differential diagnosis of ... infection by MOTT..."
3. Immune reconstitution disease (IRD) considered because the patient’s CD4 count rose from 48 to 100 cells/mm³ after ART, coinciding with worsening of a pre‑existing mycobacterial lesion. | "The patient had a diagnosis of AIDS, he was on antiretroviral therapy with increase in CD4 count and worsening of preexisting disease; hence, the diagnosis was IRD."
4. Mycobacterial culture confirming MAC supported the MOTT hypothesis but did not explain the paradoxical clinical worsening after immune recovery. | "AFB culture report ... was suggestive of M. avium complex (MAC)..."
5. Sensitivity of MAC to first‑line drugs argued against drug‑resistant TB as the cause of progression. | "AFB culture and sensitivity report showed sensitive to all first line drugs."
6. Clinical improvement after adding corticosteroids (prednisone) favored an inflammatory IRD process rather than uncontrolled infection. | "The swelling gradually became soft; skin over swelling became tense and red."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient was ultimately diagnosed with syphilis (a disease on the 21 SELECTED list). The case provides sufficient clinical, imaging, and serologic data to deduce this diagnosis, so syphilis is the primary target diagnosis.  
2. Best Breakpoint: Present the case up to the point where optic perineuritis is suspected and secondary causes are being investigated, but stop before revealing the positive syphilis serology (RPR, FTA‑ABS). This gives students enough history, exam, lumbar puncture, and MRI findings to generate a differential that includes papilledema, optic neuritis, and optic perineuritis, while preserving the mystery of the underlying infection.  
3. Author's Analytic Distinctions: The authors ruled out papilledema with normal MRI/MRV and normal opening pressure; they noted asymmetric disc edema, a trace afferent pupillary defect, and a specific pattern of RNFL thickening. Orbit MRI showed optic nerve sheath fluid and enhancement, supporting optic perineuritis. They then pursued secondary infectious causes, obtaining syphilis serology, which confirmed the diagnosis.
case_prompt:
A 41‑year‑old man was referred for blurred disc margins and possible papilledema noted by his optometrist. He was visually asymptomatic. One month earlier he had been evaluated in a hematology‑oncology clinic for swollen groin lymph nodes that were described as reactive, with no identified cause. He denied prior sexually transmitted diseases, genital lesions, penile discharge, or rash.

On ophthalmic examination, visual acuity was 20/25+ in the right eye and 20/20‑ in the left eye. Ishihara color testing was 11/11 in both eyes. A trace afferent pupillary defect was present in the left eye. Intraocular pressures were 12 mm Hg (right) and 18 mm Hg (left). Fundoscopy revealed asymmetric disc edema, more pronounced in the left eye. Optical coherence tomography showed a retinal nerve fiber layer average thickness of 188 µm in the left eye with concentric circumferential elevation and 118 µm in the right eye with inferonasal elevation.

Brain MRI and MRV with and without contrast were unremarkable, showing no mass lesions or venous occlusion. Lumbar puncture demonstrated a normal opening pressure of 18 cm H₂O, normal protein and glucose, and 72 white cells/mm³, predominantly lymphocytes.

Within two weeks he developed headaches and eye pain, especially on bending over. Repeat examination showed worsening disc edema in the right eye and enlargement of the blind spot on visual‑field testing. Because the presentation was not consistent with papilledema, an orbit MRI was obtained, which demonstrated increased optic‑nerve sheath fluid, especially posterior to the globes, and contrast enhancement of the optic‑nerve sheaths.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Papilledema considered but deemed unlikely | "Because his presentation was not consistent with papilledema..."
2. Idiopathic optic neuritis considered given unilateral visual changes, but lack of typical pain pattern and MRI findings made it less likely | "He had asymmetric disc edema, greater in the left eye... MRI and MRV were unremarkable..."
3. Optic perineuritis suggested by imaging findings of optic‑nerve sheath fluid and enhancement | "Orbit MRI ... showed increased optic nerve sheath fluid... and contrast enhancement of the optic nerve sheaths."
4. Secondary infectious/inflammatory causes explored, leading to serologic testing for syphilis | "Since the clinical and imaging findings appeared consistent with optic perineuritis, he was tested for secondary causes. He tested positive for syphilis..."
5. HIV infection evaluated as a common co‑factor for neurosyphilis, but testing was negative | "HIV testing was negative."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case’s definitive diagnosis is cutaneous cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection, which is on the 21 SELECTED diseases list (cytomegalovirus).

Ideal Breakpoint: End the presentation just after the statement that an excisional skin‑biopsy was performed and sent for pathology (“An excisional biopsy of one of the skin lesions from the upper thigh was obtained and sent for pathological examination.”). This provides the clinical picture, risk factors, and initial work‑up without revealing the histopathologic findings that confirm CMV.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished CMV infection from bacterial colonization (dense neutrophilic crust with bacteria), from fungal infection (negative PAS stain), and from mycobacterial infection (negative acid‑fast stain). Definitive proof came from characteristic viral nuclear inclusions and a positive CMV immunostain, followed by clinical response to anti‑CMV therapy.
case_prompt: A 47‑year‑old man, HIV‑negative, with a recent diagnosis of central nervous system lymphoma presented with perianal skin lesions and non‑bloody diarrhea. The lesions began as nodules that progressed to roughened plaques, sometimes ulcerating, appearing eight weeks before admission. They were multiple, scattered in the perianal area and upper thighs bilaterally, up to three centimeters in diameter. A distinct irregularly bordered lesion over the sacrum was consistent with a decubitus ulcer. Six weeks earlier he had been diagnosed with a CNS lymphoma after presenting with lower‑extremity weakness, saddle anesthesia, and fecal incontinence; imaging revealed an L1‑L2 intramedullary spinal mass, which was surgically resected and treated with high‑dose dexamethasone and radiation. He also had a right temporal lobe mass resected, pathology showing B‑cell lymphoma with T‑cell infiltration. He had no other significant past medical history or immunocompromising condition. Persistent lower‑extremity weakness confined him to bed. Because of ongoing fecal incontinence and a non‑healing sacral ulcer, he underwent a diverting colostomy. Two weeks before presentation his stools became more liquid and more frequent, without abdominal pain. The perianal lesions were painless, although sensation remained diminished from the prior spinal compression. He was on a dexamethasone taper and was transferred for further chemotherapy evaluation. Laboratory studies showed a normocytic anemia and an elevated alkaline phosphatase. An excisional biopsy of one of the skin lesions from the upper thigh was obtained and sent for pathological examination.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial colonization vs true infection – The biopsy showed a dense neutrophilic crust with numerous bacteria, suggesting a bacterial component, but there was no clinical improvement without antiviral therapy, and the lesions were atypical for common bacterial skin infections. | "A dense neutrophilic crust with numerous bacteria distributed in varying sized aggregates..."
2. Fungal infection – Periodic acid‑Schiff staining was performed to detect fungi; the stain was negative, making a fungal etiology unlikely. | "Stains with periodic acid‑Schiff ... were negative."
3. Mycobacterial infection – Acid‑fast bacilli staining was performed to assess for mycobacterial disease; the stain was negative, ruling out cutaneous tuberculosis or atypical mycobacteria. | "...and for acid‑fast bacilli were negative."
4. Cytomegalovirus infection – Endothelial cells contained magenta‑colored nuclear inclusions characteristic of CMV, and immunostaining confirmed CMV, establishing cutaneous CMV as the diagnosis. | "Some endothelial cells contained magenta‑colored nuclear inclusions consistent with cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection which was confirmed by a positive CMV immunostain."
5. Clinical response to anti‑CMV therapy – The patient's diarrhea resolved within two weeks and skin lesions healed after ganciclovir treatment, supporting CMV as the pathogenic agent. | "The diarrhea resolved within two weeks, and the skin lesions had completely healed at the time of switch to valganciclovir."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case’s final diagnosis is primary effusion lymphoma, which is not among the 21 SELECTED diseases; therefore it is classified as OUT_OF_SCOPE.
2. Best Breakpoint: End the presentation just before the sentence that declares the final diagnosis (“The final diagnosis … was indicative of primary effusion lymphoma…”). Include clinical presentation, laboratory values, imaging, cytology, immunocytochemistry panel, and molecular studies, but omit the concluding diagnostic statement.
3. Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished primary effusion lymphoma from carcinoma, melanoma, myeloid sarcoma, other B‑cell or T‑cell lymphomas, and EBV‑associated lymphoproliferations by (a) lack of solid peritoneal tumor on imaging, (b) cytologic features of large atypical cells in effusion, (c) extensive immunophenotypic panel (AE1/AE3, EMA, Melan A, MPO, etc.) to exclude non‑lymphoid neoplasms, (d) negative EBV‑EBER, (e) HHV‑8 (LANA‑1) positivity, and (f) clonality assays for IgH and TCR genes.
case_prompt:
The patient was an 88‑year‑old man of Mediterranean descent with a history of cirrhosis and chronic hepatitis B infection. He presented to clinic with a one‑month history of generalized weakness and fatigue. Physical examination showed icteric skin and sclera and abdominal distention due to ascites; no hepatosplenomegaly was appreciated.

Laboratory studies revealed macrocytic anemia (Hb 11.6 g/dL, MCV 108 fL), thrombocytopenia (platelets 113 × 10³/µL), and a normal white‑cell count (4.0 × 10³/µL). Serum chemistry showed elevated glucose (105 mg/dL), urea 32 mg/dL, creatinine 0.88 mg/dL, AST 223 U/L, ALT 155 U/L, total bilirubin 7.0 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 3.0 mg/dL, γ‑GT 50 U/L, ALP 165 U/L, LDH 241 U/L, total protein 7.4 g/dL, albumin 2.1 g/dL, CK 183 U/L. Ascitic fluid analysis demonstrated glucose 111 mg/dL, protein 2.2 g/dL, albumin 0.65 g/dL, LDH 1590 U/L, cholesterol 7 mg/dL, triglycerides 16 mg/dL.

Abdominal ultrasonography showed a cirrhotic liver with massive ascites. Contrast‑enhanced CT confirmed the ascites but showed no peritoneal implants or pathological lymphadenopathy.

Paracentesis yielded 800 mL of fluid that was processed for cytology. Thin‑Prep smears contained abundant large malignant cells with moderate basophilic cytoplasm, mostly single nuclei but occasional bi‑/multinucleated forms, coarse chromatin, irregular nuclear contours, prominent nucleoli, high mitotic activity, abnormal mitoses, and numerous apoptotic bodies.

Immunocytochemistry on cell‑block sections employed a broad panel (AE1/AE3, EMA, Vimentin, Melan A, MPO, Fascin, Perforin, Bcl‑6, CD3, CD4, CD5, CD8, CD10, CD15, CD20, CD30, CD34, CD43, CD45, CD45RO, CD138, ALK‑1, TIA‑1, LMP‑1, HHV‑8 LANA‑1). EBV infection was excluded by EBER in‑situ hybridization. Hepatitis B virus DNA was detected. PCR assays for immunoglobulin heavy‑chain (IgH) and T‑cell receptor gamma (TCR‑G) gene rearrangements were performed.

Bone‑marrow aspirate showed no evidence of lymphoma. Serology was positive for HBsAg, anti‑HBc IgG, HBeAg and negative for anti‑HBe, anti‑HBs, anti‑HCV, and anti‑HIV.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Large atypical cells in ascitic fluid suggest a malignant effusion, raising lymphoma versus metastatic carcinoma as primary considerations. | "The Thin Prep material consisted of abundant large‑sized malignant cells…arranged singly…high mitotic activity…" 
2. Absence of peritoneal masses or implants on CT argues against peritoneal carcinomatosis. | "CT… confirmed the ascites, although with no visible peritoneal implants…no pathological lymphadenopathy was detected."
3. Negative epithelial (AE1/AE3, EMA) and melanocytic (Melan A) markers exclude carcinoma and melanoma as sources of the malignant cells. | "The primary antibodies used were: AE1/AE3, EMA, … Melan A…"
4. Lack of myeloid marker (MPO) positivity rules out myeloid sarcoma. | "MPO" is listed among the antibodies investigated.
5. EBV‑encoded RNA (EBER) hybridization was negative, eliminating EBV‑associated lymphomas. | "A possible Epstein‑Barr virus (EBV) infection was excluded using the EBV‑encoded RNA (EBER) in situ hybridization test."
6. Detection of HHV‑8 LANA‑1 expression supports a HHV‑8‑associated lymphoproliferative disorder characteristic of primary effusion lymphoma. | "HHV‑8 (Latent Nuclear Antigen‑1; LANA‑1) were also investigated."
7. Clonal IgH gene rearrangement (and/or TCR‑G) indicates a clonal lymphoid proliferation, favoring lymphoma over reactive effusion. | "PCR… to detect any clonal rearrangement of the immunoglobulin heavy chain gene (IgH)… clonal T‑cell Receptor Gamma chain gene rearrangements were evaluated."
8. Bone‑marrow without lymphoma involvement indicates a primary effusion lymphoma confined to serous cavity rather than systemic disease. | "A bone‑marrow aspirate showed no evidence of lymphoma."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient’s clinical picture, serology (VDRL 1:128), and characteristic skin‑biopsy findings point to secondary syphilis, which is on the SELECTED diseases list. HIV infection is also present but already known; the mystery to be solved is syphilis.
2. Breakpoint: Present the case up to the initial laboratory and biopsy results, stopping before the authors describe initiating penicillin therapy or reporting treatment response. This includes chief complaint, history, physical exam, VDRL/HIV serology, CSF analysis, culture, and skin‑biopsy description, allowing the learner to deduce secondary syphilis without a spoiler.
3. Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished syphilis from primary syphilis (no prior genital chancre), chancroid (partner’s disease, different organism), pure bacterial infection (S. aureus culture but systemic features and serology point to syphilis), neurosyphilis (negative CSF VDRL and normal CSF), and HIV‑related dermatoses (biopsy showing plasma‑cell infiltrate rather than Kaposi spindle cells).
case_prompt:
A 30‑year‑old housewife presented with multiple, large, ulcerative lesions all over the body of 1‑month duration. She denied any history of genital lesions before the onset of the skin lesions. Concomitant symptoms of headache, fever, myalgia and leucorrhea were present. She reported two spontaneous miscarriages for which she had not taken treatment and had not had sexual contact with her husband for 6 months. Her husband, a lorry driver, had multiple extra‑ and premarital contacts, was diagnosed HIV‑positive 2 years ago, was on antiretroviral therapy, and was currently being treated for chancroid due to numerous genital ulcers.

On examination the patient was febrile. Cutaneous examination revealed multiple ulcerative, crusted lesions on the face and extremities, erosions on the lips and genital mucosa, and annular lesions with central pigmentation on the palms and soles. The axillary, epitrochlear and inguinal lymph nodes were enlarged, tender and rubbery. Initial laboratory investigations showed leukocytosis with polymorph predominance and an elevated ESR. VDRL was reactive (1:128 dilution) and HIV‑1 ELISA was positive; Western blot for p24 antigen was also positive. Pus culture from the ulcerated lesions grew Staphylococcus aureus highly sensitive to newer quinolones. CSF analysis demonstrated no abnormal intracranial pressure, pleocytosis, or elevated protein, and CSF VDRL was non‑reactive. Skin biopsy of the rupioid lesions showed pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia with ulceration, dense mid‑dermal lymphocytic infiltrate, and plasma‑cell infiltrate with obliterative vasculitis.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Secondary syphilis most likely given high‑titer reactive VDRL, characteristic palm‑sole lesions, tender rubbery lymphadenopathy, and plasma‑cell rich vasculitic biopsy pattern | "VDRL was reactive (1:128 dilution) ... Skin biopsy ... plasma cell infiltrate with obliterative vasculitis."
2. Primary syphilis excluded because the patient had no preceding genital chancre | "She did not give any history of genital lesions before the onset of skin lesions."
3. Chancroid considered unlikely as the patient’s lesions were widespread ulcerative crusted lesions rather than typical painful genital ulcers, and no Haemophilus ducreyi was isolated | "Her husband ... was being treated for chancroid" and "Pus culture ... grew Staphylococcus aureus."
4. Pure bacterial infection (S. aureus) insufficient to explain systemic features and serology; culture reflects secondary colonization | "Pus culture from the ulcerated lesions grew Staphylococcus aureus which was highly sensitive to newer quinolones."
5. Neurosyphilis ruled out by normal CSF parameters and non‑reactive CSF VDRL despite headache and fever | "CSF analysis showed no abnormalities ... CSF VDRL was nonreactive."
6. HIV‑related opportunistic skin disorders (e.g., Kaposi sarcoma) unlikely because biopsy demonstrated plasma‑cell infiltrate rather than spindle‑cell vascular proliferation | "Skin biopsy ... plasma cell infiltrate with obliterative vasculitis."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient’s illness is due to visceral leishmaniasis, which is included in the 21 SELECTED diseases list (leishmaniasis). The case also describes Schistosoma mansoni infection, but the primary mystery to be solved is the persistent Leishmania infection; therefore the target diagnosis is leishmaniasis.
2. Breakpoint: Include all data up to the second hospital admission where stool microscopy revealed S. mansoni eggs, the CT scan findings, the reactive bone‑marrow aspirate, and the laboratory abnormalities (anemia, hypoalbuminemia, high ESR, low folate/iron). Exclude the later real‑time qPCR results, the second upper‑GI endoscopy showing persistent amastigotes, and the subsequent amphotericin B deoxycholate treatment. This provides enough clues (previous proven Leishmania infection, relapse after liposomal amphotericin B, lack of response to praziquantel) for the learner to deduce refractory visceral leishmaniasis.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors confirmed Leishmania initially by serology, bone‑marrow and duodenal biopsy, and later by PCR on blood and marrow. They ruled out other etiologies by negative anti‑HIV and anti‑Trypanosoma cruzi serologies, lack of endoscopic ulceration, and failure of schistosomiasis treatment to improve symptoms. Persistence of amastigotes on repeat duodenal biopsy and positive PCR supported relapse, while the absence of Leishmania in the second marrow aspirate indicated low parasite burden rather than cure.
case_prompt: A 42‑year‑old man presented with a six‑month history of non‑bloody diarrhea accompanied by fever, splenomegaly, and pancytopenia. Serologic testing for Leishmania was positive (indirect immunofluorescence titer 1:640 and rapid test k39). Diagnosis of visceral leishmaniasis was confirmed by identification of amastigotes in bone‑marrow aspirate smears. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed duodenal erosions with fibrin, enanthema, thickened folds, and small whitish spots; duodenal biopsy showed villous enlargement with histiocytes packed with intracytoplasmic round structures consistent with Leishmania amastigotes. He received liposomal amphotericin B 4 mg/kg for 5 days, resulting in improvement of visceromegaly, fever, and normalization of white‑blood‑cell and platelet counts. However, diarrhea and anemia persisted, and his condition deteriorated. Four months later he was readmitted with worsening diarrhea, dehydration, metabolic acidosis, and electrolyte imbalance. Laboratory studies showed normochromic normocytic anemia, profound hypoalbuminemia (1.9 g/dL), ESR 120 mm/h, low serum folic acid and iron. Both vitamins were replaced and nutritional support started. Stool microscopy identified eggs of Schistosoma mansoni; he was treated with praziquantel 60 mg/kg. After four weeks the diarrhea remained unchanged, with ongoing anorexia and weight loss. Abdominal CT demonstrated mild splenomegaly, no lymphadenopathy, normal liver size, and mild dilatation of colonic loops. A repeat bone‑marrow aspiration showed only reactive changes and no Leishmania amastigotes. Lymphocyte subsets were TCD4⁺ 539/mm³, TCD8⁺ 503/mm³, TCD3⁺ 1,094/mm³. Colonoscopy was normal. Tests for anti‑Trypanosoma cruzi antibodies and HIV were negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:

case_prompt:
A 61‑year‑old woman with well‑controlled diabetes presented in March 2009 with a two‑week history of ocular pain and visual loss in the left eye. She had been diagnosed with proliferative diabetic retinopathy in both eyes and cystoid macular edema of the left eye, for which she received an intravitreal bevacizumab injection three weeks earlier and panretinal photocoagulation two weeks earlier. Post‑procedure, intraocular pressure in the left eye was managed with an anti‑glaucoma medication.

On examination, the left eye visual acuity was hand motion only. Slit‑lamp examination revealed 4+ cells and hyphema in the anterior chamber with iris neovascularization. Funduscopy showed dense vitritis and retinal vascular obliteration. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated delayed arterial filling suggestive of ocular ischemia, while carotid Doppler sonography was normal, making ocular ischemic syndrome unlikely. The right eye showed only diabetic retinopathy and laser scars.

Because dense vitritis limited further assessment, a pars plana vitrectomy was performed. Intraoperatively, necrotizing retinitis with dense retinal whitening and hemorrhage along the inferotemporal vascular arcade was observed, raising suspicion for an infectious retinitis. Undiluted vitreous was collected for polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing for herpes simplex virus (HSV), varicella‑zoster virus (VZV), and cytomegalovirus (CMV), as well as for bacterial and fungal stains and cultures.

Baseline laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count, normal CD4 (522 cells/µL) and CD8 (275 cells/µL) counts, and negative HIV antigen/antibody testing. Serum CMV IgG was positive (244.5 AU/mL) with negative IgM. The CMV antigenemia assay was positive (9/20,000 cells). No other systemic manifestations of CMV infection were present.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Infectious necrotizing retinitis warranted evaluation for viral etiologies; CMV is a known cause of such retinal lesions. | "During the vitrectomy, necrotizing retinitis with dense retinal whitening and hemorrhage ... was observed, suggestive of infectious retinitis."
2. HSV and VZV retinitis were considered because they can produce similar necrotizing retinal findings; PCR for HSV and VZV was performed to exclude them. | "PCR; Q‑CMV real time complete kit ... and cultured for herpes simplex virus (HSV), varicellar zoster virus (VZV), and CMV."
3. Bacterial and fungal endophthalmitis were considered given the dense vitritis; vitreous staining and cultures were obtained to rule them out. | "To rule out other etiologies of infectious retinitis, vitreous was also analyzed by staining and culture for bacteria and fungus."
4. Ocular ischemic syndrome was a differential because of retinal vascular obliteration and delayed arterial filling; carotid Doppler sonography was normal, decreasing its likelihood. | "No abnormal findings were observed in carotid Doppler sonography which was performed to rule out ocular ischemic syndrome."
5. HIV‑associated CMV retinitis was ruled out by normal CD4 counts and negative HIV testing, confirming the patient’s immunocompetent status. | "Blood tests did not show any immune dysfunction ... HIV antigen and antibodies were negative."
6. Systemic CMV disease was unlikely despite a positive CMV antigenemia because the patient lacked other clinical manifestations; this focused suspicion on ocular‑limited CMV infection. | "There were no other clinical manifestations of CMV infection except retinitis."
7. Final confirmation came from detection of CMV DNA in the vitreous by PCR, establishing CMV retinitis as the cause. | "PCR for CMV DNA was positive in the vitreous and negative in peripheral blood, confirming the diagnosis as CMV retinitis."
8. Negative results for HSV, VZV, bacterial, and fungal studies further supported CMV as the sole pathogen. | "The others including HSV and VZV were negative in the vitreous and blood. Neither bacteria nor fungus were observed by staining and culture."

Blood tests demonstrated neutropenia (0.9 × 10⁹/L) with a normal lymphocyte count (1.2 × 10⁹/L); HIV serology was negative. The most likely diagnoses were CMV retinitis or intraocular non‑Hodgkin’s lymphoma. A pars plana vitrectomy was planned for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes.

Intraocular lymphoma considered due to the patient’s history of follicular lymphoma and the presence of vitreous haze and atypical cells in the eye, but was ultimately excluded after PCR of vitreous fluid confirmed CMV infection, leading the authors to avoid intravitreal methotrexate: “PCR testing confirmed infectious uveitis of cytomegalovirus aetiology. A 34‑year‑old man was admitted with massive shallow ulcers of both lower extremities, fever of 39 °C and severe pain. One year earlier he had been diagnosed with nephrotic syndrome due to minimal‑change disease and treated with prednisolone and furosemide; proteinuria resolved but recurred three months after tapering steroids. On examination the inner thighs showed massive necrotic superficial ulcerations with surrounding erythema, each about 20 cm in diameter; the forearms had several reddish indurations. Blood culture grew coagulase‑negative staphylococci and repeat chest X‑ray now showed ground‑glass opacities in both perihilar regions. Neurological examination showed normal orientation, pupillary light reaction, fundoscopy, muscle tone, reflexes, and somatic sensation; there was a mild deviation of the mouth and tongue to the left on protrusion. At week 10 TDF‑FTC was temporarily withheld; she received oral Neurorubine (vitamins B1, B6, B12) for 2 weeks and became symptom‑free within 2 weeks.

She restarted the study drug at week 12, and 1 month later reported posture‑dependent numbness of the upper limbs that occurred while bending down and resolved when upright. No weakness or tremor recurred. Neurological exam was again normal. Drug levels at week 24 reflected low adherence.

At week 25 the study drug was withdrawn pending neurologic work‑up. At week 28 she reported a single dose of an oral traditional herbal medicine of unknown composition.
