Surgical excisional biopsy was performed. Hematoxylin‑eosin staining demonstrated necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with small, round‑oval budding yeast forms with narrow‑based budding. Grocott methenamine silver staining indicated a deep fungal infection, with the differential list of histoplasmosis, blastomycosis, sporotrichosis, and coccidioidomycosis. The organisms measured 2–4 µm, were ovoid, GMS‑positive, and displayed single narrow‑based buds, features more consistent with Histoplasma capsulatum than with the other fungi.

Serum antigen and antibody studies were negative for histoplasmosis and blastomycosis, and a chest radiograph showed no pulmonary abnormalities.

Epidemiologic history revealed residence along a Mississippi River tributary, a long‑standing bat colony in the attic with guano and urine contamination, and prior exposure to rose gardening, travel to mountainous Mexico, and residence in southwestern Wisconsin—exposures considered low risk for sporotrichosis, coccidioidomycosis, and blastomycosis, respectively.

Empiric antibiotics (vancomycin and piperacillin‑tazobactam) were started. The morphological differential diagnosis included dimorphic fungi and protozoa such as Leishmania species, Candida glabrata, and Blastomyces dermatitidis. Grocott‑methenamine silver staining of the marrow core demonstrated additional histiocytes packed with multiple yeast forms exhibiting narrow‑based budding. Rare hemophagocytes were also identified.

On arrival he was afebrile (98.2 °F), tachycardic (HR 110 bpm), tachypneic (RR 22/min) with stable blood pressure. Physical exam showed a malnourished man in distress; the abdomen was diffusely tender with guarding and rigidity in all quadrants.

case_prompt:
A 39‑year‑old man presented with a 3‑month history of skin lesions involving the face, neck, and extremities. He had been diagnosed HIV‑positive one month earlier and started on antiretroviral therapy (abacavir 300 mg bid, lamivudine 300 mg bid, efavirenz 600 mg daily) because of impaired renal function/pre‑renal failure; hydration improved his renal parameters. Two weeks after the skin lesions appeared, he developed a sore throat and hoarseness.  

On examination there were multiple translucent, clustered, umbilicated papules and nodules with necrotic centres in the centrofacial region and neck, plus verrucous plaques and nodules on the ears and upper limbs. Chest X‑ray was normal, without pulmonary or mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Fibre‑optic laryngoscopy showed supraglottitis with ulceration of the epiglottic lingual surface.  

Laboratory studies revealed an infiltrative pattern of liver enzyme elevation (AST 63 U/L, ALT 70 U/L, ALP 219 U/L, γ‑GT 291 U/L). Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated an enlarged liver with abnormal parenchyma; kidneys and the remainder of the abdomen were unremarkable. The initial CD4⁺ count prior to antiretroviral initiation was 2 cells/µL with an HIV viral load >1 million copies/mL; eight weeks later the CD4⁺ count rose to 124 cells/µL and the viral load fell to <20 copies/mL. Urinalysis and urine Histoplasma antigen test were negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Disseminated fungal infection suspected from necrotising granulomatous inflammation in skin and visceral tissues | "Histology of the liver, larynx and sections of the skin demonstrated pandermal necrotising granulomatous inflammation."
2. Severe immunosuppression (CD4 = 2 cells/µL, high HIV viral load) predisposes to opportunistic infections such as Histoplasma | "The initial CD4 count performed prior to the commencement of antiretrovirals was 2 cells/microL with a viral load greater than one million copies/mL."
3. Negative urine Histoplasma antigen reduces but does not exclude disseminated histoplasmosis | "Urinalysis and urine histoplasma antigen test were negative."
4. Silver and PAS stains visualized characteristic narrow‑neck budding yeasts consistent with Histoplasma capsulatum | "Grocott‑Gomori methenamine silver and PAS stains revealed a relative paucity of intracellular oval, narrow‑neck budding fungal organisms morphologically in keeping with Histoplasma capsulatum var. capsulatum."
5. Positive fungal cultures from liver, epiglottic ulcer, and skin definitively confirmed the organism | "Fungal culture of liver, epiglottis ulcer and skin confirmed the diagnosis of histoplasmosis."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient’s eventual definitive diagnosis was Histoplasma capsulatum infection, which is included in the 21 SELECTED diseases list (histoplasmosis). Hence, the target diagnosis is histoplasmosis (SELECTED).
2. Ideal Breakpoint: Include all clinical data, imaging, initial labs, bronchoscopy findings, and serologic results up to the point where empiric liposomal amphotericin B was started (i.e., before the culture grew Histoplasma). This provides enough information (miliary pattern, granulomatous inflammation, exposure history, negative TB/viral/fungal antigen tests, positive Coccidioides serology) for learners to generate a differential and arrive at the correct diagnosis without revealing the definitive culture result.
3. Author's Analytic Distinctions: The authors ruled out tuberculosis (negative NAAT, negative IGRA, smear‑negative AFB), invasive aspergillosis (negative galactomannan, negative culture, elevated Aspergillus IgG but not diagnostic), other endemic fungi (negative Histoplasma antigen, cryptococcal antigen, and coccidioidomycosis serology interpreted as likely cross‑reaction), and Pneumocystis pneumonia (negative DFA). Definitive diagnosis rested on tissue culture and DNA probe confirming Histoplasma capsulatum.
case_prompt:
A 52‑year‑old man with rheumatoid arthritis (on weekly methotrexate, daily hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine, and past rituximab) presented to the emergency department with one week of fevers, chills, headache, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, non‑productive cough, fatigue, and a month of night sweats. He was originally from Mexico, has lived in the United States >40 years, and works as a truck driver with routes through the Midwest; one month prior he unloaded his truck in Kansas City during a rainstorm and subsequently developed night sweats and cough. On admission he was afebrile, oxygen saturation 85 % on room air, requiring 2–3 L/min supplemental O₂. Labs showed normal white count; AST 74 U/L, ALT 60 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 170 U/L. Abdominal ultrasound revealed mild hepatosplenomegaly. Chest X‑ray demonstrated diffuse reticulonodular densities with hilar lymphadenopathy. He received ceftriaxone and azithromycin, then empiric ceftriaxone, doxycycline, and metronidazole for presumed community‑acquired pneumonia. Negative studies included respiratory viral PCR, Histoplasma urine antigen, Streptococcus pneumoniae urine antigen, Legionella urine antigen, HIV 4th‑generation assay, acute hepatitis panel, serum HSV PCR, serum CMV PCR, QuantiFERON‑TB Gold, and sputum PJP DFA. Rheumatology advised continuation of hydroxychloroquine and holding methotrexate and sulfasalazine.

CT chest showed diffuse micronodularity in all lobes with perilymphatic and centrilobular distribution, scattered calcified granulomas, mediastinal/hilar lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly—findings not present on scans 6 years and 1 month earlier, suggesting a miliary pattern. Three sputum AFB smears were negative; MTB NAAT on one specimen was nondetectable. Bronchoscopy revealed endobronchial nodules and plaques in the left upper lobe; biopsies were sent for aerobic, AFB, and fungal cultures. BAL Aspergillus galactomannan and PJP DFA were negative. Empiric anidulafungin and posaconazole were started for possible invasive fungal infection (including endemic fungi and aspergillosis). Serum assays for Histoplasma antigen, urine Histoplasma antigen, serum Aspergillus galactomannan, and serum Cryptococcus antigen were negative; T‑SPOT IGRA was negative; Aspergillus fumigatus IgG was elevated (13.03 U/mL). Biopsy pathology showed necrotizing granulomatous inflammation; AFB and GMS stains were negative. Four days later, Coccidioides complement fixation titer returned 1 : 8, Coccidioides IgM ELISA positive, IgG ELISA negative, and immunodiffusion showed a partial identity reaction suggestive of active coccidioidomycosis. He was started on liposomal amphotericin B; the azole and echinocandin were discontinued. His hypoxia resolved and he was discharged home.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Tuberculosis considered due to miliary pattern and night sweats; excluded by negative sputum AFB smears, nondetectable MTB NAAT, and negative IGRA (T‑SPOT) | "Three sputum AFB cultures were collected and were smear negative... MTB complex nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) was performed... was not detectable... T‑SPOT interferon‑gamma release assay was negative."
2. Invasive aspergillosis considered given diffuse micronodules; excluded by negative BAL galactomannan, negative serum galactomannan, and lack of hyphal elements on stains | "An Aspergillus galactomannan antigen and PJP DFA in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BAL) were negative... serum Aspergillus galactomannan antigen... negative."
3. Other endemic fungi (e.g., Coccidioides) considered; initial serology suggested coccidioidomycosis but later deemed possibly cross‑reactive; definitive diagnosis required culture | "Coccidioides antibody by complement fixation (CF) assay returned positive at 1 : 8... pattern of serological data suggested active coccidioidomycosis."
4. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia considered due to immunosuppression; excluded by negative sputum DFA and negative BAL DFA | "sputum Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) direct fluorescent antibody (DFA)" and "BAL ... PJP DFA ... negative."
5. Histoplasma infection considered but initial non‑culture tests were negative (urine antigen, serum antigen); ultimately confirmed by tissue culture and DNA probe | "Assays for serum Histoplasma antigen enzyme immunoassay (EIA), urine Histoplasma galactomannan antigen quantitative EIA... were negative." ... "The isolate was preliminarily identified as Histoplasma capsulatum based on morphology... tested positive for Histoplasma capsulatum by DNA probe."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient’s longstanding HIV infection is listed in past medical history only and is not the focus of diagnostic workup. The acute problem presented (severe CK elevation with tea‑colored urine, muscle pain, and elevated transaminases) is rhabdomyolysis, which is not among the 21 SELECTED diseases. Therefore the target diagnosis is an OUT_OF_SCOPE disease.
2. Breakpoint: Include information up to and including the day‑29 clinical presentation (tea‑colored urine, fever, chills, bilateral leg pain, muscle cramps) and the initial laboratory findings that reveal markedly elevated CK, AST/ALT, bilirubin, and positive urine myoglobin, together with the negative infectious work‑up. Stop before any author commentary or conclusion about the cause.
3. Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished rhabdomyolysis from sepsis, viral hepatitis, drug‑induced liver injury, and other infectious etiologies by (a) documenting negative blood/urine cultures, (b) negative hepatitis B/C and histoplasma antigens, (c) normal hepatic imaging, (d) presence of disproportionate CK elevation with myoglobinuria, and (e) temporal association with dasatinib exposure while other drugs were discontinued.
case_prompt:
A 33‑year‑old African American man was transferred for evaluation of a white‑blood‑cell count > 100 K/mm³. One month prior he had fever, chills, poor appetite, and a 10‑lb weight loss. He has a 10‑year history of HIV infection, non‑compliant with therapy for >6 months; CD4 count 847 cells/mm³, HIV viral load 101,591 copies/mL. Physical exam revealed enlarged, rubbery, non‑tender cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymph nodes. Admission labs showed WBC 110.76 K/mm³ with 29% blasts and a differential suggestive of myeloid proliferation; serum creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, ALT 14 U/L, AST 31 U/L, total bilirubin 0.5 mg/dL. He received IV fluids, allopurinol, and a new HIV regimen (emtricitabine‑tenofovir + dolutegravir). Bone‑marrow biopsy confirmed chronic myeloid leukemia in blast crisis with t(9;22) and inv(3); BCR‑ABL FISH and RT‑PCR were positive for p210 and p190 transcripts. Induction chemotherapy (cytarabine + idarubicin) plus dasatinib was started, with voriconazole prophylaxis; dasatinib dose was reduced due to interaction. By hospital day 16, bilirubin rose to 1.8 mg/dL, AST 60 U/L, ALT 41 U/L, prompting discontinuation of voriconazole. Liver ultrasound was normal. Dasatinib was resumed to 100 mg/day on day 18; LFTs normalized by day 22.
On hospital day 29 the patient developed new tea‑colored urine, fever, chills, bilateral leg pain, and muscle cramps. Blood and urine cultures remained negative. Repeat liver ultrasound was unchanged. Laboratory studies now showed total bilirubin 2.3 mg/dL, AST 1254 U/L, ALT 290 U/L, CK > 100,000 U/L, and serum creatinine 0.9 mg/dL. Urinalysis was positive for large blood but no RBCs; urine myoglobin was 220 ng/mL (reference 0‑13 ng/mL). Hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis B DNA, hepatitis C antibody, and urine histoplasma antigen were all negative. Nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A/B PCR was negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Sepsis secondary to bacterial infection was considered because of fever and chills, but repeatedly negative blood and urine cultures made infection unlikely. | "A detailed workup for the source of sepsis was negative, including blood and urine cultures."
2. Viral hepatitis (HBV, HCV) was a potential cause of transaminase elevation, yet hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis B DNA, and hepatitis C antibody were all negative. | "Hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis B DNA, hepatitis C antibody ... were all negative."
3. Invasive fungal infection (histoplasmosis) was entertained given immunosuppression, but urine histoplasma antigen was negative. | "Urine histoplasma antigen ... were all negative."
4. Influenza infection could explain fever and myalgias, but nasopharyngeal PCR for influenza A and B was negative. | "Nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B PCR was negative."
5. Drug‑induced liver injury from dasatinib or residual voriconazole was possible, yet liver ultrasound was normal, bilirubin trended down after drug adjustment, and the marked CK elevation with myoglobinuria was disproportionate to isolated hepatic injury. | "Ultrasonogram of the liver and biliary tree was normal."
6. Rhabdomyolysis due to dasatinib‑associated muscle toxicity aligns with the classic triad of tea‑colored urine, severe CK elevation, and myoglobinuria, fitting the temporal relationship after dasatinib dose increase. | "Serum creatine kinase was >100,000 U/L ... Urine myoglobin was elevated at 220 ng/ml."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case centers on desquamative interstitial pneumonia (DIP) and its acute exacerbation, which is not among the 21 SELECTED diseases; therefore the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.  
2. Best breakpoint: Include all information up to the decision to consider a DIP exacerbation but stop before the initiation of high‑dose methylprednisolone therapy (i.e., before “On the fourth hospitalization day, treatment for possible DIP exacerbation was initiated…”). This provides symptoms, imaging, labs, and the ruling‑out work‑up without revealing the therapeutic response that confirms the diagnosis.  
3. Analytic distinctions: The authors excluded infection (negative cultures, low procalcitonin), pulmonary embolism (CT angiogram negative), and heart failure (normal NT‑proBNP). Positive ANCA was noted but not pursued. After exhaustive non‑invasive work‑up failed, they entertained a DIP exacerbation, and the rapid clinical improvement after steroids served to confirm it.
case_prompt:
The patient is a 58‑year‑old Caucasian man referred to the pulmonary clinic for an abnormal high‑resolution CT chest showing ground‑glass opacities, interlobular septal thickening, minimal honeycombing, mediastinal adenopathies, and small bilateral pleural effusions. He reported progressive dyspnea and an unproductive cough. Past history included a 31‑pack‑year smoking habit, asbestos exposure, uncontrolled type II diabetes mellitus, and obesity. On examination his oxygen saturation was 93% on room air; bibasilar crackles with poor air entry were heard, without clubbing or cyanosis. Pulmonary function testing demonstrated mixed obstructive and restrictive physiology with a severely reduced diffusion capacity (DLco 44%). An extensive outpatient laboratory panel was negative except for borderline elevations in ACE, LDH, CK, and a positive ANCA. Video‑assisted thoracoscopic lung biopsy revealed classic desquamative interstitial pneumonia with areas of respiratory bronchiolitis‑interstitial pneumonia, mild fibrosis, and emphysema. He was started on a tapering course of prednisone and nicotine replacement; after seven months he improved clinically and radiographically.

Six weeks after re‑initiating smoking, he presented with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure. He was tachypneic, had worsening bibasilar crackles, decreased air entry, and required 100 % FiO₂ by non‑rebreather mask to maintain saturations >90 %. Chest X‑ray and CT angiogram showed markedly worsened bilateral ground‑glass opacities, bibasilar consolidations, mediastinal adenopathies, and a new moderate right pleural effusion; no pulmonary emboli were identified. Broad‑spectrum antibiotics (vancomycin, piperacillin‑tazobactam, azithromycin) were initiated. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 12,600 /µL without left shift, borderline procalcitonin (0.14 ng/mL), initially elevated then normalized CRP, and normal NT‑proBNP. Respiratory viral PCR panel, fungal serologies, blood cultures, sputum acid‑fast bacilli, urine streptococcus, and legionella tests were all negative. Sputum cultures grew Candida dubliniensis and Pseudomonas fluorescens, organisms considered colonizers. The patient declined bronchoscopy and thoracentesis. After four days of antibiotics with no clinical improvement and persistent imaging abnormalities, less common causes—including an exacerbation of his known desquamative interstitial pneumonia—were contemplated.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial pneumonia considered but deemed unlikely because cultures were negative, procalcitonin was only borderline, and there was no fever; “Laboratory workup was unremarkable for infection… White blood cell count was slightly elevated at 12,600 without a left shift… Procalcitonin level was borderline at 0.14 ng/mL… Additional negative tests included … blood cultures, sputum acid‑fast bacilli testing, urine streptococcus, and legionella.”  
2. Viral infection considered and excluded by a negative respiratory PCR panel; “Additional negative tests included respiratory polymerase chain reaction viral panel.”  
3. Fungal infection considered but ruled out by negative fungal serology and non‑pathogenic isolates; “Additional negative tests included … fungal serology… Sputum fungal and bacterial cultures grew Candida dubliniensis and Pseudomonas fluorescens. Although, these organisms are not generally considered pathogens in humans unless severely immunocompromised.”  
4. Pulmonary embolism excluded by CT angiography; “A chest X‑ray … and a chest CT angiogram … No pulmonary emboli were found.”  
5. Congestive heart failure excluded by normal NT‑proBNP; “NT‑proBNP was normal which excluded congestive heart failure as a cause for the pleural effusion and GGOs.”  
6. ANCA‑associated vasculitis entertained (positive ANCA) but not pursued given lack of systemic features and negative serologies; “All were negative except … positive ANCA antibodies.”  
7. Acute exacerbation of desquamative interstitial pneumonia remained plausible after other etiologies were excluded; “Because initial workup for the acute respiratory failure was inconclusive, less common etiologies were considered including DIP exacerbation.”

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient was ultimately diagnosed with disseminated histoplasmosis, which is included in the 21 SELECTED diseases list (histoplasmosis). HIV infection is also a SELECTED disease, but it was already known and not the diagnostic problem presented to the learner.
2. Ideal Breakpoint: Present the case up to the point where the bone marrow biopsy was performed and empirical steroids were started, but **exclude** the pathological description of budding yeast cells that confirmed histoplasmosis. This provides sufficient clinical, laboratory, and epidemiologic clues (fever, pancytopenia, very high ferritin/triglycerides, severe immunosuppression, travel from an endemic area) for learners to suspect disseminated histoplasmosis without revealing the definitive morphologic evidence.
3. Author's Analytic Distinctions: The authors first considered a lymphoproliferative disorder with secondary hemophagocytic syndrome because of the cytopenias and hyper‑ferritinemia, then pursued tissue diagnosis. The identification of intracellular budding yeasts on GMS/PAS stains and positive culture for *Histoplasma capsulatum* established the fungal etiology, while serology was negative, ruling out other fungal infections. Co‑infection with EBV, CMV, and HBV was documented but deemed insufficient to explain the full picture.
case_prompt: In February 2016, a 19‑year‑old woman from Ivory Coast was admitted to a peripheral hospital for persistent fever. A screening HIV‑antibody test was positive, and she was referred to the Infectious and Tropical Diseases Department. On admission she reported deep asthenia, chills, and fever up to 38.8 °C with tachycardia (110 bpm). Physical examination showed unilateral tonsillar hypertrophy and submandibular lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies revealed pancytopenia (Hb 8.7 g/dL, WBC 3,050/µL, platelets 80,000/µL), markedly elevated lactate dehydrogenase (5,201 U/L), C‑reactive protein 63.3 mg/L, ferritin > 40,000 ng/mL, and triglycerides 440 mg/dL. CD4⁺ count was 19 cells/µL and HIV‑RNA 1,787,000 copies/mL. Viral PCRs were positive for EBV‑DNA (1,297 copies/mL), CMV‑DNA (266 copies/mL), and HBV‑DNA (> 700,000,000 IU/mL). A stool test was also positive. Suspecting a lymphoproliferative disorder evolving in hemophagocytic syndrome, a bone marrow biopsy was performed and steroid therapy was initiated. Biopsies of the gut, a cervical lymph node, and the tonsil were also obtained.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Lymphoproliferative disorder with hemophagocytic syndrome considered because of fever, cytopenias, hyper‑ferritinemia, and high triglycerides | "Suspecting a lymphoproliferative disorder evolving in haemophagocytic syndrome, a bone marrow biopsy was performed and steroid treatment was started."
2. Primary viral opportunistic infections (EBV, CMV, HBV) noted but deemed insufficient to explain the full clinical picture | "the patient resulted positive for EBV‑DNA (1,297 cp/mL), CMV‑DNA (266 cp/mL), and HBV‑DNA (> 700,000,000 UI/mL)."
3. Disseminated fungal infection (Histoplasma) favored by epidemiologic exposure (West African origin) and intracellular organisms seen on histology | "Microscopical evaluation ... showed a prominent lymphohistiocytic infiltrate with budding yeast cells inside macrophages, suggestive of histoplasmosis, which was confirmed by Grocott Methenamine Silver stain (GMS) and periodic acid‑Schiff (PAS) stain."
4. Histoplasma serology negative, emphasizing need for tissue diagnosis rather than serology alone | "Histoplasma spp serology was negative, while culture of bone marrow aspirate showed H. capsulatum growth."
5. Other endemic mycoses (e.g., cryptococcosis, blastomycosis) not supported by the specific staining pattern and culture results | "the budding yeast cells were identified with GMS and PAS stains and grew as H. capsulatum in culture."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient was ultimately diagnosed with central nervous system histoplasmosis, which corresponds to **histoplasmosis** on the 21 SELECTED diseases list. HIV infection is also a SELECTED disease, but the primary teaching focus is the infectious CNS lesion; therefore the target diagnosis is histoplasmosis (with HIV as a co‑infection not required for solving the presented diagnostic puzzle).  
2. Ideal Breakpoint: Present the case up to the point where PET/CT imaging has been completed and a therapeutic trial for toxoplasmosis has failed, but before the brain biopsy result and HIV diagnosis are disclosed. This provides sufficient clinical, radiologic, and metabolic data for the learner to infer an infectious etiology—specifically histoplasmosis—without revealing the definitive microbiologic confirmation.  
3. Author's Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished an infectious cause from malignancy by (a) noting hypometabolic PET lesions relative to normal grey matter, (b) emphasizing the lack of extracerebral FDG‑avid disease, and (c) observing failure of empiric anti‑toxoplasma therapy, prompting tissue diagnosis. These steps ruled out high‑grade astrocytoma, lymphoma, and metastases and narrowed the differential to a specific fungal infection (Histoplasma capsulatum).
case_prompt: A 66‑year‑old woman, previously healthy, presented with a 2‑week history of night sweats, new‑onset headache, dizziness, intermittent double vision, and unsteady gait. On examination she ambulated with a left‑sided hemiplegic droop, leaning toward the left. Brain MRI with T1‑weighted post‑gadolinium images demonstrated multiple right temporal lobe lesions, the largest measuring 2.4 × 1.9 cm, showing intense irregular ring‑like enhancement and associated T2 hyperintensity. The radiologic differential included high‑grade astrocytoma, lymphoma, metastases, and infection. To further evaluate for malignancy, an 18F‑FDG PET/CT was performed. The scan showed no extracerebral FDG‑avid lesions; the cerebral lesions were relatively hypometabolic (maximum SUV 5.4) compared with normal grey matter (SUV 10.1 in basal ganglia, 7.6 in sensorimotor cortex), raising suspicion for an infectious process. Empiric antimicrobial therapy for toxoplasmosis was administered, but the patient did not improve.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. High‑grade astrocytoma considered because of ring‑enhancing mass lesions on MRI; excluded by PET showing low metabolic activity rather than the high FDG uptake typical of high‑grade glioma. | "the intensely enhancing cerebral lesions described on MRI were hypometabolic... which increased the likelihood of an infectious aetiology."
2. Primary CNS lymphoma considered given enhancement pattern; excluded by the same hypometabolic PET findings, as CNS lymphoma usually demonstrates high FDG avidity. | "The PET/CT scan failed to show extracerebral 18F‑FDG‑avid lesions, and the intensely enhancing cerebral lesions... were hypometabolic..."
3. Metastatic disease considered in differential; excluded by lack of extracranial FDG‑avid tumors on PET/CT. | "The PET/CT scan failed to show extracerebral 18F‑FDG‑avid lesions..."
4. Cerebral toxoplasmosis considered empirically and treated; failure to respond prompted pursuit of tissue diagnosis. | "Following the failure of a diagnostic/therapeutic trial of antimicrobials for toxoplasmosis..."
5. Other infectious etiologies (bacterial abscess, TB) less likely due to absence of systemic signs and PET pattern; the combination of night sweats, immunocompromised state (later revealed HIV) and hypometabolic lesions favored a fungal infection, ultimately confirmed as Histoplasma capsulatum. | "the lesions... increased the likelihood of an infectious aetiology."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case’s primary diagnostic challenge is disseminated histoplasmosis, which is on the 21 SELECTED diseases list. Hence the target diagnosis is **histoplasmosis** (SELECTED).
2. Best breakpoint: End the prompt after the presentation of vital signs, physical findings, chest imaging showing a diffuse miliary pattern, and initial CSF analysis, and after noting empiric antimicrobial therapy initiation. Do not include the antigen test results, culture positivity, or bone‑marrow findings that confirm histoplasmosis.
3. Author’s analytic distinctions: The authors supported histoplasmosis by positive urine/serum/CSF antigens, growth of *Histoplasma capsulatum* in respiratory and blood cultures, and compatible bone‑marrow hemophagocytosis. They ruled out bacterial sepsis (negative cultures), blastomycosis (cross‑reactive antigen), pneumocystis pneumonia (low clinical suspicion despite positive PCR), and tuberculosis (alternative cause of miliary infiltrates) through microbiologic testing and clinical context.
case_prompt:
A 54‑year‑old man with a history of probable neurosarcoidosis, lymphocytic leptomeningitis, seizures, cirrhosis, and possible ethanol use disorder presented with encephalopathy, hypoxia, and several weeks of intermittent fevers. His immunosuppressive regimen included mycophenolate 1000 mg orally twice daily and an infliximab infusion one month earlier.

On exam his temperature was 36.4 °C, blood pressure 80/52 mm Hg, heart rate 93 bpm, respiratory rate 24/min, and oxygen saturation 91 % on 10 L/min supplemental oxygen. Chest radiography revealed a diffuse miliary pattern, which was confirmed on chest CT. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed 1 white blood cell/mm³ (95 % lymphocytes), 1 red blood cell/mm³, glucose 28 mg/dL (reference 50‑70), and protein 53 mg/dL (reference 15‑45). Empiric therapy with vancomycin, piperacillin‑tazobactam, and amphotericin was started.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Disseminated fungal infection suspected due to miliary pulmonary infiltrates in an immunosuppressed host | "Conventional chest radiography ... found a diffuse miliary pattern, which was also identified on subsequent computed tomography of the chest."
2. Bacterial sepsis considered because of acute hypoxic respiratory failure; empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics initiated | "The patient received empiric vancomycin, piperacillin/tazobactam, and amphotericin for possible bacterial and fungal infections."
3. Blastomycosis entertained due to cross‑reactive antigen tests; later deemed unlikely | "Urine, serum, and CSF antigen studies were positive for histoplasmosis and blastomycosis, but the positive studies for blastomycosis were thought to be secondary to cross‑reactivity."
4. Tuberculosis considered as a cause of miliary pattern, but lack of mycobacterial evidence and positive fungal cultures shifted probability | (no direct quote; inference drawn from miliary pattern description and subsequent fungal positivity)
5. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia evaluated after positive PCR from BAL, but low clinical suspicion limited its role | "Pneumocystis jirovecii polymerase chain reaction study of the bronchoalveolar lavage was positive for which he received a complete course of trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole, although suspicion for pneumocystis pneumonia was low."
6. Histoplasma capsulatum identified definitively by culture from bronchoscopy specimen and blood, confirming disseminated histoplasmosis | "Respiratory culture obtained via bronchoscopy grew Histoplasma capsulatum. Fungal blood culture grew Histoplasma capsulatum."
7. Bone‑marrow hemophagocytosis interpreted as supportive of disseminated histoplasmosis despite negative marrow culture | "Bone marrow biopsy ... found hemophagocytosis that was thought to be consistent with the diagnosis of disseminated histoplasmosis, although the bone marrow culture had no growth of pathogens."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The autopsy disclosed noncaseating granulomata consistent with sarcoidosis, which is not included in the 21 SELECTED diseases list. Therefore the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.
2. Ideal Breakpoint: End the case presentation immediately before the autopsy findings are described, i.e., after “the eventual demise of the patient.” This provides all clinical, laboratory, and imaging data while withholding the definitive pathological clue.
3. Author's Analytic Distinctions: The authors systematically excluded bacterial, viral, fungal, mycobacterial, parasitic, and autoimmune etiologies through negative cultures, serologies, and autoantibody panels, ultimately arriving at sarcoidosis based on autopsy‑proven noncaseating granulomas.
case_prompt: A 41‑year‑old African American female presented to the emergency department with a cough, dyspnea, fevers, chills, night sweats, and fatigue. Two weeks earlier she had been prescribed oral levofloxacin for presumed pneumonia, but symptoms persisted and worsened. In the ED she was tachypneic (respiratory rate 30/min), hypoxemic (SpO₂ 87% on room air), and had diffuse bilateral crackles. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 30,000/µL, lactic acid 5 mEq/L, and a normal basic metabolic panel. Arterial blood gas revealed pH 7.17, PaCO₂ 50 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 19 mmol/L, PaO₂ 65.3 mmHg, and SaO₂ 87%. CT pulmonary angiography demonstrated extensive bilateral multifocal infiltrates with prominent hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy and no pulmonary embolism. The patient was intubated, admitted to the MICU with a presumptive diagnosis of sepsis secondary to pneumonia, and started on broad‑spectrum antibiotics. Parasite smear and initial blood cultures were negative. Bronchoscopy showed mild diffuse erythema; trans‑bronchial biopsies were not obtained due to desaturation. Bronchoalveolar lavage specimens were sent for cytology, bacterial, mycobacterial, and fungal stains and cultures. Echocardiography revealed a hyperdynamic left ventricle (EF 70%) with severe right‑ventricular dilation, hypokinesis, and an estimated right‑ventricular systolic pressure of 80 mmHg; TAPSE was 1.3 cm. The patient’s respiratory status continued to decline, requiring airway‑pressure‑release ventilation and inhaled epoprostenol. BAL remained negative for bacteria, fungi, and Pneumocystis jirovecii. Expanded workup—including fungal blood cultures, histoplasma and coccidioides serologies, a viral respiratory panel, and testing for RSV, adenovirus, influenza, parainfluenza, human metapneumovirus, HIV, EBV, CMV, leptospira, and pertussis—was all negative. Autoimmune serologies (ANA, ANCA, RF, anti‑CCP, anti‑Smith, anti‑SCL‑70, anti‑MPO, anti‑RNP, anti‑PR3) were negative; ACE level was at the high‑normal range. Despite escalating vasopressor support (norepinephrine, epinephrine, vasopressin) she developed worsening hepatic dysfunction and oliguric renal failure. On hospital day 3 she remained febrile, with a pH 6.99, PaCO₂ 47.4 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 10 mmol/L, PaO₂ 88.2 mmHg, SaO₂ 83.2%, and lactic acid 9 mEq/L. Plans for CRRT and possible ECMO were made, but shortly thereafter she suffered a pulseless electrical activity arrest and died.
diagnostic_reasoning:

T2‑hyperintense foci with enhancement involved lumbar and sacral spine, both iliac bones, and proximal femora. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis confirmed the rectal mass (9 × 5.6 × 5 cm), a left iliac lymph node (1.3 cm), a right upper‑lung nodule (0.3 cm), and no liver metastases. Bone scan and SPECT‑CT demonstrated widespread active osseous lesions throughout the spine, ribs, and pelvis.

Bone‑marrow biopsy revealed malignant infiltration by signet‑ring cells (CK20‑positive, CK7‑negative) with markedly reduced hematopoiesis. After initial cytopenias improved, treatment cycles continued with further dose reductions and supportive care. By early September his laboratory values had stabilized, though he experienced grade‑2 oral mucositis and dysphagia, leading to a brief treatment hold.

On 29 September, he presented to the emergency department with diplopia and nasal regurgitation. Vitals were stable; examination showed a left divergent squint. Moderate abdominal ascites and bilateral lower‑extremity edema were evident; cardio‑pulmonary, neurologic exams and abdominal organomegaly were unremarkable. A 36‑year‑old woman presented to the Emergency Department of the Cancer Center with fever, chills, night sweats, diarrhea, and painful oral lesions that began 3 days earlier. She had undergone liver transplantation eight years prior for biliary cirrhosis and was maintained on prednisone 5 mg daily and mycophenolate sodium 360 mg. Oral examination revealed three well‑defined shallow ulcerative lesions with fibrinous exudate and regular erythematous borders: one on the hard palate (≈1 cm), one on the vestibular and palatal gingiva between the 16 and 17 teeth (≈0.5 cm), and one on the left soft palate near the uvula (≈1 cm).

Exfoliative cytology of the oral lesions was performed and an anti‑CMV IgG test ordered. Empiric ganciclovir 300 mg three times daily was started, but no improvement occurred after 7 days. The exfoliative cytology and anti‑CMV IgG were negative, reducing the likelihood of a viral etiology. A chest X‑ray was normal, making pulmonary involvement unlikely.

A 57‑year‑old woman with hypothyroidism, hyperlipidemia, and glaucoma was referred to the interventional pulmonology clinic after chest imaging performed for a chronic dry cough revealed right lower‑lobe clusters of non‑calcified solid nodules (largest 10 × 15 mm) and an enlarged subcarinal lymph node measuring 1.4 × 2.8 cm. She denied fever, chills, anorexia, night sweats, or weight loss. She was a never‑smoker with no known environmental or occupational exposures. Physical examination and initial laboratory studies, including CBC and basic chemistry, were unremarkable.

Because of concern for an old granulomatous process (especially histoplasmosis), an endobronchial ultrasound‑guided transbronchial needle aspiration (EBUS‑TBNA) of station 7 was performed under conscious sedation. Four passes with a 21‑gauge needle were obtained. Rapid on‑site evaluation noted “excessive necrosis” from each pass. Cultures for bacteria, fungi, and acid‑fast bacilli were reported negative, and final cytology did not demonstrate infectious organisms or malignancy.

Ten days later the patient returned to the emergency department with a low‑grade fever, shortness of breath, and sharp posterior right‑sided chest pain that had worsened since the procedure. Vital signs and physical examination remained essentially normal. Laboratory testing showed a mild leukocytosis with left shift (12.5 × 10⁹/L, 76.9 % neutrophils). Repeat chest CT demonstrated a markedly enlarged subcarinal mass now measuring 5.5 × 2.6 cm, producing mass effect on adjacent vessels and the esophagus. After multidisciplinary discussion, the team elected to proceed with mediastinoscopy for further evaluation.

1. Persistent cough and incidentally discovered pulmonary nodules prompted consideration of granulomatous infection, especially histoplasmosis, which is endemic in many regions. | "The decision was made to pursue biopsy of the enlarged subcarinal LN to test for old granulomatous disease, in particular, histoplasmosis."
2. Initial EBUS‑TBNA showing excessive necrosis raised concern for necrotic tumor or infectious process, but rapid on‑site evaluation and cultures were negative for malignancy, bacteria, fungi, and AFB. | "ROSE commented on excessive necrosis from each pass. Cultures including bacterial, fungal, and acid‑fast bacteria (AFB) were negative. Final cytology was negative for infectious and malignant etiologies."

Development of fever, pleuritic chest pain, and leukocytosis after the bronchoscopic procedure suggested a post‑procedural complication such as mediastinitis or an abscess rather than a primary pulmonary neoplasm, which would be less likely to cause acute systemic symptoms. | "She presented to the Emergency Room with complaints of a low‑grade fever, shortness of breath, and sharp and posterior right‑sided chest pain which worsened since the procedure."
4. The marked increase in size of the subcarinal mass on repeat CT (from 1.4 × 2.8 cm to 5.5 × 2.6 cm) with mass effect reinforced the possibility of an infectious collection (abscess) rather than a slowly enlarging malignant node. | "CT chest was significant for a large subcarinal mass measuring 5.5 × 2.6 cm causing mass effect on adjacent vessels and esophagus."

Differential diagnoses such as lymphoma, metastatic carcinoma, tuberculous lymphadenitis, and fungal infection were considered but were less favored because prior cultures were negative, there was no evidence of systemic B symptoms, and the rapid evolution favored a suppurative process. | "Cultures including bacterial, fungal, and acid‑fast bacteria (AFB) were negative."

Intra‑operative findings of thick fluid in the mass, growth of Propionibacterium acnes, and histology showing fat necrosis with chronic inflammation confirmed an abscess as the etiology, ruling out malignancy and other granulomatous infections. | "Intraoperatively, the subcarinal mass had thick fluid inside which grew Propionibacterium acnes (P. acnes). Final histopathology showed fibroadipose tissue with fibrin, fat necrosis, and chronic inflammation consistent with abscess."

case_prompt:
A 29‑year‑old man from Delhi with no known prior comorbidities presented with a 40‑day history of fever and dry cough, and a 15‑day history of progressively worsening dyspnea. He also reported loss of appetite and a 5‑kg weight loss over the same period. On examination he was febrile, pulse 134/min, respiratory rate 36/min, blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg, and SpO₂ 92 % on room air. He was pale; there was no icterus, cyanosis, pedal edema, or lymphadenopathy. Moderate hepatosplenomegaly was noted; the lungs were clear bilaterally. 

Initial laboratory studies revealed pancytopenia (Hb 8.4 g/dL, platelets 79 ×10³/µL, WBC 3.9 ×10³/µL). Peripheral smear showed schistocytes with a corrected reticulocyte count of 1.8 %. LDH was elevated at 579 IU/L and the direct Coombs test was positive. Vitamin B12 and folate levels were normal. Electrocardiogram demonstrated a right bundle‑branch block with an S1Q3T3 pattern. B‑type natriuretic peptide was 211.6 pg/mL. Echocardiography showed moderate pulmonary arterial hypertension (PASP 43 + 10 mm Hg), moderate tricuspid regurgitation, prominent right atrium and ventricle, left ventricular ejection fraction 70 %, and a minimal pericardial effusion. 

CT pulmonary angiogram was normal, and venous Doppler ultrasonography of all four limbs showed no thrombosis. Blood and urine cultures were sterile. Serologies were negative for HIV‑1/2, rk‑39 (leishmaniasis), and Widal titers were < 1:40 for typhoidal O, H and paratyphoidal H antigens. Malaria parasites were absent on peripheral smear and quantitative buffy coat examination. ANA and anti‑dsDNA antibodies were negative; fibrinogen was low (< 150 mg/dL), triglycerides were 304 mg/dL, and ferritin exceeded 2,000 ng/mL.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Malaria excluded – peripheral smear and quantitative buffy coat showed no parasites. | "Malarial parasites were not seen on peripheral smear and quantitative buffy coat examination."
2. Visceral leishmaniasis excluded – rk‑39 antibody test negative. | "Antibodies against rk‑39 were negative."
3. HIV infection excluded – serology non‑reactive for HIV‑1/2. | "Serology for HIV 1 &2 was non-reactive."
4. Typhoid fever unlikely – low Widal titers (< 1:40). | "Widal titre was < 1:40 for typhoidal O, typhoidal H and paratyphoidal H antigen."
5. Pulmonary embolism excluded – CT pulmonary angiogram normal and lower‑limb venous Doppler studies normal. | "CT pulmonary angiogram was normal. USG Venous Doppler of all four limbs were normal."
6. Autoimmune hemolytic anemia considered but not sufficient as sole explanation – positive direct Coombs and schistocytes, yet patient also had hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, and marked inflammatory markers, prompting search for an infectious infiltrative process. | "Peripheral smear showed presence of schistocytes ... Direct coomb's test was positive. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) was found to be elevated..."
7. Disseminated histoplasmosis confirmed – bone‑marrow aspirate demonstrated intracellular and extracellular yeast morphologically consistent with *Histoplasma capsulatum*. | "Bone marrow aspirate showed ... yeast with morphology suggestive of Histoplasma capsulatum."

case_prompt:
A sixty‑four‑year‑old renal transplant recipient presented six years post‑transplant with a 36‑hour history of fever, hypotension, and asthenia, accompanied by a 7‑kg weight loss over three months. On examination she had oral white plaques and a rash on the back. Laboratory studies showed anemia (Hb 8.4 g/dL, Ht 23 %), leukopenia (2.3 × 10⁹/L), elevated C‑reactive protein (10.8 mg/dL) and ferritin (13 253 ng/mL), and acute graft dysfunction (serum creatinine rising from 3.0 to >4.0 mg/dL). Liver enzymes were normal. Her immunosuppression consisted of prednisone 5 mg/day and azathioprine 2 mg/kg/day.

On admission, blood cultures were drawn for fungi and mycobacteria; PCR for CMV and EBV, a cryptococcal latex agglutination test, and serologies for Histoplasma capsulatum and Trypanosoma cruzi were ordered. Empiric therapy with vancomycin, meropenem, and ganciclovir was started. CMV antigenemia was negative, but PCR detected 546 copies of CMV DNA. A skin lesion biopsy and cultures for fungi and mycobacteria were obtained. Thoraco‑abdominal CT and echocardiography were unremarkable. Bone‑marrow aspiration revealed erythroid hyperplasia. Upper‑GI endoscopy showed ulcerative esophagitis with intranuclear inclusions and focal esophageal candidiasis; fluconazole was added to the regimen.

The patient’s condition deteriorated with melena, mucocutaneous bleeding, hemodynamic instability, and development of disseminated intravascular coagulation. Empiric liposomal amphotericin B was started to cover histoplasmosis, and a four‑drug regimen for tuberculosis was initiated. Despite therapy, she required mechanical ventilation, vasopressor support, and developed acute hepatitis presumed secondary to amphotericin B. She died seven days after initiation of the antifungal treatment.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial sepsis was initially considered, prompting broad‑spectrum vancomycin and meropenem, but cultures remained negative and imaging showed no focus of infection. | "empiric treatment with vancomycin, meropenet, ... aiming to treat a possible bacterial infection."
2. Cytomegalovirus infection was suspected; ganciclovir was started, yet CMV antigenemia was negative and PCR load (546 copies) was modest, making it unlikely to account for the severe systemic picture. | "CMV antigenemia was negative but PCR unveiled 546 copies of the virus."
3. Epstein‑Barr virus infection was evaluated (PCR performed) but no supporting clinical or laboratory evidence was reported, leading to its exclusion. | "PCR for CMV and Epstein Barr virus (EBV)..."
4. Cryptococcosis was investigated with a latex agglutination test; the lack of a positive result argued against this diagnosis. | "latex agglutination test for cryptococcus..."
5. Candidiasis was identified endoscopically (esophageal lesions) and treated with fluconazole, but candidal disease was limited to the mucosa and could not explain the systemic sepsis‑like syndrome. | "esophageal candidiasis lesions. Fluconazole was associated..."
6. Tuberculosis was contemplated, leading to empiric four‑drug therapy, yet CT and echocardiography revealed no lesions, and no acid‑fast organisms were isolated, making active TB less likely. | "We empirically started ... a four‑drug treatment for tuberculosis."
7. Histoplasmosis remained a consideration because of the transplant status, fever, rash, mucosal lesions, cytopenias, high ferritin, and lack of an alternative source; empirical amphotericin B was started pending confirmation. | "We empirically started liposomal amphotericin B to cover histoplasmosis..."
8. Post‑mortem cultures and serology finally identified Histoplasma capsulatum in blood and skin biopsy, confirming the diagnosis. | "Histoplasma capsulatum was found in blood cultures and serology... The microbiology of the skin biopsy also isolated H. capsulatum."

case_prompt:
An 11‑year‑old girl presented with an 8‑day history of fever up to 39.4 °C occurring every 12 hours, night sweats, subjective weight loss, headaches, dizziness, nausea, intermittent right‑sided abdominal pain, anorexia, and an intermittently pruritic rash on her arms. She denied respiratory symptoms, emesis, or diarrhea.

Past medical history included multiple hospitalizations for bronchiolitis before age 2, severe varicella requiring nasogastric feeding at age 4, and hepatitis A at age 7. She was born in Central America and immigrated to the United States 4 years earlier. She had consumed unpasteurized cow milk while in Central America. A maternal uncle was diagnosed with tuberculosis several years ago, but she had not been in contact with him for more than 4 years.

On examination she was thin (weight 33.1 kg, BMI 15.5 kg/m²). Cervical lymph nodes were enlarged, mobile, and nontender bilaterally; no axillary or inguinal nodes were palpable. Small erythematous papules were present on the left antecubital fossa and the right first metacarpophalangeal joint. Mild abdominal tenderness was noted in the right upper quadrant without hepatosplenomegaly or palpable mass.

Laboratory studies on day 9 of illness showed leukopenia, anemia, mildly elevated C‑reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate > 145 mm/hr, and elevated AST/ALT. Cerebrospinal fluid was acellular with normal protein and glucose. Fourth‑generation HIV testing was positive; HIV‑1 RNA was 294,000 copies/mL in plasma and 504 copies/mL in CSF, with a CD4 count of 52 cells/µL.

Chest, abdominal, and pelvic CT revealed innumerable small nodules throughout both lungs and widespread lymphadenopathy involving cervical, axillary, hilar, mediastinal, and retroperitoneal regions; the largest retroperitoneal nodal conglomerate measured 4.4 cm. Bone‑marrow biopsy showed hypocellularity with non‑caseating granulomas. Cervical‑node biopsy demonstrated plasmacytosis and increased histiocytes without malignancy. Acid‑fast bacillus, Fite, and methenamine‑silver stains were negative in both specimens. Bronchoscopy showed no airway edema, erythema, or secretions.

Comprehensive infectious work‑up was negative: QuantiFERON‑TB Gold, mycobacterial cultures, and TB PCR from sputum, BAL fluid, lymph‑node tissue, blood, stool, and CSF were all negative; serum antibodies to *Toxoplasma gondii*, *Treponema pallidum*, *Brucella* spp., *Coccidioides immitis*, and *Histoplasma capsulatum* were negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Tuberculosis considered due to constitutional symptoms, lymphadenopathy, and pulmonary nodules; excluded by negative QuantiFERON‑TB Gold, negative mycobacterial cultures, and negative TB PCR from multiple sites. | "Evaluation for tuberculosis (TB) and non‑TB mycobacterial infections was negative, including QuantiFERON‑TB Gold, mycobacterial cultures, and/or TB PCR from sputum, bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid, lymph node tissue, blood, stool, and/or CSF."
2. Non‑tuberculous mycobacterial infection considered given immunosuppression and granulomatous pathology; excluded by identical negative cultures and PCR as above. | "Evaluation for tuberculosis (TB) and non‑TB mycobacterial infections was negative..."
3. Other endemic fungal infections (coccidioidomycosis, cryptococcosis) considered because of travel history and pulmonary findings; excluded by negative serum antibodies to *Coccidioides immitis* and *Histoplasma capsulatum* (serology) and by lack of organisms on silver staining. | "Serum antibodies to ... Coccidioides immitis, and Histoplasma capsulatum were negative."
4. Hematologic malignancy (lymphoma/leukemia) considered due to lymphadenopathy and pancytopenia; excluded by bone‑marrow hypocellularity without blast proliferation and lymph‑node biopsy showing no malignancy. | "Pathology of a bone marrow biopsy demonstrated hypocellularity and noncaseating granulomas. Lymph node biopsy revealed plasmacytosis and increased histiocytes with no evidence of malignancy."
5. HIV‑related opportunistic infections (CMV, EBV, PCP) considered in the setting of severe immunosuppression; excluded by normal CSF, lack of characteristic imaging or laboratory findings, and negative special stains. | "Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed no leukocytes and normal protein and glucose."
6. Disseminated histoplasmosis remained most consistent with (a) widespread pulmonary nodules, (b) extensive lymphadenopathy, (c) non‑caseating granulomas, (d) severe immunosuppression (CD4 = 52), and (e) negative tests for other pathogens, leading to targeted antigen testing and cultures. | "Urine and serum H. capsulatum antigens were positive with values greater than the upper limits of quantification. Ultimately, H. capsulatum grew in fungal cultures from blood, BAL fluid, and lymph node tissue."

case_prompt:
A 55‑year‑old Hispanic male presented at the request of his primary‑care provider for a 2‑month history of polyarticular joint pain (shoulders, elbows, wrists, knees), decreased appetite, and a 20‑lb weight loss. Review of systems was notable for a severely pruritic rash, chills, and fatigue that began 3 weeks prior; he denied fever, headache, alopecia, chest pain, cough, diaphoresis, dyspnea, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. Travel history included a trip to Mexico 3 months earlier; he works in landscaping.

Physical examination revealed diffuse joint tenderness without swelling or warmth and multiple raised, blanchable, erythematous papules and plaques on the back, arms, legs, and face, with leonine facies.

Laboratory studies showed:
- WBC 3,700/µL (low) with absolute lymphocytes 400/µL,
- Hemoglobin 8.6 g/dL (anemia),
- Corrected calcium 14.4 mg/dL (hypercalcemia),
- 1,25‑dihydroxyvitamin D 154 pg/mL (elevated),
- 25‑hydroxyvitamin D 20 ng/mL (low),
- PTH 1 pg/mL (suppressed),
- PTH‑related peptide 24 pg/mL (normal‑high),
- Creatinine 3.23 mg/dL (elevated),
- 24‑hour urine protein 700 mg.

Urine Bence‑Jones protein was positive at an outside lab, prompting evaluation for gammopathy. In‑house serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation, skeletal survey, and bone‑marrow biopsy were all negative for monoclonal gammopathy, infection, and malignancy.

Skin punch biopsy demonstrated non‑caseating granulomatous dermatitis, with negative stains for atypical mycobacteria, tuberculosis, and fungal organisms. CT chest showed non‑specific calcified granulomas at the hilum and left lung without hilar adenopathy or infiltrates. Renal biopsy revealed mild arterial nephrocalcinosis and segmental thickening of the glomerular basement membrane.

Additional studies were negative: tissue cultures, serum Quantiferon‑TB Gold, coccidioides antibodies, histoplasma antibodies, and blastomyces antibodies. Serum angiotensin‑converting enzyme level was normal. ECG and transthoracic echocardiogram showed no cardiac involvement.

1. Multiple myeloma (monoclonal gammopathy) was considered because of hypercalcemia, anemia, renal dysfunction, and positive urine Bence‑Jones protein; excluded by negative serum/urine protein electrophoresis, immunofixation, skeletal survey, and bone‑marrow biopsy. | "Due to positive Bence‑Jones protein … the diagnosis of gammopathy was entertained. However, an in‑house evaluation … was negative for gammopathy as well as infection and malignancy."
2. Infectious granulomatous diseases (mycobacterial TB, atypical mycobacteria, fungal infections) were considered given granulomatous skin lesions and pulmonary calcifications; excluded by negative stains on skin biopsy, negative Quantiferon‑TB, and negative serologies for coccidioides, histoplasma, and blastomyces. | "Skin punch biopsy revealed non‑caseating granulomatous dermatitis, with negative stains for atypical mycobacteria, tuberculosis and fungal organisms… Tissue cultures, serum Quantiferon TB gold, coccidioides antibodies, histoplasma antibodies, and blastomyces antibodies were all negative."
3. Sarcoidosis‑related infection (e.g., histoplasmosis) was considered because of granulomas and hypercalcemia; excluded by negative histoplasma antibodies and normal ACE level. | "Serum Angiotensin Converting Enzyme (ACE) level was normal."
4. Malignancy (solid tumor) was considered due to weight loss and hypercalcemia; excluded by negative imaging (CT chest without masses) and negative bone‑marrow biopsy. | "CT chest showed non‑specific calcified granulomas at the hilum and left lung without hilar adenopathy or infiltrates."
5. Other causes of hypercalcemia (primary hyperparathyroidism, PTH‑related peptide tumor) were ruled out by markedly suppressed PTH and only mildly elevated PTH‑related peptide. | "PTH of 1 pg/mL (normal 14‑64 pg/mL), PTH‑related protein of 24 pg/mL (normal 14‑27 pg/mL)."
6. The presence of non‑caseating granulomatous dermatitis, hypercalcemia with suppressed PTH, renal involvement, and exclusion of infectious, malignant, and plasma‑cell disorders supported sarcoidosis as the most likely diagnosis. | "By exclusion of alternative diagnoses, the patient was treated for sarcoidosis…"

case_prompt: A 14‑year‑old Hispanic male with WHIM syndrome presented with painless sudden‑onset loss of vision in the right eye for at least one week. He denied trauma, ocular pain, discharge, fever, rash, headache, or recent systemic illness. Past medical history included repaired Tetralogy of Fallot, chronic neutropenia with recurrent respiratory infections, and a prior episode of dengue fever at age 13. On examination the patient was underweight (BMI 14.5) with mild scoliosis and splenomegaly; classic WHIM features such as cutaneous warts and hypogammaglobulinemia were present. Ophthalmic assessment showed no light perception in the right eye and an afferent pupillary defect. Dilated fundus examination revealed a pale retina with widespread white subretinal infiltrates, some necrotizing, patches of subretinal fibrosis, mild vitritis, a fibrotic band extending to the optic nerve head, and a pale optic nerve. Spectral‑domain OCT demonstrated variable hyper‑reflective subretinal infiltrates throughout the macula without serous fluid and disrupted macular lamination. B‑scan ultrasound showed mild vitreous opacities, a posterior hyaloid membrane adherent to the optic disc, a vitreoschisis cavity inferiorly, and no retinal detachment or definitive eye‑wall thickening. The left eye was normal. Cranial CT scan showed mild sinusitis. Filgrastim (1 µg/kg/day) was administered, resulting in an increased ANC and increased vitritis the next day, suggesting a possible ongoing infection. Peripheral blood cultures were negative. Tests for other viral (CMV, EBV, VZV, HSV, dengue), fungal (Histoplasma, Cryptococcus), bacterial (Bartonella, Rickettsia, Legionella, Mycobacterium) and parasitic (Leishmania, Toxocara) pathogens were negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Viral necrotizing retinitis (CMV, HSV, VZV) was considered but excluded because “Tests for other viral (CMV, EBV, VZV, HSV, dengue) … pathogens were negative.”  
2. Fungal retinitis (Histoplasma, Cryptococcus) was ruled out by negative fungal testing: “Tests for … fungal (Histoplasma, Cryptococcus) … pathogens were negative.”  
3. Bacterial or mycobacterial endophthalmitis was deemed unlikely given negative blood cultures and bacterial panels: “Peripheral blood cultures were negative.” and “Tests for … bacterial (Bartonella, Rickettsia, Legionella, Mycobacterium) … pathogens were negative.”  
4. Other parasitic infections (Leishmania, Toxocara) were excluded by negative serologic testing: “Tests for … parasitic (Leishmania, Toxocara) pathogens were negative.”  
5. The pattern of necrotizing sub‑retinal infiltrates with vitritis, coupled with a positive PCR for T. gondii in vitreous fluid, confirmed ocular toxoplasmosis: “PCR testing was positive for T. gondii in vitreous fluid.”  
6. The increase in vitritis after filgrastim‑induced neutrophil recovery supported an active intra‑ocular infection rather than sterile inflammation: “Filgrastim … resulted in increased ANC and increased vitritis the next day, suggesting the possibility of an ongoing chronic infection.”

case_prompt:
A 46‑year‑old woman with a history of tobacco use presented with low‑grade fever and sudden severe right upper‑quadrant abdominal pain accompanied by nausea and vomiting. Emergent computed tomography of the abdomen demonstrated an intraluminal polypoid filling defect arising from the isthmus of the aorta and extending into the proximal descending aorta, together with infarctions of the spleen and right kidney. She was started on broad‑spectrum antibiotics for presumed sepsis and received an initial dose of heparin, which was later held to avoid hemorrhagic transformation of the infarcts.

Transthoracic echocardiography showed no valvular or cardiac source of embolus, and an agitated saline bubble study revealed no intracardiac shunting. Transesophageal echocardiography then identified a large echogenic mobile mass attached to the wall of the descending thoracic aorta. Bilateral lower‑extremity arterial Doppler ultrasonography demonstrated severe popliteal‑tibial arterial disease in the left leg.

Extensive infectious testing—including bacterial cultures, fungal panels, HIV, Bartonella henselae serology, Coxiella burnetii antibodies, Leptospira antibodies, syphilis serology, aspergillus galactomannan antigen, and histoplasma antigen—was negative. Hypercoagulability assays (DRVVT for lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibodies, homocysteine, paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria screen, protein C and S activity, antithrombin, factor V Leiden and prothrombin gene mutations) were unremarkable. Autoimmune serologies (ANA, ANCA, anti‑dsDNA, rheumatoid factor, anti‑CCP, Sjögren antibodies, MPO, PR3, complement levels, Smith and RNP antibodies) were also negative.

Given the absence of an acute limb‑ or organ‑threatening ischemia, the largely negative work‑up, and lack of a clear mechanism to remove the aortic lesion, the team elected medical management. The patient was transitioned from inpatient heparin to apixaban 5 mg twice daily plus aspirin 81 mg daily, with outpatient hematology follow‑up.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Infectious aortitis or septic emboli were considered but excluded because “Infectious work‑up was negative and included testing for bacterial infection, fungal infection, HIV, Bartonella henselae antibody, Coxiella burnetii antibodies, Leptospira antibodies, syphilis, aspergillus galactomannan antigen, and histoplasma antigen.”  
2. Hypercoagulable disorders (e.g., antiphospholipid syndrome, factor V Leiden, protein C/S deficiency) were evaluated and ruled out: “Hypercoagulability work‑up was also unremarkable and included DRVVT screening for lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibodies…, Protein C and S activity, antithrombin mutations, and factor V Leiden and prothrombin genotyping.”  
3. Her past medical history was notable for a prolonged NICU stay because of delayed oral feeding, but she had no pulmonary, cardiac, or intestinal complications of prematurity and no surgeries after NICU discharge at 6 weeks of age. There were no recent fevers or recurrent infections.

On examination she was in no acute distress, vital signs were normal, and both weight and height were below the first percentile. Physical examination revealed hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory studies showed elevated transaminases, significant hypercalcemia (4.47 mmol/L; normal 2.12‑2.74 mmol/L), a normal phosphorus level, and a appropriately suppressed parathyroid hormone. She was admitted for further evaluation.

Initial management with aggressive normal‑saline fluids, followed by furosemide and calcitonin, only partially lowered calcium. Two doses of pamidronate (0.5 mg/kg) given two days apart finally normalized calcium, and the infant was switched to a low‑calcium formula (Calcilo‑XD).

An extensive work‑up for viral, fungal, metabolic, genetic, and oncologic causes of hypercalcemia was negative. A skeletal survey showed no lytic lesions. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed no lymphadenopathy or pulmonary lesions, but confirmed hepatosplenomegaly. Because liver enzymes remained markedly elevated and hepatomegaly persisted, a liver biopsy was performed. Histology demonstrated lobular histiocytic infiltrates with well‑formed granulomas, hemophagocytosis, and increased portal/periportal and pericellular fibrosis with bridging, indicating chronicity, but no definitive etiology.

After three weeks of hospitalization, the infant was discharged home with improved weight gain, normal calcium, and improved (though still elevated) liver enzymes.

One month later she was readmitted for recurrent vomiting and poor weight gain. She remained afebrile. Laboratory testing now showed leukopenia and recurrence of hypercalcemia. The differential diagnosis included chronic granulomatous disease, immunodeficiency, tuberculosis, and hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH); screening for all was negative. HLH genotyping identified only a single allele mutation in UNC13, not sufficient to explain the phenotype. Elevated angiotensin‑converting enzyme (ACE) level (108 U/L; normal 18‑90) raised the possibility of infantile sarcoidosis. In the absence of evidence for immunodeficiency or malignancy, she was started on prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day for hypercalcemia and discharged home on steroids.

A 3‑year‑old girl (16 kg) presented with a week‑long history of vomiting, weakness, and a tremor-like movement at the right angle of the mouth. After an initial hospital stay she was discharged, but one week later developed right‑ward head tilt while speaking and reduced activity, prompting re‑admission for brain MRI and biopsy.  

During the second admission she had fever 39 °C, Glasgow Coma Scale 7 (E2V2M3), asymmetric pupils with sluggish light response, tetraparesis (strength 1/5), hyperreflexia, a positive Babinski sign with clonus, spasticity, and hand tremor. Transaminases were elevated; tests for CMV, HSV‑1, HSV‑2, syphilis, and tuberculosis were negative.  

First brain MRI (two weeks before admission) showed a large (7.8 × 8.1 × 7.9 cm) lesion involving the corpus callosum and bilateral frontal lobes with perifocal edema, adherence to the falx cerebri and lateral ventricles, and a smaller left parietal lesion with similar features; contrast‑enhancing nodules were seen in multiple lobes. The imaging pattern suggested glioblastoma with a differential of necrotizing toxoplasma encephalitis.  

Brain tissue biopsy revealed a gemistocytic cell adjacent to edematous neutrophilic stroma, extensive necrosis with caseous material, and infiltration by lymphocytes, macrophages, and epithelioid‑like cells. The initial pathology report concluded chronic inflammation consistent with brain tuberculosis. A second‑opinion review described a necrotic mass with inflammatory cells, indicating an inflammatory process without malignancy or tuberculosis.  

The patient continued anti‑tuberculosis therapy, corticosteroids, anticonvulsants, antipyretics, and mannitol. After three days her GCS improved to E4V2M3.  

A second brain MRI showed lesions in subcortical and juxtacortical regions of bilateral fronto‑temporo‑parietal, right occipital, bilateral parieto‑occipital lobes, bilateral caudate heads, putamen, and globus pallidus, without mass effect. These lesions demonstrated early sub‑acute hemorrhage in the caudate heads and cortical laminar necrosis in frontal and parietal lobes.  

Comprehensive respiratory viral PCR panels (including adenovirus, several coronaviruses, SARS‑CoV‑2, influenza, etc.) and bacterial PCRs (Bordetella spp., Chlamydia pneumoniae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae) were negative. CSF analysis showed clear fluid with 100 % mononuclear cells, leukocyte count 2 cells/mm³, protein 3 mg/dL, glucose 59 mg/dL, negative Nonne test, positive Pandy test, negative Gene Xpert for tuberculosis, and negative bacterial culture. Serum testing was negative for anti‑Histoplasma, aspergillus antibodies, autoimmune encephalitis panel, and MOG antibodies.  

The second MRI demonstrated hemorrhage and necrosis that were not consistent with resolution of a tuberculoma.

HSV-1, HSV-2 ... The second MRI showed hemorrhage and necrosis, which were inappropriate with the resolution of tuberculoma; then, the diagnosis ANEC was considered."

A 40‑year‑old woman presented to the emergency department with a one‑week history of cough, body aches, headache, fevers up to 39.4 °C, and shortness of breath. She had a 12‑year history of rheumatoid arthritis and a five‑year history of sarcoidosis (RA‑sarcoid overlap). Her immunosuppressive regimen included daily azathioprine and rituximab infusions every four months, the last given three months earlier.

Initial labs (CBC with differential, CRP, procalcitonin) were drawn, and a broad infectious screen—including COVID‑19 PCR, rapid influenza A/B antigens, urinalysis, and blood cultures—was negative or within normal limits. D‑dimer was elevated, prompting a chest CTA that showed no pulmonary embolism but revealed scattered ground‑glass opacities bilaterally. Her presentation was interpreted as consistent with an “atypical” bacterial pneumonia, and she was discharged on doxycycline.

Three days later she remained febrile and chills prompted addition of levofloxacin, followed by hospital admission where levofloxacin, ertapenem, and vancomycin were started. Further work‑up (two sets of blood cultures, LDH, serum cryptococcal antigen, urine and serum Histoplasma antigens, 1,3‑β‑D‑glucan) was broadly negative except for mildly elevated LDH. Chest X‑ray showed no lobar consolidations. Bronchoscopy with BAL yielded negative cytology, negative fungal stain, and cultures growing Streptococcus parasanguinis and Rothia dentocariosa. She was discharged on levofloxacin.

Approximately four weeks after symptom onset she continued to have fevers 38.9‑39.4 °C. With repeated negative COVID‑19 PCRs, a COVID‑19 antibody test was ordered and dexamethasone 6 mg daily plus amoxicillin were started. The next day BAL viral culture returned positive for cytomegalovirus (CMV); CMV pneumonitis was presumed and valganciclovir 900 mg twice daily was initiated. Fever improved but dyspnea, cough, and low‑grade fever persisted; COVID‑19 antibody later proved negative and dexamethasone and amoxicillin were stopped.

Five weeks after initial presentation she was readmitted with persistent fever, headache, sinus congestion, worsening cough and dyspnea on exertion, weight loss, and vague rib pain. Intravenous ganciclovir was started for presumed CMV pneumonitis. Despite therapy, fever continued for four days. Laboratory studies now showed mild transaminase elevation, anemia, leukopenia, and an extensive negative infectious panel (blood cultures, COVID‑19 PCR, respiratory viral panel, HIV Ag/Ab, Aspergillus galactomannan, Brucella serology, Coxiella serology, acid‑fast bacilli culture, Coccidioides serology, Cryptococcus antigen, 1,3‑β‑D‑glucan, EBV PCR, CMV PCR). Lumbar puncture was unremarkable. Chest CT demonstrated innumerable small pulmonary nodules throughout both lungs, many with a perilymphatic distribution, similar to a prior CT but with increased nodularity compared with imaging from six months earlier. Lung biopsy was deferred due to unsafe target.

Candida infection is not among the 21 SELECTED diseases; leishmaniasis (a SELECTED disease) was considered but ruled out. Therefore the mystery diagnosis is an OUT_OF_SCOPE disease.
2. Breakpoint: Include presentation up to the mycological examination that showed hyphae, but stop before the definitive culture results that identified Staphylococcus aureus and Candida. This provides enough clinical detail (rash morphology, lack of response to antibiotics, negative Leishmania PCR, hyphae on microscopy) for the learner to deduce a fungal skin infection without revealing the final microbiologic confirmation.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished leishmaniasis (negative PCR, endemic region), bacterial impetigo (initial response to antibiotics was absent, later cultures grew S. aureus), and fungal infection (hyphae on mycological test, response to fluconazole). They emphasized the rarity of opportunistic infections in AT and the importance of fungal cultures in confirming the diagnosis.
case_prompt: An 11‑year‑old Arab girl with ataxia‑telangiectasia diagnosed at age 1 presented with a spreading skin rash that began on her nose and later involved the nostrils and left cheek. The rash was unresponsive to a 7‑day course of amoxicillin‑clavulanic acid and topical chloramphenicol. On examination, the tip of the nose showed an erythematous plaque with a central erosion, a circinate‑elevated border, and scattered pustules; the nasal bridge and nostrils had small erythematous erosions. Her past history included recurrent pulmonary and otic infections, sclerosing cholangitis, hypothyroidism, wheelchair dependence, and recent diffuse large B‑cell lymphoma. Daily IVIG, inhaled steroids, and levothyroxine were ongoing. A PCR test for Leishmania returned negative. Mycological examination of a skin specimen revealed hyphae, but species identification was not possible because of the small sample size.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Leishmaniasis considered because of residence in an endemic region, but ruled out by negative PCR. | "Due to residence in an endemic region, leishmaniasis was initially high on the differential, but eventually, clinical suspicion and fungal cultures were of help."
2. Bacterial impetigo (Staphylococcus aureus) considered given pustular component, but lack of improvement with oral β‑lactam antibiotics and initial negative bacterial cultures made it less likely. | "Initially, she was treated with amoxicillin and clavulanic acid ... however, with no response."
3. Fungal infection suspected after hyphae were seen on mycological test despite negative Leishmania PCR, and the lesion’s circinate‑elevated border with central erosion is typical for chronic candidal or dermatophytic infection. | "A mycological test showed hyphae, but a species could not be identified due to a small sample."
4. Opportunistic infection in AT patients is rare; T‑cell function is relatively intact, so candidal infection is unusual but plausible, especially after lymphoma treatment. | "AT patients rarely acquire opportunistic infections, although they may be more susceptible to viral infections ... A case report described an AT patient with an invasive candida infection due to a functionally impaired T cell function."

case_prompt:
In October 2017 a 32‑year‑old man presented with intermittent rectal bleeding after defecation for the preceding 40 days, accompanied by cough and fever. He reported a slowly enlarging, painless perianal mass that he had first noticed five years earlier but had never sought treatment for. He was referred to the surgical unit at Gondar University Hospital for evaluation of possible colorectal carcinoma.

On examination the patient appeared well; vital signs were within normal limits. Abdominal examination revealed a palpable spleen 5 cm below the left costal margin and a liver 2 cm below the right costal margin. A 5 cm × 5 cm erythematous, nontender plaque was noted over the inner right buttock/perianal region. Digital rectal examination demonstrated a circumferential, firm rectal swelling located 4 cm from the anal verge.

A contrast‑enhanced abdominal CT scan showed a circumferential rectal mass 2.5 cm thick with extension into the mesorectum, thickened mesorectal fascia, and mesorectal lymphadenopathy (stage III); hepatosplenomegaly was also present. The radiology report concluded “rectal cancer plus hepatosplenomegaly.” A chest X‑ray was normal.

An endoscopic biopsy of the rectal lesion and a fine‑needle aspiration of the perianal plaque were performed. An HIV test performed on admission was positive, with a CD4 count of 306 cells/µL.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Colorectal carcinoma was the leading initial hypothesis because of the circumferential rectal mass, mesorectal extension, and lymphadenopathy on CT. | “The abdominal CT scan showed a circumferential rectal mass… suggestive of rectal cancer with rectal and mesorectal extension… The conclusion of the CT scan was rectal cancer plus hepatosplenomegaly.”
2. HIV‑associated opportunistic infections (e.g., lymphoma, fungal disease) were considered given the patient’s immunosuppression, but these were not supported by imaging or clinical picture. | “An HIV test was carried out at admission, and he was found to be seropositive with a CD4 count of 306.”
3. The absence of malignant cells on histology ruled out carcinoma. | “An endoscopic biopsy from the rectum showed three fragments with unremarkable mucosa… No feature of malignancy was seen in the biopsy.”
4. Identification of intracellular Leishmania amastigotes in the rectal submucosa and in the perianal lesion confirmed leishmaniasis as the cause of the mass‑like lesion. | “Numerous macrophages were stuffed with intracellular Leishmania amastigotes… FNA from the perianal lesion showed Leishman Donovan bodies (grade+3 amastigotes).”
5. Negative splenic aspiration excluded concurrent visceral leishmaniasis, indicating the disease was limited to the anorectal region. | “Splenic aspiration… was negative for Leishmania amastigotes.”
6. Clinical improvement after liposomal amphotericin B (and later miltefosine) supported the diagnosis. | “After treatment… rectal bleeding stopped, and his fever recovered… The perianal mass flattened… repeated abdominal CT scan showed reduction in the rectal lesion size.”
