A 32‑year‑old HIV‑1‑infected widow presented with a 6‑month history of progressive lethargy, anorexia, recurrent fever, vomiting, watery non‑bloody diarrhoea, and marked weight loss (from 50 kg to 21 kg over 5 months). She was unemployed and had an irregular carbohydrate‑dominant diet. 

On examination she was conscious but prostrated, severely wasted with generalized loss of muscle bulk and subcutaneous fat, and prominent bony structures. Body mass index was 10.2 kg/m² and mid‑upper‑arm circumference was 10 cm. She had hypoproteinemic hair and skin changes, dehydration, fever (37.8 °C), pallor, and oropharyngeal candidiasis; there was no lymphadenopathy. Chest, cardiovascular and abdominal examinations were normal. 

She had been on HAART (zidovudine, lamivudine, nevirapine) for 16 months with poor adherence (<70%). Viral load had fallen from 421 000 to 41 000 copies/mL, but CD4⁺ count decreased from 168 to 34 cells/µL. Full blood count showed microcytic hypochromic anaemia (packed cell volume 24%) and leukopenia (1.2 × 10³/µL). Three separate stool examinations—including modified Ziehl‑Neelsen stains for cryptosporidiosis and isosporiasis—were negative for parasites, bacteria, red or white blood cells. Serum potassium was 3.0 mmol/L and albumin 22 g/L; renal and liver function tests were otherwise normal. Chest X‑ray and abdominopelvic ultrasound were unremarkable. Hepatitis B and C serologies and a blood film for malaria parasites were negative. 

She received rehydration, empiric antimicrobial therapy for infectious diarrhoea (albendazole, ciprofloxacin, tinidazole), oral fluconazole for thrush, prophylactic co‑trimoxazole, multivitamins and haematinics.

case_prompt:
A 45‑year‑old man presented to the surgery clinic with a 30‑day history of abdominal fullness, poor appetite, and fatigue. He denied trauma, gastrointestinal disease, weight loss, or recent travel. Past medical history was notable for acute renal failure two months earlier, treated with dialysis via a jugular catheter; renal function subsequently normalized.

On examination he was asthenic, afebrile (36.7 °C), with blood pressure 130/80 mm Hg, heart rate 80 bpm, respiratory rate 16/min. Heart sounds were muffled, lungs clear, abdomen soft and non‑tender, spleen palpable 4 cm below the costal margin, no hepatomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Neurologic exam was normal.

Laboratory workup—including CBC, liver enzymes, thyroid studies, malaria smear, kala‑azar test, mononucleosis antibodies, ANA, Coombs test, blood cultures, HIV and hepatitis serologies, ECG, urinalysis, electrolytes, and creatinine—was unremarkable except for a positive rheumatoid factor. Abdominal sonography showed isolated splenomegaly. MRI of the chest and abdomen, upper GI endoscopy, and bone‑marrow aspiration/biopsy were all normal. Because of progressive splenomegaly, a diagnostic splenectomy was performed; pathology revealed no specific lesion or abscess.

Three months after splenectomy the patient developed chest pain and was referred to cardiology. Physical examination revealed a grade 3/6 diastolic murmur at the aortic area and conjunctival hemorrhage. Two‑dimensional echocardiography demonstrated an oscillating hypermobile mass (vegetation) on the aortic valve and severe aortic regurgitation. Coronary angiography was normal, and blood cultures remained negative.

3. Multiple minor Duke criteria are present: predisposing cardiac procedure (prior jugular catheter dialysis), fever absent but inflammatory marker implied by rheumatoid factor positivity, and vascular phenomena (conjunctival hemorrhage). | "Our patient presented with one major criterion and three minor criteria, thus satisfying the Duke criteria for definite endocarditis."
4. Blood cultures are repeatedly negative, raising the possibility of culture‑negative endocarditis, but does not exclude infection. | "Blood cultures were negative."
5. Non‑infective causes (e.g., Libman‑Sacks endocarditis) are unlikely because ANA and other autoimmune markers are normal. | "anti‑nuclear factor... normal."
6. Rheumatic heart disease is unlikely given the absence of a rheumatic fever history and normal inflammatory serologies. | "Only rheumatoid factor was positive."
7. Initial extensive infectious workup for splenomegaly (malaria, kala‑azar, mononucleosis, HIV, hepatitis) was negative, ruling out those as sources of the later cardiac findings. | "malaria smear, kala‑azar, infectious mononucleosis Ab, ... Serology for HIV, hepatitis and other infections ... all showed normal findings."

case_prompt:
A 32‑year‑old Caucasian man returned two days ago from a one‑month business trip to the Democratic Republic of Congo. He presented to the Infectious Diseases Unit with a 48‑hour history of high fever, headache, nausea, and epigastric pain. He had not taken malaria prophylaxis. On admission his temperature was 37.1 °C, pulse 112/min, blood pressure 120/60 mm Hg, and peripheral oxygen saturation 99 %. Laboratory testing (Table 1) showed mild leukocytosis and anemia; hepatic enzymes were within normal limits. A peripheral blood smear was positive for *Plasmodium falciparum* with 0.2 % parasitemia. Chest X‑ray and electrocardiogram were normal. He was treated with the artemether‑lumefantrine combination (Riamet) according to manufacturer recommendations (six‑dose regimen). Within 48 hours he became afebrile and a repeat smear was negative; he was discharged in good condition after 72 hours.

Fourteen days later he returned with a 48‑hour history of high fever (39.6 °C) and headache. Vital signs showed temperature 39.6 °C; other parameters were stable. Laboratory tests again demonstrated mild leukocytosis, anemia, and hepatic enzymes similar to the previous values. Blood cultures for bacteria and fungi were negative. A repeat peripheral blood smear was positive for *Plasmodium falciparum* with 2 % parasitemia. He was started on oral quinine sulfate 600 mg three times daily together with doxycycline 100 mg twice daily.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Recrudescence of malaria after artemisinin‑based therapy is suggested by the recurrence of fever and a positive *P. falciparum* smear despite prior clearance | "Blood smear was performed and resulted positive for Plasmodium falciparum with 2% parasitemia."
2. Reinfection acquired during travel is considered because the patient could have been exposed to a new infective bite during the same trip | "Two hypothesis were made: the first was that the patient's second episode was a re‑infection rather than a recrudescence..."
3. Lumefantrine resistance is entertained given recent reports of ACT failure in Southeast Asia | "...high failure rates were seen in Cambodia (13,5% in 2006), where the emergence of lumefantrine resistance could not be excluded..."
4. Inadequate drug absorption leading to sub‑therapeutic lumefantrine levels is another possible cause, despite correct dosing with meals | "...low plasma concentration of lumefantrine for an unrecognized patient's defect in intestinal absorption rather than an incorrect drug assumption..."
5. Bacterial or fungal sepsis is ruled out as blood cultures were negative and chest X‑ray/ECG were normal | "Blood cultures for bacteria and fungi were negative."
6. Other non‑malarial causes of fever (e.g., viral hepatitis, urticaria) are less likely because hepatic enzymes remained stable and no other organ system involvement was reported. | "hepatic enzymes were substantially similar to his previous values."

case_prompt:
A 54‑year‑old Ugandan male presented to Kenyatta National Hospital after being treated for severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria with intravenous quinine at a local facility. Two days after the onset of malaria treatment, he developed episodic headache, pain, numbness, coldness, and swelling of his extremities, followed by progressive darkening of the digits of his toes and hands. On arrival he was conscious, alert, oriented, but lethargic and unable to walk. He denied smoking, alcohol use, diabetes, hypertension, or prior vascular disease; his past medical history was notable only for multiple prior malaria episodes, and his father had died of stroke.

Physical examination revealed fever; abdominal, cardiovascular, respiratory, and neurological examinations were otherwise unremarkable. The skin over the affected limbs was cold, dry, wrinkled, and markedly darkened with a clear proximal demarcation; pain was present proximal to the discoloration and absent distally. Peripheral pulses were absent in the dorsalis pedis arteries. Laboratory studies showed: negative ELISA for HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and VDRL; normal urea, electrolytes, and creatinine; prolonged prothrombin time (19 sec), PT index 74 %, INR 1.36; macrocytic normochromic anemia (Hb 9.0 g/dL, MCV 89.9 fL, Hct 33.2 %); white‑blood‑cell count 4.39 × 10⁹/L with differential within normal ranges. An echocardiogram demonstrated normal cardiac chambers with type 1 left‑ventricular dysfunction and mild tricuspid regurgitation.

1. Infectious vasculitic or thrombotic etiologies (e.g., HIV‑associated vasculitis, hepatitis‑related coagulopathy, syphilis) were considered but excluded by serology. | "Investigations tested negative for HIV, HBV, HCV, and VDRL on ELISA."
2. Primary arterial occlusion from atherosclerotic disease or embolism was unlikely given the patient’s lack of cardiovascular risk factors, normal coronary/vascular imaging, and the presence of normal cardiac function on echocardiography. | "An echocardiogram was normal except for type 1 left ventricular dysfunction and mild tricuspid regurgitation."
3. Consumptive coagulopathy/DIC was evaluated; the modestly prolonged PT/INR suggested some coagulation disturbance but not the severe derangement typical of overt DIC. | "Clotting profile showed a prolonged Prothrombin time of 19 sec, Prothrombin time index of 74 %, and an INR of 1.36."
4. Hematologic causes (e.g., severe anemia, leukopenia) were present but insufficient to explain the abrupt, symmetric distal necrosis. | "A haemogram showed macrocytic normochromic anaemia (Hb 9.03 g/dL, MCV 89.9 fL …)."
5. The pattern of cold, dry, wrinkled skin with a sharp proximal demarcation and absent distal pulses, occurring after severe falciparum malaria, is characteristic of symmetrical peripheral gangrene, a non‑vasculitic, thrombotic microvascular phenomenon. | "The overlying skin cold, dry, wrinkled, and was darkened with a clear line of proximal demarcation… Pain was present in the regions proximal to the discolouration, and absent in the distal regions."

A 24‑year‑old female nurse was admitted to the emergency department on July 4, 2001 with fever, nausea, and general malaise. She had no notable past medical history except a spontaneously regressive Schönlein‑Henoch purpura in infancy. On admission, after paracetamol, her axillary temperature was 37.6 °C. She was slightly jaundiced, reported a mild headache, and denied meningeal signs. Her abdomen was depressible but tender. Urinalysis showed no hematuria or infection. Laboratory studies revealed thrombocytopenia (47.4 × 10³/µL), markedly elevated transaminases (AST 307 U/L, ALT 239 U/L), hyperbilirubinemia (total bilirubin 58 µmol/L), and a mildly raised γ‑GT (57 U/L). An abdominal ultrasound was normal. 

The patient had not traveled outside France except a brief trip to the United Kingdom years earlier and a recent car vacation in the south of France (June 23‑26). On June 21, while drawing blood from a patient being evaluated for malaria, she sustained a deep needlestick injury with an 18‑gauge peripheral venous catheter. The injury pierced her glove and entered the anterior left wrist. She reported the incident to occupational medicine the same day and was tested for HIV and hepatitis C antibodies (both negative) and confirmed immune to hepatitis B.

Ten days after the exposure (July 1) she developed fatigue, malaise, and fever (temperature reduced to 38.6 °C with paracetamol). After a brief asymptomatic interval on July 2, she experienced a second fever spike with myalgia, and on July 3 she was unable to work because of generalized pain and a temperature of 39 °C. Her mother, a biologist, learned of the needlestick and the index patient’s suspected malaria and requested a blood smear to be performed at a private laboratory. The patient was admitted to Bichat‑Claude Bernard University Hospital with suspected malaria, and a repeat blood smear was ordered.

2. HIV infection considered but excluded by negative baseline HIV test. | "She was tested for HIV ... results were negative at baseline."
3. Urinary or renal source of infection considered but excluded by normal urinalysis. | "Urinalysis did not show hematuria or signs of urinary infection."
4. Intra‑abdominal pathology considered but excluded by normal abdominal ultrasonography. | "Result of an abdominal echogram were normal."

Malaria became the leading diagnosis due to the temporal relation of the needlestick from a patient suspected of malaria, incubation period consistent with Plasmodium infection, and compatible clinical‑laboratory picture (fever, thrombocytopenia, hepatic dysfunction). | "The mother ... was aware that her daughter had sustained a needlestick injury while drawing blood from a patient in whom malaria was suspected."

case_prompt: A 30‑year‑old woman of Kenyan origin, currently 28 weeks pregnant, returned to France on June 1, 2001 after a visit to Kenya. case_prompt: A 30‑year‑old, 54‑kg female presented with severe right elbow and forearm pain following trauma. Distal neurovascular compression signs were noted in the injured limb. For the preceding 3 days she had intermittent high‑grade fever with chills, rigors, and generalized weakness. No history of cardiopulmonary disease or drug allergy was reported. On arrival her Glasgow Coma Scale was 15/15; vital signs were HR 118/min, BP 124/72 mmHg, RR 15/min, and she was febrile. Examination revealed pallor, normal cardiovascular and respiratory systems, and hepatosplenomegaly on abdominal palpation. Airway assessment was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 6.3 g/dL, total leukocyte count 14,600 /cmm; serum electrolytes, liver and renal function tests, and random glucose were within normal limits. A parasitological blood examination was ordered in addition to operative management of the fracture and neurovascular compromise. Routine monitors were applied, and the patient was pre‑medicated with IV fentanyl 2 µg/kg. Rapid‑sequence induction was performed with thiopentone and rocuronium, followed by oral intubation with a 7.5‑mm PVC cuffed tube. Anesthesia was maintained with isoflurane, vecuronium, and fentanyl. The intra‑operative course was stable for one hour.

Absence of cardiopulmonary abnormalities, normal renal and hepatic panels, and normal glucose reduce the likelihood of bacterial sepsis, viral hemorrhagic fevers, or metabolic crises. | "There was no history of any cardio‑respiratory abnormality... serum electrolytes, liver function test, renal function test and random blood sugar were within normal limits."

6. Trauma‑related causes (e.g., hemorrhagic shock, compartment syndrome) cannot explain the systemic fever, hepatosplenomegaly, and profound anemia without external blood loss. | (Implied by lack of mention of external bleeding and normal vitals aside from tachycardia.)

case_prompt: A 37‑year‑old woman returned to France in March 2004 after an 18‑day trip to Guinea, Senegal, and Sierra Leone. Three days before her return she developed fever, chills, and myalgia and self‑treated with aspirin and paracetamol; she had taken no malaria prophylaxis. The day after returning, her condition worsened with diarrhea and extreme weakness that progressed to inability to walk. Ten days after return she was admitted to a local hospital, where thick and thin blood films revealed 3 % parasitemia with *Plasmodium falciparum*. She was started on intravenous quinine and oral doxycycline (2 g per day). Three days later she remained febrile, developed conjunctival jaundice, vomiting, insomnia, and moderate hemorrhagic manifestations (epistaxis, blood in urine and feces). She was transferred to the Infectious Diseases Unit in Marseille. On admission her temperature was 39.5 °C and hepatosplenomegaly was noted. Laboratory studies showed disseminated intravascular coagulation with a platelet count of 22,000 /µL, prothrombin time 54 % above control, activated clotting time 51 s (control 34 s), fibrinogen 0.9 g/dL, and elevated AST and ALT (both 80 U/L). Because she had returned from a tropical country with fever, viral serologic tests were ordered.

1. Acute malaria confirmed by peripheral smear explains fever and parasitemia but does not fully account for severe hemorrhagic manifestations and DIC | "Thick and thin blood films showed 3% parasitemia with Plasmodium falciparum."
2. Persistent high‑grade fever, conjunctival jaundice, and hemorrhagic signs raise suspicion for another tropical infection such as dengue | "Three days later, she was still febrile and had conjunctival jaundice, vomiting, insomnia, and moderate hemorrhagic manifestations (epistaxis, blood in urine and feces)."

Laboratory evidence of DIC (marked thrombocytopenia, prolonged PT and APTT, low fibrinogen) is characteristic of severe dengue infection (dengue hemorrhagic fever) and is less typical of uncomplicated falciparum malaria | "Biologic analyses showed disseminated intravascular coagulation with platelet count of 22,000/mL, an elevated prothrombin time (54% higher than the control value), a longer activated clotting time (51 seconds versus a control value of 34 seconds), a fibrinogen level of 0.9 g/dL..."

5. The clinicians ordered viral serologies because fever after tropical travel warrants broad screening, indicating they considered dengue among other viruses | "viral serologic tests were performed because the patient had returned from a tropical country with a fever."

Other tropical infections (e.g., yellow fever, chikungunya, leptospirosis, typhoid) were considered but are less consistent with the combination of high parasitemia, DIC, and the specific hemorrhagic pattern; the authors note prior reports of dengue co‑infection with bacteria or viruses but not with malaria, highlighting the uniqueness of this case | "Only 6 published studies reported concurrent infection with dengue virus and a bacterium ... or with a virus such as Chikungunya virus."

case_prompt:
A 55‑year‑old man, lawyer, was admitted because of epigastric and right hypochondrial abdominal pain, intermittent night sweats, and a 3 kg involuntary weight loss over the preceding 8 months. He drinks ≈70 g alcohol/day and has chronic antral gastritis. He travels 18 months prior to admission to Nepal in poor‑hygiene settings. Medications include omeprazole 20 mg daily.

One year before admission the night‑sweats and abdominal pain began; routine labs (Table 1) showed normal HIV, HBV, HCV, and VDRL serologies; past CMV and EBV infections; two negative blood cultures; transthoracic echocardiography showed a well‑functioning prosthetic valve, aortic dilatation, and no vegetations; abdominal ultrasound revealed a hepatic biliary cyst. Sertraline was started for depression.

Four months before admission the pain persisted; repeat labs were again normal, protein electrophoresis was within limits. During a work trip to Brazil he developed lower‑limb leukocytoclastic vasculitis.

Because night sweats worsened and weight loss continued, he was admitted. On exam: temperature 37.1 °C, pulse 75 bpm, BP 130/75 mmHg, RR 15/min, SpO₂ 98% on room air, good oral health, no lymphadenopathy, no JVD, heart sounds with mechanical S2 and a grade II/VI systolic murmur at the aortic area, lungs clear, no peripheral stigmata of infective endocarditis. ECG: sinus rhythm with nonspecific repolarization changes.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, platelets 139 × 10³/µL, AST 61 U/L, ALT 73 U/L, ALP 110 U/L, ferritin 418 ng/mL, CRP 4.1 mg/L, ESR 15 mm/h, rheumatoid factor 318 U/mL; electrolytes and urinalysis normal. Serologies negative for HIV, HBV, HCV, Schistosoma, Borrelia, Rickettsia, Leishmania, VDRL, CMV, EBV, Toxoplasma (past infections only). Widal and Huddleson reactions, and malaria smear were negative. Two sets of blood cultures showed no growth. Protein electrophoresis demonstrated an IgG‑κ/λ monoclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. Abdominal ultrasound showed mild hepatosplenomegaly. Contrast CT of thorax‑abdomen‑pelvis confirmed hepatosplenomegaly and revealed gastric wall calcification.

Transesophageal echocardiography identified two very small echodense images on the aortic prosthetic cups, interpreted as possible surgical‑related changes or fibrosis. Ophthalmic fundus exam was normal. Liver biopsy showed infectious hepatitis without pathognomonic features and without the fibrin‑ring granulomas described in Q fever.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Typical bacterial infective endocarditis – considered due to prosthetic valve but ruled out by repeatedly negative blood cultures and absence of vegetations on transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography. | "Two sets of blood culture specimens exhibited no growth." and "no valve vegetations."
2. Viral hepatitis (HBV, HCV) – considered because of elevated transaminases but excluded by negative serologies. | "Serologies for HIV, HBV, HCV, Schistosoma, Borrelia, Rickettsia, Leishmania, and VDRL were negative."
3. Other zoonotic infections (Leishmania, Rickettsia, Borrelia, Schistosoma) – evaluated given travel history, but serologies were negative. | "Serologies for HIV, HBV, HCV, Schistosoma, Borrelia, Rickettsia, Leishmania, and VDRL were negative."
4. Typhoid fever and malaria – considered in the differential for prolonged systemic symptoms; both Widal/Huddleson reactions and Plasmodium smears were negative. | "Widal and Huddlesson reactions and research of Plasmodium spp were negative as well."
5. Non‑specific infectious hepatitis – liver biopsy showed hepatitis without characteristic Q‑fever granulomas, providing no definitive etiology. | "Liver biopsy revealed infectious hepatitis without pathognomonic features ... and with no fibrin ring granulomas described in Q fever."
6. Chronic Q fever – supported by (a) extremely high anti‑phase I IgG titer, (b) detection of C. burnetii DNA in liver tissue by PCR, and (c) fulfillment of modified Duke criteria (major serology plus minor criteria: prosthetic valve, positive RF, leukocytoclastic vasculitis, echocardiographic abnormalities). | "It revealed a high anti‑phase I IgG with an end‑point titer of 204,800 suggestive of chronic Q fever ... Specific DNA was detected in liver tissue ... Patient met one major and three minor criteria for Q‑fever endocarditis."

case_prompt:
A previously healthy 12‑month‑old boy was referred from a clinic to Kintampo Municipal Hospital (Kintampo, Ghana) after a 2‑day history of fever and vomiting. At the clinic he was diagnosed with severe anaemia secondary to malaria and received IV fluids, intramuscular quinine and a blood transfusion, but his condition deteriorated and he began passing bloody stools. Two days later he was referred to the hospital.

On arrival his conscious level was reduced; temperature was 39.5 °C, pulse 110 beats/min, respiration 60 breaths/min. He was pale; abdominal examination was normal except for periumbilical tenderness. Blood film was positive for malaria parasites. Haemoglobin was 4.2 g/dL and white‑blood‑cell count 16.4 × 10⁹/L. Neither Widal test nor stool cultures were performed. Supine abdominal X‑ray showed air‑fluid levels; erect chest X‑ray showed no subphrenic gas. Treatment for severe anaemia secondary to malaria and presumed typhoid continued with intranasal oxygen, IV fluids, whole‑blood transfusion, paracetamol, IM quinine, IV gentamicin and IV metronidazole.

After a further 2 days the child remained semiconscious and febrile, still passing blood clots in his stool. Despite another transfusion haemoglobin was 4.3 g/dL and abdominal examination remained unremarkable. An exploratory laparotomy was therefore performed.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Severe malaria causing profound anemia and gastrointestinal bleeding was considered because “Blood film was positive for malaria parasites” and the child had a haemoglobin of 4.2 g/dL with persistent fever. | “Blood film was positive for malaria parasites. Haemoglobin was 4.2 g/dL…”

A perforated hollow viscus (e.g., typhoid ulcer) was suspected because of “air‑fluid levels” on supine abdominal X‑ray, yet the erect chest X‑ray “showed no subphrenic gas,” making a large free perforation unlikely. | “Supine abdominal X‑ray showed air fluid levels. Erect chest X‑ray showed no subphrenic gas.”
4. Helicobacter pylori–related duodenal ulcer was a possible source of bleeding, but the authors note that “no test for Helicobacter pylori was performed,” leaving it unconfirmed. | “Due to resource constraint no test for Helicobacter pylori was performed.”
5. Other causes of lower GI bleeding in infants (e.g., Meckel’s diverticulum) were not discussed in the report and thus were not pursued. | (Not applicable – absent from article)

case_prompt:
A 29‑year‑old male from rural Southern Sudan, on continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis for two years, presented in May 2010 with four days of fever, dry cough, dyspnea, and abdominal discomfort. He appeared very ill, pale, and dehydrated. Vital signs: temperature 38.4 °C, respiratory rate 30/min, pulse 120 bpm, blood pressure 70/50 mmHg. Physical exam revealed tender submandibular lymph nodes; chest and cardiac examinations were unremarkable. Abdominal exam showed bilateral flank tenderness without guarding or organomegaly; the peritoneal catheter exit site was clean. No skin lesions, arthritis, or neurologic deficits were noted.

Laboratory studies: WBC 13,100/µL with 90 % neutrophils, hemoglobin 5.6 g/dL, platelets 160,000/µL, ESR > 150 mm/hr, serum albumin 1.9 g/dL, blood urea 168 mg/dL, creatinine 9.2 mg/dL; liver enzymes and electrolytes were normal. Peritoneal effluent contained 50 WBC/µL and appeared clear. Malaria blood film was negative; serologic tests for Brucella and Salmonella were negative.

The patient was admitted, rehydrated, and received 4 units of packed red blood cells. Empiric antibiotics with ceftriaxone and ciprofloxacin were started. Blood and peritoneal effluent cultures were obtained. After five days, the aerobic brain‑heart‑infusion broth became turbid; Gram stain showed tiny gram‑negative pleomorphic bacilli. Subcultures yielded non‑hemolytic, mucoid gray‑white colonies on chocolate agar, faint growth on blood agar, and no growth on MacConkey agar. A Giemsa‑stained smear demonstrated a bipolar organism. API‑20E and API‑20NE panels failed to identify the isolate but excluded Haemophilus, Actinobacillus, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, and Kingella species.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Considered malaria due to fever and anemia but excluded by negative blood film. | "Blood film for malaria was negative..."
2. Considered brucellosis because of rural exposure and undifferentiated fever; excluded by negative serology. | "serological tests for Brucella ... were negative"
3. Considered salmonellosis (enteric fever) given fever and gastrointestinal symptoms; excluded by negative serology. | "serological tests for ... Salmonella."
4. Initial broad bacterial sepsis was entertained, prompting empiric ceftriaxone and ciprofloxacin. | "started empiric antibiotic treatment with ceftriaxone, and ciprofloxacin."
5. Gram‑negative pleomorphic bacilli on direct smear suggested a fastidious organism, narrowing the field away from typical Enterobacteriaceae. | "Gram stain revealed tiny gram negative pleomorphic bacilli."
6. Bipolar (safety‑pin) appearance on Giemsa smear pointed toward organisms such as Francisella, Yersinia, or Bartonella. | "Giemsa stain smear revealed a bipolar organism."
7. Growth only on chocolate agar with faint growth on blood agar and no growth on MacConkey ruled out lactose‑fermenting enterics and many non‑fastidious gram‑negatives. | "non hemolytic mucoid gray white colonies on the chocolate agar, very faint growth ... on the blood agar, and no growth ... on the McConkey agar plate."
8. API‑20E/20NE panels failed to match any common gram‑negative rod, eliminating Haemophilus, Actinobacillus, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, and Kingella. | "Both failed to identify the organism but confirmed that it did not belong to hemophilus, actinobacillus, cardiobacterium, ekinella or kingella species."
9. The combination of pleomorphic Gram‑negative bacilli, bipolar staining, chocolate‑agar growth pattern, and exclusion of other organisms matched the known profile of Francisella tularensis. | "Thus, the organism was identified as Francisella tularensis."

case_prompt:
A 29‑year‑old previously healthy man was admitted to a peripheral hospital with a 1‑week history of fever and jaundice. Laboratory studies showed anemia (Hb 8.8 g/dL), thrombocytopenia (55 × 10³/µL), renal impairment (serum creatinine 1.5 mg/dL) and direct hyperbilirubinemia (total bilirubin 3.9 mg/dL, direct 1.9 mg/dL). Peripheral smear revealed schizonts of *Plasmodium vivax*; antigen testing for *P. falciparum* was negative. He received artesunate and clindamycin for 7 days and was discharged when afebrile, although his platelet count and renal function had not improved.

Two weeks later (one week after discharge) he returned with 3 days of vomiting, abdominal pain and oliguria. He denied fever, diarrhea, rash, bleeding or altered mental status and had no history of quinine use. He was hypertensive and pale; systemic examination was unremarkable except for a systolic murmur. Labs now showed severe anemia (Hb 4.8 g/dL), persistent thrombocytopenia (61 × 10³/µL) and worsening azotemia (creatinine 8.3 mg/dL). Peripheral smear demonstrated schistocytes; reticulocyte count was 13 %; LDH was 1242 U/L and indirect bilirubin was elevated, consistent with ongoing microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. Urinalysis revealed microscopic hematuria and proteinuria of 3.75 g/day. Coagulation studies were normal. Complement testing showed low C3 (50 mg/dL) with normal C4. ANA and HIV ELISA were negative; hepatitis B surface antigen and anti‑HCV antibodies were also negative.

He was started on five daily plasma‑exchange sessions (1.5 plasma volume each) with fresh‑frozen plasma replacement, antihypertensive therapy, intermittent hemodialysis, and packed red‑cell transfusions. After plasma exchange, platelet count rose to 150 × 10³/µL, hemoglobin stabilized at 6 g/dL and then increased, LDH fell to 206 U/L, and serum creatinine improved to 5.5 mg/dL, allowing dialysis independence. By the fourth week, hematologic remission persisted (Hb 9.1 g/dL, platelets 163 × 10³/µL) and C3 normalized.

1. Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury suggest a thrombotic microangiopathy spectrum. | "Presence of schistocytes on peripheral smear, elevated reticulocyte count (13%), elevated serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH 1242 U/L) and indirect hyperbilirubinaemia indicated ongoing microangiopathic hemolytic anemia."

case_prompt:
During October 2012, a previously healthy 31‑year‑old Canadian man presented to a Toronto hospital after 3 days of fever and severe headache. He had returned 10 days earlier from a 10‑day work trip to South Sudan, where he did not use malaria chemoprophylaxis but slept under an insecticide‑treated net.  

Initial assessment showed a blood smear positive for *Plasmodium falciparum* with 22 % parasitemia (1,100,000 parasites/µL). Laboratory values were: bilirubin 88 µmol/L (ref 5‑17), AST 105 U/L (ref 10‑38), creatinine 130 µmol/L (ref 80‑115), hemoglobin 144 g/L (ref 140‑160), platelets 17 × 10⁹/L (ref 150‑450). He received one dose each of doxycycline, atovaquone/proguanil, and artemether/lumefantrine but vomited within an hour. He was transferred to a tertiary ICU for exchange transfusion and started on intravenous artesunate (2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, 24, and 48 h) followed by a 3‑day oral atovaquone/proguanil course. Chest radiograph was normal, blood cultures were negative, and hemoglobin on admission was 125 g/L. Parasitemia became undetectable within 36 h, and he was discharged after 5 days.  

Four days after discharge, he returned with fever and “merlot‑colored” urine beginning 2 days after discharge. On re‑admission he was jaundiced. Labs showed bilirubin 89 µmol/L, LDH 1,976 U/L (ref 120‑240), hemoglobin 81 g/L, and marked hemoglobinuria; repeat thick and thin smears were negative for *Plasmodium*. Over the next days he required eight red‑cell transfusions to keep hemoglobin >75 g/L. Hemolysis persisted with a nadir hemoglobin of 68 g/L, LDH peak 3,429 U/L, and low haptoglobin (<0.12 g/L). Glucose‑6‑phosphate dehydrogenase was normal. Hemolysis resolved spontaneously 10 days after onset. At 6‑week follow‑up he was asymptomatic with hemoglobin 135 g/L. Testing did not reveal red‑cell alloantibodies, and serology was positive for schistosomiasis, strongyloidiasis, and Q‑fever—considered past infections and not contributory.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction considered but excluded because “pre‑ and post‑transfusion and follow‑up testing did not show evidence of red blood cell alloantibodies, making the possibility of a delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction unlikely.”  
2. G6PD deficiency evaluated and ruled out as “his glucose‑6‑phosphate dehydrogenase level was within reference range.”  
3. Ongoing malaria infection was excluded by negative blood smears: “multiple thick and thin blood smears were negative for *Plasmodium* spp.” and parasitemia had been undetectable within 36 h of the first admission.  
4. Prior parasitic/zoonotic infections (schistosomiasis, strongyloidiasis, Q‑fever) were deemed irrelevant: “Serologic tests showed that he was also positive for causative organisms… These diagnoses were consistent with past infections and were not considered to be contributory to the current severe hemolytic event.”  
5. Hemolysis due to other antimalarial agents (doxycycline, atovaquone/proguanil, artemether/lumefantrine) was deemed unlikely because “severe intravascular hemolysis has rarely been reported in relationship to these agents.”  
6. Drug‑induced immune hemolysis was considered but not substantiated: “We cannot exclude a potential role for drug‑induced immune hemolysis,” yet no alloantibodies or other immunologic markers were identified.

Peripheral smear demonstrated anisocytosis, poikilocytosis, polychromasia, micro‑ and macrocytosis, occasional Cabbot rings, Howell‑Jolly bodies, schistocytes, and hypersegmented neutrophils. 2. Breakpoint: End the presented information just before the PCR result is disclosed. Include history, exam, initial labs (including PPD, negative serologies, negative sputum AFB), imaging showing splenic abscesses, and note that aspiration was performed and specimens sent for microbiological/molecular testing, but omit the statement that PCR was positive.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished tuberculosis from pyogenic abscesses and other infectious etiologies by (a) lack of response to broad‑spectrum antibiotics, (b) negative bacterial cultures and Gram stain, (c) positive tuberculin skin test, (d) exclusion of other endemic infections via serology, and (e) definitive detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA by PCR on aspirated pus despite negative AFB staining.
case_prompt:
A 22‑year‑old nonsmoker, nonalcoholic male from a middle‑class family in the midwestern part of Nepal was referred to our tertiary center with intermittent fever, pain in the left lower chest, occasional nausea and vomiting, anorexia, and weight loss of three‑week duration. Symptoms did not improve with two weeks of broad‑spectrum oral and then parenteral antibiotics at a local hospital. Fever was associated with chills and rigors. Left lower chest pain was continuous with radiation to the left shoulder. There was no associated cough, shortness of breath, altered bowel or bladder habits, jaundice, headache, vomiting, joint pain, or any skin nodules. There was no history of drug abuse or sexual promiscuity. There was no history of diabetes mellitus and no past or family history of TB.  

On examination, the patient's body temperature was 102 °F, pulse 100 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, regular. Chest examination showed tenderness in the left infra‑axillary region and normal bilateral vesicular breath sounds without any additional sounds. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds without murmur. Abdominal examination showed a soft, tender left upper quadrant with Traube's space dullness; the spleen and liver were not palpable.  

Laboratory studies: complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, posteroanterior chest X‑ray, and echocardiography were normal. ESR was elevated at 58 mm/h. Purified protein derivative (PPD) was 12 mm. Three consecutive sputum samples were negative for acid‑fast bacilli (AFB). Spot serologic tests for HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C were non‑reactive. Three consecutive bacterial blood cultures and a urine culture showed no growth. Serologic tests for malaria, leptospirosis, brucellosis, and leishmaniasis were negative.  

Imaging: abdominal ultrasound revealed a 5.3 × 4.0 × 3.5 cm hypoechoic lesion at the lower pole of the spleen communicating with a ~40 ml perisplenic collection, and a 3.9 × 3.0 × 2.8 cm collection at the superior pole also communicating with perisplenic fluid. Contrast‑enhanced CT of the abdomen showed two perisplenic hypodense collections (6.9 × 5.1 × 3.2 cm inferiorly and 5.2 × 4.0 × 3.0 cm superiorly) connected with splenic parenchymal collections, suggestive of multiple splenic abscesses with perisplenic extensions.  

The patient did not improve with three weeks of empiric parenteral broad‑spectrum antibiotics. Diagnostic and therapeutic ultrasound‑guided aspiration removed approximately 30 ml of pus, which was sent for microbiological and molecular examination for Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Primary splenic tuberculosis considered because of prolonged fever, weight loss, positive tuberculin skin test, splenic abscesses in an endemic region, and lack of response to broad‑spectrum antibiotics. | "PPD was 12 mm." … "PCR for MTB was positive."
2. Pyogenic bacterial splenic abscess considered due to imaging of abscesses, but ruled out by negative blood, urine, and sputum cultures, negative Gram stain, and failure to respond to antibiotics. | "Three consecutive bacterial blood cultures and a urine culture showed no growth." … "The patient did not improve with three weeks of empiric parenteral broad‑spectrum antibiotics."
3. Brucellosis considered given systemic symptoms, but excluded by negative serology. | "Serologic tests for ... brucellosis ... were negative."
4. Leishmaniasis considered and excluded by negative serology. | "Serologic tests for ... leishmaniasis ... were negative."
5. Malaria and leptospirosis considered because of fever and were excluded by negative serology. | "Serologic tests for malaria, leptospirosis ... were negative."
6. HIV infection considered as a predisposing factor for atypical infections, but excluded by non‑reactive serology. | "Spot serological tests for human immunodeficiency virus ... were nonreactive."
7. Tuberculosis confirmed by molecular detection of MTB DNA in aspirated pus despite negative AFB staining, supporting a diagnosis of primary splenic TB. | "The pus was negative for AFB staining; however, PCR for MTB was positive."

case_prompt: A 29‑year‑old man was consulted for a sudden, febrile‑associated decline in visual acuity that was more severe in the right eye. On examination he was prostrate; visual acuity allowed him to see a waving hand with the right eye and a tenth of that with the left eye, with no improvement when using both eyes. Bilateral reactive mydriasis was present. Intra‑ocular pressure measured 11 mmHg (right) and 13 mmHg (left). Funduscopic examination revealed rounded retinal hemorrhages, some with clear centers, scattered throughout the retina and more pronounced in the right eye; bleaching areas of the retina in the macular region, again more marked on the right; and discoloration of peripheral vessels in the inferior temporal quadrant of the right eye. Fluorescein angiography showed intra‑retinal hemorrhages and retinal ischemia in the inferior temporal region of the right eye. A thick blood smear demonstrated 2 000 trophozoites per field. Complete blood count showed a microcytic hypochromic anemia with hemoglobin 11 g/L and no immature cells on peripheral smear.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Malaria confirmed by parasitologic evidence | "Thick smear was positive with two thousand trophozoides by field."
2. Lack of immature cells makes hematologic malignancy unlikely | "We noted a lack of immature cells in the blood smear."
3. Retinal findings consistent with malaria‑associated retinopathy rather than other infectious retinopathies | "Rounded retinal hemorrhages... bleaching areas of the retina in the macular area... fluorescein angiography revealed intra‑retinal hemorrhages, retinal ischemia."

2. Ideal Breakpoint: Include all presentation details, vital signs, physical findings, laboratory and imaging results, and the negative infectious work‑up (Leptospira, dengue, malaria) up to the point where the authors state “in view of encephalitis, hepatitis, myocarditis, myositis, and coagulopathy … she was suspected to have Coxsackie infection.” Do NOT include the subsequent statement of a positive Coxsackie IgM ELISA, so the learner must deduce the diagnosis before it is revealed.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors ruled out bacterial meningitis (CSF sterile, lymphocytic, normal glucose), leptospirosis, dengue, and malaria (negative serologies). They highlighted the constellation of multi‑organ involvement (encephalitis, hepatitis, myocarditis, myositis, coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia) together with a prior vesicular exanthem, pointing toward an enteroviral (Coxsackie) etiology.
case_prompt:
A 5½‑year‑old girl was hospitalized with fever for 2 days, non‑projectile vomiting for 1 day, and one episode of generalized clonic convulsion without post‑ictal drowsiness. Two months earlier she had a vesicular rash on both hands and feet that resolved spontaneously in 2–3 days, leaving tiny hypopigmented macules. There was no focal neurological deficit, altered sensorium, and developmental milestones were normal. She was up to date on immunizations.

On examination she was tachycardic (HR 110/min) and hypotensive (94/70 mmHg, systolic < 5th centile) with normal perfusion; respiratory rate was normal. General exam revealed tiny hypopigmented macules over the dorsum of both hands and on the feet. No meningeal signs were present. Mild hepatomegaly was noted; other systems were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12 g/dL, leukocyte count 13,700/µL (85 % neutrophils, 15 % lymphocytes), platelet count 130,000/µL, ESR 10 mm/h. CSF analysis: protein 83 mg/dL, glucose 79 mg/dL (serum glucose 129 mg/dL), 4 lymphocytes/hpf; bacterial culture negative, acid‑fast smear negative. Liver transaminases were elevated (AST 102 IU/L, ALT 78 IU/L). Serum creatinine 1.5 mg/dL; electrolytes and BUN normal. Coagulation studies were prolonged (PT 19.8 s, PTT 39.3 s) and serum ammonia was elevated (123 IU/L); blood glucose was low (38 mg/dL). Creatine phosphokinase was markedly elevated (2066 U/L) with CPK‑MB 13 ng/mL (normal ≤ 5.8 ng/mL). Echocardiography was normal.

Serologic testing for Leptospira IgM, dengue IgM, and malaria (OptiMAL) were negative. In view of encephalitis, hepatitis, myocarditis, myositis, and coagulopathy with thrombocytopenia and a previous rash, she was suspected to have Coxsackie infection.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial meningitis was considered but deemed unlikely because CSF showed only 4 lymphocytes, normal glucose, elevated protein, and cultures were negative. | "CSF bacterial culture did not grow any organism and smear for acid‑fast Bacillus was negative."
2. Leptospirosis was evaluated due to multi‑organ involvement, but serology was negative. | "Her Leptospira IgM ... negative."
3. Dengue infection was a differential given fever, thrombocytopenia, and transaminitis, yet IgM was negative. | "Her dengue IgM ... negative."
4. Malaria was considered because of fever and possible hepatic involvement, but rapid test was negative. | "OptiMAL test for malaria were negative."
5. Viral encephalitis (e.g., HSV, CMV) was a possibility, but the combination of myocarditis, myositis, hepatitis, coagulopathy, and prior vesicular exanthem pointed toward an enteroviral etiology rather than isolated CNS infection. | "In view of encephalitis, hepatitis, myocarditis, myositis, and coagulopathy with thrombocytopenia and a previous rash, she was suspected to have Coxsackie infection."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case’s primary mystery is spontaneous splenic rupture in a patient with sickle cell beta‑plus thalassemia, which is not included in the 21 SELECTED diseases list; therefore it is OUT_OF_SCOPE.
2. Ideal Breakpoint: Include presentation, physical exam, initial laboratory panel, sickle cell work‑up, and abdominal CT showing splenic subcapsular lacerations; stop before the sentence that declares “with the diagnosis of spontaneous splenic rupture…”.
3. Author's Analytic Distinctions: The authors ruled out common causes of splenic rupture—hematologic malignancy, hemophilia, malaria, EBV, CMV, HIV, hepatitis A‑C—by noting normal coagulation parameters, negative infectious serologies, and lack of hematologic abnormalities; the CT findings together with the sickle‑cell/beta‑thalassemia background led them to attribute the rupture to the underlying hemoglobinopathy.
case_prompt: A 32‑year‑old man presented with a 2‑day history of dull left upper quadrant pain. He denied trauma, fever, chills, sore throat, malaise, arthralgia, rash, or any bleeding. Past medical history was notable for an “unclear sickling disorder”; the patient reported sickle cell trait and childhood exchange transfusions. His mother had sickle cell disease. Vitals were stable. Physical exam revealed splenomegaly and mild tenderness in the left upper quadrant; no icterus, hepatomegaly, or lymphadenopathy was noted. Laboratory studies showed: WBC 10,400/µL, hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, hematocrit 41 %, MCV 66.8 fL, platelets 78,000/µL, aPTT 35.7 s, BUN 13 mg/dL, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, total bilirubin 2.2 mg/dL, AST 28 IU/L, ALT 33 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 56 IU/L. Further evaluation of microcytic anemia demonstrated a reticulocyte count of 1.96 %, haptoglobin 62 mg/dL, LDH 245 IU/L, serum iron 33 µg/dL, iron saturation 16 %, ferritin 269 ng/mL, and a positive sickle cell screen. Hemoglobin electrophoresis revealed 17.5 % HbA, 7.2 % HbA2, 73.8 % HbS, and 1.5 % HbF, consistent with sickle cell β⁺‑thalassemia. Abdominal CT demonstrated splenomegaly with multiple subcapsular lacerations and hematomas. No alternative cause for spontaneous splenic rupture was identified. Initial work‑up for hematologic malignancy, hemophilia, malaria, Epstein‑Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, HIV, and hepatitis A, B, C was negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Hematologic malignancy considered but deemed unlikely because leukocyte count was within normal limits and there were no peripheral smear abnormalities or lymphadenopathy. | "His symptomatology, physical examination, and initial lab tests were not consistent with the common causes of splenic rupture like hematological malignancies..."
2. Coagulopathy such as hemophilia excluded by normal aPTT and platelet count (though platelets were low, not indicative of hemophilia) and lack of personal/family bleeding history. | "...like hematological malignancies, hemophilia..."
3. Malaria ruled out by negative travel/history details and lack of fever or parasitemia; also not suggested by laboratory profile. | "...or malaria."
4. Viral infections (EBV, CMV, HIV, hepatitis A/B/C) excluded by negative serologic testing. | "Tests for Epstein‑Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, human immunodeficiency virus, and hepatitis A, B, and C viruses returned negative."
5. Traumatic rupture excluded by patient denial of recent trauma and absence of external injury. | "He denied any recent trauma."
6. Sickle cell β⁺‑thalassemia identified as the underlying hemoglobinopathy predisposing to splenic infarction and rupture, supported by electrophoresis results and prior exchange transfusions. | "Subsequent hemoglobin electrophoresis... was suggestive of sickle cell beta‑plus thalassemia."
7. Imaging confirmed splenic pathology consistent with spontaneous rupture (subcapsular lacerations, hematomas) without other intra‑abdominal pathology. | "CT scans of the abdomen showed splenomegaly with multiple splenic subcapsular lacerations and hematomas."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The post‑mortem PCR confirmed Lassa fever, which is not in the 21 SELECTED diseases list; therefore the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.
2. Ideal Breakpoint: Present the case up to the patient’s death on day 14, stopping before the statement that Lassa fever was confirmed by PCR. This provides all clinical, laboratory, and procedural data necessary for learners to generate a differential without revealing the final diagnosis.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished Lassa fever from malaria by noting persistent high‑grade fever despite appropriate antimalarial therapy, the development of leukopenia and thrombocytopenia, and hemorrhagic complications (wound bleeding, falling hemoglobin with hemolysis). They also highlighted that the initial positive malaria smear did not explain the rapid deterioration, prompting broader infectious work‑up that ultimately identified Lassa virus by PCR.
case_prompt: A 47‑year‑old male surgeon presented on February 12, 2016, with fever. He was vaccinated against yellow fever. A thick blood smear was positive for malaria, and he was started on artemether‑lumefantrine. After six days there was no clinical improvement; his high‑grade fever and generalized weakness persisted, leading to hospitalization in a private room with dedicated nursing care. On day 6 after consultation he reported fever, chills, malaise, headaches, pharyngitis, hypoacusis, and diffuse abdominal pain. Laboratory studies revealed leukopenia (1,100 cells/mm³) and thrombocytopenia (65,000 /mm³). His epigastric pain worsened, and, based on a syndrome of abdominal pain with febrile illness, an exploratory laparotomy was performed, after which the operative wound began bleeding. He was air‑lifted to Cologne, Germany, on day 13; prior to evacuation he received two units of packed red blood cells because his hemoglobin had fallen to 6.8 g/dL with evidence of hemolysis. Despite intensive care in Germany, his condition deteriorated rapidly on the second day of admission, and he died on day 14.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Persistent fever despite appropriate antimalarial therapy raises suspicion for an alternative etiology beyond malaria. | "The thick smear performed was positive for malaria and received artemether/lumefantrine without any favorable clinical course after six days."
2. Development of leukopenia and thrombocytopenia is atypical for uncomplicated malaria and suggests a systemic process such as viral hemorrhagic fever or severe sepsis. | "Laboratory tests showed leukopenia (1,100 cells/mm³) and thrombocytopenia (65,000/mm³)."
3. Hemorrhagic manifestations—including operative wound bleeding, rapid drop in hemoglobin, and signs of hemolysis—point toward a hemorrhagic viral infection rather than uncomplicated malaria or uncomplicated postoperative infection. | "He was thus air‑lifted... his hemoglobin dropped to 6.8 g/dL with evidence of hemolysis symptoms."
4. The initial positive malaria smear could represent a coinfection or incidental finding, but the lack of response to therapy and the severe hematologic abnormalities make malaria an unlikely sole cause. | "without any favorable clinical course after six days."
5. Post‑operative bacterial infection was considered because of the laparotomy, but the rapid systemic deterioration and hemorrhagic picture are more consistent with a viral hemorrhagic fever. | "exploratory laparotomy was conducted, which was followed by a bleeding on the operative wound."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient was ultimately diagnosed with Plasmodium falciparum malaria, which is on the 21 SELECTED diseases list (malaria).  
2. Best breakpoint: Include presentation, travel history, lack of chemoprophylaxis, symptom evolution, mental status change, vital signs, physical exam (jaundice), and initial laboratory abnormalities (anemia, severe thrombocytopenia, hyperbilirubinemia, markedly elevated CRP). Stop before the peripheral blood smear and rapid test results that explicitly reveal malaria parasites.  
3. Author's Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished malaria from earlier diagnoses of “common cold” by highlighting the patients’ recent travel to a malaria‑endemic region, lack of prophylaxis, severe laboratory abnormalities (thrombocytopenia, hemolysis, high bilirubin), and altered mental status, and then confirmed the diagnosis with peripheral smear and rapid antigen testing, thereby ruling out simple viral upper‑respiratory infection.
case_prompt:
A 37‑year‑old Japanese man without notable past medical history returned to Japan two weeks ago after a six‑month business trip to Nigeria. He had taken no chemoprophylaxis for malaria, used no insect repellent, and reported occasional mosquito bites. Six days before admission he developed general malaise, fever, and headache. Five days before admission he visited a local clinic and was diagnosed with a common cold, receiving loxoprofen and cefaclor. Three days before admission he returned to another clinic, again receiving a diagnosis of common cold, but his symptoms persisted and his mental state appeared altered. He was transferred by ambulance to the Japanese Red Cross Narita Hospital.

On admission his Glasgow Coma Scale was E4V4M6. Vital signs were: blood pressure 138/87 mm Hg, heart rate 126 beats/min, temperature 38.5 °C, respiratory rate 28 breaths/min, and SpO₂ 98 % on room air. Physical examination revealed slight conjunctival jaundice. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL, platelet count 17 000/µL, total bilirubin 5.1 mg/dL, and C‑reactive protein 23.14 mg/dL.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Initial consideration of a self‑limited viral upper‑respiratory infection (common cold) because of mild upper‑respiratory symptoms and outpatient diagnoses. | "diagnosed with common cold."
2. The combination of recent travel to a malaria‑endemic region, lack of prophylaxis, high fever, severe thrombocytopenia, anemia, hyperbilirubinemia, and altered mental status raised suspicion for severe malaria over a simple respiratory viral illness. | "Peripheral blood smear showed P. falciparum‑infected erythrocytes..." (confirmatory evidence that the earlier diagnoses were incorrect).
3. Confirmation of Plasmodium falciparum infection by rapid antigen test and PCR established malaria as the definitive cause, ruling out other febrile illnesses. | "A rapid immunographic test ... for P. falciparum was positive. P. falciparum infection was later confirmed by performing polymerase chain reaction."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient was ultimately diagnosed with visceral leishmaniasis caused by Leishmania donovani, which belongs to the selected disease list (leishmaniasis).  
2. Best breakpoint: Include history of prolonged fever, weight loss, laboratory evidence of inflammatory markers, evolving pancytopenia, imaging findings (splenomegaly, PET/CT marrow uptake), negative infectious work‑up, and bone‑marrow biopsy showing intracellular microorganisms, but stop before the PCR result that explicitly identifies Leishmania.  
3. Author's Analytic Distinctions: The authors systematically excluded common causes of fever of unknown origin and pancytopenia (bacterial sepsis, tuberculosis, HIV, viral infections, leptospirosis, malaria) using cultures, serologies, PCR, and interferon‑γ release assay. Imaging localized the process to bone marrow; histology demonstrated intracellular organisms, narrowing the differential to intracellular parasites. Definitive diagnosis was achieved by PCR confirmation of Leishmania DNA, distinguishing it from other intracellular pathogens or hematologic malignancies.
case_prompt:
In September 2016, a 60‑year‑old male Austrian patient presented with a three‑week history of fever of unknown origin, fatigue, and an unintentional weight loss of 6 kg. He had well‑controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypothyroidism. Travel history included two‑week trips to southern Crete (September 2015) and southern Spain (May 2016).

Physical examination was unremarkable except for splenomegaly (7.2 × 16.4 cm) on abdominal sonography. Laboratory studies showed markedly elevated C‑reactive protein (94.2–188.9 mg/L), mild normocytic, hypochromic anemia (Hb 12.5 g/dL), mild thrombocytopenia (127 × 10³/µL), and a subtly elevated γ‑glutamyltransferase. The soluble interleukin‑2 receptor was increased (5156 pg/mL). Initial chest X‑ray, urine analysis, transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography were normal.

Empiric antibiotics (initially ampicillin/sulbactam, later piperacillin/tazobactam plus vancomycin) yielded no clinical improvement. Over the next three weeks, bicytopenia progressed to severe pancytopenia requiring transfusions; lactate dehydrogenase rose to 1107 U/L, and liver enzymes (GGT, alkaline phosphatase, AST) increased. Fever persisted up to 40 °C.

Extensive infectious work‑up was negative: serial blood cultures, PCR for influenza, IgM serology for Puumala, Dobrava, and Hantaan viruses, PCR for cytomegalovirus and Epstein–Barr virus, leptospirosis antibody, malaria smear, interferon‑γ release assay for tuberculosis, and HIV antibody test. 

Positron emission tomography‑computed tomography demonstrated increased tracer uptake in both central and peripheral bone marrow. Bone‑marrow biopsy revealed numerous microorganisms within macrophages.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial sepsis considered but excluded because blood cultures remained negative and broad‑spectrum antibiotics failed to improve the patient | "Serial blood cultures were negative... Empiric antibiotic therapy... did not lead to improvement."
2. Tuberculosis evaluated due to fever and splenomegaly but ruled out by a negative interferon‑gamma release assay | "tuberculosis (negative interferon‑gamma release assay)."
3. HIV infection investigated as a cause of pancytopenia; testing was negative | "human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) (negative antibody)."
4. Viral etiologies (influenza, hantavirus, CMV, EBV) were excluded by negative PCR and IgM serologies | "tests for influenza (negative PCR), other viral infections (negative IgM antibody test for Puumala, Dobrava, and Hantaan virus, negative PCR for cytomegalovirus and Epstein‑Barr virus)."
5. Leptospirosis assessed due to travel history; serology was negative | "leptospirosis (negative antibody test)."
6. Malaria considered given febrile travel; peripheral smear was negative | "malaria (negative blood smear)."
7. Hematologic malignancy (e.g., lymphoma, leukemia) considered because of marrow PET uptake and pancytopenia; bone‑marrow biopsy showed only intracellular microorganisms without malignant cells | "Bone marrow biopsy revealed microorganisms within macrophages."
8. Visceral leishmaniasis confirmed after PCR detection of Leishmania DNA in peripheral blood and bone marrow, establishing the definitive diagnosis | "PCR from peripheral blood and bone marrow confirmed infection with Leishmania donovani."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient has Plasmodium falciparum infection, which corresponds to “malaria” on the 21 SELECTED diseases list. The case provides sufficient clinical and laboratory details (fever, severe anemia, peripheral smear with PF) to deduce malaria as the primary diagnosis.
2. Ideal Breakpoint: Include the presentation, initial smear findings, treatment courses (two oral artesunate‑SP courses, referral, initiation of parenteral quinine, clindamycin, primaquine) and the repeat smear results showing persistent ring forms, but stop before the statement that parasites cleared after 48 h. This provides enough data for learners to arrive at the diagnosis of falciparum malaria without revealing the final clearance outcome.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors emphasized (a) persistence of fever and anemia despite standard oral therapy, (b) continued presence of ring forms on repeat smears, and (c) the rapid clearance of parasites after switching to parenteral quinine‑based regimen, thereby confirming falciparum malaria and ruling out treatment failure due to non‑malaria causes.
case_prompt: A 13‑month‑old male child from Koraput district, Orissa, presented with persistent fever and severe anemia. Initial peripheral blood smear demonstrated ring forms of Plasmodium falciparum. He received a 3‑day course of oral artesunate‑sulfadoxine‑pyrimethamine, but fever persisted and parasites remained detectable. A second identical 3‑day oral regimen was given, yet ring forms were still observed on repeat smears. He was then referred to a tertiary hospital, where parenteral quinine was started together with clindamycin, and a single dose of primaquine was administered. Serial peripheral smears continued to show Plasmodium falciparum until therapy was adjusted.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Persistent fever and severe anemia in a child from a malaria‑endemic region point toward malaria as the most likely cause | "persistent fever and failure of parasite clearance after 3 days"  
2. Peripheral smear demonstrating ring forms of Plasmodium falciparum confirms infection with the malaria parasite | "smear positive for PF"  
3. Lack of parasite clearance after two courses of oral artesunate‑SP suggests drug‑resistant or inadequately absorbed falciparum malaria rather than a bacterial sepsis or viral infection, which would not produce Plasmodium on smear | "persistence of ring forms of PF in blood smear"  
4. Rapid parasitological clearance after initiating parenteral quinine plus clindamycin and primaquine supports that the organism was falciparum malaria responsive to appropriate antimalarial therapy, ruling out alternative etiologies | "parasite clearance after 48 h of initiating therapy"

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient’s presentation and investigations point to Plasmodium falciparum malaria, which is on the 21 SELECTED diseases list (malaria). No other SELECTED disease is described.
2. Ideal Breakpoint: Include data up to the point of receiving a positive PF rapid diagnostic test and the decision to start antimalarial therapy, but exclude the peripheral‑smear result that definitively confirms malaria (“ring forms of PF”). This provides enough information (fever, positive PF RDT, anemia, persistent fever) for learners to suspect malaria without revealing the final diagnostic confirmation.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors used a rapid diagnostic test to raise suspicion, performed a sickling test to exclude hemoglobinopathy‑related anemia, interpreted persistent fever despite artesunate as possible drug resistance, and finally obtained a peripheral smear to confirm Plasmodium falciparum and to document parasite clearance after alternative therapy.
case_prompt: An 8‑year‑old girl from Vizianagaram district, Andhra Pradesh, was admitted with a 10‑day history of fever. A rapid diagnostic test for *Plasmodium falciparum* was positive. She was given injection artesunate for three days and sulfadoxine‑pyrimethamine on day 2. Because of anemia and continued fever, she was referred to a higher‑level facility.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Persistent fever in a child from a malaria‑endemic area suggests malaria, supported by a positive *P. falciparum* rapid test | "PF rapid diagnostic test (RDT) was positive."
2. Anemia prompted evaluation for sickle cell disease, but the sickling test was negative, making sickle cell disease unlikely | "Sickling test was negative."
3. Lack of clinical improvement after artesunate raised concern for artesunate resistance, guiding a change to quinine‑based therapy | "Probable artesunate resistance was suspected."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient’s presentation and laboratory findings are consistent with severe malaria (Plasmodium falciparum and vivax co‑infection), which is included in the 21 SELECTED diseases list. No other SELECTED disease is prominently featured.
2. Ideal Breakpoint: End the prompt after describing the child’s initial presentation (fever, icterus) and the subsequent development of respiratory distress, hypotension, dark urine, and renal dysfunction, but before any mention of the rapid diagnostic test (RDT) results or peripheral smear findings that directly confirm malaria.
3. Author's Analytic Distinctions: The authors linked the severe clinical picture to intravascular hemolysis and sepsis, attributed delayed parasite clearance to renal failure, and used repeat smears to document parasite disappearance, thereby confirming malaria as the etiologic agent while ruling out other causes of hemolysis/AKI.
case_prompt: A 12‑year‑old girl from Visakhapatnam district, Andhra Pradesh, was admitted to a referral hospital with fever and icterus. After three days of treatment she developed respiratory distress, hypotension, cola‑colored urine, and rising renal parameters. Initial investigations showed anemia and thrombocytopenia. The clinical picture suggested intravascular hemolysis and sepsis with acute kidney injury.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Severe malaria considered because fever, icterus, hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, and rapid progression to renal failure are classic complications of Plasmodium falciparum infection | "Investigations were suggestive of intravascular hemolysis, sepsis with acute kidney injury."
2. Leptospirosis entertained given fever, icterus, dark urine, and renal dysfunction, but no exposure history or serology was provided, and subsequent parasitological testing identified malaria parasites | "She was referred after 3 days of treatment as she developed respiratory distress, hypotension, cola-colored urine, and elevated renal parameters."
3. Dengue hemorrhagic fever considered because of fever, thrombocytopenia, and plasma leakage, yet the presence of anemia, hemoglobinuria, and later detection of malaria parasites made dengue less likely | "her blood smear showed multiple PFand vivax parasites with anemia and thrombocytopenia."
4. Sepsis of bacterial origin was a differential owing to hypotension and organ failure, but the detection of malaria parasites and response to antimalarial therapy supported malaria as the primary driver | "Broad‑spectrum antibiotics and supportive measures were administered."
5. Hemolytic uremic syndrome considered due to hemolysis and renal failure, but lack of classic triad (microangiopathic hemolysis, schistocytes) and subsequent parasite clearance argued against it | "Her peripheral smear repeated after 48 h showed occasional falciparum ring forms and after 72 h, absent hemoparasites."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient’s presentation is consistent with Plasmodium falciparum malaria, which is included in the 21 SELECTED diseases list (malaria). Therefore the target diagnosis is malaria (SELECTED).
2. Best breakpoint: Include all information up to the initiation of quinine, clindamycin, and primaquine therapy, but stop before reporting parasitological clearance. This provides sufficient clinical data (fever, positive PF smear, severe complications, persistent parasitemia after artesunate) for the learner to deduce malaria without revealing the outcome.
3. Key analytic distinctions: The authors distinguished malaria from other febrile illnesses by repeated peripheral smear showing Plasmodium falciparum despite artesunate therapy, and by the classic severe malaria manifestations (ascites, icterus, hemoglobinuria). case_prompt:
A 47‑year‑old man presented in May 2016 with a five‑day history of generalized weakness that began five days prior to arrival. Four days before presentation he felt light‑headed, experienced a single episode of non‑bilious, non‑bloody vomiting, and subsequently developed right upper‑quadrant abdominal pain. Over the three days preceding admission he had several bouts of non‑bloody diarrhea accompanied by fevers up to 102 °F. Review of systems was notable for frontal headaches and dark urine; he denied recent travel or sick contacts.

The patient’s illness actually began nearly a year earlier. In July 2015, after a 20‑day stay in a Venezuelan jungle, he suffered a seizure and was treated at a local clinic with a 14‑day course of antimalarial pills (specific agents unknown). After a brief symptom‑free interval, he experienced a second episode and received another unknown antimalarial regimen in a rural town. Upon returning to the United States, he remained asymptomatic until October 2015, when a third episode of similar symptoms occurred and was treated in Miami (specific regimen not recalled). In November 2015 he had a fourth episode with fever, myalgia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and right upper‑quadrant pain; he was admitted to Elmhurst Hospital, Queens, NY, where a blood smear later identified Plasmodium species (details omitted here). He received quinine for five days, doxycycline for seven days, and primaquine for fourteen days. He was readmitted and retreated at the same hospital in January and February 2016 with the identical medication regimen; during the February admission the primaquine dose was doubled and he enrolled in directly observed therapy to ensure compliance. After completing the final primaquine course on 10 March 2016 he reported being asymptomatic.

In early May 2016 he was readmitted again for recurrent symptoms despite prior treatment courses, documented medication adherence, and no risk for new exposure. The CDC Malaria Hotline was consulted, and genotyping for CYP2D6 was ordered.

5. Consideration of drug‑resistant malaria was raised, but prior genotyping revealed a poor‑metabolizer CYP2D6 genotype, which impairs primaquine activation and explains treatment failure | "When tested for the CYP2D6 allele during his May 8th admission, he was found to have a *4/*5 allele variation, which corresponds to a poor metabolizer."

case_prompt:
A 20‑year‑old man with no past medical history presented to the emergency department with 7 days of fever, malaise, and arthralgia. On arrival he was febrile (39 °C); the remainder of the physical examination was normal. He reported ingesting unpasteurized camel’s milk, and serological testing for brucellosis was positive. Initial laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 145 g/L, white blood cells 7.6 × 10⁹/L (45.6 % lymphocytes, 49.2 % neutrophils), and platelets 4 × 10⁹/L. Chemistry revealed urea 3.6 mmol/L, creatinine 75.25 µmol/L, total bilirubin 16.1 µmol/L, ALT 48 IU/L, AST 52 IU/L. He denied using over‑the‑counter drugs, painkillers, or NSAIDs. He was advised to be admitted but left against medical advice after being prescribed doxycycline and rifampicin.

Two days later he returned with epistaxis, gingival bleeding, and hematuria. He was febrile (38.7 °C), blood pressure 110/75 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats/min. Examination revealed a non‑itchy flat purpuric rash on the lower extremities; cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal, and neurologic exams were normal. Repeat CBC showed hemoglobin 128 g/L, white blood cells 4.9 × 10⁹/L (51.8 % lymphocytes, 41.1 % neutrophils), and platelets 2 × 10⁹/L. Peripheral smear demonstrated normal red and white cells, marked thrombocytopenia with occasional giant platelets and no platelet clumps. To exclude other causes of thrombocytopenia, malaria blood film, coagulation profile, fibrinogen level, antinuclear antibody, double‑stranded DNA antibody, and serologies for HBsAg, anti‑HCV, HIV, cytomegalovirus, and Epstein‑Barr virus were all unremarkable. Brucella agglutination test remained positive (titer 1 : 1280).
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Brucellosis as the underlying infection – exposure to unpasteurized camel milk and a positive serologic test support this diagnosis. | "A history of ingesting unpasteurized camel's milk was reported, and a serological test for brucellosis was positive."
2. Immune thrombocytopenic purpura secondary to infection – severe isolated thrombocytopenia with bleeding manifestations fits ITP, and the temporal relationship to brucellosis suggests a secondary cause. | "There was severe isolated thrombocytopenia (4000), but no evidence of skin or mucous membranes bleeding."
3. Malaria excluded – malaria can cause thrombocytopenia, but the malaria blood film was negative. | "malaria blood film ... were unremarkable."
4. Autoimmune etiologies (e.g., systemic lupus erythematosus) excluded – negative ANA and anti‑dsDNA make these unlikely. | "antinuclerar antibody (ANA), double‑stranded DNA antibody (anti‑ds DNA) ... were unremarkable."
5. Viral infections (HIV, CMV, EBV, hepatitis B/C) excluded – serologies were negative. | "serological tests for HbsAg, anti‑HCV, HIV, cytomegalovirus, and Ebstein‑Barr virus all were unremarkable."
6. Drug‑induced thrombocytopenia excluded – patient denied use of over‑the‑counter drugs, painkillers, or NSAIDs. | "He denied use of any over‑the‑counter drugs, painkillers, or NSAIDs."
7. Bone‑marrow or malignant processes unlikely – peripheral smear showed normal red and white cell morphology, arguing against marrow infiltration. | "peripheral blood smear examination showed normal RBCs, WBCs morphology, and marked thrombocytopenia with occasional giant platelets and no platelet clumps."

case_prompt: A 50‑year‑old woman presented to the emergency department in South Carolina after two episodes of syncope. She stayed in an urban home, used DEET mosquito repellent, slept indoors with closed windows but no net, ate food prepared at home from a local grocery, and drank only bottled water. On examination, temperature was 100.8 °F, pulse 117/min, blood pressure 127/78 mm Hg, respirations 18/min, SpO₂ 99% on room air. She appeared comfortable, well‑nutrished, without jaundice or lymphadenopathy. Lungs were clear, heart sounds normal aside from tachycardia, abdomen non‑tender, no hepatosplenomegaly. case_prompt: A 55‑year‑old Japanese man returned from Nigeria and was admitted with a persistent high fever for 2 days. Blood smears showed parasitemia (0.05% of erythrocytes with ring forms) and PCR identified *Plasmodium falciparum*. On presentation he exhibited dysarthria, expressive aphasia, urinary incontinence, and truncal ataxia suggestive of cerebellar involvement. He appeared dazed, was unable to select appropriate words, and had a Glasgow Coma Scale of 13 (E4V4M5). He had no other signs of severe malaria. By hospital day 2 (illness day 3) parasites were no longer detectable, though neurologic deficits persisted after afebrile status on day 4. Diffusion‑weighted MRI on day 2 showed a high‑signal lesion in the splenium of the corpus callosum with reduced apparent diffusion coefficient. Cerebrospinal fluid obtained on day 10 (after platelet recovery) showed a mildly elevated cell count (6.3 cells/µL) with normal protein and glucose. Follow‑up brain MRI on day 16 demonstrated complete resolution of the splenial lesion.

1. Severe malaria considered but deemed unlikely because the patient lacked additional severe manifestations. | "He had no other signs or symptoms of severe malaria."

case_prompt:
A 16‑year‑old previously healthy teenager presented to the emergency department with a one‑week history of high‑grade intermittent fever followed by three days of severe periumbilical pain, multiple episodes of loose stools, vomiting, and jaundice. He denied drug or alcohol use, blood transfusions, recent travel, or trauma.

On examination the patient appeared ill and toxic but was alert and oriented. He was icteric, mildly dehydrated, and hemodynamically stable. Temperature was 101 °F. Respiratory rate was 32/min with SpO₂ 98 % on 4 L/min O₂ via face mask. Abdominal exam revealed tenderness with guarding in the periumbilical region and hepatosplenomegaly. The remainder of the systemic examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a deranged liver function test with direct hyperbilirubinemia (total bilirubin 4.6 mg/dL, direct 2.3 mg/dL), elevated ALP 273 U/L, AST 214 U/L, ALT 123 U/L, and G‑GT 294 U/L. Pancreatic enzymes were markedly increased (amylase 548 U/L, lipase 415 U/L). Renal function tests and complete blood count were normal.

Plain abdominal radiographs demonstrated colon cut‑off and sentinel loop signs. Abdominal ultrasound revealed a hyperechoic pancreas, distended gallbladder, and splenomegaly. Contrast‑enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen showed a bulky pancreatic tail and body with mild peripancreatic fat stranding, a distended gallbladder with minimal pericholecystic fluid, minimal ascites, and hepatosplenomegaly. There were also bilateral minimal pleural effusions with subsegmental atelectasis of posterior basal segments of both lower lobes. These findings favored acute interstitial pancreatitis (modified CTSI score 4). Using the Revised Atlanta Classification, a clinicoradiological diagnosis of interstitial edematous pancreatitis without necrosis was made. Ranson’s criteria predicted an associated mortality of 0–3 %.

The patient was admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit with a diagnosis of acute pancreatitis with impending septic shock and jaundice. Broad‑spectrum antibiotics were started after obtaining blood cultures and serologic tests. He was kept nil by mouth, received intravenous fluids, analgesics, and antipyretics.

Serological testing for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, leptospira, malaria antigen, and dengue were negative, while the Widal test was positive for Salmonella typhi “O” (1 : 320) and “H” (1 : 320). Blood cultures were drawn and pending.

1. Acute viral hepatitis (hepatitis B, C) considered because of jaundice and transaminitis, but serologies were negative. | "The serological tests for hepatitis B, C … were all reported negative..."
2. Leptospirosis considered as a cause of fever, jaundice, and pancreatitis, but leptospira serology was negative. | "The serological tests for … leptospira … were all reported negative..."
3. Malaria considered given endemic setting and fever, but malaria antigen test was negative. | "The serological tests for … malaria antigen … were all reported negative..."
4. Dengue infection considered because of fever and liver enzyme elevation, but dengue serology was negative. | "The serological tests for … dengue were all reported negative..."
