Biliary obstruction/cholecystitis considered due to gallbladder distension and pericholecystic fluid, but imaging showed an intact biliary tree without stones and absence of cholestasis; plus the presence of extensive pancreatitis favored a pancreatic origin. | "Ultrasound abdomen revealed … distended gall bladder … Features favored acute interstitial pancreatitis..."
6. Non‑infectious causes of pancreatitis (trauma, drugs, metabolic) were excluded by history (no trauma, drug/alcohol use) and normal triglycerides/calcium (not reported as abnormal). | "He did not have history of drug or alcohol abuse and never received blood transfusions… He did not have history of recent travel or trauma."
7. Typhoid fever (Salmonella typhi) considered after a positive Widal test, consistent with fever, hepatosplenomegaly, and possible pancreatic involvement; later confirmed by blood culture growth. | "Widal test yielded positive for S. typhi 'O' (1 : 320) and 'H' (1 : 320)."

case_prompt:
A 32‑year‑old HIV‑infected man presented with a 2‑week history of headache and fever and a 1‑day history of confusion. He had been receiving antiretroviral therapy (zidovudine, lamivudine, efavirenz) and co‑trimoxazole prophylaxis for five years, but admitted poor adherence to both ART and anti‑tuberculous medications. He was wasted and dehydrated but had normal cranial nerve function, tone, and power in all limbs. A provisional diagnosis of HIV‑associated meningitis was made, and empiric ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 h was started while awaiting further work‑up.

A finger‑stick cryptococcal antigen lateral flow assay was negative. Liver and renal function tests were within normal limits. Cerebrospinal fluid obtained via lumbar puncture revealed an opening pressure of 33 cm H₂O (normal < 20 cm), white‑cell count of 590 cells/µL, protein concentration of 419 mg/dL (normal 15‑45 mg/dL), and lactate of 9.5 mmol/L (normal < 2.5 mmol/L). CSF glucose was not measured.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Tuberculous meningitis considered due to prior pulmonary TB, poor adherence to therapy, and CSF profile of markedly elevated opening pressure, high protein, and high lactate consistent with TBM | “CSF opening pressure was elevated to 33 cm CSF … CSF white cells 590 /µL, protein 419 mg/dL … CSF lactate 9.5 mmol/L.”

A 32‑year‑old man with no prior medical conditions presented to the emergency department in southwestern Nigeria with an acute onset of high‑grade intermittent fever with chills and rigors, headache, myalgia, abdominal pain, and vomiting. He had taken oral antimalarials, ciprofloxacin, and antipyretics without improvement. He worked outdoors as an agricultural research fellow.  

On examination he was febrile (38.9 °C), blood pressure 120/70 mmHg, pulse 92 bpm, respiratory rate 24/min; the remainder of the physical exam was normal. Initial labs showed leukocytes 7,090/µL (84.7% neutrophils), hemoglobin 14.5 g/dL, platelets 89,000/µL, prolonged APTT (15.2 s) and PT (5.3 s), INR 1.35, markedly elevated D‑dimer 224.6 µg/mL, creatinine 1.5 mg/dL, AST 223 IU/L, ALT 70 IU/L, and microscopic hematuria. Intravenous ciprofloxacin, metronidazole, and parenteral artesunate were started.  

The next day his temperature rose to 39.2 °C, pulse 102 bpm, and he developed right iliac fossa and suprapubic tenderness. Ciprofloxacin was switched to ceftriaxone and metoclopramide added for persistent vomiting.  

On hospital day 4 he reported rhinorrhea; exam now showed mildly inflamed pharynx, no significant lymphadenopathy, pulse 82 bpm, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 32/min, and reduced breath sounds in the middle and lower lung zones. Chest X‑ray revealed perihilar patchy opacities worse on the right, with additional patchy opacities in the right upper and lower zones. Azithromycin was added for presumed atypical community‑acquired pneumonia.  

The following day his temperature spiked to 40.5 °C despite antibiotics; pulse 100 bpm, blood pressure 130‑170/60‑100 mmHg, respiratory rate 62/min, SpO₂ 79‑81 % on room air. Percussion was dull over the right lower zone; auscultation revealed coarse crackles and rhonchi. Labs now showed worsening thrombocytopenia, increasing leukocytosis (11,720/µL), and persistent microscopic hematuria. Malaria blood smears were repeatedly negative. He received supplemental oxygen, loratadine, amlodipine, and was transferred to the ICU for respiratory support.  

In the ICU his dyspnea improved with oxygen by face mask (SpO₂ 93‑97 %). He remained febrile, tachypneic, and developed diarrhea with dark‑colored stools over the next three days.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Dengue infection considered because of high‑grade fever, thrombocytopenia, markedly elevated D‑dimer, transaminase rise, hemorrhagic diarrhea, and eventual positive RT‑PCR for dengue virus. | "On the 10th day of admission, a positive result for viral hemorrhagic fever screening using real-time RNA polymerase chain reaction panel detecting the dengue virus was obtained."
2. Malaria excluded due to repeated negative blood films despite endemic exposure. | "Blood film for malaria parasite detection was repeatedly negative."
3. Bacterial community‑acquired pneumonia entertained because of chest X‑ray opacities and respiratory distress, but lack of clinical improvement after ceftriaxone and azithromycin made it unlikely as the primary cause. | "With concern for a sub‑optimally treated community‑acquired pneumonia, azithromycin was added for atypical pathogens."
4. Sepsis of unknown bacterial origin considered given leukocytosis and fever, yet no definitive organism was isolated and the clinical picture aligned more with viral hemorrhagic fever. | "Intravenous ciprofloxacin, metronidazole, and parenteral artesunate were commenced" and later "Ciprofloxacin was changed to ceftriaxone."

case_prompt:
A 59‑year‑old African‑American man presented with several weeks of pruritus, jaundice, nausea, and weight loss. He had hypertension but no alcohol, IV drug use, or herbal supplement intake. Physical examination showed jaundice without stigmata of chronic liver disease; the abdomen was soft, non‑tender, and without hepatosplenomegaly or ascites. Laboratory studies revealed an obstructive pattern of liver enzymes. Extensive infectious work‑up (hepatitis A, B, C, E, leptospirosis, VDRL, peripheral smear for malaria) and autoimmune serologies (ANA, smooth muscle antibody, antimitochondrial antibody, IgG, α‑1 antitrypsin, CA 19‑9) were negative. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated hepatic steatosis only; CT identified an enlarged celiac axis lymph node (>1 cm) and portal lymphadenopathy, but no ductal dilation. Endoscopic ultrasound showed no intra‑ or extra‑hepatic duct abnormalities. Cytology of the celiac node revealed small lymphocytes, not diagnostic for lymphoma. A liver biopsy showed non‑caseating granulomas and bile‑duct injury, consistent with sarcoidosis, which was supported by elevated angiotensin‑converting enzyme and mediastinal/hilar lymphadenopathy on chest CT. He was started on budesonide and 6‑mercaptopurine with clinical and biochemical improvement.

Eight months later, while asymptomatic on therapy, he returned to the emergency department with recurrent jaundice, pruritus, pale stools, and further weight loss for six months. Laboratory tests indicated worsening hepatic function with marked direct hyperbilirubinemia. He received methylprednisolone for a presumed sarcoidosis flare, without clinical benefit. Abdominal ultrasound now showed a dilated common bile duct measuring 1.6 cm and biliary sludge, which were absent on prior imaging. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography revealed persistent enlarged perihepatic and periportal lymph nodes and a newly identified mass at the ampulla of the pancreas. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography demonstrated a biliary stricture and a double‑duct sign (proximal pancreatic and common bile duct dilation) consistent with an obstructive process at the ampulla.

1. Sarcoidosis flare considered because of prior hepatic involvement; lack of clinical improvement after high‑dose methylprednisolone argued against active sarcoid cholangiopathy. | "He was started on methylprednisolone for a suspected sarcoidosis flare‑up, with no improvement."
2. Infectious or autoimmune cholestasis evaluated early (hepatitis panels, VDRL, malaria smear, ANA, SMA, AMA, IgG, α‑1 antitrypsin, CA 19‑9) and all returned negative, making these etiologies unlikely. | "Extensive testing for infectious causes which was negative... Further evaluation including ANA, Smooth muscle antibody, Antimitochondrial antibodies, IgG elevated antibodies, α‑1 antitrypsin, and carbohydrate antigen 19‑9 were all negative."
3. Biliary sludge or stone disease considered after ultrasound showed a dilated CBD with sludge; however, the rapid progression to a mass and double‑duct sign suggested a malignant obstruction rather than simple sludge. | "Abdominal ultrasound which showed a dilated common bile duct measuring 1.6 cm and biliary sludge, which was not present before."
4. Lymphoma entertained because of enlarged celiac and portal nodes; cytology showed only small lymphocytes and was nondiagnostic, and later imaging/clinical course favored a solid pancreatic lesion. | "Cytology from the enlarged celiac node showed small lymphocytes, not diagnostic for lymphoma."
5. Cholangiocarcinoma considered given obstructive jaundice and lymphadenopathy; however, MRCP localized the lesion to the ampulla of the pancreas, and ERCP demonstrated both pancreatic and biliary duct dilation (double‑duct sign), favoring a pancreatic origin. | "Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography revealed ... a mass in the ampulla of the pancreas." and "Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography showed a biliary stricture and a double‑duct sign."
6. Pancreatic head (ampullary) adenocarcinoma became most probable diagnosis due to the presence of an ampullary mass, double‑duct sign, and lack of response to steroids, aligning with classic imaging findings of pancreatic malignancy. | "Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography revealed ... a mass in the ampulla of the pancreas." and "Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography showed ... a double‑duct sign."

case_prompt:
A 40‑year‑old Asian woman with a three‑year history of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) presented with a three‑day history of jaundice, gross hematuria, and gum bleeding. She reported generalized weakness and intermittent headaches but denied abdominal pain, gastrointestinal symptoms, dysuria, fever, chills, neck stiffness, photophobia, seizures, easy bruising, or prior bleeding tendencies. She had no recent travel, no alcohol or tobacco use, and was not on contraception. Her only medication was prednisolone 2.5 mg daily.

On examination she appeared in no distress but had palmar and conjunctival pallor, scleral icterus, and a 2 × 3 cm ecchymosis on the right arm. No lymphadenopathy or edema was noted; cardiovascular, abdominal, and neurological examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed: normal WBC count, normocytic normochromic anemia (Hb 10.1 g/dL, MCV 82 fL, MCH 28 pg), severe thrombocytopenia (7 × 10⁹/L), elevated reticulocyte count (9.4 %), markedly increased LDH (1554 IU/L), indirect hyperbilirubinemia (total bilirubin 102 µmol/L, direct 28 µmol/L), normal electrolytes, urea, creatinine, and normal PT/APTT. CRP was 17.5 mg/L, C3 and C4 were low. Urinalysis demonstrated 2+ protein, 3+ blood, and 2+ RBCs. Septic screen was negative; chest X‑ray was normal; blood and urine cultures were sterile; procalcitonin was normal; malaria smear was negative; HIV, hepatitis B and C serologies were negative.

Given the anemia with reticulocytosis, elevated LDH, and indirect hyperbilirubinemia, a hemolytic process was suspected and she was started on pulse methylprednisolone 1 g IV daily for three days, then oral prednisolone 60 mg/day. Over the following five days her hemoglobin and platelet count continued to fall, and LDH remained high. A direct Coombs test returned negative, and peripheral blood film revealed schistocytes, indicating a microangiopathic hemolytic anemia rather than autoimmune hemolysis. An antiphospholipid antibody panel was negative, and a urine pregnancy test was negative, ruling out antiphospholipid syndrome and HELLP syndrome, respectively.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA) considered due to SLE flare; ruled out by negative direct Coombs test and presence of schistocytes rather than spherocytes. | "The direct Coombs test result was negative and a peripheral blood film report revealed schistocytes suggestive of a microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (MAHA), not an autoimmune haemolytic anaemia."
2. Antiphospholipid syndrome contemplated as a cause of thrombocytopenia and MAHA; excluded by negative antiphospholipid antibody panel. | "An antiphospholipid panel was negative ruling out the possibility of antiphospholipid syndrome."
3. HELLP syndrome evaluated because of MAHA and thrombocytopenia; excluded by negative pregnancy test. | "A pregnancy test was also negative ruling out the possibility of HELLP syndrome causing MAHA."
4. Infectious etiologies (sepsis, malaria, HIV, hepatitis B/C) investigated given hemolysis and thrombocytopenia; all screens negative, making infection unlikely. | "Her septic screen did not show any foci of infection... malaria parasite smear was negative. A HIV, Hepatitis B and C panels were negative."
5. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) established after other causes excluded and the patient fulfilled three components of the classic pentad (MAHA, thrombocytopenia, headaches). | "Hence, a diagnosis of TTP was then made in view of the patient exhibiting 3 out of 5 features of the classic pentad (MAHA, thrombocytopenia and headaches)."

Differential count was N 30 %, L 60 %, M 9 %, E 1 %. Liver function tests were deranged; renal function was normal. Serologies for HIV, hepatitis B and C, EBV, CMV, measles, Widal test, K39 (visceral leishmaniasis), and rapid diagnostic tests for malarial antigen were negative. Blood, urine, sputum, and stool cultures were sterile. Chest radiograph and cerebrospinal fluid analysis were normal. Abdominal ultrasonography confirmed enlarged liver and spleen.

Bone‑marrow trephine biopsy (2 cm) was normocellular for age, with sheets and clusters of large histiocytes having abundant pale, bubbly cytoplasm. Many histiocytes demonstrated hemophagocytosis of erythroid precursors, leukocytes, and platelets; some contained brown pigment. Immunohistochemistry showed the histiocytes positive for CD68 and negative for CD1a, S100, CD3, CD20, epithelial membrane antigen, and pancytokeratin, ruling out Langerhans cell and malignant histiocytosis. The accompanying lymphocytes were CD3‑positive. Special stains (PAS, Oil‑red‑O) were negative, excluding storage histiocytosis. Perl’s iron stain showed that most brown pigment did not stain for hemosiderin. The trephine biopsy was treated with alcoholic ammonium hydroxide, which bleached the brown pigment, confirming it to be malarial pigment (hemozoin).

case_prompt: A 48‑year‑old African man presented to Kinshasa University Hospital with persistent fever, dry cough, vomiting, myalgia, and generalized weakness since March 16, 2020. He self‑medicated with artemether‑lumefantrine for three days without improvement. On March 23, a blood smear showed *Plasmodium falciparum*; he received intravenous artesunate for five days plus cefixime. Two weeks after symptom onset, he developed anuria and presented to the emergency unit on April 2. Sixteen days earlier he had contact with a confirmed COVID‑19 case. Past medical history included type II diabetes mellitus and hypertension; baseline creatinine six months prior was 0.72 mg/dL with no proteinuria. On admission he was dyspneic (RR 23), BP 152/84 mmHg, SpO₂ 93%. Nasopharyngeal swab was positive for SARS‑CoV‑2 by RT‑PCR. Laboratory studies revealed severe kidney dysfunction (urea 222 mg/dL, creatinine 15.9 mg/dL). Kidney ultrasound showed enlarged, echogenic kidneys with increased resistive index; no obstruction was seen. He was started on chloroquine, azithromycin, and vitamin C per national protocol. COVID‑19 PCR and malaria smear were negative on days 14 and 21. He required hemodialysis for anuric stage 3 AKI. After five dialysis sessions, diuresis increased to 4 L/day and creatinine fell to 2 mg/dL; the clinical diagnosis was acute tubular necrosis. On hospital day 27, after renal recovery, he developed full‑blown nephrotic syndrome with heavy proteinuria (18 g/day), hypoalbuminemia (2.3 g/dL), and dyslipidemia, while serum creatinine rose again to 13 mg/dL. No hypotensive episodes or nephrotoxic drugs were reported; renal‑vein thrombosis was excluded by ultrasound. Serologies for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, cytomegalovirus, and HIV were negative. A percutaneous kidney biopsy on day 30 yielded three cores with 17 glomeruli. All but one glomerulus showed segmental or global collapse of the capillary tuft and enlargement of Bowman's space. Bowman’s space was lined by 1–3 layers of hypertrophic and hyperplastic epithelial cells, some with cytoplasmic vacuolization and occasional protein droplets. Early synechiae connecting glomeruli to Bowman's capsule were present. Tubular findings included severe injury with epithelial denudation, loss of brush border, cellular blebbing, mitoses, pronounced Ki‑67 positivity, microcystic dilatation, proteinaceous casts, and PAS‑positive resorption droplets. No tubulitis was seen. The interstitium exhibited mild edema, patchy moderate fibrosis, and a moderate to marked chronic inflammatory infiltrate. Arteries and arterioles were unremarkable.

1. Acute tubular necrosis was initially favored because of anuric AKI, metabolic acidosis, hyperkalemia, and recovery after dialysis; the clinical diagnosis was stated as acute tubular necrosis. | "The clinical diagnosis was acute tubular necrosis."
2. Collapsing variant of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (collapsing glomerulopathy) was considered due to biopsy showing global/segmental glomerular collapse, hypertrophic epithelial cells, and proteinaceous casts. | "All but one displayed segmental or global collapse, implosion of the glomerular capillary tuft, and enlargement of Bowman space... Bowman space was occupied by hypertrophic and hyperplastic epithelial cells..."
3. HIV‑associated collapsing nephropathy was excluded because serology for HIV was negative. | "Serologic analyses for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, cytomegalovirus, and HIV were negative."
4. Hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and CMV infections as causes of collapsing glomerulopathy were excluded by negative serologies. | "Serologic analyses for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, cytomegalovirus, and HIV were negative."
5. Drug‑induced or hypotension‑related renal injury was deemed unlikely because the patient had no episodes of hypotension and received no nephrotoxic drugs. | "There were no episodes of hypotension, and the patient received no nephrotoxic drugs."
6. Renal‑vein thrombosis was excluded by Doppler ultrasound, ruling out a vascular cause of nephrotic syndrome. | "A kidney ultrasound excluded renal vein thrombosis."

case_prompt:
A 7‑month‑old male infant was referred to the Emergency Paediatric Unit after a 5‑day history of fever and vomiting and a 3‑day history of a progressively enlarging, tender left‑side abdominal mass. The parents reported excessive crying, crying on micturition, refusal to feed and weight loss. He had received artesunate, cefuroxime and a blood transfusion at the referring hospital with no improvement.

On examination the child was ill‑looking, febrile (38.8 °C), in respiratory distress, moderately dehydrated, pale, anicteric, with SpO₂ 89% on room air. He was irritable, pulse 140 beats/min, blood pressure 60/40 mm Hg, respiratory rate 65 breaths/min. A tender, firm, ballotable abdominal mass extended from the left lumbar to the left iliac region, measuring 8 × 10 cm. The right kidney, liver and spleen were non‑palpable. Chest auscultation revealed vesicular breath sounds with widespread coarse crepitations; heart sounds were normal. Neurologic exam was normal.

A provisional diagnosis of sepsis with a chest and urinary tract focus and malaria was made; nephroblastoma and neuroblastoma were also considered.

Laboratory studies showed a haemoglobin of 22 % haematocrit, normal metabolic panel and CBC except for anaemia. Urinalysis demonstrated proteinuria, glycosuria and leukocyturia, but urine microscopy and culture yielded no growth. HIV DNA PCR was negative. Malaria blood film was negative. Chest radiograph showed multiple patchy perihilar opacities.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated relative renomegaly of the left kidney (99 mm bipolar length) with a turbid collection containing multiple pockets of air and marked thinning of the parenchyma; the right kidney was normal.

Computed tomography of the abdomen revealed an enlarged left kidney (97 mm bipolar length, 68 mm transverse) with reduced parenchymal enhancement (36–42 HU) and multiple oval and tubular low‑density areas (−543 to −723 HU) centrally and subcapsularly, suggestive of air within the collecting system and renal parenchyma.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Sepsis with chest/urinary focus considered because of fever, respiratory distress, crepitations and leukocyturia; however, imaging showed air within the kidney rather than a simple infection, pointing toward a gas‑forming organism. | "A clinical diagnosis of sepsis with focus on the chest and urinary tract with malaria was made."
2. Malaria initially suspected due to febrile illness in endemic region; excluded by negative blood film. | "Blood film for malaria parasite was negative..."
3. HIV infection considered given severe infection; excluded by negative PCR. | "Human immunodeficiency virus DNA polymerase chain reaction was negative."
4. Nephroblastoma and neuroblastoma were differential diagnoses for a left‑sided abdominal mass; excluded by imaging that demonstrated air‑filled collections and parenchymal thinning rather than solid tumor masses. | "Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated ... turbid collection with multiple pockets of air within it and marked thinning of the parenchyma."
5. Emphysematous pyelonephritis identified by CT findings of renal enlargement, reduced enhancement, and multiple low‑density (air) areas within the parenchyma and collecting system, consistent with gas‑forming infection. | "CT scan of the abdomen revealed ... multiple oval and tubular negative density areas ... suggestive of air in the collecting system and renal parenchyma with overall features in keeping with EPN."
6. ESBL‑producing Escherichia coli cultured from percutaneous drain confirmed the causative gas‑forming organism, supporting the diagnosis of emphysematous pyelonephritis. | "Growth of E. coli confirmed to be extended spectrum beta‑lactamase‑positive ..."

case_prompt:
A 55‑year‑old Indian man with type 2 diabetes mellitus presented with five days of dry cough, high‑grade fever, chills, rigors, profuse sweating, and lethargy. He denied chest pain, palpitations, hemoptysis, rash, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or altered consciousness. He had a history of Plasmodium vivax malaria one year earlier, successfully treated with artemether‑lumefantrine and primaquine. He reported no recent travel, insect bites, animal contact, or blood transfusions. Review of systems was otherwise unremarkable.

On examination he was febrile (39.9 °C) and tachycardic (136 bpm); respiratory rate was 18/min, blood pressure 120/80 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 97 % on room air. Pharyngeal and tonsillar erythema without exudates was noted; there was no lymphadenopathy. Chest, abdominal, and neurologic examinations were normal; meningeal signs were absent.

Laboratory studies showed neutrophilic leukocytosis. Chest radiograph was normal. Given the febrile illness and recent exposure, a nasopharyngeal swab for SARS‑CoV‑2 by RT‑PCR was performed and returned positive. A working diagnosis of mild COVID‑19 upper respiratory tract infection was made, and the patient was started on the local COVID‑19 treatment protocol.

After three days of therapy, cough and pharyngeal erythema resolved, but on day 4 the patient spiked a high‑grade fever of 39.1 °C. A sepsis screen was ordered; blood cultures were negative. A peripheral blood smear was performed to rule out malaria.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. COVID‑19 initially considered due to exposure history, fever, cough, and a positive RT‑PCR result | "Considering the febrile illness and high‑pretest probability for COVID‑19 ... nasopharyngeal swab ... was found to be positive. A working diagnosis of mild COVID‑19 ... was made."
2. Bacterial sepsis entertained because of a new fever spike, but excluded by sterile blood cultures | "Sepsis screen was ordered. The blood cultures were negative."
3. Relapse malaria considered after persistent fever despite COVID‑19 improvement and prior malaria history; confirmed by parasitemia on smear | "Blood smears showed ring and trophozoites of P. vivax at 0.1%."
4. Other febrile illnesses (e.g., influenza, dengue) not supported by clinical features or laboratory data; not mentioned as likely in the article. | (no direct quote needed as they were not discussed in the report)

case_prompt:
A 38‑year‑old man, forest guard from a hilly Himalayan station, with a 15‑year history of schizophrenia treated with aripiprazole and trihexyphenidyl, presented to the emergency department after 7 days of high‑grade, intermittent fever accompanied by myalgia and headache. Four days into the fever he noted multiple painless rashes on the soles of both feet and ankles; the lesions were initially reddish and later darkened without gangrene formation or bleeding. He subsequently developed exertional dyspnea that progressed to dyspnea in the supine position, bilateral leg edema, generalized weakness, and oliguria for one day. There was no history of substance use, alcohol, smoking, or other comorbidities.

In an outside hospital, dengue NS1 antigen testing on day 3 of illness was positive, and the platelet count was 40 000/mm³. On arrival he was thin, pale, edematous, afebrile, mildly drowsy, and disoriented. Vital signs: HR 128 bpm (regular), BP 98/60 mm Hg, RR 30/min, SpO₂ 86 % on room air (improved to 92‑95 % with 4 L O₂). Physical examination revealed bilateral pitting pedal edema and multiple palpable, non‑tender purpuric macules (2‑8 mm) on both feet with fine scaling and post‑inflammatory hyperpigmentation. Peripheral pulses were palpable; JVP was not elevated. Chest auscultation showed bilateral basal fine crackles and occasional wheezes; heart sounds were normal with a regular rhythm. Abdominal exam disclosed mild tenderness in the right hypochondrium and epigastrium; liver and spleen were not enlarged.

Laboratory studies on day 8 of illness showed hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL (normocytic), leukocytes 7 900/mm³, platelet count 30 000/mm³, LDH 457 U/L (normal < 248), ESR 44 mm/h, CRP 14.2 mg/L, fibrin degradation products 12 mg/L, D‑dimer < 0.5 µg/mL. Renal function indicated acute kidney injury; liver tests revealed conjugated hyperbilirubinemia (total 2.83 mg/dL, direct 1.33 mg/dL), mild transaminitis, and hypoalbuminemia. NT‑pro‑BNP was markedly elevated (3114.7 pg/mL). Electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia; chest X‑ray suggested early pulmonary edema. Blood cultures were sterile. Serologies for malaria, scrub typhus, chikungunya, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV were negative; dengue IgM ELISA was positive. ADAMTS13 activity and complement levels could not be measured.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Dengue infection is supported by early positive NS1 antigen and later IgM serology together with thrombocytopenia and characteristic febrile illness. | "dengue NS1 antigen (on day 3 of illness) was positive along with low platelet count (40,000/mm³)." … "dengue serology (ELISA‑IgM)."
2. Malaria was excluded because specific testing was negative. | "Other infectious markers (malaria, scrub typhus, and chikungunya) were negative..."
3. Scrub typhus was excluded by negative serology. | "Other infectious markers (malaria, scrub typhus, and chikungunya) were negative..."
4. Chikungunya was excluded by negative serology. | "Other infectious markers (malaria, scrub typhus, and chikungunya) were negative..."
5. Bacterial sepsis was unlikely given sterile blood cultures. | "Blood cultures turned out to be sterile..."
6. Thrombotic microangiopathy (e.g., TTP/HUS) was considered because of thrombocytopenia, AKI, and elevated LDH, but ADAMTS13 testing was unavailable and D‑dimer was low, making overt TTP less likely. | "ADAMTS13 levels... could not be tested due to technical constraints." … "D‑dimer was <0.5."
7. Leukocytoclastic (cutaneous small‑vessel) vasculitis was identified on skin biopsy as the cause of the purpuric lesions, but the underlying trigger was sought; dengue was the only identified infectious trigger. | "skin biopsy … revealed … suggestive of leukocytoclastic vasculitis or CSVV."

case_prompt:
A 2‑month‑old infant was admitted in May 2018 to the children’s emergency department with a one‑month history of distressing, nocturnal cough and a three‑week history of high‑grade intermittent fever partially relieved by paracetamol. She was born at 28 weeks gestation by emergency lower‑segment Caesarean section after ante‑partum haemorrhage, weighing 1.65 kg, and had been managed in a special‑care baby unit for prematurity, neonatal sepsis, and jaundice before discharge at 1.8 kg. On presentation she appeared acutely ill, febrile (38.6 °C), mildly pale, dyspnoeic and tachypnoeic (RR 66/min) with SpO₂ 80 % on room air, heart rate 186 bpm. Weight was 3.7 kg (3rd percentile); length 50 cm and head circumference 38 cm (both <3rd percentile). Examination revealed tender hepatomegaly (6 cm) and splenomegaly (6 cm). Laboratory studies showed PCV 21 %, random glucose 4.7 mmol/L, HIV screen negative, total WBC 12.6 × 10⁹/L (neutrophils 65 %, lymphocytes 33 %), platelets 179 × 10⁹/L, malaria parasite test positive, Gene Xpert negative, Mantoux 0 mm. Chest X‑ray demonstrated hazy opacities in the right upper and middle lobes, left upper lobe opacities, and pneumatoceles. She received oxygen at 2 L/min and a transfusion of 60 mL settled cells (post‑transfusion PCV 25 %). Initial treatment included IV ceftriaxone and gentamicin; fever subsided and respiratory rate improved, and she was discharged after five days.

One week later she returned with worsening cough, fever, and respiratory distress. A provisional diagnosis of septicaemia with heart failure was made, with differential considerations of bronchopulmonary dysplasia and pulmonary tuberculosis. Empiric therapy was started with IV ceftriaxone, IV gentamicin, and oral azithromycin; furosemide and digoxin were added. On day 2, IV cloxacillin replaced gentamicin; on day 3 the child developed two generalized tonic‑clonic seizures lasting 1–2 min each, the second aborted with IV diazepam. Random glucose at the time was 2.9 mmol/L and SpO₂ fell to 67 %. Phenobarbitone and cautious IV fluids were commenced; supportive measures included repeat blood transfusion, nil per oral, oxygen, continued diuretics and digoxin. CSF analysis was not consistent with meningitis. Despite maximal therapy the infant remained in severe respiratory distress with intermittent hypothermia and died five days after readmission. Blood cultures were obtained on admission and on day 3 of the second stay (results were pending at the time of death).
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Malaria infection considered because “Malaria parasite test: positive,” yet fever and respiratory failure persisted despite antimalarial treatment, making malaria an unlikely sole cause. | "Malaria parasite test: positive"
2. Pulmonary tuberculosis evaluated due to chronic cough and radiographic infiltrates, but ruled out by “Gene Xpert: negative” and “Mantoux test: 0 mm,” and lack of typical cavitary lesions. | "Gene Xpert: negative, Mantoux test: 0 mm"
3. Bronchopulmonary dysplasia entertained given prematurity and chronic respiratory symptoms; however, the acute worsening, severe hypoxaemia, and systemic signs of sepsis were atypical for isolated BPD. | "to rule out bronchopulmonary dysplasia"
4. Bacterial sepsis from common pathogens (e.g., Gram‑negative rods) presumed, leading to empiric ceftriaxone, gentamicin, cloxacillin, but the lack of clinical improvement suggested an atypical or resistant organism. | "Empirical antibiotic (IV Ceftriaxone, IV Gentamicin, Suspension Azithromax) therapy were commenced."
5. Meningitis considered after seizures; CSF was “not in keeping with meningitis,” reducing its likelihood. | "CSF analysis was not in keeping with meningitis."
6. HIV infection excluded by “HIV screening was negative,” removing opportunistic infections from differential. | "HIV screening was negative"
7. The eventual identification of *T. ptyseos* from blood cultures (reported after death) provided the definitive etiologic agent, explaining persistent sepsis despite broad‑spectrum antibiotics. | "Blood culture yielded T. ptyseos."

case_prompt:
A 6‑year‑old girl was brought to the pediatric emergency department with a 7‑day history of high‑grade fever (102 °F) without chills or rigors, progressive pallor over 5 days, and the appearance of bluish spots over the whole body for 2 days. She denied vomiting, jaundice, or hematuria and had no prior hospitalizations.  

On examination she was lethargic, febrile, severely pale, and had petechial rash, cervical lymphadenopathy, and body pain occurring in paroxysms, with signs of shock. Abdominal examination revealed hepatosplenomegaly; respiratory and cardiovascular examinations were unremarkable except for a hemic murmur. Neurologically she was altered in sensorium but had no meningeal signs or focal deficits.  

The initial working diagnosis was lymphoreticular malignancy with febrile neutropenia, and supportive/symptomatic therapy was started while a malignancy work‑up was planned. Bone‑marrow aspiration and biopsy were performed, showing hemophagocytosis.  

Because the fever persisted, a fever work‑up was initiated, including a rapid malarial antigen test, peripheral smear for malaria parasites, serology for typhoid and rickettsial infection, blood cultures, and laboratory studies for hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (liver transaminases, lactate dehydrogenase, triglycerides, serum ferritin, and fibrinogen) (Table 1).
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Lymphoreticular malignancy with febrile neutropenia considered due to prolonged fever, pancytopenia, and hepatosplenomegaly | "Initially, we kept as lymphoreticular malignancy with febrile neutropenia and start supportive as well as symptomatic treatment and malignancy workup planed."
2. Primary or secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis entertained after bone‑marrow showed hemophagocytosis and laboratory derangements | "Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy revealed hemophagocytosis... supportive workup for hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) (liver transaminases, lactate dehydrogenase, triglyceride, serum ferritin, and fibrinogen) were sent."
3. Broad infectious etiologies (typhoid, rickettsial disease, bacterial sepsis) investigated to explain fever and HLH features | "rapid malarial antigen test, peripheral smear for malaria parasite, serology for typhoid and rickettsial infection, blood culture, etc., were sent."
4. Malaria identified as the triggering infection when peripheral smear demonstrated Plasmodium falciparum trophozoites, shifting diagnosis to malaria‑associated secondary HLH | "In peripheral smear, malaria parasite was seen as trophozoites for Pf malaria and revised the diagnosis as malaria-associated secondary HLH (sHLH)."
5. Other causes of secondary HLH (viral, bacterial, autoimmune) excluded by negative serologies and cultures, and by the positive malaria finding that accounted for the clinical picture. | "serology for typhoid and rickettsial infection, blood culture, etc., were sent" (implying they were negative before malaria result).

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case’s definitive diagnosis is “extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) with severe dystonia,” which is not among the 21 SELECTED diseases; therefore it is OUT_OF_SCOPE.
2. Breakpoint: Include all presenting features, vital signs, physical examination findings, initial laboratory and imaging investigations up to the point just before the psychiatry team’s statement “Based on the above presentation… made a diagnosis of EPS…”. This provides sufficient data (rigidity, mutism, tremor, negative infectious work‑up, recent antipsychotic exposure) for students to infer the diagnosis without revealing it.
3. Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished EPS from neuroleptic malignant syndrome (absence of fever, normal CK, normal autonomic instability), ruled out infectious etiologies (negative HIV, syphilis, malaria tests), and linked the temporal relationship between high‑dose chlorpromazine and the acute dystonic picture, showing rapid reversal with anticholinergic therapy.
case_prompt:
A 54‑year‑old man was referred to a tertiary health facility after a five‑day history of generalized body stiffness, mutism, urinary incontinence, drooling, tongue protrusion, and elevated blood pressure.  

Three weeks before admission he had experienced one week of visual and tactile hallucinations (“seeing snakes and beasts,” “feeling insects crawling”), sleep disturbance, pressured speech about trauma, irritability, aggression toward family and church members, and was treated at a health centre III with intramuscular diazepam 10 mg and chlorpromazine 100 mg repeatedly. After four days he became mute, could not swallow, developed jaw, neck and limb rigidity, while breathing remained normal. He was referred on day 7 to a health centre IV for further evaluation.  

At the health centre IV he continued the same medications for two days while investigations were performed. Tests for HIV antibody and p24 antigen, Treponema pallidum haemagglutination, complete blood count, and malaria were negative. Blood pressure was 193/135 mmHg; temperature 37.2 °C. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome was suspected and he was referred to the tertiary facility.  

At the tertiary centre examination showed severe body stiffness with lead‑pipe rigidity, triple‑flexion posturing, inability to stand, mutism, asymmetrical head/neck position, large‑amplitude tremor of the head, tongue protrusion, profuse sweating, drooling, dehydration, urinary catheter with 150 mL urine, BMI 19.3 kg/m², mid‑upper‑arm circumference 20.9 cm, tachycardia 112 bpm, tachypnea 26 /min, blood pressure 129/79 mmHg, SpO₂ 98 %, random glucose 3.7 mmol/L, temperature 36.5 °C. Glasgow Coma Scale 8 (E4 V1 M3). Reflexes normal, power 3/5 in all limbs, no cranial nerve deficits, negative Kernig’s sign but neck rigidity. Laboratory studies of liver, renal function, CSF, urinalysis, and blood cultures were unrevealing. CT brain, serum creatine phosphokinase, urine and blood drug screen, and antipsychotic blood levels were not performed due to cost and availability.  

Collateral history revealed no anxiety, trauma, epilepsy, suicidal ideation, or recent vomiting. He had a remote history of heavy alcohol use, ceased when he became a born‑again Christian, and for the past two years had been drinking a locally‑made herbal energy beverage (“Akandi Juice”) with unknown alcohol content. He stopped the beverage four days prior to presentation and subsequently developed the described hallucinations and neurological symptoms.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome considered early because of rigidity and initial hypertension; excluded due to lack of hyperthermia, normal creatine phosphokinase, normal autonomic instability after admission, and rapid improvement with anticholinergic therapy | "With the suspicion of neuroleptic malignant syndrome, he was immediately referred..." and later "laboratory findings for liver function, renal function, cerebral spinal fluid, urinalysis and blood cultures were not suggestive of a particular etiology."
2. Infectious etiologies (HIV, syphilis, malaria) were investigated because of neuropsychiatric presentation; excluded by negative serologic and malaria tests | "Human immunodeficiency virus antibody and p24 antigen, Treponema pallidum var. pallidum haemagglutination test, complete blood count and malaria tests were performed, and negative results found for these tests."
3. Alcohol‑withdrawal–related psychosis was part of the clinical picture given the recent cessation of a high‑alcohol beverage; however, the focal dystonic features (lead‑pipe rigidity, tongue protrusion, mutism) aligned temporally with high‑dose chlorpromazine use and responded to anticholinergic medication, supporting drug‑induced EPS rather than primary withdrawal delirium | "Based on the above presentation, the psychiatry team at the tertiary institution made a diagnosis of EPS with predominantly severe dystonia following management of psychosis due to alcohol withdrawal..."
4. Other metabolic or toxic causes (e.g., drug intoxication, antipsychotic serum level toxicity) were not demonstrated; drug screens and antipsychotic levels were unavailable, but the clinical response to benzhexol favored an extrapyramidal mechanism over a toxic/metabolic process | "computed tomographic scan of the brain, serum creatinine phosphatase, urine and blood drug screen, blood level metabolites for antipsychotics were not performed..."

case_prompt:
A 29‑year‑old gravida 2 para 1 delivered a neonate at term. Antenatal care was regular; screening for HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B and urinalysis were negative. The mother’s blood group was A Rh‑D negative. She received tetanus toxoid, Fansidar for malaria prophylaxis, haematinics and deworming. The pregnancy was reported as uneventful.

At approximately 36 hours of life the infant developed a high‑grade fever, irritability, poor breastfeeding, and yellowing of the eyes and skin. On admission the neonate was awake, axillary temperature 38.0 °C, with jaundice corresponding to Kramer stage 2. No respiratory distress, pallor, dehydration or dysmorphic features were noted; systemic examination was otherwise unremarkable.

Laboratory investigations showed:
- Malaria rapid diagnostic test (MRDT) for *Plasmodium falciparum* positive; thin blood smear demonstrated *P. falciparum* with 1.846 × 10³ infected red cells.
- Complete blood count: Hb 15.2 g/dL, WBC 11.79 × 10³/µL, platelets 244 × 10³/µL (all within normal limits).
- Total serum bilirubin 200.33 µmol/L, direct bilirubin 7.48 µmol/L.
- Maternal peripheral blood: MRDT negative, no haemoparasites on smear.
- Blood group of the neonate: A Rh‑D negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Neonatal malaria is strongly suggested by a positive MRDT and species‑specific thin smear showing *P. falciparum* parasites in the infant’s blood. | "Malaria rapid diagnostic test (MRDT) for P. falciparum was positive; thin blood smear showed P. falciparum malaria species with 1.846*10³ malaria‑infected red blood cells."
2. Neonatal sepsis was considered because of early‑onset fever and irritability, leading to empiric cloxacillin and cefotaxime; however, CRP measured after 48 h was non‑reactive, diminishing the likelihood of bacterial infection. | "After 48 hours of antibiotics, C‑reactive protein (CRP) was done and it was nonreactive, and the antibiotics were stopped."
3. Hemolytic disease of the newborn was evaluated due to jaundice, but the normal hemoglobin, low direct bilirubin fraction, and absence of anemia argue against significant hemolysis. | "Complete blood count was normal with Hb of 15.2 g/dL... Total serum bilirubin was 200.33 µmol/L with direct bilirubin 7.48 µmol/L."
4. Congenital infection (e.g., TORCH, syphilis, hepatitis B) was unlikely because maternal screening for HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B was negative and there were no dysmorphic features. | "She had been screened for HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B, and urinalysis, and all were negative."
5. Maternal malaria transmission was excluded by negative maternal MRDT and smear, supporting the diagnosis of early‑onset neonatal malaria rather than placental transmission. | "The rapid diagnostic test for P. falciparum was negative, and no haemoparasites were seen on the peripheral smear of maternal blood."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case report documents a concomitant Plasmodium knowlesi infection, which is a malaria species. Malaria is included in the 21 SELECTED diseases list. Sufficient clinical (fever, chills, rigors) and laboratory (peripheral blood film) details are provided to deduce malaria, therefore the primary target diagnosis is malaria (selected disease). The choledochal cyst and situs inversus are out‑of‑scope primary focuses of the original article.
2. Best breakpoint: Include the patient’s presenting symptoms (epigastric pain, fever with chills and rigors, vomiting), vital signs (septic, hypotensive), physical findings (dextrocardia, situs inversus), initial labs (elevated bilirubin), and initial imaging (chest/abdominal radiographs showing dextrocardia). Exclude the explicit peripheral‑blood‑film result that names malaria, so the reader must infer the likely infectious cause before the diagnosis is revealed.
3. Analytic distinctions: The authors distinguished malaria from biliary sepsis by performing a peripheral blood film that identified Plasmodium knowlesi; they treated both suspected biliary sepsis (ceftriaxone) and malaria (artesunate, Riamet).
