A 20‑year‑old Zambian male student in China was transferred to our hospital with a 10‑day history of high fever (up to 40.8 °C) associated with chills, fatigue, vomiting, and diarrhea, followed by 3 days of unconsciousness and incontinence. His friend experienced identical symptoms after a shared meal but recovered without medical care. Initial blood work at a local hospital showed a leukocyte count of 5,680 cells/mm³ with 90.6 % neutrophils, platelet count of 12,000 cells/mm³, C‑reactive protein of 257.3 mg/L, and procalcitonin > 100 ng/mL. Empiric cefoperazone‑sulbactam (2 g IV) was started and blood cultures were drawn. He was transferred to Zhejiang Provincial People's Hospital on 14 October 2019.

On admission his temperature was 40.8 °C, respiratory rate 35 /min, pulse 157 beats/min, blood pressure 85/42 mmHg. He was intubated for hypoxemia. Neurologic examination revealed coma (GCS 5) and neck rigidity. Laboratory studies confirmed markedly elevated inflammatory markers, hepatic injury (ALT 73 U/L), hyperbilirubinemia (total bilirubin 206.6 µmol/L), and renal dysfunction (creatinine 279.2 µmol/L). Computed tomography of the head, chest, and abdomen demonstrated a possible minor subdural effusion in the right fronto‑parieto‑temporal region and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, with no abdominal abnormalities.

After admission he required mechanical ventilation and continuous renal replacement therapy. Platelet count rose to 50,000 cells/mm³ after transfusion. Lumbar puncture showed turbid yellow CSF with opening pressure 400 mmH₂O, positive Pandy’s test, glucose 1.53 mmol/L, leukocytes 1,585.8 cells/µL, and protein > 300 mg/dL. Initial consideration was gut‑derived intracranial infection, and linezolid (1.2 g/day) plus meropenem (6.0 g/day) were started. A blood culture from the prior hospital grew Gemella morbillorum; subsequent cultures of blood, CSF, stool, and other specimens were negative.

Metagenomic next‑generation sequencing (mNGS) of blood and CSF identified multiple oral microbiome organisms. A repeat head CT performed on hospital day 4 showed a patchy low‑density focus in the right frontal lobe and an arc‑shaped low‑density lesion in the right fronto‑parieto‑temporal region. After excluding communicable diseases such as malaria and dengue fever, the patient was admitted to the intensive care unit.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Sepsis of unknown origin considered due to high fever, leukocytosis, and markedly elevated CRP/PCT | "Suspecting 'infectious fever', blood culture was taken first, and cefoperazone sulbactam was administered intravenously..."
2. Malaria and dengue fever excluded early because of epidemiologic screening and negative tests | "After excluding communicable diseases such as malaria and dengue fever, he was admitted to the intensive care unit(ICU)."
3. Gut‑derived intracranial infection initially favored because of preceding gastrointestinal symptoms | "Since the patient started with gastrointestinal symptoms, gut‑derived intracranial infection was first considered..."
4. Odontogenic source entertained after mNGS detected oral flora in blood and CSF despite a normal oral examination | "The results of mNGS in blood and CSF revealed several oral microbiomes..." and "From the above results, odontogenic intracranial infection was suspected."
5. Primary pulmonary infection deemed less likely as the initial chest CT showed only inflammation without defined abscesses, and neurological findings predominated | "Computed tomography(CT) of the head, chest, and abdomen was taken and revealed a possibly minor subdural effusion...and bilateral pulmonary inflammation..."
6. Brain abscess diagnosis supported by CT demonstration of low‑density intracranial lesions and CSF pattern of high protein, low glucose, and neutrophilic pleocytosis | "a patchy low-density focus of the right frontal lobe and a minor arc‑shaped low-density lesion of the right fronto‑parieto‑temporal region were seen on rechecked head CT."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient was ultimately diagnosed with visceral leishmaniasis (kala‑azar), which corresponds to **leishmaniasis** on the 21 SELECTED diseases list.  
2. Breakpoint: Present the case up to the point where the emergency metagenomic next‑generation sequencing (mNGS) result is ordered, but **exclude** the mNGS findings that identified Leishmania. This gives enough clinical, laboratory, and imaging data (prolonged fever, splenomegaly, cytopenias, travel history, negative routine infectious work‑up) for a learner to consider leishmaniasis without revealing the definitive result.  
3. Analytic Distinctions: The authors differentiated leishmaniasis from sepsis, malignancy, decompensated cirrhosis, COVID‑19, fungal infections, and other parasitic diseases using negative routine tests, lack of response to broad‑spectrum antibiotics, and finally positive mNGS and rK39 serology.
case_prompt:
A 47‑year‑old male technical staff presented to the emergency department on December 28, 2020 with a four‑month history of recurrent fever that had worsened over the past month and was now accompanied by profuse watery diarrhea. The fever had initially begun abruptly with temperatures up to 39.9 °C, occurring in the afternoon and resolving after several hours, and was associated with headache, myalgia, and nausea. Antipyretics and oral artemisinin provided minimal relief, and multiple hospital visits failed to establish a diagnosis. After a brief afebrile period following discharge from a local hospital in October 2020, the fever returned with a sustained temperature of 39 °C and diarrhea occurring more than ten times per day, described as yellow liquid stool.

Past medical history was notable for malaria diagnosed six years earlier while he was in Africa, treated with oral quinine. He reported hypersensitivity to all quinolones.

On admission, vital signs were significant for fever; laboratory studies showed: hemoglobin 83 g/L, platelet count 16 × 10⁹/L, white‑blood‑cell count 2.82 × 10⁹/L with neutrophils 84 % and lymphocytes 8 %; procalcitonin 0.87 ng/mL. Blood cultures grew methicillin‑resistant coagulase‑negative Staphylococci. SARS‑CoV‑2 nucleic‑acid test was negative. Cryptococcal antigen, fungal (G) test, and galactomannan were all negative. Serologies for Schistosoma japonicum, Echinococcus granulosus, liver fluke, Plasmodium (antigen and smear), hepatitis A, hepatitis B, autoimmune liver disease, AFP, and CEA were negative. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated an enlarged liver and spleen. Contrast‑enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen revealed cirrhosis, splenomegaly, portal hypertension with collateral vessels, and peritoneal effusion. The working differential at this stage included sepsis, fever of unknown origin (infection versus tumor), and decompensated Child‑Pugh B cirrhosis. An emergency metagenomic next‑generation sequencing (mNGS) test on peripheral blood was ordered for further evaluation.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Sepsis considered due to fever and positive blood culture, but the isolate (methicillin‑resistant coagulase‑negative Staphylococci) was likely a contaminant and the patient failed to improve with moxifloxacin therapy. | "Even after being treated with moxifloxacin anti‑infective therapy, the patient continued to suffer from recurrent fever."
2. Tumor (malignancy) entertained as a cause of FUO, yet imaging showed only cirrhosis and splenomegaly without mass lesions, and tumor markers AFP and CEA were negative. | "Autoimmune liver, alpha fetoprotein (AFP), and carcinoembryonic antigen were negative."
3. Decompensated cirrhosis considered; the patient had Child‑Pugh B cirrhosis with portal hypertension, but cirrhosis alone could not explain persistent high‑grade fever and severe diarrhea. | "The following diagnosis was considered: sepsis, fever of undetermined origin (FUO): infection? The tumor? Child‑Pugh B stage of decompensated cirrhosis."
4. COVID‑19 excluded by a negative SARS‑CoV‑2 nucleic‑acid test. | "Novel Coronavirus nucleic acid test: negative."
5. Cryptococcosis and other invasive fungal infections ruled out by negative cryptococcal antigen, fungal G test, and galactomannan. | "The cryptococcus antigen test, fungal G test, and GM test were negative."
6. Other parasitic infections (Schistosoma, Echinococcus, liver fluke, malaria) excluded by negative serologies/antigen tests and blood smear. | "The schistosoma japonicum IgG antibody, echinococcus granulosus antibody, liver fluke antibody test, plasmodium antigen test, and blood smear test were all negative."
7. Leishmaniasis identified when mNGS detected Leishmania DNA and was corroborated by a positive rK39 antibody test, establishing the diagnosis of kala‑azar. | "The blood mNGS test results on the 4th day of admission detected Leishmania infantum and Leishmania donovani... One day later, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention performed an rK39 antibody test and the result appeared positive; therefore, the clinical diagnosis of kala‑azar was made."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient’s primary disease is a primary lung malignancy (non‑small cell lung cancer). This condition is not on the 21 SELECTED diseases list, so the target diagnosis is classified as OUT_OF_SCOPE.
2. Best breakpoint: End the presentation immediately before the bronchoscopy biopsy result (“pathological diagnosis of PSC”) is disclosed. At this point, the reader has the chief complaint, smoking history, PET‑CT findings of a large, invasive lung lesion with metabolically active lymph nodes, and bronchoscopy visualization of obstructing necrotic material—sufficient to formulate a differential that leads to the final diagnosis without revealing it.
3. Key analytic distinctions: The authors differentiated a malignant thoracic tumor from inflammatory lymphadenopathy based on PET‑CT metabolic activity, invasive imaging characteristics, and histopathology (biopsy). The lack of prior infectious disease history (e.g., tuberculosis, malaria) helped exclude infectious etiologies. The large size, mediastinal invasion, and smoking history supported primary lung cancer over benign cystic lesions.
case_prompt:
A 50‑year‑old man presented on August 22, 2021 with cough and expectoration of unclear origin. He had a 35‑year history of smoking one pack per day and consumed about 100 mL of alcohol daily. He denied any prior infectious diseases such as dysentery, malaria, viral hepatitis, or tuberculosis, and there was no family history of cancer aside from his father’s death from esophageal cancer.

On August 23, 2021, positron emission tomography‑computed tomography (PET‑CT) demonstrated a large cystic‑solid lesion measuring 8.6 × 5.9 × 9.9 cm extending from the right hilum to the right upper lobe. The lesion was interpreted as a right thoracic malignant tumor, invading the mediastinum adjacent to the superior vena cava and the main right pulmonary artery. Multiple enlarged lymph nodes were identified in both hila, the mediastinum, and the right supraclavicular fossa; the largest measured 1.5 × 1.4 cm and showed mildly to moderately increased metabolic activity, thought to represent lymph node inflammation (Figure 1A).

On August 26, 2021, electronic bronchoscopy revealed stenosis of the right upper lobe opening with obstruction of the lumen by necrotic material (Figure 1B). A bronchoscopic biopsy of the superior lobe of the right lung was performed; the pathological result was pending at this stage.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Primary lung malignancy suggested by a large invasive cystic‑solid lesion with high metabolic activity on PET‑CT in a heavy smoker | "considered to be a right thoracic malignant tumor" and "large cystic solid lesion ... invaded mediastinum adjacent superior vena cava and main right pulmonary artery."
2. Metastatic disease from an extrathoracic primary considered less likely because no other primary tumor was identified and the lesion’s location and SUV pattern were consistent with a primary lung process | "large cystic solid lesion ... in the lung field from the right hilum to the right upper lobe."
3. Infectious or inflammatory lymphadenitis (e.g., tuberculosis) considered but deemed unlikely given the patient’s denial of prior infectious disease history and the PET‑CT metabolic pattern suggesting malignancy rather than infection | "multiple enlarged lymph nodes ... with mild to moderate increase in metabolism, which was considered as multiple lymph node inflammation."
4. Benign cystic pulmonary lesion (e.g., bronchogenic cyst) considered but excluded due to aggressive features such as mediastinal invasion, rapid growth, and necrotic obstruction seen on bronchoscopy | "bronchoscopy revealed stenosis ... obstruction of the lumen by necrotic material."
5. Definitive diagnosis established by histopathology after bronchoscopy biopsy, confirming malignant carcinoma (PSC) | "electronic bronchoscopy biopsy ... led to a pathological diagnosis of PSC."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient’s presentation and subsequent serologic confirmation fulfill criteria for dengue infection, which is included in the 21 SELECTED diseases list. No other SELECTED disease is present.
2. Ideal Breakpoint: Present the case up to the description of imaging that revealed acute portal vein thrombosis, including initial vital signs, physical findings, laboratory abnormalities, and negative microbiology/immunology work‑up, but stop before the statement confirming anti‑DENV‑1 IgM positivity.
3. Author's Analytic Distinções: The authors established dengue by serology, while systematically excluding bacterial sepsis, other arboviral or viral infections, malaria, Chagas disease, leptospirosis, thrombotic microangiopathies, inherited thrombophilias, antiphospholipid syndrome, hemolytic anemia, and autoimmune vasculitides through cultures, serologies, coagulation panels, complement studies, and auto‑antibody testing.
case_prompt:
In October 2019, a 51‑year‑old woman from a rural area of Santander, Colombia, was admitted with a 5‑day history of fever and shivers accompanied by epigastric pain, vomiting, diarrhea, and an episode of hematemesis. Her past medical history included hypertension and dyslipidemia; she was taking enalapril, hydrochlorothiazide, atorvastatin, and aspirin.

On examination she was hemodynamically unstable with tachycardia, hypotension requiring vasopressors, delayed capillary refill, and signs of dehydration. Petechiae were noted on the extremities. Cardiopulmonary auscultation revealed bilateral basal rales. Abdominal palpation showed painful hepatomegaly extending 4 cm below the costal margin.

Laboratory studies demonstrated pancytopenia with severe thrombocytopenia (7 000 cells/mm³). Liver function tests showed transaminases elevated approximately 50‑fold, LDH > 1000 U/L, normal bilirubin, and normal alkaline phosphatase, suggesting a hepatocellular injury with an ischemic component. Coagulation testing revealed a prolonged PTT with a normal PT.

Chest X‑ray and abdominal ultrasound showed free fluid in the abdomen, pleural effusion, and hepatomegaly. Echocardiography identified bubbles in the right cardiac chambers without evidence of a shunt. Doppler ultrasonography of the portal and mesenteric veins and a contrast‑enhanced CT scan during the portal venous phase demonstrated an image compatible with acute complete non‑cirrhotic thrombosis of the proximal portal vein.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Dengue infection – severe febrile illness with petechiae, profound thrombocytopenia, transaminase elevation, capillary leak, distributive shock, and serologic confirmation. | "She was serologically confirmed positive for anti-DENV-1 IgM by ELISA."
2. Bacterial sepsis – considered because of fever and shock, but blood, urine, and stool cultures were negative. | "Cultures of the blood, urine, and stool yielded normal results."
3. Malaria – excluded by negative blood‑smear testing. | "Malaria ... tests in blood smear were negative."
4. Chagas disease – excluded by negative blood‑smear testing. | "Chagas tests in blood smear were negative."
5. Viral hepatitis (A, B, C) – excluded by serology. | "Hepatitis A, B, and C virus infections were ruled out serologically."
6. Cytomegalovirus infection – excluded by serology. | "CMV ... infections were ruled out serologically."
7. HIV infection – excluded by serology. | "HIV ... infections were ruled out serologically."
8. Leptospirosis – excluded by serology. | "Leptospira infections."
9. Thrombotic microangiopathies – screening showed no abnormality. | "Screening for TMAs ... did not reveal any abnormality."
10. Inherited thrombophilia (protein C/S deficiency, factor V Leiden, hyperhomocysteinemia, antithrombin III deficiency) – negative screening. | "Screening for ... protein C and S deficiency, factor V Leiden, hyperhomocysteinemia, and ATIII deficiency."
11. Antiphospholipid syndrome – negative screening. | "She was screened for antiphospholipid syndrome..."
12. Hemolytic anemia – no evidence on laboratory evaluation. | "There was no evidence of hemolytic anemia."
13. ADAMTS13 deficiency – normal activity level. | "ADAMTS 13 levels were normal."
14. Systemic autoimmune disease (SLE) – negative ANA and anti‑dsDNA. | "ANAs, anti-dsDNA ... were also negative."
15. ANCA‑associated vasculitis – negative ANCAs. | "ANCAs were also negative."
16. COVID‑19 – not tested; first national case occurred later, making infection unlikely. | "She was not tested for COVID-19 given that the first case reported in our country occurred in March 2020."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case ultimately diagnoses thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), which is not among the 21 SELECTED diseases; therefore the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.  
2. Best Breakpoint: End the presentation just before the explicit statement “TTP was diagnosed.” Include the clinical presentation, neurologic findings, hematologic labs, repeat CBC, coagulation profile, LDH, bilirubin, renal function, blood‑film results, PLASMIC score, and repeat head CT showing periventricular bleed. This provides sufficient data for learners to deduce TTP without revealing the authors’ final label.  
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished TTP from stroke, uterine bleed, hematologic malignancy, and other causes of seizures/hemorrhage by (a) demonstrating microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with schistocytes, (b) severe thrombocytopenia with normal coagulation studies, (c) markedly elevated LDH, (d) high PLASMIC score indicating high probability of ADAMTS‑13 deficiency, and (e) exclusion of infectious etiologies (HIV, hepatitis, malaria) and malignancy through negative serologies and blood‑film.
case_prompt:
A 40‑year‑old African female was referred to the Emergency Department for a stroke confirmed by CT scan. She had 1‑day history of slurred speech, facial asymmetry, and left upper and lower limb weakness. Past history included hypertension (non‑compliant for 2 weeks), two prior strokes 5 years earlier, menorrhagia for 10 years, and encephalitis at 8 months of age. Medications were amlodipine and lisinopril.

On examination she was afebrile (36.8 °C), pulse 81 bpm, respirations 20/min, BP 103/67 mmHg. She was severely pale with purpuric patches on flexural areas of elbows, knees, and posterior lower legs. Neurologic exam showed left‑sided power 1/5; other systems were unremarkable.

Initial labs: Hb 4.3 g/dL, platelets 18 × 10⁹/L, WBC 10.47 × 10⁹/L, normal renal function. Initial working diagnosis comprised acute ischemic stroke, abnormal uterine bleeding from a leiomyoma, possible hematologic malignancy, and a bleeding diathesis. Samples were sent for blood film, malaria smear, LDH, uric acid, coagulation profile, HIV, ANA, hepatitis B/C, plus ECG, echocardiogram, abdominal‑pelvic ultrasound, and chest X‑ray. She received 1 unit whole blood and physiotherapy. By days 2–3 her limb power improved to 4/5.

On day 4 she developed tonic‑clonic seizures and progressive jaundice. Repeat CBC: Hb 6.2 g/dL, WBC 13.5 × 10⁹/L, platelets 22 × 10⁹/L. Coagulation: INR 1.16, PT 9.8 s, APTT 33.9 s, PTT 0.92 s. LDH 2 611 U/L (ref 135‑214), uric acid 0.4 mmol/L (ref 0.13‑0.39), direct bilirubin 19.86 µmol/L, indirect bilirubin 34.7 µmol/L, globulin 25.7 g/L. HIV, hepatitis B/C, ECG, chest X‑ray, malaria smear, AST, ALT, and ANA were normal. Thyroid function was normal.

The working diagnosis was revised to recurrent seizures with differentials of recurrent stroke with hemorrhagic transformation, post‑stroke seizures, intracranial infection (meningoencephalitis), electrolyte encephalopathy, and intracranial hemorrhage from idiopathic or acquired thrombocytopenia. Repeat head CT showed a periventricular bleed. Blood‑film comment revealed normocytic normochromic RBCs, ++ schistocytes, occasional normoblasts, few polychromatic cells, neutrophilic leukocytosis with left shift, and reduced platelets without clumping, suggestive of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. The PLASMIC score was calculated, yielding 7 (high risk) with a 96.2 % probability of severe ADAMTS‑13 deficiency. A repeat renal panel showed urea 31.7 mmol/L (ref 2.1‑7.1) and creatinine 492 µmol/L (ref 62‑106).
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Acute ischemic stroke with left hemiparesis was considered because of focal neurologic deficits and CT evidence of stroke | "The initial working diagnosis was an acute ischemic stroke with left hemiparesis..."
2. Abnormal uterine bleeding from leiomyoma was entertained due to longstanding menorrhagia and severe anemia | "...Abnormal uterine bleeding from a uterine leiomyoma..."
3. Hematologic malignancy was part of the differential given profound pancytopenia and purpuric rash | "...hematological malignancy..."
4. Primary bleeding diathesis was evaluated because of severe thrombocytopenia and purpuric lesions | "...bleeding diathesis."
5. Recurrent stroke with hemorrhagic transformation was reconsidered after seizures and new CT bleed | "...recurrent stroke with hemorrhagic transformation..."
6. Post‑stroke seizures were a possibility given tonic‑clonic activity after the initial event | "...poststroke seizures..."
7. Intracranial infection (meningoencephalitis) was listed due to seizures and neurologic decline | "...intracranial infections such as meningoencephalitis..."
8. Electrolyte encephalopathy was contemplated as a metabolic cause of seizures | "...electrolyte encephalopathy..."
9. Intracranial hemorrhage from idiopathic or acquired thrombocytopenia was considered because of low platelets and new bleed | "...intracranial hemorrhage from idiopathic or acquired thrombocytopenia."
10. Infectious etiologies (HIV, hepatitis B/C, malaria) were ruled out by negative serologies and blood smear | "HIV, Hepatitis B and C, ... blood film for malaria parasite ... were all normal."
11. Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia indicated by schistocytes pointed toward a thrombotic microangiopathy rather than malignancy | "schistocytes ++ ... suggestive of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia."
12. Normal coagulation parameters (INR, PT, APTT) argued against disseminated intravascular coagulation | "Clotting profile results showed an INR of 1.16, PT - 9.8 s, APTT - 33.9 s..."
13. Markedly elevated LDH and bilirubin supported hemolysis | "LDH was 2 611 U/L... both direct and indirect bilirubin were high..."
14. High PLASMIC score (7) conferred >96 % risk of severe ADAMTS‑13 deficiency, strongly favoring thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura | "the PLASMIC score... yielded a total score of 7 (high risk) and a 96.2% risk of severe ADAMTS13 deficiency."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient’s clinical picture culminates in a diagnosis of **malaria** (P. falciparum), which is included in the 21 SELECTED diseases list. Hence the target diagnosis is malaria (selected disease).
2. Best breakpoint: End the case presentation just before the malaria rapid diagnostic test result and the thick/thin smear confirmation are disclosed. Include chief complaint, travel history, symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam, and initial laboratory findings (CBC, renal panel, CRP) that allow the learner to suspect malaria without revealing the definitive positive test.
3. Author’s analytic distinctions: The authors distinguished malaria from bacterial sepsis (absence of sepsis signs), from other enteric infections (negative stool cultures), and confirmed malaria by parasitologic evidence (RDT, thick/thin smear) and by the presence of high parasitemia and malaria‑related organ dysfunction (acute renal failure, thrombocytopenia, elevated CRP).
case_prompt:
A 22‑year‑old student from Paris presented after fainting during a hike in the rainforest of French Guiana. He arrived at the local health centre in poor general condition, with fever, vomiting, and watery diarrhea. He had returned 11 days earlier from a 4‑month stay in Cameroon, during which he experienced two malaria episodes that were treated with artesunate and an unidentified tablet, respectively, while self‑administering Artemisia annua herbal tea for prophylaxis. Five days before presentation he developed symptoms while in Paris, sought care in Kourou, and was diagnosed by thick and thin blood smears as positive for *Plasmodium falciparum*. He declined the prescribed antimalarial, continued the herbal tea, and three days after arriving in the village was found by police unable to walk, febrile, and severely ill. 

Physical examination at the health centre showed no signs of sepsis, bleeding, hypoglycemia, or dyspnea; neurological exam was normal. Initial laboratory studies revealed: hemoglobin 12.7 g/dL, leukocytes 8 ×10⁹/L, platelets 19 ×10⁹/L, alkaline reserve 20.8 mmol/L, urea 16.4 mmol/L (reference 2.8‑8.1), creatinine 135 µmol/L (reference 59‑104), bilirubin 45.8 µmol/L (reference <21), and C‑reactive protein 205.4 mg/L (reference <5). The patient had ongoing watery diarrhea but no further vomiting after receiving metoclopramide. Renal function deteriorated on repeat testing (creatinine 325 µmol/L, urea 26.1 mmol/L, eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73 m²). Lactate was normal (1.6 mmol/L). No other features of severe malaria were noted at that time.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Malaria suspected due to recent travel to endemic areas (Cameroon, French Guiana) and febrile illness with gastrointestinal symptoms. | "He had returned from a 4‑month stay in Cameroon... diagnosed through thick and thin blood smears that were positive for *P. falciparum*."
2. Severe malaria considered because of high parasitemia and organ dysfunction (acute renal failure, thrombocytopenia, marked inflammatory response). | "Thick and thin blood smears were positive for *P. falciparum* with a parasitemia of 1.62% of erythrocytes... worsening of the renal function with creatinine dosed at 325 µmol/L... platelet count 19 G/L... CRP 205.4 mg/L."
3. Bacterial sepsis evaluated and excluded on exam (no signs of sepsis) and laboratory data. | "Physical examination showed no sign of sepsis, bleeding, hypoglycemia or dyspnea."
4. Other enteric infections ruled out by negative stool cultures and parasitology. | "Stool cultures as well as stool parasitology were screened and no pathogens were found."
5. Alternative malaria treatment strategies (IV artesunate) were debated but not pursued because the patient improved clinically, supporting that the initial therapy was adequate for severe malaria. | "It was decided not to switch treatment for IV artesunate because the patient's clinical state was already improving after the first dose of artemether/lumefantrine."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case describes progressive cognitive impairment with imaging evidence of encephalomalacia and a recent acute cerebellar infarct. No disease from the 21 SELECTED list is diagnosed; the likely diagnosis (vascular cognitive impairment/dementia) is OUT_OF_SCOPE.
2. Breakpoint: Include all clinical history, physical exam, laboratory results, and imaging up to the brain MRI on 22 September 2021 (which shows punctate DWI hyperintensity indicating an acute cerebellar infarct and chronic encephalomalacia). Exclude any discussion or concluding statement that names the final diagnosis.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors ruled out infectious etiologies (negative hepatitis, syphilis, HIV serologies), metabolic deficiencies (normal vitamin B12, folate, thyroid), and psychiatric depression (lack of response to neuro‑nutritional therapy). The progressive imaging changes and acute diffusion restriction guided them toward a vascular cause of the cognitive decline.
case_prompt:
The patient is a 33‑year‑old male automobile factory worker who presented to a cognitive‑impairment clinic on 15 September 2021 with a 3‑year history of memory decline, worsening over the preceding 5 months. Three years ago he noted recent‑memory impairment, reduced responsiveness during conversation, occasional incoherence, and emotional indifference, although he remained able to work. Two years prior he underwent cranial MRI (17 December 2019) that showed encephalomalacia in the right basal ganglia, frontal lobe and cerebral atrophy. Five months before admission his memory loss progressed, with inability to recall the previous day’s events, difficulty learning new lyrics, and transient typing difficulty. A repeat MRI on 31 August 2021 demonstrated expansion of encephalomalacia to bilateral frontal lobes, right insula, and right temporo‑occipital junction. Lumbar puncture revealed normal opening pressure, clear CSF, and normal routine, biochemical and immune studies. He received nutritional and intellectual‑promotion therapy without significant improvement and was admitted to the neurology department.

Past medical history is unremarkable for hypertension, diabetes, coronary or cerebrovascular disease, hepatitis, tuberculosis, malaria, trauma, transfusion, or drug allergy. He reported emotional trauma in 2011, a dog bite with rabies vaccination in 2018, and a 10‑year smoking history (20 cigarettes/day). Family history includes an uncle with early‑onset memory impairment.

Physical examination: T 36.5 °C, P 52/min, R 17/min, BP 127/87 mmHg. Cardiorespiratory exam was normal. Neurological exam showed clear consciousness, fluent language, intact orientation and calculation, impaired recent memory, normal pupils, normal ocular movements, intact cranial nerves, grade V limb strength, normal tone, brisk tendon reflexes, negative Babinski, and no frontal release signs.

Routine blood work, coagulation profile, serum immune panel, liver and kidney function, lipids, glucose, hs‑CRP, homocysteine, thyroid function, folic acid, vitamin B12, ferritin, hepatitis A‑C serologies, syphilis and HIV tests, urine and stool studies were all unremarkable. ECG showed sinus rhythm; ambulatory ECG was normal. Cardiac echocardiography revealed mild valvular regurgitation without intracardiac shunt. Abdominal and urinary system doppler ultrasound were normal.

Brain MRI on 22 September 2021 showed punctate hyperintensity on diffusion‑weighted imaging of the right cerebellum consistent with an acute cerebral infarction, along with cerebral atrophy and varying degrees of encephalomalacia. Magnetic resonance angiography demonstrated no significant vascular morphological abnormalities. Neuropsychological testing revealed multidomain cognitive decline, especially delayed recall deficits, emotional apathy and sleep disturbances. Automated AI‑based brain volumetric analysis demonstrated reduced gray and white matter proportions and decreased volumes of bilateral thalamus, caudate, putamen, frontal, parietal, occipital, temporal lobes and especially the cerebellum.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Infectious etiologies such as tuberculosis, syphilis, and HIV were considered but excluded by negative serologic testing and lack of clinical signs. | "immune panel (hepatitis A, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, syphilis and HIV) showed no significant abnormalities."
2. Metabolic causes (vitamin B12, folate, thyroid dysfunction) were ruled out by normal laboratory values. | "serum ... folic acid, vitamin B12, ... thyroid function ... showed no significant abnormalities."
3. Primary psychiatric depression was unlikely because cognitive symptoms persisted despite neuro‑nutritional and intellectual‑promotion therapy. | "His symptoms were not significantly improved after treatment with nutritional nerve and intellectual promotion."
4. Vascular etiology was supported by MRI evidence of chronic encephalomalacia and a new acute cerebellar infarct on DWI, indicating ischemic injury underlying the cognitive decline. | "MRI ... showed punctate hyperintensity on diffusion‑weighted imaging of the right cerebellum, suggesting an acute cerebral infarction, cerebral atrophy and encephalomalacia foci."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient’s definitive diagnosis is Plasmodium falciparum infection – malaria, which is included in the 21 SELECTED diseases list. He also has chronic hepatitis B, an OUT_OF_SCOPE condition, but the teaching focus will be on malaria.
2. Best Breakpoint: Stop the presentation just before the peripheral blood smear and blood parasite test results are presented. This includes the chief complaint, travel history, vital signs, physical exam (unremarkable), initial laboratory abnormalities, imaging findings (ileus without obstruction), and the decision to admit for possible sepsis with empiric antibiotics. No mention of malaria confirmation or hepatitis B results is included.
3. Author's Analytic Distinctions: The authors considered infectious sepsis of unknown source, ruled out common viral respiratory pathogens with negative tests, excluded mechanical bowel obstruction via imaging, and ultimately identified malaria parasites on peripheral smear, which confirmed the diagnosis despite the initial broad empiric antibiotic coverage.
case_prompt:
A 27-year-old man with a past history of recurrent malaria presented with three days of high‑grade fevers, chills, generalized aches, and three episodes of non‑bloody, non‑bilious emesis. He had not had a bowel movement since symptom onset and had poor oral intake due to vomiting. Two weeks earlier he returned to the United States after a month in Guinea, West Africa, where he was bitten by mosquitoes several times. He recalled multiple childhood malaria infections, the last about 12 years ago.

A 65‑year‑old man was admitted because of generalized weakness, coughing, and sputum production. Two months earlier he had developed weakness, sweating, anorexia, and an intermittent cough with whitish sputum that slowly worsened. He recalled eating raw pork several times 20 years ago; there was no relevant family history.  

Vital signs on admission: temperature 36 °C, pulse 98/min, respiration 20/min, blood pressure 110/75 mmHg.  

Physical examination: the patient appeared weak and chronically ill, alert, with poor nutritional status. Conjunctivae and corneas were normal. Lungs were clear, without crackles or wheezes. Cardiac exam showed normal S1, normally split S2, no murmurs. Abdomen revealed mild right‑upper‑quadrant tenderness; the liver was palpated four fingerbreadths below the costal margin. Neurologic exam was unremarkable. Multiple subcutaneous nodules were noted on the upper extremities and axillae.  

Laboratory data: hemoglobin 13.9 g/dL, hematocrit 41.8 %, white‑cell count 8 700/µL with 4 % eosinophils, BUN 5 mg/dL, creatinine 1.3 mg/dL, total protein 8.1 g/dL, albumin 4.3 g/dL, AST 42 U/L, ALT 32 U/L; HBsAg and anti‑HBs were negative. Urine and stool studies were normal.  

Sputum acid‑fast bacilli stain and cytologic examination were negative. Pulmonary function testing was within normal limits (FEV₁ 4.1 L, FEV₁/FVC 87 %).  

Chest radiograph demonstrated multiple nodular densities throughout both lower lung fields. Computed tomography of the brain and chest showed multiple nodular and small calcified densities.  

A biopsy of a subcutaneous nodule was performed on hospital day 4.

4. Definitive diagnosis established by histopathology: “A biopsy of a subcutaneous nodule … upon microscopic examination, a bladder worm … and … cysticercus … was observed.” This finding confirmed neurocysticercosis.

A 35‑year‑old man presented with sudden bilateral loss of vision and periorbital swelling. He reported fever and pedal edema. His past medical history was membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, for which he had been receiving oral prednisone (dose not specified) and an ACE inhibitor for the prior seven months. Ocular examination showed light‑perception vision with inaccurate ray projection in both eyes. Slit‑lamp exam revealed 2+ anterior chamber cells and pigment on the anterior lens surface bilaterally. Fundus examination demonstrated hazy media, inferotemporal retinal detachment, sub‑retinal exudates, intraretinal hemorrhages, dilated veins and narrowed arteries. Intra‑ocular pressure (IOP) was 16 mmHg in each eye. Blood pressure was 160/100 mmHg with bradycardia. An initial impression of hypertension‑related exudative retinal detachment was made, although atypical central serous chorioretinopathy and Vogt‑Koyanagi‑Harada syndrome were also considered. He was given hydrocortisone 200 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, cefixime 200 mg twice daily, and amlodipine 5 mg daily.

Two days later he developed generalized hypotony, staggering gait, truncal ataxia, buccal and proximal weakness, and decreased plantar reflexes. Neurology considered a pontomedullary lesion or cytomegalovirus meningitis. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was normal. Brain MRI showed multiple cystic‑enhancing lesions in both cerebral hemispheres, thought to represent tuberculomas or neurocysticercosis. He was started on anti‑tubercular therapy (ATT) and oral steroids.

Four days after initiating ATT he experienced a generalized tonic‑clonic seizure. Repeat contrast MRI demonstrated disseminated parenchymal lesions. Despite antiepileptic therapy he initially improved for two weeks, then worsened. Ocular findings now included restricted abduction, sluggish pupils, 3+ anterior chamber cells, and markedly elevated IOPs (66 mmHg right, 52 mmHg left). Fundus exam showed increased exudates, higher retinal detachment, and vitreous cells. Disseminated toxoplasma infection or malignancy were considered. An aqueous tap PCR was negative for malignant cells, tuberculosis, CMV, HSV, VZV, and toxoplasma.

An Ahmed glaucoma valve was placed in the left eye after failure of maximal medical therapy; postoperative examination showed a stony‑hard eye with severe conjunctival chemosis and shallow anterior chamber. Five weeks after presentation a pars‑plana vitrectomy with vitreous biopsy was performed. Intravitreal vancomycin, ceftazidime, and voriconazole were administered, and fortified topical antibiotics plus natamycin were started for presumed fungal endophthalmitis. Smears and cultures of ocular tissue were negative for bacteria and fungi.

Subsequent work‑up showed no lumbar puncture opening pressure, severe conjunctival chemosis, exposure keratopathy, and conjunctival abscesses. CSF was negative for CMV and Cryptococcus. Blood serologies were negative for HIV, TORCH pathogens, CMV, and HSV. Blood cultures showed no bacterial or fungal growth. Bone‑marrow biopsy was normal.

Because of progressive systemic decline and severe cachexia, repeat brain MRI revealed a large right parieto‑occipital mass, bilateral globe deformities, intra‑ocular hemorrhages, and extra‑ocular soft‑tissue inflammation. A multiloculated intracerebral abscess was drained, and a brain biopsy was performed.

A 34‑year‑old right‑handed Hispanic male presented after a new‑onset generalized seizure while driving. He emigrated from Mexico 15 years earlier and had not returned for 6 years; his work required travel throughout the United States, including Texas, Louisiana, Virginia, Florida, and Nebraska, and he had lived in Alabama for the past 11 years. At an outside hospital, non‑contrast CT of the head and subsequent MRI revealed a large, multilobulated cystic lesion in the left fronto‑temporal region. Lumbar puncture with CSF analysis, culture, cytology, and flow cytometry were unremarkable. He was started on oral phenytoin and discharged with outpatient follow‑up.

In clinic, neurologic examination was normal. Review of the outside imaging showed a non‑contrast CT head with a 6.5 × 4.5 × 4 cm multilobulated cystic lesion centered around the sylvian fissure, producing significant mass effect, a 0.5 cm midline shift, and central calcifications. MRI demonstrated T2‑hyperintensity identical to CSF, minimal wall signal on FLAIR, no diffusion restriction on DWI, and no peripheral contrast enhancement. Serum cysticercosis IgG antibodies were positive.

He received dexamethasone 8 mg IV every 8 h the day prior to surgery and continued phenytoin. A contrast‑enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis was performed to exclude metastatic disease and hydatid cysts and was unremarkable. The next day, a left pterional craniotomy was performed. After opening the dura, chronic inflammation of the superficial pia and arachnoid was noted. A Touhey needle was inserted into the temporal cyst and aspirated 6 mL of clear fluid, allowing brain relaxation. During sylvian dissection the cyst began to evaginate, ruptured, and its contents spilled into the subarachnoid space; copious irrigation and a second dose of dexamethasone were given. The cyst complex was then removed en bloc with no residual lesion apparent.

Post‑operatively the patient had no neurological deficits. Non‑contrast CT head and MRI on postoperative day 1 showed expected encephalomalacia around the resection cavity without residual lesion. He completed a 14‑day oral albendazole course (400 mg twice daily) with a tapering steroid regimen and was discharged on postoperative day 5. At outpatient follow‑up he was well; surveillance CT demonstrated stable left fronto‑temporal encephalomalacia and no recurrence.

Three years later she experienced another severe headache with nausea and vomiting, which responded to steroids; thereafter she had recurrent episodes of headache and vomiting every 2–3 years, requiring several hospitalizations. Since 2003 she had been taking oral steroids (deflazacort 6 mg to 30 mg) almost continuously and reported that lumbar punctures temporarily alleviated her headaches.

In 2005 she developed progressive gait disturbance and forgetfulness confirmed by her husband; two years later urinary incontinence began, rendering her unable to perform household chores. She had been operated for benign thyroid cysts in 2003 and was on thyroxine therapy.

At first interview, neurologic examination showed an unsteady, wide‑based gait, inability to walk in tandem, slight retropulsion, and bilateral papilledema in regression. She scored 24 on the Mini‑Mental State Examination (MMSE); verbal fluency was markedly reduced (7 animals/min, 7 words beginning with “p”/min). The remainder of the neurologic exam was unremarkable.

A CSF analysis performed in July 2008 disclosed 35 leukocytes (predominantly lymphomononuclear cells with 5 % eosinophils), protein 77 mg/dL, a high gammaglobulin concentration (27 %; normal 7‑14 %), and normal glucose. Serologic tests for toxoplasmosis, cytomegalovirus, Epstein‑Barr virus (both IgG and IgM), and HIV were all negative.

In October 2008 magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed mild communicating hydrocephalus. A ventriculoperitoneal shunt was placed, producing almost immediate clinical improvement. A subsequent CT scan confirmed resolution of hydrocephalus and a slight increase in the right Sylvian fissure.

The patient returned in May 2010 reporting rapid improvement after shunting, but recurrence of headache, somnolence, mental confusion, and urinary incontinence began 8 months earlier. Examination now showed no papilledema but a broad‑based gait; MMSE was 23 with verbal fluency of 6 animals/min. CT demonstrated increased ventricular dilation. Brain MRI revealed moderate hydrocephalus, the shunt catheter tip in the right lateral ventricle, and multiple cystic lesions in the right Sylvian fissure lacking a scolex, with peripheral enhancement and a “bunch of grapes” appearance.

Dexchlorpheniramine 6 mg daily (2 mg three times daily) and a tapering course of dexamethasone (starting at 12 mg daily, tapering over 20 days) were initiated, resulting in slight improvement. In September 2010 a new ventriculoperitoneal shunt was inserted, leading to marked clinical recovery. Follow‑up MRI after three years showed resolution of hydrocephalus, marked reduction in the number of Sylvian fissure cysts, persistent slight peripheral enhancement, and high T2/FLAIR signal.

case_prompt:
A 64‑year‑old woman underwent haploidentical allogeneic hematopoietic stem‑cell transplantation (HSCT) for acute myeloid leukemia secondary to myelodysplastic syndrome in September 2016. Conditioning consisted of reduced‑dose thiotepa, Busulfan, and fludarabine, with GVHD prophylaxis including cyclosporine, methotrexate, rabbit anti‑thymocyte globulin, basiliximab, and mycophenolic acid. She developed acute gastrointestinal GVHD on day +100, treated with steroids, and subsequently experienced multiple cytomegalovirus reactivations, sarcopenia, and a femoral head fracture.

On day +320 post‑transplant she presented with nausea, vomiting, nystagmus, diplopia, and severe cutaneous purpura. Brain CT revealed a right multicystic cerebellar mass with perilesional edema compressing the fourth ventricle; MRI confirmed these findings. Congenital abnormalities such as cavernous malformations were excluded. Infectious (tuberculotic, echinococcal, toxoplasmotic) and neoplastic etiologies were deemed possible, prompting a suboccipital craniotomy for lesion excision. The attempted biopsy produced only normal cerebellar tissue with polymorphonuclear leukocytes; no neoplastic cells or fungal hyphae were identified. Fundoscopic examination showed no cystic lesions. QuantiFERON‑TB Gold and tuberculin skin testing were negative.

Empiric meropenem plus clindamycin was initiated without clinical or radiologic improvement. After 20 days, high‑dose intravenous trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole was started for suspected cerebral toxoplasmosis (donor and patient were IgG positive pre‑HSCT). Two weeks later the patient’s symptoms persisted and MRI demonstrated progression of the multicystic lesions with increased edema and early cerebellar herniation. New neurological findings included an intention tremor, bilateral hypoacusia, and severe hematologic toxicity.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Congenital vascular malformation (cavernous malformation) considered but excluded because the lesions were new and not previously reported, and imaging did not show characteristic features. | "As the lesions were not previously reported, we ruled out congenital abnormalities such as cavernous malformations."
2. Tuberculoma considered; ruled out by negative interferon‑gamma release assay and negative tuberculin skin test. | "The fundus oculi assessment did not show cystis. Moreover, the quantiferon and TB skin test (or PPD test) were negative."
3. Echinococcal cyst considered; lack of supporting clinical or serologic evidence led to its exclusion (implicit from differential list and absence of positive findings). | "Since other differential diagnosis, including infectious (tuberculotic, echinococcal, and toxoplasmotic cysts) … required a histological assessment..."
4. Cerebral toxoplasmosis suspected due to donor and patient IgG positivity; high‑dose TMP‑SMX was given but there was no clinical or radiologic improvement, making toxoplasmosis unlikely. | "High‑dose intravenous trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole for a suspicious cerebral toxoplasmosis ... was given ... In absence of clinical and radiological improvement..."
5. Bacterial brain abscess or other bacterial infection considered; empiric meropenem and clindamycin failed to produce clinical or imaging response. | "Although prompt empiric antibiotic combination of meropenem and clindamycin was started, clinical and neuroradiological response was not achieved."
6. Neoplastic process considered; biopsy specimens showed only normal cerebellar tissue without neoplastic cells, arguing against tumor. | "No neoplastic cells … were seen."
7. Fungal infection considered; histology showed no fungal hyphae, reducing likelihood of fungal etiology. | "No … fungal hyphae were seen."
8. Neurocysticercosis ultimately diagnosed by applying revised diagnostic criteria: presence of multicystic lesions without discernible scolex, compatible neurological signs, and epidemiologic exposure (rural residence, household contact). | "we applied the revised diagnostic criteria for Taenia solium infection and discovered that our patient presented a definitive diagnosis of NCC …"

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case’s definitive diagnosis is spinal syphilitic gumma, which is a manifestation of syphilis. “syphilis” is on the SELECTED diseases list, so the target diagnosis is syphilis (SELECTED).
2. Ideal Breakpoint: Include all presenting data up to the point where the authors first state their diagnostic impression (“spinal syphilitic gumma was strongly suspected”). Stop after reporting the negative ancillary serologies (AQP4‑IgG, ANA, RF, tuberculosis antibody, neurocysticercosis antibody, tumor marker) so that the learner has the clinical picture, MRI findings, CSF results, and positive syphilis serology but no explicit statement of the diagnosis.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors differentiate spinal tumor from inflammatory granuloma based on MRI characteristics; they rule out tuberculosis and neurocysticercosis with negative specific antibodies; they confirm syphilis with positive TPPA and high TRUST titers in serum and CSF; HIV negativity and other autoimmune panels further narrow the differential.
case_prompt:
A 46‑year‑old male worker was admitted with 5 days of bilateral lower‑limb numbness, lower back pain, and irregular defecation, the pain gradually spreading to the upper abdomen. Examination showed muscle strength 4/5 in the lower extremities and 5/5 in the upper extremities, with hyperalgesia below the T7 level. Deep tendon reflexes in the arms and legs were normal, as were abdominal reflexes; no pathologic reflexes were elicited. He had a history of hypertension and compensated kidney failure, without prior trauma, cancer, diabetes, or allergic disease.

Spinal MRI demonstrated swelling of the thoracic cord with a long‑segment diffuse high‑signal intensity and a heterogeneous nodule with a hypointense center at T7 on T2‑weighted images. Post‑gadolinium imaging showed peripheral enhancement of the nodule in the dorsal aspect of the cord, while the diffuse high‑signal lesion did not enhance. Brain MRI was normal.

Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed an elevated leukocyte count (120 cells/µL, 76 % lymphocytes) and increased protein (84 mg/dL); glucose and chloride were normal. Syphilis serology was positive: TPPA reactive and TRUST titers of 1/128 in serum and 1/32 in CSF. HIV testing was negative. Serologic testing for AQP4‑IgG, antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, tuberculosis antibody, neurocysticercosis antibody, and tumor markers were all negative. The patient denied any prior venereal disease, unprotected commercial sex, homosexuality, and reported no current skin or mucosal lesions.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Spinal tumor considered due to a focal intramedullary nodule on MRI | "Performance of MRI may indicate spinal tumors or inflammatory granuloma such as syphilis, tuberculosis, and neurocysticercosis."
2. Inflammatory granuloma (syphilis) supported by positive TPPA and high TRUST titers in serum and CSF | "Syphilis serology including the Treponema pallidum particle agglutination (TPPA) and toluidine red unheated serum test (TRUST) demonstrated positive results. The TRUST titer of serum and CSF were 1/128 and 1/32, respectively."
3. Tuberculosis excluded by negative specific antibody test | "Normal results were observed in the tests for ... tuberculosis antibody ..."
4. Neurocysticercosis excluded by negative specific antibody test | "Normal results were observed in the tests for ... neurocysticercosis antibody ..."
5. Autoimmune demyelinating disease (NMOSD, MS) deemed unlikely due to negative AQP4‑IgG and normal brain MRI | "Normal results were observed in the tests for AQP4‑IgG ... Brain MRI was normal."
6. HIV‑related opportunistic infections ruled out by negative HIV serology | "Serological test for HIV was negative."
7. CSF findings (lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein) consistent with neurosyphilis rather than tumor | "CSF examination showed elevated cell (120/mul, 76 % lymphocytes) and protein levels (84 mg/dl)..."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The report’s main diagnostic conclusion is “blue nevus syndrome,” which is not among the 21 SELECTED diseases. Neurocysticercosis, a SELECTED disease, is only mentioned as past medical history without a current diagnostic work‑up. Therefore the target diagnosis for the teaching case is the out‑of‑scope disease.
2. Ideal Breakpoint: End the prompt just before the sentence that states the definitive histopathologic diagnosis (“Based on these findings, the diagnosis of blue nevus syndrome was made.”). Include the initial neurologic presentation, skin lesion description, neuro‑imaging findings, and the subsequent respiratory deterioration, but omit the pathology results that confirm the syndrome.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished the vascular malformations seen on imaging (consistent with cavernous‑type lesions) from infectious or inflammatory processes, used skin‑biopsy histology to identify characteristic hyalinized vascular proliferations, and finally integrated clinical, imaging, and histologic data to assign the rare “blue nevus syndrome.”
case_prompt:
A 74‑year‑old man was admitted to the emergency department with sudden aphasia, left facial palsy, and difficulty swallowing. His sister and son had been diagnosed with epilepsy, presumably due to neurocysticercosis. The patient had a history of structural epilepsy thought to be secondary to intraparenchymal neurocysticercosis and had received a single course of albendazole; he had been on carbamazepine 200 mg twice daily for most of his life with good seizure control (approximately one seizure per year).

On examination he had disseminated skin lesions on the upper thorax, abdomen, and all limbs and mucous membranes. The lesions were violet and skin‑colored nodules and macules, 0.5 mm to 2 cm in size; nodular neoformations were rubbery, adherent, and appeared vascular. Skin biopsies were taken.

Neurologic examination revealed bilateral abducens nerve palsy, left central facial palsy, left soft‑palate palsy with a diminished ipsilateral gag reflex, tongue deviation to the left, a discrete left‑body weakness with an ipsilateral extensor plantar response, and left‑side dysmetria on finger‑to‑nose testing.

Brain CT showed a large right frontal hematoma in acute and subacute phases with perilesional edema, multiple calcified intraparenchymal lesions, and a punctiform hemorrhage within the medulla oblongata. CT angiography confirmed multiple heterogeneous contrast‑enhancing vascular malformations in the cortical and subcortical areas of both cerebral hemispheres. Brain MRI demonstrated a moderately differentiated hyperintense lesion in the right frontotemporal region (≈ 27 × 38 mm) with abundant edema and irregular core, additional lesions in the right occipital lobes (~ 10 mm), a left temporal pole lesion (10.5 mm), and numerous supra‑ and infratentorial punctate hypointense foci on T2* GRE consistent with cavernous‑type lesions.

The following week the patient developed respiratory distress. Thoracic CT revealed multilobar pneumonia; broad‑spectrum intravenous antibiotics were started, and Staphylococcus aureus was isolated from blood and sputum cultures. He died a few days later, and an autopsy was performed.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Neurocysticercosis considered as cause of prior epilepsy but not responsible for the acute presentation | "He was diagnosed with structural epilepsy suspected to be secondary to intraparenchymal neurocysticercosis..."
2. Cerebral cavernous malformations (CCM) suggested by imaging pattern of heterogeneous contrast‑enhancing vascular lesions and punctate hypointense foci | "multiple heterogeneous contrast‑enhancing vascular malformations... This pattern was consistent with CCM‑like lesions..."
3. Infectious etiology (e.g., bacterial meningitis or brain abscess) ruled out by lack of meningeal signs and negative CSF data (not reported) and later identified as Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia causing pneumonia rather than CNS infection | "Staphylococcus aureus was isolated from the blood and sputum samples."
4. Primary vascular tumors (e.g., hemangioma) deemed less likely because skin lesions were multiple, systemic, and histology showed hyalinized vascular proliferations rather than neoplastic endothelial proliferation | "skin lesions with multiple vascular proliferations with areas of dilated and congestive venous vessels, ectasia, and extensively hyalinized..."
5. Blue nevus syndrome ultimately diagnosed based on combined cutaneous vascular histology and systemic vascular malformations | "Based on these findings, the diagnosis of blue nevus syndrome was made."

1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient’s lesion is confirmed as neurocysticercosis, which appears on the 21 SELECTED diseases list. Therefore the target diagnosis is neurocysticercosis (selected).
2. Breakpoint: Stop the case presentation before the MRI description is interpreted as “most consistent with racemose NCC” and before the worm is explicitly identified. Include CT findings, MRI description of a lobulated cystic fourth‑ventricular mass with internal linear enhancement, but omit the phrase “racemose NCC” and any mention of a visible worm.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors used (a) imaging characteristics (ventriculomegaly, transependymal flow, fourth‑ventricle obstruction, cystic mass with linear enhancement) to narrow the differential; (b) epidemiologic exposure (childhood residence in Mexico) to favor NCC; (c) exclusion of tuberculosis infection; (d) definitive pathology showing a mature Taenia solium plerocercoid larva after surgical removal.
case_prompt:
A 36‑year‑old woman with a remote history of adult‑onset seizures presented with a one‑year history of progressively worsening bilateral headaches accompanied by vertigo and intermittent nausea. The headaches were worse at night and on awakening, then improved throughout the day. She denied any recent neurologic deficits.

A non‑contrast CT scan of the head revealed ventriculomegaly with transependymal CSF flow and evidence of obstruction at the fourth ventricle. Subsequent MRI demonstrated obstructed hydrocephalus secondary to a lobulated cystic mass within the fourth ventricle, displaying a streak of internal linear enhancement. Neurologic examination was unremarkable.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Tuberculosis causing intraventricular cystic lesions was considered but ruled out by negative testing. | "she was negative for tuberculosis infection."
2. Neoplastic cystic tumors (e.g., ependymoma, pilocytic astrocytoma) were possible given a fourth‑ventricular cystic mass, but lack of solid enhancing components and the patient’s endemic exposure made these less likely. | "MRI demonstrated obstructed hydrocephalus secondary to a lobulated cystic mass within the fourth ventricle, with a streak of internal linear enhancement."
3. Other parasitic cysts (e.g., echinococcosis) were considered; however, the patient’s only risk factor was childhood residence in Mexico, where Taenia solium is endemic. | "Our infectious disease colleagues were consulted and found no other risk factors for NCC aside from living in Mexico until the age of 8."
4. Auto‑infection from gastrointestinal colonization was hypothesized to explain a new active lesion in a patient with prior seizure history, supporting a parasitic etiology over neoplastic causes. | "Given her longstanding history of seizures, but recent presentation with an active lesion, it was felt that she may have been auto‑infecting."
5. Definitive confirmation came from surgical pathology showing a mature Taenia solium plerocercoid larva, establishing neurocysticercosis as the cause of the cystic mass. | "Gross examination and pathology demonstrated a mature T. solium plerocercoid larvae..."

1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case ultimately diagnoses a tumefactive multiple sclerosis relapse, which is not among the 21 SELECTED diseases; therefore the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.  
2. Ideal Breakpoint: Include all information up to the decision to obtain a stereotactic brain biopsy, ending before the biopsy pathology results are presented. This provides sufficient history, exam, imaging, and laboratory data for the learner to generate a differential and pursue the correct diagnostic work‑up without revealing the final diagnosis.  
3. case_prompt:
A 51‑year‑old Mediterranean man with an 8‑year history of relapsing‑remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS) was admitted on suspicion of a relapse. He had been treated sequentially with glatiramer acetate, natalizumab (discontinued early 2017 due to rising anti‑JC virus antibody index), and fingolimod (started 3 months before admission).  

Eight days before admission he noted progressive left lower‑limb weakness and worsening gait; he could stand unaided and walk a few steps with unilateral assistance (EDSS 6.0).  

At admission the differential was an MS relapse versus progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML). Brain MRI showed bihemispheric confluent T2 white‑matter lesions without change, described as typical for PML. CSF analysis demonstrated a normal white‑cell count (2 cells/µL) with mildly increased lactate and glucose, normal albumin quotient, positive oligoclonal bands with intrathecal IgG and IgM synthesis. PCR, microbiologic and serologic studies were negative for JCV (PCR and antibody index), HSV‑1, HSV‑2, VZV, EBV, and HIV. Evoked potentials showed corticospinal tract impairment to the right leg, bilateral tibial nerve somatosensory abnormalities, and bilateral visual system involvement.  

He received IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for five days, with slight improvement. Two days later he became somnolent, mute, developed bilateral horizontal gaze palsy, tetraplegia, and bilateral Babinski signs (EDSS 9.5). Repeat MRI demonstrated progression of bihemispheric confluent white‑matter lesions. He developed aspiration pneumonia requiring intubation and tracheostomy.  

High‑dose steroids and seven cycles of plasma exchange were administered without clinical improvement; subsequent MRI showed further gadolinium enhancement and increased T2 lesion load.  

Because of negative laboratory results and radiologic features atypical for PML, additional differentials were entertained: tumefactive MS relapse, neurocysticercosis, neurosarcoidosis, intracerebral lymphoma, atypical PML, and other viral encephalitis. CSF and serology were negative for neurocysticercosis; chest CT and ACE/sIL2R were negative for sarcoidosis; CSF and imaging were not supportive of lymphoma; EEG was normal.  

To distinguish between a tumefactive MS relapse and a less likely intracerebral lymphoma, a stereotactic biopsy of a right frontal‑lobe lesion was performed.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. MS relapse considered due to acute neurological worsening and prior disease course | "On suspicion of an MS relapse, the patient was treated with IV methylprednisolone…"  
2. PML considered because of prior natalizumab exposure and rising anti‑JCV index; excluded by negative JCV PCR/antibody and atypical MRI | "Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)... were all negative (including JCV PCR, JCV CSF/serum antibody index)..." and "radiological findings atypical for PML…"  
3. Neurocysticercosis included as a common CNS parasite; excluded by negative CSF and serology and unusual MRI appearance | "The negative results of the CSF analysis and serology argued against a neurocysticercosis… presentation on MRI imaging was judged unusual."  
4. Neurosarcoidosis considered; excluded by normal chest CT and negative ACE and sIL2R | "For sarcoidosis, a CT scan of the chest and laboratory tests for ACE and sIL2R were added; both proved negative."  
5. Intracerebral lymphoma considered; CSF negative and imaging not typical, biopsy later to rule out | "The negative CSF findings and radiological presentation also argued against an intracerebral lymphoma but did not definitely exclude one."  
6. Atypical PML remains in differential but dismissed due to the above negative virology and imaging features | same as point 2.  
7. Other viral encephalitis (HSV, VZV, EBV, HIV) considered; excluded by comprehensive PCR panel negative | "PCR, microbiological, and serological study findings were all negative (including ... HSV‑1 PCR, HSV‑2 PCR, VZV PCR, EBV PCR, and HIV PCR)."  
8. HHV‑6 encephalitis entertained after tissue PCR showed low copies of HHV‑6 DNA; uncertainty persisted until histopathology clarified the lesion | "PCR analysis revealed low copy numbers of human herpesvirus 6 (HHV‑6) DNA in tissue…" and "Given the diagnostic uncertainty between HHV‑6 encephalitis and tumefactive MS lesions…"

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case ultimately diagnoses fibromatosis, which is not included in the 21 SELECTED diseases list; therefore the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.  
2. Ideal Breakpoint: Present the case up to the point where MRI provides a differential (neurocysticercosis vs fibromatosis) but before the open‑biopsy pathology results that confirm fibromatosis. This gives sufficient clinical, imaging, and epidemiologic clues for the learner to formulate a diagnosis without revealing it.  
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors used imaging characteristics (soft‑tissue mass with calcifications, diffusion restriction, hypovascularity) to generate a differential that included neurocysticercosis and fibromatosis. Definitive diagnosis was achieved by histopathology showing a benign spindle‑cell lesion with immunoprofile (vimentin+, beta‑catenin focal+, SMA+, S100‑) consistent with fibromatosis, thereby excluding neurocysticercosis.
case_prompt:
A 78‑year‑old retired farmer from Tamil Nadu presented with a 6‑month history of a gradually enlarging swelling on the right side of the neck, now measuring about 10 × 8 cm. Over the past 2 months he noted dull, aching pain localized to the mass, without radiation, weakness, sensory loss, or constitutional symptoms. Past medical history includes hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and benign prostatic hyperplasia; he is not diabetic.

Physical examination revealed a globular, firm, well‑defined, mobile mass over the right shoulder extending from 8 cm below the mastoid tip to the scapular spine, with pinchable overlying skin and no warmth or tenderness. Neurologic examination of the right upper limb was normal, and shoulder range of motion was preserved.

Plain radiographs of the neck demonstrated a soft‑tissue mass in the inferior neck with multiple ovoid calcifications. Fine‑needle aspiration cytology was inconclusive. Magnetic resonance imaging of the neck showed an ill‑defined, lobulated lesion within the right trapezius muscle (C6‑T2 level), measuring 4.0 × 7.0 × 5.4 cm. The lesion was isointense on T1, exhibited mild diffusion restriction, appeared heterogeneous on T2 and STIR sequences, and was hypovascular on Doppler evaluation. No hemorrhagic foci or calcifications were seen within the lesion on MRI. The radiology report listed a differential diagnosis of neurocysticercosis or fibromatosis.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Neurocysticercosis considered because the lesion contained multiple ovoid components and calcifications on plain radiograph, features that can be seen in parasitic cysts; however, the MRI lacked the classic cystic, scolex‑containing appearance and showed a solid, hypovascular mass, making this diagnosis less likely. | "MRI again was reported with a differential of neurocysticercosis or fibromatosis."
2. Fibromatosis (desmoid tumor) entertained due to the lesion’s firm, infiltrative nature, lack of necrosis, and homogeneous spindle‑cell appearance on imaging; definitive confirmation came from open biopsy demonstrating benign spindle‑cell proliferation with immunohistochemistry positive for vimentin, focal beta‑catenin, and SMA, and negative for S100, which is characteristic of fibromatosis. | "Open biopsy was done which showed benign spindle cell lesion ... The tumor cells were positive for vimentin, focally positive for beta‑catenin, and smooth muscle actin (SMA) ... The cells were negative for S100. Hence, the lesion was suggestive of fibromatosis."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case ultimately confirms neurocysticercosis, which is included in the 21 SELECTED diseases list. Therefore, the target diagnosis is neurocysticercosis (selected).
2. Best Breakpoint: End the presentation just before the ELISA serologic result and molecular PCR confirmation are disclosed. Include the patient’s presentation, travel/exposure history, seizure, vital signs, imaging findings, negative infectious work‑up, and brain‑biopsy histology, but stop prior to the statement “While awaiting ELISA serologic assay results, which later returned positive for cysticercosis…”.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished neurocysticercosis from tuberculoma, bacterial abscess, fungal infection, and toxoplasmosis by (a) epidemiologic exposure, (b) ring‑enhancing lesion without scolex, (c) exhaustive negative microbiologic cultures and stains (including GeneXpert MTB/RIF), and (d) histology showing granulomatous inflammation without organisms, ultimately confirmed by serology and PCR.
case_prompt:
A 35‑year‑old Indian male with no prior medical history presented after a witnessed first‑onset generalized tonic‑clonic seizure lasting ten minutes, followed by a postictal period of drowsiness. He had no preictal symptoms and denied fever, night sweats, weight loss, or anorexia. He was born in Tamil Nadu, emigrated to Singapore six years earlier, and travels annually to rural villages in India where he drinks well water and consumes local food. On exam his temperature was 37.8 °C; blood pressure, heart rate, and oxygen saturation were normal. Neurologic examination was unremarkable, with no focal deficits.

Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (WBC 18.4 × 10⁹/L) without eosinophilia; renal, hepatic, electrolytes, and routine biochemistry were within normal limits. HIV serology was non‑reactive. Two sets of blood cultures and serum cryptococcal antigen were negative. Three stool examinations for ova, cysts, and parasites were also negative. A non‑contrasted CT of the brain revealed an ill‑defined 8‑mm hypodense lesion with a hyperdense rim in the left basal temporal region, surrounded by mild vasogenic edema. MRI delineated a solitary ring‑enhancing lesion measuring 1.2 × 1 cm with thick smooth peripheral enhancement; no clearly defined scolex or mural nodule was seen. A serum sample was sent to an overseas reference centre for cysticercosis ELISA testing.

Neurosurgical biopsy via left minicraniotomy yielded a slightly hardened pale white‑yellow lesion containing milky white exudate. Histology showed granulomatous inflammation with epithelioid histiocytes, multinucleated giant cells lining a fibrous cyst wall, mixed inflammatory infiltrate, and necrosis. No cysticercus larva was identified. Stains for fungi (GMS) and acid‑fast bacilli (Ziehl‑Neelsen) were negative, as were immunohistochemical stains for Toxoplasma. Microbiologic evaluation—including Gram stain, aerobic and anaerobic cultures, fungal smear, acid‑fast smear, and GeneXpert MTB/RIF assay—did not detect any organisms.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Neurocysticercosis considered due to endemic exposure (annual travel to rural India, consumption of local food and water) and a solitary ring‑enhancing brain lesion typical of cysticercal lesions, even though a scolex was not visualized. | "He returns to India annually... rural areas with farms housing farm animals... MRI ... solitary ring‑enhancing lesion ... no clearly‑defined scolex..."
2. Tuberculoma considered because granulomatous inflammation is characteristic of TB and the region is endemic; excluded by multiple negative TB tests (acid‑fast stain, GeneXpert MTB/RIF, cultures). | "No fungi or acid‑fast bacilli were found on ... Ziehl‑Neelsen ... GeneXpert MTB/RIF assay ... negative."
3. Bacterial brain abscess considered given leukocytosis and ring‑enhancing lesion; excluded by negative blood cultures, negative Gram stain, and sterile aerobic/anaerobic cultures. | "Two sets of blood cultures were negative... Microbiologic testing did not identify causative organisms on Gram stain, aerobic and anaerobic culture."
4. Fungal infection considered (cryptococcal antigen tested); excluded by negative serum cryptococcal antigen and negative GMS stain. | "Serum Cryptococcal antigen was nonreactive... No fungi ... on Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) stain."
5. Cerebral toxoplasmosis considered; excluded by negative immunohistochemical staining for Toxoplasma. | "No Toxoplasma organisms were identified on immunohistochemical staining."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case describes a cystic lesion in the sellar region confirmed by histology and serology as cysticercosis. This corresponds to “neurocysticercosis,” which is included in the 21 SELECTED diseases list.
2. Best breakpoint: Include presentation, neurological exam, pituitary hormonal results, and MRI findings up to the description of the cystic sellar mass. Exclude the surgical approach, intra‑operative findings, histology, and postoperative serology, as these directly reveal the final diagnosis.
3. Author’s analytic distinctions: The authors used a normal pituitary hormonal panel to argue against endocrine tumors, noted the lack of contrast enhancement on MRI to differentiate from solid sellar neoplasms, and provided definitive proof through microscopic identification of a parasitic wall and a positive lentil‑lectin blot.
case_prompt: A 45‑year‑old woman residing in an area endemic for cysticercosis presented with chronic severe headaches and a progressive 6‑month decline in visual acuity. She first noticed blurring of vision in the left eye, resulting in bumping into objects on her left side, followed later by similar symptoms in the right eye. Neurological examination revealed visual acuities of 20/60 (right) and 20/80 (left), isochoric pupils measuring 2 mm with normal light reflexes, and a bitemporal hemianopia. Extra‑ocular movements were full, and funduscopic examination was unremarkable. Pituitary hormonal assays were within normal limits. Brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a cystic lesion in the sellar and suprasellar region measuring 17 × 20 × 22 mm, hyperintense on T2‑weighted images and hypointense on T1, with no capsule enhancement after contrast administration. The mass caused upward displacement and compression of the optic chiasm.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Normal pituitary hormone profile argues against a functional pituitary adenoma or other endocrine sellar tumors. | "Pituitary hormonal assay was carried out and was found to be normal."
2. The cystic nature of the lesion without contrast enhancement is atypical for solid sellar neoplasms such as adenoma, craniopharyngioma, or meningioma. | "Brain magnetic resonance (MR) showed a cystic image ... hyperintense on T2 sequence and hypointense on T1 with **no capsule enhancement** on the contrast study..."
3. Histologic identification of a parasitic wall with wavy cuticle and inflammatory infiltrate confirms a cysticercal cyst. | "Histological examination revealed a parasitic wall characterized by wavy, dense cuticle, and focal globular structure, surrounding inflammatory, mononuclear lymphocytic reaction..."
4. Positive lentil‑lectin glycoprotein EL‑Blot provides serologic confirmation of cysticercosis. | "Postoperative lentil lectin glycoprotein enzyme‑linked immunoelectrotransfer blot was positive."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case ultimately diagnoses schistosomiasis, which is not on the 21 SELECTED diseases list; therefore the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.  
2. Breakpoint: Include all clinical data up to the serological panel results (including the positive schistosoma IgM/IgG) but stop before the authors state “a schistosoma infestation (schistosomiasis) was diagnosed.” This provides sufficient clues (travel history, retroperitoneal lesion, biopsy showing microorganisms, serology) without revealing the final label.  
3. Analytic Distinctions: Authors first pursued an endocrine/neoplastic work‑up (paraganglioma, catecholamine‑producing tumor, neuroendocrine tumor) using catecholamine labs, MIBG scan, octreotide scan, and biopsy. When those were non‑diagnostic, they shifted to an infectious evaluation, using travel history, Mantoux test, and a broad serologic panel to rule out other tropical infections (echinococcosis, leishmaniasis, Taenia solium, etc.) and finally identified schistosome antibodies as the only positive result, leading to treatment and lesion regression.
case_prompt:
A 45‑year‑old Caucasian man was referred to endocrinology after an incidental retroperitoneal, para‑aortic lesion was seen on abdominal CT performed for abdominal pain. The CT showed a 4 cm nonspecific lesion between the celiac trunk and superior mesenteric artery, “suggestive of neuroendocrine tumor as the first possibility.” Past medical history included smoking, Barrett’s esophagus, hiatus hernia, gastroesophageal reflux disease (on omeprazole), sleeve gastrectomy (2015) and cholecystectomy (2017).

Initial laboratory evaluation for a suspected paraganglioma revealed: glucose 79 mg/dL, creatinine 0.69 mg/dL, ALT 22 IU/L, ferritin 73 ng/mL, NSE 19 ng/mL (reference < 16), CEA 2.6 ng/mL, CA 19‑9 12 IU/mL, chromogranin A 3.3 nmol/L, hemoglobin 15.4 g/dL, neutrophils 51.7 %, lymphocytes 33.4 %, eosinophils 5.3 %. Total and fractional catecholamines, total metanephrines, and 24‑hour urinary 5‑OH‑indoleacetic acid were normal.

Whole‑body scintigraphy with metaiodobenzylguanidine showed no clear signs of a catecholamine‑producing tumor. Whole‑body 99mTc‑octreotide SPECT/CT demonstrated the para‑aortic mass without pathological tumor uptake.
