The patient is a 10‑year‑old female born at 33 weeks gestation after precipitous labor complicated by chorioamnionitis; she required a 1‑month NICU stay but had no intraventricular hemorrhage or retinopathy. Development was age‑appropriate until 17 months, when she presented to the emergency department with a 90‑minute seizure characterized by limpness, left‑ward eye deviation, jaw clenching, and generalized rigidity. Initial head CT was normal; brain MRI showed periventricular leukoencephalopathy and EEG demonstrated excessive beta artifact with background slowing. The following day she developed right‑sided facial twitching, left hemiplegia, and facial droop; repeat MRI revealed subtle parietal diffusion restriction thought to represent acute ischemia, with stable periventricular leukomalacia, and MRA was unremarkable. EEG then showed right hemispheric slowing. Over the next 5 days she had persistent left hemiplegia, which improved gradually with steroids. A third MRI remained stable and a subsequent EEG showed a symmetric background with improvement.

At 23 months she was hospitalized for febrile seizures requiring intubation; EEG demonstrated left‑hemispheric slowing without epileptiform discharges. Refractory seizures continued, often necessitating airway support. At 25 months an EEG captured recurrent left frontal epileptiform discharges and an electrographic seizure arising from the left hemisphere, unresponsive to midazolam, lorazepam, fosphenytoin, or levetiracetam. Developmental regression and progressive neurologic decline ensued. By age 4 a follow‑up MRI remained stable, showing persistent periventricular leukomalacia.

At age 5 she experienced an 18‑hour status epilepticus episode; MRI then showed diffuse bilateral T2/FLAIR white‑matter hyperintensity with diffusion restriction. Subsequent imaging demonstrated new volume loss, encephalomalacia, and ex‑vacuo ventricular dilatation. EEGs over the next years displayed evolving patterns of left‑sided slowing, generalized background slowing, intermittent sharp‑slow complexes, and multifocal spike‑and‑wave discharges. At age 8, after another status epilepticus, MRI revealed patchy cortical T2 hyperintensities; EEG showed high‑amplitude generalized delta activity with multifocal spikes and excessive beta activity. At age 9 she presented with sudden right‑sided weakness and facial droop; MRI showed chronic hydrocephalus without acute cerebrovascular injury, and she was started on verapamil.

Extensive diagnostic work‑up was performed throughout: serum acylcarnitine, ceruloplasmin, CRP, pyruvic acid, vitamin D, cerebrospinal fluid lactic acid, cysticercosis antibodies, amino acids, a mitochondrial disorder panel, Factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutations, epilepsy gene panels, SCN1A large deletion/duplication test, chromosomal microarray, and cardiac evaluation—all negative. Two polymorphisms in SCN1A (3199 A>G) and SCN1B (629 T>C) were identified but have been observed in healthy individuals and are not disease‑associated. The patient is compound heterozygous for MTHFR C677T and A1298C polymorphisms; although linked to hyperhomocysteinemia, her homocysteine level was normal.

Given the lack of a definitive explanation, a trio whole‑exome sequencing (XomeDxPlus) was ordered.

Neurologic examination revealed an upper‑motor‑neuron‑type weakness (4/5) in the right upper and lower extremities, increased temperature sensitivity on the right side, and gait abnormalities affecting the right lower extremity. Reflexes were intact and cranial nerves were normal.

Non‑contrast head CT demonstrated widespread cystic lesions throughout the cerebral hemispheres. Brain MRI showed numerous bilateral intraparenchymal cystic enhancing lesions, some with internal hemorrhagic components. The largest lesion was in the left paramedian frontoparietal lobe (5.0 × 3.4 × 4.0 cm) with significant mass effect, distorting the corpus callosum and left lateral ventricle. Additional lesions involved the left caudate head, left basal ganglia (with a prominent rim of hemorrhagic products), and the right superior frontal gyrus (1.8 × 1.5 × 1.6 cm). The septum pellucidum was shifted ~5 mm to the right.

Chest and abdominal CT showed no primary or metastatic masses. Syphilis serology was nonreactive, and the Quantiferon test was reactive; the patient had no prior latent TB therapy. CSF analysis revealed 10 WBC/mm³, protein 69 g/L, glucose 70 mmol/L, and atypical cells raising concern for malignancy. Additional infectious work‑up (VDRL, blood cultures, AFB stain, serum Cryptococcus antigen, HIV serology, galactomannan, Fungitell, toxoplasma serology) was negative.

Four days later he returned with persistent erythema and a new ulcerated lesion with central eschar. He reported subjective fever the day before but had no respiratory, gastrointestinal, or systemic symptoms. Vital signs revealed tachycardia (100 bpm); laboratory studies showed a neutrophil‑predominant leukocytosis of 11,600 /mm³ (reference 3,500‑10,000). At the outpatient infectious‑disease visit one week later, the eschar had enlarged but was non‑tender. Laboratory testing revealed anemia (Hb 8.0 g/dL) and marked transaminase elevations (ALT 153 U/L, AST 108 U/L) and alkaline phosphatase 688 U/L. Blood cultures for fungi, mycobacteria, and bacteria were drawn; urine antigen testing for Histoplasma capsulatum, serum Aspergillus galactomannan, and cryptococcal antigen were ordered. Stool studies were negative for parasites, Cryptosporidium, and enteropathogenic bacteria. Oral ulcers were clinically compatible with herpetic stomatitis; IV acyclovir was started, and TMP‑SMX prophylaxis for PJP was initiated but later replaced by oral dapsone and pyrimethamine due to a local allergic reaction.

On day 1, a contrast‑enhanced chest CT demonstrated a ground‑glass and micronodular miliary pattern, “suggesting both PJP and either histoplasmosis or milliary tuberculosis.” Consequently, a bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was planned. Empiric therapy with IV clindamycin 600 mg q8h, oral primaquine 30 mg/day, and IV amphotericin B 50 mg/day was begun for presumed histoplasmosis, and the patient’s zidovudine‑containing regimen was switched to emtricitabine/tenofovir plus efavirenz because of anemia.

A laparoscopic liver biopsy was performed; specimens were sent for histology, Gram stain, KOH preparation, ZN stain, modified Kinyoun stain for Nocardia, bacterial, fungal, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis cultures, and GeneXpert MTB/RIF Ultra testing. Sputum ZN staining showed no acid‑fast bacilli, and tuberculosis treatment was not started. By day 5, aerobic bacterial cultures of liver tissue were negative. On day 6, serum Aspergillus galactomannan was positive (index 3.27 > 0.5). HIV viral load decreased to 74 copies/mL by day 8; hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis B core IgM, hepatitis B DNA, hepatitis C antibody, and cryptococcal antigen were all negative. Creatinine rose to 1.34 mg/dL, attributed to amphotericin B nephrotoxicity. By day 11, creatinine peaked at 1.6 mg/dL; amphotericin B infusion was prolonged over 24 h, and renal function improved by day 14.

On day 15, a BAL sample was obtained via fiberoptic bronchoscopy to detect Mycobacterium tuberculosis, fungi, or bacteria.

1. Chest CT showing ground‑glass and micronodular miliary pattern generated a differential of PJP, histoplasmosis, or miliary tuberculosis. | "ground‑glass and micronodular miliary pattern (Figure 1), suggesting both PJP and either histoplasmosis or milliary tuberculosis."

case_prompt:
A 50‑year‑old farmer presented with fever and a serosanguineous, discharging swelling over the dorsum of the right foot. The lesion began 18 months earlier as a small 1–2 cm nodule without pain or discharge and gradually enlarged to involve the entire dorsum. There was no history of trauma, diabetes, hypertension, or known tuberculosis. Three months prior he had been diagnosed with tuberculosis at a local hospital and received anti‑tubercular therapy for two months without improvement, after which treatment was stopped.

Physical examination showed a grossly swollen right foot with intense erythema, numerous well‑demarcated nodular lesions of varying size, and several inflamed sinus openings discharging dried pus. The foot was deformed and tender; the right leg veins were dilated with pitting edema extending to the knee. Discharge was yellowish, purulent, and foul‑smelling, without visible granules.

Vital signs revealed mild fever. Laboratory studies: hemoglobin 10 g/dL, total leukocyte count 11,900/mm³ (80 % neutrophils), ESR 40 mm/h. HIV serology negative; liver, renal function tests and electrolytes were normal. Radiographs of the right foot showed soft‑tissue density occupying the inter‑metatarsal and metatarsophalangeal joint spaces with spreading of the 2nd and 3rd inter‑metatarsal joints, but no bone involvement.

A smear of the aspirated pus stained with Gram’s stain revealed thin, long, branching, Gram‑positive filamentous bacilli. On modified Ziehl‑Neelsen stain (1 % H₂SO₄ decolorizer) the filaments were weakly acid‑fast.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Chronic, progressive foot swelling with multiple sinus tracts suggested a mycetoma‑type process, leading to consideration of actinomycetoma versus eumycetoma. | "numerous elevated, well‑demarcated small to large nodular lesions with few discharging sinuses."
2. Prior empirical anti‑tubercular therapy without clinical improvement argued against tuberculosis as the etiologic agent. | "patient was diagnosed as having tuberculosis and treated with anti‑tubercular drugs... there was no improvement even after 2 months."
3. Gram stain showing thin, branching, Gram‑positive filamentous bacilli pointed toward filamentous bacteria such as Nocardia or Actinomyces rather than typical pyogenic cocci. | "revealed thin, long, branching, Gram‑positive filamentous bacilli."
4. Weakly acid‑fast staining differentiated Nocardia (weakly acid‑fast) from Mycobacterium (strongly acid‑fast) and from non‑acid‑fast actinomycetes, narrowing the diagnosis toward nocardial infection. | "On modified Ziehl‑Neilson stain ... the filaments were weakly acid fast."
5. Absence of bone involvement on radiographs made classic eumycetoma (often associated with bone destruction) less likely and favored a superficial actinomycetoma. | "there was no bone involvement."
6. Histopathology (described later in the article) showed basophilic granules without eosinophilic peripheral material, a pattern more consistent with actinomycetoma rather than eumycetoma. | "Few irregular lobulated light basophilic granules were present. The granules are not bordered at the periphery by the eosinophilic material."
7. Definitive culture grew dry, chalky white to cream colonies identified as Nocardia species, confirming the organism suggested by microscopy. | "A small, dry, granular, wrinkled chalky white to cream colored colonies were grown... The colonies were identified as Nocardia species... as N. asteroides."

case_prompt:
A 20‑year‑old woman presented to an ambulatory care center with progressively worsening headaches over two weeks. She had recently been treated for a presumed mycoplasma infection. She denied fever, but reported a sore throat 3–4 days before presentation without cough. She lived on a farm with a friend who had previously been treated for fungal meningitis. No tobacco, alcohol, intravenous drug use, or recent sexually transmitted infections were reported. 

On exam she was afebrile, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, alert and oriented, with no adenopathy. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 12.4 × 10³/µL (87 % neutrophils, no bands); serology was negative for mycoplasma and HIV‑1. Neurologic examination was normal. Brain MRI demonstrated a 3.5 × 1.3 × 1.9 cm contrast‑enhancing lesion in the left temporal lobe with mild midline shift. Specialists considered a differential of a non‑infectious process (favored), a neoplastic process, or infection. Empiric therapy with vancomycin, meropenem, and dexamethasone was initiated. The lesion was surgically resected; intra‑operative cultures for aerobic, anaerobic, mycobacterial, and fungal organisms were obtained and later reported negative. Gram stain, modified acid‑fast bacillus stain, and fungal stains were also negative, and PCR testing for infectious agents was negative. Post‑operative care included continued vancomycin for 10 days; postoperative imaging confirmed gross‑total resection and the patient remained neurologically intact on postoperative days 1 and 30.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Infectious etiology considered but excluded because “Anaerobic and aerobic cultures as well as gram, modified acid fast bacillus, and fungal stains were negative” and “Brain tissue polymerase chain reaction analysis ... was negative for infectious agents.” |
2. Specific bacterial agents such as Nocardia and Mycobacteria excluded: “Special stains for bacteria including Nocardia and Mycobacteria were negative.” |
3. Fungal infection excluded: “The Grocott's Methenamine Silver GMS stains revealed no fungal organisms.” |
4. Viral and protozoal infections excluded: “There were no giant cells, viral inclusions, Herpes Simple x1 or 2, cytomegalovirus, Epstein‑Barr virus, or Toxoplasma immunoreactivity.” |
5. Neoplastic process considered but not supported by pathology; absence of tumor cells and presence of abundant plasma cells and histiocytes with crystals led authors to favor a non‑neoplastic, non‑infectious lesion. |
6. Non‑infectious inflammatory process supported by histology showing “fibrotic lesion with an extensive chronic inflammatory infiltrate of CD138‑immunoreactive plasma cells, CD68‑immunoreactive macrophages and monocytes and S100‑immunoreactive histiocytes,” and “numerous periodic acid‑Schiff (PAS) staining rhomboid crystals.” |
7. Final diagnosis established by demonstration of light‑chain restriction: “These demonstrated overwhelmingly lambda light chain restriction” and electron microscopy showing “intracellular but also extracellular rhomboid and diamond‑shaped crystals,” leading to the conclusion that “the findings ... were considered consistent with CSH, light chain subtype.”

case_prompt:
A 67‑year‑old male non‑smoker with a past history of ischemic heart disease (status post coronary artery bypass graft) and bronchiectasis was diagnosed with angioimmunoblastic T‑cell lymphoma, stage III B, in December 2004. He had been treated with prednisone, mycophenolate mofetil and subcutaneous alemtuzumab. In October 2006 he was readmitted with a two‑week history of fever, productive cough with yellowish sputum, and mild dyspnea. He denied chest or abdominal pain, headache or any bleeding. On examination he appeared unwell and in mild respiratory distress. Temperature was 38.7 °C, BP 112/68 mmHg, pulse 92/min, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO₂ 93 % on room air. He was pale; there was no cyanosis, leg edema, jaundice or external lymphadenopathy. Lung examination revealed decreased inspiratory volumes with coarse crackles over the mid and lower lung fields bilaterally. Cardiovascular, abdominal and neurological examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed: WBC 1.83 × 10⁹/L (neutrophils 1.1, lymphocytes 0.3), hemoglobin 109 g/L, platelets 315 × 10⁹/L; renal and hepatic panels were normal. Blood, urine, stool cultures and CMV antigen test were negative. Chest radiograph displayed bronchiectatic changes in both lower lobes with bilateral nodular infiltrates consistent with severe pneumonia. He was started on IV piperacillin‑tazobactam, gentamicin, supplemental oxygen and IV fluids. Initial partial response was followed by worsening fever and respiratory distress; on day 8 his blood pressure fell to 85/45 mmHg. Septic screens were repeated and antibiotics were escalated to IV meropenem and vancomycin, after which his blood pressure improved and fever subsided. A repeat chest CT showed bronchiectatic cavities in the lower lobes, bilateral nodular infiltrates, segmental consolidation and pleural thickening. Echocardiogram revealed no vegetations, valvular abnormalities or pericardial effusion, and brain CT showed no space‑occupying lesions. Bronchoscopy was performed.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial pneumonia due to common pathogens – considered because of productive cough, fever, infiltrates, but initial cultures (blood, urine, stool) were negative and the patient did not improve on broad‑spectrum beta‑lactam plus aminoglycoside therapy. | "Blood, urine, stool cultures and CMV antigen test were all negative."
2. Viral pneumonia (including CMV) – considered given immunosuppression; CMV antigen testing was negative. | "Blood, urine, stool cultures and CMV antigen test were all negative."
3. Tuberculosis – considered due to chronic pulmonary infiltrates; BAL was negative for acid‑fast bacilli. | "BAL fluid was negative for acid fast bacilli."
4. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia – considered in immunocompromised host; BAL negative for pneumocystis carinii. | "BAL fluid was negative for ... pneumocystis carinii."
5. Endocarditis with septic pulmonary emboli – considered because of fever and shock; echocardiogram showed no vegetations. | "Echocardiogram showed no vegetations, pericardial effusions or valvular defects."
6. Pulmonary malignancy/metastasis – considered given lymphoma history; BAL cytology negative for malignant cells. | "BAL fluid ... malignant cells."
7. Nocardiosis – confirmed when BAL fluid showed gram‑positive branching rods later identified as Nocardia asteroides, and sputum cultures grew the same organism. | "BAL fluid showed ... gram positive rods identified later on as Nocardia asteroides." / "sputum cultures grew branching gram positive rods identified as N. asteroides."
8. Aspergillosis – confirmed by positive fungal stains identifying Aspergillus niger and a positive galactomannan assay. | "Special stains for fungi were positive and the fungus was identified as Aspergillus niger (A. niger)." / "Aspergillus galactomannan test was positive."

case_prompt: A 77‑year‑old Korean man with a history of well‑controlled hypertension was transferred from a local clinic because of dyspnea and right‑sided chest pain that began after a fall from his bed two days earlier. In the emergency department his oxygen saturation was 89.7% on room air and rose to 97% with 5 L supplemental oxygen. Vital signs and electrocardiogram were otherwise normal. Chest radiography showed a right‑sided pleural effusion, and a chest tube was placed. The drained fluid was reddish, containing >10,000 red blood cells/L and 850 leukocytes/L (96% polymorphonuclear cells). Laboratory studies revealed a leukocyte count of 6,900/L with 97.2% neutrophils, C‑reactive protein 27.8 mg/dL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 53 mm/hr, and lactate dehydrogenase 575 IU/L. Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR performed on the pleural fluid was negative. Contrast‑enhanced chest CT demonstrated bilateral pleural effusions with pleural thickening. Pleural fluid cytology showed no malignant or severe inflammatory changes. Whole‑body PET/CT demonstrated diffuse hypermetabolism of both pleural surfaces, interpreted as more suggestive of inflammation than malignancy. The patient was empirically started on a third‑generation cephalosporin and an aminoglycoside. On hospital day 7 he developed fever, and a repeat CT on day 15 showed worsening pneumonia, yet repeated sputum, pleural fluid, and blood cultures remained negative. He required transfer to the intensive care unit for altered mental status and respiratory distress, and was placed on a ventilator.

case_prompt: A 51-year-old man presented with three weeks of progressive headaches, nausea, vomiting, left hip pain, and fatigue. Neurologic examination revealed a left‑leaning antalgic gait and difficulty with tandem and heel‑to‑toe walking. Brain MRI demonstrated extensive leptomeningeal enhancement with a small focus of nodular parenchymal enhancement and nonspecific T2 white‑matter hypointensities. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was consistent with aseptic meningoencephalitis, showing lymphocytic predominance, elevated total protein, and increased IgG. Over the ensuing week his lower‑extremity strength declined. A repeat lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 45 cm H₂O and elevated protein; brain MRI was unchanged, while spine MRI revealed diffuse leptomeningeal nodular enhancement of the cervical, thoracic, and cauda equina nerve roots. Empiric therapy for a central nervous system fungal infection was started pending CSF serology and cultures. Multiple therapeutic lumbar punctures yielded persistently elevated nucleated cells and protein with low glucose but no diagnostic organism. A right temporal brain biopsy was performed; surgical pathology initially suggested Nocardia asteroides, later determined to be a contaminant. His neurological status continued to worsen with intermittent leg weakness and seizure‑like episodes. Because of the diagnostic dilemma, a cauda equina biopsy was performed three weeks after the brain biopsy. Frozen section of the nerve root demonstrated pigmented cells.

case_prompt:
A 64‑year‑old man presented to Jichi Medical University Hospital with left‑eye visual loss and floaters in the right eye. He had been receiving 40 mg oral prednisolone daily for >6 weeks for interstitial pneumonia associated with rheumatoid arthritis. Past medical history was notable for metastatic rectal cancer, intestinal obstruction, and pericarditis.

Ophthalmic examination showed best‑corrected visual acuity of 20/20 in the right eye and 8/200 in the left eye. Funduscopy revealed round yellowish‑white subretinal lesions with retinal hemorrhage in both eyes.

Laboratory studies demonstrated elevated anti‑Toxoplasma, anti‑Herpes simplex virus IgG, anti‑HSV IgM, and anti‑cytomegalovirus IgG titers, together with low total lymphocyte and CD4‑positive lymphocyte counts. White‑blood‑cell count, C‑reactive protein, and β‑D‑glucan levels were not increased. Blood cultures and whole‑body contrast CT were unremarkable.

Empiric oral anti‑Toxoplasma (acetylspiramycin 1,800 mg/day) and antiviral (valganciclovir 1,800 mg/day) therapy was started, but ocular lesions progressed. Diagnostic vitrectomy of the left eye performed 4 weeks after presentation yielded no pathogens on broad‑range PCR, multiplex PCR, or cultures. Broad‑spectrum antibiotics (imipenem/cilastatin and amikacin) were given under suspicion of bacterial infection including Nocardia, without improvement. Intravitreal injections of ceftazidime, vancomycin, and voriconazole were administered at 6 weeks, yet lesions worsened and visual acuity declined to light perception.

At 7 weeks, left‑eye exenteration was performed; Gram‑negative rods were seen on Gram stain of the tissue, but cultures grew only Candida albicans. Systemic levofloxacin and high‑dose fosfluconazole were started, and intravitreal ceftazidime, vancomycin, and voriconazole were given to the right eye from weeks 8 to 10. Broad‑range PCR of vitreous fluid obtained at 8 weeks showed 7.19 × 10⁴ copies/mL bacterial 16S ribosomal RNA and 1.85 × 10⁵ copies/mL fungal 28S ribosomal RNA, indicating a fungus‑dominant mixed infection.

The subretinal abscess in the right eye enlarged toward the fovea, and visual acuity fell to 2/200. Vitrectomy combined with cataract extraction and silicone oil tamponade was performed at 10 weeks; C. albicans was cultured from the vitreous fluid. Continued systemic antifungal therapy resulted in lesion healing under silicone oil, and the fundus remained stable at 1 year 4 months with visual acuity 4/200.

1. Toxoplasma gondii infection was considered due to elevated anti‑Toxoplasma IgG, but lesions expanded despite high‑dose oral acetylspiramycin, indicating lack of therapeutic response. | "The lesions expanded in both eyes... administration of oral anti‑Toxoplasma ... was initiated. However, the lesions expanded in both eyes."
2. Herpes simplex virus (HSV) encephalitis/endophthalmitis was entertained because of elevated anti‑HSV IgG and IgM; however, antiviral therapy with valganciclovir failed to halt progression. | "Administration of oral anti‑Toxoplasma ... and anti‑viral drugs (valganciclovir 1,800 mg/day) was initiated. However, the lesions expanded in both eyes."
3. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis was a differential given anti‑CMV IgG positivity, yet no improvement with antiviral therapy and absence of typical CMV retinal findings argued against it. | "Laboratory studies showed elevated ... anti‑cytomegalovirus IgG antibodies... However, the lesions expanded in both eyes."
4. Nocardia or other bacterial endophthalmitis was suspected (patient immunosuppressed, Gram‑negative rods later seen); broad‑spectrum antibiotics (imipenem/cilastatin, amikacin, later ceftazidime/vancomycin) produced no clinical benefit, and cultures remained negative, lowering its likelihood. | "Broad‑spectrum antibiotic treatment (imipenem/cilastatin ...) was initiated, under suspicion of bacterial infections including Nocardia. However, the lesions did not improve."
5. case_prompt:
A 70‑year‑old man was transferred from a nearby intensive‑care unit. He had sudden‑onset clonic seizures involving the right hemisoma. Computed tomography (CT) of the brain demonstrated multiple ring‑enhancing lesions. He was receiving empiric metronidazole and cefotaxime. His past medical history was notable for a 2‑year IgA myeloma (ISS stage II) treated initially with MPV protocol and subsequently with lenalidomide plus dexamethasone (eleven cycles, partial response). No trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis had been given; chemotherapy was discontinued on admission.

Two months earlier he had a subcutaneous abscess on the left shoulder of unknown origin that was drained; microbiology was non‑diagnostic because of mixed flora. He lived in a small rural hamlet and retired from construction work ten years prior.

On arrival his temperature was 36.5 °C, heart rate 92/min, blood pressure 150/90 mmHg, and Glasgow Coma Scale 15. He was alert and oriented. A 35‑year‑old man presented with sudden bilateral loss of vision and periorbital swelling. He also reported fever and pedal edema. Intra‑ocular pressure was 16 mmHg bilaterally. Blood pressure was 160/100 mmHg with bradycardia. An initial impression of hypertension‑related exudative retinal detachment was made, though atypical central serous chorioretinopathy and Vogt‑Koyanagi‑Harada syndrome were also listed as differentials. Two days later he developed generalized hypotony, staggering gait, truncal ataxia, buccal and proximal weakness, and decreased plantar reflexes. Neurology considered a pontomedullary lesion or cytomegalovirus meningitis; cerebrospinal fluid analysis was normal. Brain MRI demonstrated multiple cystic‑enhancing lesions in both cerebral hemispheres, described as suggestive of tuberculomas or neurocysticercosis. He was started on anti‑tubercular therapy and oral steroids.

Four days after commencing ATT, he suffered a generalized tonic‑clonic seizure. Repeat contrast MRI showed disseminated parenchymal lesions. Ophthalmic status worsened with restricted abduction, sluggish pupils, 3+ anterior chamber cells, intra‑ocular pressures of 66 mmHg (right) and 52 mmHg (left), increased exudates, higher retinal detachment, and vitreous cells. A diagnosis of disseminated toxoplasma or malignancy was considered; aqueous PCR was negative for malignant cells, tuberculosis, CMV, HSV, VZV, and toxoplasma. An Ahmed glaucoma valve was placed in the left eye, after which the left eye became stony hard with severe conjunctival chemosis and a shallow anterior chamber.

Five weeks after presentation, suspicion of metastatic endophthalmitis prompted a pars‑plana vitrectomy with vitreous biopsy. Intravitreal vancomycin, ceftazidime, and voriconazole were administered, and fortified topical antibiotics and natamycin were started for presumed fungal endophthalmitis. All smears and cultures for bacteria and fungi were negative. Subsequent work‑up revealed negative cerebrospinal fluid for CMV and Cryptococcus, negative blood serology for HIV, TORCH, CMV, and HSV, and a normal bone‑marrow biopsy.

Because of progressive systemic decline and severe cachexia, a repeat brain MRI showed a large right parieto‑occipital mass, bilateral globe deformities, intra‑ocular hemorrhages, and extra‑ocular soft‑tissue inflammation. case_prompt:
A 75‑year‑old woman with no significant past medical history presented with sudden‑onset left‑sided weakness over a few days. She denied fever, headache, nausea, vomiting, recent travel, trauma, or drug use. Examination showed left facial palsy with forehead sparing and a distal‑predominant left hemiparesis (MRC grade 4 proximally, grade 3 distally in the upper limb; grade 4 in the lower limb). Deep tendon reflexes were brisk with extensor plantar responses; sensory examination was normal and meningeal signs were absent.

Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood count, electrolytes, liver tests, coagulation profile, ESR, and CRP. Serology was positive for syphilis (RPR and Treponema pallidum hemagglutination assay). Autoimmune serologies (ANA, ANCA), HIV test, rheumatoid factor, complement levels, and tumor markers (CA15‑3, CA 19‑9, CEA, AFP) were within normal limits; CA 125 was markedly elevated. ECG and echocardiogram were unremarkable.

Brain MRI showed multiple small lesions in the bilateral frontal cortex and subcortex, primarily involving the right internal capsule, with rim enhancement on gadolinium‑enhanced T1 images. MR angiography was normal. Initial differential diagnoses included metastatic brain tumors and infections such as neurosyphilis or bacterial abscesses.

Further work‑up: blood cultures and procalcitonin were negative; CSF analysis showed normal protein (41.4 mg/dL), glucose (58.4 mg/dL), and cell count (WBC 1/mm³), with minimal reactivity on CSF FTA‑ABS IgG and negative CSF VDRL, cytology, and cultures for mycobacteria and fungi. Whole‑body CT did not reveal a primary malignancy. FDG‑PET/CT demonstrated a hypermetabolic lesion in the cervical spinal cord, and cervical MRI showed high signal intensity from C2‑C6 with heterogeneous enhancement involving the left pyramidal tract.

A stereotactic brain biopsy of a left frontal lesion was performed. Histopathology revealed collections of foamy histiocytes with mild perivascular lymphocytic infiltration and an unknown filamentous, branching, Gram‑positive microorganism within histiocytes, brain tissue, and perivascular spaces. The organism stained positive with Gomori methenamine silver, negative with acid‑fast and Warthin‑Starry stains. Empiric therapy with sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim and amikacin was started to cover Nocardia and Actinomyces, later switched to imipenem after liver enzyme elevation. DNA sequencing was ordered for definitive identification.

Her antiretroviral regimen consisted of lamivudine/zidovudine plus lopinavir/ritonavir, and she received trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole (800/160 mg) three times weekly for prophylaxis.

Lung fields were clear bilaterally; no lymphadenopathy was palpable. Laboratory studies showed LDH 217 U/L (normal 100‑190), albumin 2.0 g/dL, hemoglobin 10.7 g/dL, white blood cell count 7.9 ×10³/µL with 71 % neutrophils, 16 % lymphocytes, 12 % monocytes, and normal eosinophils and basophils.

Chest CT demonstrated subcarinal, pre‑vascular, and right hilar lymphadenopathy, multiple bilateral pulmonary masses and nodules (largest cavitating lesion in the left upper lobe measuring 4.2 × 4.2 cm), a right cardiophrenic‑angle mass (2.2 × 4.6 cm), bilateral pleural effusions with compressive atelectasis of the lower lobes, and fibrotic changes in the left apex.

Initial work‑up revealed negative sputum Gram stain and bacterial cultures, three negative acid‑fast bacilli sputum smears, and a negative purified protein derivative test. Fever persisted for four days (101‑102 °F) before subsiding; nausea and vomiting attributed to TMP/SMX developed.

Bronchoalveolar lavage of the lingula and five transbronchial biopsies of the left upper lobe were obtained. All cultures and smears returned negative, and cytology was negative for malignancy and PCP. TMP/SMX was stopped pending results, while azithromycin and ceftriaxone were continued. Three days later, fever and malaise recurred, prompting re‑initiation of TMP/SMX due to suspicion for nocardiosis. A head CT showed sinus disease (maxillary, frontal, ethmoid) without other abnormalities. That day, two transthoracic core‑needle biopsies were performed in the left upper‑lobe cavitating pleural‑based mass.

An 8‑year‑old girl was referred to Inkosi Albert Luthuli Central Hospital with a 4‑month history of chronic purulent sputum, severe weight loss and constitutional symptoms. There was no known tuberculosis (TB) contact, although her 6‑year‑old brother had similar symptoms. They lived on a farm in rural KwaZulu‑Natal, South Africa. She had initially been assessed as having pulmonary TB and started on standard four‑drug anti‑TB therapy (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) at a provincial hospital based on clinical presentation and chest radiography. GeneXpert and TB cultures were negative. ESR was >140 mm/hr, monocytes 2.56 × 10⁹/L, globulin fraction 37 g/L, and HIV test was negative.

After two months of TB treatment she deteriorated, presenting with severe respiratory distress. Chest X‑ray revealed a right pleural effusion; thoracentesis yielded pus and an intercostal chest drain was placed. She developed respiratory failure and was transferred to the pediatric ICU for mechanical ventilation. Examination showed marked wasting (weight 24 kg, z‑score –2 to –3), pallor, clubbing, axillary lymphadenopathy, absent breath sounds on the right and left‑sided crackles, a firm 7‑cm hepatomegaly, 3‑cm splenomegaly, and encephalopathy with meningism. An initial assessment of disseminated TB was made. TB regimen was continued with ethambutol changed to ethionamide, and meropenem was added.

Urgent CT brain showed age‑incongruent cerebral and cerebellar involutional changes without basal enhancement, hydrocephalus, or raised intracranial pressure. Lumbar puncture revealed lymphocytes 28 × 10⁶/L, neutrophils 12 × 10⁶/L, glucose 1.1 mmol/L, protein 2.5 g/L, chloride 122 mmol/L. Admission labs showed white blood cells 45.3 × 10⁹/L (neutrophils 35 × 10⁹/L, monocytes 4.99 × 10⁹/L), platelets 1 169 × 10⁹/L, ESR >140 mm/hr, and procalcitonin 52 ng/dL. Repeat GeneXpert and TB cultures remained negative.

CT chest demonstrated destruction of the right lung with bronchiectasis and cavities. The patient was intubated, ventilated, and continued on both anti‑TB drugs and broad‑spectrum antibiotics pending further results.

Typical bacterial pneumonia/sepsis considered given severe neutrophilic leukocytosis and high procalcitonin, but lack of response to meropenem alone and presence of cavitary bronchiectatic disease suggested an atypical organism. | "Meropenem was added to the treatment…white blood cells were 45.3 × 10⁹/L…procalcitonin 52 ng/dL."

case_prompt: A 29‑year‑old woman with recently diagnosed systemic lupus erythematosus involving hemolytic anemia, cerebritis, lupus nephritis, cardiomyopathy (EF 33 %) and interstitial pneumonia was discharged after two weeks of hospitalization on mycophenolate mofetil, hydroxychloroquine and a tapering course of prednisolone. Laboratory studies showed WBC 16.3 K/µL, hemoglobin 8.6 g/dL, platelets 124 K/µL, potassium 3.0 mEq/L, sodium 125 mEq/L, magnesium 1.6 mg/dL, folate 5.7 ng/mL, CK 455 U/L, LDH 310 U/L, albumin 2.9 g/dL, CRP 16.9 mg/L, lactate 3.1 mmol/L, procalcitonin 0.14 ng/mL, D‑dimer 10.56 µg/mL FEU. CT pulmonary angiogram demonstrated bilateral infiltrates (more extensive on the left) and excluded pulmonary embolism. Abdominal ultrasound showed hepatomegaly. During hospitalization he recalled recent exposure to sick kittens and mice. Testing for Hantavirus, Q fever, leptospirosis, and toxoplasmosis was ordered, and doxycycline was continued empirically. case_prompt:

Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis (18.1 × 10⁹/L) and a markedly elevated C‑reactive protein (165.7 mg/L). Arterial blood gas showed mild hypoxemia (PaO₂ 8.7 kPa). On admission his pulse was 94/min, respiratory rate 20/min, blood pressure 102/68 mm Hg, and temperature 40 °C. Lung examination showed symmetrical chest movement, normal percussion, and diminished breath sounds in the right lower lung field; heart, abdomen, extremities, skin, and neurologic examinations were unremarkable. Invasive fungal infection (e.g., aspergillosis) was evaluated; galactomannan was low (0.34 µg/L) and cryptococcal antigen was negative, making fungal etiology unlikely despite an elevated fungal G test. | "negative Cryptococcus haemolyticus capsule antigen test, GM [Galactomannan] antigen test result of 0.34 µg/L, 'fungal G test' result of 56 ng/L."

case_prompt: A 54‑year‑old male ceramic worker with no prior immune dysfunction was admitted for a persistent fever lasting 19 days. He reported occasional cough and joint soreness but denied other symptoms. On examination his temperature was 38.4 °C; all other vital signs and systemic examinations (pulmonary, abdominal, cardiac, neurologic) were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis 20.72 × 10⁹/L with 87.4 % neutrophils, elevated C‑reactive protein 90.61 mg/L, and a slightly increased procalcitonin of 0.173 ng/mL. On day 5, endobronchial ultrasound‑guided transbronchial needle aspiration (EBUS‑TBNA) was performed using a virtual bronchoscopic navigation system to reach the lesion. Purulent exudate was obtained; biopsy revealed abundant purulent secretions with few lymphocytes and macrophages. Microscopic analysis of the aspirate smear showed numerous weakly acid‑fast and branching filamentous rod bacteria.

Microscopy demonstrated weakly acid‑fast, branching filamentous rods, a morphology characteristic of Nocardia and distinct from strongly acid‑fast mycobacteria. | "Microscopic analysis revealed numerous weakly acid‑fast and branching filamentous rod bacteria were identified from the samples on the aspirate smear."

case_prompt:
A 63‑year‑old Japanese woman presented with a 3‑day history of fever, exertional dyspnea, and a non‑productive cough. She had been receiving oral steroids for three months for interstitial pneumonia secondary to mixed connective‑tissue disease. Two months earlier she experienced life‑threatening toxic epidermal necrolysis after sulfamethoxazole‑trimethoprim (SXT) given for PCP prophylaxis, treated with steroid pulse therapy and plasma exchanges. Atovaquone prophylaxis was stopped because of nausea and anorexia, leaving her without PCP chemoprophylaxis. She also had a prior anaphylactic reaction to ganciclovir for CMV enteritis.

On arrival she was alert (GCS E4V5M6). Vital signs: BP 117/78 mmHg, HR 90 bpm, T 37.8 °C, RR 26/min, SpO₂ 85 % on room air. With 2 L/min nasal O₂, ABG showed pH 7.464, pCO₂ 33.4 mmHg, pO₂ 94.7 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 22.4 mEq/L, PaO₂/FiO₂ 326 mmHg, A‑a DO₂ 70.3 mmHg. No wheezes or crackles were heard.

Laboratory data: WBC 6,700/µL, CRP 3.75 mg/dL, LDH 499 IU/L, KL‑6 595 U/mL. Chest X‑ray showed bilateral, diffuse, symmetric reticular interstitial shadows. Chest CT demonstrated bilateral, asymmetric, patchy mosaic attenuation with peripheral ground‑glass opacities. The differential diagnosis considered included PCP, CMV pneumonia, and pulmonary edema due to heart failure. An additional blood test revealed an elevated β‑D‑glucan level of 155 pg/mL (normal ≤20 pg/mL). CMV antigenemia and IgM antibodies were negative. HIV antibody testing was negative and CD4 count was normal. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated normal cardiac function.

1. PCP considered because β‑D‑glucan, a fungal cell‑wall component that includes Pneumocystis jirovecii, was markedly elevated | "An additional blood test showed an increased level (155 pg/mL, normal: ≤20 pg/mL) of beta‑D‑glucan (a cell wall component of most fungi, including Pneumocystis jirovecii)..."

3. Pulmonary edema due to heart failure considered but excluded by normal cardiac function on echocardiography | "Transthoracic echocardiography revealed normal cardiac function."

The combination of immunosuppression from prolonged steroids, characteristic CT findings (ground‑glass opacities, mosaic pattern), and high β‑D‑glucan made PCP the most likely diagnosis among the differentials | "Based on these findings, the following differential diagnoses were considered: PCP, CMV pneumonia, and pulmonary edema due to heart failure."

case_prompt:
A 68‑year‑old man presented with a three‑month history of paroxysmal cough producing white mucous sputum, accompanied by chest distress, shortness of breath, and bilateral lower‑limb numbness. He had a 50‑year smoking history (20 cigarettes per day) but quit five months prior. Physical examination revealed rough breath sounds bilaterally without rhonchi or moist rales; lymph nodes were not enlarged and cardiac and abdominal examinations were unremarkable.

Chest CT (05 March 2022) showed a mixed‑density mass measuring ≈12.6 × 7.6 cm in the left upper lobe with bronchial truncation, localized thinning of the left pulmonary artery, and multiple small patchy and nodular high‑density shadows in the surrounding lung and left lower lobe. Cranial MRI identified an abnormal signal in the left lateral ventricle, presumed cavernous hemangioma. Bronchoscopy (09 March 2022) revealed a cauliflower‑like neoplasm obstructing the left upper lobe bronchial orifice; the left lower lobe opening was mildly compressed. Tumor markers were elevated (CEA 6 mg/ml, CA125 88.18 U/ml, CK19 12.91 ng/ml, NSE 33.72 ng/ml). Pathology from bronchoscopic biopsy demonstrated moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma (CK5/6 +, CK7 –, P40 +, P63 +, Ki‑67 50‑60 %). The patient received two cycles of DP chemotherapy (docetaxel + cisplatin) followed by a single dose of camrelizumab immunotherapy (25 April 2022). During the second chemotherapy cycle he experienced severe gastrointestinal toxicity and bone‑marrow suppression, with leukopenia (WBC 1.3 × 10⁹/L) and neutropenia (NEU 0.23 × 10⁹/L). He declined further chemotherapy.

On 21 May 2022 the patient developed coughing up ≈20 mL of blood‑streaked sputum. Repeat chest CT (22 May 2022) showed the left upper‑lobe tumor had decreased in size, but the multiple small nodules and patchy high‑density shadows in both lungs had become more extensive, raising concern for pneumonia or infection related to immune checkpoint inhibition. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage was performed; a 13‑item nucleic‑acid respiratory pathogen panel was positive for *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*. Acid‑fast bacillus staining of the lavage fluid was also positive.

case_prompt: A 59‑year‑old man with diffuse large B‑cell lymphoma (stage IA) received six cycles of R‑CHOP chemotherapy. Two weeks after the fifth cycle he was readmitted for response assessment. He complained of intermittent mild cough with scant white sputum. Vital signs were normal; lung auscultation was clear; there was no lymphadenopathy. Laboratory testing showed leukocytosis, lymphocytopenia, moderate anemia, elevated C‑reactive protein, normal procalcitonin, and normal serum 1‑3‑β‑D‑glucan. Hepatic and renal panels were within normal limits. Sputum cultures grew no pathogens; serum CMV PCR was undetectable; HIV testing was repeatedly non‑reactive. Chest X‑ray revealed patchy bilateral shadows. PET‑CT demonstrated decreased tibial tumor burden but multiple patchy, cord‑like pulmonary opacities with increased FDG uptake, interpreted as pneumonia. Empiric cefoperazone and levofloxacin were started. Despite therapy, the patient developed daily fevers up to 38.9 °C. On day 8 of admission he progressed to dyspnea and hypoxemia (SpO₂ 90% on room air) with an oxygenation index ≈100, suggesting acute respiratory distress syndrome. Non‑infectious drug‑induced lung injury considered (e.g., chemotherapeutic toxicity); deemed unlikely as timing coincided with severe immunosuppression and imaging showed ground‑glass opacities rather than typical drug‑related patterns. case_prompt: A 52‑year‑old man with a history of allogeneic bone‑marrow transplantation (33 years prior) presented with advanced BRAF‑mutated colorectal cancer with multiple lung, liver, and peritoneal metastases. He underwent transverse colostomy for colonic obstruction. Baseline chest CT showed multiple pulmonary nodules from metastases but no fibrosis. He received first‑line FOLFIRI + bevacizumab; on day 6 of the first cycle he developed a fleeting fever that resolved with naproxen. After the second chemotherapy cycle, on day 15, his SpO₂ fell to 92 % in room air, prompting admission. CT revealed subtle bilateral ground‑glass opacities without tumor progression. Bronchoscopy showed a normal airway; BAL cultures and PCR for pneumocystis jirovecii and CMV DNA were negative. Transbronchial lung biopsy demonstrated metastatic colon cancer but no inflammation. Serum LDH, KL‑6, and β‑D‑glucan were normal. White‑blood cell count was 2,740/µL (neutrophils 1,140/µL, lymphocytes 880/µL); interferon‑γ release assay for tuberculosis was negative. He was started on levofloxacin. Four days later his cough and dyspnea worsened, with expanding bilateral interstitial infiltrates on CT and a rise in KL‑6 to 531 U/mL. On day 6 of this admission, high‑dose methylprednisolone (1 g/day) and piperacillin‑tazobactam were given, leading to rapid clinical improvement and radiographic resolution by day 21. Steroids were tapered to oral prednisolone 30 mg/day by day 22, then to 20 mg/day by day 33. On day 39, he developed abdominal pain; CT showed a retroperitoneal hematoma and pseudoaneurysm, managed with intra‑arterial embolization while maintaining prednisolone. On day 43 lung infiltrates recurred; methylprednisolone pulse therapy was re‑initiated on day 44, tapered to 125 mg/day by day 47, and nasal high‑flow oxygen started on day 49. Intravenous cyclosporine (150 mg/day) was added on day 49. On day 51 laboratory tests showed AST 32 U/L, ALT 53 U/L, ALP 351 U/L, GGT 236 U/L, total bilirubin 3.0 mg/dL, and CRP 3.89 mg/dL. The patient’s condition remained critical, and additional antimicrobial agents (micafungin) were started pending further infectious work‑up.

1. Drug‑induced interstitial lung disease (DILD) was initially favored because ground‑glass opacities appeared after chemotherapy and improved rapidly with high‑dose steroids. | "CT showed slight bilateral ground‑glass shadows... methylprednisolone (1 g/day) was administered... respiratory condition improved rapidly."

CMV antigen positive cell count was 200‑206... ganciclovir (500 mg/day) was added."

case_prompt:

After three cycles, creatinine rose to 346 µmol/L and BUN to 9.58 mmol/L; abdominal CT showed no urinary obstruction, and urinalysis revealed trace protein, microscopic hematuria (1600/µL) and an elevated urine microalbumin/creatinine ratio (53.04 mg/g). Two weeks later he developed cough with yellow sputum containing blood, intermittent epistaxis, fever up to 39 °C with chills, and blood pressure 152/84 mmHg. Laboratory studies showed: WBC 12.03 ×10⁹/L, hemoglobin 60 g/L, neutrophils 95.4 %, HS‑CRP 157.14 mg/L, procalcitonin 7.47 ng/mL, IL‑6 113.10 pg/mL, creatinine 537 µmol/L, BUN 22.06 mmol/L, PaO₂ 62 mmHg (room air), fibrinogen 6.04 g/L, D‑dimer 950 ng/mL. Autoimmune serologies were negative for ANA, anti‑dsDNA, RF, C3, C4, anti‑GBM, and anti‑SSA/SSB, but anti‑MPO was 152.82 RU/mL and anti‑PR3 was 98.48 RU/mL. Sputum culture grew Klebsiella pneumoniae. Chest CT demonstrated multiple bilateral lesions with diffuse pulmonary alveolar hemorrhage around the hilum and ground‑glass opacities. Nasopharyngeal MRI showed chronic sinus inflammation. A kidney biopsy performed four months after chemotherapy revealed capillary loop necrosis with cellular, fibrocellular, and fibrous crescents; immunofluorescence was negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial pneumonia (Klebsiella) considered because sputum culture was positive, yet it does not explain the crescentic glomerulonephritis and diffuse alveolar hemorrhage. | "Sputum culture revealed the presence of Klebsiella pneumoniae… Chest CT showed multiple lesions…with diffuse pulmonary alveolar hemorrhage…"  
2. Anti‑GBM disease considered but excluded by negative anti‑GBM antibodies. | "anti‑GBM…were negative."  
3. Lupus nephritis / immune‑complex vasculitis excluded by negative ANA, anti‑dsDNA, and normal complement levels. | "The antinuclear antibody, anti‑dsDNA…C3, C4…were negative."  
4. Drug‑induced AAV favored over malignancy‑related vasculitis because renal function and urinalysis were normal before chemotherapy and vasculitic manifestations appeared after XELOX + trastuzumab exposure. | "Malignant tumors can also lead to vasculitis, but the patient's renal function and urine routine were normal before and after the resection…vasculitis occurred after chemotherapy."  
5. Dual positivity for MPO‑ANCA and PR3‑ANCA suggested a drug‑induced process rather than idiopathic AAV. | "If a patient tests positive for both MPO and PR3‑ANCA, it suggests that the disease may be drug‑induced."  
6. Tuberculosis and Legionella infections were later identified by tNGS but deemed secondary to immunosuppression; they could not account for the initial renal pathology. | "tNGS examination revealed…Legionella pneumophila…Mycobacterium tuberculosis…Yeast‑like Pneumocystis jirovecii…Although the tuberculosis culture and acid‑fast staining were negative, tuberculosis infection was still considered."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient’s primary unresolved infection is Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, which is on the SELECTED diseases list. Although Mycobacterium tuberculosis reads were detected, subsequent investigations suggested it was not the pathogenic cause, making PJP the focus.
2. Breakpoint: Include presentation, lymphoma background, prior therapies, bronchoscopy findings, initial CT comment (“two lung infections should be considered”), negative routine microbiology, BAL‑F NGS results, initial antimicrobial regimen, development of drug‑induced liver injury, persistent fever, worsening respiratory parameters, and the key laboratory abnormalities. Stop before the authors explicitly classify the illness as “severe PJP.”
3. Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished PJP from tuberculosis (negative T‑cell response, sputum PCR, cultures), from bacterial pneumonia (negative Gram stain and cultures), and from drug toxicity (liver enzyme rise without explaining respiratory failure). The high burden of PJP reads on NGS and the clinical picture of hypoxemia with interstitial infiltrates guided the final diagnosis.
case_prompt:
A 41‑year‑old man with relapsed refractory diffuse large B‑cell lymphoma (MYC, BCL‑2, BCL‑6 expression) had received multiple regimens including R‑CHOP, R‑GDP, venetoclax, obutinib, and immune checkpoint inhibitors. He was transferred to a tuberculosis referral hospital after bronchoscopy revealed no bacteria on Gram stain, no fungal growth in culture, no PJP cysts on Grocott’s silver stain, and no acid‑fast bacilli on smear; however, BAL‑fluid next‑generation sequencing identified 5,225 reads of Pneumocystis jirovecii and four reads of Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

On admission his computed tomography scan suggested that two lung infections should be considered first. Initial management comprised meropenem, trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole (TMP‑SMX) 1.44 g q6 h for presumed PJP, and rifampicin, isoniazid, and levofloxacin for tuberculosis, together with methylprednisolone 40 mg q12 h, ganciclovir prophylaxis, and tiopronin for liver protection.

Six days later he developed drug‑induced liver injury (ALT 269 U/L, AST 299 U/L) accompanied by nausea and vomiting, prompting reduction of TMP‑SMX to 0.96 g q8 h and addition of micafungin for PJP. After four more days his repeat CT scan showed progression of the pulmonary infiltrates. He remained febrile up to 40.4 °C, dyspneic, and complained of chest tightness. Arterial blood gas revealed type 2 respiratory failure with PaO₂ 57 mmHg; SaO₂ was 89 % at rest. Laboratory studies showed procalcitonin 5.32 ng/mL, C‑reactive protein 167.53 mg/L, lactate dehydrogenase 564 U/L, and white‑blood‑cell count 2.7 × 10⁹/L.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. High burden of Pneumocystis reads on BAL‑fluid NGS points to PJP as the dominant pathogen | "BALF‑NGS found 5,225 PJP reads and four Mycobacterium tuberculosis reads."
2. Absence of bacteria on routine microbiology makes bacterial pneumonia unlikely | "The routine microbiological examination did not detect any pathogenic bacteria; Gram staining did not show any bacteria; the culture did not show fungal growth."
3. Negative T‑cell receptor clustering and lack of MTB DNA/RNA in sputum argue against active tuberculosis | "The immune response to MTB by T‑cell receptor clustering was negative, and MTB complex from sputum samples, non‑tuberculous mycobacterial DNA, and tuberculosis DNA and RNA were negative."
4. Drug‑induced liver injury explains hepatic enzyme elevation but not respiratory failure | "Unfortunately, the patient developed drug‑induced liver injury after six days of treatment, with ALT levels up to 269 U/L and AST levels up to 299 U/L."
5. CMV retinitis is noted but does not account for pulmonary findings | "The patient developed ... cytomegalovirus retinitis..."
6. Persistent high fever, severe hypoxemia (PaO₂ 57 mmHg, SaO₂ 89 %), and extensive interstitial shadowing on CT are classic for severe PJP | "Based on the persistent fever, tachypnoea, PaO₂ of 57 mmHg, arterial oxygen saturation (SaO₂) of 89 % at rest, and extensive interstitial shadowing on chest CT, the patient was classified as having severe PJP."

case_prompt:
A 70‑year‑old woman with Philadelphia‑like CRLF2‑overexpressing B‑cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia achieved complete remission after induction chemotherapy in August 2021. She subsequently received consolidation therapy with blinatumomab, beginning on September 10. On the second day of infusion she had a sub‑febrile temperature, attributed to mild cytokine‑release syndrome and treated with loxoprofen. On day 9 of blinatumomab she developed intermittent fever without respiratory symptoms; white‑blood‑cell count rose to 18.1 × 10⁹/L and chest computed tomography showed subtle infiltrates and nodules. Empiric piperacillin/tazobactam, acyclovir, and trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis were started, but fever persisted.

On day 17 of blinatumomab the patient developed marked dyspnea; pulse oximetry fell to 78 % on room air. Repeat chest CT demonstrated diffuse ground‑glass opacities with scattered small nodules. Laboratory studies revealed a lymphocyte count of 0.59 × 10⁹/L, C‑reactive protein increased from 2.41 to 109.75 mg/L (reference < 3 mg/L), lactate dehydrogenase rose from 250 to 413 U/L (reference < 250 U/L), and the serum β‑D‑glucan level was 298.6 pg/mL (reference < 100.5 pg/mL). The patient reported a dry, non‑productive cough.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Cytokine‑release syndrome (CRS) considered due to recent blinatumomab initiation; however, the patient’s fever persisted beyond the typical transient CRS window and was accompanied by progressive hypoxemia and radiographic changes, making CRS less likely. | "On the second day of blinatumomab infusion, she presented with subfebrile fever, which was thought attributed to mild cytokine release syndrome... However, on the 9th day after blinatumomab use, she experienced intermittent fever... On the 17th day of blinatumomab treatment, she developed obvious shortness of breath, and her pulse oxygen saturation decreased to 78%."  
2. Bacterial pneumonia considered because of fever and infiltrates; empiric piperacillin/tazobactam was administered, yet the patient failed to improve and cultures were negative, arguing against bacterial etiology. | "The patient received empiric treatment with piperacillin/tazobactam... Despite treatment, the fever persisted."  
3. Viral reactivation (e.g., HSV, CMV) considered, prompting acyclovir therapy; lack of clinical response and absence of viral PCR findings diminished this possibility. | "The patient received ... acyclovir... Despite treatment, the fever persisted."  
4. Drug‑induced pulmonary toxicity from blinatumomab considered, but the pattern of diffuse ground‑glass opacities with nodules, markedly elevated β‑D‑glucan, and lymphopenia are more characteristic of an opportunistic fungal infection. | "Chest CT showed diffuse GGO with scattered small nodules... beta‑D‑glucan assays showed 298.6 (reference <100.5) pg/mL, all indicative of possible PCP infection."  
5. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) supported by (a) profound lymphopenia, (b) high serum β‑D‑glucan, (c) elevated LDH, (d) diffuse ground‑glass opacities with nodules on CT, (e) dry cough, and (f) later confirmation by pathogen‑specific sequencing. | "her lymphocyte count decreased to 0.59 × 10⁹/L, C‑reactive protein increased... LDH increased... beta‑D‑glucan assays showed 298.6... all indicative of possible PCP infection. The dry cough... prompted next‑generation sequencing of peripheral blood, which tested positive for pneumocystis jirovecii without evidence of other pathogens."

2. Breakpoint: Include all information up to the point where the bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) metagenomic next‑generation sequencing result is mentioned. The prompt will present the initial presentation, treatment course, persistent muscle weakness, development of seizures, PICU admission, physical exam findings, laboratory abnormalities, and imaging (chest CT, cerebral CT/MRI, EEG, CSF) but will stop before the sentence that states “pneumocystis jirovecii was detected…”.

Author's Analytic Distinctions: The authors identified the opportunistic infection by NGS of BAL fluid, distinguished it from bacterial/viral causes by normal CRP and absence of pathogens in CSF, considered macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) due to hyperferritinemia and thrombocytopenia, and attributed seizures to CNS involvement of active JDM. These distinctions allowed them to initiate targeted plasmapheresis and anti‑pneumocystis therapy.
case_prompt:
An 11‑year‑old boy presented with a one‑month history of proximal muscle weakness and a heliotrope rash. On admission his CMAS score was 12, serum CK was 4,718 U/L, EMG showed myogenic changes, and muscle biopsy demonstrated perifascicular atrophy with inflammatory infiltrates and strong MHC‑I expression. Myositis‑specific antibody testing was positive for anti‑NXP2 (IgG 115.42 RU/ml) and anti‑Ro‑52; ANA was 1:320. He met criteria for definite juvenile dermatomyositis (total score 14.9). Initial therapy included IVIG 2 g/kg, IV methylprednisolone (IVMP) 500 mg/day × 3 days, oral prednisone 2 mg/kg/day, and one dose of IV cyclophosphamide 500 mg.

Despite treatment, muscle weakness persisted and dysphagia developed. Two weeks later he suffered tonic‑clonic seizures progressing to status epilepticus, requiring sedation, endotracheal intubation, and transfer to the PICU. Examination revealed marked skin and periorbital edema, blood pressure 126/81 mmHg, bilateral positive Babinski signs, and otherwise unremarkable cardiac, pulmonary, and abdominal findings.

Laboratory studies showed AST 269 U/L, ALT 76 U/L, LDH 1,200 U/L, CK 4,784 U/L, white blood cell count 17.15 × 10⁹/L with 91.4 % neutrophils, hemoglobin 137 g/L, platelet count 39 × 10⁹/L, normal C‑reactive protein, ferritin >2,000 ng/mL, triglycerides 2.56 mmol/L, and mildly elevated CSF protein (64 mg/dL) with normal glucose, cell count, and no bacterial or viral evidence. Echocardiography was normal. Chest CT demonstrated bilateral lung infiltrates with partial consolidation. Cerebral CT showed blurred gray‑white matter differentiation; contrast‑enhanced MRI revealed abnormal signals in the left parieto‑occipital lobe and thalamus. MRA and MRV were negative. EEG displayed diffuse background slow waves (2–5 Hz).
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Persistent immunosuppression and new bilateral lung infiltrates in a child with JDM raise suspicion for opportunistic infection, especially Pneumocystis jirovecii | "Chest CT indicated bilateral lung infiltrates and partial consolidation."
2. Absence of fever, normal C‑reactive protein, and lack of sputum culture data make a typical bacterial pneumonia less likely | "C‑reactive protein level was within normal range."
3. No viral pathogens identified in CSF and normal glucose and cell count argue against viral encephalitis or viral pneumonia as primary causes | "no evidence of bacteria or viruses" in CSF study.
4. Hyperferritinemia and thrombocytopenia could indicate macrophage activation syndrome, but the patient lacked fever and other classic MAS criteria, prompting further evaluation | "Considering that the patient presented with hyperferritinemia and thrombocytopenia, macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) could not be ruled out, despite the absence of fever."
5. Seizures were attributed to CNS involvement of active JDM rather than an infectious process, based on muscle enzyme trends and rising NXP2 antibody titers | "we concluded that the patient was in the active stage of JDM, and seizures were attributed to CNS involvement."
6. Metagenomic next‑generation sequencing of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid identified Pneumocystis jirovecii, confirming the opportunistic infection and guiding antifungal therapy | "pneumocystis jirovecii was detected in the metagenome next‑generation sequencing analysis of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid on PICU hospitalization day 6, so antifungal treatments were administered."

case_prompt:
A 52‑year‑old woman was admitted for persistent afternoon fever and fatigue lasting more than one month. Body temperature fluctuated between 37.1°C and 38.2°C, accompanied by cough with scant sputum. Initial work‑up showed elevated AST (80 IU/L), markedly increased LDH (947 IU/L), high CRP (20.8 mg/L) and IL‑6 (47.99 pg/mL). Procalcitonin was mildly elevated (0.09 ng/mL). Arterial blood gas revealed pH 7.45, PCO₂ 29.5 mmHg, PO₂ 63 mmHg, SaO₂ 93%. Mycoplasma pneumoniae antibodies were positive at titers up to 1:320. Cryptococcal antigen was negative; CD4 proportion was 50.85%. Chest CT demonstrated multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules, mainly in the upper lobes, described as inflammatory nodules, with mild interlobular septal thickening suggesting mild pulmonary edema. Contrast‑enhanced abdominal CT showed multiple mildly enhancing renal cortical nodules and a 1.1 cm hypodense right hepatic posterior‑lobe lesion thought to be inflammatory.

Initial empiric moxifloxacin failed to improve fever. Subsequent serologies yielded inconclusive antihistone and anti‑mitochondrial antibodies, borderline anti‑dsDNA and ANA, normal thyroid panel, and no ANCA abnormalities. Antibiotics were escalated to piperacillin‑tazobactam, minocycline, and doxycycline without defervescence. Next‑generation sequencing of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid detected Staphylococcus aureus, Pneumocystis carinii, and human herpesvirus‑5; therapy was switched to meropenem, vancomycin, and high‑dose trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole, after which fever resolved temporarily. Despite negative repeat blood cultures, intermittent low‑grade fever persisted, and a SARS‑CoV‑2 (COVID‑19) PCR later returned positive. A PET‑CT was suggested but declined.

Ultrasound of the liver revealed a 1.4 × 1.1 cm hypoechoic nodule beneath the capsule of the right posterior lobe, with clear margins and no Doppler flow. Contrast‑enhanced ultrasound showed rapid uniform hyper‑enhancement in the arterial phase, early wash‑out in the late arterial phase, and slight reduced enhancement in portal and delayed phases, describing a “fast in and fast out” pattern typical of malignant hepatic lesions. Because of the lesion’s size and location, a laparoscopic liver biopsy was planned.

Bacterial pneumonia was considered due to cough and fever, but sputum and pharyngeal cultures were non‑diagnostic and the patient did not improve with broad‑spectrum antibiotics. | "Sputum and pharyngeal bacteria culture did not show obvious abnormalities... antibiotics were adjusted... but the patient still had a recurrent fever."

Mycoplasma infection was suggested by positive titers, yet the lack of clinical response to moxifloxacin made it unlikely as the sole cause. | "Mycoplasma pneumonia antibody: titer 1:40 ... 1:320 retained (+/‑); Moxifloxacin was used as an anti‑infective therapy... however, it did not produce satisfactory results."

Staphylococcus aureus infection was identified by NGS of BAL fluid, prompting vancomycin therapy, but fever persisted, indicating it was not the primary driver. | "Detection of Staphylococcus aureus, pneumocystis carinii and human herpes virus type 5… antibiotics were adjusted to meropenem+vancomycin, and the patient did not have fever after treatment with compound sulfamethoxazole against pneumocystis."

Pneumocystis pneumonia was diagnosed via NGS and treated with trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole, leading to temporary fever resolution, yet recurrent fever continued, suggesting another underlying process. | "Detection of ... pneumocystis carinii… the antibiotics were adjusted… the patient did not have fever after treatment with compound sulfamethoxazole against pneumocystis."

case_prompt: A 53‑year‑old man with a grade III pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor and widespread metastases had been treated with multiple chemotherapy regimens and, from September 2022, with the RET inhibitor pralsetinib. After an initial month of therapy he developed Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteremia with septic emboli and cervical spondylodiscitis, which resolved after discontinuation of pralsetinib and prolonged antibiotics. Subsequent infections included two episodes of pneumonia treated with amoxicillin‑clavulanic acid and piperacillin‑tazobactam, and a lumbar spondylodiscitis due to P. aeruginosa confirmed by vertebral biopsy. Extensive immunologic work‑up at that time showed grade I lymphopenia, profound hypogammaglobulinemia with isolated IgG deficiency, and normal CD4/CD8 ratios; HIV, hepatitis B and C serologies were negative. Pralidated therapy was resumed, but three weeks later he presented with febrile hypoxemia and persistent lymphopenia. A thoracic CT scan demonstrated disseminated, poorly delineated pulmonary lesions, which were initially interpreted as possible disease progression.

1. Persistent lymphopenia and selective IgG deficiency suggested an acquired immunodeficiency predisposing to opportunistic infections | "Grade I lymphopenia was identified without concomitant neutropenia... plasmatic protein electrophoresis identified deep hypogammaglobulinemia with specific IgG deficiency."
2. Recurrent Pseudomonas infections raised concern for bacterial pneumonia, but the current pulmonary lesions were atypical for bacterial patterns and cultures were negative | "Repeated blood culture (bacterial and fungal) was performed and remained negative."
3. Tuberculosis was considered because of vertebral involvement, but histology of the biopsy did not demonstrate mycobacterial disease | "histology did not show the presence of bone tuberculosis or tumor progression."

Tumor progression was a leading differential given new pulmonary nodules on CT, yet the pattern was poorly delimited and inconsistent with the known response profile; no new metastatic lesions were confirmed on imaging at that time | "pulmonary lesions... were first interpreted as disease progression."
5. HIV infection could predispose to Pneumocystis, but serology was negative, ruling it out as a cause of immunosuppression | "Broad‑spectrum serology, including human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and hepatitis B and C, was negative."
6. The definitive diagnosis of Pneumocystis pneumonia was established when respiratory secretions tested positive for the organism, confirming the etiology of the pulmonary lesions | "pulmonary secretion was positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii."

case_prompt:
A 51‑year‑old man was admitted with a 3‑day history of fever, asthma, cough, and purulent sputum production. He reported occasional dark‑red blood streaks in the sputum and right‑sided chest pain. He had a past history of non‑infectious uveitis treated with methylprednisolone and cyclosporine (2022).  

On examination his temperature was 38.9 °C, heart rate 130 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min. Physical findings included a “moon face,” limb muscle atrophy, and reduced subcutaneous fat. Lung examination revealed solid percussion notes over the right lower zone, coarse breath sounds, and wet rales in both lower lungs; limb strength and tone were normal.  

Laboratory studies showed a white‑blood‑cell count of 10.62 × 10⁹/L with 82.9 % neutrophils. T‑lymphocyte subsets demonstrated CD3⁺CD4⁺ percentage of 12.52 % (CD4⁺/CD8⁺ ratio 0.34), absolute lymphocyte count 45 cells/µL. HIV antibody test, serum Aspergillus galactomannan, Aspergillus IgG, Candida mannan antigen, and Candida IgG were all negative.  

Chest computed tomography demonstrated unevenly reduced attenuation throughout both lung fields with mosaic change, interstitial thickening, solid nodules, ground‑glass nodules, halo signs surrounding some lesions, flake‑like high‑density shadows with rough edges in the right lower lobe, patchy low‑density necrosis, and multiple nodular high‑density shadows in all lobes.  

Fiberoptic bronchoscopy showed congestion and edema of the posterior basal mucosa of the right lower lobe. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid was collected and sent for smear, culture, and metagenomic next‑generation sequencing (mNGS).

Chest computed tomography performed at an outside hospital showed ground‑glass opacities in both upper lobes. Her past medical history was notable for triple‑negative breast cancer treated with left breast‑conserving surgery on February 29, 2024 followed by three cycles of adjuvant doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide; she had completed chemotherapy on May 6, 2024 and subsequently received pegfilgrastim for leukopenia (initial leukocyte count 2.69 × 10⁹/L).

Initial laboratory studies (Table 1) showed anemia (Hb 8.0 g/dL) and markedly elevated liver enzymes (ALT 153 U/L, AST 108 U/L, ALP 688 U/L). Blood cultures for fungi, mycobacteria, and bacteria were obtained; urinary Histoplasma antigen, serum Aspergillus galactomannan, and Cryptococcus antigen were ordered. Stool studies were negative for parasites, Cryptosporidium, and enteropathogenic bacteria. Oral ulcers were clinically compatible with herpetic stomatitis; IV acyclovir was started, and TMP‑SMX prophylaxis for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) was initiated.

Because of a local allergic reaction on day 1, PJP prophylaxis was switched to oral dapsone and pyrimethamine with calcium folinate. A colonoscopy and contrast‑enhanced head CT were unremarkable. Chest CT showed a ground‑glass and micronodular miliary pattern, suggesting both PJP and either histoplasmosis or miliary tuberculosis. Consequently, a bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) specimen was sent for Ziehl‑Neelsen staining. On day 2, PJP prophylaxis was stopped; clindamycin + primaquine therapy was begun, and IV amphotericin B deoxycholate was started for suspected histoplasmosis. Zidovudine/lamivudine was replaced with emtricitabine/tenofovir + efavirenz due to anemia. Liver biopsy was performed because of markedly elevated transaminases, and tissue was sent for histology, Gram, KOH, Ziehl‑Neelsen, modified Kinyoun (Nocardia), bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial cultures, as well as GeneXpert MTB/RIF Ultra.

By day 4, sputum Ziehl‑Neelsen staining showed no acid‑fast bacilli, and tuberculosis treatment was withheld. On day 6, serum Aspergillus galactomannan returned positive (index 3.27; cutoff >0.5). By day 8, hepatitis B surface antigen, anti‑HBc IgM, hepatitis B DNA, and hepatitis C antibody were all negative, and cryptococcal antigen was also negative. Creatinine rose to 1.34 mg/dL, attributed to amphotericin B nephrotoxicity. On day 11, acute kidney injury (creatinine 1.6 mg/dL) prompted a 24‑hour infusion of amphotericin B, with subsequent renal improvement by day 14. On day 15, a second BAL was obtained to detect Mycobacterium tuberculosis, fungi, or bacteria.

1. PJP considered due to ground‑glass CT pattern and HIV immunosuppression | "ground‑glass and micronodular miliary pattern (Figure 1), suggesting both PJP and either histoplasmosis or milliary tuberculosis."
2. Histoplasmosis considered because of endemic exposure, hepatomegaly, elevated liver enzymes, and miliary pattern | "painful hepatomegaly without jaundice" and "high level of liver enzymes x3 times the upper limit of normal ... raising suspicion of hepatic infiltration."
3. Tuberculosis included in differential due to miliary pattern; excluded after negative sputum ZN stain and GeneXpert | "no acid‑fast bacilli were observed" and "microbiological results ... for M. tuberculosis ... were negative."
4. Aspergillosis considered after positive serum galactomannan (index 3.27) | "The result of the test was 3.27 (cutoff index >0.5 is reported as positive)."
5. Cryptococcosis ruled out by negative cryptococcal antigen | "cryptococcal antigen test yielded negative results."
6. Viral hepatitis (B and C) excluded by serology and PCR | "Hepatitis B surface antigen ... was measured at 0.51 COI ... hepatitis B DNA PCR test result was less than 117 IU/mL ... antibody test for hepatitis C showed 0.05 COI."
7. Nocardia infection evaluated (modified Kinyoun stain) but not reported as positive; thus excluded | "samples were sent for ... modified Kinyoun stain for Nocardia spp."
8. Herpetic stomatitis diagnosed clinically and treated with acyclovir; not the cause of systemic illness | "oral ulcers clinically compatible with herpetic stomatitis. IV acyclovir 500 mg every eight hours was initiated."
9. Final confirmation of histoplasmosis achieved by positive urine antigen and later blood culture isolation of H. capsulatum | "Histoplasma urine antigen (IMMY, Norman, OK, USA) was detected." and "H. capsulatum infection was confirmed through fungal isolation from blood cultures."

1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient ultimately was diagnosed with Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, which is on the 21 SELECTED diseases list (pneumocystis). A 62‑year‑old woman with mixed‑phenotype acute leukemia was admitted for first‑line consolidation chemotherapy (FLAG‑Ida + sorafenib). After induction she had two episodes of febrile neutropenia due to piperacillin/tazobactam‑resistant Klebsiella oxytoca bacteremia, treated with meropenem and later discharged when clinically stable.

Twelve days after discharge she was readmitted for consolidation therapy in a positive‑pressure hemato‑oncology ward. Antiviral (acyclovir) and antifungal (posaconazole) prophylaxis were given; no routine bacterial or Pneumocystis prophylaxis was administered. Eleven days into chemotherapy she again developed febrile neutropenia; blood cultures again grew resistant K. oxytoca, and she was treated with meropenem, later de‑escalated to cefepime.

On day 25 of chemotherapy, while profoundly neutropenic (WBC 0.06 × 10⁹/L), she developed a new febrile syndrome. Laboratory trends showed a rapid drop in hemoglobin (from 8.6 to 6.8 g/dL) and new unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia; potassium and LDH were unreportable due to hemolysis. Hours later she became agitated, somnolent, complained of abdominal discomfort, and desaturated. Urine was visibly red. Contrast‑enhanced CT of chest and abdomen was unremarkable except for an air‑dense lesion in the right hepatic lobe, without evidence of bleeding.

She required aggressive hydration, multiple red‑cell transfusions, and was transferred to the ICU for septic shock with respiratory, renal, hepatic, and neurologic dysfunction. Broad‑spectrum antibiotics (meropenem + vancomycin) were continued. Urine analysis showed mild erythrocyturia despite gross hematuria, suggesting hemoglobinuria.

Because of progressive respiratory insufficiency, a repeat chest CT showed bilateral consolidations with a ground‑glass appearance. Empiric amphotericin B was started for possible invasive fungal infection. A broncho‑alveolar lavage was performed; fungal cultures and galactomannan assays (blood and lavage) were negative, and β‑D‑glucan testing was unavailable. A PCR assay for Pneumocystis jirovecii was performed.

case_prompt:
A 66‑year‑old African American man presented with a 1‑week history of progressive shortness of breath and bilateral calf pain. He reported occasional productive cough and denied chest pain, hemoptysis, night sweats, palpitations, or dyspnea. Past medical history included peripheral vascular disease, prostate cancer treated with prostatectomy and penile implant, and an 8‑year incarceration history. He had a significant smoking history but no alcohol or street drug use; family history was notable for lung cancer.

Chest radiography was followed by a computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest, which revealed a left upper‑lobe mass measuring 4.5 × 5.5 × 5 cm with mediastinal and right hilar adenopathy; no pleural or pericardial effusion was seen. CT of the head and a bone scan showed no metastasis.

A CT‑guided fine‑needle aspiration of the left lung mass demonstrated an inflammatory necrotic background with several large aggregates of fungi. On Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) stain, the hyphae were of uniform diameter, septated, and branched at 45°, morphologically compatible with Aspergillus species. A special stain for acid‑fast bacilli (AFB) was negative, and no tumor cells were identified. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7.7 g/dL, white blood cell count 7.7 × 10³/µL (absolute neutrophils 4.6 × 10³/µL, monocytes 0.6 × 10³/µL, lymphocytes 3.2 × 10³/µL), serum creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, BUN 14 mg/dL. 2. Mycobacterial infection (tuberculosis) considered given cavitary lesion, but excluded by negative acid‑fast bacilli stain. | “A special stain for Acid Fast Bacilli (AFB) was negative.”

Non‑Aspergillus fungal infection considered, yet GMS morphology (uniform diameter, septation, 45° branching) was described as “morphologically compatible with Aspergillus species,” supporting Aspergillus over other fungi. | “On Gomori Methanamine Silver (GMS) stain, the hyphae had uniform diameter, septation and branching at 45 degree, morphologically compatible with aspergillus species.”

Viral, bacterial, or Pneumocystis etiologies were later evaluated with bronchoalveolar lavage; all cultures and direct fluorescent antibody tests were negative, further narrowing the diagnosis to a fungal etiology. | “BAL … returned negative for mycobacterium, fungus, legionella and cytomegalovirus… BAL fluid was negative for … Pneumocystis carinii.”
