case_prompt:
A 39‑year‑old woman with type 1 diabetes and AIDS (CD4 166 cells/µL, undetectable HIV load) presented on June 5, 2009 with three days of fever, non‑productive cough, generalized weakness, and worsening dyspnea. She was on antiretroviral therapy (combivir, efavirenz) and trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole but was non‑compliant. She had a sick child at home with an influenza‑like illness and a past history of pleuropericardial Nocardia infection, recurrent pleural effusions, and hepatomegaly of unknown cause.  

On admission she was febrile (101 °F), tachycardic (109 bpm), hypotensive (86/52 mm Hg), tachypneic (22 /min) with oxygen saturation 88 % on room air. Physical exam revealed decreased breath sounds at the bases, hepatomegaly, and bilateral lower‑extremity edema. Laboratory studies showed leukopenia (3,000 cells/mm³ with 93 % neutrophils), hemoglobin 12.7 g/dL, platelets 118,000/mm³, BUN 66 mg/dL, creatinine 2.9 mg/dL, CPK 2,276 IU/L, lactate 3.6 mmol/L (anion gap 13). Chest radiograph demonstrated a moderate right pleural effusion and retrocardiac air‑space disease.

Over 48 hours she deteriorated, requiring ICU transfer, intubation, pressor support, and continuous venovenous hemofiltration. Repeat testing for influenza virus, respiratory fluorescent antibodies, and viral culture remained negative, as did blood cultures and urine Legionella antigen. Thoracentesis yielded transudative fluid negative for acid‑fast bacilli, bacteria, and fungi. Chest imaging later showed a right‑sided pneumothorax and worsening bilateral infiltrates. On hospital day 5 bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage was performed; cytology was negative for Pneumocystis jiroveci, viral inclusions, fungi, acid‑fast bacilli, bacteria, and mycobacteria, but clusters of filamentous organisms were observed.

Definitive diagnosis required molecular testing; RT‑PCR of a nasopharyngeal swab returned positive for pandemic (H1N1) 2009, confirming the viral etiology | "Diagnosis was based on a positive result for pandemic (H1N1) 2009 by real-time reverse transcription‑PCR (RT‑PCR) for a nasopharyngeal swab specimen."

case_prompt:
A 38‑year‑old man presented to the emergency department with cough, dyspnea, and hemoptysis. One week earlier he had inhaled large amounts of dust while sanding and dry‑sweeping a cement floor‑patching compound that contained 1%–5% crystalline quartz silica and was highly alkaline (pH 12). He experienced mucosal irritation during work and felt ill each night after his shifts. After three days he stopped working; over the weekend his symptoms progressed to chills and fever, and he was prescribed antibiotics and an inhaler at a walk‑in clinic. His pulmonary symptoms worsened, prompting ED presentation and admission.

Past history included childhood asthma and a remote one‑pack‑year smoking history. Physical examination revealed diffuse bilateral crackles and expiratory wheezes throughout all lung fields. After two nebulized albuterol/Atrovent treatments his arterial blood gas on room air showed pH 7.45, PCO₂ 36 mm Hg, PO₂ 56 mm Hg. Laboratory studies were notable for WBC 17.7 ×10³/µL; hemoglobin 15 g/dL, hematocrit 42 %; chemistry panel, CPK, and troponin were normal. Chest radiograph demonstrated a diffuse interstitial pattern. Serial acid‑fast bacilli tests and sputum cultures were negative for Mycobacterium, Pneumocystis, and Streptococcus pneumoniae.

Two days after admission the patient’s hypoxemia worsened, necessitating intubation and pressure ventilation. Fiberoptic bronchoscopy revealed bloody secretions; bronchoalveolar lavage fluid showed no particulate matter and no evidence of bacterial infection. A transesophageal echocardiogram showed normal left‑ventricular function (EF 65 %) without significant valvular disease and a trivial pericardial effusion. The patient did not improve with oral antibiotics and could not be weaned from ventilation.

2. Bacterial pneumonia contemplated; sputum cultures and AFB stains were negative for common pathogens. | "Serial AFB tests and sputum cultures were negative for mycobacterium, pneumocystis, and streptococcus pneumoniae."
3. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia considered; excluded by negative AFB, BAL, and histologic stains. | "BAL fluid showed no particulate matter or evidence of bacterial infection." and "Lung biopsy stains also conclusively ruled out ... pneumocystis ..."
4. Fungal infection entertained; histopathology did not reveal fungi. | "Lung biopsy stains also conclusively ruled out fungi..."
5. Asthma exacerbation evaluated; limited response to bronchodilators and progressive respiratory failure argued against isolated bronchospasm. | "He did not respond to oral antibiotics and made no progress in weaning off ventilation..."
6. Anti‑GBM (Goodpasture’s) disease supported by systemic renal findings (hematuria, proteinuria) and a positive anti‑GBM antibody with linear IgG/C3 deposition on renal and lung biopsy. | "At this time the patient tested positive for the anti‑GBM antibody and he was diagnosed with Goodpasture's syndrome." and "renal biopsy... demonstrated... linear immunofluorescence reactions (IgG, IgM, C3) on glomerular basement membranes."

case_analysis:

case_prompt:
A 5‑month‑old boy was admitted to the intensive‑care unit for respiratory insufficiency after three days of fever, cough, and worsening dyspnea. He had oral thrush, bilateral pulmonary rales, and hepatosplenomegaly. He was BCG‑vaccinated at birth and had a history of recurrent infections (conjunctivitis, otitis media, persistent oral thrush). There was no consanguinity; two maternal uncles had died of pneumonia in infancy.  

Chest radiograph showed absence of a thymus and bilateral pulmonary opacities. An immunologic panel confirmed severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID), later genotyped as an IL2RG missense mutation.  

Bronchoalveolar lavage yielded Candida albicans, Pneumocystis jiroveci, and acid‑fast bacilli. Abdominal ultrasound revealed an enlarged spleen containing multiple nodules.  
The clinical team initiated trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole and a four‑drug antituberculous regimen (isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, levofloxacin), along with antifungal prophylaxis and immunoglobulin replacement.

SCID predisposes to opportunistic infections, explaining the oral thrush, recurrent bacterial infections, and the presence of Candida, Pneumocystis, and acid‑fast bacilli in the BAL. | "He had been vaccinated at birth with BCG… The immunologic panel confirmed the hypothesis of SCID… The bronchoalveolar lavage was positive for Candida albicans, Pneumocystis jiroveci, and acid‑fast bacilli."

Alternative mycobacterial etiologies (e.g., Mycobacterium avium complex) were considered less likely because the patient had received a BCG vaccine and the clinical course fit BCG dissemination; definitive PCR later confirmed BCG. | "The BCG primer‑specific polymerase chain reaction quickly identified the infection by BCG…"

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case centers on pulmonary infection by Mycobacterium lentiflavum, a nontuberculous mycobacterium. This organism is not among the 21 SELECTED diseases; therefore the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.
2. Ideal Breakpoint: Include all clinical information up to, but not including, the definitive identification of the organism (the statement “Two months after hospitalization, the diagnosis of M. lentiflavum was obtained…”). This gives the learner enough data—persistent acid‑fast bacilli, negative PCR for M. tuberculosis/avium, scotochromogenic culture, susceptibility profile, exclusion of HIV, chronic granulomatous disease, and other pathogens—to deduce a nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary infection without revealing the exact species.

Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished the NTM infection from re‑activation tuberculosis (negative PCR), from Mycobacterium avium complex (negative PCR), from other bacterial/viral atypical pneumonias (negative serologies), from Pneumocystis carinii (negative cultures), and from immunodeficiency states (negative HIV, normal lymphocyte subsets, normal macrophage killing test). case_prompt:
In February 2000, a 67‑year‑old woman with a remote history of pulmonary tuberculosis 47 years earlier developed progressive dyspnea, productive cough, hemoptysis, weight loss, weakness, and low‑grade fever. Chest radiograph showed post‑tuberculous fibrodystrophy of the right upper lobe. Ziehl‑Neelsen smear was positive, and a nontuberculous mycobacterium was isolated. Drug‑susceptibility testing demonstrated sensitivity to rifampin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide and resistance to streptomycin and isoniazid; she received isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, and rifampin for three months without microbiologic change. Persistent acid‑fast bacilli and positive cultures were interpreted as colonization, and treatment was stopped.

In March 2002, she was admitted with worsening productive cough, dyspnea, hemoptysis, fever, and further weight loss. Repeat radiograph and CT revealed extensive reticulonodular changes and a new opacity in the left middle lobe. Sputum smear remained positive for acid‑fast bacilli; PCR specific for *M. tuberculosis* and *M. avium* DNA was negative, and routine mycobacterial cultures grew an unidentified scotochromogenic mycobacterium. HIV testing was negative, and lymphocyte subset analysis was normal. A macrophage killing test excluded chronic granulomatous disease. Cultures of sputum and broncholavage for routine bacteria and fungi, including *Pneumocystis carinii*, were negative. Serologic assays for *Chlamydia pneumoniae*, *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*, and *Legionella* spp. (including urinary antigens) were also negative. Susceptibility testing showed sensitivity to clarithromycin, ethambutol, isoniazid, streptomycin, rifabutin, cycloserine, and terizidon, with resistance to rifampin, amikacin, kanamycin, pyrazinamide, and ofloxacin. Clarithromycin therapy was started, leading to afebrile status after 10 days, modest radiographic improvement, and marked clinical recovery.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Reactivation pulmonary tuberculosis considered due to prior TB history and persistent AFB; excluded because PCR for *M. tuberculosis* DNA was negative. | "PCR specific for M. tuberculosis and M. avium DNA was negative"
2. Mycobacterium avium complex infection considered; excluded by the same negative PCR result for *M. avium*. | "PCR specific for M. tuberculosis and M. avium DNA was negative"
3. HIV‑associated immunodeficiency as a predisposing factor; excluded by a negative HIV test and normal lymphocyte subsets. | "HIV test ... was negative" and "Lymphocyte subsets by flow cytometry ... showed normal values"
4. Chronic granulomatous disease as a host defect; excluded by a normal macrophage killing test. | "a killing test ... was performed, and a diagnosis of chronic granulomatosis disease was excluded"
5. Other bacterial or fungal pathogens (including *Pneumocystis carinii*); excluded by negative sputum and broncholavage cultures. | "Cultures ... did not identify other pathogens"
6. Atypical bacterial pneumonias (*Chlamydia pneumoniae*, *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*, *Legionella* spp.); excluded by negative serologic and urinary antigen tests. | "Serologic tests ... produced negative results"
7. Drug‑resistant tuberculosis considered because of prior treatment; excluded by susceptibility profile showing sensitivity to rifampin (initially) but later resistance, and by PCR negativity for *M. tuberculosis*. | "susceptibility tests ... showed sensitivity to rifampin" and later "resistance to rifampin"
8. Nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary infection (unspecified); supported by persistent AFB positivity, isolation of a scotochromogenic mycobacterium, and clinical improvement after clarithromycin, which is active against many NTM. | "routine cultures for mycobacteria yielded unidentified scotochromogenic mycobacterium" and "treatment with clarithromycin was initiated" and "patient ... progressive improvement"

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case ultimately identifies cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection as the etiologic agent of pulmonary alveolar proteinosis. CMV is on the 21 SELECTED diseases list.
2. Best Breakpoint: Include all information up to the bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) findings (PAS‑positive material, lipid‑laden macrophage index 120) but stop before the laboratory result that confirms CMV (the indirect fluorescent antibody positivity and serum IgM/IgG). This provides sufficient clinical and pathologic data for a learner to infer a viral etiology (CMV) causing secondary PAP without revealing the definitive test.
3. Author's Analytic Distinctions: The authors excluded bacterial, fungal, mycobacterial, and Pneumocystis etiologies through negative cultures, special stains (GMS, Ziehl‑Neelsen), and lack of malignant cells; they highlighted the characteristic PAS‑positive alveolar proteinosis pattern and a markedly elevated lipid‑laden macrophage index, then confirmed CMV with specific immunofluorescence and serology, establishing causality.
case_prompt:
A 23‑month‑old girl was brought to the hospital with one week of worsening fevers, productive cough, and increased work of breathing. Over the preceding three months she had been treated repeatedly for presumed upper respiratory infections with inhaled β‑agonists, inhaled steroids, oral steroids, and several courses of oral antibiotics. Her past medical history was notable for prematurity, severe anemia requiring intra‑uterine transfusions, a diagnosis of congenital dyserythropoietic anemia type II at 20 months confirmed by bone‑marrow biopsy, and placement of a Port‑a‑Cath for chronic transfusions.

On presentation her temperature was 37.9 °C, heart rate 156 bpm, respiratory rate 50/min, oxygen saturation 83 % on room air (improved to 98 % on 1 L/min nasal cannula), and blood pressure 115/61 mm Hg. She was in mild distress with increased work of breathing. Physical examination revealed moderate frontal bossing, an open anterior fontanelle, a II/IV systolic ejection murmur, diffuse bilateral rales without wheezing, hepatomegaly (liver 4 cm below the costal margin) and splenomegaly (palpable to the umbilicus). No clubbing, cyanosis, or peripheral edema were noted.

Chest radiograph demonstrated diffuse ground‑glass alveolar infiltrates that were chronic compared with a film obtained one year earlier. Blood, urine, and respiratory cultures were obtained, and empirical therapy with oral azithromycin and intravenous ceftriaxone was initiated.

By day 3, transthoracic echocardiography showed a patent foramen ovale but no cardiomyopathy; abdominal ultrasound confirmed hepatosplenomegaly. A repeat chest X‑ray was unchanged, and a chest CT was offered but declined by the parents.

Despite four days of antibiotics the patient continued to have intermittent fevers and required supplemental oxygen; chest radiographs remained unchanged. Bronchoscopy on day 5 revealed normal airway anatomy. The bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid was cloudy, without evidence of aspiration or malignant cells. Special stains were negative for Pneumocystis jirovecii (GMS) and acid‑fast bacilli (Ziehl‑Neelsen). Cultures of BAL fluid for bacteria, fungi, AFB, RSV, and influenza yielded no growth. Differential cell count of the BAL fluid showed 68 % macrophages, 12 % polymorphonuclear leukocytes, and 10 % lymphocytes. Light microscopy with periodic acid‑Schiff (PAS) stain demonstrated abundant amorphous material within pulmonary macrophages and in larger extracellular aggregates, suggestive of pulmonary alveolar proteinosis. The lipid‑laden macrophage index was 120.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial pneumonia considered due to fever, cough, infiltrates, but cultures of blood, urine, and BAL were negative and the patient did not improve after 4 days of ceftriaxone and azithromycin. | "Despite 4 days of antibiotics, the patient continued to spike intermittent fevers and was still on oxygen treatment, and there still were no changes on chest radiograph."
2. Viral pneumonia (non‑CMV) entertained given persistent fever and immunocompromised state, yet initial viral cultures (RSV, influenza) from BAL were negative and no specific viral test had been performed. | "Fungal, bacterial, AFB, RSV, and influenza cultures of BAL fluid revealed no growth."
3. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia considered because of immunocompromise and diffuse infiltrates; ruled out by negative GMS stain. | "Grocott's methenamine silver (GMS) stain was negative for Pneumocystis jirovecii."
4. Mycobacterial (tuberculosis) infection considered given chronic infiltrates and hepatosplenomegaly; excluded by negative Ziehl‑Neelsen stain and lack of AFB growth. | "Ziehl‑Neelsen stain was negative for acid‑fast bacilli (AFB)."
5. Fungal infection considered; excluded by negative fungal cultures and stains. | "Fungal … cultures of BAL fluid revealed no growth."
6. Aspiration pneumonitis considered because of cloudy BAL fluid, but no evidence of aspiration material or malignant cells was seen. | "BAL fluid was cloudy in appearance and revealed no evidence of aspiration or malignant cells."
7. Malignancy (leukemia or lymphoma) considered given hepatosplenomegaly and systemic symptoms; excluded by lack of malignant cells in BAL and normal peripheral counts (not detailed but implied). | "BAL fluid ... revealed no evidence of … malignant cells."
8. Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP) identified by PAS‑positive proteinaceous material within macrophages and a high lipid‑laden macrophage index, establishing a pattern consistent with PAP. | "PAS stain was positive for abundant amorphous material within the pulmonary macrophages … suggesting pulmonary alveolar proteinosis … The lipid‑laden macrophage (LLM) index was 120."
9. Cytomegalovirus infection identified as the cause of secondary PAP after specific testing; CMV is a known viral trigger of PAP in immunocompromised hosts. | "BAL fluid was positive for cytomegalovirus (CMV) by indirect fluorescent antibody testing and serum CMV IgG and IgM antibodies were detected."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case’s final diagnosis is idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis, which is not among the 21 SELECTED diseases list; therefore the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.
2. Best Breakpoint: Include presentation, history, physical exam, initial labs, imaging (CXR, HRCT), pulmonary function tests, BAL findings, and mention that a VATS biopsy was performed, but stop before reporting the pathologic results that revealed idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors ruled out infectious etiologies (negative cultures, PCR, BAL stains), autoimmune vasculitides (negative ANA, ENA, ANCA, anti‑GBM), TB (negative skin test), HIV and hepatitis (negative serologies), gastrointestinal sources of hemorrhage (negative endoscopy/colon), and neoplastic or granulomatous disease (absence of lesions on biopsy). Persistence of diffuse alveolar hemorrhage with hemosiderin‑laden macrophages and exclusion of all known causes led to the diagnosis of idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis.
case_prompt:
A 27‑year‑old Greek man presented to the pulmonary outpatient clinic with relapsing fever spikes up to 38.7 °C, generalized fatigue, and discomfort. Earlier oral antibiotics (β‑lactam plus macrolide) had failed, and he was transferred for further evaluation. Two years prior he had been hospitalized for fever of unknown origin, which improved with high‑dose corticosteroids, though the cause was never determined. He was a light smoker (5 pack‑years) with no drug use or known environmental exposures.

On examination he was febrile, otherwise well‑appearing, without dyspnea (respiratory rate 12/min) or tachycardia (HR 70 bpm). Arterial PO₂ was 84 mm Hg. No clubbing, skin lesions, lymphadenopathy, or joint swelling were noted. Lung auscultation revealed mild end‑inspiratory crackles in both lower zones; other systems were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed microcytic iron‑deficiency anemia (Hct 35.9 %, Hgb 11.9 g/dL, MCV 69.7 fL, Fe 19 mg/dL) with normal ferritin, B12, folate, white blood cell count, liver and renal panels, and CRP. ESR was elevated at 65 mm/h. Urinalysis was normal, and 24‑hour protein excretion was 60 mg/dL. Chest X‑ray demonstrated bilateral lower‑lobe alveolar infiltrates. He received intravenous piperacillin‑tazobactam, moxifloxacin, and a brief course of oseltamivir (stopped after a negative H1N1 sputum smear).

Autoimmune serologies (ANA, ENA, ANCA, anti‑GBM) were negative; tuberculin skin test, HIV, hepatitis B and C serologies were also negative. A positive stool Mayer test for blood prompted endoscopic evaluation, but gastroscopy and colonoscopy with biopsies showed no evidence of inflammatory bowel disease, malignancy, or celiac disease (negative anti‑tTG IgA/IgG).

Pulmonary function testing revealed normal volumes with a markedly elevated DLCO (120 % predicted), suggestive of alveolar hemorrhage. High‑resolution CT of the chest showed diffuse bibasilar ground‑glass opacities consistent with alveolar hemorrhage. Bronchoalveolar lavage identified abundant hemosiderin‑laden macrophages (>40 % of cells) while cultures and stains for bacteria, mycobacteria, fungi, viruses, and Pneumocystis were negative.

Because his condition worsened with increasing dyspnea, rising ESR and CRP, and falling hemoglobin, a video‑assisted thoracoscopic (VATS) lung biopsy from the right middle lobe was performed to further investigate the cause of the hemorrhage.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Infectious pneumonia considered due to fever and infiltrates but excluded by lack of clinical response to broad‑spectrum antibiotics and negative cultures/stains. | "He was initially treated with a course of oral antibiotics... with poor clinical response." and "BAL fluid specimens were negative for routine bacterial, mycobacterial, fungal, and viral as well as Pneumocystis stains and cultures."
2. Influenza H1N1 infection evaluated and excluded after negative sputum PCR. | "sputum smear was negative for H1N1."
3. Tuberculosis considered given pulmonary infiltrates; excluded by negative tuberculin skin test and negative BAL for mycobacteria. | "The tuberculin skin test was negative."
4. HIV‑related opportunistic infection ruled out by negative HIV serology. | "His HIV test was also negative."
5. Hepatitis B/C‑related vasculitis excluded by normal antibody titers. | "his hepatitis B and C antibody titers were within normal range."
6. Autoimmune vasculitis (ANCA‑associated, anti‑GBM, collagen vascular disease) considered because of diffuse alveolar hemorrhage but excluded by negative ANA, ENA, ANCA, and anti‑GBM antibodies. | "Laboratory tests for collagen vascular disease and vasculitis, including ANA, ENA, ANCA, and anti‑GBM antibodies, were also negative."
7. Inflammatory bowel disease as a source of pulmonary hemorrhage considered after positive stool blood test, but endoscopic biopsies showed no IBD, malignancy, or celiac disease. | "positive Mayer stool test for erythrocytes... gastroduodenal biopsies were performed and findings were inconsistent with both inflammatory bowel disease and malignancy as well as celiac disease."
8. Malignancy or granulomatous disease considered but excluded by lack of lesions on imaging and, later, by biopsy showing no granulomas (though biopsy results are beyond the breakpoint, the decision to biopsy reflects the need to exclude these entities). | "Extensive pathologic evaluation of the lung specimen divulged... absence of any specific pathology such as granulomas or evidence of vasculitis/capillaritis."
9. Drug‑induced pulmonary hemorrhage unlikely due to absent exposure history to illicit drugs, toxins, or occupational fumes. | "He reported no exposure to illicit drugs, environmental, and occupational allergens or toxic fumes, chemicals, and dust."
10. Idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis remained as diagnosis of exclusion after all above causes were ruled out and BAL showed abundant hemosiderin‑laden macrophages consistent with alveolar hemorrhage. | "BAL demonstrating increased numbers of hemosiderin‑laden macrophages (>40 % of total number of macrophages)."

case_analysis:

case_prompt:
A 66‑year‑old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus was referred to hematology after a colonoscopy performed for symptomatic anemia. Following the procedure she developed melena, hematuria, extensive subcutaneous hemorrhage, and a retroperitoneal hematoma. Specific coagulation studies demonstrated a strong factor VIII inhibitor (234 BU) and a residual factor VIII activity of <1 % (reference 50‑150 %). Initial management consisted of high‑dose oral prednisone 50 mg daily and cyclophosphamide 100 mg daily. After three weeks there was no improvement in APTT, inhibitor level, or factor VIII activity, prompting initiation of four weekly infusions of rituximab 375 mg/m². Six weeks after starting rituximab, the APTT, inhibitor titer, and factor VIII activity began to improve, and by five months after rituximab the APTT and factor VIII levels had normalized.

case_prompt:
A 64‑year‑old man was evaluated after an acute cerebrovascular accident. He had no prior symptoms. Past medical history was notable for hyperlipidemia; he smoked 20 cigarettes per day and drank alcohol occasionally. Medications were omeprazole and atorvastatin. Physical examination revealed only a few basal rales on pulmonary auscultation.

Laboratory studies showed mild hypoproteinemia, hypercholesterolemia, and markedly elevated angiotensin‑converting enzyme (ACE) at 83 U/L (reference ≤ 55 U/L). Complete blood count, renal, hepatic, and thyroid panels, serum protein electrophoresis, immunoglobulin levels, serum free light chains, β₂‑microglobulin, antinuclear antibodies, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate were all within normal limits. Urine analysis demonstrated increased immunoglobulin light chains, predominantly λ (2.8 mg/dL; normal ≤ 0.39 mg/dL). Echocardiography revealed left‑ventricular hypertrophy with preserved ejection fraction. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed a restrictive pattern with diffuse infiltrative cardiomyopathy and marked subendocardial wall thickening of both ventricles.

Given suspicion for a systemic infiltrative disease, an abdominal subcutaneous flat biopsy was performed and was normal. Subsequently, a bronchoscopic biopsy with bronchoalveolar lavage was obtained; the lavage specimens were stained and cultured to exclude Pneumocystis jirovecii and mycobacterial infection.

case_prompt:
A 55‑year‑old woman from Guyana with a 10‑year history of seropositive rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and prior latent tuberculosis (incomplete isoniazid, completed 4‑month rifampin) presented with worsening respiratory symptoms. Her RA had been refractory to methotrexate 20 mg weekly, hydroxychloroquine 400 mg daily, and chronic prednisone (10–20 mg daily). Leflunomide caused severe alopecia, and adalimumab failed to improve disease and produced a rash 7 years earlier. She was then placed on weekly subcutaneous etanercept 50 mg, achieving good joint control for 3 years without pulmonary or mediastinal abnormalities on chest CT; etanercept was stopped 3 years ago because of insurance issues.

Three years later she developed cough and dyspnea. Laboratory studies showed ESR 40 mm/h, CRP 1.35 mg/dL, negative ANA, hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL, WBC 10.3 K/µL, platelets 296 K/µL, and normal renal and hepatic panels. High‑resolution CT revealed bilateral lower‑lobe ground‑glass opacities. Echocardiography was normal. Methotrexate was discontinued, after which her cough and shortness of breath improved. Bronchoscopy showed no endobronchial lesions; bronchial lavage cultures for bacteria, fungi, mycobacteria, and pneumocystis were negative, and cytology was negative for malignancy. Transbronchial biopsy demonstrated focal emphysematous changes and mild interstitial pneumonitis.

Given active RA, prednisone was increased to 10 mg twice daily and etanercept 50 mg weekly was restarted. Her arthritis improved, and prednisone was tapered to 5 mg every other day. After 12 months of etanercept therapy, repeat HRCT showed resolution of the ground‑glass opacities but newly enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes measuring 2.3 × 3.1 cm. Mediastinoscopy was performed and revealed enlarged right anterior lymph nodes.

Sarcoidosis induced by TNF‑α inhibitor (etanercept) considered after development of mediastinal lymphadenopathy despite prior radiographic improvement, and was confirmed by non‑necrotizing epithelioid granulomas with negative infectious studies. | "Tissue biopsy showed nonnecrotizing epithelioid granulomata." and "All infectious studies of lymph node tissues were negative."

case_prompt:

case_prompt:

She denied respiratory infection symptoms, had no relevant occupational or environmental exposures, and had quit smoking ten years earlier (ten‑pack‑year history). On hospital day 2 his dyspnea worsened with hypoxemia requiring supplemental oxygen. A non‑contrast volumetric chest CT showed diffuse micronodules with central cavitation and bronchial wall thickening, described as “most suspicious for mycobacterial or fungal infection” and notably “no ground glass opacities.” Based on these imaging findings, the team discontinued PCP therapy, initiated anti‑tuberculosis treatment, and consulted pulmonary services for bronchoscopy.

Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid from the right middle lobe contained 87 % histiocytes, 6 % neutrophils, 4 % lymphocytes, and 3 % eosinophils. Routine cultures of bronchial washings were negative. On hospital day 5 his respiratory status worsened, requiring non‑invasive positive‑pressure ventilation, and cyclophosphamide 500 mg was administered intravenously.

A 25‑year‑old man with no prior medical history presented to the emergency department in November 2018 with sudden onset of psychotic symptoms (paranoid delusions, auditory hallucinations, marked anxiety) accompanied by fever, cough, and generalized asthenia. He had returned ten days earlier from a one‑week trip to Greece and reported unprotected sexual contact with a man two months before and during travel.  

On admission he was febrile (38.5 °C) and exhibited pharyngitis, oral candidiasis, and a skin rash. Laboratory studies showed elevated C‑reactive protein (18 mg/L), mild anemia (hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL) with low reticulocytes (37 × 10⁹/L), lymphopenia (500 cells/µL), neutropenia (600 cells/µL), and thrombocytopenia (90 × 10⁹/L). HIV‑1 serology was positive, confirmed by immunoblot, with a viral load of 5.47 × 10⁶ copies/mL and CD4⁺ count of 90 cells/µL. Neuroleptic (cyamemazine, risperidone) and benzodiazepine therapy were started for psychosis and anxiety, and the patient was transferred to the infectious diseases service.  

Two weeks after symptom onset, repeat HIV viral load was 6.85 × 10⁶ copies/mL with CD4⁺ count of 30 cells/µL and global lymphopenia (including CD8⁺ and NK cells). The immunoblot displayed gp120 and gp41 reactivity with weak ambiguous p24/p31 bands, a pattern compatible with acute primary infection; the patient had never been screened for HIV before. A review of records showed a normal lymphocyte count a year earlier. His recent partner was concurrently diagnosed with HIV.  

Lumbar puncture, EEG, and brain MRI were unremarkable. Thoraco‑abdominal and pelvic CT demonstrated homogeneous hepatosplenomegaly and several interstitial pulmonary lesions (micronodules and reticulations). Sputum cultures and bronchoalveolar lavage were negative for Pneumocystis jirovecii and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Serologies for hepatitis A, B, C, E, toxoplasmosis, and syphilis were negative; EBV and CMV viral loads were undetectable. Genotypic testing identified an HIV‑1 CRF19‑cpx strain.  

Combination antiretroviral therapy (tenofovir, emtricitabine, raltegravir) was initiated two weeks after diagnosis, and cotrimoxazole prophylaxis for Pneumocystis pneumonia was started. Despite cART and neuroleptic treatment, psychotic symptoms, fever, chills, and sweats persisted, and the patient developed bilateral muscle rigidity. He required intensive care, and a neuroleptic malignant syndrome was diagnosed; extrapyramidal signs resolved after discontinuation of neuroleptics, yet fever and night sweats continued.  

Laboratory reassessment revealed worsening pancytopenia (hemoglobin 7.0 g/dL, platelets 50 × 10⁹/L, neutrophils 600 cells/µL), hyperferritinemia, elevated transaminases, and mildly increased triglycerides. The team hypothesized hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) triggered by acute primary HIV infection. Sternal bone‑marrow aspiration showed macrophage activation without overt hemophagocytosis; stains for Leishmania were negative, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex PCR was negative. An empiric course of intravenous immunoglobulin (1 g/kg for 2 days) was given without clinical improvement.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Acute primary HIV infection considered as trigger of HLH | "We hypothesized that the patient had a hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) triggered by an acute primary HIV infection."
2. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome entertained because of rigidity and fever after neuroleptic use | "A neuroleptic malignant syndrome was diagnosed, and extrapyramidal syndrome recovered after stopping neuroleptic treatment."
3. Opportunistic infections (Pneumocystis jirovecii, Mycobacterium tuberculosis) investigated due to HIV and pulmonary findings; ruled out by negative sputum cultures and BAL | "Sputum cultures and bronchoalveolar lavage showed no Pneumocystis nor tuberculosis infection."
4. Viral co‑infections (HBV, HCV, HAV, HEV, EBV, CMV, toxoplasmosis, syphilis) excluded by serology and undetectable viral loads | "No co‑infection with HAV, HBV, HCV, HEV, toxoplasmosis nor syphilis was found. EBV and CMV viral loads were undetectable."
5. Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis remained plausible because of fever, cytopenias, hyperferritinemia, organomegaly | "blood tests showed worsening pancytopenia...hyperferritinemia...We hypothesized that the patient had a hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH)..."
6. Bone‑marrow aspiration provided evidence of macrophage activation but no hemophagocytosis and no Leishmania, reducing likelihood of Leishmania at that stage | "Sternal bone marrow aspiration was performed showing signs of macrophages activation without hemophagocytosis. No Leishmania was found on bone marrow aspirate smears..."
7. Empiric intravenous immunoglobulin administered for presumed immune‑mediated HLH, lack of response suggested an infectious trigger not addressed | "An empiric treatment with intravenous immunoglobulins 1 g/kg for 2 days was administered; no clinical response was observed."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient ultimately developed a Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP), which is on the SELECTED diseases list (pneumocystis). Although the original case report focuses on diffuse large B‑cell lymphoma (out‑of‑scope), the secondary opportunistic infection meets the criteria for a SELECTED disease and can be isolated as the mystery diagnosis.
2. Breakpoint: End the case presentation after the decision to send a blood sample for next‑generation sequencing (NGS) to identify the pathogen, but before the NGS result is disclosed. At this point, readers have the clinical picture (severe neutropenia, respiratory failure, CT findings, positive β‑D‑glucan, negative sputum for hyphae) that allow deduction of PCP without revealing the definitive test.
3. Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished PCP from bacterial pneumonia (lack of response to piperacillin‑tazobactam), from invasive fungal disease (negative sputum for hyphae, limited response to voriconazole), and confirmed the diagnosis with NGS. These points will guide the reasoning steps.
case_prompt: A 53‑year‑old married woman with diabetes was admitted for diffuse large B‑cell lymphoma involving the central nervous system. After six cycles of chemotherapy she developed severe myelosuppression with a white blood cell count of 300 mm³. She then experienced fulminant respiratory failure accompanied by low‑grade fever and dry cough. Empiric therapy with piperacillin‑tazobactam showed no clinical improvement. A chest CT scan demonstrated pulmonary consolidation in the lower lobes surrounded by extensive ground‑glass opacities on both sides. A β‑D‑glucan assay was positive, and sputum microscopy was negative for hyphae and spores. The patient required mechanical ventilation in the intensive care unit and was treated with broad‑spectrum antibiotics, voriconazole, trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole, and adjunctive dexamethasone. Because of the unclear etiology, a blood sample was sent for next‑generation sequencing (NGS) to detect potential pathogens.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Severe neutropenia predisposes to opportunistic infections, especially Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. | "she experienced severe myelosuppression and had an extremely low white cell count (300/mm3)."
2. The pattern of diffuse ground‑glass opacities with peripheral consolidations on CT is classic for PCP. | "CT lung screening revealed pulmonary consolidation in the inferior lobes surrounded by a wide range of ground‑glass opacity effusions on both sides."
3. Positive β‑D‑glucan supports a fungal or Pneumocystis infection, while sputum negative for hyphae makes invasive aspergillosis unlikely. | "The beta‑D‑glucan assay test was positive and the sputum sample was negative for hyphae and spores."
4. Lack of clinical response to piperacillin‑tazobactam argues against typical bacterial pneumonia. | "Piperacillin‑tazobactam treatment had no therapeutic efficacy."
5. Empiric voriconazole (targeting invasive fungi) did not lead to rapid improvement, reducing the likelihood of other fungal pathogens. | "several broad‑spectrum antibiotics, and antifungal therapy with voriconazole and trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole (TMP‑SMX) were also added."
6. NGS identified Pneumocystis DNA, confirming the diagnosis. | "The results confirmed a PCP infection, and we increased the dose of TMP‑SMX."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case concludes with a diagnosis of Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection (with associated ARDS and cold‑agglutinin hemolysis). Mycoplasma pneumoniae is not among the 21 SELECTED diseases, therefore the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.  
2. Breakpoint: End the presentation just before the BAL microbiology result that identified Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Include the initial presentation, negative SARS‑CoV‑2 and other pathogen PCRs, imaging findings, clinical deterioration, ICU course, and the laboratory evidence of hemolysis with cold agglutinins. Exclude the sentence stating that BAL was positive for Mycoplasma.  
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors ruled out COVID‑19, influenza, TB, Legionella, typical bacterial pathogens, and Pneumocystis by negative PCR/BAL cultures and by imaging patterns inconsistent with COVID‑19. They then highlighted hemolysis with cold agglutinins as a classic clue for Mycoplasma infection, confirmed by positive BAL PCR, leading to targeted antimicrobial therapy and rapid clinical improvement.
case_prompt:
On 14 March 2020 a 36‑year‑old man presented to the emergency unit with fever, dry cough, and head and limb aches that began three days earlier. He was otherwise healthy, having completed a half‑marathon the week before. On admission he had reduced general condition and shortness of breath; auscultation revealed crackles in the right upper lobe. SARS‑CoV‑2 infection was suspected, and he was admitted to the ICU. Initial microbiological sampling and chest imaging were performed. Empiric antibiotics (piperacillin/tazobactam and clarithromycin) were started. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for SARS‑CoV‑2 was negative, as were the results for influenza, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and Legionella spp. After two days, because inflammatory markers remained elevated and the patient worsened, antibiotic therapy was escalated to meropenem, linezolid, and fosfomycin. Chest CT showed a diffuse interstitial reticular pattern, multilobular patchy ground‑glass opacification, and consolidation of the right upper lobe.

The patient required high‑flow oxygen for a week, then was intubated with a PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio of 130. Despite proning, his respiratory status declined (PaO₂/FiO₂ 108, hypercapnia, respiratory acidosis), and vasopressor support increased. On 22 March the ECMO team was consulted for possible transfer. Review of laboratory and imaging findings led the team to abandon the COVID‑19 hypothesis and to suspect atypical pneumonia. Meropenem was continued (monitored by serum levels) and clarithromycin was re‑added.

Laboratory studies on admission revealed elevated bilirubin and lactate dehydrogenase, low haptoglobin, and macrocytic hyper‑regenerative anemia with hemoglobin 5.3 g/dL (scvO₂ 67%), indicating hemolysis. A Coombs’ test was positive for cold agglutinins. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was performed for microbiological sampling and to further evaluate for SARS‑CoV‑2 infection.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. COVID‑19 initially considered due to fever, cough, and ground‑glass opacities; excluded because PCR was negative and imaging later described “mainly right‑sided pneumonia, not typical for COVID‑19” | “Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for SARS‑CoV‑2 was negative… Imaging showed mainly right‑sided pneumonia, not typical for COVID‑19, and the hypothesis of COVID‑19 was abandoned.”
2. Influenza, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and Legionella spp. considered; excluded by negative PCR panels | “PCR for SARS‑CoV‑2 was negative, as were the results for influenza, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and Legionella spp.”
3. Typical bacterial pneumonia (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae) considered; excluded by negative BAL cultures and atypical radiographic pattern | “Microbiological results from a BAL … were negative for … Streptococcus pneumoniae.”
4. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia considered in severe respiratory failure; excluded by negative BAL PCR | “Microbiological results … were negative for Pneumocystis jirovecii.”
5. Atypical pneumonia suspected; hemolysis with cold agglutinins pointed toward Mycoplasma pneumoniae, which was confirmed by BAL PCR | “Coombs' test revealed cold agglutinins the same day.” and “Microbiological results … were … positive for Mycoplasma (M.) pneumoniae.”

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case’s definitive pathogen identified on tissue biopsy is Pneumocystis jiroveci, which corresponds to “pneumocystis” on the 21 SELECTED diseases list. Therefore, the target diagnosis is pneumocystis (PCP).  
2. Best Breakpoint: Stop the case presentation just before the core‑needle biopsy pathology result that confirms Pneumocystis. Include all data up to the bronchoscopy findings, the negative BAL/culture results, the restart of TMP/SMX for presumed nocardiosis, and the sinus CT, but exclude the sentence describing organisms morphologically consistent with Pneumocystis on GMS stain. This gives students enough clinical, radiologic, and microbiologic information to generate and prioritize a differential without revealing the definitive diagnosis.  
3. Key Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished PCP from bacterial pneumonia, tuberculosis, nocardiosis, and malignancy by (a) negative bacterial cultures and AFB smears, (b) lack of response to broad‑spectrum antibiotics, (c) persistence of fever despite initial TMP/SMX discontinuation, (d) negative cytology for malignancy, and (e) ultimate histopathologic identification of organisms on GMS stain, which ruled in PCP and ruled out the other considerations.
case_prompt:
A 51‑year‑old woman was admitted with three weeks of cough—initially dry then producing a small amount of clear sputum—and six days of subjective fevers, chills, and dyspnea on exertion. She reported worsening malaise, fatigue, and dyspnea the day before admission. Past medical history was significant for HIV infection diagnosed two years earlier (CD4 count 220 cells/µL two months prior), cervical dysplasia treated with cone biopsy, and chronic anemia. She denied recent travel or sick contacts and was on lamivudine/zidovudine plus lopinavir/ritonavir; TMP/SMX 800/160 mg three times weekly was being taken for PCP prophylaxis.

On examination she was febrile 102 °F, pulse 84 beats/min, respirations 22/min, blood pressure 86/50 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 99 % on room air. Lung fields were clear with bilateral breath sounds; no lymphadenopathy was appreciated. Laboratory studies showed LDH 217 U/L (reference 100‑190), albumin 2.0 g/dL, hemoglobin 10.7 g/dL, white blood cell count 7.9 ×10³/µL (71 % neutrophils, 16 % lymphocytes, 12 % monocytes, 0.4 % eosinophils, 0.8 % basophils).

Chest CT demonstrated subcarinal, prevascular, and right hilar lymphadenopathy; numerous bilateral pulmonary masses and nodules, the largest a cavitating lesion in the left upper lobe measuring 4.2 × 4.2 cm, and a second mass at the right cardiophrenic angle (2.2 × 4.6 cm). Bilateral pleural effusions with compressive atelectasis of the lower lobes and left apical fibrosis were also noted.

The patient was admitted with “pneumonia of uncertain etiology,” placed on airborne isolation for tuberculosis, and started on ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily, azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, and TMP/SMX 2 double‑strength tablets orally every 8 hours. Sputum Gram stain and bacterial culture, three acid‑fast bacilli smears, and a purified protein derivative test were negative. She remained intermittently febrile (101‑102 °F) for four days, then became afebrile and reported nausea/vomiting attributed to TMP/SMX, leading to its discontinuation.

Five days after admission, fiberoptic bronchoscopy was performed. Airways appeared normal; bronchoalveolar lavage of the lingula and five transbronchial biopsies of the left upper lobe were obtained. All cultures and smears were negative, and cytology was negative for malignancy and for PCP. TMP/SMX was stopped, while azithromycin and ceftriaxone were continued. Three days later, fever and malaise recurred; because nocardiosis was suspected, TMP/SMX was restarted. A head CT showed disease of the maxillary, frontal, and ethmoid sinuses but no other pathology.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial pneumonia considered due to cough and fever; empiric ceftriaxone and azithromycin were started, but lack of clinical improvement and negative sputum cultures argued against it. | "Sputum Gram stain and bacterial culture ... were negative."
2. Tuberculosis entertained because of cavitary lung lesion and lymphadenopathy; patient was placed on airborne isolation, yet three AFB smears and a PPD test were negative. | "Sputum Gram stain and bacterial culture, 3 Acid-Fast Bacilli sputum smears and purified protein derivative testing were negative."
3. Nocardiosis was suspected after recurrence of fever following TMP/SMX discontinuation, prompting its re‑initiation, but there was no microbiologic evidence from bronchoscopy or cultures to support it. | "Because of suspicion for nocardiosis, TMP/SMX was restarted."
4. Pulmonary malignancy considered given multiple masses and nodules; transbronchial biopsies and cytology were performed but showed no malignant cells. | "Cytology was negative for malignancy and PCP."
5. Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia remained in the differential because the patient was HIV‑positive with a CD4 count near the typical risk threshold, had diffuse pulmonary nodules, and responded clinically to TMP/SMX re‑challenge, despite negative BAL cytology. | "She became afebrile and ... improved after TMP/SMX was restarted."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case’s principal diagnosis is drug‑induced pneumonitis, which is not included in the 21 SELECTED diseases list → OUT_OF_SCOPE.
2. Ideal Breakpoint: Present the case up to the point where imaging shows new ground‑glass opacities and the infectious/autoimmune work‑up is reported negative, but before the authors state “she was started on IV methylprednisolone with an empirical diagnosis of drug induced pneumonitis.”
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors excluded bacterial, mycobacterial, fungal, viral and pneumocystis infections with cultures and PCR; they excluded connective‑tissue disease with serologies; they contrasted the new GGOs with prior subpleural metastases to argue for acute interstitial lung disease rather than tumour progression; finally, the temporal association with palbociclib therapy led them to label the process as drug‑induced pneumonitis.
case_prompt:
A 67‑year‑old post‑menopausal woman with hormone‑positive metastatic breast cancer diagnosed in February 2019 (multiple bony metastases and bilateral subpleural lung metastases <1 cm) had undergone fixation of a pathological femoral fracture. Her past history included well‑controlled hypertension and asymptomatic bronchiectasis diagnosed two years earlier. She was receiving zoledronic acid, palbociclib, and letrozole, with marked reduction of the breast lesion and improvement of bone pain.

Four months after initiating palbociclib, she developed a dry, non‑productive cough and worsening exertional dyspnea without fever. She was non‑neutropenic and had normal renal and hepatic function. Arterial blood gas demonstrated hypoxaemia consistent with type 1 respiratory failure. High‑resolution CT of the thorax, compared with baseline imaging, revealed multiple new patchy and confluent ground‑glass opacities throughout both lungs, described as suggestive of acute interstitial lung disease.

A comprehensive work‑up was performed. Blood and sputum cultures for bacteria, mycobacteria, and fungi were negative, and PCR testing for viruses and mycobacteria was also negative. Serologic testing for connective‑tissue disease—including ANA, anti‑dsDNA, rheumatoid factor, and anti‑CCP—was negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial, mycobacterial, fungal, viral, or pneumocystis pneumonia was considered but excluded because “blood and sputum cultures was negative for bacterial, mycobacterial, fungal infections, influenza and pneumocystis carinii.”  
2. Connective‑tissue disease–related interstitial lung disease was considered but ruled out as “Serological workup for underlying connective tissue disorder ... was also negative.”  
3. Progression of metastatic breast cancer to the lungs was considered; however, the imaging showed “multiple new patchy and confluent ground glass opacities (GGOs) in bilateral lung fields, suggestive of acute interstitial lung disease (ILD)” which differs from the prior stable subpleural metastases.  
4. Drug‑induced pneumonitis from palbociclib was deemed most likely given the temporal relationship with drug initiation and exclusion of other causes, leading to an empirical diagnosis of drug‑induced pneumonitis.

1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case describes infection with human coronavirus HKU1, which is not among the 21 SELECTED diseases. Therefore the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.

case_prompt: A 67‑year‑old woman with arterial hypertension, type II diabetes, thyroidectomy, osteoporosis, hyperlipidemia, and rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate and corticosteroids presented in August 2019 with progressive dyspnea at rest and fatigue over the past two days. Examination showed an afebrile patient with crackles throughout both lung fields. Blood pressure was 100/80 mmHg, heart rate 120 beats/min, oxygen saturation 79 % on room air, and temperature 36.5 °C. ECG demonstrated sinus tachycardia. Arterial blood gas on room air revealed pO₂ 40 mmHg, pCO₂ 35 mmHg, pH 7.48, HCO₃⁻ 29.2 mmol/L. Chest radiograph displayed patchy diffuse infiltrates, predominately in the left lower lobe. CBC was normal; biochemistry was unremarkable except for LDH 311 U/L (normal < 225), glucose 263 mg/dL (normal 60‑100), and CRP 122.3 mg/L (normal < 6). Urinalysis was normal. RT‑PCR for Influenza A and B from nasopharyngeal/oropharyngeal samples was negative. Urinary antigen tests for Legionella pneumophila and Streptococcus pneumoniae, serology for Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and blood cultures were all negative. The patient received 60 % oxygen via Venturi mask and empirical IV ceftriaxone, azithromycin, and trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole. After two days she deteriorated, required intubation, and was transferred to the ICU. Chest CT showed diffuse ground‑glass opacities in all lung fields and bilateral pleural effusions. Echocardiography demonstrated normal ejection fraction and valve function. Bronchoscopy with bronchial washings and BAL from the lingula and right middle lobe was performed; cytologic and microbiologic studies of the specimens were negative. Direct immunofluorescence and PCR for Pneumocystis jirovecii in BAL were negative and trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole was stopped.

1. Bacterial pneumonia (Legionella, Streptococcus pneumoniae) was considered given diffuse infiltrates, but urinary antigen tests were negative. | “Urinary antigen tests for Legionella pneumophila and Streptococcus pneumoniae … were negative.”
2. Atypical bacterial pneumonia (Mycoplasma) was evaluated, yet serologic testing was negative. | “Serological testing for Mycoplasma pneumonia … were negative.”
3. Influenza infection was a potential cause of acute respiratory failure, but RT‑PCR for Influenza A and B returned negative. | “RTau‑PCR test for Influenza A and B … were negative.”
4. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia was high on the differential because of immunosuppression, but direct immunofluorescence and PCR on BAL were negative, leading to discontinuation of trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole. | “Direct immunofluorescence and PCR for Pneumocystis jirovecii in BAL were negative and administration of trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole was discontinued.”
5. Broad‑range bacterial and fungal cultures of bronchial washings and BAL were unrevealing, further lowering the likelihood of a conventional infectious etiology. | “Cytological and microbiological examination of bronchial washings and BAL was negative.”
6. Multiplex respiratory virus panel performed on BAL identified human coronavirus HKU1 as the sole pathogen, correlating with the clinical picture and explaining recovery without pathogen‑specific therapy. | “Respiratory virus panel test … revealed HCoV‑HKU1.”

1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case’s definitive diagnosis is Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, which belongs to the SELECTED disease list (“pneumocystis”).
2. Best Breakpoint: End the prompt after describing the patient’s worsening respiratory status and the decision to obtain bronchoscopy, but before reporting the BAL results that confirmed P. jirovecii. case_prompt:
A 17‑year‑old male kidney‑transplant recipient presented with a one‑week history of subfebrile temperature, dry cough, and dyspnea on exertion, accompanied by generalized fatigue for over three weeks and a 4‑kg weight loss. On examination he was tachycardic (128 bpm), SpO₂ 89% on room air, required 2–3 L/min oxygen to maintain saturation >92%, and had a temperature of 37.2 °C. Blood pressure was 124/80 mmHg. A dry, maculopapular rash was noted on the upper trunk and neck, and fungal changes of the toenails were present. Lung auscultation was normal.

Laboratory studies showed a rise in serum creatinine with eGFR falling to 32 mL/min/1.73 m², CRP 79.2 mg/L, tacrolimus level 5.7 ng/mL, and normal complete blood count, albumin, liver enzymes, and electrolytes. CMV viremia was low (51 copies/mL). Tuberculosis screening was negative (TST and IGRA). Atypical bacterial serologies and nasopharyngeal PCR panels were negative, and two SARS‑CoV‑2 nasopharyngeal PCR tests were negative. Chest radiograph revealed fine bilateral interstitial infiltrates with edema. Chest CT demonstrated bilateral ground‑glass opacities, basal pneumatoceles, and heterogeneous centrilobular and peribronchovascular consolidations.

Immunosuppression (tacrolimus, methylprednisolone, MMF) and antihypertensive therapy were continued. Topical antifungal agents were started for the nail and skin lesions. On hospital day 2, while awaiting bronchoscopy, the patient’s respiratory rate and oxygen requirement rose sharply, necessitating up to 12 L/min supplemental O₂ and a further decline in eGFR to 27 mL/min/1.73 m². A bronchoscopy was performed for bronchoalveolar lavage.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. PCP considered due to subfebrile fever, dry cough, hypoxemia, weight loss, and characteristic CT findings of bilateral ground‑glass opacities in an immunosuppressed host | "Chest CT scan ... showed bilateral ground glass opacities, pneumatoceles ... and diffuse ... consolidation foci."
2. CMV pneumonia contemplated because of detectable CMV viremia and post‑transplant status, but low viral load made it less likely initially | "CMV viremia was present at 51 copies/ml."
3. Bacterial pneumonia in differential given respiratory symptoms, but excluded by negative serologies and nasopharyngeal PCR | "Atypical bacterial infections were excluded with negative serological testing and negative nasopharyngeal swab PCR."
4. COVID‑19 ruled out by two negative SARS‑CoV‑2 PCR tests | "PCR tests for SARS‑CoV‑2 from nasopharyngeal swabs were negative twice."
5. Tuberculosis excluded via negative tuberculin skin test and interferon‑gamma release assay | "Tuberculosis was excluded with both negative Tuberculin skin test (TST) and Interferon‑gamma release assay."
6. Primary fungal infection considered because of toenail fungus and rash, leading to topical therapy; systemic fungal disease not supported by imaging or labs | "Topical antifungal treatment was prescribed for suspected fungal etiology of toenail and skin lesions while microbiological tests were ongoing."
7. Definitive diagnosis established by BAL PCR detecting P. jirovecii, confirming PCP | "BALF sample tested positive for P. jirovecii."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient develops a new infectious complication that is not yet identified; laboratory work‑up eventually reveals Pneumocystis jirovecii infection, which is on the SELECTED diseases list (pneumocystis). Although COVID‑19 (covid_19) is also present, it was already diagnosed early, so the primary teaching target is pneumocystis.
2. Breakpoint: Include all data up to the performance of bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and the list of assays ordered on the BAL fluid, but stop before reporting the BAL results (i.e., before mention of a positive P. jirovecii immunofluorescence or the initiation of trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole). This provides the learner with persistent fever, worsening ground‑glass opacities, lymphopenia, hypogammaglobulinemia, and a broad infectious work‑up that is still unrevealing.

Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors systematically excluded bacterial superinfection (no clinical response to ceftaroline + levofloxacin), fungal infection (negative β‑D‑glucan, galactomannan), mycobacterial disease (negative GeneXpert for M. tuberculosis), and other viral reactivations (negative CMV‑DNA, VZV‑DNA). Persistence of SARS‑CoV‑2 RNA was noted, but the acute worsening prompted BAL, which identified Pneumocystis jirovecii as the cause of the refractory respiratory syndrome.
case_prompt:
A 64‑year‑old woman from Campania with arterial hypertension, occult HBV infection (on lamivudine), and a follicular variant non‑Hodgkin lymphoma in remission (last rituximab dose June 2020) presented with low‑grade fever and dysgeusia on 31 August 2020. Nasopharyngeal swab on 5 September was positive for SARS‑CoV‑2 RNA. She was admitted on 26 September with dyspnea, oxygen saturation 93% on room air, PaO₂ 68 mmHg, and fever 37.8 °C. High‑resolution chest CT showed bilateral ground‑glass opacities (GGO) and peripheral consolidations. She received methylprednisolone, ceftriaxone, and enoxaparin. A repeat CT on 14 October showed marked regression of lesions, but in early December fever recurred with a three‑fold rise in C‑reactive protein; a third CT demonstrated bilateral increase of GGO. SARS‑CoV‑2 RNA remained positive, prompting transfer on 11 December to a university infectious‑disease unit.

On admission she was hemodynamically stable, receiving omeprazole, atorvastatin, folic acid, lamivudine, and olmesartan/hydrochlorothiazide. Laboratory tests revealed glucose 150 mg/dL, ferritin 860 ng/mL, LDH 319 U/L, CRP 1.43 mg/dL, WBC 4,230/mm³ with lymphocytes 423/mm³ (CD4⁺ 28%, absolute 118/mm³; CD8⁺ 50%, absolute 211/mm³), hemoglobin 10 g/dL, normal neutrophils, and IgG 2.6 g/L (hypogammaglobulinemia). Blood, urine, and sputum cultures and serology for intracellular bacteria were negative; Legionella and a respiratory viral panel were also negative. She received 20 g intravenous immunoglobulin for two days. Lymph‑node ultrasound was normal, and oncology confirmed lymphoma remission, withholding further rituximab.

She was classified as WHO clinical progression scale class 4 and treated from 11 to 17 December with ceftaroline 600 mg BID and levofloxacin 750 mg daily for presumed bacterial superinfection, without improvement. Two consecutive β‑D‑glucan assays were negative. A CT on 26 December showed bilateral GGOs with a severity score of 11/20. Bronchoalveolar lavage was performed on 28 December; the fluid was sent for galactomannan, CMV‑DNA, VZV‑DNA, PCR for respiratory viruses, microscopy, bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial cultures, and a GeneXpert assay for Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
diagnostic_reasoning:

case_prompt: A 19‑year‑old male with relapsed Philadelphia chromosome‑like B‑cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia underwent a haploidentical stem cell transplant. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain revealed multiple ring‑enhancing lesions suggestive of septic emboli (Figure 1A). Magnetic resonance angiography showed no intracranial aneurysm, and transthoracic echocardiography revealed no intracardiac shunt, valve disease, or vegetation. Antibiotics were broadened to vancomycin and meropenem for presumed disseminated B. cereus. Despite clearance of B. cereus from the bloodstream, fever persisted. The patient was known to be IgG seropositive for Toxoplasma gondii, and trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX) was started empirically from days +22 to +25, but was stopped after negative T. gondii PCR from blood, cerebrospinal fluid, and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) specimens. A comprehensive workup was negative for Aspergillus, Pneumocystis jirovecii, Cryptococcus, and viral infections. On day +51 the patient acutely developed respiratory failure and worsening somnolence. Chest CT showed diffuse ground‑glass opacities. He was transferred to the pediatric intensive care unit, where he required mechanical ventilation, vasoactive support, and plasma exchange for thrombocytopenia‑associated multiple organ failure. case_prompt:
A 20‑year‑old man with immune‑mediated aplastic anemia refractory to prior immunosuppression underwent an unrelated donor peripheral stem cell transplant. Toxoplasma serologies were not obtained during his pre‑transplant evaluation per institutional practice. His early post‑transplant course was uneventful, and he was discharged home on post‑transplant day +21. On day +52 he was readmitted for fever and diarrhea. He remained febrile despite broad‑spectrum antibiotics and antifungals. His respiratory status worsened, leading to PICU transfer on day +61, intubation, and placement on venous‑venous ECMO within 24 hours. The ECMO course was complicated by shock, marked hyperferritinemia, and acute kidney injury requiring renal replacement therapy. 

Immune dysregulation was managed with pulse methylprednisolone (2 g/day) followed by a prolonged steroid taper, plasma exchange, tocilizumab, and etanercept, later switched to infliximab. Hyperinflammation improved and he was decannulated from ECMO on day +73. On day +90, fever recurred during a steroid taper; additional tocilizumab, infliximab, and pulse methylprednisolone were given. Cytokine panels showed rising markers, and by day +94 hyperferritinemia peaked at 202,000 ng/mL, prompting anakinra and repeat plasma exchange. Despite these measures, he continued to develop refractory multiorgan dysfunction, severe hypoxemic respiratory failure, and catecholamine‑refractory shock. At the family’s request, life‑sustaining measures were withdrawn on day +95.
