case_prompt:
A 58‑year‑old never‑smoking housewife presented to the Department of Pulmonary and Critical Care Medicine with cough, dyspnea, and intermittent fever. She had a history of untreated leukopenia of unknown origin. Chest CT showed scattered solid nodules in both lungs, a fibrous striped shadow in the medial segment of the right middle lobe, and slight left hilar enlargement. Broad‑spectrum antibiotics were started, but her condition worsened, evolving into severe pneumonia with type I respiratory failure; SpO₂ fell to 70 % on 5 L/min nasal cannula, prompting transfer to the ICU.

On ICU admission she was febrile (38.6 °C), tachycardic (105 bpm), tachypneic (35 /min), blood pressure 118/77 mmHg, and SpO₂ 93 % on 5 L/min O₂. Lung auscultation revealed coarse breath sounds and wet rales bilaterally; pitting edema was present in both lower extremities. Laboratory studies showed WBC 8.54 × 10⁹/L with 89.7 % neutrophils, CRP >200 mg/L, procalcitonin 1.67 ng/mL, ALT 48 U/L, AST 68 U/L. Autoimmune panels (ANA, ANCA, RF) were negative. Blood cultures, 1‑3‑β‑D‑glucan, galactomannan, T‑spot, cryptococcal antigen, EBV DNA, and CMV DNA were all negative. Fiberoptic bronchoscopy with BAL revealed extensive bronchial mucosal hyperemia and edema; fungal culture grew Candida albicans, while bacterial and mycobacterial cultures were negative. PCR assays for viruses, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and Chlamydia were negative; no Pneumocystis was detected, and tumor cytology was negative. Contrast‑enhanced CT demonstrated bilateral ground‑glass opacities and consolidations with mildly enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes.

On ICU day 2 the patient’s respiratory status declined further, with radiographic progression of bilateral infiltrates. She required mechanical ventilation and venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV‑ECMO). That same day a bedside transbronchial cryobiopsy (TBCB) was performed, obtaining three specimens from the outer and posterior basal segments of the left lower lobe.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial pneumonia was considered because of fever, cough, and infiltrates, but the patient deteriorated despite broad‑spectrum antibiotics. | "Broad‑spectrum antibiotics were administered, the patient's clinical status worsened..."
2. Viral etiologies (including COVID‑19) were evaluated; all viral nucleic‑acid tests were negative. | "All virus, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and Chlamydia nucleic acid amplification tests were negative."
3. Fungal infection was investigated; cultures grew only Candida albicans, while serum β‑D‑glucan, galactomannan, and other fungal antigens were negative, making invasive fungal disease unlikely. | "Fungal cultures were positive for Candida albicans… 1‑3‑beta‑D‑glucan (BDG) assay, galactomannan (GM) tests… were negative."
4. Mycobacterial tuberculosis was ruled out by negative T‑spot and mycobacterial cultures. | "T‑spot… were negative. Cultures for bacteria and mycobacteria were negative."
5. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia was excluded because PCR and staining did not detect the organism. | "No pneumocystis infection was identified."
6. Autoimmune vasculitis or connective‑tissue disease was unlikely given negative ANA, ANCA, and RF. | "Autoimmune tests including anti‑neutrophil antibody (ANA), anti‑neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA), and rheumatoid factor (RF) were negative."
7. Malignancy was considered but tumor cytology from BAL was negative. | "tumor cytology was negative."
8. Histopathology from the transbronchial lung biopsy showed fibroblasts intermixed with loose connective tissue and collagen in alveoli and distal bronchioles, findings characteristic of organizing pneumonia. | "histological examination revealed fibroblasts intermixed with loose connective tissue and collagen in the alveoli and the distal bronchioles… These findings were typical of OP."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient ultimately had pneumocystis pneumonia (pneumocystis) and later tuberculosis. Pneumocystis is on the SELECTED diseases list, making it the target diagnosis for this teaching case.  
2. Ideal Breakpoint: End the presentation just before the definitive microbiologic confirmation of PCP (the finding of cysts in sputum). Include chief complaint, history of immunosuppression, vital/respiratory status, laboratory values (LDH, T‑reg count), chest CT description, physical exam findings, and the empiric treatment regimen; omit any statement that PCP was later confirmed or that the patient improved.  
3. Author's Analytic Distinctions: The authors highlighted the immunocompromised state, elevated LDH, interstitial CT pattern, and lack of typical bacterial signs to favor PCP, while still covering Aspergillus (treated with caspofungin) and other atypical pathogens (added moxifloxacin) as alternative possibilities.
case_prompt: A 66‑year‑old man presented to the hospital with fever for 3 days and dyspnea for 1 day. He had been diagnosed with malignant pemphigus vulgaris and had received prednisolone, methylprednisolone and other immunosuppressive drugs for the past 9 years. On admission he was in respiratory failure. The absolute count of regulatory T lymphocytes was 156.67 cells/µL and lactate dehydrogenase was increased to 457 IU/L. Chest computed tomography showed multiple flaky, fuzzy, and high‑density opacities in both lungs with interstitial changes. He had obvious hypoxia, no prior respiratory symptoms, and no other infections. On respiratory examination the lungs did not have many rales. Because of his immunocompromised state, PCP was regarded as a possible etiology; Aspergillus infection could not be excluded, and other atypical pathogens were also considered. He was started on trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole (3 tablets twice daily), caspofungin (loading dose 70 mg then 50 mg daily), steroids, and moxifloxacin.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Immunocompromised host with interstitial CT pattern raises suspicion for PCP | "PCP, usually treated with sulfonamides, was considered a possible etiology because of his immunocompromised state."
2. Aspergillus infection could not be excluded, prompting antifungal therapy | "Caspofungin is a good treatment of choice for Aspergillus infection, which could not be excluded."
3. Potential other atypical pathogens warranted coverage with a fluoroquinolone | "For other atypical pathogens, moxifloxacin should be added."
4. Lack of prominent rales and absence of prior respiratory infections made typical bacterial pneumonia less likely | "On respiratory examination, the patient did not have many rales in the lungs."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case ultimately identifies Pneumocystis infection, which is listed in the 21 SELECTED diseases (pneumocystis). Therefore, the target diagnosis is pneumocystis.
2. Ideal Breakpoint: Include all information up to the second EBUS procedure where tissue sampling remained nondiagnostic (no malignancy on cytology, no flow cytometry clone, no cultures sent). Exclude the thoracic surgical resection and the pathological findings (necrotizing granulomas, GMS stain showing Pneumocystis) that reveal the definitive diagnosis.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors first pursued a malignancy work‑up (PET‑CT hypermetabolism, bronchoscopy with EBUS, cytology and flow cytometry) to rule out primary lung cancer or lymphoma recurrence. When these minimally invasive methods were nondiagnostic, they proceeded to VATS resection, where histopathology with special stains (acid‑fast bacilli, GMS) differentiated infectious etiologies, ultimately demonstrating Pneumocystis organisms.
case_prompt:
A 76‑year‑old man with a history of peripheral T‑cell lymphoma treated with six cycles of CHOP was referred for abnormal imaging. Initial imaging showed enlarged mediastinal lymphadenopathy, particularly within the right paratracheal and subcarinal regions, as well as prominent mesenteric, retroperitoneal, and pelvic lymphadenopathy. A surveillance CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis performed two months after therapy showed dramatic improvement. However, a new 1.2 cm pulmonary nodule was seen in the superior‑medial aspect of the right lower lobe just lateral to the distal bronchus intermedius. A subsequent PET‑CT scan revealed this nodule to be hypermetabolic with a standardized uptake value of 5.7, raising suspicion for a possible primary pulmonary malignancy. 

The patient underwent bronchoscopy with linear endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS). After passing the scope into the distal bronchus intermedius and rotating the probe to face the posterior wall, the pulmonary nodule was identified on ultrasound. A 22‑gauge needle was used to obtain tissue. Cytology showed no evidence of malignant cells, and flow cytometry showed no discrete clonal B‑cell or atypical T‑cell population. No tissue was sent for culture. 

Follow‑up CT imaging two months later showed enlargement of the nodule to 1.8 cm and two new 1 cm nodules in the peripheral basal right lower lobe. A repeat EBUS was performed; the area of interest was identified, and a 22‑gauge needle was used with suction, taking up to fifteen passes. Rapid on‑site evaluation did not confirm the presence of lymphocytes. Cytology was again nondiagnostic. No tissue was sent for culture.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Primary pulmonary malignancy considered because the PET‑CT nodule was hypermetabolic (SUV 5.7) | "PET‑CT scan revealed this nodule to be hypermetabolic with a standardized uptake value (SUV) of 5.7, raising the suspicion for a possible primary pulmonary malignancy."
2. Recurrent lymphoma considered given prior peripheral T‑cell lymphoma, but excluded by lack of malignant cells and no clonal lymphoid population on flow cytometry | "Cytology showed no evidence of malignant cells, and flow cytometry showed no discrete clonal B‑cell or atypical T‑cell population."
3. Mycobacterial infection considered; acid‑fast bacilli stain later proved negative, arguing against tuberculosis | "Acid‑fast bacilli stain was negative."
4. Pneumocystis infection confirmed by special fungal stain showing characteristic organisms within necrotizing granulomas | "Grocott methenamine silver (GMS) stain demonstrated clusters of organisms compatible with Pneumocystis in the center of these granulomas."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case ultimately describes chronic non‑infectious pulmonary inflammation in a patient with autosomal dominant Hyper‑IgE syndrome. This condition is not among the 21 SELECTED diseases, so the final mystery diagnosis is classified as OUT_OF_SCOPE.  
2. Best breakpoint: End the presentation just before the decision to treat with prednisolone for presumed non‑infectious inflammation. Include the full history, imaging, microbiology, immunology, and biopsy results that failed to identify an infectious or malignant cause, but omit the statement that therapy was switched to steroids.  
3. Analytic distinctions: The authors ruled out Aspergillus infection (negative cultures, PCR, galactomannan, and biopsy), mycobacterial disease (negative BAL, cultures, IGRA), bacterial pathogens (treated but not explaining cavity progression), Pneumocystis infection (identified by PCR and treated), and malignancy (normal brush biopsies and needle biopsy). Persistence of the cavitary lesion despite antifungal therapy and lack of pathogen detection led them to label the process non‑infectious inflammation.
case_prompt:
The patient had a childhood history of recurrent otitis media and a documented pneumonia at age 6. Physical features were typical of autosomal dominant Hyper‑IgE syndrome, including retained primary teeth, a broad nasal bridge, and a history of onychomycosis without mucosal fungal disease. He denied asthma.  

For several years he reported a mild, productive, clear‑coloured sputum each morning but no dyspnoea, weight loss, or fever. Pulmonary function testing demonstrated normal dynamic and static volumes as well as normal diffusion capacity.  

Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) performed in April 2017 grew Streptococcus pneumoniae (penicillin‑sensitive) and Achromobacter species; a PCR panel was positive for an opportunistic pneumonia pathogen and the patient was treated with sulfamethoxazole‑trimethoprim. Subsequent BAL specimens (February 2018) showed no growth of bacteria, fungi, or mycobacteria; microscopy and PCR for Aspergillus species were negative, as was serum galactomannan. Serum Aspergillus‑specific IgG antibody was undetectable (0.0 AU/mL).  

Immunologic studies revealed normal IgG and IgM, markedly elevated IgA (6.22 g/L) and reduced IgG2 (1.53 g/L). Total serum IgE was mildly increased at 158 IU/mL (reference < 115). The interferon‑γ release assay was negative.  

Imaging showed a right‑upper‑lobe cavitary lesion with a “fungal‑ball”‑like appearance on HRCT (March 2017) and high FDG uptake on PET/CT (May 2017). Follow‑up scans demonstrated progression of the cavity and new infiltrates despite 11 months of voriconazole therapy. A repeat BAL cultured Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which was treated with intravenous tazobactam and ciprofloxacin; repeat galactomannan remained negative.  

Bronchoscopic brush biopsies yielded normal respiratory epithelial cells, and a CT‑guided coarse needle biopsy demonstrated chronic inflammation without malignant cells or any fungal elements.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Chronic pulmonary aspergillosis considered because of cavity with “fungal‑ball” appearance and PET FDG uptake, but excluded by multiple negative Aspergillus cultures, PCR, galactomannan, serology, and biopsy lacking fungal elements. | "BAL was negative for Aspergillus sp. and other fungal moulds... PCR and microscopy for Aspergillus sp. were negative as well... CT‑guided biopsy showed chronic inflammation with no evidence of ... any fungal infection."
2. Mycobacterial tuberculosis considered given cavitary disease, but excluded by negative BAL microscopy and cultures, and a negative IGRA. | "BAL showed negative microscopy for Mycobacterium sp. The BAL culture for Mycobacterium sp. was negative as well. The interferon gamma release assay (IGRA) test was also negative."
3. Bacterial infection (S. pneumoniae, Achromobacter, P. aeruginosa) identified but deemed insufficient to explain persistent cavitation; treated with appropriate antibiotics without radiologic resolution. | "BAL culture positive for Streptococcus pneumoniae... Achromobacter sp... patient received phenoxymethylpenicillin... later Pseudomonas aeruginosa was cultured and treated with IV tazobactam and ciprofloxacin."
4. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia identified by PCR and treated with sulfamethoxazole‑trimethoprim; while present, it did not account for the cavitary lesion’s progression. | "PCR was positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii, which was treated with Sulfatrim."
5. Malignancy considered because of cavitary lung lesion, but excluded by normal brush biopsy cells and needle biopsy showing only chronic inflammation with no malignant cells. | "Superdimension‑bronchoscopy with brush biopsies: normal cells. A CT‑guided transthoracic coarse needle biopsy showed chronic inflammation with no evidence of malignancy."
6. Other opportunistic fungal infections (e.g., histoplasmosis, cryptococcosis) not supported by any positive cultures, serology, or histopathology, and thus excluded. | "BAL was negative for Aspergillus sp. and other fungal moulds... Galactomannan antigen test was negative."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient’s acute illness is confirmed to be COVID-19 pneumonia, which is listed as “covid_19” in the 21 SELECTED diseases. Therefore, the target diagnosis is covid_19.
2. Ideal Breakpoint: Present the case up to the point where the positive SARS‑CoV‑2 PCR result and characteristic CT findings are described, including initial labs and exclusion of bacterial and Pneumocystis pneumonia, but stop before any therapeutic interventions (monoclonal antibodies, baricitinib, dexamethasone) are introduced.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors diagnosed COVID‑19 by combining (a) a positive nasopharyngeal PCR with Delta‑variant sequencing, (b) typical ground‑glass opacities involving ~40 % of lung parenchyma on CT, and (c) exclusion of bacterial pneumonia (negative cultures/Gram stain) and Pneumocystis pneumonia (normal LDH, atypical imaging distribution). These data distinguished COVID‑19 from other infectious pneumonias in an immunosuppressed host.
case_prompt:
A 74‑year‑old woman with limited systemic sclerosis (diagnosed 2015), hypertension, hyperlipidemia, hypothyroidism, and a BMI of 32 kg/m² presented to the emergency department in December 2021 with progressive dyspnea, fever, and cough that had begun 7 days earlier. She had received rituximab two months earlier and completed a SARS‑CoV‑2 vaccination schedule (two doses of BNT162b2 followed by a booster with ChAdOx1), but no anti‑spike antibodies were detectable at admission.

On examination she was ill‑appearing, dyspneic, febrile (38.6 °C), respiratory rate 21/min, and oxygen saturation 97 % on room air. Laboratory studies showed lymphopenia (400 cells/µL), CRP 143 mg/L, D‑dimer 1,605 ng/mL, ferritin 109 ng/mL, and IL‑6 239.9 pg/mL. A nasopharyngeal SARS‑CoV‑2 PCR assay was positive; sequencing identified the Delta variant. No SARS‑CoV‑2 spike antibodies were present.

Chest CT demonstrated typical ground‑glass opacities consistent with COVID‑19 pneumonia involving approximately 40 % of the lung parenchyma. Blood and sputum cultures were negative, and Gram stains showed no bacteria. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia was considered unlikely because lactate dehydrogenase levels were normal and the imaging pattern was predominantly posterobasal segmental rather than diffuse.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. COVID‑19 pneumonia is most likely given the acute respiratory symptoms, fever, positive SARS‑CoV‑2 PCR, and characteristic ground‑glass opacities on CT. | "Nasopharyngeal SARS‑COV‑2‑PCR assay was positive and subsequent sequencing revealed infection with the Delta variant... CT‑scans showed typical ground glass opacities consistent with COVID‑19 pneumonia..."
2. Bacterial pneumonia was considered but ruled out by negative blood and sputum cultures and lack of organisms on Gram stain. | "Blood and sputum cultures were obtained for the differential diagnosis of bacterial pneumonia, which was excluded based on the negative cultures and Gram staining."
3. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia was a differential in this immunosuppressed patient, but was excluded because lactate dehydrogenase was normal and imaging showed predominantly posterobasal segmental involvement rather than the diffuse pattern typical of PCP. | "Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia was ruled out based on normal lactate dehydrogenase levels and imaging findings showing predominantly posterobasal segmental involvement."
4. Non‑infectious causes (e.g., drug‑induced lung injury, progression of systemic sclerosis‑related interstitial lung disease) were less plausible given the acute onset, positive viral PCR, and the absence of prior lung involvement on prior imaging. | "She had no dyspnea or cough before; lung involvement was ruled out by prior PFTs and high‑resolution CT."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case centers on Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, which corresponds to **pneumocystis** on the 21 SELECTED diseases list.
2. Best Breakpoint: Include all data up to the Gram‑stain result of the broncho‑alveolar lavage fluid (“Gram stain of the BALF revealed many Gram‑negative organisms.”). Exclude the subsequent metagenomic next‑generation sequencing (mNGS) findings that definitively identified P. jirovecii, so that the learner must deduce the diagnosis from clinical, radiologic, and preliminary laboratory clues.
3. Author's Analytic Distinctions: 
   • Broad infectious work‑up (culture, smear, GeneXpert MTB, galactomannan) was negative, narrowing the differential. 
   • Empirical coverage for bacterial, viral (CMV), and fungal pathogens was initiated while awaiting definitive testing. 
   • mNGS of serum and BALF identified P. jirovecii; results were corroborated by qPCR and Sanger sequencing, providing the decisive evidence. 
   • Alternative opportunistic pathogens (CMV, Aspergillus, Mycobacterium tuberculosis) were systematically excluded by negative specific assays.
case_prompt:
A 69‑year‑old woman was admitted on December 26, 2020 with a one‑week history of progressive weakness in her arms and legs. She denied fever, cough, rhinorrhea, asthma, COPD, smoking, or exposure to pets or poultry. She reported no known contact with suspected COVID‑19 cases and a prior PCR test for SARS‑CoV‑2 was negative. Her past medical history was notable for rheumatoid arthritis treated chronically with steroids; methotrexate, leflunomide and prednisone had been added recently.

On initial evaluation her temperature was 36.2 °C, blood pressure 142/83 mmHg, pulse 105 bpm, respiratory rate 20/min. Fine moist rales were heard in the lower lung fields. Muscle strength was 5/5 in the upper limbs and 3/5 in the lower limbs. That night she developed sudden dyspnea and low‑grade fever; arterial blood gas showed hypoxemia (pO₂ 68 mmHg, pCO₂ 21.6 mmHg). Chest CT demonstrated diffuse effusion and ground‑glass opacities bilaterally.

Laboratory studies revealed pancytopenia with marked lymphopenia, elevated serum creatinine (230.5 µmol/L) and BUN (16.6 mmol/L). She was transferred to the ICU on December 28 due to worsening respiratory failure (SpO₂ 85% on mask oxygen, RR 31/min, HR 138/min) and septic shock (MAP 66/42 mmHg, SOFA 18). Intubation, mechanical ventilation, fluid resuscitation and vasopressors were started.

Bronchoscopy with broncho‑alveolar lavage (BAL) was performed. BAL fluid was sent for culture, smear, GeneXpert MTB, galactomannan assay, and metagenomic next‑generation sequencing (mNGS). Empiric therapy for possible opportunistic infections (trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole, acyclovir) and broad‑spectrum antibiotics were initiated. Bone‑marrow biopsy on hospital day 2 showed hemophagocytosis.

Cultures of sputum, urine and blood remained negative. Gram stain of the BAL fluid revealed many gram‑negative organisms.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. COVID‑19 infection considered but excluded | "She did not contact suspected COVID‑19 cases, with negative PCR results for COVID‑19..."
2. Bacterial pneumonia considered but cultures were negative and no specific pathogen isolated | "The sputum, urine, and blood cultures returned with negative results... Gram stain of the BALF revealed many Gram‑negative organisms."
3. Tuberculosis considered; GeneXpert MTB was negative | "...including culture, smear, GeneXpert MTB..."
4. Invasive aspergillosis considered; galactomannan test was negative | "...and galactomannan test."
5. Cytomegalovirus infection considered among opportunistic pathogens; other diagnostic tests did not detect any pathogenic microorganism | "Considering that the patient was highly suspected of opportunistic infections, such as PJP or cytomegalovirus infection..."
6. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia ultimately identified by mNGS, confirmed by qPCR and sequencing, establishing the definitive diagnosis | "mNGS revealed P. jirovecii in both serum and BALF... The PCR products were sequenced by Sanger and finally identified as P. jirovecii, confirming the mNGS results."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient has disseminated infection with Nocardia farcinica, which is on the SELECTED diseases list (nocardiosis). Co‑infections (CMV, Pneumocystis, Aspergillus) are also present, but the primary mystery to be solved before the breakpoint is the Nocardia infection; thus the target diagnosis is nocardiosis.
2. Breakpoint: Include presentation up to admission vital signs, routine laboratory values, imaging findings, and CSF analysis, but stop **before** any mention of next‑generation sequencing (NGS) results that identify specific pathogens. This provides enough clues (immunosuppression, brain lesions, pulmonary ground‑glass opacities, neutrophilic CSF) for learners to hypothesize opportunistic infections while keeping the exact pathogen concealed.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors used NGS to pinpoint Nocardia farcinica as the dominant organism, distinguished it from CMV and Pneumocystis by sequence counts and therapeutic response, and later confirmed Aspergillus by sputum culture when clinical response plateaued despite appropriate anti‑nocardial therapy.
case_prompt:
A 62‑year‑old man received oral dexamethasone (2.25 mg tid) and ornidazole (0.5 g bid) after a tooth extraction. Ten days later he developed fever (39 °C) with chills, headache, abdominal bloating, tinnitus, and hearing loss. Local hospital therapy failed and he was transferred three days later.

On admission: temperature 38.6 °C, blood pressure 134/74 mmHg, respiration 16/min, heart rate 75/min, fully conscious.

Laboratory studies: WBC 4.40 × 10⁹/L, neutrophils 89.8 %, lymphocytes 0.17 × 10⁹/L, CD4⁺ count 32 cells/mm³, CRP 14.38 mg/L, creatinine 37.05 µmol/L, pH 7.399, procalcitonin 0.123 ng/mL, 1,3‑β‑d‑glucan 253.73 pg/mL.

MRI of the brain revealed multiple lesions; contrast‑enhanced MRI showed multiple abnormal enhancing shadows suggestive of hematogenous dissemination. Chest CT demonstrated multiple ground‑glass opacities in the anterior segment and lower lobe of the left lung.

Cerebrospinal fluid analysis: WBC 1,352 × 10⁶/L, neutrophils 92 %, glucose 0.59 mmol/L, protein 1.48 g/L.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Nocardia farcinica infection strongly implicated by high‑throughput sequencing showing abundant Nocardia reads in CSF and blood, indicating a disseminated nocardial disease. | "NGS of the patient's CSF reported 37,235 sequences from N. farcinica... Blood NGS reported 61 sequences from Nocardia farcinica..."
2. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) considered because NGS detected CMV sequences in CSF and blood, but the low sequence count relative to Nocardia and modest clinical response to ganciclovir suggested CMV was a co‑infection rather than the primary cause. | "8 sequences from human cytomegalovirus... 543 sequences from human cytomegalovirus... treatment with ganciclovir, the patient's symptoms improved slightly..."
3. Pneumocystis jirovecii was contemplated owing to its detection in blood NGS and the patient’s severe CD4⁺ lymphopenia, yet absence of the organism in respiratory cultures and lack of classic PCP radiographic pattern argued against it as the main pathogen. | "8 sequences from P. jirovecii... N. farcinica and P. jirovecii were not found in the sputum culture..."
4. Aspergillus fumigatus infection emerged later, confirmed by sputum culture and new CT lesions, indicating a secondary opportunistic fungal infection that required voriconazole after limited response to anti‑nocardial therapy. | "sputum culture was positive for A. fumigatus and lung CT showed new lesions."
5. Common bacterial meningitis and tuberculosis were deemed less likely given the patient’s low procalcitonin, negative bacterial cultures, and lack of typical imaging or laboratory hallmarks for TB. | "procalcitonin level of 0.123 ng/mL... blood cultures remained negative..."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case’s ultimate diagnosis is “transient pneumonitis induced by a COVID‑19 mRNA vaccine,” which is not among the 21 SELECTED diseases; therefore the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.  
2. Ideal Breakpoint: Include all presenting data up to the point where extensive infectious work‑up is reported negative and chest CT shows rapid radiographic improvement, but stop before the authors state the final diagnosis of vaccine‑induced pneumonitis. This provides enough information (fever, cough, dyspnea, CT findings, negative microbiology) for students to reason toward the diagnosis without a spoiler.  
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors first considered interstitial lung disease and infectious etiologies (viral, bacterial, atypical, mycobacterial, fungal, Pneumocystis). They systematically excluded each with negative antigen, PCR, serology, culture, and beta‑D‑glucan tests, and demonstrated rapid radiographic and clinical resolution, supporting a transient, non‑infectious pneumonitis attributable to the recent mRNA vaccine.
case_prompt:
A 76‑year‑old woman with stable rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate presented with malaise and high‑grade fever (>39 °C) five days after receiving a second dose of the BNT162b2 mRNA COVID‑19 vaccine. Ten days after vaccination she developed a persistent cough and dyspnea, and 17 days after vaccination she was admitted to an outside hospital for persistent fever. Laboratory studies at that time showed a white blood cell count of 4,990/µL, lactate dehydrogenase 477 U/L, and C‑reactive protein 6.4 mg/dL. An antigen test for SARS, serum (1,3)-β‑D‑glucan, and blood cultures were negative; testing for Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, and sputum culture were not performed. Chest computed tomography revealed infiltrates and ground‑glass opacities throughout all lung fields, and a provisional diagnosis of interstitial lung disease was made. She was transferred to our hospital 21 days after vaccination.

On admission her temperature was 36.5 °C, blood pressure 110/60 mmHg, pulse 65 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and SpO₂ 98 % on room air. Physical examination showed stable rheumatoid arthritis without new joint findings. Laboratory results were: WBC 5,420/µL, RBC 3.77 × 10⁶/µL, hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, hematocrit 35.5 %, platelets 404 × 10³/µL, CRP 1.47 mg/dL, LDH 311 U/L, Krebs von den Lungen‑6 (KL‑6) 452.4 U/mL, surfactant protein D 226 ng/mL; rheumatoid factor, anti‑CCP, and ANA were negative.

Further testing showed negative results for Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, tuberculosis (T‑Spot), and antigen tests for Cryptococcus, Candida, Aspergillus, cytomegalovirus, and SARS‑CoV‑2. Serum β‑D‑glucan, blood cultures, and PCR for Pneumocystis jirovecii DNA from respiratory samples were also negative. Repeat chest CT performed four days later demonstrated a marked improvement in the infiltrates and ground‑glass opacities.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Interstitial lung disease (ILD) considered because of diffuse ground‑glass opacities on CT; however, rapid radiographic improvement within days is atypical for chronic ILD. | "Chest CT showed a significant improvement compared to the chest CT performed 4 days earlier."
2. COVID‑19 infection considered due to recent vaccination and fever; excluded by negative SARS‑CoV‑2 antigen test and absence of typical viral prodrome. | "Tests for ... SARS‑CoV‑2 antigen were negative."
3. Bacterial pneumonia considered; excluded by negative blood cultures and lack of sputum culture, plus low WBC count. | "The antigen test for SARS, serum B‑D glucan, and blood culture was negative."
4. Atypical bacterial infections (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia) considered; not tested initially, later explicitly negative. | "Tests for Mycoplasma, Chlamydia ... were negative."
5. Tuberculosis considered given chronic immunosuppression; excluded by negative T‑Spot. | "Tests for ... tuberculosis (T‑Spot) ... were negative."
6. Fungal infections (Aspergillus, Candida, Cryptococcus) considered; excluded by negative antigen assays and serum β‑D‑glucan. | "Antigen tests for Cryptococcus, Candida, Aspergillus ... were negative."
7. Cytomegalovirus pneumonia considered; excluded by negative CMV antigen test. | "Cytomegalovirus antigen ... were negative."
8. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia considered in immunosuppressed host; excluded by negative PCR for Pneumocystis DNA. | "PCR for Pneumocystis jirovecii DNA were also negative."
9. Vaccine‑induced transient pneumonitis ultimately favored because of temporal association with mRNA vaccination, absence of infectious agents, and spontaneous clinical and radiographic resolution. | (Implied by the overall negative work‑up and rapid improvement described above.)
final_diagnosis: transient pneumonitis induced by a COVID-19 mRNA vaccine -> OUT_OF_SCOPE

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The primary disease being worked up in the case is BCR::ABL‑positive chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), which is not on the 21 SELECTED diseases list. Although the patient later develops pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (a SELECTED disease), the diagnostic challenge presented before the breakpoint focuses on establishing the CML diagnosis. Therefore, the final answer must be formatted as an OUT_OF_SCOPE disease.
2. Breakpoint: Include all information up to the point where bone‑marrow morphology is described (consistent with atypical CML) but stop before the cytogenetic finding of the Philadelphia chromosome and the explicit statement of BCR::ABL‑positive CML. This gives the learner sufficient clinical, laboratory, and marrow data to formulate the correct diagnosis without revealing the definitive genetic result.
3. Analytic Distinctions: The authors differentiated CML from atypical CML, leukemoid reaction, and other myeloproliferative neoplasms by (a) demonstrating a left‑shifted neutrophilia with circulating blasts, (b) marrow findings of hypercellularity with increased myeloid lineage, and (c) ultimately identifying the t(9;22) translocation and BCR::ABL positivity, which ruled out atypical CML and reactive causes.
case_prompt: A 79‑year‑old man with a known history of triple‑negative primary myelofibrosis presented in August 2021 after a syncopal episode. On admission his performance status was ECOG 2. His past medical history included a mechanical aortic valve replacement (2009), resection of a myxoid liposarcoma (2011), and monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance diagnosed in 2016. EBV serology indicated past infection, while quantitative PCR detected 3,359 copies/mL, suggesting possible reactivation.

Transesophageal echocardiography identified numerous floating prosthetic strands in the left ventricular outflow tract and mild mitral valve prolapse without vegetations. Contrast‑enhanced chest CT demonstrated postoperative changes of the mechanical ascending‑aortic prosthesis. ^18F‑FDG PET‑CT demonstrated intense uptake in the periaortic region and marked splenic medullary uptake, findings compatible with a reactive‑infectious process or an underlying hematologic disease. Because both possibilities could not be excluded, a bone‑marrow biopsy was undertaken.

Head, neck, lung, cardiac and abdominal examinations were unremarkable; ophthalmic exam showed no uveitis. No penile swelling or induration, skin rash, or peripheral edema.

Laboratory studies demonstrated cholestatic pattern with ALT 211 U/L, AST 101 U/L, total bilirubin 1.41 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.72 mg/dL, and low albumin 3.2 g/dL. CBC, BUN and creatinine were normal. Serologic testing for hepatitis A, B, C, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, and Epstein‑Barr virus was negative; extensive autoimmune and metabolic work‑up was unrevealing. Liver MRI showed mild fatty infiltration and borderline splenomegaly (~13 cm) without renal abnormalities.

Urinalysis revealed 3+ protein; quantitative testing showed an albumin‑creatinine ratio of 1,295.8 mg/g and a protein‑creatinine ratio of 972.4 mg/g (reference <150 mg/g). The A/G ratio was 0.8.

Rapid plasma reagin (RPR) was markedly reactive at 1:128, and Treponema pallidum hemagglutination (TPHA) was positive with a titer of 1:2,560. HIV antibody test was negative. Serum immunoglobulins were within normal limits except IgE 766 IU/mL (reference <100). A kidney biopsy was performed. Light microscopy of 15 glomeruli revealed well‑perfused, non‑sclerosed units with focal segmental thickening of capillary loops, mild mesangial matrix expansion, and mild tubular atrophy. Direct immunofluorescence showed moderate diffuse granular capillary wall staining for IgG, C1q, C3, kappa and lambda light chains. Electron microscopy did not demonstrate definitive electron‑dense deposits along capillary loops or in the mesangium, but granular deposits along the glomerular basement membrane were identified.

Three months later he presented to the emergency department with mild fever, non‑productive cough, nocturnal sweats, and inability to walk. Examination showed a thin, ill‑looking patient (63 kg) with BP 154/95 mmHg, HR 104 bpm, temperature 38.2 °C, SpO₂ 95 %. Neurologic exam revealed preserved proprioception, negative Babinski, Hoffman, and Lasègue signs; muscle strength 3/5 proximally, poor squat test, but symmetric active patellar reflexes. Cardiovascular exam noted tachycardia without murmurs; lung auscultation revealed bi‑basal crackles, predominantly on the right. Skin showed pityriasis‑versicolor‑like eruptions on upper limbs and thorax; the scrotum had hypochromic vitiligo‑like macules. No lymphadenopathy was present.

Initial investigations showed: iPTH 205 ng/L (reference 15‑65), 1,25‑OH D₃ 24 pmol/L (43‑148), 25‑OH D₃ 38 nmol/L (75‑200) with normal calcium‑phosphate product. Sputum smear, urine and blood cultures, and three separate blood cultures were negative. Mantoux test was non‑reactive. Chest X‑ray demonstrated an interstitial pattern in both lung fields with a normal‑sized mediastinum. Transthoracic Doppler‑echocardiography revealed mild concentric left‑ventricular hypertrophy and a calcified bicuspid aortic valve with mild regurgitation but no aortitis. Abdominal‑pelvic ultrasound showed mild splenomegaly and poorly differentiated kidneys with acquired cystic disease. Fundoscopy identified proliferative retinopathy and an incidental syphilitic‑appearing uveitis.

The patient was empirically started on ceftriaxone 1.5 g post‑dialysis, resulting in marked clinical improvement within one week; ceftriaxone was continued for a total of two weeks. The patient’s spouse was subsequently screened and found to have serologic evidence of syphilis, prompting referral for intramuscular benzathine‑penicillin therapy.

1. Lumbar disc disease considered because of proximal weakness; ruled out by lack of progressive radicular pain and minimal findings on CT/EMG – “lumbar CT scan showed diffuse degenerative changes associated with a disc protrusion at L3‑L4 level” and “EMG/NCS showed evidence of a pending left external popliteal sciatic nerve without evidence of diffuse symmetrical polyneuropathy.”

A 43‑year‑old homosexual man with known HIV infection presented to the emergency department with one week of nausea, vomiting, and severe abdominal pain. The pain was diffuse, intermittent, dull, and most prominent in the epigastrium and right upper quadrant, worsening with oral intake. On examination, he was afebrile, normotensive, and his abdomen was soft, nondistended, and diffusely tender, especially in the right upper quadrant with voluntary guarding. A macular, darkly pigmented rash was present on the palms and soles, and bilateral nontender inguinal lymphadenopathy was appreciated. Genitourinary and rectal examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and renal function. CD4 count on admission was 394 cells/mm³. Liver enzymes were markedly elevated (alkaline phosphatase 712 IU/L, AST 262 IU/L, ALT 481 IU/L) with a total bilirubin of 1.7 mg/dL. Lipase was 1396 U/L. Initial imaging with abdominal X‑ray was non‑diagnostic. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a contracted gallbladder without visible stones. case_prompt:
A 67‑year‑old man presented with progressive central vision loss in the right eye for one month, without photopsia, night blindness, headache, or other extra‑ocular symptoms. Past medical history was notable for pulmonary emphysema; family history was non‑contributory. Best‑corrected visual acuity was 0.08 (right eye) and 1.2 (left eye); relative afferent pupillary defect was absent. Slit‑lamp examination revealed moderate anterior vitreous cells in both eyes. Funduscopy showed swollen optic discs surrounded by serous retinal detachment, dilated tortuous veins in both eyes, and a subretinal opaque exudation at the fovea of the right eye. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated early hyperfluorescence with late leakage from the optic disc and retinal venous wall staining in both eyes, and early hyperfluorescence at the fovea of the right eye. Indocyanine green angiography was essentially normal except for slight late‑phase hypofluorescence corresponding to the right‑eye foveal lesion. Optical coherence tomography displayed serous retinal detachment adjacent to the optic disc in both eyes and a dome‑shaped hyperreflective lesion extending from the inner nuclear layer to the photoreceptor layer at the right‑eye fovea; the left‑eye macular IS/OS line remained intact. Goldmann perimetry revealed a 20 × 20 ° blind‑spot enlargement in both eyes and a 10 × 10 ° central scotoma in the right eye. Visual‑evoked potentials showed normal P100 latencies bilaterally, and brain/orbital MRI was unremarkable.

Two weeks later, visual acuity declined to 0.02 (right) and 0.3 (left) with worsening optic‑disc swelling in both eyes and new serous detachment at the left macula. Single bright‑flash electroretinography showed normal a‑waves bilaterally and a slightly reduced b‑wave in the left eye. Serologic screening for infections (including syphilis and Bartonella henselae) and autoantibodies for systemic autoimmune disease returned within normal limits.

Based on these findings, oral prednisolone 30 mg daily was started under the working diagnosis of bilateral neuroretinitis. Systemic work‑up identified extensive‑stage small‑cell lung carcinoma, and chemotherapy was initiated. After five months, optic‑disc swelling resolved, foveal scarring remained in the right eye, and visual acuity improved to 0.08 (right) and 1.2 (left).

1. Infectious retinitis (syphilis, Bartonella) considered but excluded because “Results of serological screening tests for infection, including syphilis and anti‑Bartonella henselae antibody … were within normal limits.”  
2. Primary inflammatory optic neuropathy / autoimmune optic neuritis considered; excluded by normal visual‑evoked potentials, unremarkable brain/orbital MRI, and lack of systemic autoantibodies: “P100 latency … showed no prolongation … Brain and orbital MRI revealed no abnormalities.”  
3. Typical bilateral neuroretinitis initially presumed, yet progression despite steroids and the presence of an underlying malignancy prompted reconsideration: “based on a diagnosis of bilateral neuroretinitis” followed by detection of small‑cell carcinoma.

Paraneoplastic retinopathy (cancer‑associated retinopathy) supported by temporal correlation of ocular inflammation with tumor recurrence and by detection of onconeural antibodies (recoverin, CRMP‑5, alpha‑enolase): “Immunoblot analyses … detected autoantibodies against recoverin, CRMP‑5, and alpha‑enolase … Two months after recurrence of carcinoma, optic disc swelling also recurred.”  
5. Alternative paraneoplastic antibodies (e.g., carbonic anhydrase II) tested and found negative, narrowing the diagnosis to the identified antibody profile: “but not carbonic anhydrase II (data not shown).”

A 58‑year‑old African‑American woman presented to the emergency department with a superotemporal marginal corneal ulcer of the left eye, two clock hours in length with mild thinning. Uncorrected visual acuity was 20/30 right and 20/50 left; both eyes showed diffuse punctate corneal epitheliopathy. Past medical history was notable for chronic alcoholism (6–12 beers/day since age 34), chronic pancreatitis, diarrhea, liver cirrhosis, cholecystectomy, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, >50 pack‑year smoking history, and prior gastrointestinal bleed. She lived in an urban U.S. setting.

Initial corneal cultures grew alpha‑hemolytic streptococcus and catalase‑positive Gram‑positive cocci identified preliminarily as coagulase‑negative Staphylococcus. She was started on hourly topical moxifloxacin 0.5% in the left eye and artificial tears bilaterally. Three days later she returned with unchanged exam except mild injection of the right eye; treatment was continued with the same antibiotics and increased artificial tears.

Six days after the initial visit she presented to an outpatient office with bilateral marginal corneal ulcers, each with >50 % thinning parallel to the limbus; the left eye also had a small hypopyon. Visual acuity was 20/40 right, 20/80 left. She was lost to follow‑up for over a week, then returned to the emergency department 17 days after first presentation with severe bilateral vision loss and painful swelling of the left lower lid of 2‑day duration. On admission, vision was hand motions bilaterally. The right eye had deep marginal thinning inferiorly for 6 clock hours; the left eye had deep stromal thinning temporally for 5 clock hours and a tender erythematous left lower lid. Diffuse severe bilateral corneal edema with hypopyon (1.5 mm right, 1.0 mm left) was present; B‑scan ultrasonography of the fundus was unremarkable.

Corneal cultures grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus hominis from the right eye, and Staphylococcus warneri and Staphylococcus lugdunensis from the left eye. Fortified vancomycin (25 mg/mL) hour‑ly and moxifloxacin 0.5% hour‑ly were initiated bilaterally, later adjusted to vancomycin every 2 h and fortified tobramycin (14 mg/mL) every 2 h after culture results. Intravenous cefazolin (1 g q8h) was given for left lower lid cellulitis, with resolution. Amniotic membrane grafts and a bandage contact lens were placed on hospital day 4. A urinary tract infection yielded vancomycin‑resistant Enterococcus treated with linezolid.

Laboratory evaluation showed mild protein malnutrition (total protein 6.5 g/dL), BMI 21.4, hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypomagnesemia, and hypocalcemia. Testing ruled out HIV, tuberculosis, syphilis, sarcoidosis, rheumatoid arthritis, hepatitis A, B, C, and Wegener granulomatosis. ANA titer was 40 with a fine speckled pattern; Sjögren panel (SS‑A/Ro, SS‑B/La, Smith, RNP) was negative. ESR and CRP were normal.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial keratitis due to Gram‑negative and Gram‑positive organisms | "Cultures from admission grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus hominis from the right eye and Staphylococcus warneri and Staphylococcus lugdunensis from the left eye."
2. Multidrug‑resistant Enterococcus urinary infection complicating the hospital course | "A urinary tract infection found during hospitalization was culture‑positive for vancomycin‑resistant Enterococcus and was treated with linezolid."
3. Possible autoimmune vasculitis (Wegener granulomatosis) considered but excluded | "Testing ruled out … Wegener granulomatosis."
4. Infectious systemic etiologies (HIV, tuberculosis, syphilis, hepatitis) evaluated and excluded | "Testing ruled out HIV, tuberculosis, syphilis, … hepatitis A, B, C."
5. Inflammatory systemic diseases (sarcoidosis, rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren syndrome) evaluated and excluded | "Testing ruled out … sarcoidosis, rheumatoid arthritis… Sjogren syndrome testing … were all negative."
6. Nutritional deficiency (vitamin A deficiency) identified as underlying predisposing factor | "Testing revealed a marked vitamin A deficiency, with a level of 0 µg/dL (reference range 18‑77)."
7. Malnutrition and chronic alcoholism supporting a deficiency state | "The patient had mild protein malnutrition with total protein 6.5 g/dL… Laboratory analysis showed hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypomagnesemia, and hypocalcemia."

2. Ideal Breakpoint: Include all presentation details, symptom evolution, imaging, and laboratory findings up to but not including the explicit statement “Overall the patient was diagnosed as having nonceliac gluten sensitivity…”. This provides sufficient data (autoimmune‑type antibodies to wheat antigens, normal tTG, extensive white‑matter lesions, negative infectious work‑up) for the learner to reason toward the correct diagnosis without a spoiler.

Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors differentiate IBS from an organic process by the emergence of systemic symptoms and abnormal labs; they contrast SLE (positive ANA, anemia, elevated ESR) with the later neurological picture; they rule out multiple sclerosis by atypical MRI findings; they exclude infectious etiologies through exhaustive CSF and serum testing; finally they demonstrate gluten‑related autoimmunity via a broad wheat‑protein IgG/IgA panel while tTG remains negative, leading to the NCGS diagnosis.
case_prompt:
A 49‑year‑old woman presented with abdominal pain, constipation, acid reflux, and headache. Initial evaluation by an internist showed a normal complete blood count except for a hemoglobin of 10.8 g/dL, and a normal chemistry panel including liver enzymes. Further biochemical and immunological testing—including ANA, rheumatoid factor, T₃, T₄, and TSH—were all within normal limits. Because of persistent gastrointestinal discomfort she was referred for gastroenterology. Upper endoscopy and H. pylori testing were normal, and she was diagnosed with irritable bowel syndrome; treatment with a beta‑blocker and esomeprazole magnesium led to moderate symptom improvement.

Four years later she returned with her prior gastrointestinal complaints plus new malaise, blurred vision, facial rash, intermittent sleepiness, irritability, and breathing problems. Laboratory studies now revealed hemoglobin 9.7 g/dL, MCV 72 fL, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 46 mm/hr, ANA 1 : 80, mildly elevated IgA smooth‑muscle antibody, while double‑stranded DNA and extractable nuclear antibodies were negative. Based on these findings a rheumatologist diagnosed systemic lupus erythematosus and initiated steroid therapy, which modestly improved her overall condition but her anemia persisted and ESR fluctuated.

Two years after that, she developed difficulty urinating together with tingling and sensory disturbances in the trunk and legs, prompting neurologic referral. She reported a band‑like sensation across the trunk and reduced visual acuity (8/46 right eye, 8/23 left eye) with minimal eye pain but normal eye movements. Laboratory evaluation again showed low hemoglobin, microcytic indices, and low ferritin (14 mg/L). Brain MRI demonstrated extensive white‑matter abnormalities that were not typical of multiple sclerosis; cerebrospinal fluid analysis was unremarkable. Comprehensive infectious studies of blood and CSF were negative for bacterial and viral agents, including syphilis, mycobacteria, Borrelia, EBV, CMV, HTLV, and herpes‑6. Visual evoked potentials revealed delayed conduction in both optic nerves.

Given these findings, a broad serologic panel assessing IgG and IgA antibodies against wheat proteins and peptides was ordered. The panel demonstrated IgG antibodies against wheat antigens, alpha‑gliadin 33 and 17 mer, gamma‑ and omega‑gliadin, glutenin, gluteomorphin, prodynorphin, gliadin‑tTG complex, wheat germ agglutinin, and glutamic acid decarboxylase‑65. IgA antibodies were detected against wheat antigens and wheat germ agglutinin. Both IgG and especially IgA antibodies to tissue transglutaminase were within the normal range. Additional testing showed 2–4‑fold elevation of antibodies against ganglioside, cerebellar, synapsin, myelin basic protein, collagen, thyroglobulin, thyroid peroxidase, and aquaporin‑4. Upper GI endoscopy with biopsy revealed normal histology and intra‑epithelial lymphocyte counts.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Irritable bowel syndrome was initially presumed because gastrointestinal symptoms were present with normal endoscopy and H. pylori testing. | "Both endoscopy and H. pylori test results were normal. The patient was diagnosed with irritable bowel syndrome..."
2. Systemic lupus erythematosus was diagnosed after anemia, elevated ESR, and low‑titer ANA, despite negative dsDNA and ENA, leading to steroid treatment. | "Based on the available evidence, a diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) was made by a rheumatologist, and treatment with steroids was commenced."
3. Multiple sclerosis was considered due to visual loss and sensory deficits, but MRI showed atypical extensive white‑matter lesions and CSF was normal, making MS unlikely. | "MRI scan of the brain showed extensive white matter abnormalities not typical of multiple sclerosis, and no abnormalities were detected in CSF examination."
4. Neuromyelitis optica was entertained because of optic involvement and white‑matter changes, yet aquaporin‑4 antibodies were only modestly elevated and the clinical picture did not fulfill diagnostic criteria. | "Antibodies against … aquaporin‑4 were tested, and all were 2‑4 fold above the reference range."
5. Infectious etiologies (syphilis, mycobacteria, Borrelia, EBV, CMV, HTLV, herpes‑6) were systematically excluded by serology and CSF studies. | "Blood and CSF examination showed no evidence of bacterial and viral infection including syphilis, mycobacteria, borrelia, EBV, CMV, HTLV, and herpes type‑6."
6. Celiac disease was ruled out because tissue transglutaminase IgG/IgA antibodies were normal and duodenal biopsies lacked villous atrophy or increased intra‑epithelial lymphocytes. | "Both IgG and in particular IgA tested against tTg were within the normal range... Upper GI endoscopy and biopsy revealed normal histology and intraepithelial lymphocytes."
7. Nonceliac gluten sensitivity was supported by a broad IgG/IgA antibody response to multiple wheat proteins and peptides despite normal tTG, together with multisystem neurological manifestations that improved after gluten‑free diet. | "Comprehensive IgG and IgA panel ... revealed IgG against wheat antigens ... IgA antibodies were detected against wheat antigens ... both IgG and in particular IgA tested against tTg were within the normal range."

case_prompt: A 57‑year‑old African American man with a remote history of alcohol abuse was brought to the emergency department because of worsening memory. He was a poor historian and could not provide pertinent details. Vitals were within normal limits. He displayed a flat affect and scored 14/30 on the Mini‑Mental State Examination. Cranial nerves were intact. Motor strength was 5/5 in all muscle groups except 4+/5 in the left iliopsoas. Sensory testing revealed mildly reduced vibration and pinprick sensation in the bilateral feet. A Babinski reflex was present on the left, Romberg sign was positive, and gait was wide‑based. Urine toxicology was negative; blood alcohol level was <10 mg/dL. Laboratory studies were notable for HbA1c 5.4%, LDL 64 mg/dL, TSH 2.07 µIU/mL, vitamin B12 402 pg/mL, folate 13.6 ng/mL, and a negative HIV screen. MRI of the brain showed moderate leukoaraiosis and global volume loss. CTA revealed a right‑dominant vertebral artery, mild calcification of the cavernous segment of the left ICA without stenosis, and a hypoplastic A1 segment of the right ACA. Transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrated an ejection fraction of 50% with no patent foramen ovale, intracardiac shunt, or valvular abnormalities. Serum rapid plasma reagin was reactive at a 1 : 32 titer, and the specific treponemal MHA‑TP test was also reactive; antiphospholipid antibodies were negative. He received a single dose of intramuscular benzathine penicillin 2.4 million units for latent syphilis. Lumbar puncture yielded CSF glucose 69 mg/dL, protein 62.4 mg/dL, RBC 5 cells/mm³, and WBC 3 cells/mm³ (95 % lymphocytes, 5 % monocytes); Gram stain and culture were negative. CSF VDRL was reactive with a titer of 1 : 8, and he was started on intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G 3 million units every 4 hours for confirmed neurosyphilis.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Positive serum treponemal and non‑treponemal tests indicate systemic syphilis infection. | "His serum RPR was reactive (1 : 32 titer) along with a reactive MHA‑TP."
2. Reactive CSF VDRL confirms central nervous system involvement by Treponema pallidum, establishing neurosyphilis. | "CSF VDRL was reactive with a titer of 1 : 8."
3. Absence of HIV infection excludes HIV‑related opportunistic CNS disease. | "HIV screen negative."
4. Normal antiphospholipid antibodies and lack of cardiac shunt make antiphospholipid syndrome and paradoxical emboli unlikely. | "Patient had negative antiphospholipid antibody." and "no PFO or intracardiic shunt by bubble study."
5. CTA showed no significant arterial stenosis or occlusion to explain acute neurologic deficits, reducing likelihood of atherosclerotic large‑vessel stroke. | "Mild calcification of the cavernous segment of the left ICA without stenosis."
6. MRI findings of moderate leukoaraiosis and global atrophy are chronic changes, not acute infarction, supporting an infectious/inflammatory etiology rather than primary ischemic stroke. | "MRI of the brain showed moderate leukoaraiosis and global volume loss."
7. The focal left‑leg weakness, neglect, and dysarthria emerged after treatment, suggesting a Jarisch‑Herxheimer reaction rather than a new vascular event. | "Six hours after the first dose, patient was found on floor... new onset mild dysarthria."
8. Alternative infectious causes (e.g., bacterial meningitis) are excluded by negative Gram stain, culture, and low CSF WBC count. | "Gram stain and CSF culture were negative."

case_prompt:
A 36‑year‑old Hispanic man presented to the emergency department with a one‑week history of right groin pain. The pain was aching, rated 6–8/10, worsened by walking and relieved after about 10 minutes of rest. It had progressively intensified, producing a painful limp. He denied morning stiffness, rash, fever, back pain, or other joint complaints. He had taken occasional nonsteroidal anti‑inflammatory drugs with minimal relief.

He also reported subtle left‑sided weakness of the upper and lower extremities that began three years earlier and had slowly progressed, without causing functional limitation, falls, incontinence, or pain. An MRI of the brain obtained two years prior was reported as normal.

On examination, the right hip showed no erythema, swelling, or inguinal lymphadenopathy. Passive range of motion was limited and painful, especially forced internal rotation; the “log roll” and straight‑leg raise tests elicited pain. Bilateral hyperpigmentation from the knees to the toes and mild pitting edema of the lower extremities were noted; peripheral pulses were palpable.

Cranial nerve testing revealed a left spinal accessory nerve deficit (inability to shrug the left shoulder) and left hypoglossal nerve involvement (tongue fasciculation with deviation to the left). The remaining cranial nerves were intact and meningeal signs were absent.

Motor testing demonstrated left‑sided upper and lower extremity weakness (4/5) with exaggerated deep‑tendon reflexes, increased tone, a positive Babinski sign, and ankle clonus. Right‑sided strength was normal. Sensory examination showed loss of vibration and position sense in the left lower extremity and pain‑temperature deficits in the left arm and a cape‑like distribution across the shoulders and upper torso (anteriorly to T2, posteriorly to L1). Rectal tone was normal.

Laboratory studies were unremarkable: serum RPR and VDRL for syphilis were negative; chemistry panel, vitamin B12, folate, and complete blood count were within normal limits.

Plain radiograph of the right hip was normal. MRI of the right hip demonstrated a wedge‑shaped subcortical area of enhancement with adjacent bone‑marrow edema in the posterior aspect of the femoral head, suggesting either avascular necrosis or early changes of a neurogenic joint.

MRI of the cervical and thoracic spine showed a 9 mm inferior displacement of the cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum, compressing the craniocervical junction, together with extensive syringohydromyelia of the cervical and thoracic cord.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Avascular necrosis of the femoral head was considered because of subcortical enhancement and marrow edema on hip MRI. | "MRI of the right hip joint showed a wedge shaped subcortical enhancement with adjacent bone marrow edema ... suggestive of avascular necrosis ..."
2. Charcot arthropathy secondary to underlying neurologic disease was considered as an alternative explanation for the hip findings. | "... suggestive of avascular necrosis or early radiological signs Charcot arthropathy considering the patient's underlying neurological disease."
3. Neurosyphilis was evaluated given the cranial nerve deficits, but serologic testing was negative. | "Serological tests for syphilis, that included serum RPR and VDRL, were negative ..."
4. The characteristic tonsillar herniation on spinal MRI identified a structural hindbrain abnormality, differentiating it from other causes of progressive unilateral weakness such as demyelinating disease or peripheral neuropathy. | "MRI of the cervical and thoracic spine ... showed a 9 mm inferior herniation of the cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum, compressing the craniocervical junction ... and extensive cervical and thoracic spinal cord syringohydromyelia."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case’s definitive diagnosis is neurosyphilis, which belongs to the SELECTED disease list as “syphilis”.  
2. Breakpoint: Include all presenting symptoms, psychiatric findings, neurologic signs, prior viral encephalitis label, antipsychotic treatment, and the positive serum syphilis serologies (VDRL, TPA, TRUST). Stop before the lumbar‑puncture CSF results and before the initiation of penicillin therapy, so that the target diagnosis can be inferred without explicit confirmation.  
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished syphilis from viral encephalitis, primary psychiatric illness, drug‑induced parkinsonism, and HIV infection by (a) persistent neuro‑psychiatric decline despite antipsychotics, (b) positive treponemal serology (TPA, TRUST), (c) CSF VDRL reactivity confirming neurosyphilis, and (d) dramatic clinical improvement after appropriate penicillin therapy.
case_prompt:
A 15‑year‑old girl was admitted in January 2012 because she had become increasingly nervous and withdrawn since October 2011. Her mother reported that the girl no longer communicated with others, showed restlessness and whole‑body tremors, could not care for herself, and stopped bathing. She had a several‑day fever in October 2011; chest X‑ray and abdominal ultrasound were normal. She was diagnosed with viral encephalitis at a local hospital and received a short, unspecified treatment. She was then transferred to a local mental hospital where brain MRI showed mild atrophy; she was prescribed sulpiride (max 1.2 g/day) and benzhexol (max 8 mg/day) without improvement, and her tremors worsened.  

On admission she exhibited visual hallucinations, persecutory delusions, flattening of affect, disorganized thought, and four‑limb rigidity. Neurology was consulted for the tremors and rigidity, and all antipsychotics were stopped. The neurologist recommended repeat MRI, lumbar puncture, and a Venereal Disease Research Laboratory (VDRL) serum test because of rare entities such as HIV infection. Serum testing was positive for Treponema pallidum antibody (TPA); TRUST titer was 1:4; and the T. pallidum particle‑agglutination test was positive. The mother later disclosed that the patient had been raped in 2009.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Viral encephalitis considered initially because of prior fever and a normal chest X‑ray/ultrasound, but lack of improvement and progressive neuro‑psychiatric decline argued against it | “She was diagnosed as having viral encephalitis at the local hospital… It was found that the patient's condition did not improve, and her tremors became increasingly more severe.”  
2. Primary psychiatric disorder (e.g., schizophrenia) suggested by hallucinations, delusions, and flat affect, yet the presence of rigidity, tremor, and lack of response to antipsychotics made this unlikely | “After admission, we found that the patient had visual hallucinations, persecutory delusions… four‑limb rigidity… we also stopped all antipsychotic treatments.”  
3. Drug‑induced parkinsonism from sulpiride/benzhexol considered because of rigidity and tremor, but symptoms persisted and worsened despite dosage adjustments, and antipsychotics were discontinued without improvement | “She was prescribed sulpiride… and benzhexol… However, it was found that the patient's condition did not improve, and her tremors became increasingly more severe.”  
4. HIV infection entertained as a rare cause of neuro‑psychiatric manifestations, prompting VDRL testing; negative HIV work‑up (not directly stated) and positive treponemal serology shifted focus | “The neurologist suggested… VDRL serum test under the suspicion of some rare diseases, such as human immunodeficiency virus infection.”  
5. Neurosyphilis (target diagnosis) supported by positive serum treponemal tests (TPA, TRUST, particle‑agglutination) and compatible neuro‑psychiatric picture, later confirmed by reactive CSF VDRL | “The VDRL serum test yielded positive results with respect to the T. pallidum antibody (TPA)… we then found a titer of 1:4 with respect to the toluidine red unheated serum test (TRUST)… The patient’ mother finally confessed that the patient had been raped in 2009.”

case_prompt: Mrs. ZNA, a 29‑year‑old Malay housewife, Gravida 4 Para 2+1, presented for antenatal booking at a primary‑care clinic with a one‑week history of polyuria, polydipsia, and lethargy. An ultrasound dated the fetus at 11 weeks. A fasting blood glucose of 11.0 mmol/L led to a diagnosis of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) and she was referred for further management. She also complained of genital itching with a whitish vaginal discharge; a high vaginal swab grew Candida, and she was treated accordingly. Routine labs were performed: hepatitis B and HIV serologies were negative, but the rapid plasma reagin (RPR) was reactive at a 1 : 16 titre, and a Syphilis IgG test was positive. diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Positive RPR at a higher titre than the previous 1 : 8 suggests active infection or reinfection | “The serology tests for hepatitis B and HIV were negative. However, the rapid plasma reagin (RPR) was reactive at 1:16 titration.”
2. Positive treponemal IgG confirms presence of treponemal antibodies, supporting a diagnosis of syphilis | “The diagnosis of syphilis was confirmed by a positive Syphilis IgG result.”
3. History of prior treated syphilis with a lower titre, now increased, indicates reinfection rather than persistent serology | “She admitted to the treatment of syphilis during her previous pregnancy in 2010… previous syphilis record showed the RPR titre was 1:8 but no subsequent follow‑up.”

2. Best Breakpoint: Stop the case presentation just before the laboratory results that confirm syphilis are disclosed. Include presentation, ocular examination, imaging, and the list of ordered tests, but omit the sentence reporting reactive RPR and FTA‑Abs.

case_prompt: A 39‑year‑old healthy Caucasian female from rural Nebraska presented with a 2‑week history of bilateral flashes and left eye pain associated with redness in both eyes. She denied prior eye discharge, trauma, surgeries, or chronic medical conditions. Visual acuity was 20/20 bilaterally. Slit‑lamp examination showed 1+ conjunctival injection in the right eye and 2+ in the left; corneas were clear. Anterior chamber cells were 0.5+ (right) and 2+ (left) with non‑granulomatous flare. Pupils were equal, reactive, and without RAPD. The left eye had trace nuclear sclerosis, pigment deposits in the crystalline lens, and 1+ vitreous cell. Intraocular pressure was normal. Fundus exam revealed mild optic disc edema (right > left) with a cup‑to‑disc ratio of 0.3, and a subtle peripheral retinal elevation with a well‑defined area of whitening in the left eye; macula and vessels were unremarkable. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated hyperfluorescence corresponding to the peripheral whitening with perivascular leakage in the left eye and optic disc leakage in both eyes. B‑scan of the superonasal quadrant showed no corresponding elevation or abnormality. OCT of the lesion revealed retinal infiltration with hyperreflective dots. Anterior chamber paracentesis was performed at the slit lamp and sent for herpes simplex virus (HSV) and varicella zoster virus (VZV) PCR and gram stain. Additional laboratory tests ordered included CBC, CMP, ESR, CRP, syphilis serology, HSV and VZV titers, HIV antibodies, chest X‑ray, and MRI of the brain and orbit with and without contrast. The patient was not treated with steroids while awaiting laboratory results.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Viral uveitis (HSV or VZV) considered due to anterior chamber inflammation; PCR testing was obtained to evaluate this possibility. | "Anterior chamber paracentesis... sent for herpes simplex virus (HSV) and varicella zoster virus (VZV) PCR and gram stain."
2. HIV‑related ocular disease considered as a potential cause of bilateral uveitis; excluded by negative serology. | "HIV antibodies were negative"
3. Syphilitic uveitis confirmed by serologic evidence of active infection; reactive RPR and FTA‑Abs established the diagnosis. | "rapid plasma regain (RPR) and fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption (FTA-Abs) were both reactive."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient has laboratory‑confirmed syphilis (positive VDRL and TPHA) and neurological signs consistent with neurosyphilis. Syphilis is on the 21‑disease SELECTED list, so it is the primary target diagnosis. The report also describes a concurrent squamous cell carcinoma of the palate, which is OUT_OF_SCOPE, but the teaching focus will be on diagnosing syphilis.
2. Ideal Breakpoint: Include the chief complaint, past history (penile ulcer scar, nasal twang, palate ulcer), physical examination findings (palatal perforation, tongue leukoplakia, cervical lymphadenopathy, pyramidal signs), and initial laboratory data (elevated ESR, serum VDRL 1:1, TPHA positive, CSF VDRL negative, HIV negative). Stop before describing the histopathology of the palatal lesion, so the learner must rely on clinical and serologic information to arrive at syphilis.
3. Author's Analytic Distinctions: The authors used serologic testing (VDRL, TPHA) to confirm treponemal infection, correlated the neurological findings with possible neurosyphilis, and performed biopsies to rule out or identify a malignant process that could mimic the oral lesions. They highlighted the coexistence of carcinoma but emphasized that the systemic features were explained by syphilis.
case_prompt: A 74‑year‑old man presented with a long‑standing nasal twang and nasal regurgitation. Over the past month he noted a swelling over the palate that had ulcerated. He recalled a penile ulcer at age 18 following a premarital exposure. Examination revealed a 1 cm × 1 cm white patch on the ventral tongue, a 1.5 cm × 1 cm perforation of the hard palate with indurated, sloughing margins, and a 2 cm × 2 cm atrophic scar on the prepuce. Cervical nodes were firm to hard. Neurological assessment showed bilateral pyramidal signs. Laboratory studies demonstrated a raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate, a serum VDRL titre of 1:1, and a positive treponema pallidum hemagglutination assay. Cerebrospinal fluid VDRL and HIV tests were negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Chronic oral ulceration with palate perforation raises suspicion for granulomatous infection; the history of a prior penile ulcer and a preputial scar points toward prior treponemal disease. | "He gives a history of penile ulcer at the age of 18... An atrophic scar of 2 cm × 2 cm was present over the prepuce."
2. Positive non‑treponemal (VDRL 1:1) and treponemal (TPHA) serology confirm active syphilis infection. | "His erythrocyte sedimentation rate was raised, venereal disease research laboratory (VDRL) was 1:1 and treponema pallidum hemagglutination assay was positive."
3. Bilateral pyramidal signs suggest central nervous system involvement, compatible with neurosyphilis, especially when serology is positive and CSF VDRL is negative (early neurosyphilis may have false‑negative CSF VDRL). | "Neurological evaluation revealed features suggestive of bilateral pyramidal signs."
4. Elevated ESR is a nonspecific marker of inflammation supporting an active infectious process. | "His erythrocyte sedimentation rate was raised."
5. HIV infection can predispose to oral lesions and neurosyphilis; a negative CSF HIV test makes HIV‑related immunosuppression unlikely. | "His cerebrospinal fluid VDRL and HIV were negative."
6. Squamous cell carcinoma of the palate was considered because of ulcerated oral lesions; however, the serologic profile and systemic findings are more coherently explained by syphilis, with carcinoma representing a concurrent but separate pathology. | "Biopsy from palatal lesion showed squamous cells with nuclear hyperchromasia and high mitotic index extending beyond the basement membrane."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The newborn’s condition (bilateral microphthalmia/anophthalmia) is not among the 21 SELECTED infectious diseases; therefore the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.  
2. Best Breakpoint: Include the prenatal maternal history, delivery details, initial ophthalmologic findings (bilateral palpebral occlusion, entropion, small palpebral fissures, empty reduced orbital cavities), and the decision to obtain extensive imaging studies, but **exclude** the imaging results that explicitly describe microphthalmia and anophthalmia. This provides enough information for learners to formulate a differential and anticipate imaging without revealing the final diagnosis.

A 36‑year‑old man was brought to the emergency department with a 5‑day history of sharp pain, redness, and photophobia in his right eye. He denied any eye trauma or contact lens use. Eight years earlier he had experienced four mild episodes of unilateral alternating peripheral ulcerative keratitis (PUK), more frequent in winter. His past medical history was notable for chronic hepatitis C infection of at least 10 years’ duration and prior intravenous drug use (cocaine, heroin), discontinued after incarceration and now on methadone 45 mg/day. There was no history of connective‑tissue disease.

On examination, best‑corrected visual acuity was 20/30 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. Oculomotility was normal; the right eye was mildly painful. Biomicroscopy of the right eye showed deep conjunctival hyperemia, a ring‑shaped peripheral ulcer extending from 3 to 6 o’clock with a dense white stromal infiltrate, and an adjacent area of mild diffuse non‑necrotizing scleritis. No signs of ocular rosacea or blepharitis were present. Tyndall and flare were absent. Intraocular pressure was 17 mm Hg bilaterally. The left eye was unremarkable except for two discrete peripheral ring‑like leucomas sparing the limbus, without thinning. Posterior segments were normal in both eyes.

He was started on topical ofloxacin 0.3 % every 2 hours, oxytetracycline ointment three times daily, cyclopentolate 1 % twice daily, and artificial tears. After five days, because of lack of improvement, oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day was added, leading to marked clinical response. Within two weeks his visual acuity returned to 20/20 and the anterior‑segment inflammation resolved.

Laboratory work‑up was negative for connective‑tissue disease antibodies (antinuclear antibodies, anti‑double‑strand DNA, ANCA, rheumatoid factor, liver‑kidney microsomal type 1, anti‑SSA/Ro, anti‑SSB/La) and complement levels were normal. Serologies for syphilis, HIV, and hepatitis B virus were negative, and interferon‑γ release assay was nondiagnostic. Complete blood count, urinalysis, and liver function tests were within normal limits except for a two‑fold elevation in hepatic transaminases. Hepatitis C viral load was >2.6 million IU/mL (genotype 1a). Cryoglobulin screening revealed mixed type 2 cryoglobulins without rheumatoid‑factor activity (86 µg/mL).

1. Infectious keratitis (bacterial, viral, fungal) considered due to stromal infiltrate; excluded because there was no response to intensive topical antibiotics and cultures/serologies were negative. | "After a 5‑day course of topical ofloxacin … lack of clinical improvement … systemic corticosteroids … with good clinical response."
2. Syphilis‑related ocular disease considered; excluded by negative serology. | "Infectious serology for syphilis … was also negative."
3. HIV‑associated ocular manifestations considered; excluded by negative HIV serology. | "Infectious serology for … HIV … was also negative."
4. Autoimmune connective‑tissue diseases (e.g., granulomatosis with polyangiitis, rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus) considered because PUK is a known manifestation; excluded by comprehensive negative autoimmune panel and normal complement levels. | "Systemic workout was negative for CTD (antinuclear antibodies, anti‑double strand‑DNA, ANCAs, Rheumatoid factor, …), with normal complement levels."
