case_prompt:
A 43‑year‑old Hispanic man presented with a 2‑week history of frontal headache, fever, nausea, and vomiting. Past history was notable for herpes zoster ophthalmicus two years earlier. Vital signs on admission were within normal limits. Neurologic examination showed mild cervical stiffness and pain with neck motion; no focal deficits were observed.

Laboratory studies revealed a normal white blood cell count (6.7 k/µL), anemia (hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL), and a normal platelet count (172 K/µL). A rapid HIV test was reactive; CD4 count was 83 cells/µL and HIV viral load 51,080 copies/mL. Serum rapid plasma reagin (RPR) was reactive with a titer of 1:1024, and CSF VDRL was also reactive, leading to a diagnosis of neurosyphilis. Initial CSF analysis showed 73 leukocytes/mm³ (96 % lymphocytes), protein 112 mg/dL, and glucose 37 mg/dL. The patient was started on ceftriaxone, vancomycin, and acyclovir, then switched to intravenous penicillin for neurosyphilis.

Three days later his headache and neck pain worsened, accompanied by nausea, vomiting, slurred speech, and visual hallucinations. MRI demonstrated T2/FLAIR hyperintensity involving the left middle cerebellar peduncle, vermis, and right cerebellar hemisphere. Repeat lumbar puncture showed 267 leukocytes/mm³ (74 % lymphocytes), protein 94 mg/dL, glucose 8 mg/dL, and a positive CSF cryptococcal antigen titer of 1:640. India ink stain and fungal culture were negative. He was treated with amphotericin B lipid complex and flucytosine for cryptococcal meningitis, later transitioned to oral fluconazole.

After completing induction therapy and a two‑week course of intravenous penicillin, he was discharged stable. Two weeks later he began antiretroviral therapy (tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine and darunavir‑ritonavir). At one‑month follow‑up he reported malaise, dizziness, slurred speech, and left‑hand clumsiness. Examination revealed an ataxic gait and saccadic eye movements. Repeat MRI showed improvement of supratentorial leptomeningeal enhancement but progression of posterior‑fossa leptomeningeal enhancement and T2/FLAIR signal abnormality.

He was readmitted; opening pressure on lumbar puncture was elevated (26 cm H₂O). CSF analysis revealed 2 leukocytes, normal glucose and protein, rare encapsulated yeasts on India ink, and a decreased cryptococcal antigen titer of 1:80. He was restarted on amphotericin B and flucytosine for a possible relapse of cryptococcal meningitis.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Neurosyphilis considered initially because serum RPR and CSF VDRL were reactive with high titers. | "Serum RPR was reactive with a titer of 1 : 1024 dils. VDRL from CSF was also reactive."
2. Cryptococcal meningitis diagnosed after CSF cryptococcal antigen returned strongly positive (1 : 640) and the patient improved with antifungal therapy. | "Cryptococcus antigen from CSF was positive with a titer of 1 : 640 dils... He was started on amphotericin B lipid complex and flucytosine for cryptococcal meningitis."
3. Bacterial meningitis deemed less likely given lymphocytic predominance, low glucose, and lack of response to broad‑spectrum antibiotics, plus negative Gram stain and cultures. | "CSF analysis revealed high WBC count (73 leukocytes/mm3) with lymphocytic predominance (96%)."
4. Relapse of cryptococcal meningitis suspected on readmission because of persistent symptoms, elevated opening pressure, and presence of rare yeasts on India ink despite previous therapy. | "Opening pressure was elevated (26 cm H2O). India ink stain revealed rare encapsulated yeasts."
5. Tuberculosis meningitis entertained due to progressive posterior‑fossa leptomeningeal enhancement on MRI, near‑sterile CSF (2 WBC), normal glucose and protein, and falling cryptococcal antigen titers, suggesting another pathogen. | "Repeat MRI showed improvement of leptomeningeal enhancement supratentorially but progression of leptomeningeal enhancement and T2/FLAIR signal abnormality within the posterior fossa."
6. Definitive diagnosis of tuberculous meningitis was confirmed when CSF culture grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis. | "CSF culture from recent hospital admission grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis."

case_prompt:
A 51‑year‑old man presented with a two‑ to three‑month history of intermittent akinesia of the hands. His occupation required frequent long‑ and short‑haul flights. The remainder of his history was unremarkable.

Physical examination demonstrated cogwheel rigidity of the upper limbs and impaired vibration sense limited to the upper body, extending caudally to the level of the anterior superior iliac spine. He was positive on both the Unterberger and Romberg tests. Gait was normal; there was no tremor, nystagmus, or pain. Long‑term memory appeared intact. The remainder of the neurological exam was normal.

Routine blood tests were insignificant. Analysis of genomic DNA from leukocytes by gas‑liquid chromatography revealed the presence of epoxy‑oleic acid DNA adducts, which were localized to the N‑formyl peptide receptors using DNA microarrays. Comprehensive testing for other possible causes—including gonorrhoea, hepatitis B core antibodies, hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C antibodies, HTLV‑1, IgG and IgM antibodies to syphilis, antibodies to Chlamydia species, HIV‑1 and HIV‑2 p24 antigen, and VDRL—were all negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Infectious etiologies such as syphilis, HIV, hepatitis B/C, HTLV‑1, gonorrhoea, and chlamydia were considered but excluded by negative serologic testing. | "testing for gonorrhoea, hepatitis B core antibodies, hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C antibodies, HTLV‑1, IgG and IgM antibodies to syphilis, ... antibodies to chlamydia species, as well as the HIV duo ... and VDRL tests" were negative.
2. Routine laboratory evaluation failed to reveal metabolic or hematologic abnormalities that could explain the movement disorder. | "Routine blood tests were insignificant."
3. The detection of epoxy‑oleic acid DNA adducts localized to N‑formyl peptide receptors suggested a toxin‑related pathogenesis rather than a primary neurodegenerative process. | "Investigation for DNA adducts ... showed the presence of epoxy‑oleic acid, which was localised to the N‑formyl peptide receptors (FPRs) using DNA microarrays."
4. The clinical constellation of cogwheel rigidity, akinesia, and selective vibration loss is characteristic of a parkinsonian syndrome, supporting the diagnosis of toxin‑induced parkinsonism after other causes were excluded. | "Physical examination revealed cogwheel rigidity in the upper limbs and impaired vibration sense..."

A 61‑year‑old Vietnamese man with coronary artery disease, peripheral vascular disease, and abdominal aortic aneurysm underwent axillary‑bifemoral bypass and bilateral lower‑extremity thromboembolectomy. Preoperatively he developed malaise, productive cough, and a 5‑lb weight loss over five weeks. He smoked, worked as an electronics engineer, denied night sweats, tuberculosis exposure, recent travel, or animal contact, although he noted a cattle field along his route to work.

Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate >120 mm/hr, leukocytosis 18.8 × 10⁹/L (82% neutrophils), and hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL. Chest CT revealed bilateral ground‑glass opacities, most prominent in the right lower lobe, without a mass lesion. QuantiFERON‑TB test was negative, as were serologic tests for Treponema pallidum, Cryptococcus, Histoplasma, Coccidioides, and Brucella. Because malignancy remained a concern, a second CT‑guided core biopsy one week later showed identical necrotic tissue with no evidence of malignancy.

2. Malignancy considered but excluded because two separate core biopsies revealed only necrotic tissue and no malignant cells. | "first biopsy revealed ischemic necrosis ... no evidence of malignancy" and "second ... showed no evidence of malignancy."

7. Mycobacterial infection excluded by negative acid‑fast bacilli stain. | "AFB ... stains were negative for acid‑fast bacilli."

case_prompt:
A 57‑year‑old Chinese male presented to the emergency department with transient left upper and lower limb weakness, left facial droop, and slurred speech lasting about 30 minutes. He denied prior similar events. Past medical history was notable for HIV infection on HAART for four years; he was a nonsmoker and had no family history of stroke.

On arrival, vital signs were stable with blood pressure 165/98 mmHg. Physical examination showed dysarthria, left facial droop, and left‑sided pronator drift; NIHSS score was 3. Non‑contrast brain CT demonstrated an acute right middle cerebral artery (MCA) territorial infarct with mild right frontoparietal mass effect (ASPECTS 5). Thrombolysis was not administered.

He was admitted to the stroke unit and started on aspirin 100 mg and atorvastatin 40 mg. His HAART regimen included abacavir, efavirenz, and lamivudine; the last CD4 count (one year prior) was 533 cells/µL, and HIV viral load performed a week earlier was detectable but <20 copies/mL.

Initial labs were unremarkable: normal ECG, troponin, glucose, urea, electrolytes, liver function, coagulation profile, and complete blood count. Lipid panel showed LDL‑c 2.28 mmol/L; HbA1c <4.3 %. Blood pressure readings during admission remained normal, and no antihypertensive therapy was needed. Chest X‑ray, transthoracic echocardiogram, bilateral carotid Doppler ultrasound, and 24‑hour Holter monitor were all normal.

MRI of the brain confirmed the right MCA territory infarct. Time‑of‑flight MRA suggested mild stenosis of the mid‑distal right M1 segment of the MCA without flow limitation. Given the lack of conventional cardiovascular risk factors, a thrombophilia and autoimmune panel was ordered (results not detailed). CT angiography of the circle of Willis showed bilateral moderate luminal irregularity in the M2 branches of the MCAs (more pronounced on the right) and less pronounced changes in the A2 segments of the anterior cerebral arteries, raising suspicion for small‑ to medium‑vessel vasculitis.

A lumbar puncture was performed. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed 203 white blood cells (90 % lymphocytes) and elevated protein at 0.81 g/L (reference 0.10–0.40 g/L).

1. Large‑vessel atherosclerotic stroke considered but unlikely because the patient had no traditional cardiovascular risk factors, LDL‑c was modest, and imaging showed only mild MCA stenosis without significant flow limitation. | "In view of the absence of known cardiovascular risk factors... CT angiography... raising suspicion for small to medium vessel vasculitis."
2. Cardioembolic source evaluated and excluded by normal ECG, troponin, transthoracic echocardiography, and 24‑hour Holter monitoring. | "His chest radiograph, transthoracic echocardiography, Doppler ultrasound of bilateral carotids, and 24‑hour Holter monitoring were normal."
3. Hypertensive small‑vessel disease deemed unlikely due to normal blood pressure readings throughout admission and lack of antihypertensive therapy. | "His subsequent inpatient blood pressure readings were normal and antihypertensive agents were not required."
4. Hypercoagulable or thrombophilic states investigated; although results are not detailed, the work‑up was performed because of the atypical presentation. | "In view of the absence of known cardiovascular risk factors, a thrombophilia and autoimmune workup was performed."
5. Primary inflammatory vasculitis (e.g., primary CNS vasculitis, autoimmune vasculitis) considered; imaging suggested vasculitic changes, but autoimmune work‑up was pending and CSF findings of lymphocytic pleocytosis with elevated protein are common in infectious vasculitis. | "CT angiography... raising suspicion for small to medium vessel vasculitis."

Infectious vasculitis, specifically neurosyphilis, became the leading diagnosis after CSF showed lymphocytic pleocytosis and high protein, findings compatible with neurosyphilis, and would be confirmed by a positive CSF VDRL (not yet disclosed at this breakpoint). | "A lumbar puncture was performed, which showed 203 white blood cells (WBC) with lymphocytes accounting for 90%... case_prompt:
A 66‑year‑old Japanese woman presented with bilateral blurred vision that began 4 months earlier. She had initially been diagnosed with conjunctivitis and treated with antibacterial eye drops. During that period she developed general fatigue and lumbar pain, leading to a diagnosis of bilateral exudative pleural effusions at a private clinic and subsequent referral to our hospital. Past medical history was notable for breast cancer treated 2 years earlier; however, pleural fluid cytology was negative for malignant cells and imaging (CT, MRI) showed no evidence of recurrence. Pleural fluid analysis showed an exudate with specific gravity 1.304, cell count 397 /µL (neutrophils 4 %, lymphocytes 62 %, macrophages 34 %), LDH 105 U/L, ADA 8.7 U/L, total protein 4.4 g/dL, rheumatoid factor < 10 IU/mL, antinuclear antibodies (+‑), and sterile cultures. Orthopedic evaluation identified multiple spondylitis; MRI of the spine and bone scintigraphy demonstrated lesions consistent with SAPHO syndrome, which was also supported by longstanding palmoplantar pustulosis. She was started on antibiotics and NSAIDs.

Seven days after admission, ophthalmology evaluation revealed best‑corrected visual acuity of 0.6 in each eye, intraocular pressures of 18 mm Hg (right) and 16 mm Hg (left), and shallow anterior chambers without keratic precipitates or cells. Fundoscopy showed bilateral annular choroidal detachment with exudative serous retinal detachment involving the macula. Optical coherence tomography demonstrated sub‑retinal fluid, a wavy retinal pigment epithelium line, and thickened choroid in both eyes. Fluorescein angiography displayed multiple areas of pinpoint dye leakage from the RPE, and indocyanine green angiography revealed multiple zones of choroidal hypoperfusion. B‑scan ultrasonography confirmed choroidal detachment without scleral thickening or masses.

Differential diagnosis showed no evidence of diseases such as uveal effusion syndrome, posterior scleritis, or choroidal metastasis, and laboratory markers of other types of uveitis including sarcoidosis, syphilis, and tuberculosis were negative. Moreover, autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody‑associated vasculitis were considered unlikely because specific antibodies were absent.

2. Posterior scleritis can mimic choroidal detachment, yet B‑scan ultrasonography did not reveal the characteristic “T sign” or scleral involvement. | "...posterior scleritis... B‑scan ultrasonography confirmed choroidal detachment with no associated scleral thickening..."
3. Choroidal metastasis was excluded because cytology of pleural fluid was negative for malignant cells and systemic imaging showed no neoplastic lesions. | "...choroidal metastasis... no malignant cells were observed in cytology examination, and no malignancy was detected by CT and MRI."
4. Sarcoidosis can produce granulomatous uveitis, but laboratory markers (e.g., ACE) were not elevated and specific tests were negative. | "laboratory markers of other types of uveitis including sarcoidosis... were negative."
5. Syphilis is a known cause of posterior uveitis; serologic testing was negative, ruling it out. | "...syphilis... were negative."

Visual acuity was doubtful light perception in OD and 3/60 in OS. The right eye was phthisical. Anterior segment exam of OS showed aphakia and a greyish pupillary reflex. Indirect ophthalmoscopy demonstrated a total rhegmatogenous retinal detachment in OS; intra‑ocular pressure (IOP) in OS was 10 mm Hg.

Pre‑surgical laboratory screening (complete blood count, differential, plasma glucose, hepatitis B, HIV, syphilis) was unremarkable. She underwent 23‑gauge trans‑conjunctival retinal detachment repair with 360° endolaser, silicone oil endotamponade (1000 cSt), and 7‑0 polyglactin sutures placed in a shoelace pattern.

Five days post‑operatively she returned with left‑eye pain; visual acuity had improved to 6/60 and IOP was 22 mm Hg. Examination revealed localized episcleral congestion and white discharge over the sclerotomy site and lid margins, without frank suppuration. A high index of suspicion for infection was maintained and a scleral abscess was suspected; samples were sent for microbial analysis. Empiric topical antibiotics (moxifloxacin 0.5% six times daily, tobramycin 0.3% six times daily), topical prednisolone acetate 1% hourly, and timolol 0.5% twice daily were started.

Microbial analysis showed no organisms on microscopy or culture on blood, chocolate, and Sabouraud agar, nor in infusion broths. Repeat hematologic studies (CBC, plasma glucose, renal function) remained unremarkable.

Infectious scleral abscess (bacterial) considered because of postoperative pain, white discharge, and episcleral congestion; ruled out by sterile cultures and lack of organism growth. | "Microbial analysis showed no organisms on microscopy or culture on agar plates (blood, chocolate, and Sabroud's) and infusion broths."

4. Systemic autoimmune scleritis (e.g., granulomatosis with polyangiitis) considered but not supported by normal systemic labs and lack of systemic symptoms. | "Hematologic investigations (complete blood count, plasma glucose and renal function tests) were unremarkable."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case describes a primary cutaneous CD30+ lymphoproliferative disorder (lymphomatoid papulosis type A), which is not among the 21 SELECTED diseases; therefore the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.
2. Breakpoint: Include all information up to but not including the authors’ statement of the proposed diagnosis. This comprises the patient’s presentation, physical findings, extensive infectious serologies, biopsy histology, and immunophenotypic results, allowing the learner to synthesize a diagnosis without the authors’ explicit conclusion.
3. Analytic Distinctions: The authors differentiated lymphomatoid papulosis from other cutaneous lymphomas, sarcoidosis, histiocytosis, and infectious mimics by (a) the presence of CD30⁺ (>75%) T‑cell infiltrate with CD3⁺, CD4⁺, MUM1⁺ phenotype; (b) high Ki‑67 (~80%) yet epidermal sparing and psoriasiform hyperplasia; (c) negative cultures and serologies for infectious agents; and (d) lack of systemic involvement on imaging and bone‑marrow studies.
case_prompt: A 27‑year‑old man with a history of expanding skin lesions was referred after a 7‑day course of oral cefuroxime failed to improve the lesions. Examination revealed a 3 × 3 cm nodular, incipiently ulcerated, crumbly lesion on the extensor surface of the left thigh and numerous dome‑shaped, reddish, smooth papules and nodules on the trunk, limbs, neck, periorbital area, and genitalia; some sites showed perilesional scaling. Palms, soles, and mucous membranes were spared. The patient reported several months of fatigue but no consistent systemic B symptoms. Differential diagnoses considered included lymphomatoid papulosis, other cutaneous lymphomas, sarcoidosis, histiocytosis, and cutaneous infections (leishmaniasis, atypical mycobacterial infection, bacillary angiomatosis). Laboratory testing showed an elevated Bartonella quintana titer (1/80); all other serologies (CMV, EBV, HIV, HBV, HCV, Toxoplasma, Treponema pallidum, Leishmania, Coxiella burnetii, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, Quantiferon, RF, IgA, IgG, IgM, C3, C4, ANA, ENA) were negative. Ophthalmologic and ENT evaluations were normal. Two skin biopsies (ulcerated thigh lesion and non‑ulcerated back lesion) yielded negative bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial cultures. Histology demonstrated a diffuse lymphocytic infiltrate in the reticular dermis composed of small, medium, and large lymphocytes with occasional anaplastic nuclei, interspersed neutrophils and histiocytes, and spared epidermis with psoriasiform hyperplasia. Immunophenotyping showed CD3⁺, CD30⁺ (>75%), CD4⁺, MUM1⁺, CD8⁻, ALK‑1⁻, CD15⁻, and TIA‑1‑/⁺ (≈20%); Ki‑67 was ~80%. Peripheral blood smear, peripheral blood immunophenotype, and bone‑marrow biopsy were unremarkable, and CT of neck, thorax, and abdomen showed no lymphadenopathy.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Lymphomatoid papulosis considered because of multiple recurrent papulonodular lesions with CD30⁺ T‑cell infiltrate and high Ki‑67, while epidermis is spared; | "Immunophenotypically the lymphocytes were CD3+..., CD30+ (>75%...), CD4+, MUM1+, CD8-, ALK-1-, CD15-, ... Ki-67 ~80%."
2. Other primary cutaneous CD30⁺ T‑cell lymphomas excluded by the presence of anaplastic nuclei, diffuse infiltrate, and lack of systemic disease; | "CT‑scan of neck‑thorax‑abdomen showed no lymphadenopathy" and "Peripheral blood smear... normal."
3. Sarcoidosis ruled out by absence of non‑caseating granulomas on histology and negative systemic imaging; | "Histology revealed a diffuse lymphocytic infiltration... no granulomatous pattern."
4. Histiocytosis excluded because histology lacked characteristic histiocyte proliferation and immunophenotype did not show CD1a or S100 positivity; | "Histology revealed a diffuse lymphocytic infiltration... accompanied by a variable number of neutrophils and histiocytes" but immunophenotype was CD30⁺ T‑cells, not histiocytic markers.
5. Cutaneous leishmaniasis excluded by negative Leishmania serology and lack of amastigotes on biopsy; | "serology for ... Leishmania ... were negative" and cultures were negative.
6. Atypical mycobacterial infection excluded by negative mycobacterial cultures and lack of granulomatous inflammation; | "Bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial cultures from the specimens were negative."
7. Bacillary angiomatosis excluded by negative Bartonella serology (titers low and no clinical response to doxycycline) and absence of vascular proliferative pattern; | "Laboratory examination revealed an increased serum title of Bartonella quintana (1/80) ... doxycycline ... with no change."
8. Viral infections (CMV, EBV, HIV, HBV, HCV, Toxoplasma) ruled out by negative serologies; | "serology for CMV, EBV, HIV, HBV, HCV, Toxoplasma... were negative."
final_diagnosis: primary cutaneous CD30+ lymphoproliferative disorder -> OUT_OF_SCOPE

case_prompt:
A 56‑year‑old man with seronegative rheumatoid arthritis (on abatacept and sulfasalazine), peripheral neuropathy, obstructive sleep apnea, and a right total hip arthroplasty performed 9 years earlier presented to clinic with a 3‑month history of malaise and low‑grade temperature (99 °F). He had returned 3 months earlier from a mission trip to Honduras. One month after returning he developed low‑grade fever, unintentional weight loss, night sweats, and mild congestion; a course of amoxicillin did not improve symptoms. Progressive right hip pain ensued. A bone scan was unremarkable. Fever rose to 103 °F, prompting hospital admission. The patient denied other travel, animal exposure, tobacco, or drug use; he drank only bottled water in Honduras.  

On examination the extremities were atraumatic, with mild discomfort on internal rotation of the right hip; otherwise the exam was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed WBC 6.3 K/µL, hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, ESR 25 mm/h, and normal liver transaminases. Extensive infectious work‑up was negative, including malaria smear/Ag, HIV Ag/Ab, syphilis Ab, Histoplasma Ag/Ab, Coccidioides serology, Cryptococcal Ag, Bartonella and Brucella IgG/IgM, T‑Spot TB, Chikungunya IgG, and two sets of blood cultures. Chest radiograph and echocardiogram were unremarkable. A two‑view hip radiograph showed the prosthesis without periprosthetic lucency or fracture. A tagged white‑blood‑cell scan demonstrated no increased uptake. MRI of the right hip (non‑contrast) revealed fluid collections medial to the lesser trochanter, interpreted as hematoma or pseudotumor.  

Joint aspiration yielded grossly purulent fluid. Gram stain showed no organisms. Routine bacterial cultures (aerobic and anaerobic) showed no growth after 5 days.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Common pyogenic prosthetic joint infection – considered because of purulent aspiration and fever, but routine aerobic/anaerobic cultures remained negative after 5 days. | "Aspirate routine culture was negative, with no growth at 5 days on aerobic and anaerobic culture."
2. Tuberculous prosthetic joint infection – plausible given weight loss, night sweats, immunosuppression, but T‑spot TB was negative. | "The following infection diagnostics were negative: … T spot TB …"
3. Fungal prosthetic infection – entertained due to immunosuppression, yet fungal cultures yielded no growth. | "Fungal cultures remained negative."
4. Brucellosis – considered given travel and systemic symptoms, but Brucella IgG/IgM were negative. | "Bartonella and Brucella IgG/IgM" (negative).
5. Histoplasmosis – possible endemic exposure, but Histoplasma serum Ag and Ab were negative. | "Histoplasma serum Ag and Ab" (negative).
6. Coccidioidomycosis, Cryptococcosis, Chikungunya – evaluated by serology; all were negative, making these etiologies unlikely. | "Coccidiodes serology, Cryptococcal serum Ag, … Chikungunya IgG" (negative).
7. Atypical mycobacterial infection (non‑tuberculous) – persisted despite negative routine cultures; later acid‑fast bacilli grew after prolonged incubation, identified as MAC, confirming the diagnosis. | "Aspirate grew acid‑fast bacteria at 10 days, identified later as MAC."

Author's Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished the true pathogen from numerous potential causes of culture‑negative endocarditis by (a) exhaustive targeted PCR and serologic testing for fastidious organisms (e.g., *Bartonella*, *Brucella*, *Coxiella*), (b) a negative broad‑range 16S rDNA PCR suggesting low bacterial load or PCR inhibition, and (c) confirmation with three independent bioinformatic pipelines applied to NGS data that overwhelmingly identified *Cardiobacterium hominis* while negative controls remained clean.
case_prompt:
In May 2018, a 58‑year‑old man, an independent painter, presented to the emergency department with breathlessness, chest tightness, and chills persisting for a couple of weeks. He had a good dental status and no recent dental procedures. Physical examination showed signs of heart failure; there were no splenomegaly, peripheral embolic lesions, large‑vessel emboli, cutaneous lesions, or retinal/conjunctival lesions. Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography demonstrated moderate to severe aortic regurgitation and a 15 × 8 mm mobile vegetation on the right aortic leaflet. Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis (12.4 × 10⁹ cells/L), mild anemia (hemoglobin 130 g/L), and elevated C‑reactive protein (87.3 mg/L). Infective endocarditis was suspected, and empiric antibiotics (amoxicillin, amoxicillin/clavulanic acid, and gentamicin) were started on day 0. On day 3, the patient underwent aortic valve replacement with implantation of a biological valve. Before pathogen identification, antibiotic therapy was empirically switched to ceftriaxone, a third‑generation cephalosporin.

Five sets of blood cultures obtained at 30‑minute intervals on day 0, prior to antibiotics, remained negative after 7 days of incubation. Culture of the excised valve and vegetation on standard enriched media was also negative. Indirect detection methods for infectious agents were all negative, including specific PCR assays for *Chlamydophila pneumoniae*, *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*, *Bordetella* spp. (oropharyngeal samples), *Treponema pallidum*, *Tropheryma whipplei*, *Brucella* spp., *Bartonella henselae*, and *Bordetella quintana* (valve tissue and blood); a *Legionella pneumophila* urinary antigen test; and serologies for *Coxiella burnetii*, *Bartonella henselae*, and *Brucella* spp. Broad‑range 16S rDNA PCR performed on a fragment of the aortic valve was negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Culture‑negative infective endocarditis due to common bacterial pathogens considered | "Suspecting an infective endocarditis, empiric treatment was started..."
2. Blood culture–negative endocarditis from fastidious organisms (e.g., *Bartonella*, *Brucella*, *Coxiella*) ruled out by targeted PCR and serology negativity | "Results of indirect detection of infective agents were also negative. These included: ... PCR tests for ... Brucella spp....; ... serologies for Coxiella burnetti, Bartonella henselae, and Brucella spp."
3. *Legionella pneumophila* infection excluded by negative urinary antigen test | "Legionella pneumophila urinary antigen test" was performed and found negative.
4. Broad‑range 16S rDNA PCR failure suggesting low bacterial load or PCR inhibition, not confirming any specific organism | "The broad-range 16S rDNA PCR performed on a fragment of the aortic valve revealed negative."
5. Endocarditis caused by *Cardiobacterium hominis* (HACEK group) ultimately identified by metagenomic next‑generation sequencing, which provided a dominant (>97%) read assignment to this organism across three bioinformatic pipelines, while negative extraction controls showed no Cardiobacterium reads | "The results obtained by either approach suggested an infection caused by Cardiobacterium hominis... Cardiobacterium was the only genus identified... with a dominance of C. hominis for both DNA extracts."
final_diagnosis: Infective endocarditis due to Cardiobacterium hominis -> OUT_OF_SCOPE

case_prompt:
In May 2017, a 27‑year‑old man presented with a 2‑week history of progressive throat irritation and hoarseness. He first noticed a foreign‑body sensation after a cold, which then worsened and affected his voice. Direct laryngoscopy at a local hospital revealed multiple warty, cauliflower‑like masses within the arytenoid cartilage, on the laryngeal side of the epiglottis, and at the right ventricular band. He was diagnosed with respiratory papillomatosis and underwent neoplasm excision. Histopathology showed papillomatous hyperplasia of the mucous epithelium, hypergranulosis, mild atypical hyperplasia, and vacuolar degeneration of epithelial cells; Ki‑67 labeling index was 10 %, and HPV‑16 was detected.

He was lost to follow‑up and returned four months later with recurrent hoarseness and dysphagia. After repeat excision, symptoms recurred two months later and worsened.

In January 2018 he presented to our hospital. He denied prior asthma, reflux esophagitis, fevers, rashes, or headache. He reported oral sex with a partner who had genital warts. He denied smoking or alcohol use. Rapid plasma reagin, Treponema pallidum particle agglutination assay, and HIV antibody tests were all negative.

Repeat laryngoscopy again demonstrated lesions at the laryngeal side of the epiglottis and within the arytenoid cartilage. Biopsy showed papillomatous hyperplasia of the mucous epithelium with vacuolar degeneration, a low Ki‑67 proliferation index (10 % positive), and immunohistochemistry positive for HPV‑16. PCR of the lesion also identified HPV‑16 DNA.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Malignancy such as squamous cell carcinoma was considered due to the presence of airway masses, but histopathology demonstrated benign papillomatous hyperplasia without atypia, arguing against cancer. | "The pathological changes showed papillomatous hyperplasia of the mucous epithelium and vacuolar degeneration in epithelium cells..."  
2. Syphilitic infection was a differential because of possible laryngeal lesions; however, serologic testing was negative. | "He was negative in the rapid plasma reagin test (RPR), Treponema pallidum particle agglutination assay (TPPA)..."  
3. HIV‑associated lesions were entertained given the recurrent nature, but HIV antibody testing was negative. | "and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) antibody test."  
4. Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis was supported by the characteristic warty lesions, low Ki‑67 index, and definitive detection of HPV‑16 by immunohistochemistry and PCR. | "HPV‑16 was found in the lesion... We also detected HPV‑DNA in the neoplasm sample with polymerase chain reaction (PCR) technique, and HPV‑16 subtype was also found."

case_prompt:
A 67‑year‑old man was admitted for progressive elevation of liver enzymes. Three months earlier he had presented to the emergency department with fatigue, decreased appetite, and abdominal pain and was found to have elevated transaminases. Outpatient gastroenterology work‑up for viral hepatitis, alpha‑1 antitrypsin deficiency, primary biliary cirrhosis, Wilson disease, and autoimmune hepatitis was largely inconclusive. Over the next two months he developed distal weakness and numbness that spread proximally, ataxia requiring a walker, right‑sided weakness, and intermittent severe radiating back pain. Imaging of the head, brain, and spine was unremarkable. On admission he reported anorexia, 18‑lb weight loss, weakness, lower‑extremity edema, “rusty” colored urine, and sharp pains in his back, groin, and legs lasting minutes to hours. Ten days prior he noticed a non‑itchy painless rash that began on his arms and spread to his torso, palms, and thighs. He denied alcohol, tobacco, or drug use. He was sexually active with 5–10 male partners in the past year. No recent travel, sick contacts, antibiotics, or herbal supplements.

Physical examination showed mild scleral icterus, bilateral pitting edema of the lower extremities, and diminished pinprick and light‑touch sensation in both legs. The skin displayed a nontender maculopapular rash on the palms, thighs, chest, and scalp. A 1–2 cm nontender chancre was present on the posterior penile shaft.

Laboratory studies revealed total bilirubin 5.9 mg/dL, AST 201 U/L, ALT 116 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase 1,048 U/L. Abdominal CT demonstrated hepatomegaly with heterogeneous attenuation, patent hepatic vasculature, no focal lesions, and mild splenomegaly. HIDA scan showed patent cystic and common bile ducts. MRCP showed no extra‑hepatic biliary obstruction. A liver biopsy was performed.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Viral hepatitis considered due to transaminase elevation but excluded because viral hepatitis panel was negative in prior outpatient work‑up. | "workup for viral hepatitis ... was largely inconclusive."
2. Alpha‑1 antitrypsin deficiency considered as cause of liver injury but excluded by normal levels in prior work‑up. | "workup for ... alpha‑1 antitrypsin deficiency ... was largely inconclusive."
3. Primary biliary cirrhosis considered given cholestatic pattern but excluded by negative antimitochondrial antibodies and imaging without biliary dilatation. | "workup for ... primary biliary cirrhosis ... was largely inconclusive."
4. Wilson disease considered because of hepatic dysfunction; excluded by normal ceruloplasmin and absence of Kayser‑Fleischer rings. | "workup for ... Wilson's disease ... was largely inconclusive."
5. Autoimmune hepatitis considered given elevated AST/ALT; excluded by negative autoantibodies and lack of interface hepatitis on biopsy. | "workup for ... autoimmune hepatitis was largely inconclusive."
6. Drug‑induced or herbal supplement liver injury considered but denied use of medications, antibiotics, or herbal products. | "He denied ... use of antibiotics or herbal supplements."
7. Alcoholic liver disease considered but denied alcohol consumption. | "He denied use of alcohol..."
8. Metastatic or infiltrative liver disease considered; imaging showed no focal lesions and vasculature patent, making this unlikely. | "Abdominal CT scan showed hepatomegaly with heterogeneous attenuation, patent hepatic vasculature, no focal lesions."
9. Cholestatic obstruction (biliary) considered; MRCP and HIDA scans demonstrated patent ducts without obstruction. | "MRCP showed no extrahepatic biliary obstruction."
10. Neurologic causes (e.g., multiple sclerosis, spinal cord compression) considered; MRI of brain and spine were unremarkable, making central lesions unlikely. | "Imaging of his head, brain, and spine was unremarkable."

13. Neurosyphilis considered due to neurologic symptoms; excluded by non‑reactive CSF VDRL and modest CSF pleocytosis. | "lumbar puncture ... showed ... nonreactive CSF VDRL titer, ... thus ruling out neurosyphilis."

case_prompt:
A 93‑year‑old Caucasian woman was referred for a three‑month history of right cervical adenopathies. Past history included cutaneous sarcomatoid carcinoma of the face excised four years earlier. She denied fever, weight loss, night sweats, respiratory symptoms, or prior tuberculosis exposure. Physical examination revealed an enlarged, mobile, painful right cervical lymph node; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable.

Contrast‑enhanced CT of the cervico‑thoraco‑abdominal‑pelvic region showed a right cervical mass with multiple adenopathies and fibrotic lesions in the upper right lung lobe; no other adenopathies or neoplastic lesions were identified.

Fine‑needle aspiration of the cervical node yielded a non‑caseous granulomatous process. Ziehl‑Neelsen staining was negative, as was PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and cultures were unrevealing. The patient was placed under surveillance. Subsequent work‑up identified an IgG‑lambda monoclonal gammopathy; renal function, calcium metabolism, hemoglobin, urinary free light chains, and beta‑2‑microglobulin were all normal. Peripheral blood immunophenotyping demonstrated a polyclonal B‑cell population. Serologies for syphilis, HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C were negative. An interferon‑γ release assay (QuantiFERON) returned positive.

Two months later the cervical adenopathies enlarged and developed cutaneous fistulization with suppurative lymphadenitis. Swab culture grew Staphylococcus aureus, treated with cefuroxime with only modest improvement. Excisional biopsy of the node showed granulomas with caseous necrosis and suppuration. PCR testing of the tissue was negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Nocardia, Mycobacterium avium complex, Toxoplasma gondii, Aspergillus fumigatus, Bartonella spp., Treponema pallidum, and Leishmania infantum.

1. Tuberculous lymphadenitis considered due to chronic cervical adenopathy, caseating granulomas, and positive QuantiFERON despite negative initial stains. | "Considering the presence of persistent cervical lymphadenopathy with caseous granulomas, a positive QuantiFERON test, and the exclusion of other potential causes, the hypothesis of cervical tuberculous lymphadenitis was strongly suspected..."
2. Sarcoidosis entertained because of non‑caseous granulomas on initial FNA, but later development of caseation and lack of systemic sarcoid features made it unlikely. | "Fine needle aspiration ... yielded a noncaseous granulomatous process."
3. Bacterial suppurative lymphadenitis (e.g., Staphylococcus aureus) suggested by fistulization and positive wound swab, yet the chronic course, granulomatous histology, and limited response to cefuroxime argued against it as sole cause. | "Microbiologic examination of a suppuration swab was positive for Staphylococcus aureus and the patient was treated with cefuroxime, displaying only slight improvement."

5. Mycobacterium avium complex excluded by negative PCR for MAC. | "PCR assessment of the samples was negative for ... Mycobacterium avium complex ..."
6. Fungal infections (Aspergillus) excluded by negative PCR for Aspergillus fumigatus. | "PCR assessment of the samples was negative for ... Aspergillus fumigatus ..."
7. Bartonella (cat‑scratch disease) excluded by negative PCR. | "PCR assessment of the samples was negative for ... Bartonella spp."
8. Treponema pallidum (syphilis) excluded by negative PCR and negative serology. | "Serology tests for syphilis ... were negative" and "PCR assessment ... negative for ... Treponema pallidum."
9. Leishmania infection excluded by negative PCR. | "PCR assessment ... negative for ... Leishmania infantum."
10. Metastatic carcinoma or lymphoma considered given prior skin carcinoma and monoclonal gammopathy, but immunophenotyping showed a polyclonal B‑cell population and histology lacked neoplastic cells. | "Peripheral blood immunophenotyping demonstrated a polyclonal B cell population." and "There was no evidence of Reed‑Sternberg cells or neoplastic cells."

case_prompt:
A 46‑year‑old male worker was admitted with a 5‑day history of bilateral lower‑limb numbness, lower back pain, and irregular defecation that gradually spread to the upper abdomen. On examination, muscle strength was grade 4/5 in the lower extremities and grade 5 in the upper extremities; hyperalgesia was present below the T7 level. Muscle tension, deep tendon reflexes in the arms and legs, abdominal reflexes, and pathologic reflexes were all normal. The patient had a past history of hypertension and compensated renal failure; there was no history of trauma, cancer, diabetes, or allergic disease.

Spinal MRI revealed swelling of the thoracic cord with a long‑segment diffuse high‑signal intensity and a heterogeneous nodule with a hypointense center at T7 on T2‑weighted images. Post‑gadolinium images showed peripheral enhancement of the dorsal nodule, while the diffuse high‑signal lesion showed no enhancement. Brain MRI was normal. The authors noted that “MRI may indicate spinal tumors or inflammatory granuloma such as syphilis, tuberculosis, and neurocysticercosis.”

Cerebrospinal fluid analysis demonstrated an elevated cell count (120 cells/µL, 76 % lymphocytes) and increased protein (84 mg/dL) with normal glucose and chloride. Syphilis serology was positive: TPPA and TRUST were reactive, with TRUST titers of 1:128 in serum and 1:32 in CSF. case_prompt:
A 46‑year‑old man presented to the emergency department with a 3‑month history of progressive lower‑limb swelling, a persistent non‑productive cough, and vague abdominal discomfort that had worsened over the past week. He had a prior traumatic lower‑limb amputation and a heavy smoking history; no other comorbidities were reported. On exam he was afebrile, had marked pedal edema, sub‑centimeter inguinal lymph nodes, and extensive penile ulceration. Cardiovascular, respiratory and neurological examinations were normal; the abdomen was minimally tender.

Urine dipstick showed significant proteinuria. Laboratory studies revealed: urine protein‑creatinine ratio 0.317 g/mmol, serum creatinine 58 µmol/L, calcium 3.12 mmol/L, ALT 33 U/L, GGT 349 U/L, ALP 461 U/L. Serology was negative for HIV and hepatitis B; Treponema pallidum antibody (TPAb) screening was positive. A rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test performed later returned a titre of 1:256.

Chest radiography identified a suspicious left lower‑lobe mass with multiple smaller pulmonary nodules. Contrast‑enhanced chest CT the next day confirmed an irregular left lower‑lobe mass (37 × 28 × 26 mm) with multiple posterior subpleural nodules, sub‑centimetre mediastinal and bilateral hilar nodes, no pleural effusion, and background paraseptal emphysema.

Given the raised calcium, cholestatic liver profile, proteinuria, and imaging findings, the provisional diagnosis was metastatic lung cancer with nephrotic‑syndrome‑type proteinuria. A CT‑guided lung biopsy was performed.

Histology of the lung specimen showed no atypia or malignancy; instead there was a dense plasma cell infiltrate with multiple granulomas, some showing early central necrosis, and scattered anthracotic pigment. Stains for acid‑fast bacilli (Ziehl‑Neelsen), fungi (PAS, Grocott), and bacteria (Gram) were all negative, and bacterial cultures yielded no growth. The case team noted the positive RPR result but considered it an unrelated finding at this stage and ordered further immunohistochemical studies.

1. Metastatic lung carcinoma was initially favored because of the solitary lung mass, multiple nodules, hypercalcemia, and hepatic enzyme elevation; however, biopsy “reported no evidence of atypia or malignancy” and showed granulomatous inflammation, arguing against carcinoma. | “Provisional histology of the lung mass reported no evidence of atypia or malignancy… there was a marked plasma infiltrate with multiple granulomas…”
2. Tuberculosis was considered given granulomas and pulmonary nodules, but Ziehl‑Neelsen staining “showed no acid‑fast bacilli” and cultures were negative, making TB unlikely. | “There were no acid‑fast bacilli identified after Ziehl‑Neelsen…”
3. Fungal infection (e.g., histoplasmosis, aspergillosis) can produce granulomas; however, PAS and Grocott stains were negative for fungi. | “…or fungi after Periodic Acid‑Schiff and Grocott staining…”
4. Nocardiosis or other bacterial infections were entertained, but Gram stain showed no organisms and cultures remained sterile. | “Gram stain showed no organisms and subsequent bacterial culture was negative.”
5. Sarcoidosis can present with non‑caseating granulomas and hilar nodes, yet the presence of a “positive… RPR” and later tissue positivity for T. pallidum made sarcoidosis less consistent; additionally, sarcoidosis does not explain the penile ulceration or hypercalcemia of this magnitude. | “The granulomatous inflammation and positive TPAb supported a final diagnosis of pulmonary syphilis…”

Syphilis (pulmonary involvement) was ultimately supported by: a positive serologic screen (TPAb, RPR 1:256), lung biopsy granulomas with early necrosis, and immunohistochemistry that demonstrated T. pallidum antigen. | “T. pallidum antibody was positive… The granulomatous inflammation and positive TPAb supported a final diagnosis of pulmonary syphilis…”
7. Syphilitic nephropathy explained the proteinuria; renal biopsy showed “mild mesangial proliferative glomerulonephritis, keeping with syphilitic nephropathy,” fitting the systemic treponemal infection. | “Renal biopsy… showed mild mesangial proliferative glomerulonephritis, keeping with syphilitic nephropathy.”

case_prompt:
A 47‑year‑old man presented with a two‑week history of headaches, progressive diplopia, and right eyelid ptosis. He denied other neurologic symptoms; review of systems was negative. Past medical history was unremarkable; he smoked 10 pack‑years and reported unprotected same‑sex intercourse with multiple partners over the past decade. Visual acuity was 20/30 OD and 20/20 OS. Ocular examination revealed 80 prism diopters of exotropia with marked hypotropia; the right eye showed severe deficits in elevation, adduction, and depression from the primary position, while abduction and incyclotorsion were preserved. The right pupil was dilated and poorly reactive to light and accommodation; no relative afferent pupillary defect was noted. The remainder of the cranial nerve, anterior segment, fundus, and neurologic examinations were normal. An isolated complete pupil‑involving right oculomotor nerve palsy was diagnosed.

Given the presentation, aneurysmal compression was suspected and urgent brain computed tomography angiography (CTA) was obtained but came back normal. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated thickening and enhancement of the right oculomotor nerve at the level of the interpeduncular and suprasellar cisterns, without leptomeningeal or other cranial nerve enhancement. Complete blood count, glycated hemoglobin, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C‑reactive protein were within normal limits. Chest radiography showed no hilar adenopathy or signs of tuberculosis. Serologic testing revealed a reactive Treponema pallidum enzyme immunoassay confirmed by a rapid plasma reagin (RPR) titer of 1:16. HIV testing and interferon‑gamma release assay for tuberculosis were negative. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis demonstrated elevated protein (0.83 g/L) and lymphocytic pleocytosis (30 × 10⁶/L).

1. Aneurysmal compression considered due to acute painful third‑nerve palsy; ruled out by normal CTA. | "Given the clinical presentation, aneurysmal compression was suspected and urgent brain computed tomography angiography (CTA) was obtained but came back normal."

Microvascular ischemic neuropathy (e.g., diabetic or hypertensive) considered; deemed unlikely because glycated hemoglobin, ESR, and CRP were normal and the patient had no vascular risk factors. | "Complete blood count, glycated hemoglobin, erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C‑reactive protein serum levels were normal."
3. Tuberculous meningitis considered; excluded by negative chest radiography, negative IGRA, and lack of leptomeningeal enhancement on MRI. | "Chest radiography did not reveal hilar adenopathy or signs of tuberculosis." and "Testing for ... tuberculosis (interferon gamma release assay, IGRA) was negative."

Neurosyphilis considered due to positive serum treponemal tests, compatible CSF findings (elevated protein, lymphocytic pleocytosis), and focal cranial nerve enhancement, making it the most plausible diagnosis. | "The initial treponemal test (Treponema pallidum enzyme immunoassay) was reactive and was confirmed by a positive rapid plasma reagin test (at a 1:16 titer)." and "Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis demonstrated elevated protein levels ... and lymphocytic pleocytosis ..."

Her husband reported that two months earlier she had been at her baseline, but over the ensuing weeks she developed waxing and waning mentation problems, selective mutism, minimal social engagement, and a 20‑lb weight loss due to poor intake. Six weeks prior, she tested positive for COVID‑19 by nasopharyngeal RT‑PCR despite being asymptomatic respiratorily; MRI brain, 1‑hour EEG, and CSF were normal, and she was discharged after brief improvement. Two weeks later, she returned with severe hypertension (190/101 mmHg), flaccid extremities, and incomprehensible sounds; she was intubated, received lorazepam for presumed seizure, and was extubated the next day with full alertness. After a brief interval of independence, she again developed urinary and fecal incontinence, worsening selective mutism, and was readmitted.

On admission she was drowsy but oriented to month and year with intact limb strength, brisk reflexes, decreased pinprick sensation in both feet, and impaired proprioception in the lower extremities. No dysdiadochokinesia or Babinski sign was present. A lorazepam trial produced transient improvement in conversation, followed by inappropriate laughter, pressured speech, and unsteady gait; these changes resolved within an hour.

A 24‑hour EEG was normal (post‑dominant rhythm 8‑9 Hz, no seizures). MRI brain was unremarkable; lumbar spine MRI showed multilevel degenerative changes without cord compression. Laboratory studies revealed serum copper 11 µg/dL (normal 70‑175), ceruloplasmin 6 mg/dL (normal 18‑53), and serum zinc at the upper limit of normal (126 µg/dL, normal 60‑130). B12 was elevated; folate was normal. Lumbar puncture showed opening pressure 7 cm H₂O, mild lymphocytic pleocytosis (12 cells/µL), normal glucose and protein, negative cytology, and negative PCR for HSV 1/2, West Nile, bacterial pathogens, and SARS‑CoV‑2. An autoimmune encephalitis panel (anti‑NMDA‑R, LGI1, GAD65, GABA‑B, CASPR2, AMPA‑R) was negative, as were HIV, syphilis, acid‑fast bacilli, ANA, SS‑A/SS‑B, and ribosomal P antibodies. Morning cortisol was normal.

Autoimmune encephalitis (including anti‑NMDA receptor) entertained given neuropsychiatric features; excluded by negative comprehensive autoimmune encephalitis panel and serologies (ANA, Sjögren, ribosomal P). | "University of Pennsylvania autoimmune encephalitis evaluation CSF panel... returned negative. case_prompt:
A 43‑year‑old man with a past history of migraine presented to the emergency department two hours after the abrupt onset of diplopia, altered speech, and fluctuating decreased level of consciousness. He denied any toxic or drug ingestion. On examination he had right‑dominant femoral hemiparesis, binocular strabismus with limited convergence and vertical eye movements, non‑reactive miotic pupils, and a Glasgow Coma Scale that waxed between 8 and 10.

Echocardiogram demonstrated a 75 % left ventricular ejection fraction, mild mitral valve prolapse with mild regurgitation, and mild pericardial effusion. Chest CTA revealed small bilateral pleural effusions, larger on the left, causing compressive atelectasis. Repeat SARS‑CoV‑2 PCR and antigen tests were negative. Three months after the first dose he received the second identical vaccine dose. Eighteen days later he was hospitalized for an unintended 13‑kg weight loss over two months, intermittent fever (38 °C), bilateral posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, pruritic salmon‑pink rash, asthenia, and persistent arthralgia of shoulders, hands, and knees.
