A 57‑year‑old man presented with a 2‑week history of sudden‑onset, progressively worsening shortness of breath and dry cough. He denied chest pain, palpitations, hemoptysis, fever, weight change, or diurnal variation of dyspnea. He reported no known contact with COVID‑19‑positive individuals or tuberculosis patients. He had received the first dose of the AstraZeneca/Covishield COVID‑19 vaccine two weeks before symptom onset. Past medical history was notable for hypertension, hyperlipidemia, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hidradenitis suppurativa diagnosed in 2006, for which he had received biological therapy for one year. He denied recent travel or exposure to industrial chemicals or gases and had no family members with similar illness.

On admission his blood pressure was 136/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98 % on room air. Chest auscultation revealed reduced air entry bilaterally with bibasal crepitations; there was no pallor, cyanosis, icterus, or clubbing. Other systemic examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.3 g/dL, total leukocyte count 5 440 µL⁻¹ (neutrophils 59.7 %, lymphocytes 19.1 %, eosinophils 5.0 %, monocytes 13.8 %), platelet count 225 000 µL⁻¹, ESR 68 mm/h, normal renal function, and liver enzymes within normal limits (total bilirubin 5.5 µmol/L, ALT 18.3 IU/L, AST 16 IU/L, ALP 80 IU/L, total protein 72.9 g/L, albumin 37.2 g/L, globulin 35.7 g/L).

Chest X‑ray demonstrated patchy bilateral infiltrates. Computed tomography pulmonary angiography showed bilateral diffuse patchy consolidation without pulmonary embolus and a few mediastinal reactive lymph nodes. Bronchoscopy revealed mild bilateral inflammation, most prominent in the right upper lobe lingula and right middle lobe, with no endobronchial lesion or mucous secretion.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Tuberculosis – positive molecular detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis from bronchial washings confirmed the infection. | "TB PCR Gene Expert of bronchial washing came positive for mycobacterium tuberculosis."
2. Sarcoidosis – later considered due to persistent infiltrates and confirmed by non‑caseating granulomas on bronchial biopsy. | "A bronchial biopsy ... showed a non‑caseating granuloma with minimal inflammatory cell infiltrate compatible with sarcoidosis."
3. Pulmonary embolism – excluded because CT pulmonary angiography demonstrated no embolus. | "CT pulmonary angiography ... revealed ... no pulmonary embolus."
4. COVID‑19 – deemed unlikely given absence of known exposure to a COVID‑19 case. | "There was no history of contact with the COVID‑19‑positive case."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case ultimately establishes pulmonary tuberculosis, which is on the 21 SELECTED diseases list. Although malaria (also a SELECTED disease) was identified early, the teaching focus will be on the later, more challenging diagnosis of tuberculosis.
2. Ideal Breakpoint: Stop the presentation just before the authors state “A diagnosis of PTB was made and she was commenced on anti‑tuberculosis drugs…”. Include all presenting symptoms, physical findings, imaging, and laboratory results up to the GeneXpert test result (which was negative), but omit the explicit decision to treat for TB.
3. Author's Analytic Distinctions: The authors contrasted acute bronchopneumonia/heart failure from PDA versus a chronic infectious etiology (TB) based on persistent weight loss, recurrent pneumonia, radiographic pattern, and lack of response to antibiotics; they also noted a positive malaria smear that did not explain the chronic course, and they used GeneXpert (negative) yet still diagnosed TB clinically.
case_prompt:
A 9‑month‑old female infant was brought to the emergency department with a 2‑week history of poor weight gain since birth, cough, and high‑grade continuous fever. She had developed fast breathing for one week and, for the preceding 24 hours, was unable to suckle from her breast despite her mother’s attempts. Review of systems revealed orthopnea, easy fatigability, excessive sweating, but no cyanosis, edema, or seizures.

On examination the infant was severely pale and in marked respiratory distress with subcostal and intercostal recessions, nasal flaring and an oxygen saturation of 85 % on room air. She weighed 6 kg (44 % of expected, > –3 Z‑score) and was 72 cm tall (0.8 Z‑score). Respiratory rate was 60 breaths/min with diffuse crepitations. Cardiovascular examination showed an active precordium, displaced apex to the 5th left intercostal space lateral to the mid‑clavicular line, tachycardia at 160 bpm, and a grade 3/6 continuous systolic murmur best heard at the left lower sternal border radiating to the axilla. Abdomen revealed a reducible umbilical hernia and tender hepatomegaly (liver palpable 4 cm below the right costal margin). Dysmorphic facial features included upward‑slanting palpebral fissures, low‑set ears, and a flattened nasal bridge suggestive of a chromosomal abnormality.

Initial laboratory studies demonstrated leukocytosis (WBC 22.7 × 10⁹/L), anemia (hematocrit 28 %), hypokalemia (2.4 mmol/L), hypocalcemia (non‑ionic calcium 1.09 mmol/L), and a negative HIV serology. Chest radiograph showed diffuse perihilar mottled and fluffy opacities in all lung zones bilaterally, cardiomegaly with a cardiothoracic ratio of 61 %, and splaying of the carina consistent with cardiogenic pulmonary edema. Electrocardiogram revealed sinus tachycardia, right atrial enlargement, right ventricular hypertrophy, and right axis deviation. Echocardiography identified a 0.4 cm patent ductus arteriosus with left‑to‑right shunt at 74 mmHg. A peripheral blood smear was positive for malaria parasites.

The working diagnosis at this stage was severe bronchopneumonia with heart failure in the setting of an acyanotic congenital heart disease (patent ductus arteriosus) and a probable chromosomal abnormality (Down syndrome), complicated by malnutrition. The infant was started on parenteral antibiotics, diuretics, supplemental oxygen, nutritional rehabilitation, vitamin D, antimalarial therapy, and hematinics. She stabilized, was discharged, and referred for surgical ligation of the PDA, which was performed successfully six months later.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Severe bronchopneumonia with heart failure due to PDA was considered because of fever, cough, diffuse crackles, cardiomegaly, and a continuous murmur; however, the persistence of symptoms despite appropriate antibiotics and diuretics suggested another process. | "initial working diagnosis was severe bronchopneumonia in heart failure… she was stabilized… discharged…"
2. Congenital heart disease (PDA) explained the cardiomegaly and murmur, but did not account for chronic weight loss, recurrent fevers, and progressive respiratory symptoms after PDA ligation. | "Echocardiography showed: 0.4 cm PDA…"
3. Down syndrome (chromosomal abnormality) was suggested by dysmorphic features, but chromosomal disorders are not directly linked to the infectious pattern observed. | "dysmorphic features… probably Downs syndrome."
4. Acute malaria infection was identified (positive peripheral smear) and treated, yet the infant’s cough and weight loss continued for months, indicating malaria was not the primary driver of the chronic presentation. | "The malaria parasite was positive."
5. Tuberculosis was entertained due to prolonged fever, weight loss, recurrent pneumonia, and chest X‑ray showing bilateral perihilar mottled opacities; GeneXpert was negative but clinical suspicion remained high, leading to a therapeutic trial. | "Chest X‑ray (Figure 3) showed bilateral perihilar mottled opacity. GeneXpert test showed mycobacteria tuberculosis was not detected. A diagnosis of PTB was made…"

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient ultimately was found to have active Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection, which is on the 21 SELECTED diseases list (tuberculosis). Therefore, tuberculosis is the target diagnosis for this teaching case.
2. Best Breakpoint: Include the initial presentation, lung cancer work‑up, treatment with chemotherapy and immunotherapy, subsequent hemoptysis, and the chest CT findings on 22 May 2022 that show new/more extensive bilateral nodular and patchy high‑density shadows. Exclude the definitive microbiologic results (positive MTB nucleic‑acid test and acid‑fast stain) so that the learner must infer the likely diagnosis before it is revealed.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished tuberculosis from tumor progression, ICI‑associated pneumonitis, bacterial pneumonia, and other opportunistic infections by (a) noting the pattern of new lesions and hemoptysis, (b) reporting prior negative microbiologic work‑up, (c) emphasizing that CT could not exclude infection, and (d) finally confirming TB with nucleic‑acid testing and acid‑fast staining.
case_prompt:
A 68‑year‑old man was admitted with a three‑month history of paroxysmal cough producing white sputum, chest distress, shortness of breath, and numbness of both lower limbs. He had a 50‑year smoking history (20 cigarettes/day) but quit five months earlier. Physical examination showed rough breath sounds without rhonchi or moist rales; lymph nodes were not enlarged and cardiac and abdominal exams were normal.

Contrast‑enhanced chest CT (5 March 2022) revealed a mixed‑density mass 12.6 × 7.6 cm in the left upper lobe with truncated bronchi, localized thinning of the left pulmonary artery, and multiple small patchy and nodular high‑density shadows in the surrounding lung and lower lobe. Cranial MRI showed a presumed cavernous hemangioma. Tracheoscopy (9 March 2022) identified a cauliflower‑like neoplasm obstructing the left upper‑lobe bronchial orifice. Tumor markers were elevated (CEA 6 mg/ml, CA125 88.18 U/ml, CYFRA 19‑1 12.91 ng/ml, NSE 33.72 ng/ml). Pathology from bronchoscopy biopsy demonstrated moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma (CK5/6+, P40+, P63+, Ki‑67 50‑60%). Etiological examinations for bacteria, fungus, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Pneumocystis carinii, Actinomyces, Nocardia, and cytomegalovirus were negative.

The final diagnosis at that stage was left‑upper‑lobe squamous cell carcinoma, cT4N3M0 IIIC, with obstructive pneumonia. As he had no surgical indication, he received two cycles of docetaxel‑cisplatin chemotherapy (15 March and 5 April 2022), followed by camrelizumab immunotherapy (25 April 2022). He subsequently developed severe gastrointestinal toxicity and bone‑marrow suppression, leading him to decline further chemotherapy.

On 21 May 2022 the patient began coughing up about 20 ml of blood‑stained sputum. A repeat chest CT on 22 May 2022 showed that the primary tumor in the left upper lobe was smaller than before, but multiple small nodules and patchy high‑density shadows in both lungs were more extensive, a pattern that “could not exclude pneumonia or infection associated with ICIs.”
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Tumor progression versus infection: New bilateral nodular infiltrates and hemoptysis could represent cancer spread, yet the primary lesion had decreased in size, suggesting an alternative process. | "CT showed that the lung cancer in the upper lobe of the left lung was less extensive than before, while multiple small nodules and small patchy high‑density shadows in both lungs were more extensive than before, which could not exclude pneumonia or infection associated with ICIs."
2. Immune‑checkpoint inhibitor–associated pneumonitis: Considered because of recent PD‑1 blockade, but typical ICI pneumonitis usually presents with ground‑glass opacities and less hemoptysis; the pattern of nodular infiltrates is atypical. | "could not exclude pneumonia or infection associated with ICIs."
3. Bacterial pneumonia: Unlikely as routine blood tests were normal and there was no fever; prior bacterial cultures were negative. | "There were no abnormalities in the routine blood test."
4. Other opportunistic infections (Pneumocystis, Nocardia, CMV, fungal): Systematically excluded by negative etiologic examinations before immunotherapy. | "No abnormalities were found in etiological examinations for bacteria, fungus, M. tuberculosis, Pneumocystis carinii, Actinomyces, nocardiosis, and cytomegalovirus."
5. Reactivation of latent tuberculosis: Immunosuppression from chemotherapy and PD‑1 blockade increases TB risk; subsequent bronchoalveolar lavage nucleic‑acid testing was positive for MTB and acid‑fast staining confirmed the organism, establishing active TB. | "The patient was diagnosed with a tracheoscopy and a 13‑item nucleic acid test for respiratory pathogens in the lavage fluid, which was positive for MTB. Moreover, the acid‑fast bacillus stain test was positive."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case’s primary diagnosis is eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA), which is not on the 21 SELECTED diseases list → OUT_OF_SCOPE.
2. Best breakpoint: End the presentation just before the sentence that explicitly mentions “raised the suspicion for eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA).” Include all clinical data, imaging, and labs up to the autoimmune work‑up results, but exclude the authors’ diagnostic conclusion.
3. Key analytic distinctions: The authors excluded an infectious etiology (negative respiratory pathogen panel, negative TB test, bronchoscopy without infection), ruled out alveolar hemorrhage, considered but dismissed uremic pericarditis because of eosinophilia and ECG findings, and found negative ANCA/anti‑GBM and normal complement, narrowing the differential to EGPA supported by adult‑onset asthma, chronic sinusitis, eosinophilia, and pulmonary opacities.
case_prompt:
A 27‑year‑old man presented with a 3‑week history of epistaxis, cough, chest pain, haemoptysis, and bilateral lower‑extremity swelling. Past medical history included post‑streptococcal glomerulonephritis leading to chronic kidney disease stage 5, non‑crystal‑proven gout, and several episodes of shortness of breath, wheezing, dry cough, and sinus congestion over the prior 2 years that responded to glucocorticoids and were presumed to be asthma. He lived in Ohio, denied recent travel, tuberculosis exposure, smoking, or recreational drug use.

On exam he was hemodynamically stable, appeared pale, had friction rubs on cardiac auscultation, bilateral crackles, diffuse sinus tenderness, and nasal crusting without deformity or septal perforation; no purpuric rash was noted.

Laboratory studies showed normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 7.6 g/dL, baseline ≈ 12 g/dL), leukocytosis 16.39 × 10³/µL with 79 % neutrophils, 10 % eosinophils (absolute eosinophil count 1740/µL), creatinine 22.44 mg/dL, BUN 223 mg/dL, high‑sensitivity troponin 264 ng/L, and BNP > 70 000 pg/mL. ECG revealed sinus tachycardia without ST‑segment elevation or T‑wave inversion.

Chest radiograph demonstrated diffuse air‑space opacities bilaterally. Non‑contrast chest CT showed multifocal bilateral ground‑glass and consolidative opacities involving all lobes, a cavitary lesion in the left lower lobe, and trace pericardial and bilateral pleural effusions. Echocardiogram indicated normal left ventricular systolic function (EF 61 %) and a small pericardial effusion without tamponade.

He was started on urgent hemodialysis for severe fluid overload and presumed uremic pericarditis. An extensive respiratory infectious work‑up—including viral panel, Legionella and Streptococcus pneumoniae urine antigens, and a tuberculosis test—was negative. Bronchoscopy revealed no alveolar hemorrhage or infectious process; bronchoalveolar lavage fluid contained 6 % eosinophils. Autoimmune testing showed an elevated IgE of 567 kU/L, negative ANCA and anti‑GBM antibodies, and normal complement C3 and C4. Sinus CT demonstrated severe diffuse mucosal thickening in most sinuses.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Infectious etiologies considered but excluded because “An extensive respiratory infectious work‑up, including a viral panel, Legionella and Streptococcus pneumoniae urine antigens and a tuberculosis test, was negative.”  
2. Alveolar haemorrhage ruled out as “He underwent bronchoscopy, which showed no evidence of alveolar haemorrhage or underlying infectious process.”  
3. Uremic pericarditis initially considered; however, “Uraemic pericarditis was considered … However, owing to other accompanying clinical features, inconsistent ECG findings and the presence of eosinophils, alternative aetiologies were explored.”  
4. ANCA‑associated vasculitis other than EGPA deemed less likely due to “Autoimmune work‑up was notable for … negative ANCA …”  
5. Anti‑GBM disease excluded by “negative … anti‑GBM antibodies.”  
6. Complement‑mediated disorders considered but dismissed because “normal complement levels (C3 and C4).”  
7. EGPA diagnosis supported by the constellation of adult‑onset asthma, chronic sinusitis, peripheral and tissue eosinophilia, and pulmonary opacities: “The combination of presumed diagnosis of adult‑onset asthma, sinonasal symptoms, peripheral and tissue eosinophilia, and pulmonary opacities on CT chest raised the suspicion for eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA).”

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient was ultimately diagnosed with tuberculosis (TB), which is on the 21 SELECTED diseases list. Sufficient clinical, imaging, immunologic (IGRA), and microbiologic (culture) data are provided to deduce TB, making it the primary target diagnosis.
2. Ideal Breakpoint: End the presentation just before the culture result confirming Mycobacterium tuberculosis is disclosed. Include the initial obstetric complications, hysteroscopic findings, granulomatous pathology, the differential list, negative Ziehl‑Neelsen/auramine stains, chest X‑ray, and a positive IGRA. Omit any statement that the tissue culture grew M. tuberculosis or that it was rifampicin‑resistant.
3. Author's Analytic Distinctions: The authors used (a) histopathology showing necrotic granulomatous inflammation, (b) exclusion of common mimickers (negative ZN/auramine stains, negative actinomyces cultures), (c) immunologic evidence supporting TB (positive IGRA), and (d) imaging (CT, PET‑CT) to locate an extrapulmonary granuloma, thereby confirming TB and ruling out autoimmune vasculitis and actinomycosis.
case_prompt:
At 38 years old, a woman was pregnant. A normal ultrasound at 10 weeks gestation showed no anomalies. At 18 weeks she experienced vaginal bleeding; ultrasound revealed a sub‑placental hematoma. The fetus had no structural abnormalities and cervical length measured 27 mm. Cervical swabs for gonorrhea, chlamydia, bacterial vaginosis, and yeast, as well as a PAP smear, were unremarkable. She returned with another bleeding episode and cramps and delivered prematurely at 22 weeks. Delivery was complicated by a retained placenta, which was removed by vacuum curettage and sent for pathology. Pathology showed necrotic granulomatous inflammation.

At a routine postpartum visit the patient reported continuous irregular vaginal bleeding and lower abdominal pain. Ultrasound demonstrated a 13 mm intrauterine homogeneous structure suspicious for retained placental tissue. She underwent hysteroscopy; a large amount of thick, yellow, fibrotic tissue was visualized but could only be partially resected, and the procedure was halted due to fluid loss. Pathology again reported granulomatous inflammation without placental tissue. A differential diagnosis of tuberculosis, actinomyces species, autoimmune vasculitis, and other autoimmune diseases was generated. Additional endometrial tissue was obtained for pathology and culture to evaluate actinomyces and tuberculosis. Ziehl‑Neelsen and auramine stains were negative. Blood was drawn for IGRA (QuantiFERON‑TB) and a broad autoimmune panel (IL‑2R, ANCAs, ENA, antibodies). A recent chest X‑ray performed for shortness of breath showed no lung disease, and the IGRA was positive.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Granulomatous inflammation in uterine tissue suggests an infectious or inflammatory cause; tuberculosis classically produces caseating granulomas. | "Pathology report showed a necrotic granulomatous inflammation..."
2. Actinomyces can cause chronic granulomatous lesions in the genital tract; cultures and special stains were ordered to detect it. | "More tissue was collected ... to examine for actinomyces and TB."
3. Autoimmune vasculitis or other autoimmune diseases can mimic granulomatous inflammation; autoimmune serologies were obtained to assess. | "A differential diagnosis was drawn up; TB, actinomyces species, auto‑immune vasculitis, and auto‑immune diseases."
4. Negative Ziehl‑Neelsen and auramine stains argue against abundant acid‑fast bacilli but do not exclude TB, especially extrapulmonary disease. | "The Ziehl‑Neelsen (ZN) and auramine testing results were negative."
5. Positive IGRA indicates prior sensitization to Mycobacterium tuberculosis and supports TB over other etiologies. | "...the QFT‑TB was positive..."
6. Normal chest X‑ray reduces likelihood of active pulmonary TB, but extrapulmonary TB can occur without pulmonary involvement. | "A recent X‑ray of the lungs ... showed no signs of lung diseases."
7. Actinomyces infection is less likely given lack of characteristic sulfur granules and negative cultures (to be reported). | "culture results ... for actinomyces" (implied negative in subsequent work‑up).
8. Autoimmune vasculitis was deemed less probable because specific autoantibodies (ANCAs, ENA) were not reported as positive. | "blood was taken for ... ANCAs, ENA, and antibodies."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient has confirmed brucellosis (Brucella abortus and Brucella melitensis serology) which is one of the 21 SELECTED diseases. Although acquired TTP is the primary focus of the report, the presence of sufficient clinical and laboratory data to diagnose brucellosis makes it the primary target diagnosis according to Rule 1.
2. Breakpoint: Include all information up to, but not including, the ADAMTS‑13 activity results and the definitive statement that the presentation is “specific to acquired TTP.” Thus the prompt ends after the report of Brucella serology and the initiation of doxycycline‑rifampin therapy.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors initially considered immune‑mediated thrombocytopenia (ITP) and TTP, performed bone‑marrow studies, and evaluated infectious etiologies (viral, TB). The presence of non‑caseating granulomas prompted a broad infectious work‑up, leading to the identification of high‑titer Brucella antibodies; negative EBV/CMV/HIV and QuantiFERON‑TB excluded other common triggers. The response to anti‑brucellosis therapy, together with serology, supported brucellosis as the underlying cause.
case_prompt:
A 9‑year‑old previously healthy Syrian boy was admitted with a 1‑day history of epistaxis, hematemesis, hematuria, and melena associated with periumbilical abdominal pain. He had been complaining of pallor, decreased activity and appetite, and weight loss for the preceding month, with a noticeable increase in pallor one week before admission. On examination he was hypoactive, pale, and jaundiced; he was normothermic and hemodynamically stable. Systemic examination revealed hepatosplenomegaly and a small palpable lymph node in the supraclavicular and inguinal regions. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed bi‑cytopenia: platelet count 11 × 10⁹/L, hemoglobin 97 mg/L, white‑blood‑cell count 10.2 × 10⁹/L, and reticulocyte count 2.45 %. Peripheral smear demonstrated red‑blood‑cell fragmentation (schistocytes) at 1.45 % and neutrophilic toxic granulation. LDH was 1,021 U/L, AST 46 IU/L, ALP 143 IU/L, total bilirubin 41.3 µmol/L (direct 12.7 µmol/L). Urinalysis revealed hematuria and hemoglobinuria. Coagulation studies were normal; fibrinogen was 1.72 g/L. Coombs test was negative.

Initial management assumed atypical immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP); the patient received two doses of IVIG 1 g/kg without response, and platelet and hemoglobin levels continued to fall. Bone‑marrow aspiration and biopsy were performed; the aspirate showed megakaryocytes suggesting immune destruction, while the biopsy revealed frequent small epithelioid non‑necrotizing granulomas. Viral serologies for EBV, CMV, and HIV were negative, and QuantiFERON‑TB Gold was negative. Abdominal ultrasound and chest/abdominal CT demonstrated splenomegaly without significant lymphadenopathy.

Given the patient’s recent consumption of unpasteurized goat milk and cheese in a Brucella‑endemic region, Brucella serology was obtained and returned with titers of Brucella abortus 1:5,120 and Brucella melitensis 1:20,480 (both markedly elevated). A regimen of doxycycline (5 mg/kg orally twice daily) and rifampin (20 mg/kg orally twice daily) was started for six weeks. Following initiation of anti‑brucellosis therapy, the patient no longer required fresh frozen plasma transfusions, and his platelet and hemoglobin levels began to improve, with a concurrent decline in LDH.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) was considered because of isolated thrombocytopenia, but lack of response to IVIG and ongoing hemolysis made it unlikely. | "Initially, the patient was diagnosed with atypical idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) and treated with Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG) 1 g/kg. He received two doses of IVIG without response, and his Hgb and platelet counts declined further."
2. Thrombotic microangiopathy (including TTP) was entertained due to schistocytes and elevated LDH, prompting plasma exchange; however definitive ADAMTS‑13 data were not yet available at the breakpoint. | "The final result of BMA revealed peripheral destruction of blood cells, indicating microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA), likely TTP..."
3. Infectious triggers (viral EBV, CMV, HIV) were investigated because infections can precipitate MAHA; all tests were negative. | "Viral surveillance, including EBV, CMV, and HIV were negative."
4. Tuberculosis was evaluated given granulomatous bone‑marrow findings; QuantiFERON‑TB Gold was negative, reducing its likelihood. | "QuantiFERON‑TB Gold was negative."
5. Sarcoidosis was a differential for non‑caseating granulomas, but lack of pulmonary/lymph node enlargement and negative systemic findings made it less plausible. | "Considering that this is a nonspecific finding that could be attributed to various etiologies, including infections (viral, bacterial, and tuberculosis), infiltrating diseases such as sarcoidosis..."
6. Brucellosis emerged as a strong candidate because of endemic exposure (unpasteurized goat products) and markedly elevated serologic titers; initiation of doxycycline‑rifampin coincided with clinical improvement. | "Since Brucella is endemic in Saudi Arabia and the patient had recently consumed a significant amount of unpasteurized goat milk and cheese, brucella titers were sent, and the result showed Brucella abortus 1:5,120 ... Brucella melitensis 1:20,480... A combination of Doxycycline... and Rifampin... was commenced... Once starting the anti‑brucellosis management, the patient did not require further FFP transfusion... platelets count and hemoglobin levels recovered to the normal range."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient was ultimately diagnosed with tuberculosis, which is on the 21 SELECTED diseases list. Although schistosomiasis was also identified, it is not on the list; therefore the primary target diagnosis is tuberculosis.
2. Ideal Breakpoint: Present the case up to the point where the pancreatic biopsy was sent for GeneXpert testing, but before the positive result is disclosed. This includes symptoms, transplant history, imaging findings, initial endoscopy, surgical exploration, histopathology showing schistosomiasis, and the decision to pursue a TB work‑up.
3. Author's Analytic Distinctions: The authors ruled out pancreatic malignancy by histology, considered schistosomiasis as an incidental finding, and pursued TB testing (GeneXpert) because the mass persisted despite malignancy being excluded; the positive GeneXpert result confirmed TB as the etiology of the pancreatic lesion.
case_prompt:
A 54‑year‑old woman presented with three months of abdominal pain, anorexia, hematochezia, post‑prandial fullness, and a 20‑kg weight loss. Four years earlier she had undergone orthotopic liver transplantation; she had not been screened for latent tuberculosis infection and had received no isoniazid prophylaxis. She was on tacrolimus and mycophenolate without episodes of acute rejection. She originated from a tuberculosis‑endemic region but denied known exposure.

On admission to the general surgery service, abdominal CT revealed a dilated pancreatic duct, a finding confirmed by magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) that also showed an expansive pancreatic process. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) identified a vegetating lesion at the major duodenal papilla, raising suspicion for pancreatic neoplasia with duodenal invasion.

Exploratory laparotomy uncovered a ~6 cm tumor in the pancreatic head, infiltration of the hepatic hilum and duodenum, ascites, and secondary lesions in jejunal loops. Biopsies of liver, jejunum, and pancreatic tissue were obtained, and a Roux‑en‑Y gastrojejunostomy was performed.

Histopathology demonstrated mild chronic liver disease with a biliary pattern, chronic atrophic pancreatitis without malignancy, and chronic inflammatory schistosomal fibrosing reaction with numerous viable eggs in peritoneal and jejunal lesions. The infectious disease team was consulted, and the patient received two doses of praziquantel 20 mg/kg for peritoneal schistosomiasis.

Because malignancy was excluded, a differential diagnosis of tuberculosis was entertained. The patient underwent a repeat EGD, and a new biopsy of the pancreatic mass was obtained and sent for GeneXpert testing for Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Pancreatic neoplasia considered due to imaging and duodenal papilla lesion, but ruled out by histopathology showing no malignant cells | "Histopathological analysis ... chronic atrophic pancreatitis without signs of malignancy in the pancreas lesions."
2. Schistosomiasis identified in peritoneal and jejunal specimens, suggesting an infectious etiology, yet the pancreatic mass persisted despite antiparasitic therapy, making it an unlikely sole cause of the mass | "chronic inflammatory schistosomal fibrosing reaction, with the presence of numerous viable eggs of the parasite in the peritoneum jejunal lesions."
3. Tuberculosis pursued after malignancy exclusion; GeneXpert testing ultimately yielded a positive result confirming Mycobacterium tuberculosis as the cause of the pancreatic lesion | "The exam yielded a positive result and characterized the bacteria as being sensitive to rifampicin."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case ultimately identified Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection (tuberculous meningitis and urinary TB). Tuberculosis is on the 21 SELECTED diseases list, so the target diagnosis is “tuberculosis”.
2. Ideal Breakpoint: End the case presentation just before the mNGS result that confirmed MTB. Include the patient’s worsening urinary symptoms, imaging findings, cerebrospinal fluid analysis, and the statement that the team decided to send CSF for metagenomic next‑generation sequencing. Exclude the sentence “Day 13 mNGS results showed Mycobacterium tuberculosis…”.
3. Author's Analytic Distinctions: The authors initially considered complicated urinary tract infection, interstitial cystitis, lupus encephalopathy, cerebral hemorrhage/infarction, and other infectious causes (bacterial, fungal). They used urine cultures, CSF studies (negative bacterial, fungal, TB antibody/DNA), imaging, and lack of response to broad‑spectrum antibiotics to rule these out, ultimately relying on mNGS detection of MTB to confirm the diagnosis.
case_prompt:
A 52‑year‑old man with a 14‑year history of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and lupus nephritis, maintained on prednisone 10 mg/d, leflunomide 20 mg/d, and hydroxychloroquine 0.4 g/d, was admitted for recurrent urinary urgency, frequency, dysuria, and elevated serum creatinine over the past 18 months. His urinary symptoms first appeared in 2013, improved with antibiotics, recurred in 2019 with poor response to anti‑infective therapy, and persisted despite repeated urine tests showing leukocyturia but no growth on culture.

On 13 January 2021 he was evaluated for rising creatinine and received herbal therapy. On 11 July 2022 he was readmitted to nephrology. Urine analysis revealed 434.1 WBC/µL, 53.7 RBC/µL, and 64.9 bacteria/µL; ESR 44 mm/h, CRP 16.82 mg/L; creatinine 124 µmol/L, urea 8.58 mmol/L; ANA +1:320, anti‑dsDNA 131.1 IU/mL. Ultrasound showed a right kidney stone, left hydronephrosis, and left ureteral dilatation; CT demonstrated bilateral renal calculi, left bladder wall thickening with hydronephrosis, and a cyst in the right kidney. Differential considerations included complicated urinary tract infection and interstitial cystitis.

On day 18, urethral stricture dilatation, transurethral cystoscopy, hydrodistension, and cystocentesis biopsy were performed; pathology showed transverse muscle with scant fibrous and fatty tissue. By day 24, urine WBC rose to 951.3/µL, RBC to 1258.8/µL, and bacteria to 274.7/µL. He was discharged after clinical stabilization.

He returned on 16 August 2022 with increased urinary frequency, urgency, gross hematuria, fever 38.8 °C, and unresponsiveness. Labs: WBC 10.22 ×10⁹/L, RBC 4.36 ×10¹²/L, platelets 203 ×10⁹/L; urine: leukocytes 2618.5/µL, bacteria 2937.7/µL, numerous RBCs; creatinine 121 µmol/L, urea 5.64 mmol/L. He received bladder irrigation and piperacillin‑tazobactam.

On day 3, he became unconscious; brain MRI showed punctate DWI high signal in the pons, small lacunar infarcts in bilateral frontal lobes, mild periventricular white‑matter demyelination, mild sinusitis, and mild intracranial arterial stenoses. Cerebral hemorrhage and infarction were considered unlikely; no meningeal enhancement was seen. Persistent fever and altered consciousness prompted consideration of lupus encephalopathy, and methylprednisolone 40 mg/d was added with limited improvement.

Physical examination revealed diffuse abdominal tenderness with positive shifting dullness and reduced breath sounds at both lung bases. She had been on antituberculous treatment (fixed‑dose combination of isoniazid, pyrazinamide, rifampicin, and ethambutol for 56 days, followed by isoniazid, rifampicin, and ethambutol for 14 months) for sixteen months for drug‑sensitive spinal tuberculosis (Pott’s disease) as per national guidelines, with an extended regimen after orthopaedic consultation. She was advised bed rest but continued household work and attended orthopaedic and infectious‑disease clinics irregularly.

She denied cough, weight loss, anorexia, night sweats, fever, trauma, heavy lifting, or known TB contact. No past major medical or surgical history; no substance misuse, incarceration, or refugee camp stays.

Physical examination: afebrile, weight 50 kg (BMI 21.6 kg/m²). Marked tenderness over dorso‑lumbar spine with severe limitation of motion on bending or rising from bed. Respiratory, neurological, and cardiovascular examinations were normal.

Laboratory studies: hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL, total leukocyte count 5,800/mm³ (71 % neutrophils, 19 % lymphocytes), ESR 63 mm (first hour), CRP 21 mg/L. Induced sputum smear for acid‑fast bacilli and mycobacterial culture were negative; HIV 1/2 test non‑reactive.

Imaging: Plain radiograph of lumbar spine showed destruction of the lower L1 shelf and upper L2 shelf. Chest radiograph was unremarkable. MRI at treatment initiation (16 months ago) demonstrated bone‑marrow edema in D12 and L1 with cortical destruction of posterior D12, without pre‑vertebral, paravertebral, or psoas collections. Follow‑up MRI at presentation revealed significant collapse of L1 with cortical destruction and marrow edema, partial collapse of D12 with loss of D12‑L1 height, mild edema in D11 and L2, multiple tiny pre‑ and paravertebral collections, large bilateral psoas abscesses (right 27 × 57 mm, left 25 × 12 mm), mild kyphosis, and a small anterior epidural collection.

Drug‑sensitive spinal tuberculosis – initially diagnosed and treated, but disease progression despite 16 months of appropriate therapy suggested treatment failure. | "Due to the deterioration of her condition evident clinically and on the MRI, a detailed workup with suspicion of drug resistance was done."
2. Non‑tuberculous or pyogenic spinal infection – considered unlikely because pus obtained later was positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis by nucleic‑acid amplification, confirming a mycobacterial etiology. | "The direct smear of pus for acid‑fast bacilli was negative. case_prompt:
A 24‑year‑old woman from Angola, resident in Portugal since 2017, presented in January 2022 with an inaugural seizure and dyspnea. She was eupneic on room air with oxygen saturation 100 %. Neurological examination revealed right homonymous hemianopsia and a left positive Babinski sign. Laboratory tests showed hyponatremia (130 mmol/L) and markedly elevated C‑reactive protein (26.2 mg/dL); complete blood count, liver and renal panels were within normal limits. Screening for influenza A/B, SARS‑CoV‑2, Legionella pneumophila, Streptococcus pneumoniae, HIV, chronic and acute hepatitis B and C were all negative, as were repeat autoimmune markers.  

Chest computed tomography demonstrated a cavitation with adjacent extensive consolidation and air bronchograms in the left upper lobe. Bronchoalveolar lavage revealed positive acid‑fast bacilli stains. Brain magnetic resonance imaging showed multiple sub‑centimetric lesions with T2 hypodensity and ring enhancement after contrast, involving the right occipital, frontal and anterior temporal regions as well as the left internal temporal and parasagittal occipital regions with ipsilateral cerebellar involvement.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Prior diagnosis of Kikuchi’s disease was considered as a cause of the new neurologic symptoms, but the presence of pulmonary cavitation and acid‑fast bacilli on BAL made an infectious etiology more likely. | "Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) showed positive acid‑fast bacilli (AFB) stains..."

4. Viral respiratory infections (influenza A/B, SARS‑CoV‑2) and HIV were excluded by targeted PCR and serology panels. | "Influenza A and B, SARS‑CoV‑2... HIV... were ruled out."
5. Autoimmune vasculitis or other systemic inflammatory disorders were deemed unlikely because extensive autoimmune serologies (ANCA, ANA, dsDNA, MPO, etc.) remained negative. | "Autoimmune markers were again negative."
6. Fungal meningitis (Cryptococcus) and other opportunistic infections were ruled out by negative CSF studies (including Cryptococcus antigen). | "CSF... negative for AFB and Mtb PCR." (implicit exclusion of other pathogens)
7. The constellation of a cavitary pulmonary focus, disseminated brain lesions, and acid‑fast bacilli on BAL strongly points toward Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. | "BAL showed positive acid‑fast bacilli (AFB) stains" and imaging described "multiple subcentimetric lesions with ring enhancement," findings typical for tuberculous granulomas.

3. Key Analytic Distinctions (from the article):
   - Absence of sexual exposure and negative VDRL argued against common sexually transmitted epididymitis.
   - Gram stain and aerobic culture failed to isolate bacterial pathogens, making typical bacterial epididymo‑orchitis unlikely.
   - Ultrasound showed heterogeneous testicular tissue with a sinus tract, a pattern more compatible with chronic infectious processes such as TB rather than simple acute epididymitis or cyst.
   - The previous wrist lesion raised a remote suspicion of musculoskeletal TB, supporting a disseminated TB hypothesis despite earlier negative microbiology.
   - The definitive CBNAAT detection of MTBC confirmed the tubercular etiology, while the lack of growth on Lowenstein‑Jensen medium highlighted the paucibacillary nature of the disease.
case_prompt:
A 23‑year‑old unmarried male student from Haryana, India, presented with a one‑month history of left scrotal swelling. Fifteen days prior, a purulent discharge emanated from a single sinus on the posterior surface of the scrotum, and he reported intermittent fever for one week. He denied sexual activity, urethral discharge, prior surgery, or trauma. Empiric doxycycline (100 mg BID) for presumed sexually transmitted disease had been ineffective.

Past medical history was notable for a one‑year‑old right wrist swelling following trauma. Investigations of the wrist showed leukocytosis (12,890/µL) with neutrophilia (66.6 %) and monocytosis (8.3 %). CRP was 4.8 mg/dL, ESR 15 mm/h, and rheumatoid factor was negative. MRI revealed ill‑defined enhancing soft‑tissue thickening and bone marrow edema of the carpal bones and adjacent joints, suggesting an infectious etiology (tuberculosis versus post‑traumatic regional pain syndrome). Ziehl‑Neelsen staining and CBNAAT of the wrist biopsy were negative for acid‑fast bacilli and MTBC, respectively. The patient received prednisolone, sulfasalazine, and etoricoxib for three months without improvement; anti‑tubercular therapy was not initiated.

On current examination, the left testis was mildly swollen with induration of the epididymis; the right testis was normal. Systemic examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed CRP 4.8 mg/dL, ESR 9 mm/h, negative rheumatoid factor, anti‑CCP, ANA, hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C antibodies, and HIV antibodies; VDRL was non‑reactive. Scrotal ultrasound demonstrated heterogeneous echotexture of the left testis and epididymis with a small sinus tract extending to the cutaneous plane; the left epididymal head and body were bulky (≈15 mm) with increased vascularity, consistent with left epididymitis. The right testis appeared normal.

A swab from the discharging sinus was obtained for microbiological studies. Gram stain showed no pus cells or organisms, and aerobic culture after 48 hours yielded only skin contaminants.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Common sexually transmitted epididymitis considered but deemed unlikely because the patient denied sexual activity, had no urethral discharge, and VDRL was non‑reactive. | "The patient was unmarried and denied having a sexual partner... The venereal disease research laboratory (VDRL) test was non-reactive."
2. Typical bacterial epididymo‑orchitis was entertained; however, Gram stain showed no organisms and aerobic cultures grew only skin contaminants, making a pyogenic bacterial cause improbable. | "Gram staining, which did not show pus cells or microorganisms. Aerobic culture grew skin contaminants..."
3. Epididymal cyst or simple acute epididymitis was suggested by ultrasound but the presence of a chronic sinus tract and persistent symptoms for weeks argued against a purely cystic or acute process. | "Ultrasound... showed heterogeneous echotexture... and a small sinus tract extending to the cutaneous plane... A differential diagnosis of left epididymo‑orchitis/epididymal cyst was made."
4. Tubercular epididymo‑orchitis considered due to chronicity, sinus formation, lack of response to doxycycline, and prior wrist disease suggestive of musculoskeletal TB. | "The wrist swelling clinically did not improve after the above treatment... after one year of wrist swelling, the patient presented with... discharging sinuses from the left testis."
5. Definitive confirmation of Mycobacterium tuberculosis by molecular testing (GeneXpert) with trace MTBC detection and susceptibility to rifampicin and isoniazid established the diagnosis. | "In the Ziehl‑Neelsen stain, acid‑fast bacilli were not seen. A CBNAAT was performed using GeneXpert (Ultra), in which MTBC was detected (trace) and rifampicin resistance was indeterminate... line probe assay... detected the MTBC and was susceptible to rifampicin and isoniazid."
6. Lack of growth on Lowenstein‑Jensen medium was compatible with the paucibacillary nature of genitourinary TB, supporting the diagnosis despite negative culture. | "The Lowenstein‑Jensen culture didn't grow Mycobacterium tuberculosis."

case_prompt:
A 10‑year‑old boy from an eastern Indian tribal family presented with a 7‑day history of fever and projectile vomiting. The fever was low‑grade and continuous with occasional spikes; vomiting increased from 1–2 episodes daily to 4–5 episodes by admission. One and a half years earlier he had frontal headaches; a CT scan then showed frontal bone erosion with a hypodense scalp collection, reported as osteomyelitis, for which he received unspecified injections.

On examination his vital signs were normal and a BCG scar was present. Swelling was noted in the right submandibular and supra‑orbital regions, and a single verrucous plaque was seen over the left knee. Neurologically he was conscious but spoke incoherently, GCS 14, with neck stiffness, increased tone in all extremities, and bilateral extensor plantar responses; cranial nerves were intact, and there was no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Fundoscopy was normal.

Pus aspirated from the submandibular swelling yielded sterile culture. Initial cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed neutrophilic predominance, elevated protein and low glucose; CSF and blood cultures were sterile. Empirical intravenous ceftriaxone and vancomycin were started for suspected pyogenic meningitis. After seven days there was no improvement in fever spikes or sensorium.

A repeat CSF examination demonstrated 100 % lymphocytes, elevated protein and low glucose, with sterile culture. Dermatology evaluated the knee plaque as “tuberculous verrucous cutis.” Contrast‑enhanced brain CT revealed osteolytic lesions of multiple skull bones with granulations and a small extracalvarial collection in the right frontal bone, while the brain parenchyma appeared normal.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Pyogenic bacterial meningitis was initially suspected because of fever, neck stiffness, and neutrophilic CSF; it was excluded by sterile CSF and blood cultures and lack of clinical response to ceftriaxone‑vancomycin therapy. | "suspecting pyogenic meningitis... no improvement in the fever spike and sensorium of the patients after seven days of antibiotics."
2. Tuberculous meningitis became the leading diagnosis due to the subacute course, shift to lymphocytic CSF with persistent low glucose and high protein, sterile cultures, osteolytic skull lesions on CT, and a cutaneous lesion interpreted as tuberculous verrucous cutis. | "repeat CSF examination was done, which showed 100% lymphocytes with elevated protein and low glucose... The lesion on the left knee appeared to be tuberculous verrucous cutis... contrast‑enhanced CT scan of the brain revealed osteolytic lesions of multiple skull bones... most likely of infectious origin."

1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case’s definitive diagnosis is hepatic tuberculosis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection). Tuberculosis is on the 21 SELECTED diseases list, so the target diagnosis is a SELECTED disease.

This gives students enough data (fever, weight loss, hepatomegaly, hepatic lesion, necrotic lymphadenopathy, negative AFB sputum, negative bacterial cultures, negative amoebic serology) to formulate a differential and suspect extrapulmonary TB without revealing the definitive test outcome.

Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors first considered common causes of liver abscess (pyogenic, amoebic) and ruled them out with negative bacterial cultures and a negative Entamoeba IgG ELISA. They also performed sputum AFB smear to assess pulmonary TB, which was negative, emphasizing the need to look for extrapulmonary disease. Definitive confirmation was achieved through CBNAAT detecting MTB and granulomatous caseating histology, which together distinguished TB from other infectious or neoplastic processes.
case_prompt: A 46‑year‑old woman presented with intermittent fever for two months, mild epigastric and right‑upper‑quadrant abdominal pain for one month, anorexia, and a 10–12 kg weight loss over the preceding two months. She had no known comorbidities. On examination she was thin (BMI 16), afebrile, pulse 98 /min, BP 106/60 mm Hg, respirations 24/min, SpO₂ 95% on room air. She was pale and had cervical lymphadenopathy (2 × 1 cm right, 1 × 1 cm left) and inguinal lymphadenopathy (4 × 3 cm right, 2 × 1 cm left). Abdominal exam revealed moderate right‑upper‑quadrant tenderness and hepatomegaly. Laboratory studies showed mild normocytic anemia, leukocytosis, elevated ESR, and elevated alkaline phosphatase; other routine tests were normal. Chest X‑ray was unremarkable. Contrast‑enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a well‑defined, peripherally enhancing hypodense lesion measuring 34 × 36 × 32 mm in segments VI–VII of the right hepatic lobe, coalescing with a sub‑centimetric lesion suggestive of a liquefied hepatic abscess. Multiple enlarged, centrally necrotic lymph nodes were seen at the splenic hilum, porta hepatis, upper abdomen, retroperitoneum, bilateral iliac vessels, obturator region, and inguinal region, suggesting an infectious process; tuberculosis needed to be ruled out. An Entamoeba histolytica IgG ELISA and bacterial cultures of the hepatic pus were also ordered to exclude amoebic and pyogenic liver abscesses.

A 59‑year‑old male, non‑smoker, presented with a three‑day history of worsening cough and episodes of moderate haemoptysis (~60 mL/day). He had been successfully treated for pulmonary tuberculosis ten years earlier and subsequently developed chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with bronchiectasis, for which he used long‑term inhalational bronchodilators and corticosteroids. Over the past three years he had occasional self‑limiting mild haemoptysis (~20 mL). Viral serologies for HIV, HCV, and HBV were negative.

Serum Aspergillus fumigatus‑specific IgG was positive.

Primary lung malignancy (e.g., bronchogenic carcinoma) was a differential due to cavitary lesion, but BAL cytology showed no malignant cells and imaging lacked lymphadenopathy or pleural effusion. | "Bronchoalveolar lavage... malignant cells" and "There was no evidence of mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy or pleural effusion."

Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis supported by the combination of a host factor (long‑term corticosteroid use), a radiologic sign (air‑crescent sign), and a positive fungal biomarker (BAL galactomannan). | "The presence of one host factor... one clinical factor; positive 'air‑crescent' sign on HRCT chest, and one microbiological factor; and positive BAL galactomannan collectively suggested the diagnosis..."

case_prompt:
A 19‑year‑old man from the Andean region of Peru, employed at a poultry market for the past 7 months, presented with a 3‑week history of dry cough, headache and a feverish sensation. Five months earlier he had a brief episode of cough with mild hemoptysis that resolved spontaneously. Ten days before admission he developed stabbing chest pain and diaphoresis; one week prior he had a 125 mL hemoptysis episode during sport, followed by two episodes of 250 mL hemoptysis the day before presentation.

On arrival to the emergency department his blood pressure was 108/63 mmHg, pulse 109 bpm, respiratory rate 26 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Physical examination revealed decreased vesicular murmur over the left anterior hemithorax with wet crackles. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11 g/dL, leukocyte count 11 277 /mm³ (eosinophils 162), CRP 244 mg/L, and D‑dimer 2.72 µg/mL. Serologies for HIV, HTLV, hepatitis B and C were negative. Chest CT demonstrated a lobar consolidation with cavitation in the left upper lobe (segment 3) and adjacent rib cage collapse.

Bronchoscopy revealed inflammation and erythema of the left upper bronchus with active bleeding; bronchoalveolar lavage samples were obtained for acid‑fast bacilli (AFB) smear and culture. Empiric anti‑tuberculosis therapy (isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide) and intramuscular codeine were started while awaiting results. Four days after bronchoscopy, direct microscopy of the lavage fluid showed trophozoites of Lophomonas sp. with long, irregular flagella, without additional staining.

Tuberculosis considered due to hemoptysis, cavitary lung lesion, and occupational exposure; initial AFB smear and GeneXpert were negative, leading to discontinuation of anti‑TB therapy. | "clinical and radiological suspicion of TB, treatment with a sensitive scheme... Although the AFB results were negative... it was decided to continue the antituberculosis treatment and to conduct a GeneXpert assay..."
2. Pulmonary lophomoniasis identified by direct microscopic observation of Lophomonas trophozoites in bronchoalveolar lavage, providing a definitive etiologic clue and prompting a switch to metronidazole. | "Four days after the bronchofibroscopy, the results of bronchoalveolar lavage indicated the presence of trophozoites of Lophomonas sp. with long and irregular flagella..."
3. Other bacterial or fungal pneumonias were not supported by laboratory data (no neutrophilic leukocytosis, normal eosinophils, negative serologies) and were not mentioned as primary considerations in the report. | "Serological testing was negative for HIV, HTLV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C."

case_analysis:

3. Author’s analytic distinctions: The authors ruled out tuberculosis (negative smear, culture, GeneXpert), excluded HIV/HTLV infection (negative serology), and identified the etiologic agent with MALDI‑TOF MS, linking the empyema to an oral anaerobe and chronic pericoronitis as the source.
case_prompt:
A 28‑year‑old man from a peri‑urban area of Lima, employed as a motorcycle taxi driver, presented to the emergency department after 34 days of persistent fever, chills, weight loss, dyspnea, and leukocytosis. Five years earlier he had completed individualized therapy for multidrug‑resistant pulmonary tuberculosis.  

Initially he experienced moderate left rib‑cage pain, palpitations, and high fever; an electrocardiogram was normal and a chest X‑ray performed on day 4 of illness was reported as “normal.” Fever (38 °C) and chills continued, alongside neutrophilic leukocytosis. He also developed abdominal pain and weight loss. Serology for HIV 1‑2 was non‑reactive and three sputum samples were negative for acid‑fast bacilli. Abdominal ultrasound and stool studies were unremarkable, leading to hospital admission for persistent symptoms.  

On examination the patient was thin, with a heart rate of 110 bpm, blood pressure 100/70 mmHg, oxygen saturation 96 % on room air, moderate dehydration, and abolition of vesicular breath sounds over the middle and lower thirds of the left hemithorax. Laboratory studies showed rising leukocyte counts and C‑reactive protein.  

On hospital day 9 (illness day 42) thoracentesis yielded 600 mL of purulent, greenish fluid; a thoracic drainage tube was placed. The following day intravenous antibiotics were started. By hospital day 12 (illness day 45) fever and leukocytosis resolved, and the drainage fluid was no longer purulent. A CT scan on day 15 (illness day 48) demonstrated a marked reduction in left‑sided pleural fluid volume. Subsequent chest ultrasound on day 22 (illness day 55) measured the residual empyema at 73 mL.  

Initial work‑up for tuberculosis included HIV and HTLV serology (both non‑reactive) and sputum and urine cultures for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, all negative. GeneXpert MTB/RIF performed on pleural fluid was also negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Tuberculous empyema considered because of prior multidrug‑resistant TB; excluded by multiple negative microbiologic tests – “Culture and smear tests for Mycobacterium tuberculosis in sputum and urine were also negative” and “both of which were negative” for MGIT and GeneXpert.  
2. HIV‑associated opportunistic infection considered given immunosuppression; excluded by serology – “Serology for immunodeficiency virus infection (HIV 1‑2) … were nonreactive.”  
3. Non‑tuberculous bacterial empyema suspected; definitive pathogen identified by mass‑spectrometry – “The MALDI‑TOF MS test was used for detecting common germs and was positive for P. micra.” This finding, together with the dental source, confirmed an anaerobic oral flora‑related empyema.

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case focuses on nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary disease (NTM-PD) caused by Mycobacterium europaeum, which is not included in the 21 SELECTED diseases list; therefore the final diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.
2. Breakpoint: Present the case up to the receipt of the mNGS results (identifying Mycobacterium europaeum, Moraxella catarrhalis, and human herpesvirus‑4) but stop before the authors explicitly state that NTM‑PD is considered. This provides sufficient clinical, imaging, and laboratory data for students to formulate the diagnosis without revealing it.
3. Analytic Distinctions: The authors ruled out tuberculosis (negative AFB smear, T‑SPOT, and TB PCR), bacterial pneumonia (only scant alpha‑hemolytic streptococcus), fungal infection (negative CrAg, BDG, GM, Aspergillus antigen), and malignancy (bronchoscopic pathology showed no malignant cells). The presence of a high‑read count Mycobacterium europaeum on mNGS, together with cavitary lesions, led to the NTM‑PD diagnosis.
case_prompt:
On November 16, 2022, a 51‑year‑old male weld‑er was admitted for recurrent tightness of breath lasting more than two years. He had been diagnosed with occupational welding pneumoconiosis stage I and had been away from dust exposure for 10 months. Two years earlier he experienced dyspnea that improved with deep inspiration and occasional mild cough. Prior imaging showed scattered large nodular shadows in the upper lobes with pleural calcification (CT, July 2017) and extensive interstitial changes (X‑ray, May 2018). On November 9, 2022 a repeat chest CT revealed bilateral nodules and a cavity in the posterior segment of the left upper lobe, suggesting possible secondary pulmonary infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis. However, sputum acid‑fast bacilli smears and T‑SPOT.TB were negative.

On admission (day 1) vital signs were: temperature 36.6 °C, pulse 72 /min, respirations 20 /min, blood pressure 129/89 mmHg, weight 58 kg. Lung auscultation was unremarkable; cardiac exam was normal. case_prompt:
A 67‑year‑old Caucasian woman presented for evaluation of a possible prosthetic infection after a total left hip replacement performed 16 months earlier. Three years prior she had developed left hip pain and limitation, leading to the arthroplasty; pre‑operative chest X‑ray and labs were normal except an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR = 94 mm/h). The postoperative course was uneventful and she was discharged five days after surgery.

Sixteen months after the operation she began to experience pain and limited movement at the prosthetic site. Two months later a computed tomography (CT) scan of the hip identified a suspect iliopsoas abscess, confirmed by peripheral blood mononuclear cells labeled with 99 mTc. Her condition worsened with increasing local pain and a mild irregular fever, prompting admission for ultrasound‑guided needle aspiration of the 102 × 53 mm abscess. Cultures of aspirate and blood (aerobic and anaerobic) were obtained, and empiric intravenous linezolid 600 mg twice daily was started. Fever rose, and all cultures remained negative. After one week of unsuccessful medical therapy, surgical exploration revealed a pseudocyst adjacent to the prosthesis; dense, cloudy fluid and tissue biopsies were obtained. Intravenous antibiotics (teicoplanin 400 mg, gentamicin 160 mg, ciprofloxacin 800 mg) were initiated. Fever resolved after four days, and the patient was discharged without further antibiotics; repeat cultures were negative. Histopathology showed fibrous tissue with acute and chronic inflammation and a nonspecific granulomatous pattern.

Twenty days later she reported mild fever and a painful, fluctuant nodule along the superior internal surface of the left thigh near the surgical scar. The nodule was surgically drained, yielding abundant cloudy fluid; cultures again were negative. A deep fistula (~5 cm) with discrete greenish, odorless secretion persisted. On admission her vital signs were normal, but physical examination revealed poor general condition and striking brownish discoloration of the skin on the hands, feet, palmar and plantar folds, nipples, linea alba, and oral mucosa. Laboratory studies showed: RBC 4.53 × 10⁹/L, hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL, platelets 336 × 10⁹/L, WBC 8.2 × 10⁹/L (60.9 % neutrophils, 24.2 % lymphocytes), ESR 89 mm/h, C‑reactive protein 75 mg/L. Tuberculin skin test (5 IU PPD) was positive; QuantiFERON‑TB Gold was 3.08 IU/mL (cut‑off 0.35 IU/mL). Serum cortisol at 8 a.m. was 9.5 µg/dL (normal 4.3–22.4); ACTH 2300 pg/mL (normal 10–60). Anti‑cortical antibodies were negative; repeat cortisol and ACTH were 5.5 µg/dL and 1490 pg/mL. An experimental whole‑blood interferon‑γ assay to RD1‑selected peptides was positive (2.6 IU/mL; cut‑off 0.7 IU/mL). Gram and Ziehl‑Neelsen stains were performed on fistula fluid; PCR for the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex was pending.

Hip, abdominal, and chest CT scans demonstrated a periprosthetic abscess extending into the left psoas muscle, slight bilateral adrenal enlargement with calcifications, and mild fibrosis of both upper lung lobes.

case_prompt:
A 31‑year‑old non‑smoking male presented with a long‑standing history of chronic intermittent cough since childhood, each episode lasting two to three days and often initiated or worsened after heavy meals. He also reported recurrent chest infections but denied hemoptysis, dyspnea, dysphagia, or choking. Systemic examination was unremarkable; he used inhalers and cough suppressants as needed. 

Chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral apical pleural thickening with fibro‑atelectatic changes in the right upper lobe. Barium esophagography revealed marked dilatation of the entire esophagus, more prominent in the proximal third, with free passage of contrast into the stomach and no strictures at the distal end or gastro‑esophageal junction; these findings were interpreted as suggestive of a neurological cause or an esophageal motility disorder. 

Esophageal manometry showed an aperistaltic esophagus, although assessment of the lower esophageal sphincter was not possible.

7. Direct visualization of a smooth tracheoesophageal opening on upper GI endoscopy confirmed the fistula → “Upper GI endoscopy revealed the presence of smooth tracheoesophageal opening (fistula) in the upper 3rd of the anterior wall of the esophagus at 25 cm from the incisor teeth.” 
8. CT imaging corroborated the fistulous connection at the sternoclavicular level, solidifying the diagnosis → “CT scan of chest confirmed the presence of the TEF at the level of sternoclavicular joint along with dilated esophagus.”

In early March 2003, a 26‑year‑old man was admitted to a general medical ward of the Prince of Wales Hospital; he had been ill for 1 week with fever, chills, and rigor. He had had a cough productive of whitish sputum for 2 weeks. He also had diarrhea and had vomited several times before his admission. A complete blood profile on admission showed a leukocyte count 3.1 × 10⁹/L, absolute neutrophil count 2.0 × 10⁹/L, lymphocyte count 0.7 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 112 × 10⁹/L, and hemoglobin 14.7 g/dL. The patient had mild renal impairment, with a creatinine of 119 µmol/L, urea and electrolytes within normal limits, and alanine transaminase mildly elevated at 90 IU/L (normal < 58 IU/L). Bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and albumin levels were normal. C‑reactive protein was 6.5 mg/L (normal < 9.9 mg/L). A diagnosis of atypical or viral pneumonia was suspected because of the low leukocyte count and normal C‑reactive protein. Other laboratory tests were performed, including blood, sputum, and urine cultures, nasopharyngeal aspirate for influenza and parainfluenza, indirect immunofluorescence for respiratory syncytial viral antigen detection, and atypical pneumonia titer (for adenovirus, psittacosis, Q fever, influenza A and B, and mycoplasma). The patient received treatment with intravenous amoxicillin‑clavulanate and oral clarithromycin.

After admission his high fever and productive cough, now with thick, yellowish sputum, persisted. He also complained of progressive dyspnea, headache, dizziness, generalized malaise, and myalgia. His pulse and blood pressure were normal, and his oxygen saturation was approximately 98 % on room air. A sputum culture yielded normal oral flora, and sputum smears were negative for acid‑fast bacilli. Nasopharyngeal aspiration was negative for influenza viruses A and B, respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, and parainfluenzavirus types 1, 2, and 3, with the use of commercial immunofluorescence assay. A chest radiograph on day 4 showed progression of pneumonia, with consolidation changes over the right upper and lower lobes. A repeat complete blood profile showed a leukocyte count of 5.4 × 10⁹/L with persistent lymphopenia and a platelet count of 98 × 10⁹/L. Amoxicillin‑clavulanate was therefore changed to intravenous cefotaxime, 1 g every 8 h; clarithromycin (500 mg twice a day) was continued. As the patient’s condition deteriorated progressively and he had difficulty in expectorating sputum, salbutamol, 0.5 g four times a day, driven by a jet nebulizer at 6 L of oxygen per minute, was given to assist mucociliary clearance. His oxygen saturation remained normal without supplemental oxygen.

A 22‑year‑old woman was admitted through the emergency department with sudden‑onset severe headache, vomiting, and bilateral visual dimness (visual acuity 6/60). She had been diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus one year earlier with grade 3 nephropathy and had received pulse cyclophosphamide followed by chronic oral prednisolone 7.5 mg/day, which she continued up to admission. She had no prior ophthalmic problems and her mental status was normal.

During hospitalization she developed a low‑grade fever and her visual loss progressed; by the third hospital day she had no light perception in either eye. Pupils were dilated and non‑reactive. Laboratory studies showed mild anemia, thrombocytopenia, and fasting hyperglycemia (144 mg/dL) attributed to prolonged steroid use. Because of papilledema, a non‑contrast CT scan of the brain was performed, revealing a calcified mass in the suprasellar region with surrounding edema and obstructive hydrocephalus, along with mild cerebral atrophy. The Mantoux test was negative (patient on steroids). Sputum microscopy was negative for acid‑fast bacilli and chest radiography was normal. The patient reported household contact with a sputum‑positive tuberculosis case three months earlier. Hormonal studies were within normal limits. - Plaque 2: left side of the back, ~6 × 3 cm;

A 33‑year‑old previously healthy manual laborer presented with a 6‑day history of intermittent fever with chills and rigors followed by a 5‑day history of sudden weakness in both lower limbs, complete loss of sensation below the nipples, and urinary retention. The lower limbs were hypotonic with 0/5 power; deep tendon and superficial reflexes were absent, plantars unelicitable. Sensation to touch, pin‑prick, temperature, and vibration was absent bilaterally below the D4 level; perianal sensation was lost and the anal sphincter was lax. Neck rigidity and Kernig’s sign were negative; no spinal tenderness or lymphadenopathy was noted.

Laboratory studies showed a normal total leukocyte count (9700 /mm³) and ESR of 4 mm in the first hour. HIV ELISA was negative; blood and urine cultures were sterile. CSF analysis revealed abundant polymorphonuclear cells, low glucose, and elevated protein. CSF serology was positive for anti‑herpes simplex type I IgG, varicella‑zoster IgG, and anti‑dengue virus IgG and IgM antibodies. CSF Gram stain, fungal stain, and acid‑fast bacilli smear were negative and cultures grew no organism.

MRI of the cervical and dorsal spine demonstrated mild thickening of the cord from C4 to D2 with T2 hyperintensity and no gadolinium enhancement. Screening lumbar MRI (sagittal) revealed a small intradural mass isointense to cord on T1W and T2W images, without contrast enhancement, attached to the conus and filum terminale. Subsequent contrast‑enhanced lumbar MRI confirmed the lesion encircled by cord tissue.

Given the neutrophil‑predominant CSF and the lumbar mass, the patient underwent D12–L3 laminectomy. Intraoperatively a thin, clear arachnoid was noted; yellowish, purulent material loosely adhered to the conus medullaris and filum terminale. The material was evacuated, and samples were sent for histopathology, bacterial, fungal, and tubercular studies. Histopathology showed nonspecific inflammation with abundant neutrophils and few lymphocytes; all stains and cultures remained negative. Empirical intravenous antibiotics (cefoperazone, amikacin, metronidazole) were started for a presumed pyogenic abscess.

One week later the patient developed paresthesias in both upper limbs. Repeat MRI showed expansion of the cervical‑dorsal lesion now spanning C4 to D12 (holocord) with patchy meningeal enhancement. Cervico‑dorsal laminectomy (C4–D4) was performed; intra‑operative findings included yellow‑white cheesy material within the white matter without a clear plane from neural tissue. Additional biopsies again revealed nonspecific neutrophilic inflammation; repeat Gram, fungal, and AFB stains and cultures were negative. The patient continued on empirical antibiotics, supportive care, low‑molecular‑weight heparin, and physiotherapy.

Viral acute transverse myelitis was considered because of the preceding febrile illness and rapid flaccid weakness; however, CSF showed neutrophil predominance and low glucose, which are atypical for viral infection. | "CSF microscopic examination showed plenty of polymorphs, reduced sugars, and elevated proteins, which were unusual for viral etiology."

A 58‑year‑old man was referred to an outpatient clinic with a two‑month history of progressive shortness of breath, dry cough, fatigue, anorexia and unintentional weight loss. Occupationally he worked for 20 years as a warehouse stacker with moderate dust exposure followed by 20 years in an administrative role. case_prompt:
A 37‑year‑old Caucasian man working as a mechanic presented to the emergency department with a solitary swelling on the right side of his chest wall. On this occasion a tissue sample was sent for histology and microbiology. The clinical impression at that time was hidradenitis suppurativa.

Histology was reported as “chronic inflammation with multinucleate giant cells along with foci of caseating necrosis surrounded by granulomas”. No acid‑fast bacilli were demonstrated on special stains, but the diagnosis was considered probable tuberculosis.

The patient was referred to respiratory physicians for treatment of tuberculosis.

case_prompt:
A 21‑year‑old Japanese male presented to the outpatient department with sporadic nausea for 2 months, abdominal discomfort for 1 month, and worsening headache. He had a cysto‑peritoneal (CP) and ventriculo‑peritoneal (VP) shunt placed in infancy for hydrocephalus due to a suprasellar arachnoid cyst, with the VP shunt replaced twice by age 13. The CP cranial tube had been removed previously, leaving the extracranial tube in the mediastinum adherent to surrounding organs. He had a prior diagnosis of slit ventricle syndrome but was otherwise functional, with mild mental retardation and no systemic risk factors or foreign travel.

A few days before presentation he developed fever and mild consciousness disturbance. Examination showed temperature 38.9 °C, restlessness, and marked abdominal distension; there were no meningeal signs or focal neurological deficits. Laboratory data revealed a white blood cell count of 10,900/mm³ and C‑reactive protein 31.8 mg/dL. Chest X‑ray was normal. Brain and abdominal CT scans demonstrated enlarged lateral ventricles, a large peritoneal cyst surrounding the distal end of the peritoneal tube, and fluid in the sheath surrounding the tube, suggesting shunt blockage and increased intracranial pressure. Chest CT showed no abnormalities in the lung fields or subcutaneous chest tissues. The provisional diagnosis was shunt malfunction due to an undefined peritoneal abnormality.

External drainage of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) from the lateral ventricles and the abdominal cyst was performed. CSF was clear; cyst fluid was xanthochromatic. CSF chemical screening was negative. Cyst fluid analysis showed 1,495 cells/mm³ (69 monocytes, 1,426 polymorphonuclear cells) and protein 1.4 g/dL. Empiric antibiotics for abdominal infection were started and bacterial cultures obtained, but no pathogen was isolated.

Symptoms improved after placement of the external drainage system, yet the cyst fluid re‑accumulated and mild inflammation persisted despite antibiotics. A second procedure involved CT‑guided transcutaneous drainage of the cyst, but the fluid re‑collected. A third intervention, laparotomy, revealed no membranous wall (defining a pseudocyst), no malignancy in the omentum, and no ascites. Throughout, cytologic examinations for malignancy were negative and bacterial cultures remained sterile.

3. Malignancy evaluated because of abdominal mass and cystic fluid, but excluded by negative cytology | "All cytological examinations for malignancies were negative."

Simple pseudocyst formation without infection considered after laparotomy showed no membrane or malignancy, yet persistent inflammation suggested an infectious etiology | "Laparotomy... revealed no membrane surrounding the abdominal cyst (defining it as a pseudocyst), no malignancies within the omentum, and no ascites."

case_prompt:
A 32‑year‑old man presented to the surgical clinic with multiple left axillary lymph nodes that had been present for eight months, preceded by furuncles in the axilla. He had taken intermittent treatments from several practitioners without relief and subsequently developed low‑grade fever (100‑101 °F). There was no family or past history of tuberculosis, weight loss, anorexia, or jaundice.

Physical examination revealed three discrete, firm, mobile lymph nodes in the left central axilla, ranging from 0.8 to 2.0 cm, the largest being painful. A Montoux test was negative. Laboratory studies showed an elevated ESR of 28 mm/hr; other hematologic parameters and coagulation profile were normal. Chest radiograph was unremarkable. Smears stained with hematoxylin‑eosin, Giemsa, and Ziehl‑Neelsen (ZN) were cellular, showing intact and degenerated neutrophils, histiocytes, eosinophils, loose epithelioid cell granulomas, giant cells, and a variable number of lymphocytes, with extensive caseous necrosis in the background. Polymerase chain reaction as well as culture for Mycobacterium tuberculosis was positive."

Initial provisional diagnosis of tuberculosis alone was challenged when parasitic hooklets were seen, prompting the addition of a co‑existent echinococcal infection. | "On palpation ... provisional diagnosis of tuberculosis ... Alerted by this discovery, a further search revealed scolices of Echinococcus."

case_prompt:
A 52‑year‑old previously healthy man was referred from a pneumology hospital in Yaoundé for evaluation of suspected heart failure. He reported shortness of breath on moderate exertion associated with a dry cough of two days duration, worse at night. He denied fever, weight loss, night sweats, chest pain, lower‑extremity swelling, or hemoptysis. Past history was unremarkable except for exposure to a patient with tuberculosis ten years ago; he was a never‑smoker and did not consume alcohol.

Physical examination: well‑built, no acute distress; blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, pulse 70/min, respiratory rate 19/min, temperature 36.9 °C, weight 71 kg, BMI 25.2 kg/m². Respiratory exam revealed clear breath sounds without wheezes or crackles. Cardiovascular exam showed a regular rhythm, no murmurs, no accentuation of the pulmonary component of the second heart sound, no jugular venous distension, and no peripheral edema.

Chest radiograph demonstrated an enlarged cardiac silhouette and a right middle‑lung lobe cavitary lesion with regional lymphadenopathy. ECG showed sinus rhythm, incomplete right bundle‑branch block, and T‑wave inversions in V1–V3. Echocardiography revealed a dilated right atrium and right ventricle, severe tricuspid regurgitation, and severe pulmonary artery hypertension with a pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 80 mmHg; left‑ventricular ejection fraction was 70 %.

Laboratory studies: WBC 4,300/mm³, hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL, platelets 315,000/mm³, serum creatinine 11.92 mg/L, C‑reactive protein 54.4 mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 46 mm (first) and 59 mm (second), fasting blood sugar 1 g/L, AST 19.9 IU/L, ALT 15.6 IU/L, negative HIV serology, INR 1.10.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Pulmonary embolism considered due to acute dyspnea, severe pulmonary hypertension, and right‑heart dilation on echo | "Echocardiography showed dilated right atrium, dilated right ventricle, severe tricuspid regurgitation and severe pulmonary artery hypertension; Pulmonary Artery Systolic Pressure (PASP): 80 mmHg."
2. Pulmonary hypertension from other causes (e.g., primary pulmonary arterial hypertension) deemed less likely because imaging revealed a focal cavitary lung lesion and the clinical picture was acute rather than chronic | "Chest radiograph revealed an enlarged cardiac silhouette, a right middle lung lobe cavitary lesion with regional lymphadenopathy."
3. Deep‑vein thrombosis ruled out as a source of emboli | "Ultrasound studies did not show evidence of deep venous thrombosis."
4. Acute heart failure of left‑sided origin excluded by normal left‑ventricular ejection fraction and absence of pulmonary congestion on exam | "Ejection fraction of the left ventricle was 70%." and "auscultation revealed clear breath sounds without wheezes nor crackles."
5. Pulmonary tuberculosis identified later but not responsible for the acute hemodynamic findings | "Sputum was found to contain numerous acid‑fast bacilli on direct microscopy (>15 bacilli/field). Culture results was positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis."
6. Lung malignancy excluded by bronchial biopsy showing severe dysplasia without carcinoma | "Bronchial biopsy showed severe dysplasia of bronchial epithelium with absence of carcinoma."
7. Final confirmation of embolic obstruction demonstrated on CT angiography showing filling defects in the pulmonary arteries | "thoracic Computed Tomographic scan with contrast was performed which showed bilateral proximal pulmonary emboli."
