Guillain‑Barré syndrome (Miller Fisher/Bickerstaff variants) was favored due to peripheral neuropathy, albuminocytologic dissociation (high CSF protein with modest pleocytosis), normal EMG/MRI, and preceding C. jejuni seropositivity | “Considering the peripheral nerve injury and cerebrospinal fluid protein cell separation, GBS secondary to C. jejuni infection was specifically classified as Miller Fisher syndrome (MFS) and Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis.”

case_prompt: A 16‑year‑old male student from Jieyang City, Guangdong Province was admitted on 11 November 2020 with a 6‑month history of intermittent dry cough without fever, chest pain, or known exposures to birds or soil. Chest CT performed on 19 October at a local hospital showed a lung shadow suspicious for tuberculosis, prompting referral. On admission, physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests revealed a white blood cell count of 7.20 × 10⁹/L, neutrophils 51.9 % (3.73 × 10⁹/L), and C‑reactive protein 9 mg/L. Both T‑SPOT and purified protein derivative (PPD) skin test were positive (13 × 14 mm). Serial sputum acid‑fast stains on 13, 14, and 15 November were negative. A chest plain film and contrast‑enhanced CT on 13 November demonstrated cavitary lesions in the left lower lobe and right lung, interpreted as possible pyogenic inflammation, fungal infection, or secondary tuberculosis. Empiric cefotaxime‑sulbactam 2.25 g intravenously twice daily was started. After 10 days, repeat CT showed little change. Immunoglobulin levels, T‑cell subsets, and HIV testing were normal. Bronchoscopy on 17 November displayed congested and edematous bronchial mucosa throughout both lungs; bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) cytology showed respiratory epithelium and few neutrophils, without malignant cells. Tracheoscopic brushings were similarly non‑diagnostic. BALF GeneXpert for Mycobacterium tuberculosis was negative, as were tests for MTB‑DNA and rpoB; the (1→3)-β‑D‑glucan assay was <37.5 pg/mL. No acid‑fast bacilli, bacteria, spores, or hyphae were observed microscopically. A second bronchoscopy on 20 November confirmed bilateral bronchitis, and BALF was sent for metagenomic next‑generation sequencing (mNGS).

1. Tuberculosis considered due to positive T‑SPOT, positive PPD, and cavitary lesions on imaging; excluded because multiple sputum smears and GeneXpert were negative and there was no radiographic response after anti‑tuberculous‑suspicion treatment. | "T‑SPOT and pure protein derivative (PPD) skin test (13 × 14 mm) were positive... GeneXpert (-): MTB‑DNA: negative, rpoB: negative."
2. Bacterial pyogenic pneumonia suggested by cavitary lesions and initial empiric cefotaxime‑sulbactam; excluded because after 10 days of appropriate antibiotics, chest CT showed little change and cultures remained negative. | "After 10 days of regular treatment, the chest CT scan showed little change compared with pre‑treatment."
3. Common fungal infection (e.g., Aspergillus) entertained given cavitary lesions; G test was negative and microscopy showed no hyphae, lowering this possibility. | "G test revealed <37.50 pg/ml. No acid‑fast bacilli, bacteria, spores, or hyphae were found."
4. Malignancy considered during bronchoscopy; cytology of BALF and brushings showed no cancer cells, effectively ruling it out. | "Microscopic examination of bronchial lavage fluid (BALF) ... no cancer cells."

Opportunistic infection by Cryptococcus neoformans ultimately identified: unbiased mNGS of BALF yielded a specific read of C. neoformans, which was subsequently confirmed by CrAg‑LFA (titer 1:80) and fungal culture, establishing pulmonary cryptococcosis as the definitive diagnosis. | "mNGS result came back and showed one specific read of C. neoformans... case_prompt:
A 38‑year‑old man employed in an automotive parts manufacturing plant presented with jaundice in mid‑January 2022. On January 28, he was evaluated at a local hospital where laboratory testing showed markedly elevated transaminases (AST 1,140 IU/L, ALT 2,650 IU/L), γ‑glutamyl transpeptidase 215 IU/L, total bilirubin 9.41 mg/dL and direct bilirubin 6.77 mg/dL. Abdominal computed tomography demonstrated acute hepatitis with mild hepatosplenomegaly. He was transferred to the gastroenterology department for further evaluation. The patient denied recent use of hepatotoxic medications (herbal remedies, antifungals, anti‑tuberculosis drugs, anti‑inflammatory agents), had no drug allergies, no relevant family history, never smoked, and consumed a bottle of soju twice weekly. He was diagnosed with acute hepatitis of unidentified etiology and managed as an outpatient.

One week later (February 4) his jaundice improved and liver enzymes decreased (AST 662 IU/L, ALT 482 IU/L, total bilirubin 5.5 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 2.7 mg/dL). He attended the occupational and environmental medicine clinic on February 9 and reported tolerable condition with continued improvement.

On February 15, he returned to gastroenterology because abdominal discomfort and jaundice had recurred 4–5 days earlier. He was admitted due to deteriorating condition and rising liver enzymes (AST 937 IU/L, ALT 409 IU/L, total bilirubin 18.8 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 9.9 mg/dL). Complete blood count and coagulation profile were normal (prothrombin time 23.3 s, INR 2.00, APTT 41.4 s). Serologic testing to exclude viral and autoimmune hepatitis yielded: anti‑HAV IgG negative, anti‑HAV IgM negative, HBsAg negative, anti‑HCV negative, HIV Ag/Ab negative, ANA (IF) positive at 1:320 dilution, anti‑smooth muscle antibody negative, ANCA negative, AMA negative, anti‑LKM antibody negative, anti‑dsDNA IgG within normal range. Abdominal ultrasonography showed findings compatible with acute hepatopathy and reactive gallbladder wall thickening. Elastography revealed a mean shear‑wave velocity of 3.26 ± 0.24 m/s, suggestive of stage 4 fibrosis, which the team interpreted as acute inflammatory change rather than established cirrhosis. The patient received hydration and conservative treatment, and liver function normalized before discharge after eight days. Follow‑up 20 days later showed AST 33 IU/L and ALT 13 IU/L.

1. Viral hepatitis excluded by negative serologies for HAV, HBV, HCV and HIV. | "anti‑HAV IgG (-), anti‑HAV IgM (-), HBs Ag (-), anti‑HCV (-), HIV Ag/Ab (-)"  
2. Autoimmune hepatitis considered due to ANA 1:320 but ruled out because specific auto‑antibodies (anti‑smooth muscle, anti‑LKM, AMA, dsDNA) were negative and clinical course was acute. | "ANA (IF) (1:320 dilution), anti‑smooth muscle Ab (-), ANCA (-), AMA (-), anti‑LKM Ab (-), and anti‑dsDNA IgG ... within normal range"  
3. Drug‑induced hepatitis deemed unlikely since the patient reported no recent use of known hepatotoxic agents, including herbal medicines, antifungals, anti‑TB drugs, or anti‑inflammatory drugs. | "The patient had not recently taken hepatotoxic medications such as herbal medicines, antifungal drugs, anti‑tuberculosis drugs, or anti‑inflammatory drugs"  
4. Alcoholic liver injury considered low probability given modest alcohol intake (one bottle of soju twice weekly) and absence of chronic consumption pattern. | "He drank a bottle of soju twice per week."  
5. Ischemic or congestive hepatopathy not supported; he was hemodynamically stable with normal coagulation and no cardiac history. | "Complete blood count was normal, and coagulation factors were also normal (prothrombin time 23.3 seconds, INR 2.00, ...)"  
6. Occupational toxic hepatitis later identified as the plausible cause after workplace investigation revealed high chloroform concentrations, but this information was not available at the diagnostic breakpoint. | "It has been determined to be the main cause of toxic hepatitis."

case_prompt: On 21 November 2018, an 11‑year‑old boy presented with a productive cough, fever, and weight loss for four weeks. He was dyspneic, febrile (39 °C), blood pressure 110/60 mmHg, heart rate 120/min, oxygen saturation 85% on room air, respiratory rate 20/min. Leukocyte count was 28 260/µL (84% neutrophils, 11% lymphocytes, 4.4% monocytes), hemoglobin 9.5 g/dL, platelets 550 × 10⁹/L, ESR 150 mm/h; biochemistry was normal. Chest CT showed bilateral diffuse air‑space disease. Sputum smear for acid‑fast bacilli and TB PCR were negative. Empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics (linezolid, gentamicin, meropenem) were started, later replaced by antituberculosis therapy after clinical deterioration, which was discontinued after negative TB PCR and smear. On 29 November, sputum smear revealed yeast with pseudohyphae and budding cells; cultures grew Candida tropicalis. Amphotericin was added, and the patient improved. On 15 December, bronchoscopy showed diffuse bronchitis with necrotic mainstem bronchi. Immunoglobulin levels were normal (IgG 10.4 g/L, IgA 2.81 g/L, IgM 0.675 g/L, IgE 26.3 IU/mL). Total protein 8.1 g/dL, albumin 2.4 g/dL. Oxidative burst measurement with DHR assay showed patient result 0.3% compared with control 98‑100%.

1. Bacterial pneumonia (MRSA) considered due to prior neck infection, but persistent fever despite vancomycin/clindamycin and later broad‑spectrum antibiotics made it unlikely. | "He was sent home in good condition. Symptoms started… with daily high‑grade fever and productive cough."
2. Tuberculosis considered because of chronic cough and weight loss; empiric therapy was started but discontinued after negative AFB smear and PCR. | "A direct smear of sputum for acid‑fast bacilli and tuberculous mycobacteria PCR was negative." and "antituberculosis treatment … later discontinued after getting the negative PCR and AFB smear results."

A 55‑year‑old woman with no past medical history presented initially with three weeks of oral mucosal hemorrhage. Laboratory studies revealed a marked leukocytosis of 88.1 × 10⁹/L with left‑shifted granulocyte precursors, thrombocytosis (640 × 10⁹/L), elevated LDH (647 U/L), and a positive BCR‑ABL p210 RT‑PCR. Eleven months later she returned with sudden respiratory distress, tachycardia (HR 137 bpm), tachypnea (RR 34/min), hypotension (BP 89/64 mmHg), and a two‑month cough. Chest examination revealed moist rales at the bases. Sputum culture grew Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, filamentous fungi, and trace Aspergillus fumigatus. Labs showed WBC 6.78 × 10⁹/L, platelets 269 × 10⁹/L, and procalcitonin 1.035 ng/mL. Viral serologies (TORCH, influenza, EBV, CMV) and fungal markers (β‑D‑glucan, galactomannan) were negative. Chest CT demonstrated ground‑glass opacities, patchy shadows, multiple nodules in both lungs, and enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes. She was diagnosed with septic shock and treated with biapenem and voriconazole, resulting in clinical improvement.

Three months later she developed fever (max 38.5 °C). CT showed enlargement of left‑lung masses. CT‑guided percutaneous lung biopsy revealed extensive necrosis; periodic acid‑silver methenamine stain was negative. Bronchoscopy yielded thick yellow secretions; BAL fluid NGS identified EBV and Actinomyces odontolyticus. She received penicillin sodium and acyclovir with symptomatic improvement.

One month thereafter she presented with worsening cough, white sputum, and intermittent fever (max 38.5 °C). CT showed reduction of the upper‑lobe left‑lung mass but increase of the lower‑lobe mass. Repeat bronchoscopy revealed a white substance in the dorsal segment of the left lower lobe; BAL NGS now detected EBV and Enterobacter cloacae complex. A second CT‑guided lung biopsy was performed. Histopathology demonstrated proliferation and vascular infiltration of polymorphic lymphoid cells. Immunohistochemistry showed the tumor cells were positive for Pax5, CD20, Bcl‑2, EBER, and Ki‑67 (≈60 %); negative for Bcl‑6, c‑MYC, CD10, TdT, CD34, CD117, and MPO. MUM‑1 was positive (≈20 %). Adjacent T‑cells stained CD3 and CD7. Tuberculosis PCR on the tissue was negative; stains for mycobacteria and fungi were negative. PET/CT revealed intense FDG uptake in the dorsal, posterior basal, and lateral basal segments of the left lower lobe, with no FDG activity in mediastinal nodes, excluding secondary nodal involvement. Bone marrow aspiration showed no lymphoma. BCR‑ABL transcripts were undetectable. Serum EBV DNA was 2.07 × 10⁴ IU/mL (normal < 5 × 10³) and LDH was 348 U/L.

The patient was a 36‑year‑old female who presented with left‑sided chest pain that began more than one month ago and had worsened over the preceding 10 days. She reported recurrent pulmonary infections with cough and sputum production. Her highest recorded temperature was 38.5 °C; she denied chest tightness or dyspnea. Physical examination revealed a barrel‑shaped chest, but auscultation and palpation of the lungs were unremarkable, and cardiac examination was normal. Multidetector spiral CT of the chest (lung window) demonstrated that the bilateral basal lung isthmus was connected, extending behind the pericardium and crossing the midline. The left lower lobe basal segment showed sparse lung markings with increased transparency, and patchy opacities were noted near the spine at the bases of both lungs. A distinct pleural interface was seen between the isthmus and the left lung. Transparent imaging highlighted isthmus lung tissue (arrow). Three‑dimensional bronchial rendering revealed thinner bronchial branches in the left lower lobe compared with the right, with cystic changes at the origin of the left lower lobe. The outer and posterior basal segments of the left lower lobe fused proximally, with distal branches appearing sparse. Thoracic CT‑angiography showed consolidation in the basal segments of both lower lobes, more prominent on the left, and multiple calcified nodules within the left lesion. The arterial supply to the bilateral lesions arose directly from the adjacent trunk of the thoracic aorta (arrows).

A 5‑year‑old boy was evaluated for bronchiectasis discovered on a recent high‑resolution chest CT. The caregiver reported no recurrent cough, expectoration, hemoptysis, chest pain, fever, night sweats, weight loss, or sinusitis. Fiberoptic bronchoscopy demonstrated condensed secretions in the right lower lobe bronchus. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) next‑generation sequencing identified a high read count of *Tropheryma whipplei* (13,200 reads). Electron microscopy of bronchial biopsy showed mild inflammatory changes in the cilia without ultrastructural features of primary ciliary dyskinesia. No evidence of tuberculosis, viral infection, or autoimmune vasculitis was found.

In April 2012 two adult men presented to the outpatient department with acute fever and myalgia, prompting admission.

**Case 1 – 28‑year‑old man**  
He was bitten on the right index finger by a squirrel 48 hours before presentation. Within 24 hours he developed myalgia, fever, and general weakness. On examination he had a 10 mm cut‑like wound on the distal right index finger with minimal local inflammation; the rest of the physical exam was unremarkable except for slight reduced vigilance. Within hours he entered shock (BP 70/50 mm Hg, HR up to 120/min) and required oxygen, IV fluids, amoxicillin (later ceftriaxone and cloxacillin), corticosteroids, and adrenaline, after which consciousness returned. The next day he had fever up to 39 °C, edema of both hands and lower legs, and, 48 hours after admission (4–5 days after the bite), vesicles appeared on all four extremities, the gluteal region, and the scrotum, later forming clear‑fluid bullae up to 15 mm. Lesions were absent on the face, palms, and soles. No lymphadenopathy was noted. On day 4 of admission he experienced epistaxis and hematemesis that resolved spontaneously within 12 hours. Initial coagulation studies were unavailable. The team isolated the patient and, on appearance of the rash, raised clinical suspicion for MPXV infection despite unfamiliarity with the virus in the region. Blood, vesicular fluid, and a skin‑lesion biopsy were dispatched to the regional reference laboratory. Eight days after hemorrhage onset laboratory data showed a modest AST rise to 66 IU/L (normal 15–46) and thrombocytopenia (91 × 10⁹/L; normal 150–350). Tests for filovirus and Dengue were negative.

**Case 2 – 26‑year‑old farmer**  
Four days later a 26‑year‑old farmer from a nearby village arrived with 24 hours of myalgia, fever, and vesicular lesions on the lower arms and legs, including the palms; few lesions were present on the trunk and face, none on the soles. Edema of the hands, lower legs, and feet was noted, with puffy, livid, painful distal fingertip lesions. Enlarged axillary, inguinal, and femoral lymph nodes up to 20 mm were palpable. He reported no animal contact other than pigs and no travel. On admission his temperature was 40 °C; the same evening he developed epistaxis and bloody stools that resolved spontaneously within 12 hours. He received cloxacillin, ibuprofen, and paracetamol. Over the following days his general condition improved, but the distal fingertip lesions progressed to demarcated necrosis. Blood, vesicular fluid, and a skin‑lesion biopsy were sent to the reference laboratory. Eight days after hemorrhage onset labs showed AST 109 IU/L, GGT 161 IU/L, and a platelet count at the lower limit of normal (150 × 10⁹/L). Filovirus, Yellow Fever, and Dengue virus infections were ruled out.

Abdominal ultrasound showed hepatomegaly. Serologies for hepatitis A, B, C, Epstein–Barr virus, and cytomegalovirus were negative. Repeat dengue serology was positive, and DF‑related hepatitis was considered. Because of an uncertain vaccination history and the ongoing yellow‑fever outbreak, a yellow‑fever PCR was ordered, but the result was not available before discharge. He was discharged after one week with improving labs (AST 259 U/L, ALT 638 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 153 U/L, platelets 294 000 /mm³, total bilirubin 2.25 mg/dL).

Forty days later he returned with persistent fatigue, jaundice, and pruritus. Laboratory tests now showed total bilirubin 19.2 mg/dL, AST 1037 U/L, ALT 2289 U/L, GGT 669 U/L, and INR 1.05. An extensive work‑up—including viral hepatitis serologies, EBV, CMV, ceruloplasmin, ferritin, and autoimmune markers (ANA, anti‑smooth muscle, anti‑mitochondrial antibodies, gamma‑globulin)—was unrevealing. Liver biopsy demonstrated lobular hepatitis with mild neutrophilic infiltration, frequent hepatocyte ballooning, macro‑ and microvacuolar steatosis, and occasional apoptotic bodies. He was discharged after a modest decline in bilirubin, still without a definitive diagnosis.
